whyNot.D: 0.1 K is (0.5 × 400) ÷ 2000; the formula has been turned upside down.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A 1.0 kW electric heater is placed in water that is already boiling at 100 °C. How long does it take to boil away 0.2 kg of the water? (specific latent heat of vaporisation of water = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹; assume all the heater's energy goes into the water)
questions.explanation: Heat needed Q = mL = 0.2 × 2.26 × 10⁶ = 4.52 × 10⁵ J. The heater supplies 1.0 kW = 1000 J every second, so t = Q ÷ P = 4.52 × 10⁵ ÷ 1000 = 452 s.

whyNot.A: 4520 s uses a power of 100 W; 1.0 kW is 1000 W.
whyNot.C: 2260 s is L ÷ P; it leaves out the 0.2 kg mass of water.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A fixed mass of gas has a volume of 600 cm³ at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 27 °C. Its pressure is changed to 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa and its temperature to 127 °C. What is its new volume?
questions.explanation: Use the general gas law P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ with kelvin temperatures: T₁ = 27 + 273 = 300 K, T₂ = 127 + 273 = 400 K. V₂ = P₁V₁T₂ ÷ (T₁P₂) = (1.0 × 10⁵ × 600 × 400) ÷ (300 × 2.0 × 10⁵) = 400 cm³.

whyNot.B: 300 cm³ allows for the doubled pressure but ignores the temperature rise, which makes the gas expand.
whyNot.A: 1600 cm³ multiplies by the pressure ratio instead of dividing; a higher pressure squeezes the gas into a smaller volume.
whyNot.C: 1411 cm³ uses the Celsius temperatures 27 and 127; the gas laws need kelvin temperatures.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A student on the Obudu Plateau, high above sea level, finds that water boils there at a temperature below 100 °C. Why does this happen?
options: Water at high altitude contains fewer dissolved impurities
The specific heat capacity of water is smaller at high altitude
The air is colder, so less heat is needed to make the water boil
The atmospheric pressure is lower, so the saturated vapour pressure of the water equals it at a lower temperature
questions.explanation: A liquid boils when its saturated vapour pressure equals the external (atmospheric) pressure. High up, the atmospheric pressure is lower, so the water's vapour pressure reaches it at a lower temperature, and the boiling point falls below 100 °C.

whyNot.C: The temperature of the surrounding air does not set the boiling point; pressure does. Cold air only makes the water take longer to heat.
whyNot.A: Dissolved impurities raise the boiling point, and there is no reason for plateau water to be purer.
whyNot.B: The specific heat capacity of water does not change with altitude, and it affects how fast water heats, not the temperature at which it boils.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror. The mirror is turned through an angle of 15° while the incident ray stays fixed. Through what angle does the reflected ray turn?
questions.explanation: Turning the mirror through θ changes the angle of incidence by θ, and the angle of reflection by θ as well, so the reflected ray turns through 2θ. 2 × 15° = 30°.

whyNot.C: 15° assumes the reflected ray turns by the same angle as the mirror; both the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection change, so it turns twice as much.
whyNot.B: 7.5° halves the angle instead of doubling it.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: An object is placed 10 cm from a converging lens. The lens forms a real image that is three times the size of the object. What is the focal length of the lens?
questions.explanation: Magnification m = v ÷ u, so v = 3 × 10 = 30 cm (real image on the other side of the lens). Using 1/f = 1/u + 1/v (real-is-positive): 1/f = 1/10 + 1/30 = 4/30, so f = 30 ÷ 4 = 7.5 cm.

whyNot.A: 30 cm is the image distance v, not the focal length.
whyNot.D: 20 cm is v − u; the lens formula adds the reciprocals 1/u and 1/v.
whyNot.B: 40 cm is u + v; f = uv ÷ (u + v), not u + v.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Which of the following properties of light shows that light is a transverse wave?
questions.explanation: Only transverse waves can be polarised, because polarisation means restricting the vibrations to one plane at right angles to the direction of travel. Longitudinal waves vibrate along the direction of travel, so they cannot be polarised. Light can be polarised (for example by Polaroid sheets), so it is transverse.

whyNot.C: Sound, a longitudinal wave, is also reflected (echoes), so reflection does not show light is transverse.
whyNot.D: Sound also diffracts round corners and through doorways; all waves diffract.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: In a stationary wave set up on a string, the distance between two neighbouring nodes is 0.25 m. The frequency of vibration is 200 Hz. What is the speed of the waves on the string?
questions.explanation: Neighbouring nodes are half a wavelength apart, so λ = 2 × 0.25 = 0.50 m. Speed v = fλ = 200 × 0.50 = 100 m s⁻¹.

whyNot.D: 50 m s⁻¹ uses 0.25 m as the wavelength; the node-to-node distance is only half a wavelength.
whyNot.B: 200 m s⁻¹ uses a wavelength of 1.0 m, which is four times the node-to-node distance.
whyNot.C: 800 m s⁻¹ is 200 ÷ 0.25; the speed is frequency × wavelength.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Ada stands 170 m in front of a tall cliff and claps her hands once. How long after the clap does she hear the echo? (speed of sound in air = 340 m s⁻¹)
questions.explanation: The sound travels to the cliff and back, a total distance of 2 × 170 = 340 m. Time = distance ÷ speed = 340 ÷ 340 = 1.0 s.

whyNot.D: 0.5 s is the time to reach the cliff only; the echo must also travel back to Ada.
whyNot.C: 2.0 s doubles the time twice; the total path is 340 m, which takes 1.0 s.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: The refractive index of a glass block is 1.5. What is the speed of light in the glass? (speed of light in air = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
questions.explanation: Refractive index n = speed of light in air ÷ speed of light in the glass. So speed in glass = 3.0 × 10⁸ ÷ 1.5 = 2.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Light slows down in the denser medium.

whyNot.A: 4.5 × 10⁸ multiplies by n; light travels more slowly in glass, so you must divide.
whyNot.D: 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ is the speed in air; light slows down when it enters glass.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Two small charges of +2 μC and +3 μC are 0.3 m apart in air. What is the size of the electrostatic force between them? (k = 1/(4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)

whyNot.C: 0.18 N divides by r = 0.3 instead of r² = 0.09; the force follows an inverse-square law.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Capacitors of 3 μF and 6 μF are connected in series. What is their combined capacitance?
questions.explanation: For capacitors in series, 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ = 1/3 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2, so C = 2 μF. In series the combined capacitance is smaller than the smallest one.

whyNot.B: 9 μF adds the values directly; that rule is for capacitors in parallel.
whyNot.A: 18 μF is the product 3 × 6 without dividing by the sum (3 + 6).

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Lenz's law states that an induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change producing it. This law is a consequence of the law of conservation of
questions.explanation: Because the induced current opposes the change, work must be done (for example, pushing a magnet into a coil) to produce it. That work is converted into electrical energy. If the induced current helped the change instead, electrical energy would appear from nothing, breaking the law of conservation of energy.

whyNot.A: Conservation of charge is the basis of Kirchhoff's current (junction) rule, not of Lenz's law.
whyNot.D: Conservation of momentum governs collisions and explosions; Lenz's law is about the work done to produce the induced current.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: In a metre bridge experiment, an unknown resistor R is in the left gap and a standard 6 Ω resistor is in the right gap. The balance point is 40.0 cm from the left end of the 100 cm wire. What is the value of R?
questions.explanation: At balance, R ÷ 6 = l₁ ÷ l₂, where l₁ = 40.0 cm (the left side) and l₂ = 100 − 40.0 = 60.0 cm. R = 6 × 40 ÷ 60 = 4.0 Ω.

whyNot.D: 9.0 Ω swaps the lengths (6 × 60 ÷ 40); R is in the left gap, so it goes with the 40 cm length.
whyNot.A: 2.4 Ω is 6 × 0.40; it compares 40 cm with the whole 100 cm wire instead of with the 60 cm on the other side.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A pure inductor of inductance 0.1 H is connected to a 50 Hz a.c. supply. What is its inductive reactance? (π = 3.14)
questions.explanation: Inductive reactance X_L = 2πfL = 2 × 3.14 × 50 × 0.1 = 31.4 Ω.

whyNot.D: 5.0 Ω is just f × L; the formula includes 2π.
whyNot.A: 15.7 Ω is πfL; the 2 in 2πf has been left out.
whyNot.C: 0.032 Ω is 1 ÷ (2πfL); that reciprocal form is how capacitive reactance is built, 1 ÷ (2πfC), not inductive reactance.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A galvanometer of resistance 99 Ω gives a full-scale deflection when a current of 1 mA flows through it. What resistance must be connected in parallel with it (a shunt) to convert it into an ammeter that reads up to 100 mA?
questions.explanation: At full scale, 1 mA flows through the galvanometer and the remaining 100 − 1 = 99 mA must flow through the shunt. They are in parallel, so they share the same p.d.: 1 mA × 99 Ω = 99 mA × R_s. R_s = (0.001 × 99) ÷ 0.099 = 1.0 Ω.

whyNot.B: 100 Ω is far too large; a shunt must have a small resistance so that most of the current goes through it.
whyNot.A: 0.01 Ω is the ratio 1 mA ÷ 100 mA, not a resistance; it leaves out the galvanometer's 99 Ω.
whyNot.D: 9.9 Ω would let too much current through the galvanometer: the shunt would carry only 10 times the meter current, giving a full-scale reading of 11 mA.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment, in which a few alpha particles bounced back from a thin gold foil, showed that
options: most of the atom's mass and all its positive charge are concentrated in a tiny nucleus
electrons move round the nucleus only in fixed energy levels
atoms of the same element can have different masses
the atom is a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it
questions.explanation: Most alpha particles passed straight through, so the atom is mostly empty space. A very few were deflected through large angles or bounced back, which needs a strong repulsion from a tiny, massive, positively charged centre: the nucleus.

whyNot.B: Fixed energy levels come from Bohr's model, based on line spectra, not from the scattering experiment.
whyNot.D: This is Thomson's 'plum pudding' model, which the scattering experiment disproved.
whyNot.C: Atoms of different masses (isotopes) were shown by mass spectrometry, not by alpha scattering.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: The work function of a metal is 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is its threshold frequency? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
questions.explanation: At the threshold frequency f₀, the photon energy just equals the work function: hf₀ = W. So f₀ = W ÷ h = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ ÷ 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ = 0.5 × 10¹⁵ = 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

whyNot.D: 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ is h ÷ W, which is upside down.
whyNot.C: 5.0 × 10¹⁵ Hz is a power-of-ten slip: 0.5 × 10¹⁵ equals 5.0 × 10¹⁴, not 5.0 × 10¹⁵.
whyNot.B: 2.2 × 10⁻⁵² is W × h; you must divide the energy by h.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A radioactive isotope of iodine has a half-life of 8 days. What fraction of a sample of it has decayed after 24 days?
questions.explanation: 24 days = 24 ÷ 8 = 3 half-lives. The fraction remaining is (½)³ = 1/8. The fraction that has decayed is 1 − 1/8 = 7/8.

whyNot.D: 1/8 is the fraction still undecayed; the question asks for the fraction that has decayed.
whyNot.A: 3/4 is the fraction decayed after only two half-lives (16 days); 24 days is three half-lives.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: In the radioactive decay ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + X, what is X?
questions.explanation: Mass number and atomic number must balance. X has mass number 226 − 222 = 4 and atomic number 88 − 86 = 2. A particle with A = 4 and Z = 2 is a helium nucleus, ⁴₂He: an alpha particle.

whyNot.B: A beta particle (an electron) has mass number 0 and would raise the atomic number by 1, not lower it by 2.
whyNot.A: A gamma ray has no mass or charge, so it cannot change the mass number or atomic number.
whyNot.D: A neutron has mass number 1 and atomic number 0, which does not balance the equation.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Electrons in an X-ray tube are accelerated through a potential difference of 33 kV. What is the maximum frequency of the X-rays produced? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
questions.explanation: The maximum photon energy equals the kinetic energy gained by one electron: E = eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 33 000 = 5.28 × 10⁻¹⁵ J. Then f_max = E ÷ h = 5.28 × 10⁻¹⁵ ÷ 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ = 8.0 × 10¹⁸ Hz.

whyNot.A: 8.0 × 10¹⁵ Hz uses 33 V instead of 33 kV = 33 000 V.
whyNot.D: 1.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ is h ÷ eV, which is upside down.
whyNot.B: 5.3 × 10⁻¹⁵ is the photon energy in joules; it still has to be divided by h to give a frequency.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Pure silicon is doped with a small amount of boron, which has three valence electrons. What kind of material is produced?
options: An insulator, because boron removes all the free electrons
An intrinsic semiconductor, because no extra electrons are added
A p-type semiconductor, with holes as the majority carriers
An n-type semiconductor, with electrons as the majority carriers
questions.explanation: Silicon has four valence electrons. Each boron atom (a trivalent impurity) has only three, so one bond around it is missing an electron: a hole. These holes act as positive charge carriers, so the doped silicon is a p-type semiconductor with holes as the majority carriers.

whyNot.D: n-type material is made with pentavalent impurities such as phosphorus or arsenic, which donate an extra electron.
whyNot.A: Doping increases the number of charge carriers, so the material conducts better, not worse.
whyNot.B: An intrinsic semiconductor is the pure, undoped material; adding boron makes it extrinsic.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Which of the following is a derived quantity?
questions.explanation: A derived quantity is obtained by combining fundamental quantities. Velocity = displacement ÷ time, so it is derived from length and time (unit m s⁻¹). Mass, time and temperature are fundamental (base) quantities with base units kg, s and K.

whyNot.C: Mass is a fundamental quantity; its SI base unit is the kilogram.
whyNot.B: Time is a fundamental quantity; its SI base unit is the second.
whyNot.D: Thermodynamic temperature is a fundamental quantity; its SI base unit is the kelvin.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A simple pendulum is 0.4 m long. What is its period of oscillation? (g = 10 m s⁻², π = 3.14)

whyNot.D: 0.63 s is π√(l/g); the formula has 2π.
whyNot.B: 3.97 s is 2π√l; it leaves out g.
whyNot.C: 12.6 s is 2π√(l × g); l must be divided by g.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A ball of mass 0.5 kg is moving at 4 m s⁻¹. What is its kinetic energy?
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy = ½mv² = ½ × 0.5 × 4² = ½ × 0.5 × 16 = 4 J.

whyNot.D: 8 J is mv²; it leaves out the ½.
whyNot.C: 2 J is mv, which is the momentum (in kg m s⁻¹), not the kinetic energy.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A 2 kg trolley moving at 6 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley. The two trolleys stick together after the collision. What is their common velocity just after the collision?
questions.explanation: Momentum is conserved. Momentum before = 2 × 6 + 1 × 0 = 12 kg m s⁻¹. After, the combined mass is 3 kg, so 3v = 12 and v = 4 m s⁻¹.

whyNot.B: 6 m s⁻¹ ignores the extra mass; sharing the momentum with the 1 kg trolley must slow the moving trolley down.
whyNot.D: 3 m s⁻¹ simply halves the speed; the momentum is shared by 3 kg in total, not split equally.
whyNot.C: 12 is the total momentum in kg m s⁻¹, not a velocity.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A wire 2.0 m long with a cross-sectional area of 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m² stretches by 1.0 mm when a load of 100 N hangs from it. What is the Young modulus of the material of the wire?
questions.explanation: Stress = F ÷ A = 100 ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.0 × 10⁸ Pa. Strain = extension ÷ original length = 1.0 × 10⁻³ ÷ 2.0 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴. Young modulus = stress ÷ strain = 1.0 × 10⁸ ÷ 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa.

whyNot.C: 1.0 × 10⁸ Pa is only the stress; it must still be divided by the strain.
whyNot.B: 2.0 × 10⁸ Pa uses the extension in millimetres (1.0) instead of metres (1.0 × 10⁻³ m).
whyNot.D: 5.0 × 10¹⁰ Pa calculates strain as extension × length instead of extension ÷ length.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A stone is thrown horizontally at 10 m s⁻¹ from the top of a cliff 45 m high. How far from the foot of the cliff does it land? (g = 10 m s⁻², ignore air resistance)
questions.explanation: Vertically the stone starts from rest: 45 = ½ × 10 × t², so t² = 9 and t = 3 s. Horizontally the speed stays at 10 m s⁻¹, so distance = 10 × 3 = 30 m.

whyNot.A: 90 m uses t = 9 s; that is t², and you must take the square root to get t = 3 s.
whyNot.D: 45 m is the height of the cliff, not the horizontal distance.
whyNot.B: 450 m multiplies the speed by the height; the horizontal speed must be multiplied by the time of flight.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: During the day, a cool breeze blows from the sea onto the land in coastal towns such as Lagos. This sea breeze is caused mainly by
options: radiation of heat from the sea towards the land
the land cooling down faster than the sea during the day
convection currents set up because the land heats up faster than the sea
conduction of heat from the warm sea to the cooler land
questions.explanation: Land has a lower specific heat capacity than water, so in the day it heats up faster than the sea. Air over the land warms, expands, becomes less dense and rises. Cooler, denser air from over the sea moves in to take its place. This convection current is felt as the sea breeze.

whyNot.D: Air is a poor conductor, and in the day the sea is cooler than the land, not warmer.
whyNot.B: In the day the land warms faster than the sea; the land cools faster at night, which gives the land breeze.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: The linear expansivity of a metal is 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹. What is its cubic expansivity?
questions.explanation: Cubic (volume) expansivity γ is about three times the linear expansivity α: γ = 3α = 3 × 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ = 3.6 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹.

whyNot.A: 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹ is 2α, the area (superficial) expansivity.
whyNot.B: 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ divides by 3 instead of multiplying; a volume expands more than a length.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A 0.1 kg metal block at 100 °C is dropped into 0.2 kg of water at 25 °C. The final steady temperature of the mixture is 30 °C. Ignoring heat losses and the heat taken by the container, what is the specific heat capacity of the metal? (specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)
questions.explanation: Heat lost by metal = heat gained by water. Metal: 0.1 × c × (100 − 30) = 7c. Water: 0.2 × 4200 × (30 − 25) = 4200 J. So 7c = 4200 and c = 600 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

whyNot.B: 300 uses the water's mass (0.2 kg) for the metal; the metal's mass is 0.1 kg.
whyNot.A: 560 uses a fall of 75 K for the metal (100 − 25); the metal cools only to the final temperature, 30 °C, a fall of 70 K.
whyNot.C: 3600 uses a rise of 30 K for the water; the water warms from 25 °C to 30 °C, only 5 K.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A fixed mass of gas has a volume of 273 cm³ at 0 °C. What is its volume at 50 °C if the pressure stays constant?
questions.explanation: Charles's law: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ with kelvin temperatures. T₁ = 273 K and T₂ = 50 + 273 = 323 K. V₂ = 273 × 323 ÷ 273 = 323 cm³.

whyNot.C: 223 cm³ subtracts the temperature rise; a gas heated at constant pressure expands.
whyNot.A: 273 cm³ assumes no change, but a gas heated at constant pressure expands.
whyNot.B: 546 cm³ doubles the volume, as if the kelvin temperature had doubled; it has risen only from 273 K to 323 K.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how pure water behaves when it is heated from 0 °C to 4 °C?
options: It expands, so its density decreases
It expands at first and then contracts
It contracts, so its density increases
Its volume and density stay the same
questions.explanation: Water shows anomalous expansion: between 0 °C and 4 °C it contracts as it is heated, so its density increases. It has its smallest volume and greatest density at 4 °C. Above 4 °C it expands on heating like most liquids.

whyNot.A: Expanding on heating is what water does above 4 °C, not between 0 °C and 4 °C.
whyNot.B: The order is wrong: water contracts all the way from 0 °C to 4 °C, and only then starts to expand.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: How much heat is needed to change 0.05 kg of water at 100 °C into steam at 100 °C? (specific latent heat of vaporisation of water = 2.3 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹)
questions.explanation: The temperature does not change, so only latent heat is needed: Q = mL = 0.05 × 2.3 × 10⁶ = 1.15 × 10⁵ J.

whyNot.B: 4.6 × 10⁷ J divides L by the mass; the heat needed is mass × latent heat.
whyNot.A: 2.3 × 10⁶ J is the heat for 1 kg; it leaves out the 0.05 kg mass.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Which of the following is a longitudinal wave?
options: A wave on a plucked guitar string
questions.explanation: In a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate along the direction in which the wave travels, forming compressions and rarefactions. Sound in air travels this way. Light and radio waves are electromagnetic (transverse), and a wave on a string is transverse.

whyNot.B: Light is an electromagnetic wave, which is transverse.
whyNot.D: On a plucked string the string moves sideways while the wave runs along it, so the wave is transverse.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: An object is placed 10 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Where is the image formed?
options: 6 cm in front of the mirror
30 cm in front of the mirror
questions.explanation: Using 1/v = 1/f − 1/u (real-is-positive): 1/v = 1/15 − 1/10 = (2 − 3)/30 = −1/30, so v = −30 cm. The minus sign means the image is virtual, 30 cm behind the mirror. This fits the rule that an object inside the focal length of a concave mirror gives a virtual, upright, magnified image.

whyNot.D: The distance is right, but the negative v means the image is virtual and behind the mirror, not real and in front.
whyNot.A: 6 cm in front comes from adding 1/15 + 1/10; the reciprocals must be subtracted.
whyNot.C: 5 cm is just 15 − 10; the mirror formula uses reciprocals, not the distances themselves.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Total internal reflection can take place only when light
options: travels from a denser to a less dense medium at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
travels from a less dense to a denser medium at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
strikes a polished plane mirror at an angle of incidence greater than 45°
travels from a denser to a less dense medium at an angle of incidence smaller than the critical angle
questions.explanation: Two conditions are needed. The light must be going from an optically denser medium (such as glass or water) towards a less dense one (such as air), where it bends away from the normal. And the angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle, so that no refracted ray can leave and all the light is reflected back.

whyNot.B: Going into a denser medium the light bends towards the normal, so there is always a refracted ray and no critical angle.
whyNot.D: Below the critical angle, most of the light refracts out of the denser medium.
whyNot.C: Reflection at a mirror is ordinary reflection at a surface, not total internal reflection.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A string 0.5 m long is fixed at both ends. Waves travel along the string at 200 m s⁻¹. What is the frequency of the fundamental note it produces?
questions.explanation: In the fundamental mode there is a node at each end and one antinode in the middle, so the length is half a wavelength: λ = 2L = 1.0 m. f = v ÷ λ = 200 ÷ 1.0 = 200 Hz.

whyNot.A: 400 Hz takes the wavelength as equal to the length of the string (0.5 m); in the fundamental it is twice the length.
whyNot.C: 100 Hz uses λ = 4L, which applies to a pipe closed at one end, not a string fixed at both ends.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: An FM radio station in Abuja broadcasts at a frequency of 100 MHz. What is the wavelength of its radio waves? (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)

whyNot.B: 0.33 m is f ÷ c, which is upside down.
whyNot.A: 3.0 × 10⁶ m uses 100 Hz; the frequency is 100 MHz, that is 100 × 10⁶ Hz.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A converging lens has a focal length of 25 cm. What is its power?
questions.explanation: Power P = 1 ÷ f, with f in metres. f = 25 cm = 0.25 m, so P = 1 ÷ 0.25 = +4.0 dioptres. A converging lens has a positive power.

whyNot.D: +0.04 D uses f in centimetres (1 ÷ 25); the focal length must be in metres.
whyNot.C: A negative power belongs to a diverging lens; this lens is converging.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Why is soft iron, rather than steel, used for the core of the electromagnet in an electric bell?
options: It is magnetised and demagnetised easily
It keeps its magnetism after the current is switched off
It is not attracted by permanent magnets
It is a better conductor of electricity than steel
questions.explanation: In an electric bell the electromagnet must switch on and off many times a second as the circuit is made and broken. Soft iron gains magnetism quickly when current flows and loses it almost at once when the current stops, so the armature can spring back each time. Steel keeps its magnetism, so the armature would stay stuck.

whyNot.B: Keeping magnetism is a property of steel, used for permanent magnets; it would stop the bell working.
whyNot.D: The core is not part of the electric circuit, so its electrical conductivity is not the reason.
whyNot.C: Soft iron is strongly attracted by magnets; it is a ferromagnetic material.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Three resistors, each of 6 Ω, are connected in parallel. What is their effective resistance?
questions.explanation: For resistors in parallel, 1/R = 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2, so R = 2 Ω. For n equal resistors in parallel, R = (one resistance) ÷ n = 6 ÷ 3 = 2 Ω.

whyNot.A: 18 Ω adds the resistances; that rule is for resistors in series.
whyNot.B: 3 Ω is the result for only two 6 Ω resistors in parallel.
whyNot.D: 0.5 Ω is 1/R; you must take the reciprocal at the end.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A cell of e.m.f. 6.0 V drives a current of 1.0 A through a 5.0 Ω resistor. What is the internal resistance of the cell?
questions.explanation: E = I(R + r). So 6.0 = 1.0 × (5.0 + r), which gives 5.0 + r = 6.0 and r = 1.0 Ω. The 'lost volts' inside the cell are Ir = 1.0 V.

whyNot.D: 6.0 Ω is E ÷ I, the total resistance of the circuit; the external 5.0 Ω must be taken away.
whyNot.A: 5.0 Ω is the external resistor, not the resistance inside the cell.
whyNot.C: 11 Ω adds E ÷ I and R; the external resistance must be subtracted, not added.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: The magnetic flux through a coil of 200 turns changes steadily by 0.03 Wb in 0.1 s. What is the average e.m.f. induced in the coil?
questions.explanation: Faraday's law: E = N × (change in flux ÷ time) = 200 × (0.03 ÷ 0.1) = 200 × 0.3 = 60 V.

whyNot.A: 0.3 V is the rate of change of flux for one turn; it leaves out the 200 turns.
whyNot.C: 6 V is N × change in flux; it still has to be divided by the time, 0.1 s.
whyNot.B: 0.6 V multiplies by the time instead of dividing by it.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A household in Kano uses three 100 W bulbs for 5 hours every day. If electricity costs ₦50 per kWh, what is the cost of running the bulbs for 30 days?
questions.explanation: Total power = 3 × 100 W = 300 W = 0.3 kW. Time = 5 h × 30 days = 150 h. Energy = 0.3 × 150 = 45 kWh. Cost = 45 × ₦50 = ₦2,250.

whyNot.A: ₦750 is the cost for one bulb only; there are three bulbs.
whyNot.B: ₦75 is the cost for one day (0.3 × 5 × 50); the question asks for 30 days.
whyNot.C: ₦2,250,000 uses watts instead of kilowatts; electricity is charged per kilowatt-hour.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A circuit contains an inductor of 0.1 H in series with a capacitor of 10 μF. At what frequency does resonance occur? (π = 3.14)

whyNot.A: 1000 is 1 ÷ √(LC), which is the angular frequency ω in rad s⁻¹; divide by 2π to get the frequency in Hz.
whyNot.C: 318 Hz is 1 ÷ (π√(LC)); the formula has 2π.
whyNot.D: 6.3 × 10⁻³ is 2π√(LC); the formula is the reciprocal of this.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Cathode rays, produced in a discharge tube at very low pressure, are streams of
questions.explanation: Cathode rays come from the negative electrode (cathode) and are deflected by electric and magnetic fields in the way expected for negative charges. J. J. Thomson showed they are streams of fast-moving electrons.

whyNot.D: Protons are positive; cathode rays bend the way negative charges do.
whyNot.A: Neutrons are uncharged, but cathode rays are deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
whyNot.C: X-rays are produced when cathode rays hit a target, and being uncharged they are not deflected by fields.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Light whose photons each carry 4.0 eV of energy falls on a metal of work function 2.5 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons, in joules? (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
questions.explanation: Einstein's photoelectric equation: KE_max = hf − W = 4.0 − 2.5 = 1.5 eV. Convert to joules: 1.5 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

whyNot.C: 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J is the whole photon energy (4.0 eV); the work function must be subtracted.
whyNot.D: 1.04 × 10⁻¹⁸ J adds the work function (6.5 eV) instead of subtracting it.
whyNot.A: 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ J writes 1.5 eV without converting it; 1 eV is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, not 10⁻¹⁹ J.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A radioactive nuclide has a half-life of 693 s. What is its decay constant? (take ln 2 = 0.693)
questions.explanation: The half-life and decay constant are linked by T½ = ln 2 ÷ λ, so λ = 0.693 ÷ T½ = 0.693 ÷ 693 = 1.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹.

whyNot.B: 1.0 × 10³ is 693 ÷ 0.693, which is upside down.
whyNot.C: 1.4 × 10⁻³ is 1 ÷ 693; it leaves out the factor ln 2 = 0.693.
whyNot.D: 4.8 × 10² multiplies 693 by 0.693; λ = ln 2 ÷ T½.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: The mass defect of a helium-4 nucleus, ⁴₂He, is 0.0304 u. What is its binding energy per nucleon? (1 u is equivalent to 931 MeV)
questions.explanation: Total binding energy = mass defect × 931 MeV = 0.0304 × 931 = 28.3 MeV. Helium-4 has 4 nucleons (2 protons and 2 neutrons), so binding energy per nucleon = 28.3 ÷ 4 = 7.08 MeV.

whyNot.A: 28.3 MeV is the total binding energy of the nucleus; it must be shared among the 4 nucleons.
whyNot.C: 14.2 MeV divides by 2, the number of protons; nucleons include both protons and neutrons.
whyNot.D: 0.0076 MeV divides the mass defect by 4 but never converts it to energy with 931 MeV per u.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Which of the following describes nuclear fusion?
options: An unstable nucleus gives out an alpha particle and becomes a new element
An electron falls to a lower energy level and gives out a photon
Light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus and release energy, as in the sun
A heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei after absorbing a neutron
questions.explanation: Fusion is the joining (fusing) of light nuclei, such as isotopes of hydrogen, to form a heavier nucleus. The products have slightly less mass than the reactants, and the lost mass appears as energy (E = mc²). This is the main source of the sun's energy.

whyNot.D: This describes nuclear fission, used in nuclear power stations.
whyNot.A: This describes alpha decay, a natural radioactive process.
whyNot.B: This is how atoms emit light (line spectra); it involves electrons, not the nucleus.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: An atom emits a photon of energy 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is the wavelength of the photon? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)

whyNot.B: 4.5 × 10¹⁴ is E ÷ h, the frequency in hertz, not a wavelength.
whyNot.A: 1.5 × 10⁶ is E ÷ (hc), which is upside down.
whyNot.C: 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ is h ÷ E; the speed of light c has been left out.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Which subatomic particle has a relative mass of about 1 and carries no electrical charge?
questions.explanation: The neutron is found in the nucleus, has a relative mass of about 1 (like the proton) and has no charge. The proton has a mass of about 1 but a charge of +1, and the electron has a charge of −1 and a mass of only about 1/1840.

whyNot.A: A proton has about the same mass but carries a +1 charge.
whyNot.D: An electron carries a −1 charge and is almost massless compared with the neutron.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: When magnesium burns in oxygen, magnesium oxide is formed. What type of bond holds the particles of magnesium oxide together?
questions.explanation: Magnesium (2, 8, 2) is a metal that loses two electrons to form Mg²⁺, and oxygen (2, 6) is a non-metal that gains two electrons to form O²⁻. Transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal gives an electrovalent (ionic) bond between the oppositely charged ions.

whyNot.C: Covalent bonds form by sharing electrons, usually between two non-metals.
whyNot.B: Metallic bonding holds atoms together in a pure metal, not in a metal oxide.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: How many electrons, protons and neutrons are there in the aluminium ion ²⁷₁₃Al³⁺?
questions.explanation: The atomic number 13 gives 13 protons. Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 27 − 13 = 14. A neutral atom has 13 electrons; the 3+ charge means 3 electrons have been lost, so the ion has 13 − 3 = 10 electrons.

whyNot.A: 13 electrons is the neutral atom; the 3+ ion has lost three electrons.
whyNot.D: 27 is the mass number (protons + neutrons), not the number of neutrons.
whyNot.B: 16 electrons would be a 3− ion, formed by gaining electrons.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: The carbon atom in methane, CH₄, forms four single covalent bonds and has no lone pairs. What is the shape of the methane molecule?
questions.explanation: Four bonding electron pairs around carbon repel one another equally and get as far apart as possible, pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron with bond angles of about 109.5°. So methane is tetrahedral.

whyNot.C: Linear shapes arise from two electron pairs, as in CO₂.
whyNot.B: Trigonal planar arises from three electron pairs, as in BF₃.
whyNot.D: A bent shape needs lone pairs on the central atom, as in H₂O.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following Period 3 elements has the highest first ionisation energy?
questions.explanation: Across a period, nuclear charge increases while the outer electrons stay in the same shell, so the outer electrons are held more tightly and ionisation energy generally rises. Chlorine is furthest to the right of the four, so it needs the most energy to remove an outer electron.

whyNot.B: Sodium, at the start of the period, has the lowest first ionisation energy of the four.
whyNot.D: Magnesium's value is higher than sodium's and aluminium's but still far below chlorine's.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Boron has two isotopes, ¹⁰B and ¹¹B. Its relative atomic mass is 10.8. What is the percentage abundance of ¹⁰B?
questions.explanation: Let the abundance of ¹⁰B be x%, so ¹¹B is (100 − x)%. Then (10x + 11(100 − x)) ÷ 100 = 10.8, so 1100 − x = 1080 and x = 20. Boron is 20% ¹⁰B and 80% ¹¹B; the average (10.8) is closer to 11 because ¹¹B is more abundant.

whyNot.D: 80% is the abundance of ¹¹B, the heavier isotope.
whyNot.A: 50% of each would give a relative atomic mass of 10.5, not 10.8.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: What volume is occupied by 0.5 mol of hydrogen gas at s.t.p.? [Molar volume = 22.4 dm³ at s.t.p.]
questions.explanation: One mole of any gas occupies 22.4 dm³ at s.t.p. So 0.5 mol occupies 0.5 × 22.4 = 11.2 dm³.

whyNot.D: 22.4 dm³ is the volume of one whole mole, not half a mole.
whyNot.B: 44.8 dm³ comes from dividing 22.4 by 0.5 instead of multiplying.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: What is the mass of 0.25 mol of calcium trioxocarbonate(IV), CaCO₃? [C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40]
questions.explanation: Molar mass of CaCO₃ = 40 + 12 + (3 × 16) = 100 g mol⁻¹. Mass = moles × molar mass = 0.25 × 100 = 25 g.

whyNot.C: 100 g is the mass of one mole, not 0.25 mol.
whyNot.B: 400 g comes from dividing 100 by 0.25 instead of multiplying.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Methane burns in oxygen: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l). What volume of oxygen is needed to burn 20 cm³ of methane completely, all volumes measured at the same temperature and pressure?
questions.explanation: By Gay-Lussac's law, gases react in simple volume ratios equal to their mole ratios. CH₄ : O₂ = 1 : 2, so 20 cm³ of methane needs 2 × 20 = 40 cm³ of oxygen.

whyNot.B: 20 cm³ assumes a 1 : 1 ratio, ignoring the 2 in front of O₂.
whyNot.D: 10 cm³ inverts the ratio (it would be the volume of CH₄ needed for 20 cm³ of O₂).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: How many atoms are present in 0.1 mol of ammonia, NH₃? [Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹]
questions.explanation: Number of molecules = 0.1 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²². Each NH₃ molecule contains 4 atoms (1 N + 3 H), so the number of atoms = 4 × 6.02 × 10²² = 2.408 × 10²³ ≈ 2.41 × 10²³.

whyNot.A: 6.02 × 10²² is the number of molecules; each molecule has 4 atoms.
whyNot.B: 1.81 × 10²³ counts only the 3 hydrogen atoms in each molecule.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: 6.5 g of zinc is added to 100 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. What volume of hydrogen is produced at s.t.p.? [Zn = 65; molar volume = 22.4 dm³ at s.t.p.]
questions.explanation: Moles of Zn = 6.5 ÷ 65 = 0.10 mol. Moles of HCl = 1.0 × 100/1000 = 0.10 mol. Zinc needs 2 × 0.10 = 0.20 mol HCl, so HCl is the limiting reagent. 2 mol HCl give 1 mol H₂, so 0.10 mol HCl gives 0.05 mol H₂ = 0.05 × 22.4 = 1.12 dm³.

whyNot.C: 2.24 dm³ assumes all the zinc reacts, but there is not enough acid for that.
whyNot.A: 4.48 dm³ treats each mole of HCl as giving two moles of H₂.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: 2.86 g of hydrated sodium trioxocarbonate(IV), Na₂CO₃·xH₂O, was heated to constant mass and 1.06 g of the anhydrous salt remained. What is the value of x? [H = 1, C = 12, O = 16, Na = 23]
questions.explanation: Molar mass of Na₂CO₃ = 46 + 12 + 48 = 106 g mol⁻¹, so moles of Na₂CO₃ = 1.06 ÷ 106 = 0.010 mol. Mass of water lost = 2.86 − 1.06 = 1.80 g = 1.80 ÷ 18 = 0.10 mol. Ratio Na₂CO₃ : H₂O = 0.010 : 0.10 = 1 : 10, so x = 10 (washing soda, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O).

whyNot.B: 7 does not match the mole ratio of water to anhydrous salt.
whyNot.C: 1 is the monohydrate; it would lose only 0.18 g of water here.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following is a property of dilute acids?
options: They feel soapy to the touch.
They turn blue litmus paper red.
They turn red litmus paper blue.
They have a pH greater than 7.
questions.explanation: Dilute acids contain hydrogen ions, H⁺(aq), which turn blue litmus red. They have a pH below 7 and taste sour. Turning red litmus blue, a soapy feel and pH above 7 are properties of alkalis.

whyNot.C: Turning red litmus blue is a property of alkalis.
whyNot.A: A soapy feel is typical of alkalis, which react with oils on the skin.
whyNot.D: A pH greater than 7 means the solution is alkaline.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following gases dissolves in water to form an alkaline solution?
questions.explanation: Ammonia reacts with water: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. The hydroxide ions make the solution alkaline (it turns red litmus blue). The other three gases form acidic solutions.

whyNot.A: Hydrogen chloride dissolves to form hydrochloric acid.
whyNot.D: Sulphur(IV) oxide forms trioxosulphate(IV) acid, H₂SO₃.
whyNot.C: Carbon(IV) oxide forms weak trioxocarbonate(IV) acid, H₂CO₃.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Crystals of washing soda, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, left open to the air slowly lose part of their water of crystallisation and become a white powder. This property is called
questions.explanation: An efflorescent substance gives up some or all of its water of crystallisation to the atmosphere when exposed, so the crystals crumble to a powder. Washing soda is a common example.

whyNot.D: A deliquescent substance absorbs so much water from the air that it dissolves in it (e.g. CaCl₂, NaOH).
whyNot.B: A hygroscopic substance absorbs water from the air without dissolving (e.g. concentrated H₂SO₄).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: What mass of sodium hydroxide is needed to prepare 500 cm³ of a 0.20 mol dm⁻³ solution? [H = 1, O = 16, Na = 23]
questions.explanation: Moles needed = concentration × volume in dm³ = 0.20 × 500/1000 = 0.10 mol. Molar mass of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g mol⁻¹. Mass = 0.10 × 40 = 4.0 g.

whyNot.B: 8.0 g is what 1 dm³ of the solution would need, not 500 cm³.
whyNot.A: 0.10 is the number of moles, not the mass in grams.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: What is the basicity of ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH?
questions.explanation: Basicity is the number of replaceable (ionisable) hydrogen atoms in one molecule of the acid. In CH₃COOH only the hydrogen of the –COOH group ionises (CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺); the three hydrogens of the CH₃ group are bonded to carbon and are not replaceable. So the basicity is 1.

whyNot.A: 4 counts every hydrogen atom, but only the –COOH hydrogen is replaceable.
whyNot.B: 2 is the basicity of acids such as H₂SO₄, which have two replaceable hydrogens.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: 25.0 cm³ of a sodium trioxocarbonate(IV) solution required 20.0 cm³ of 0.25 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid for complete neutralisation, using methyl orange. Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. What is the concentration of the Na₂CO₃ solution in g dm⁻³? [C = 12, O = 16, Na = 23]
questions.explanation: Moles of HCl = 0.25 × 20.0/1000 = 0.0050 mol. From the equation, moles of Na₂CO₃ = 0.0050 ÷ 2 = 0.0025 mol in 25.0 cm³. Concentration = 0.0025 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.10 mol dm⁻³. Molar mass of Na₂CO₃ = 106 g mol⁻¹, so concentration = 0.10 × 106 = 10.6 g dm⁻³.

whyNot.B: 21.2 g dm⁻³ ignores the 1 : 2 mole ratio and treats the reaction as 1 : 1.
whyNot.D: 0.10 is the concentration in mol dm⁻³, not in g dm⁻³.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: In terms of electron transfer, oxidation is defined as
questions.explanation: Oxidation is the loss of electrons by a species, so its oxidation number increases. Reduction is the gain of electrons. A memory aid is OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.

whyNot.C: Gain of electrons is reduction.
whyNot.A: Gaining protons describes a base in acid-base reactions, not oxidation.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of sulphur in tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid, H₂SO₄?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen is +1 and oxygen is −2, and the compound is neutral. So 2(+1) + S + 4(−2) = 0, giving S − 6 = 0 and S = +6. This matches the (VI) in its name.

whyNot.D: +4 is sulphur's oxidation number in SO₂ and H₂SO₃.
whyNot.A: −2 is sulphur's oxidation number in H₂S and metal sulphides.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed using carbon electrodes. Which substance is liberated at the anode?
questions.explanation: The melt contains only Pb²⁺ and Br⁻ ions. Negative Br⁻ ions move to the positive anode and are oxidised: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻, giving brown bromine vapour. Lead is deposited at the cathode.

whyNot.C: Lead forms at the cathode, where Pb²⁺ gains electrons.
whyNot.A: There is no water in a melt, so no hydrogen can be formed.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: In the reaction H₂S + Cl₂ → 2HCl + S, which substance is the reducing agent?
questions.explanation: Sulphur changes from −2 in H₂S to 0 in S, so H₂S loses electrons (is oxidised). A substance that is oxidised gives electrons to another substance and is therefore the reducing agent. Chlorine goes from 0 to −1, so Cl₂ is the oxidising agent.

whyNot.C: Cl₂ gains electrons (0 → −1); it is the oxidising agent.
whyNot.A: HCl and S are products, not the reagents that donate or accept electrons.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: In a Daniell cell, a zinc rod dips into zinc tetraoxosulphate(VI) solution and a copper rod dips into copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) solution, connected by a salt bridge. In the external wire, electrons flow
options: from the copper rod to the zinc rod
from the zinc rod to the copper rod
through the salt bridge from zinc to copper
questions.explanation: Zinc is higher than copper in the electrochemical series, so zinc atoms are oxidised (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻) and the electrons travel through the external wire to the copper rod, where Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. The zinc rod is the negative electrode.

whyNot.A: Copper is less reactive, so it receives electrons rather than releasing them.
whyNot.D: The salt bridge carries ions, not electrons.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: The same quantity of electricity is passed through silver trioxonitrate(V) solution and copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) solution connected in series. If 2.16 g of silver is deposited, what mass of copper is deposited? [Ag = 108, Cu = 64]
questions.explanation: Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag: moles of Ag = 2.16 ÷ 108 = 0.020 mol, so 0.020 mol of electrons (0.020 F) passed. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu: 0.020 mol of electrons deposits 0.020 ÷ 2 = 0.010 mol of Cu = 0.010 × 64 = 0.64 g.

whyNot.D: 1.28 g forgets that each Cu²⁺ ion needs two electrons.
whyNot.A: Equal charge does not deposit equal masses; it depends on molar mass and ionic charge.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following is an unsaturated hydrocarbon?
questions.explanation: C₂H₄ (ethene) fits CₙH₂ₙ, the general formula of the alkenes, and contains a carbon–carbon double bond, so it is unsaturated. The others fit CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ and are saturated alkanes with only single bonds.

whyNot.D: C₂H₆ (ethane) is an alkane with only single bonds.
whyNot.A: C₃H₈ (propane) is an alkane with only single bonds.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂COOH?
questions.explanation: The molecule has three carbon atoms in its chain (prop-), including the carbon of the –COOH group, and the –COOH group makes it an alkanoic acid (-oic acid). So it is propanoic acid.

whyNot.C: Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, has only two carbon atoms.
whyNot.A: Propan-1-ol has an –OH group, not a –COOH group.
whyNot.D: Propanal has an aldehyde –CHO group.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C₄H₁₀?
questions.explanation: Four carbon atoms can be joined in only two ways: a straight chain, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ (butane), or a three-carbon chain with a methyl branch on the middle carbon, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃ (2-methylpropane). Any other drawing is one of these two.

whyNot.A: 1-methylpropane is just butane drawn bent, so it is not a third isomer.
whyNot.C: 4 counts the carbon atoms, not the isomers.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Which reagent can be used to distinguish ethanoic acid from ethanol in the laboratory?
questions.explanation: Ethanoic acid is an acid, so it reacts with NaHCO₃ to give effervescence of carbon(IV) oxide: CH₃COOH + NaHCO₃ → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂. Ethanol is neutral and gives no gas. A test that gives different results is the one that distinguishes them.

whyNot.D: Sodium metal reacts with both, giving hydrogen gas each time.
whyNot.C: Neither compound has a C=C bond, so neither decolourises bromine water.
whyNot.A: Both mix completely with water, so water shows no difference.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Ethene burns completely in oxygen: C₂H₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O. What mass of carbon(IV) oxide is produced when 7.0 g of ethene is burnt? [H = 1, C = 12, O = 16]
questions.explanation: Molar mass of C₂H₄ = 24 + 4 = 28 g mol⁻¹, so moles = 7.0 ÷ 28 = 0.25 mol. Each mole of ethene gives 2 mol CO₂, so 0.50 mol CO₂ is formed. Molar mass of CO₂ = 44 g mol⁻¹, so mass = 0.50 × 44 = 22 g.

whyNot.A: 11 g uses a 1 : 1 ratio and ignores the 2 in front of CO₂.
whyNot.D: 44 g is the mass of one mole of CO₂, not of 0.50 mol.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: 10 cm³ of a gaseous hydrocarbon burns completely in exactly 30 cm³ of oxygen, producing 20 cm³ of carbon(IV) oxide. All volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure. What is the formula of the hydrocarbon?
questions.explanation: For CₓHᵧ + (x + y/4)O₂ → xCO₂ + (y/2)H₂O, volumes are in the mole ratio. 10 cm³ of hydrocarbon gives 20 cm³ CO₂, so x = 2. It uses 30 cm³ O₂, so x + y/4 = 3, giving y/4 = 1 and y = 4. The hydrocarbon is C₂H₄ (ethene).

whyNot.A: C₂H₆ would need 3.5 volumes of oxygen per volume (35 cm³), not 30 cm³.
whyNot.C: C₂H₂ would need only 2.5 volumes of oxygen (25 cm³).
whyNot.B: C₃H₆ would give 30 cm³ of CO₂, not 20 cm³.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: The elements in Group VII of the Periodic Table, such as chlorine and bromine, are known as the
questions.explanation: Group VII elements (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine) have seven outer electrons and are called the halogens, meaning 'salt formers', because they combine with metals to form salts such as NaCl.

whyNot.C: The alkali metals are Group I (e.g. sodium, potassium).
whyNot.B: The noble gases are Group 0 (or VIII), e.g. neon and argon.
whyNot.D: The alkaline earth metals are Group II (e.g. magnesium, calcium).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: The atomic number of an element is the number of
options: protons and neutrons in its atom
electrons in the outermost shell of its atom
neutrons in the nucleus of its atom
protons in the nucleus of its atom
questions.explanation: The atomic (proton) number, Z, is the number of protons in the nucleus. It identifies the element; in a neutral atom it also equals the number of electrons.

whyNot.A: Protons plus neutrons gives the mass number, A.
whyNot.B: The outermost electrons are the valence electrons, which relate to the group number.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following compounds contains both ionic and covalent bonds?
questions.explanation: Sodium hydroxide is made of Na⁺ ions and OH⁻ ions held by ionic bonds, but within each OH⁻ ion the oxygen and hydrogen atoms share a pair of electrons in a covalent bond. So NaOH has both kinds of bond.

whyNot.D: MgCl₂ contains only Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held by ionic bonds.
whyNot.C: HCl is a covalent molecule with no ions in the pure compound.
whyNot.A: CH₄ has only covalent C–H bonds.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Solid metals such as copper conduct electricity because they contain
options: positive ions that can move through the structure
delocalised electrons that can move through the structure
molecules with shared pairs of electrons
negative ions held in fixed positions
questions.explanation: In metallic bonding, the outer electrons of the metal atoms are delocalised: they form a 'sea' of electrons around a lattice of positive ions. These mobile electrons carry the current when a voltage is applied.

whyNot.A: The positive ions in a solid metal stay fixed in the lattice; they only vibrate.
whyNot.D: Metals do not contain negative ions; the lattice is made of positive ions.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Across a period of the Periodic Table from left to right, the atomic radius generally decreases. This is because
options: the atoms lose electrons more easily
the nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell
the number of electron shells decreases
questions.explanation: Along a period, each element has one more proton than the one before, so the nuclear charge increases. The added electrons go into the same outer shell and shield one another poorly, so the stronger nucleus pulls the outer shell closer and the atoms get smaller.

whyNot.C: All elements in a period have the same number of occupied shells.
whyNot.A: Atoms on the right of a period actually lose electrons less easily.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: What is the total number of electrons in the tetraoxosulphate(VI) ion, SO₄²⁻? [Atomic numbers: O = 8, S = 16]
questions.explanation: Electrons in the neutral atoms = 16 (S) + 4 × 8 (O) = 48. The 2− charge means the ion has gained 2 extra electrons, so the total is 48 + 2 = 50.

whyNot.A: 48 counts only the electrons of the neutral atoms and ignores the 2− charge.
whyNot.C: 46 subtracts the 2 electrons, as if the ion were positive.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: How many moles are present in 9.8 g of tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid, H₂SO₄? [H = 1, O = 16, S = 32]
questions.explanation: Molar mass of H₂SO₄ = 2(1) + 32 + 4(16) = 98 g mol⁻¹. Moles = mass ÷ molar mass = 9.8 ÷ 98 = 0.10 mol.

whyNot.D: 1.0 mol would be 98 g of the acid.
whyNot.A: 10 mol comes from dividing 98 by 9.8 instead of 9.8 by 98.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: How many moles of sodium ions, Na⁺, are present in 0.5 mol of sodium tetraoxosulphate(VI), Na₂SO₄?
questions.explanation: Each formula unit of Na₂SO₄ contains 2 Na⁺ ions. So 0.5 mol of Na₂SO₄ contains 2 × 0.5 = 1.0 mol of Na⁺ ions.

whyNot.B: 0.5 mol is the amount of the salt (and of SO₄²⁻ ions), not of Na⁺.
whyNot.D: 0.25 mol divides by 2 instead of multiplying.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Ammonium trioxonitrate(V), NH₄NO₃, is used as a fertiliser. What is the percentage by mass of nitrogen in it? [H = 1, N = 14, O = 16]
questions.explanation: Molar mass of NH₄NO₃ = 14 + 4(1) + 14 + 3(16) = 80 g mol⁻¹. It contains two nitrogen atoms, mass 2 × 14 = 28 g. Percentage of N = 28 ÷ 80 × 100 = 35%.

whyNot.C: 17.5% counts only one of the two nitrogen atoms.
whyNot.B: 28 is the mass of nitrogen in grams per mole, not a percentage.
whyNot.D: 60% is the percentage of oxygen (48 ÷ 80 × 100).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: What is the mass of 4.48 dm³ of ammonia gas, NH₃, at s.t.p.? [H = 1, N = 14; molar volume = 22.4 dm³ at s.t.p.]
questions.explanation: Moles of NH₃ = 4.48 ÷ 22.4 = 0.20 mol. Molar mass of NH₃ = 14 + 3 = 17 g mol⁻¹. Mass = 0.20 × 17 = 3.4 g.

whyNot.D: 1.7 g is the mass of 0.10 mol (2.24 dm³).
whyNot.A: 17 g is the mass of one mole, which would occupy 22.4 dm³.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: An oxide of iron contains 70% iron by mass. What is its empirical formula? [O = 16, Fe = 56]
questions.explanation: In 100 g there are 70 g Fe and 30 g O. Moles: Fe = 70 ÷ 56 = 1.25; O = 30 ÷ 16 = 1.875. Divide by the smaller: Fe = 1, O = 1.5. Multiply by 2 to get whole numbers: Fe : O = 2 : 3, so the formula is Fe₂O₃.

whyNot.B: FeO contains about 78% iron (56 ÷ 72).
whyNot.D: Fe₃O₄ contains about 72% iron (168 ÷ 232).
whyNot.C: FeO₂ would contain about 64% iron, and it is not a common oxide of iron.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Potassium trioxochlorate(V) decomposes on heating: 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂. What mass of KClO₃ must be heated to produce 3.36 dm³ of oxygen at s.t.p.? [O = 16, Cl = 35.5, K = 39; molar volume = 22.4 dm³ at s.t.p.]
questions.explanation: Moles of O₂ = 3.36 ÷ 22.4 = 0.15 mol. From the equation, 3 mol O₂ come from 2 mol KClO₃, so moles of KClO₃ = 0.15 × 2/3 = 0.10 mol. Molar mass of KClO₃ = 39 + 35.5 + 48 = 122.5 g mol⁻¹. Mass = 0.10 × 122.5 = 12.25 g.

whyNot.B: 18.38 g treats the mole ratio as 1 : 1 (0.15 mol of KClO₃).
whyNot.A: 6.13 g divides the moles of O₂ by 3 but forgets to multiply by 2 (0.05 mol of KClO₃).
whyNot.D: 24.50 g is the mass for 0.20 mol, double the amount needed.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: An aqueous solution has a pH of 2. The solution is
questions.explanation: On the pH scale, values below 7 are acidic, 7 is neutral and above 7 is alkaline. The lower the pH, the higher the hydrogen ion concentration, so pH 2 is strongly acidic.

whyNot.C: Weakly acidic solutions have pH values just below 7, such as 5 or 6.
whyNot.A: Strongly alkaline solutions have pH values near 14.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Which gas is given off when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to zinc granules?
questions.explanation: A metal above hydrogen in the activity series displaces hydrogen from a dilute acid: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. The gas burns with a 'pop' when a lighted splint is brought near.

whyNot.D: Chlorine stays in the salt, zinc chloride, as Cl⁻ ions.
whyNot.B: Carbon(IV) oxide is given off when an acid reacts with a trioxocarbonate(IV), not with a metal.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Hydrochloric acid is described as a strong acid because it
options: contains many hydrogen atoms in each molecule
questions.explanation: The strength of an acid depends on how far it ionises in water. HCl ionises completely: HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻. A weak acid such as ethanoic acid ionises only partly. Strength is different from concentration, which is the amount of acid per dm³.

whyNot.A: Concentration describes how much acid is dissolved; a dilute strong acid is still strong.
whyNot.C: HCl has only one hydrogen atom per molecule.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most suitable drying agent for ammonia gas?
questions.explanation: Ammonia is a basic gas, so it must be dried with a basic drying agent that does not react with it. Calcium oxide is basic and is used for this. Acidic drying agents react with ammonia, and calcium chloride forms a compound with it.

whyNot.A: Concentrated H₂SO₄ is an acid and reacts with ammonia to form ammonium tetraoxosulphate(VI).
whyNot.B: Anhydrous calcium chloride absorbs ammonia to form a complex (CaCl₂·8NH₃).
whyNot.C: Phosphorus(V) oxide is an acidic oxide and reacts with ammonia.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: How many moles of hydrogen ions are present in 50 cm³ of 0.20 mol dm⁻³ tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid, H₂SO₄? (Assume the acid is fully ionised.)
questions.explanation: Moles of H₂SO₄ = 0.20 × 50/1000 = 0.010 mol. Each H₂SO₄ gives 2 H⁺ ions (H₂SO₄ → 2H⁺ + SO₄²⁻), so moles of H⁺ = 2 × 0.010 = 0.020 mol.

whyNot.C: 0.010 mol is the amount of acid; it forgets that the acid is dibasic.
whyNot.D: 0.20 is the concentration, not the number of moles in 50 cm³.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: 55.0 cm³ of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid is mixed with 45.0 cm³ of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide solution. What is the pH of the resulting solution? (Assume complete ionisation.)
questions.explanation: Moles of HCl = 0.10 × 0.0550 = 0.0055 mol; moles of NaOH = 0.10 × 0.0450 = 0.0045 mol. They react 1 : 1, leaving 0.0055 − 0.0045 = 0.0010 mol of H⁺ in a total volume of 100 cm³ (0.100 dm³). [H⁺] = 0.0010 ÷ 0.100 = 0.010 mol dm⁻³, so pH = −log₁₀(0.010) = 2.

whyNot.D: pH 1 is the pH of the original 0.10 mol dm⁻³ acid, before any was neutralised.
whyNot.B: pH 7 would need exactly equal moles of acid and alkali; here the acid is in excess.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: A goldsmith in Kano wants to electroplate a brass spoon with silver. The spoon should be made the
questions.explanation: In electroplating, the object to be coated is made the cathode, where metal ions gain electrons and are deposited: Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag. A piece of silver is used as the anode and a silver salt solution as the electrolyte.

whyNot.A: The anode is the silver metal, which dissolves to replace the Ag⁺ ions.
whyNot.B: The electrolyte is the solution of silver ions, not the spoon.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Household bleach contains sodium oxochlorate(I), NaOCl. What is the oxidation number of chlorine in this compound?
questions.explanation: Sodium is +1 and oxygen is −2, and the compound is neutral. So (+1) + (−2) + Cl = 0, giving Cl = +1. This matches the (I) in oxochlorate(I).

whyNot.A: −1 is chlorine's oxidation number in chlorides such as NaCl.
whyNot.D: +5 is chlorine's oxidation number in trioxochlorate(V), such as KClO₃.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Water acidified with dilute tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid is electrolysed using platinum electrodes. What is the ratio of the volume of hydrogen to the volume of oxygen collected, at the same temperature and pressure?
questions.explanation: Cathode: 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂. Anode: 4OH⁻ → 2H₂O + O₂ + 4e⁻. The same 4 mol of electrons produce 2 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂, so the volume ratio of hydrogen to oxygen is 2 : 1, matching the formula H₂O.

whyNot.C: 1 : 2 swaps the gases; more hydrogen than oxygen is produced.
whyNot.A: 1 : 1 ignores that each O₂ needs four electrons but each H₂ needs only two.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: In the reaction 2FeCl₂ + Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃, what happens to iron?
options: Its oxidation number does not change.
questions.explanation: In FeCl₂, each Cl is −1, so Fe is +2. In FeCl₃, Fe is +3. An increase in oxidation number (loss of an electron) is oxidation, so iron is oxidised from +2 to +3. Chlorine is reduced from 0 to −1.

whyNot.A: The change is from FeCl₂ to FeCl₃, i.e. +2 to +3, not the reverse.
whyNot.D: Iron starts as Fe²⁺ in FeCl₂, not as the free element (0).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following metals will NOT liberate hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: Only metals above hydrogen in the electrochemical (activity) series can displace hydrogen from dilute acids. Copper is below hydrogen, so it does not react with dilute HCl. Magnesium, zinc and iron are above hydrogen and give hydrogen gas.

whyNot.C: Zinc is above hydrogen and reacts readily with dilute HCl.
whyNot.A: Magnesium is well above hydrogen and reacts vigorously.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: How long will it take a current of 2.0 A to deposit 0.54 g of aluminium during the electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide? [Al = 27; F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹]
questions.explanation: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al. Moles of Al = 0.54 ÷ 27 = 0.020 mol, needing 3 × 0.020 = 0.060 mol of electrons. Charge Q = 0.060 × 96 500 = 5790 C. Time t = Q ÷ I = 5790 ÷ 2.0 = 2895 s.

whyNot.A: 965 s treats aluminium as Al⁺, needing only one electron per atom.
whyNot.B: 5790 is the charge in coulombs; it still has to be divided by the current.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following compounds is an alkanoic acid?
questions.explanation: Alkanoic acids contain the carboxyl group, –COOH. CH₃COOH (ethanoic acid, the acid in vinegar) has this group.

whyNot.D: CH₃CH₂OH (ethanol) has an –OH group; it is an alkanol.
whyNot.A: CH₃CHO (ethanal) has a –CHO group; it is an alkanal.
whyNot.C: CH₃COOCH₃ (methyl ethanoate) is an ester (–COO–).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: In petroleum refining, heavy fractions are cracked. The main purpose of cracking is to
options: break large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful ones such as petrol and alkenes
join small alkene molecules into long polymer chains
separate crude oil into fractions by their boiling points
remove sulphur compounds from crude oil
questions.explanation: Cracking uses heat (and often a catalyst) to break long-chain alkanes, which are in low demand, into shorter alkanes for petrol and alkenes such as ethene, which are used to make plastics.

whyNot.C: Separating by boiling point is fractional distillation, not cracking.
whyNot.B: Joining small alkene molecules is polymerisation, the reverse idea.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: The chain has four carbon atoms (but-) and one C=C double bond (-ene). Numbering from the end nearest the double bond, it starts at carbon 1, so the name is but-1-ene.

whyNot.A: But-2-ene is CH₃CH=CHCH₃, with the double bond between carbons 2 and 3.
whyNot.B: Butane has no double bond.
whyNot.C: Prop-1-ene has only three carbon atoms.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following polymers is made by condensation polymerisation?
questions.explanation: In condensation polymerisation, monomers join and a small molecule such as water or HCl is given off at each link. Nylon is formed this way from a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid (or its acid chloride). The other three are addition polymers made from alkene monomers with nothing given off.

whyNot.D: Poly(ethene) is an addition polymer of ethene.
whyNot.A: Poly(chloroethene), PVC, is an addition polymer of chloroethene.
whyNot.B: Poly(phenylethene), polystyrene, is an addition polymer.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Ethyne is prepared by adding water to calcium dicarbide: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → C₂H₂ + Ca(OH)₂. What volume of ethyne at s.t.p. is obtained from 6.4 g of CaC₂? [C = 12, Ca = 40; molar volume = 22.4 dm³ at s.t.p.]
questions.explanation: Molar mass of CaC₂ = 40 + 2(12) = 64 g mol⁻¹, so moles = 6.4 ÷ 64 = 0.10 mol. One mole of CaC₂ gives one mole of C₂H₂, so 0.10 mol of ethyne is formed, occupying 0.10 × 22.4 = 2.24 dm³.

whyNot.D: 4.48 dm³ uses the 2 in front of H₂O as if it applied to ethyne.
whyNot.A: 22.4 dm³ is the volume of one whole mole of gas.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following is an isomer of ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH?
questions.explanation: Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures. Ethanol is C₂H₆O. Methoxymethane, CH₃OCH₃, is also C₂H₆O, but its oxygen links the two carbon atoms (an ether), so it is a structural isomer of ethanol.

whyNot.C: CH₃CHO (ethanal) is C₂H₄O, two hydrogen atoms fewer than ethanol.
whyNot.B: CH₃OH (methanol) is CH₄O; it is a homologue of ethanol, not an isomer.
whyNot.D: CH₃COOH (ethanoic acid) is C₂H₄O₂.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which part of a cell contains the chromosomes and controls the activities of the cell?
questions.explanation: The nucleus holds the chromosomes, which carry the genes (DNA). The genes direct which proteins and enzymes the cell makes, so the nucleus controls the cell's activities and its inheritance.

whyNot.D: The cytoplasm is where many reactions happen, but it does not hold the chromosomes.
whyNot.A: The mitochondrion releases energy by aerobic respiration; it does not control the whole cell.

questions.subject: biology
questions.context: A student looks at a cell from a hibiscus leaf under a light microscope and draws it. The drawing shows a firm outer wall, a thin membrane just inside it, many small green oval bodies near the edge, a nucleus pushed to one side, and a large space labelled X in the centre. X is filled with a watery liquid and is surrounded by its own thin membrane.
questions.stem: What is the main function of the structure labelled X?
options: It traps light energy for photosynthesis
It stores cell sap and keeps the cell firm (turgid)
It controls which substances enter and leave the cell
questions.explanation: X is the large central vacuole. It stores cell sap (water with dissolved sugars and salts). When it is full of water it presses the cytoplasm against the cell wall, making the cell turgid, which keeps soft plant parts such as leaves firm.

whyNot.A: Trapping light is done by the green oval bodies, the chloroplasts.
whyNot.D: Controlling entry and exit of substances is the job of the cell membrane.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Some human red blood cells are placed in distilled water. What happens to them after a few minutes?
options: They take in water but stay the same size because of the cell wall
They take in water by osmosis, swell and burst
They lose water by osmosis and shrink
They lose salts by diffusion and become plasmolysed
questions.explanation: Distilled water has a higher water potential than the cytoplasm of red cells, so water enters the cells by osmosis. Animal cells have no cell wall to resist the pressure, so the cells swell and burst (haemolysis).

whyNot.C: Cells shrink only in a more concentrated solution, such as strong salt water.
whyNot.A: Red blood cells have no cell wall; only plant cells are protected by one.
whyNot.D: Plasmolysis happens to plant cells that lose water, not to animal cells in pure water.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: During mitosis, at which stage do the chromosomes line up across the equator (middle) of the spindle?
questions.explanation: In prophase the chromosomes shorten and become visible; in metaphase they line up on the equator of the spindle; in anaphase the chromatids are pulled to opposite poles; in telophase new nuclei form.

whyNot.A: In prophase the chromosomes condense but are not yet arranged on the equator.
whyNot.D: In anaphase the chromatids are moving apart to the poles.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A block of agar is a cube with sides of 2 cm. What is its surface area to volume ratio?
questions.explanation: Surface area = 6 faces × (2 × 2) cm² = 24 cm². Volume = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cm³. Ratio = 24 : 8 = 3 : 1. Larger organisms have a smaller ratio, which is why they need special transport and exchange systems.

whyNot.D: 1 : 3 puts volume before surface area.
whyNot.A: 6 : 1 is the ratio for a 1 cm cube (6 cm² to 1 cm³).

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Two test tubes contain starch solution and salivary amylase. Tube 1 is kept at 37 °C. In tube 2 the amylase was boiled before it was added. After 20 minutes iodine solution is added to both. Which result is expected?
options: Tube 1 stays brown and tube 2 turns blue-black
Tube 1 turns blue-black and tube 2 stays brown
questions.explanation: At 37 °C amylase digests the starch to maltose, so iodine stays brown in tube 1. Boiling denatures the enzyme (its active site loses its shape), so the starch in tube 2 is not digested and turns iodine blue-black.

whyNot.B: This would mean the active enzyme in tube 1 did nothing.
whyNot.D: This reverses the result: it is the boiled enzyme that cannot work.

questions.subject: biology
questions.context: A diagram shows a human heart seen from the front. Of its four chambers, the one labelled P has the thickest muscular wall. The largest artery of the body, which arches over the top of the heart, leaves chamber P.
questions.stem: Which chamber is P?
questions.explanation: The aorta leaves the left ventricle. This chamber has the thickest wall because it must pump blood with high pressure all round the body, while the right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs.

whyNot.B: The right ventricle pumps blood into the pulmonary artery, and its wall is thinner.
whyNot.A: The atria only push blood into the ventricles, so their walls are thin.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A lack of vitamin D in the diet of young children, together with little sunlight, causes
questions.explanation: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium and phosphate for building bones. Without it, children's bones stay soft and bend, a condition called rickets.

whyNot.A: Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C.
whyNot.D: Beriberi is caused by a lack of vitamin B1 (thiamine).
whyNot.C: Night blindness is caused by a lack of vitamin A.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which sequence shows the correct path of an impulse in a simple reflex arc, such as pulling the hand away from a hot pot?
options: Receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector
Effector → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → receptor
Receptor → relay neurone → sensory neurone → motor neurone → effector
Receptor → motor neurone → relay neurone → sensory neurone → effector
questions.explanation: The receptor in the skin detects the heat. The sensory neurone carries the impulse to the spinal cord, a relay neurone passes it on, and the motor neurone carries it to the effector (arm muscle), which contracts.

whyNot.D: The sensory neurone must come first, carrying the impulse from the receptor.
whyNot.B: The effector is the end of the arc, not the start.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: On a hot afternoon a farmer in Kano sweats a great deal and drinks very little water. How does his body respond to save water?
options: More ADH is released, so the kidneys reabsorb more water and he passes a small volume of concentrated urine
Less ADH is released, so the kidneys reabsorb more water and he passes concentrated urine
More ADH is released, so the kidneys reabsorb less water and he passes a large volume of dilute urine
More insulin is released, so the kidneys stop producing urine
questions.explanation: When the blood becomes too concentrated, the pituitary gland releases more antidiuretic hormone (ADH). ADH makes the collecting ducts of the kidney more permeable, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood and only a little concentrated urine is produced.

whyNot.B: Less ADH would make the kidneys reabsorb less water, not more.
whyNot.C: ADH increases water reabsorption; it does not reduce it.
whyNot.D: Insulin controls blood glucose, not water balance.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A maize seedling on a classroom windowsill bends towards the window. Which explanation is correct?
options: Cells on the lit side divide faster because they make more food by photosynthesis
Auxin collects on the shaded side of the shoot, so cells there grow longer than cells on the lit side
Auxin collects on the lit side of the shoot, so cells there grow longer than cells on the shaded side
Light destroys all the auxin, so the shoot stops growing on both sides
questions.explanation: Light from one side causes auxin to move to the shaded side of the shoot tip. In shoots, auxin makes cells elongate, so the shaded side grows faster and the shoot curves towards the light (positive phototropism).

whyNot.C: If the lit side grew faster, the shoot would bend away from the light.
whyNot.D: The shoot keeps growing; it is uneven growth that causes bending.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: The left ventricle of a student pumps out 70 cm³ of blood at each beat, and her heart beats 72 times per minute. What volume of blood does it pump in one minute?
questions.explanation: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 70 cm³ × 72 beats per minute = 5 040 cm³ per minute (about 5 dm³).

whyNot.D: 142 cm³ is 70 + 72; the two values must be multiplied, not added.
whyNot.B: 504 cm³ is out by a factor of ten.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A vegetation zone covers much of Nigeria's Middle Belt around towns such as Minna and Makurdi. It has tall grasses up to about 3 m high, scattered trees such as locust bean and shea, a dry season with bush fires, and annual rainfall of roughly 1 000 to 1 500 mm. Which zone is this?
questions.explanation: Tall grass with scattered fire-resistant trees and moderate rainfall describes the Guinea savanna, the largest vegetation zone in Nigeria, lying between the rainforest in the south and the drier Sudan savanna to the north.

whyNot.A: The Sahel savanna, in the far north-east, has short sparse grass and much lower rainfall.
whyNot.C: The rainforest has tall trees in a closed canopy and much higher rainfall, with little grass.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In a food chain the producers trap 20 000 kJ of energy. If only 10% of the energy at each trophic level is passed on to the next, how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
questions.explanation: Producers 20 000 kJ → primary consumers 10% = 2 000 kJ → secondary consumers 10% = 200 kJ → tertiary consumers 10% = 20 kJ. Energy is lost at each step as heat from respiration, in faeces and in uneaten parts.

whyNot.A: 200 kJ is what reaches the secondary consumers.
whyNot.B: 2 000 kJ is what reaches the primary consumers.
whyNot.D: 2 kJ would be one step further, at the quaternary level.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which instrument is used to measure the relative humidity of the air in a habitat?
questions.explanation: A hygrometer (for example a wet-and-dry bulb thermometer) measures relative humidity, the amount of water vapour in the air compared with the most it could hold at that temperature.

whyNot.C: An anemometer measures wind speed.
whyNot.D: A rain gauge measures the amount of rainfall.
whyNot.A: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Small ferns grow on the trunk of an oil palm. The ferns get support and a place in the light, and the palm is neither helped nor harmed. This relationship is
questions.explanation: In commensalism one organism benefits and the other is unaffected. The ferns (epiphytes) benefit from support and light, while the oil palm neither gains nor loses.

whyNot.D: In parasitism the host is harmed; the ferns take no food from the palm.
whyNot.A: In mutualism both partners benefit, but the palm gains nothing.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: After an oil spill in a creek in the Niger Delta, many fish die. Which is the main reason?
options: The oil raises the water temperature until it boils
The oil makes the water too salty for fish
The oil adds too many nitrates, causing eutrophication
The oil film on the surface reduces the oxygen dissolving into the water
questions.explanation: Crude oil spreads as a film over the water surface. This cuts down the oxygen dissolving from the air into the water, and oil also coats the gills of fish, so the fish cannot get enough oxygen and die.

whyNot.C: Eutrophication is caused by fertiliser and sewage runoff rich in nitrates and phosphates, not by crude oil.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which type of soil holds the most water after heavy rain?
questions.explanation: Clay has very tiny particles packed closely together, with many small pore spaces that hold water tightly. It therefore retains more water than coarse-textured soils.

whyNot.A: Sandy soil has large particles and large pore spaces, so water drains away quickly.
whyNot.C: Loamy sand is still mostly sand, so it drains well.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In guinea pigs, black coat (B) is dominant over white coat (b). Two heterozygous black guinea pigs are mated several times and produce 64 young in total. How many of the young are expected to be white?
questions.explanation: Bb × Bb gives BB : Bb : bb in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1, so 1/4 of the young are bb (white). 1/4 × 64 = 16.

whyNot.A: 32 would be half, which is the expected number of heterozygous (Bb) young.
whyNot.D: 48 is the expected number of black young (3/4 of 64).

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A man of blood group A (genotype IᴬIᴼ) marries a woman of blood group B (genotype IᴮIᴼ). What is the probability that their first child will be blood group O?
questions.explanation: The man makes gametes Iᴬ or Iᴼ, and the woman makes Iᴮ or Iᴼ. The four equally likely offspring are IᴬIᴮ (AB), IᴬIᴼ (A), IᴮIᴼ (B) and IᴼIᴼ (O). Only one of the four is group O, so the probability is 1/4.

whyNot.A: 1/2 is the probability that the child carries at least one Iᴬ allele.
whyNot.D: Both parents carry the recessive Iᴼ allele, so an IᴼIᴼ child is possible.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In humans, the sex of a baby is decided by
options: the number of autosomes in the egg
whether the egg carries an X or a Y chromosome
