whyNot.D: Ghanaian women writers include Ama Ata Aidoo; Bâ was Senegalese and wrote in French.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: Ama Ata Aidoo, author of the play The Dilemma of a Ghost, is from
questions.explanation: Ama Ata Aidoo was a Ghanaian playwright, poet and novelist. The Dilemma of a Ghost (1965) is about a Ghanaian man who returns home with an African-American wife.

whyNot.A: She was not Nigerian; the play is set in Ghana.
whyNot.C: The Senegalese woman writer often studied is Mariama Bâ.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: Which Nigerian poet, author of Labyrinths, died fighting in the Nigerian Civil War in 1967?
questions.explanation: Christopher Okigbo, one of Nigeria's most important modern poets, was killed in 1967 early in the Civil War. His collected poems were published as Labyrinths.

whyNot.B: J. P. Clark lived until 2020.
whyNot.A: Gabriel Okara lived until 2019.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: The novels People of the City and Jagua Nana, set in Lagos, were written by
questions.explanation: Cyprian Ekwensi is known for lively novels of Lagos city life, including People of the City (1954) and Jagua Nana (1961).

whyNot.C: Amos Tutuola wrote The Palm-Wine Drinkard, based on Yoruba folklore.
whyNot.A: Elechi Amadi wrote The Concubine, set in a traditional village.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: On a map drawn to a scale of 1:50,000, the distance between two villages is 6 cm. What is the actual distance on the ground?
questions.explanation: 1:50,000 means 1 cm on the map is 50,000 cm on the ground. 6 × 50,000 = 300,000 cm. Since 100,000 cm = 1 km, 300,000 cm = 3 km.

whyNot.D: 30 km comes from dividing by 10,000 instead of 100,000 when changing centimetres to kilometres.
whyNot.C: 6 km treats the scale as 1 cm to 1 km, which is 1:100,000.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A map has the statement scale '1 cm represents 5 km'. What is this scale written as a representative fraction (R.F.)?
questions.explanation: Change both sides to the same unit. 5 km = 5 × 100,000 cm = 500,000 cm. So 1 cm on the map represents 500,000 cm on the ground, giving an R.F. of 1:500,000.

whyNot.C: 1:50,000 comes from using 10,000 cm in a kilometre instead of 100,000 cm.
whyNot.B: 1:5,000,000 adds one zero too many; 5 km is 500,000 cm.

questions.subject: geography
questions.context: On a map of scale 1:25,000, point P is a spot height of 450 m and point Q is a spot height of 250 m. The straight-line distance from P to Q on the map is 8 cm.
questions.stem: What is the average gradient between P and Q?
questions.explanation: Vertical interval = 450 − 250 = 200 m. Horizontal equivalent = 8 × 25,000 = 200,000 cm = 2,000 m. Gradient = VI ÷ HE = 200 ÷ 2,000 = 1/10, which is 1 in 10.

whyNot.B: 1 in 20 uses a scale of 1:50,000 instead of the map's 1:25,000.
whyNot.D: 1 in 1,000 compares 200 m with 200,000 cm without first changing both to the same unit.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: In a six-figure grid reference such as 346723, what do the first three figures give?
questions.explanation: Grid references always give the easting first (read along the bottom of the map from west to east), then the northing (read up the side). So 346 is the easting and 723 is the northing.

whyNot.C: The northing is given by the last three figures, not the first three.
whyNot.B: A grid reference fixes a position; heights are shown by contours and spot heights.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The bearing of town Q from town P is 060°. What is the bearing of P from Q?
questions.explanation: The back bearing differs from the forward bearing by 180°. Since 060° is less than 180°, add 180°: 060° + 180° = 240°.

whyNot.D: 300° is 360° − 60°, which reflects the line across the north–south line instead of reversing it.
whyNot.B: 120° is 180° − 60°, which is not the reverse direction.

questions.subject: geography
questions.context: On a topographical map, a set of contour lines bends into sharp V shapes. The point of each V faces towards the higher contour values, and a thin blue line runs through the points of the Vs.
questions.stem: Which relief feature is shown?
questions.explanation: Where contours cross a valley they bend upstream, so the V points towards higher ground. The blue line running through the Vs is the river flowing along the valley floor.

whyNot.B: On a spur the Vs point towards lower ground, not higher ground.
whyNot.C: A col is a low dip between two hills, shown by contours that narrow like an hour-glass, not by Vs.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A rectangular farm measures 4 cm by 3 cm on a map of scale 1:50,000. What is its actual area?
questions.explanation: At 1:50,000, 1 cm represents 0.5 km. So the sides are 4 × 0.5 = 2 km and 3 × 0.5 = 1.5 km. Area = 2 × 1.5 = 3 km².

whyNot.B: 12 km² multiplies the map lengths (4 × 3) without converting them to kilometres.
whyNot.D: 6 km² converts only one side (12 × 0.5); for an area the factor 0.5 must be applied to both sides (0.25 per cm²).

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: On a contour map, what do contour lines that are drawn very close together indicate?
questions.explanation: Contours join places of equal height. When they are close together, the land rises through the same vertical interval over a short horizontal distance, which means the slope is steep.

whyNot.D: A gentle slope is shown by contours that are widely spaced.
whyNot.A: Flat land has few or no contours crossing it.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A footpath measures 7.5 cm on a map of scale 1:20,000. How long will a man walking steadily at 3 km per hour take to cover the path?
questions.explanation: Ground distance = 7.5 × 20,000 = 150,000 cm = 1.5 km. Time = distance ÷ speed = 1.5 ÷ 3 = 0.5 hour, which is 30 minutes.

whyNot.A: 15 minutes is the time for 0.75 km, half the real distance.
whyNot.C: 50 minutes comes from treating 0.5 hour as 50 minutes; 0.5 hour is 30 minutes.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A map of scale 1:25,000 is reduced so that every length on it becomes half as long. What is the scale of the reduced map?
questions.explanation: After reduction, 1 cm on the new map equals 2 cm on the old map. 2 cm on the old map represents 2 × 25,000 = 50,000 cm on the ground. So the new scale is 1:50,000 (a smaller scale).

whyNot.A: 1:12,500 is what you get when the map is enlarged to twice the size, not reduced.
whyNot.B: 1:100,000 would mean the lengths were reduced to a quarter, not a half.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Granite, formed when magma cools slowly deep inside the earth's crust, is an example of
questions.explanation: Granite forms from magma that cools slowly underground. Slow cooling gives large crystals, and rocks formed inside the crust are called intrusive (plutonic) igneous rocks.

whyNot.C: Sedimentary rocks form from layers of deposited particles, not from cooled magma.
whyNot.D: Extrusive igneous rocks, such as basalt, cool quickly on the surface and have small crystals.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which instrument is used in a weather station to measure the relative humidity of the air?
questions.explanation: A hygrometer (often wet-and-dry bulb thermometers) measures the moisture in the air. The difference between the wet and dry bulb readings is used to find relative humidity.

whyNot.A: An anemometer measures wind speed.
whyNot.D: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Town A is on longitude 30°E and town B is on longitude 15°W. When the local time at A is 2.00 p.m., what is the local time at B?
questions.explanation: The two towns are on opposite sides of Greenwich, so add the longitudes: 30° + 15° = 45°. The earth turns 15° in one hour, so 45° = 3 hours. B is west of A, so its time is behind: 2.00 p.m. − 3 hours = 11.00 a.m.

whyNot.C: 5.00 p.m. adds the 3 hours; places to the west are behind, so the hours must be subtracted.
whyNot.B: 1.00 p.m. subtracts the longitudes (30° − 15° = 15°) even though the towns are on opposite sides of Greenwich.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Marble is a metamorphic rock formed by the action of great heat and pressure on
questions.explanation: When limestone (mainly calcium carbonate) is subjected to great heat and pressure, its crystals recrystallise to form marble.

whyNot.D: Shale is changed into slate, not marble.
whyNot.C: Sandstone is changed into quartzite, not marble.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: In which stage of a river's course is an ox-bow lake most likely to form?
options: At the source of the river
questions.explanation: In the lower course the river flows slowly over a wide flat floodplain and develops large meanders. Erosion narrows a meander neck until the river cuts through it, leaving the old loop cut off as an ox-bow lake.

whyNot.C: In the upper course the river is cutting down steeply in a V-shaped valley and does not form wide meanders.
whyNot.D: A waterfall is a feature of the upper course where vertical erosion dominates.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Temperature falls with height at an average rate of 6.5 °C per 1,000 m. If the temperature at sea level is 28 °C, what is the temperature on top of a hill 2,000 m high?
questions.explanation: Fall in temperature = 6.5 × (2,000 ÷ 1,000) = 13 °C. Temperature at the top = 28 − 13 = 15 °C.

whyNot.B: 21.5 °C uses the fall for only 1,000 m.
whyNot.D: 41 °C adds the fall instead of subtracting it; temperature decreases with height.
whyNot.C: 13 °C is the amount of the fall, not the temperature at the top.

questions.subject: geography
questions.context: Mean monthly temperatures (°C) for a station: Jan 27, Feb 28, Mar 29, Apr 29, May 28, Jun 26, Jul 25, Aug 25, Sep 26, Oct 27, Nov 28, Dec 26.
questions.stem: What is the mean annual temperature of the station?

whyNot.C: 4.0 °C is the annual range of temperature (29 − 25), not the mean.
whyNot.A: 29.0 °C is the highest monthly mean, not the average of all twelve months.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which planet of the solar system is nearest to the sun?
questions.explanation: In order of distance from the sun the planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Mercury is the closest.

whyNot.B: Venus is the second planet from the sun.
whyNot.C: Mars is the fourth planet, just beyond the earth.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which of the following is true on 22 December (the December solstice)?
options: The midday sun is overhead at the Equator
The midday sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn
The northern hemisphere has its longest day
The Arctic Circle has 24 hours of daylight
questions.explanation: Because the earth's axis is tilted at 23½°, the overhead midday sun reaches its most southerly position, the Tropic of Capricorn (23½°S), around 22 December. The southern hemisphere then has its longest day, while the northern hemisphere has its shortest day and the Arctic Circle has 24 hours of darkness.

whyNot.C: The northern hemisphere has its longest day around 21 June, when the sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer.
whyNot.A: The sun is overhead at the Equator at the equinoxes (about 21 March and 23 September).
whyNot.D: In December the Arctic Circle is tilted away from the sun and has 24 hours of darkness.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which of these is a characteristic of the tropical rainforest?
options: Trees that shed their leaves in a long dry season
Tall evergreen trees arranged in layers
questions.explanation: The tropical rainforest has heavy rainfall and high temperatures all year, so trees grow tall, stay green (evergreen) and form several layers or storeys, with a dense canopy.

whyNot.B: Short grasses with scattered trees describe savanna vegetation.
whyNot.D: Coniferous trees with needle-shaped leaves belong to cool temperate (taiga) forests.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A state has a population of 2,400,000 people and an area of 8,000 km². What is its population density?
questions.explanation: Population density = total population ÷ land area = 2,400,000 ÷ 8,000 = 300 persons per km².

whyNot.A: 3,000 has one zero too many; check the division carefully.
whyNot.B: 3.3 divides area by population (8,000 ÷ 2,400) and shifts the decimal; density is people per unit area.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Houses that are built in a long line on both sides of a main road form which settlement pattern?
questions.explanation: A linear (ribbon) settlement stretches along a line such as a road, railway, river or coast, because people want easy access to the route.

whyNot.C: A nucleated settlement has houses clustered closely around a centre, not strung out along a line.
whyNot.A: In a dispersed settlement houses are scattered far apart across the countryside.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which means of transport is most suitable for moving crude oil and natural gas continuously over long distances on land?
questions.explanation: Pipelines carry liquids and gases continuously, cheaply and safely once built, so they are used to move crude oil and gas from fields to refineries, terminals and power stations.

whyNot.A: Lorries carry small loads at a high cost per tonne and cannot move oil continuously.
whyNot.C: Air transport is far too expensive for bulky, low-value cargo such as crude oil.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Cement factories, such as the one at Ewekoro, are usually located near limestone deposits mainly because
options: cement is a perishable product that must be sold quickly
cement factories need very large amounts of skilled labour
limestone is bulky and loses weight in manufacture, so it is cheaper to process it near the quarry
limestone is found only near large cities
questions.explanation: Limestone is heavy and much of its weight is lost during processing. Moving the raw material far would cost more than moving the finished cement, so the factory is sited at the raw material (a raw-material-oriented industry).

whyNot.A: Cement is not perishable; it can be stored for a long time if kept dry.
whyNot.D: Limestone deposits are often in rural areas, such as Ewekoro in Ogun State.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A population pyramid with a very broad base that narrows quickly towards the top shows a population with
options: a low birth rate and a long life expectancy
a high birth rate and a short life expectancy
questions.explanation: The broad base means a large share of children, which comes from a high birth rate. The rapid narrowing upwards shows that few people survive to old age, so life expectancy is short. This is typical of many developing countries.

whyNot.A: A low birth rate and long life expectancy give a narrow base and wide upper bars.
whyNot.C: A declining number of births would make the base narrower than the bars just above it.

questions.subject: geography
questions.context: A country's visible trade in one year (₦ billion). Exports: crude oil 600, cocoa 90, other goods 60. Imports: machinery 500, food 330.
questions.stem: What is the country's balance of trade for the year?
questions.explanation: Total exports = 600 + 90 + 60 = ₦750 billion. Total imports = 500 + 330 = ₦830 billion. Balance of trade = exports − imports = 750 − 830 = −₦80 billion. A negative figure is a deficit (unfavourable balance).

whyNot.C: The size is right, but imports are greater than exports, so the balance is a deficit, not a surplus.
whyNot.A: ₦750 billion is total exports only; imports must be subtracted.
whyNot.B: ₦330 billion is the food import bill alone, not the difference between total exports and total imports.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which of the following is a tertiary economic activity?
questions.explanation: Tertiary activities provide services rather than goods. Banking, transport, trade, teaching and health care are tertiary activities.

whyNot.A: Fishing takes resources directly from nature, so it is a primary activity.
whyNot.C: Textile manufacturing turns raw materials into goods, so it is a secondary activity.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: In a country, 45% of the population is under 15 years, 5% is over 64 years and 50% is aged 15–64. What is the dependency ratio?
questions.explanation: Dependency ratio = (dependants ÷ working-age population) × 100 = ((45 + 5) ÷ 50) × 100 = 100. This means there is one dependant for every person of working age.

whyNot.B: 50 is the percentage of dependants, not the ratio of dependants to workers.
whyNot.D: 90 uses only the young dependants (45 ÷ 50 × 100) and leaves out the old.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which of these is a push factor that drives young people from rural areas to cities in Nigeria?
options: Better job opportunities in the cities
Lack of social amenities in the villages
questions.explanation: Push factors are conditions in the place of origin that make people want to leave, such as lack of electricity, pipe-borne water and good schools in the villages.

whyNot.A: Better jobs in the cities attract people to the destination, so they are a pull factor.
whyNot.B: Better city hospitals are a pull factor at the destination.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: What is a conurbation?
options: A small village with houses scattered among farmland
A large urban area formed when neighbouring towns grow and merge into one built-up area
A settlement that grew up around a single mine
A city that has lost most of its population
questions.explanation: As neighbouring towns grow outwards, the countryside between them is built over until they join into one continuous built-up area, called a conurbation. Lagos and its surrounding towns are an example.

whyNot.A: Scattered houses among farmland describe a dispersed rural settlement.
whyNot.C: A settlement built around a mine is a mining town, which need not have merged with others.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: At which town do the Rivers Niger and Benue meet?
questions.explanation: The River Benue joins the River Niger at Lokoja in Kogi State. Below the confluence the combined river flows south to the Niger Delta.

whyNot.D: Onitsha is on the Niger, downstream of the confluence.
whyNot.C: Makurdi is on the Benue, upstream of the confluence.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Kainji Dam, Nigeria's first major hydroelectric dam, was built across which river?
questions.explanation: Kainji Dam was built across the River Niger in Niger State and completed in the late 1960s. It created Kainji Lake and generates hydroelectric power.

whyNot.C: The River Kaduna is dammed at Shiroro, not at Kainji.
whyNot.B: No major hydroelectric dam on the Benue is called Kainji.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which Nigerian city is best known for coal mining?
questions.explanation: Coal has been mined in the Enugu area since the early twentieth century, which earned Enugu the name 'Coal City'.

whyNot.A: Jos is famous for tin and columbite mining, not coal.
whyNot.B: Kano is a commercial centre known for groundnuts and trade, not coal.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The harmattan, a dry and dusty wind that blows over Nigeria between about November and February, comes from the
questions.explanation: The harmattan is the north-east trade wind (tropical continental air mass). It blows from the Sahara Desert, so it is dry and carries fine dust.

whyNot.A: Winds from the Atlantic Ocean are moist and bring rain, not dry dust.
whyNot.C: The Gulf of Guinea is the source of the moist south-west winds of the rainy season.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which is the correct order of Nigeria's vegetation zones from the coast northwards?
options: Mangrove swamp, Guinea savanna, rainforest, Sahel savanna, Sudan savanna
Mangrove swamp, rainforest, Guinea savanna, Sudan savanna, Sahel savanna
Sahel savanna, Sudan savanna, Guinea savanna, rainforest, mangrove swamp
Rainforest, mangrove swamp, Sudan savanna, Guinea savanna, Sahel savanna
questions.explanation: Rainfall decreases from the coast inland, so vegetation changes from mangrove swamp on the coast, to rainforest, then Guinea savanna, Sudan savanna and finally Sahel savanna in the far north-east.

whyNot.D: Mangrove swamp lies on the coast, south of the rainforest.
whyNot.C: This is the order from north to south, not from the coast northwards.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which group of states forms the main cocoa-producing area of Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Cocoa needs heavy rainfall, high temperatures and deep, well-drained forest soils. These are found in the south-western forest belt, especially Ondo, Osun, Ogun and Oyo States.

whyNot.B: Kano, Katsina and Jigawa are too dry for cocoa; they grow groundnuts, millet and cotton.
whyNot.C: Borno, Yobe and Bauchi lie in the dry savanna north-east.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Tin and columbite are mined mainly in which part of Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Tin and columbite occur in the granite rocks of the Jos Plateau, in Plateau State, where they have been mined for over a century.

whyNot.B: The Niger Delta is famous for crude petroleum and natural gas.
whyNot.C: The Sokoto Plains are sedimentary lowlands known for limestone and phosphate, not tin.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which is the highest peak in Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Chappal Waddi, in the Gotel Mountains of Taraba State near the Cameroon border, is about 2,400 m high and is the highest point in Nigeria.

whyNot.C: Olumo Rock in Abeokuta is a famous granite outcrop but is far lower.
whyNot.D: The Obudu Plateau in Cross River State is high, but it is a plateau, not Nigeria's highest peak.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which best explains why annual rainfall in Nigeria decreases from the south to the north?
options: The harmattan blows mainly over the south
The north is nearer the Equator than the south
The moist south-west winds from the Atlantic reach the south earlier and stay there longer
The north is at a higher altitude than the south
questions.explanation: Rain is brought by moist south-west winds (tropical maritime air) from the Atlantic. They reach the coastal south first and remain there for most of the year, but reach the far north only for a short period, so the rainy season and the total rainfall decrease northwards.

whyNot.A: The harmattan affects the north most strongly; it is the south that receives the rain-bearing winds.
whyNot.B: The south, not the north, is nearer the Equator.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which is the main geographical advantage of the site of the Ajaokuta Steel Complex in Kogi State?
options: It is in the middle of the Niger Delta oil fields
It lies on the Atlantic coast for easy export
It is close to the iron ore at Itakpe and lies beside the River Niger
It is close to the coal mines of Kano
questions.explanation: A steel plant needs large amounts of iron ore and water and cheap transport for heavy goods. Ajaokuta is near the Itakpe iron ore deposits and on the bank of the River Niger, which supplies water and a transport route.

whyNot.D: Kano has no coal mines; Nigeria's coal is mainly in the Enugu area.
whyNot.B: Kogi State is inland; it has no Atlantic coastline.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Mount Kilimanjaro, the highest mountain in Africa, is located in
questions.explanation: Mount Kilimanjaro is in north-eastern Tanzania, close to the border with Kenya. It is a volcanic mountain and the highest peak in Africa.

whyNot.D: Kenya's highest mountain is Mount Kenya; Kilimanjaro is just across the border in Tanzania.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Suez Canal links which two bodies of water?
options: The Red Sea and the Indian Ocean
The Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean
The Mediterranean Sea and the Red Sea
The Mediterranean Sea and the Atlantic Ocean
questions.explanation: The Suez Canal in Egypt joins the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea, so ships between Europe and Asia do not have to sail round Africa.

whyNot.B: The Atlantic and Pacific Oceans are linked by the Panama Canal.
whyNot.D: The Mediterranean and the Atlantic are joined naturally by the Strait of Gibraltar.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which is the largest lake in Africa?
questions.explanation: Lake Victoria, shared by Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania, is the largest lake in Africa by area. It is also a source of the White Nile.

whyNot.D: Lake Tanganyika is very deep and long, but its area is smaller than Lake Victoria's.
whyNot.B: Lake Volta is a man-made lake behind the Akosombo Dam and is smaller than Lake Victoria.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Kariba Dam, which supplies hydroelectric power to Zambia and Zimbabwe, is built across which river?
questions.explanation: The Kariba Dam stands on the River Zambezi on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe, forming Lake Kariba.

whyNot.D: The Congo is dammed at Inga in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, not at Kariba.
whyNot.A: The Orange River flows through South Africa and Namibia, far from Kariba.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Copperbelt, an important copper-mining region of Africa, is found in
questions.explanation: The Copperbelt lies in northern Zambia (extending into the Democratic Republic of the Congo). Copper is Zambia's main export.

whyNot.D: Ghana is noted for gold, cocoa and bauxite, not a copper belt.
whyNot.C: Senegal is known for groundnuts and phosphates.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The temperate grasslands of North America are called the
questions.explanation: Temperate grasslands have local names: Prairies in North America, Pampas in South America, Steppes in Eurasia, Veld in South Africa and Downs in Australia.

whyNot.C: The Pampas are in South America, mainly Argentina.
whyNot.D: The Veld is in South Africa.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which part of Africa has a Mediterranean type of climate, with hot dry summers and mild wet winters?
options: The south-western tip of South Africa, around Cape Town
questions.explanation: Mediterranean climate occurs on the western sides of continents at about 30°–40° from the Equator. In Africa it is found along the north-west coast and the south-western tip around Cape Town, which gets most of its rain in winter.

whyNot.A: The Congo Basin has an equatorial climate with rain all year.
whyNot.C: The Nigerian coast has a tropical climate with rain mainly in the hot season.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Ruhr, one of the world's major heavy-industrial regions, grew up mainly because of local deposits of coal and its position on the River Rhine. In which country is it?
questions.explanation: The Ruhr is in western Germany. Rich coal deposits and cheap transport along the Rhine and canals made it a centre of iron and steel, chemicals and engineering.

whyNot.A: Japan's industrial regions lie on its coasts and rely on imported raw materials.
whyNot.B: Canada's main industrial belt is around the Great Lakes and St Lawrence.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Akosombo Dam on the River Volta in Ghana was built mainly to provide electricity for
questions.explanation: The Volta River Project produced hydroelectric power at Akosombo chiefly to run an aluminium smelter at Tema, since smelting aluminium uses very large amounts of electricity. It also supplies homes and industries.

whyNot.D: Jos is in Nigeria; Ghana's Akosombo power was built for Ghana's own aluminium industry.
whyNot.B: Kumasi is a commercial and timber centre, not a copper-refining town.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Great Rift Valley of East Africa was formed mainly by
questions.explanation: Tension in the earth's crust caused parallel faults. The land between the faults sank (or the sides rose), producing a long, steep-sided valley called a rift valley.

whyNot.B: Glaciers carve U-shaped valleys in cold mountain regions; East Africa's rift is a tectonic feature.
whyNot.D: River deposition builds floodplains and deltas, not deep, steep-sided rift valleys.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: On a map of scale 1:100,000, a road measures 4.5 cm. What is the actual length of the road?
questions.explanation: At 1:100,000, 1 cm on the map represents 100,000 cm, which is exactly 1 km. So 4.5 cm represents 4.5 km.

whyNot.B: 45 km treats 1 cm as 10 km.
whyNot.D: 9 km doubles the distance, as if the scale were 1:200,000.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which statement scale is the same as a representative fraction of 1:250,000?
questions.explanation: 1:250,000 means 1 cm represents 250,000 cm. Divide by 100,000 to change centimetres to kilometres: 250,000 ÷ 100,000 = 2.5 km.

whyNot.D: 25 km comes from dividing by 10,000 instead of 100,000.
whyNot.A: 250 m (0.25 km) comes from dividing by 1,000,000 instead of 100,000.
whyNot.B: 250 km comes from dividing by 1,000, which does not change centimetres into kilometres.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: What is the true bearing of a place that lies exactly south-west of an observer?
questions.explanation: Bearings are measured clockwise from north. East is 090°, south is 180° and west is 270°. South-west lies halfway between south and west: (180 + 270) ÷ 2 = 225°.

whyNot.D: 135° is south-east.
whyNot.C: 315° is north-west.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: On a contour map, a low point or dip on a ridge between two hills is called a
questions.explanation: A col (saddle) is a low gap between two higher points on a ridge. Contours on each side of it bend away from each other, giving an hour-glass shape.

whyNot.A: A spur is a tongue of high land projecting into lower ground.
whyNot.D: A knoll is a small, rounded hill, not a dip.

questions.subject: geography
questions.context: On a topographical map, a borehole lies inside the grid square whose bottom-left corner is formed by easting line 34 and northing line 72. Measured in tenths of the square, the borehole is 6 tenths east of easting 34 and 3 tenths north of northing 72.
questions.stem: What is the six-figure grid reference of the borehole?
questions.explanation: Write the easting first: 34 plus 6 tenths gives 346. Then the northing: 72 plus 3 tenths gives 723. The grid reference is 346723.

whyNot.C: 723346 gives the northing before the easting; eastings always come first.
whyNot.B: 343726 swaps the tenths, putting the 3 with the easting and the 6 with the northing.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Two towns are 18 km apart on the ground. On a map they are 36 cm apart. What is the representative fraction of the map?
questions.explanation: Change the ground distance to centimetres: 18 km = 18 × 100,000 = 1,800,000 cm. R.F. = map distance ÷ ground distance = 36 ÷ 1,800,000 = 1 ÷ 50,000, so 1:50,000.

whyNot.D: 1:500,000 has one zero too many from a slip in the conversion.
whyNot.A: 1:20,000 comes from dividing 36 by 18 and wrongly treating the answer as the scale.

questions.subject: geography
questions.context: On a map, a set of contour lines forms V shapes. The point of each V faces towards lower contour values (lower ground), and there is no river along the Vs.
questions.stem: Which relief feature is shown?
questions.explanation: A spur is a finger of high land sticking out into lower ground. Its contours form Vs (or Us) that point downhill, towards lower values.

whyNot.D: In a valley the Vs point uphill, towards higher ground, and a river often runs through them.
whyNot.C: A plateau is a broad, flat-topped upland with widely spaced contours on top and steep edges.

questions.subject: geography
questions.context: On a map, the contours on one side of a hill are widely spaced near the summit and become closer and closer together towards the foot of the hill.
questions.stem: What type of slope does this show?
questions.explanation: Close contours mean steep ground and wide contours mean gentle ground. Here the slope is gentle at the top and steep at the bottom, so it bulges outwards: a convex slope.

whyNot.B: A concave slope is steep at the top and gentle at the bottom, so its contours are close near the summit and wide near the foot.
whyNot.D: A uniform slope has contours spaced evenly all the way down.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: On a topographical map, a dot with a number beside it, such as •412, which gives the height of that exact point above sea level, is called a
questions.explanation: A spot height is a dot on a map with a number showing the height, in metres, of that exact point above sea level.

whyNot.C: A contour is a line joining many places of the same height, not a single dot.
whyNot.B: A grid reference is a set of figures used to locate a point, not a height.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A square plot of land measures 2 cm by 2 cm on a map of scale 1:25,000. What is its actual area?
questions.explanation: At 1:25,000, 1 cm represents 25,000 cm = 0.25 km. Each side is 2 × 0.25 = 0.5 km. Area = 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25 km².

whyNot.B: 0.5 km² multiplies 2 cm² by 0.25 once; for an area the conversion must be applied to both sides.
whyNot.C: 4 km² multiplies the map lengths without converting them to kilometres.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which instrument is used to measure the speed of the wind?
questions.explanation: An anemometer has cups that spin in the wind. The faster the wind blows, the faster the cups turn, and the speed is read off a dial.

whyNot.B: A wind vane shows the direction the wind comes from, not its speed.
whyNot.D: A hygrometer measures humidity.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which movement of the earth causes day and night?
options: Movement of the moon round the earth
Revolution of the earth round the sun
Rotation of the earth on its axis
questions.explanation: The earth spins (rotates) on its axis once in about 24 hours. The side facing the sun has day and the side facing away has night.

whyNot.B: Revolution round the sun takes about 365¼ days and, with the tilt of the axis, causes the seasons.
whyNot.C: The tilt of the axis causes seasons and changing day lengths, not day and night themselves.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which of the following is a sedimentary rock?
questions.explanation: Sandstone is made of grains of sand deposited in layers and then compressed and cemented together, so it is a sedimentary rock.

whyNot.A: Granite is an igneous rock formed from cooled magma.
whyNot.C: Marble is a metamorphic rock formed from limestone.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Slate is a metamorphic rock formed from
questions.explanation: Shale, a fine-grained clay rock, is changed by heat and pressure into slate, which splits into thin flat sheets.

whyNot.D: Limestone is changed into marble.
whyNot.B: Sandstone is changed into quartzite.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A narrow, steep-sided V-shaped valley with waterfalls and rapids is typical of which stage of a river's course?
questions.explanation: In the upper course the river flows fast down steep slopes and erodes mainly downwards (vertical erosion), cutting a narrow V-shaped valley. Hard rock bands produce waterfalls and rapids.

whyNot.B: In the lower course the valley is wide and flat, with meanders and floodplains.
whyNot.D: A delta forms at the mouth by deposition, not by vertical erosion.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: At a certain temperature, a cubic metre of air holds 12 g of water vapour, but it could hold 16 g if it were saturated. What is the relative humidity of the air?
questions.explanation: Relative humidity = (actual water vapour ÷ water vapour needed to saturate the air) × 100 = (12 ÷ 16) × 100 = 75%.

whyNot.B: 133% inverts the fraction (16 ÷ 12); relative humidity cannot exceed 100%.
whyNot.A: 25% is the shortfall from saturation (4 ÷ 16), not the humidity.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Mangrove trees in coastal swamps are adapted to waterlogged, salty mud mainly by having
options: very deep tap roots to reach underground water
questions.explanation: Stilt (prop) roots hold the tree firmly in soft mud, and breathing roots (pneumatophores) stick up above the mud to take in air, because waterlogged mud has little oxygen.

whyNot.A: Thick fire-resistant bark is an adaptation of savanna trees to bush fires.
whyNot.B: Deep tap roots help desert and savanna plants find water; mangroves are surrounded by water.

questions.subject: geography
questions.context: A weather station in northern Nigeria records its hottest month mean as 32 °C (April) and its coolest month mean as 24 °C (January).
questions.stem: What is the annual range of temperature at the station?
questions.explanation: Annual range of temperature = mean of the hottest month − mean of the coolest month = 32 − 24 = 8 °C.

whyNot.D: 28 °C is the average of the two months, not the range.
whyNot.A: 56 °C adds the two temperatures instead of subtracting.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A crescent-shaped sand dune, with its horns pointing in the direction the wind is blowing, is called a
questions.explanation: A barchan forms where wind blows steadily from one direction across a desert with limited sand. Sand moves faster at the edges, so the ends (horns) are pushed ahead downwind, giving a crescent.

whyNot.A: A seif is a long, narrow ridge-shaped dune lying parallel to the wind.
whyNot.D: A mesa is a flat-topped table-like hill left by erosion, not a sand dune.
whyNot.B: A wadi is a dry, steep-sided valley in a desert.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Place X is on longitude 45°E. When the local time at X is 6.00 p.m., what is the local time at Greenwich (0°)?
questions.explanation: The earth turns 15° in one hour, so 45° = 45 ÷ 15 = 3 hours. Greenwich is west of X, so its time is behind: 6.00 p.m. − 3 hours = 3.00 p.m.

whyNot.A: 9.00 p.m. adds the 3 hours; places to the west are behind in time.
whyNot.C: 3.00 a.m. gets the hours right but wrongly changes p.m. to a.m.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which of these is a primary economic activity?
questions.explanation: Primary activities take resources directly from nature. Fishing, farming, mining and lumbering are primary activities.

whyNot.C: Car assembly is manufacturing, a secondary activity.
whyNot.A: Teaching is a service, so it is a tertiary activity.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A settlement in which the houses are packed closely together around a central point, such as a market or a road junction, is described as
questions.explanation: In a nucleated settlement the buildings are grouped tightly around a centre (nucleus). Defence, a water point or a market often draws houses together.

whyNot.B: Dispersed settlements have houses scattered widely over the land.
whyNot.D: A linear settlement is stretched out along a road, river or coast.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A country has a birth rate of 40 per 1,000 and a death rate of 15 per 1,000 people per year. Ignoring migration, what is its rate of natural increase?
questions.explanation: Natural increase = birth rate − death rate = 40 − 15 = 25 per 1,000. As a percentage: 25 ÷ 1,000 × 100 = 2.5% per year.

whyNot.C: 25% treats 25 per 1,000 as 25 per 100.
whyNot.B: 5.5% adds the birth and death rates instead of subtracting.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which goods are best suited to transport by air?
questions.explanation: Air transport is fast but expensive per tonne, so it suits light, high-value or perishable goods that must arrive quickly, such as fresh flowers and medicines.

whyNot.A: Iron ore and coal are bulky and low in value; they go by rail or ship.
whyNot.B: Crude petroleum is moved by pipeline or tanker ship.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Bakeries are usually located close to the people who buy their bread mainly because
options: bakeries need very large amounts of water power
bread is too heavy to transport by road
flour can be found only in towns
bread is perishable and must reach buyers fresh
questions.explanation: Bread goes stale quickly and is bulkier than its raw materials, so bakeries are market-oriented: they are sited near consumers to deliver fresh bread cheaply every day.

whyNot.C: Flour is easily transported; it is not tied to towns.
whyNot.B: Bread is light; the issue is freshness, not weight.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Entrepôt trade is best described as
options: trade carried out only within a country
importing goods and re-exporting them to other countries
selling goods from door to door
exchange of goods for goods without money
questions.explanation: In entrepôt trade, a port imports goods, often stores, sorts or repacks them, and then re-exports them to other countries. Singapore is a famous entrepôt.

whyNot.A: Trade within a country is home (internal) trade.
whyNot.D: Exchange of goods for goods without money is barter.

questions.subject: geography
questions.context: State A has a population of 3,600,000 and an area of 12,000 km². State B has a population of 2,000,000 and an area of 5,000 km².
questions.stem: Which statement about the two states is correct?
options: Both states have the same population density
State A is more densely populated, by 100 persons per km²
State B is more densely populated, by 100 persons per km²
State B is more densely populated, by 1,600 persons per km²
questions.explanation: Density of A = 3,600,000 ÷ 12,000 = 300 persons per km². Density of B = 2,000,000 ÷ 5,000 = 400 persons per km². B is denser by 400 − 300 = 100 persons per km², even though A has more people.

whyNot.B: A has the larger population, but density depends on area too; A's density is lower.
whyNot.D: 1,600 comes from subtracting the populations in thousands instead of comparing densities.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: In the study of settlements, the 'site' of a town refers to
options: the position of the town in relation to surrounding places
the main function of the town
the actual piece of land on which the town is built
the number of people living in the town
questions.explanation: Site means the land the settlement stands on, with features such as a hilltop, a river crossing or a dry point. Situation means its position in relation to the surrounding area, routes and other settlements.

whyNot.A: Position in relation to surrounding places is the town's situation, not its site.
whyNot.B: Function describes what the town does, such as trade or administration.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Optimum population is best defined as the population at which
options: every family has exactly two children
the population is the largest the land can hold
available resources are used to give the highest standard of living per person
the birth rate equals the death rate
questions.explanation: Optimum population is the ideal balance between people and resources: with the technology available, the resources are fully used and output per person (standard of living) is highest. Fewer people means under-population; more means over-population.

whyNot.D: Equal birth and death rates give zero natural increase, which can occur at any population size.
whyNot.B: The largest population the land can hold would be beyond the optimum and lower living standards.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: What is a population census?
options: An official count of all the people in a country at a given time
A survey of the land area of a country
questions.explanation: A census is an official counting of all the people in a country at a particular time, usually with details such as age, sex and occupation. Governments use it for planning.

whyNot.A: Recording births is vital registration, which records events as they happen.
whyNot.D: A voters' register lists only adults who registered to vote, not the whole population.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: In which year did Abuja officially replace Lagos as the capital of Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Abuja was chosen as the new Federal Capital Territory in 1976, but the seat of government formally moved from Lagos to Abuja in December 1991.

whyNot.A: 1976 is when the decision to create Abuja was taken; the move happened later.
whyNot.C: 1960 is the year of Nigeria's independence, when Lagos was the capital.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: In which Nigerian state is the Nigerian part of Lake Chad found?
questions.explanation: Lake Chad lies in the far north-east of Nigeria, in Borno State, where Nigeria meets Niger, Chad and Cameroon.

whyNot.C: Sokoto is in the far north-west, far from Lake Chad.
whyNot.A: Plateau State is in the centre of the country.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The River Benue flows into Nigeria from which neighbouring country?
questions.explanation: The River Benue rises in the highlands of northern Cameroon and flows westwards into Nigeria, joining the Niger at Lokoja.

whyNot.D: The River Niger, not the Benue, enters Nigeria from Niger Republic.
whyNot.A: Benin Republic lies to the west; the Benue comes from the east.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Nigeria's first commercial discovery of crude oil was made in 1956 at
questions.explanation: Crude oil was first found in commercial quantities in 1956 at Oloibiri, in present-day Bayelsa State in the Niger Delta.

whyNot.B: Kaduna has an oil refinery, but no oil was discovered there.
whyNot.D: Ewekoro is known for limestone and cement, not oil.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Ewekoro in Ogun State is important for which mineral, used to make cement?
questions.explanation: Ewekoro has large limestone deposits, which are the main raw material for the cement factory there.

whyNot.A: Tin is mined on the Jos Plateau.
whyNot.D: Coal is mined around Enugu.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The famous 'groundnut pyramids' of the past, made of stacked bags of groundnuts for export, were a well-known sight in
questions.explanation: Groundnuts grow well in the light sandy soils and moderate rainfall of the northern savanna. Kano was the main collecting centre, where bags were stacked into pyramids before being railed to the coast.

whyNot.C: Port Harcourt is in the oil-rich south, too wet for groundnuts.
whyNot.B: Enugu is known for coal, not groundnuts.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which vegetation zone, with short grasses and scattered thorny trees such as acacia, covers most of Kano and Sokoto States?
questions.explanation: The Sudan savanna lies in the drier north, where the rainy season is short. It has short grasses and scattered drought-resistant trees such as acacia, baobab and shea.

whyNot.A: Rainforest is found in the wet south.
whyNot.C: Mangrove swamps grow on the salty coast and in the Niger Delta.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Rainfall in southern Nigeria shows two peaks in the year with a short, drier spell in between. What is this drier spell usually called?
questions.explanation: Southern Nigeria has a double maximum of rainfall, with peaks around June–July and September–October. Between them, around August, rainfall drops for a short time; this is known as the 'August break' or little dry season.

whyNot.C: The harmattan is the dry dusty wind of the main dry season, around November to February.
whyNot.D: The dry season is the long period of little rain, not a short break between two rainfall peaks.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Tea is grown on the Mambilla Plateau in Taraba State mainly because
options: the high altitude gives cool temperatures suited to tea
the plateau has the lowest rainfall in Nigeria
it is in the Sahel savanna
it lies on the coast with salty soils
questions.explanation: Temperature falls with height. The Mambilla Plateau is high (over 1,500 m), so it is cooler than the surrounding lowlands and has good rainfall, giving conditions like those of tea-growing highlands.

whyNot.B: Tea needs plenty of rain; the driest parts of Nigeria are in the far north.
whyNot.D: The Mambilla Plateau is far inland on the eastern border.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which country borders Nigeria to the west?
questions.explanation: Nigeria's neighbours are Benin to the west, Niger to the north, Chad to the north-east and Cameroon to the east. The Atlantic Ocean (Gulf of Guinea) lies to the south.

whyNot.A: Cameroon borders Nigeria to the east.
whyNot.B: Niger borders Nigeria to the north.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which is the largest hot desert in the world?
questions.explanation: The Sahara in northern Africa covers about 9 million km², making it the largest hot desert in the world.

whyNot.C: The Kalahari in southern Africa is much smaller than the Sahara.
whyNot.D: The Atacama in South America is very dry but small in area.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Into which sea does the River Nile flow?
questions.explanation: The Nile flows northwards through Sudan and Egypt and enters the Mediterranean Sea through a large delta near Alexandria and Cairo.

whyNot.A: The Red Sea lies east of Egypt; the Nile does not drain into it.
whyNot.B: The Atlantic receives rivers such as the Niger and the Congo.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Panama Canal links which two oceans?
questions.explanation: The Panama Canal cuts across the narrow Isthmus of Panama in Central America, joining the Atlantic Ocean (through the Caribbean Sea) to the Pacific Ocean.

whyNot.D: Ships between the Atlantic and Indian Oceans either sail round Africa or use the Suez Canal and Red Sea.
whyNot.A: The Pacific and Indian Oceans meet around Indonesia and Australia.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Witwatersrand (the Rand) in South Africa is world-famous for the mining of
questions.explanation: The Witwatersrand around Johannesburg has some of the richest gold deposits ever found. Gold mining there led to the growth of Johannesburg.

whyNot.B: Copper is associated with the Copperbelt of Zambia and the DR Congo.
whyNot.A: Bauxite is mined in countries such as Guinea and Ghana.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Aswan High Dam was built across which river?
questions.explanation: The Aswan High Dam is on the River Nile in southern Egypt. It controls floods, stores water for irrigation in Lake Nasser and produces hydroelectric power.

whyNot.C: The Zambezi is dammed at Kariba and Cahora Bassa.
whyNot.A: The Volta is dammed at Akosombo in Ghana.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Kalahari Desert lies mainly in which country?
questions.explanation: The Kalahari is a semi-desert in southern Africa covering most of Botswana and parts of Namibia and South Africa.

whyNot.A: Egypt is in the Sahara, in northern Africa.
whyNot.C: Morocco borders the Sahara in the north-west of Africa.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Equator passes through which of these countries?
questions.explanation: The Equator (0° latitude) crosses Africa through countries such as Gabon, the Congo, DR Congo, Uganda, Kenya and Somalia.

whyNot.D: Nigeria lies wholly north of the Equator, from about 4°N to 14°N.
whyNot.C: South Africa lies far south of the Equator, around the Tropic of Capricorn and beyond.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Japan became a leading industrial nation even though it has few minerals. Which of these best explains this?
options: It has very large deposits of iron ore and coal
It is a landlocked country with good road links
It has vast areas of flat land for farming
It imports raw materials and uses skilled labour and advanced technology
questions.explanation: Japan lacks most raw materials, so it imports them by sea to coastal factories. A highly skilled workforce, advanced technology and large capital investment allow it to turn these imports into high-value goods for export.

whyNot.A: Japan has only small deposits of coal and iron ore and must import most of its needs.
whyNot.C: Japan is mountainous; flat land is scarce.
whyNot.B: Japan is an island country surrounded by sea, not landlocked.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Namib Desert on the south-west coast of Africa is very dry mainly because of
options: its great height above sea level
questions.explanation: The cold Benguela Current cools the air above it. Cool air is stable and holds little moisture, so winds blowing onto the coast bring fog but almost no rain, creating a coastal desert.

whyNot.C: The Namib is a lowland coastal desert, not a high plateau.
whyNot.D: The Guinea Current is a warm current off West Africa, far from the Namib.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), set up by the Treaty of Lagos in 1975, has its headquarters in
questions.explanation: ECOWAS was founded in Lagos in 1975 to promote trade and economic co-operation in West Africa. Its Commission has its headquarters in Abuja, Nigeria.

whyNot.A: Addis Ababa is the headquarters of the African Union, not ECOWAS.
whyNot.D: Accra is the capital of Ghana, a member state, but not the ECOWAS headquarters.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Mrs Aondona grows yam, maize and vegetables on two hectares in Benue State mainly to feed her household, selling only a small surplus. This type of agriculture is called
questions.explanation: Subsistence agriculture is farming done mainly to meet the food needs of the farmer and family. It is usually small-scale, and only the little left over is sold.

whyNot.A: Commercial agriculture produces mainly for sale and profit, not for the household.
whyNot.B: Plantation agriculture is large-scale growing of one cash crop such as oil palm or rubber.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which of these industries depends directly on agriculture for its main raw material?
questions.explanation: A textile mill spins and weaves cotton lint, which is a farm product. This is one way agriculture supplies raw materials to industry (agro-allied industry).

whyNot.A: Cement is made from limestone, a mineral, not a farm product.
whyNot.D: Steel is made from iron ore, a mineral.
whyNot.C: A refinery processes crude oil, a mineral resource.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Under Nigeria's Land Use Act of 1978, land in each state is vested in
options: the traditional ruler of each town
questions.explanation: The Land Use Act (1978) vests all land within the territory of each state in the Governor, who holds it in trust for the people and grants rights of occupancy.

whyNot.D: Before the Act, traditional rulers held communal land in many places, but the Act transferred this control to the Governor.
whyNot.C: Family ownership is a customary (traditional) tenure system that the Act replaced as the basis of ownership.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: In many Nigerian communities a farmer's land is shared among all his children when he dies. The main problem this causes for agriculture is
options: a sharp rise in the price of farm produce
loss of soil nutrients by leaching
fragmentation of land into small, scattered plots
shortage of improved seeds and seedlings
questions.explanation: When land is divided among heirs generation after generation, each holding becomes smaller and plots become scattered. Small fragmented plots make mechanisation and large-scale farming difficult.

whyNot.B: Leaching is caused by heavy rainfall washing nutrients down the soil, not by inheritance.
whyNot.D: Seed shortage is a problem of supply of inputs, not of how land is inherited.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The Operation Feed the Nation (OFN) programme was launched in 1976 by the government of
questions.explanation: OFN was launched in 1976 by the military government headed by General Olusegun Obasanjo. It encouraged everyone, including students and civil servants, to grow food.

whyNot.A: Shehu Shagari's civilian government launched the Green Revolution programme in 1980.
whyNot.B: Gowon's government had been overthrown in July 1975, before OFN began.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: In shifting cultivation, the fertility of the soil is restored mainly by
options: applying large amounts of inorganic fertiliser
irrigating the land during the dry season
leaving the land to fallow under natural vegetation
planting the same crop on it every year
questions.explanation: In shifting cultivation the farmer abandons a piece of land after a few years of cropping. Natural vegetation grows back, adds organic matter and recycles nutrients, so the soil recovers.

whyNot.A: Shifting cultivators are typically small-scale farmers who rely on fallow, not on bought fertiliser.
whyNot.D: Planting the same crop every year (monocropping) uses up the same nutrients and lowers fertility.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: In the taungya system practised in some Nigerian forest reserves, farmers are allowed to
options: fell mature trees for sale as timber
grow food crops between young forest trees
burn the undergrowth to hunt animals
graze cattle freely inside the reserve
questions.explanation: Taungya is a form of agroforestry. Farmers plant food crops such as maize or yam between newly planted forest tree seedlings; they weed the plot while farming, which helps the young trees establish.

whyNot.D: Free grazing would damage the young trees, so it is not part of taungya.
whyNot.A: Taungya is about establishing new trees, not felling mature ones.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Cocoa in Nigeria is grown mainly in the rainforest belt of the South-West rather than in the Sudan savanna of the far North chiefly because cocoa needs
options: cool temperatures found only at high altitude
a long dry season to ripen its pods
sandy soils that drain very quickly
high, well-distributed rainfall and high humidity
questions.explanation: Cocoa is a shade-loving tree crop of the humid tropics. It needs heavy rainfall spread through most of the year, high humidity and deep, well-drained but moisture-retaining soils, which the rainforest belt provides.

whyNot.B: A long dry season stresses cocoa trees; that is a feature of the savanna, which is why cocoa does poorly there.
whyNot.C: Very sandy, fast-draining soils dry out and cannot hold the moisture cocoa needs.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A farmer practises bush fallowing in which each plot is cropped for 1 year and then left fallow for 4 years. What is the least total land she needs so that 2 hectares are under crops every year?
questions.explanation: One full cycle is 1 year cropped + 4 years fallow = 5 years, so only 1 out of every 5 plots is cropped in a given year. To crop 2 ha each year she needs 2 × 5 = 10 ha in total.

whyNot.A: 8 ha counts only the fallow land (2 × 4) and leaves out the 2 ha being cropped.
whyNot.C: 6 ha adds 2 + 4 instead of multiplying by the length of the cycle.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which Federal Government programme, launched in 2015 through the Central Bank of Nigeria, gives smallholder farmers inputs and loans that they repay with their harvested produce?
questions.explanation: The Anchor Borrowers' Programme was launched by the CBN in November 2015. It links smallholders to processors (anchors), gives them inputs on credit and lets them repay with produce such as rice or maize.

whyNot.C: OFN was a 1976 campaign to encourage food production, not a CBN loan scheme.
whyNot.A: The Green Revolution was launched in 1980.
whyNot.B: River Basin Development Authorities were set up in the 1970s to develop water resources and irrigation.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Yam is usually propagated by planting
questions.explanation: Yam is propagated vegetatively using seed yams (small whole tubers) or setts cut from larger tubers. The minisett technique uses small 25–30 g pieces to multiply planting material quickly.

whyNot.A: Stem cuttings are used for cassava, not yam.
whyNot.C: Suckers are used for plantain, banana and pineapple.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Groundnut and cowpea can improve the nitrogen content of the soil because their roots
options: carry nodules containing nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium bacteria
absorb nitrogen gas directly from the air in the soil
release nitrates that they make in their leaves
kill the bacteria that cause denitrification
questions.explanation: Legumes form root nodules in which Rhizobium bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into compounds the plant can use. When the roots and residues decay, the soil gains nitrogen.

whyNot.B: Plants cannot use nitrogen gas directly; only certain bacteria can fix it.
whyNot.D: Legumes do not kill denitrifying bacteria; they add nitrogen through fixation.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Cassava mosaic disease, which causes yellow mottled and distorted cassava leaves, is caused by
options: a fungus spread mainly by wind-borne spores
a nematode spread mainly in irrigation water
a bacterium spread mainly by aphids
a virus spread mainly by whiteflies
questions.explanation: Cassava mosaic disease is caused by cassava mosaic viruses. The whitefly Bemisia tabaci spreads it from plant to plant, and it is also carried in infected stem cuttings. Control includes resistant varieties and clean cuttings.

whyNot.A: Fungal diseases of cassava exist, but mosaic is viral.
whyNot.C: Cassava bacterial blight is the bacterial disease of cassava, and aphids are not its main vector.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Black pod disease, which turns cocoa pods dark brown to black and rots the beans, is caused by
questions.explanation: Black pod is a fungal disease caused by Phytophthora species. It spreads in wet, humid weather. It is controlled by removing infected pods, improving air flow by pruning, and spraying copper-based fungicides.

whyNot.D: Swollen shoot is a different cocoa disease, caused by a virus spread by mealybugs.
whyNot.A: Capsids (mirids) are insect pests that damage cocoa shoots and pods; they are not the cause of black pod.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Maize is planted at a spacing of 75 cm between rows and 25 cm within rows, with one plant per stand. What is the plant population per hectare? (1 ha = 10,000 m²)
questions.explanation: Area per plant = 0.75 m × 0.25 m = 0.1875 m². Plant population = 10,000 m² ÷ 0.1875 m² = 53,333 plants per hectare.

whyNot.D: 13,333 comes from 10,000 ÷ 0.75, which ignores the within-row spacing.
whyNot.C: 133,333 comes from a decimal slip, dividing by 0.075 instead of 0.1875.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A farmer wants to apply 92 kg of nitrogen per hectare to 2.5 ha of maize using urea, which contains 46% nitrogen. How many 50 kg bags of urea does she need?
questions.explanation: Urea needed per hectare = 92 ÷ 0.46 = 200 kg. For 2.5 ha: 200 × 2.5 = 500 kg. Number of 50 kg bags = 500 ÷ 50 = 10 bags.

whyNot.B: 4 bags is the urea for only 1 ha (200 kg ÷ 50).
whyNot.A: 5 bags comes from treating the 230 kg of nitrogen needed as if it were urea (230 ÷ 50 ≈ 5).

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The older, lower leaves of a maize crop turn pale yellow, starting from the tip and moving along the midrib, while the plants stay short. The nutrient most likely lacking is
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is mobile in the plant, so when it is short the plant moves it from older leaves to young ones. The older leaves turn yellow first (chlorosis), typically in a V-shape from the tip along the midrib in maize, and growth is stunted.

whyNot.A: Calcium is immobile, so its deficiency shows first in young leaves and growing points.
whyNot.D: Iron is also immobile; its deficiency causes yellowing between the veins of young leaves.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: In oil palm breeding, the high-yielding thin-shelled Tenera palm is obtained by crossing
questions.explanation: Dura palms have thick shells, and Pisifera palms are shell-less but usually female-sterile. Crossing Dura (as the female) with Pisifera (as the pollen parent) gives Tenera, which has a thin shell and a thick, oil-rich mesocarp. NIFOR distributes such hybrid seed.

whyNot.D: Dura × Dura gives Dura, with a thick shell.
whyNot.C: Pisifera palms are usually female-sterile, so they cannot bear the fruit for such a cross.
whyNot.A: Tenera × Pisifera gives a mixture of Tenera and Pisifera offspring, not pure Tenera.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which type of soil has the highest water-holding capacity?
questions.explanation: Clay has the finest particles and the smallest pore spaces, giving a very large total surface area that holds water tightly. It therefore retains the most water, though it drains poorly.

whyNot.D: Sandy soil has large particles and large pores, so water drains through it quickly.
whyNot.C: Sandy loam holds more water than sand but much less than clay.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: In the nitrogen cycle, the conversion of ammonium compounds in the soil to nitrites is carried out by
questions.explanation: Nitrification happens in two steps: Nitrosomonas oxidises ammonium to nitrite, and then Nitrobacter oxidises nitrite to nitrate, which plants absorb.

whyNot.C: Nitrobacter carries out the second step, nitrite to nitrate.
whyNot.A: Rhizobium fixes atmospheric nitrogen in legume root nodules.
whyNot.B: Pseudomonas is associated with denitrification, which returns nitrogen gas to the air.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: An adult male goat is called a
questions.explanation: The adult male goat is a buck (also called a billy), the female is a doe, and the young is a kid.

whyNot.D: A ram is an adult male sheep.
whyNot.B: A boar is an adult male pig.
whyNot.A: A bull is an adult male of cattle.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: How many days does it take a fertile chicken egg to hatch under normal incubation?
questions.explanation: The incubation period of the domestic fowl is 21 days, whether the eggs are under a broody hen or in an incubator.

whyNot.A: About 28 days is the incubation period for duck and turkey eggs.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: In a cow, which compartment of the stomach is called the true stomach because it secretes digestive juices like the human stomach?
questions.explanation: The ruminant stomach has four parts: rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum. Only the abomasum secretes gastric juice with acid and enzymes, so it is called the true stomach.

whyNot.C: The rumen is the largest part, where microbes ferment fibre, but it secretes no digestive enzymes.
whyNot.D: The omasum absorbs water from the food; it is not glandular like the abomasum.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Newcastle disease, which causes twisted necks, gasping and sudden death in chickens, is best prevented by
options: debeaking the birds at an early age
adding antibiotics to the drinking water
questions.explanation: Newcastle disease is caused by a virus. Antibiotics do not kill viruses, and there is no cure, so prevention by vaccinating the flock on schedule, together with good hygiene, is the main control.

whyNot.D: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not on the Newcastle disease virus.
whyNot.B: Debeaking prevents cannibalism and feather pecking, not viral disease.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A farmer in a tsetse-infested area of southern Nigeria wants a cattle breed that tolerates trypanosomiasis. Which breed should he choose?
questions.explanation: N'Dama (like the Muturu) is a humpless West African breed that is trypanotolerant: it can survive and produce in areas where tsetse flies spread trypanosomiasis, which kills many zebu cattle.

whyNot.D: White Fulani is a zebu breed of the drier North and is highly susceptible to trypanosomiasis.
whyNot.C: Red Bororo is also a susceptible zebu breed kept by pastoralists in the savanna.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Young chickens on deep litter become dull, with ruffled feathers and blood-stained droppings. The disease is most likely coccidiosis, which is caused by
questions.explanation: Coccidiosis is caused by protozoan parasites of the genus Eimeria, which damage the lining of the intestine and cause bloody droppings. It spreads on damp, dirty litter and is controlled with coccidiostats and dry litter.

whyNot.B: Viral poultry diseases include Newcastle disease and Gumboro, not coccidiosis.
whyNot.D: Salmonella causes fowl typhoid and pullorum, not coccidiosis.
whyNot.C: Aspergillus causes aspergillosis (brooder pneumonia), a breathing disease.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which of the following is a catfish commonly raised in Nigerian fish ponds?
questions.explanation: Clarias gariepinus, the African catfish, is the most widely farmed fish in Nigeria. It grows fast, tolerates low oxygen because it can breathe air, and fetches a good price.

whyNot.B: Oreochromis niloticus is the Nile tilapia, not a catfish.
whyNot.A: Lates niloticus is the Nile perch.
whyNot.D: Cyprinus carpio is the common carp.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A batch of broilers ate 2,100 kg of feed and gained a total of 1,000 kg of live weight. What is their feed conversion ratio?
questions.explanation: Feed conversion ratio = feed eaten ÷ weight gained = 2,100 ÷ 1,000 = 2.1. The birds needed 2.1 kg of feed for every 1 kg of gain; the lower the FCR, the more efficient the birds.

whyNot.A: 0.48 is weight gain ÷ feed (1,000 ÷ 2,100), the inverse of the FCR.
whyNot.C: 4.2 doubles the correct value.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.context: A farmer has maize containing 9% crude protein (CP) and soybean meal containing 44% CP. She uses the Pearson square to mix them into a feed containing 20% CP.
questions.stem: What percentage of the mixture should be soybean meal?
questions.explanation: Pearson square: parts of soybean meal = 20 − 9 = 11; parts of maize = 44 − 20 = 24; total = 35 parts. Soybean meal = 11 ÷ 35 × 100 = 31.4% (and maize = 68.6%).

whyNot.D: 68.6% is the share of maize, not soybean meal.
whyNot.A: 20% is the target protein level of the feed, not the share of soybean meal.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Goats grazing on marshy land near a river become thin and anaemic, with swelling under the jaw. A post-mortem shows liver flukes. The intermediate host of this parasite is
questions.explanation: The liver fluke (Fasciola) passes part of its life cycle in water snails (Lymnaea). Larvae leave the snail and encyst on wet grass, which grazing animals eat. Draining marshy pastures and controlling snails breaks the cycle.

whyNot.A: The tsetse fly transmits trypanosomes, not liver flukes.
whyNot.B: Ticks transmit diseases such as babesiosis (red water), not flukes.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The reward paid for the use of land as a factor of production is
questions.explanation: Each factor of production earns a reward: land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest and the entrepreneur earns profit.

whyNot.B: Wages are the reward for labour.
whyNot.D: Interest is the reward for capital.
whyNot.C: Profit is the reward for the entrepreneur.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: In a farmers' cooperative society, the principle of democratic control means that
options: the oldest members take all the decisions
government officials appoint the management committee
each member has one vote, whatever the size of his shares
members vote according to the number of shares they hold
questions.explanation: Cooperatives are controlled democratically: every member has one vote regardless of how much capital he has contributed. This is one of the principles that distinguishes a cooperative from a company.

whyNot.D: Voting by number of shares is how a joint-stock company works, not a cooperative.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A farmer grew maize on 1.5 ha and harvested 4 tonnes per hectare, which she sold at ₦350,000 per tonne. Her variable costs were ₦1,250,000 and her fixed costs were ₦200,000. What was her gross margin?
questions.explanation: Total revenue = 1.5 × 4 × ₦350,000 = ₦2,100,000. Gross margin = total revenue − total variable costs = ₦2,100,000 − ₦1,250,000 = ₦850,000. Fixed costs are not deducted in a gross margin.

whyNot.A: ₦650,000 also deducts the fixed costs; that is net profit, not gross margin.
whyNot.B: ₦2,100,000 is the total revenue before any costs are taken away.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which of these is a fixed cost to a poultry farmer?
options: Cost of feed for the birds
Cost of vaccines for each batch
Annual rent on the poultry house
questions.explanation: Fixed costs stay the same whatever the level of output in the short run. The rent on the house is paid whether the farmer keeps 500 birds or 1,000. Feed, vaccines and chicks rise with the number of birds, so they are variable costs.

whyNot.A: Feed cost rises as more birds are kept, so it is variable.
whyNot.C: The number of chicks bought changes with the size of the batch, so it is a variable cost.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: An extension agent plants a plot of a new maize variety with the recommended fertiliser beside a farmer's usual variety, so that farmers can compare the yields at harvest. This method is called
questions.explanation: A result demonstration shows farmers the outcome (result) of a new practice, often side by side with the old one, so they can see the difference in yield for themselves.

whyNot.C: A method demonstration shows how to carry out a practice step by step, such as how to apply fertiliser.
whyNot.D: A farm and home visit is an individual contact between the agent and one farmer.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A farm tractor bought for ₦18,000,000 is expected to last 10 years and then be sold as scrap for ₦3,000,000. Using the straight-line method, what is its annual depreciation?
questions.explanation: Straight-line depreciation = (cost − scrap value) ÷ useful life = (₦18,000,000 − ₦3,000,000) ÷ 10 = ₦15,000,000 ÷ 10 = ₦1,500,000 per year.

whyNot.D: ₦1,800,000 ignores the scrap value (18,000,000 ÷ 10).
whyNot.B: ₦2,100,000 adds the scrap value instead of subtracting it.
whyNot.C: ₦300,000 is the scrap value divided by 10.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Sorting harvested oranges into groups by size and quality before sale, so that buyers pay according to quality, is the marketing function of
questions.explanation: Grading (and standardisation) sorts produce into classes of similar size and quality. Good grades fetch higher prices and buyers can trust what they pay for.

whyNot.A: Assembling is collecting produce from many farmers into one place.
whyNot.B: Processing changes the form of the produce, for example oranges into juice.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A list of all the assets on a farm, such as land, buildings, tools and livestock, with their values at a given date, is called
questions.explanation: An inventory record lists everything the farm owns, with quantities and values, at a particular date (usually the start or end of the year). It helps the farmer know the worth of the business.

whyNot.A: A farm diary records the day-to-day activities on the farm.
whyNot.C: A sales record shows what was sold, to whom and at what price.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.context:
Output of yam from a fixed plot as more workers are employed:
Number of workers: 1, 2, 3, 4
Total output (bags): 10, 24, 34, 40
questions.stem: What is the marginal product of the third worker?
questions.explanation: Marginal product is the extra output from one more worker. With 2 workers output is 24 bags; with 3 it is 34 bags. MP of the third worker = 34 − 24 = 10 bags. MP falls from 14 (second worker) to 10, showing diminishing returns.

whyNot.C: 34 bags is the total product with three workers, not the extra output.
whyNot.D: 11.3 bags is the average product (34 ÷ 3).
whyNot.A: 6 bags is the marginal product of the fourth worker (40 − 34).

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which of these is an informal source of credit to farmers in Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Esusu, ajo or adashe groups are informal: members contribute regularly and each takes the pooled money in turn, without bank regulation or collateral. Banks are formal, regulated sources of credit.

whyNot.A: Commercial banks are formal, licensed lenders.
whyNot.C: The Bank of Agriculture is a government-owned formal lender.
whyNot.B: Microfinance banks are licensed and regulated by the CBN, so they are formal.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which tool is best for pruning the branches of orange trees?
questions.explanation: Secateurs are strong scissor-like shears designed to cut small branches and twigs cleanly, which is what pruning requires.

whyNot.B: A mattock is used for digging hard ground and uprooting stumps.
whyNot.A: A rake gathers trash and levels soil.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: After a field has been ploughed, which implement is used to break the large clods into a fine tilth?
questions.explanation: Harrowing is secondary tillage: the harrow breaks up the clods left by the plough, levels the soil and prepares a fine seedbed.

whyNot.B: A ridger forms ridges after the soil has been prepared.
whyNot.D: A planter places seeds in the soil.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: In the diesel engine of a farm tractor, the fuel is ignited by
options: a flame from the exhaust pipe
the heat of air that has been highly compressed
the battery heating the fuel tank
a spark from the spark plug
questions.explanation: A diesel engine is a compression-ignition engine. Air is compressed so much that it becomes very hot; when diesel is injected into it, the fuel ignites without a spark plug.

whyNot.D: Spark plugs are used in petrol (spark-ignition) engines, not diesel engines.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The part of a tractor that transfers power from the engine to drive implements such as a rotavator or slasher is the
questions.explanation: The power take-off is a rotating splined shaft at the rear of the tractor. Implements with moving parts connect to it and are driven by the engine's power.

whyNot.B: The drawbar is for pulling (towing) trailed implements, not for turning their moving parts.
whyNot.D: The radiator cools the engine.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which machine cuts a crop such as rice, threshes it and cleans the grain in one operation?
questions.explanation: A combine harvester combines reaping, threshing and winnowing (cleaning) in a single machine, so the grain comes out ready for drying and storage.

whyNot.B: A disc plough is for primary tillage.
