questions.explanation: Angel Jibril (Gabriel) is the angel of revelation. He brought the Qur'an to the Prophet over about 23 years, starting in the Cave of Hira.

whyNot.B: Mika'il is the angel associated with rain and provision.
whyNot.D: Israfil is the angel who will blow the trumpet on the Last Day.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Prophet Muhammad (SAW) received the first revelation while meditating in
questions.explanation: The Prophet used to retreat to the Cave of Hira on Jabal an-Nur near Makkah. There, in Ramadan 610 CE, Jibril came to him with the first verses of Surah al-'Alaq.

whyNot.D: The Cave of Thawr is where he hid with Abu Bakr during the Hijrah.
whyNot.B: Arafat is the plain where pilgrims stand during Hajj.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Over about how many years was the Qur'an revealed to Prophet Muhammad (SAW)?
questions.explanation: Revelation began when the Prophet was 40 (610 CE) and continued until shortly before his death at 63 (632 CE), about 23 years: roughly 13 in Makkah and 10 in Madinah.

whyNot.D: 13 years is roughly the Makkan period only.
whyNot.A: 10 years is roughly the Madinan period only.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Why did Caliph Uthman ibn Affan have official copies of the Qur'an made and sent to the main cities of the Muslim world?
options: To add verses that were revealed after the Prophet's death
Because the Qur'an had never been written down before
To end disputes among Muslims over differences in recitation
To translate the Qur'an into Persian and Greek
questions.explanation: As Islam spread, people in different regions recited with differences, and disputes arose. Uthman had copies made from the compilation kept by Hafsah, in the dialect of Quraysh, sent them to the provinces, and ordered other copies destroyed, to keep the Muslims united on one text.

whyNot.B: The Qur'an was written down during the Prophet's lifetime and compiled into one copy under Abu Bakr.
whyNot.A: Revelation ended with the Prophet's death; nothing was added afterwards.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Surah al-Fil (Surah 105) tells the story of
options: Prophet Sulayman and his army of jinn and birds
the People of the Cave who slept for many years
Abrahah's army with elephants, destroyed when it came to attack the Ka'bah
Prophet Nuh and the great flood
questions.explanation: Surah al-Fil reminds the Quraysh how Allah sent flocks of birds (ababil) pelting stones of baked clay on the army of Abrahah, which had come with an elephant to destroy the Ka'bah in the year the Prophet was born.

whyNot.A: Sulayman's army is described in Surah an-Naml, not al-Fil.
whyNot.B: The People of the Cave appear in Surah al-Kahf.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which surah contains the verses 'He neither begets nor is begotten, and there is none comparable to Him'?
questions.explanation: Surah al-Ikhlas (Surah 112) is a short, four-verse statement of tawhid: Allah is One, the Eternal Refuge; He neither begets nor is begotten, and nothing is comparable to Him.

whyNot.D: Al-Falaq teaches seeking refuge in Allah from evils such as envy and darkness.
whyNot.C: Al-Kafirun separates the worship of believers from that of idol-worshippers.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Surah Quraysh (Surah 106) reminds the Quraysh of Allah's favour in making which activity safe for them?
options: Their wars against the tribe of Banu Sa'd
Their winter and summer trade journeys
Their fishing trips on the Red Sea
questions.explanation: Surah Quraysh mentions the Quraysh's caravan journeys in winter and summer, and tells them to worship the Lord of the Ka'bah, who fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear.

whyNot.C: The Quraysh did not make a yearly pilgrimage to Jerusalem; the surah speaks of trade journeys.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: According to Surah at-Takathur (Surah 102), what distracts people until they 'visit the graves'?
options: Fear of their enemies in battle
Rivalry in piling up worldly gains
Too much travel in search of knowledge
questions.explanation: Surah at-Takathur warns that competing for more wealth, children and status distracts people until death comes. It adds that on that Day they will be asked about the blessings they enjoyed.

whyNot.B: Prayer and fasting are acts of worship the Qur'an praises; the surah criticises worldly rivalry.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Surah al-Kafirun was revealed in response to which situation?
options: The hypocrites in Madinah refused to march out to the Battle of Uhud
The Muslims lost hope after the Prophet's death
Quraysh leaders proposed that the Prophet worship their gods for a time and they would worship Allah for a time
The Jews of Madinah asked the Prophet about the soul
questions.explanation: Leaders of the Quraysh offered a compromise: alternate worship of their idols and of Allah. Surah al-Kafirun rejected it firmly: 'I do not worship what you worship... For you is your religion, and for me is my religion.'

whyNot.D: The question about the soul (ruh) is answered in Surah al-Isra' (17:85).
whyNot.B: The Prophet's death came long after this Makkan surah was revealed.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: In Surah al-Humazah, what is 'al-Hutamah'?
options: The crushing Fire prepared for slanderers who hoard wealth
A spring of water in Paradise
The record book of a person's deeds
The bridge over Hell on the Day of Judgement
questions.explanation: Surah al-Humazah (Surah 104) warns the backbiter and slanderer who collects wealth and counts it, thinking it will make him live forever. He will be thrown into al-Hutamah, the Fire of Allah that rises over the hearts.

whyNot.B: Springs in Paradise have other names, such as Salsabil.
whyNot.D: The bridge over Hell is called as-Sirat.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: In hadith studies, the 'matn' of a hadith is
options: the text or content of the hadith
the compiler who recorded it in a book
the place where the hadith was spoken
the chain of people who narrated it
questions.explanation: A hadith has two parts: the isnad (chain of narrators) and the matn (the actual words or content). Scholars examine both before accepting a hadith.

whyNot.D: The chain of narrators is the isnad.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: The two hadith collections regarded by Sunni scholars as the most authentic (the Sahihayn) were compiled by
questions.explanation: The Sahih of al-Bukhari and the Sahih of Muslim are together called the Sahihayn ('the two Sahihs'). Their compilers accepted only hadith meeting very strict conditions.

whyNot.C: Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi compiled Sunan collections, which include some hasan and weak hadith.
whyNot.D: Malik compiled al-Muwatta' and Ahmad compiled the Musnad; neither is one of the two Sahihs.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which Companion of the Prophet (SAW) narrated the largest number of hadith?
questions.explanation: Abu Hurayrah stayed close to the Prophet for about three years after accepting Islam and devoted himself to learning, so he narrated more hadith than any other Companion (over 5,000).

whyNot.A: Abu Bakr was the closest companion, but he narrated relatively few hadith.
whyNot.C: Zayd ibn Thabit is known as a scribe of revelation and compiler of the Qur'an.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: In the hadith of Jibril, how did the Prophet (SAW) define ihsan?
options: To testify that there is no god but Allah and Muhammad is His messenger
To worship Allah as though you see Him, for though you do not see Him, He sees you
To believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers and the Last Day
To give charity secretly so that the left hand does not know what the right gives
questions.explanation: In the hadith of Jibril (narrated by Umar), Jibril asked about Islam, iman and ihsan. The Prophet described ihsan as worshipping Allah as if you see Him, knowing that He sees you. It is the highest level of the religion.

whyNot.A: The shahadah was given in the answer about Islam, not ihsan.
whyNot.C: Belief in Allah, angels, books, messengers and the Last Day was the answer about iman.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: A report falsely attributed to the Prophet (SAW), which he never said, is classified as
questions.explanation: Mawdu' means fabricated. Scholars of hadith identified fabricated reports by examining narrators known to lie and texts that contradict the Qur'an or established Sunnah.

whyNot.D: A mutawatir hadith is reported by so many narrators at each stage that it could not have been invented.
whyNot.A: A hasan hadith is a good, acceptable hadith.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: According to the hadith on changing evil, 'whoever among you sees an evil should change it with his hand; if he cannot, then with his tongue; if he cannot, then with his heart'. What does the Prophet (SAW) say about changing it with the heart?
options: It is only for scholars and rulers
It is the best form of jihad
It is the weakest level of faith
questions.explanation: This hadith, narrated by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri in Sahih Muslim, ends: 'and that is the weakest of faith.' Hating evil in the heart is the minimum required when a person cannot act or speak against it.

whyNot.B: The hadith presents the heart as the last resort, not the best form of striving.
whyNot.A: The hadith addresses 'whoever among you', meaning every believer.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: A man asked the Prophet (SAW) for advice, and he replied repeatedly with the same words. This short hadith in an-Nawawi's Forty Hadith is
options: 'Love of one's homeland is part of faith.'
questions.explanation: Abu Hurayrah reported (al-Bukhari) that a man asked for advice and the Prophet said, 'Do not become angry,' repeating it several times. Controlling anger protects a person from many sins.

whyNot.B: 'Seek knowledge even in China' is widely quoted, but scholars of hadith judge it weak or fabricated.
whyNot.D: 'Love of one's homeland is part of faith' is a popular saying that scholars do not accept as an authentic hadith.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: 'The halal is clear and the haram is clear, and between them are doubtful matters.' What does this hadith teach a Muslim to do?
options: Treat every doubtful matter as fully lawful
Ask a ruler to decide every doubtful matter
Stay away from doubtful matters to protect one's religion and honour
Avoid all lawful things that are pleasant
questions.explanation: In this hadith (narrated by an-Nu'man ibn Bashir) the Prophet (SAW) explained that whoever avoids doubtful matters protects his religion and honour, while whoever falls into them may fall into the haram, like a shepherd grazing near a protected pasture.

whyNot.A: The hadith warns against doubtful matters; it does not declare them lawful.
whyNot.D: Lawful things are permitted; the hadith concerns only doubtful ones.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Why did the Prophet (SAW), in the early period, discourage the general writing down of his sayings?
options: Because writing materials were forbidden in Islam
So that his words would not be mixed up with the Qur'an
So that his sayings would be forgotten after his death
Because the Companions could not read or write at all
questions.explanation: While the Qur'an was still being revealed, the Prophet said, 'Do not write anything from me except the Qur'an' (Sahih Muslim), so that his words would not be confused with revelation. Later, some Companions such as Abdullah ibn Amr were allowed to write hadith.

whyNot.D: Several Companions could write; some served as scribes of revelation.
whyNot.C: The Prophet told his Companions to convey his teachings, so he did not want them forgotten.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: How are the hadith arranged in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal?
options: In the order in which the hadith were spoken
According to their grade, from sahih to da'if
According to the Companions who narrated them
According to topics of law, from purification to inheritance
questions.explanation: A musnad groups hadith under the name of the Companion who narrated them, for example all of Abu Bakr's narrations together. Collections such as the Sunan are arranged instead by topics of law.

whyNot.D: Arrangement by legal topics is the method of Sunan and Sahih collections.
whyNot.B: The Musnad does not sort its hadith by grade.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: To which prophet was the Zabur (Psalms) revealed?
questions.explanation: The Qur'an names the revealed books: the Tawrah to Musa, the Zabur to Dawud, the Injil to Isa, and the Qur'an to Muhammad (SAW). Scrolls (suhuf) were also given to Ibrahim.

whyNot.B: Prophet Musa received the Tawrah.
whyNot.D: Prophet Isa received the Injil.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: What is the first of the five pillars of Islam?
questions.explanation: The hadith 'Islam is built on five' lists the shahadah first: testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. Then come salat, zakat, sawm and Hajj.

whyNot.A: Salat is the second pillar.
whyNot.C: Hajj is the fifth pillar, required once in a lifetime for those who are able.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: During Hajj, pilgrims walk or run seven times between which two hills?
questions.explanation: The sa'y is walking seven times between Safa and Marwah. It recalls Hajar, wife of Prophet Ibrahim, searching for water for her baby Isma'il before the well of Zamzam appeared.

whyNot.B: Arafat and Muzdalifah are places where pilgrims stay, not two hills of the sa'y.
whyNot.D: Uhud and Thawr are mountains connected with the Prophet's life, not Hajj rites.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which angel will blow the trumpet to announce the end of the world and the Resurrection?
questions.explanation: In Islamic belief, Angel Israfil is charged with blowing the trumpet (as-sur). At the first blast everything will perish, and at the second the dead will be raised.

whyNot.D: Jibril brings revelation to the prophets.
whyNot.A: Munkar, with Nakir, questions the dead in the grave.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: When should zakat al-fitr be paid?
options: On the Day of Arafah during Hajj
Before the Eid al-Fitr prayer at the end of Ramadan
At the beginning of the Islamic new year
questions.explanation: Zakat al-fitr is a small charity, about one sa' of staple food per person, paid at the end of Ramadan before the Eid al-Fitr prayer. It purifies the fasting person and lets the poor also celebrate Eid.

whyNot.A: The Day of Arafah (9 Dhul-Hijjah) is during Hajj, months after Ramadan.
whyNot.D: The Eid al-Adha sacrifice is a separate act of worship.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which of the following makes a ritual bath (ghusl) obligatory before a Muslim can pray?
questions.explanation: Ghusl, washing the whole body, is required after janabah (sexual discharge or intercourse), and after menstruation or post-natal bleeding ends. Minor impurities only need wudu.

whyNot.A: Passing wind only breaks wudu, which is renewed by performing wudu again.
whyNot.D: Passing urine also needs only wudu, not ghusl.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: In Islamic law, an act that is discouraged, which earns reward if avoided but no punishment if done, is described as
questions.explanation: Islamic law grades acts into five categories: wajib (obligatory), mandub (recommended), mubah (permitted), makruh (disliked) and haram (forbidden). Makruh acts are better avoided but are not sinful.

whyNot.B: Haram acts are forbidden and are punished if done.
whyNot.D: Mubah acts are neutral: no reward or punishment either way.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: The belief that Allah alone is the Creator, Owner and Sustainer of the universe is called
questions.explanation: Rububiyyah comes from Rabb (Lord). Tawhid ar-rububiyyah is affirming that Allah alone creates, owns and controls all things. Uluhiyyah is directing all worship to Him alone, and al-asma' wa as-sifat is affirming His names and attributes.

whyNot.C: Tawhid al-uluhiyyah is about worship being for Allah alone.
whyNot.A: Tawhid al-asma' wa as-sifat is about Allah's names and attributes.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: A man deliberately has sexual relations with his wife during the daytime in Ramadan. Apart from making up the day, which of the following is one of the recognised forms of expiation (kaffarah) for this act?
questions.explanation: According to the hadith of the man who did this (al-Bukhari and Muslim), the expiation is to free a slave; if that is not possible, to fast two consecutive months; if that is not possible, to feed sixty poor people. (In the Maliki school a person may choose among these.)

whyNot.A: Fasting three days is part of the expiation for a broken oath (Qur'an 5:89).
whyNot.D: Feeding ten poor people is also an expiation for a broken oath, not for this act in Ramadan.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Malam Sani owns 40 goats that have grazed freely for a full lunar year. What is the zakat due on them?
questions.explanation: The nisab for sheep and goats is 40. From 40 up to 120 animals the zakat is one sheep or goat; two are due from 121 to 200. So 40 freely grazing goats owned for a lunar year owe one goat.

whyNot.D: Four goats would be one-tenth of the flock; zakat on livestock uses fixed scales, not a percentage.
whyNot.C: Forty is exactly the nisab, so zakat is already due.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Who was the first woman to accept Islam?
questions.explanation: When the Prophet came home shaken after the first revelation, his wife Khadijah comforted him and believed in his message, becoming the first woman (and, by most accounts, the first person) to accept Islam.

whyNot.C: Aishah was a child at the time and married the Prophet years later.
whyNot.D: Sumayyah was an early Muslim and the first martyr of Islam, but not the first woman to believe.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: How old was Prophet Muhammad (SAW) when he received the first revelation?
questions.explanation: The Prophet was about 40 years old when Jibril first came to him in the Cave of Hira in 610 CE.

whyNot.A: 25 was his age when he married Khadijah.
whyNot.C: 53 was his age at the Hijrah to Madinah.
whyNot.B: 63 was his age when he died.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: At what age did Prophet Muhammad (SAW) pass away in Madinah?
questions.explanation: The Prophet died in Madinah in 11 AH (632 CE) at the age of 63 (in lunar years). He was buried in the room of his wife Aishah, next to his mosque.

whyNot.D: 60 is too low; he was 53 at the Hijrah and lived about ten more years in Madinah.
whyNot.A: 70 is too high; he died ten years after the Hijrah, at 63.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: The year in which both Khadijah and Abu Talib died is known as
questions.explanation: Around 619 CE, the Prophet lost his wife Khadijah, his greatest supporter at home, and his uncle Abu Talib, his protector among the Quraysh. Because of this double grief, the year is called the Year of Sorrow ('Am al-Huzn).

whyNot.A: The Year of the Elephant is the year of the Prophet's birth.
whyNot.C: The Year of Delegations (9 AH) is when many Arab tribes sent delegations to accept Islam.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: When some Muslims migrated to Abyssinia to escape persecution in Makkah, which ruler protected them?
questions.explanation: Around 615 CE the Prophet advised some followers to go to Abyssinia, whose Christian king, the Negus, was known for justice. When the Quraysh asked for their return, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib recited from Surah Maryam, and the Negus refused to hand them over.

whyNot.C: Heraclius later received a letter from the Prophet inviting him to Islam, but he did not shelter the emigrants.
whyNot.D: Muqawqis also received a letter from the Prophet years later, from Madinah.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: What was the first mosque built by Prophet Muhammad (SAW) on his way to Madinah during the Hijrah?
questions.explanation: On arriving at Quba, on the outskirts of Madinah, the Prophet stayed some days and laid the foundation of Masjid Quba, the first mosque built in Islam. He then moved into Madinah and built Masjid an-Nabawi.

whyNot.A: Masjid an-Nabawi was built after he entered Madinah itself.
whyNot.C: Masjid al-Haram surrounds the Ka'bah in Makkah, which was built long before.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which important act of worship was made obligatory during the Night Journey and Ascension (al-Isra' wa al-Mi'raj)?
questions.explanation: During the Mi'raj, the Prophet (SAW) ascended through the heavens, and Allah made the five daily prayers obligatory on the Muslims. Fasting and zakat were made obligatory later, in Madinah.

whyNot.D: Fasting in Ramadan was made obligatory in Madinah in 2 AH (Qur'an 2:183).
whyNot.C: Hajj became obligatory later in the Madinan period.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: In which year did the Muslims conquer Makkah, after which the Prophet (SAW) declared a general pardon for its people?
questions.explanation: After the Quraysh's allies broke the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, the Prophet marched on Makkah with about 10,000 men in 8 AH (630 CE). The city was taken almost without fighting, the idols around the Ka'bah were destroyed, and its people were pardoned.

whyNot.A: 6 AH is the year of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah.
whyNot.C: 10 AH is the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Why was the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan, given the title Dhun-Nurayn ('Possessor of the Two Lights')?
options: He married two daughters of the Prophet, one after the other
He led the prayer in both Makkah and Madinah
He compiled the Qur'an twice during his caliphate
He built two great mosques in Madinah
questions.explanation: Uthman married the Prophet's daughter Ruqayyah. After her death, he married another daughter, Umm Kulthum. Because he married two of the Prophet's daughters, he was called Dhun-Nurayn.

whyNot.C: Uthman standardised the copies of the Qur'an once; the title has nothing to do with this.
whyNot.D: The title refers to his marriages, not to building mosques.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: What was the main purpose of the Constitution of Madinah (Sahifat al-Madinah)?
options: To give the terms of peace between the Muslims and the Quraysh of Makkah
To fix the number of rak'ahs in each daily prayer
To divide the booty taken at the Battle of Badr
To set out the rights and duties of Muslims, Jews and other groups living together in Madinah
questions.explanation: Soon after the Hijrah, the Prophet drew up a written agreement among the Muhajirun, the Ansar, the Jewish tribes and others in Madinah. It made them one community for defence, protected each group's religion and rights, and made the Prophet the final judge in disputes.

whyNot.B: The details of the prayer come from the Prophet's Sunnah, not from this document.
whyNot.A: Peace terms with the Quraysh came later, in the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah (6 AH).

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Sankore, a famous centre of Islamic learning in West Africa, was located in which city?
questions.explanation: Timbuktu, on the Niger bend, became a great city of scholarship under the Mali and Songhai empires. The Sankore mosque and its scholars attracted students from across West and North Africa.

whyNot.A: Kano was an important Hausa centre of trade and learning, but Sankore was in Timbuktu.
whyNot.C: Kukawa was a 19th-century capital of Bornu.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: As leader of the jihad and the Sokoto Caliphate, Usman dan Fodio held the title
questions.explanation: In 1804 Usman dan Fodio's followers gave him the title Amir al-Mu'minin, 'Commander of the Faithful', known in Hausa as Sarkin Musulmi. The Sultans of Sokoto have kept this title.

whyNot.D: Mai was the title of the rulers of Kanem-Bornu.
whyNot.C: Mansa was the title of the rulers of Mali.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: In 1804, Usman dan Fodio and his followers made a hijrah (migration) from Degel to escape the hostility of the ruler of Gobir. Where did they go?
questions.explanation: Following the example of the Prophet's Hijrah, Usman dan Fodio and his community left Degel for Gudu in February 1804. There he was chosen as Amir al-Mu'minin, and the jihad against Gobir began.

whyNot.D: Kano was conquered later by the jihadists; it was not the place of the hijrah.
whyNot.C: Ilorin joined the caliphate later as an emirate.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which leader successfully defended Bornu against the Fulani jihadists in the early 19th century and argued with Muhammad Bello in letters about the jihad?
questions.explanation: When the jihadists attacked Bornu, the scholar Muhammad al-Amin al-Kanemi led its defence. In his letters he asked why the jihad was waged against Bornu, a Muslim state, and Muhammad Bello replied in defence of it.

whyNot.B: Idris Alooma ruled Bornu in the 16th century, long before the jihad.
whyNot.A: Abdullahi dan Fodio was a leader of the jihad, not a defender of Bornu.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: The Songhai Empire, a major Muslim power, was brought to an end by an invading army from Morocco at the Battle of Tondibi in
questions.explanation: In 1591 a Moroccan army with firearms defeated the Songhai army at Tondibi. Timbuktu and Gao were occupied, and scholars such as Ahmad Baba were later taken to Morocco.

whyNot.B: 1493 is when Askia Muhammad came to power in Songhai.
whyNot.D: 1324 is the year of Mansa Musa's pilgrimage.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: After the jihad, the Sokoto Caliphate was divided into two parts for administration. Which leader was put in charge of the western part, with headquarters at Gwandu?
questions.explanation: Usman dan Fodio gave his brother Abdullahi the western emirates, ruled from Gwandu, and his son Muhammad Bello the eastern emirates, ruled from Sokoto.

whyNot.C: Muhammad Bello ruled the eastern part from Sokoto.
whyNot.A: Al-Kanemi led Bornu, which resisted the jihad.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: The famous Moroccan traveller who visited the Mali Empire in the 14th century and wrote about the Muslims there was
questions.explanation: Ibn Battuta visited Mali in 1352–1353 during the reign of Mansa Sulayman. He praised the people's devotion to Friday prayer and to memorising the Qur'an, and their sense of justice.

whyNot.D: Ibn Khaldun was a North African historian who wrote about Mali but did not travel there.
whyNot.B: Leo Africanus visited West Africa in the 16th century, during Songhai's time.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: To which Sufi order (tariqah) did Usman dan Fodio belong?
questions.explanation: Usman dan Fodio and his family belonged to the Qadiriyyah, the order traced to Shaykh Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani. It was the main Sufi order in Hausaland during the jihad.

whyNot.B: The Tijaniyyah spread in Nigeria mainly after the jihad, helped by al-Hajj Umar al-Futi, who visited Sokoto in the time of Muhammad Bello.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Who was the first Mai (king) of Kanem to accept Islam?
questions.explanation: Mai Humai (Hume) Jilmi, who ruled in the late 11th century, is remembered as the first Muslim king of Kanem. He was taught by the scholar Muhammad ibn Mani.

whyNot.B: Idris Alooma ruled in the 16th century and is known as a great reformer, not the first Muslim king.
whyNot.D: Dunama Dibbalemi, in the 13th century, strengthened Islam in Kanem but came after Humai.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: The North African scholar Muhammad al-Maghili wrote 'The Obligations of Princes', a guide to Islamic government, for which ruler of Kano?
questions.explanation: Al-Maghili of Tlemcen visited Kano in the late 15th century and advised Sarkin Kano Muhammad Rumfa, a reforming Muslim ruler. He wrote 'The Obligations of Princes' to guide him on just Islamic rule.

whyNot.A: Ali Yaji ruled Kano in the 14th century, when Islam was introduced there by Wangarawa scholars from Mali.
whyNot.C: Usman dan Fodio lived about three centuries after al-Maghili, although he drew on his writings.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the coefficient of x² in the binomial expansion of (1 + 2x)⁵.
questions.explanation: The general term of (1 + 2x)⁵ is ⁵Cᵣ(2x)ʳ. For x², r = 2: ⁵C₂ × 2² = 10 × 4 = 40.

whyNot.D: 10 is ⁵C₂ alone; the 2 in 2x must also be squared.
whyNot.B: 20 multiplies ⁵C₂ by 2 instead of by 2² = 4.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the term independent of x in the expansion of (x + 2/x)⁶.
questions.explanation: The general term is ⁶Cᵣ x^(6 − r) (2/x)ʳ = ⁶Cᵣ 2ʳ x^(6 − 2r). It is independent of x when 6 − 2r = 0, so r = 3. The term is ⁶C₃ × 2³ = 20 × 8 = 160.

whyNot.B: 20 is ⁶C₃ alone; the factor 2³ = 8 from (2/x)³ is left out.
whyNot.A: 120 uses ⁶C₃ × 6 instead of ⁶C₃ × 2³.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Given that (5x + 1)/((x + 1)(x − 1)) ≡ A/(x + 1) + B/(x − 1), find the value of A.
questions.explanation: Multiply through: 5x + 1 ≡ A(x − 1) + B(x + 1). Put x = −1: −5 + 1 = A(−2), so −4 = −2A and A = 2. (Putting x = 1 gives 6 = 2B, so B = 3.)

whyNot.B: 3 is the value of B, the constant over (x − 1).
whyNot.D: −2 comes from a sign slip when dividing −4 by −2.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Evaluate the determinant of the matrix with rows (3, −2) and (4, 5).
questions.explanation: For rows (a, b) and (c, d) the determinant is ad − bc = 3 × 5 − (−2) × 4 = 15 + 8 = 23.

whyNot.D: 7 comes from 15 − 8, forgetting that −(−2 × 4) is +8.
whyNot.B: −23 computes bc − ad, the wrong order.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: The functions f and g are defined on the real numbers by f(x) = 2x − 3 and g(x) = x². Find f(g(−2)).
questions.explanation: Work from the inside: g(−2) = (−2)² = 4. Then f(4) = 2 × 4 − 3 = 5.

whyNot.D: 49 is g(f(−2)) = (−7)², the composition in the wrong order.
whyNot.A: −7 is f(−2), which ignores g altogether.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: When P(x) = x³ − 2x² + kx + 6 is divided by (x − 2), the remainder is 4. Find the value of k.
questions.explanation: By the remainder theorem the remainder is P(2) = 8 − 8 + 2k + 6 = 2k + 6. Setting 2k + 6 = 4 gives 2k = −2, so k = −1.

whyNot.C: 1 comes from a sign slip when solving 2k = −2.
whyNot.A: 5 comes from 2k = 4 + 6, adding the 6 instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Which statement is the contrapositive of "If Musa studies, then he passes"?
options: If Musa does not pass, then he did not study
If Musa passes, then he studied
If Musa studies, then he does not pass
If Musa does not study, then he does not pass
questions.explanation: The contrapositive of p ⇒ q is ~q ⇒ ~p: negate both parts and swap them. Here p is "Musa studies" and q is "he passes", so the contrapositive is "If Musa does not pass, then he did not study". It is logically equivalent to the original.

whyNot.B: This is the converse, q ⇒ p, which is not equivalent to the original.
whyNot.D: This is the inverse, ~p ⇒ ~q, which only negates without swapping.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A committee of 3 is to be chosen from 5 boys and 4 girls. In how many ways can this be done if the committee must contain exactly 2 girls?
questions.explanation: Choose 2 of the 4 girls in ⁴C₂ = 6 ways and 1 of the 5 boys in ⁵C₁ = 5 ways. By the multiplication principle the total is 6 × 5 = 30.

whyNot.D: 84 is ⁹C₃, the number of committees of 3 with no condition.
whyNot.C: 60 treats the choices as ordered (multiplies by 2!) when order does not matter in a committee.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the inverse of the matrix M with rows (2, 1) and (5, 3).
questions.explanation: det M = 2 × 3 − 1 × 5 = 1. The inverse is (1/det) × (swap the leading diagonal, change the signs of the other two): rows (3, −1) and (−5, 2). Check: (2)(3) + (1)(−5) = 1 and (2)(−1) + (1)(2) = 0.

whyNot.B: This is the negative of the inverse; det M is +1, not −1.
whyNot.D: This is the transpose of the correct inverse; the off-diagonal entries are in the wrong places.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the range of values of x for which x² − 5x + 6 < 0.
questions.explanation: Factorise: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3). The graph is a U-shaped parabola cutting the x-axis at 2 and 3, so it is below the axis (negative) between the roots: 2 < x < 3.

whyNot.A: This is where the expression is positive (outside the roots).
whyNot.D: −3 and −2 are the roots of x² + 5x + 6, a sign slip in factorising.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the centre and radius of the circle x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0.
questions.explanation: Compare with x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0: 2g = −6 so g = −3; 2f = 4 so f = 2; c = −12. The centre is (−g, −f) = (3, −2) and the radius is √(g² + f² − c) = √(9 + 4 + 12) = √25 = 5.

whyNot.A: This takes the centre as (g, f) instead of (−g, −f).
whyNot.B: Radius 1 comes from √(9 + 4 − 12), using +c instead of −c.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the equation of the tangent to the circle x² + y² = 25 at the point (3, 4).
questions.explanation: The radius from the centre (0, 0) to (3, 4) has gradient 4/3. The tangent is perpendicular to it, so its gradient is −3/4. Through (3, 4): y − 4 = −3/4(x − 3), so 4y − 16 = −3x + 9, giving 3x + 4y = 25.

whyNot.A: 4x − 3y = 0 is the line of the radius (the normal), not the tangent.
whyNot.D: 4x + 3y = 25 does not pass through (3, 4): 12 + 12 = 24.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the unit vector in the direction of 3i − 4j.
questions.explanation: The magnitude is |3i − 4j| = √(3² + (−4)²) = √25 = 5. Divide the vector by its magnitude: (3/5)i − (4/5)j, which has length 1.

whyNot.D: 7 is 3 + 4, the sum of the components, not the magnitude.
whyNot.C: This swaps the components, so it points in a different direction.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the angle between the vectors a = 2i + j and b = i + 3j.

whyNot.B: 60° needs cos θ = 1/2, which is not what the dot product gives.
whyNot.A: 90° would need a · b = 0, but here a · b = 5.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the perpendicular distance of the point (2, 3) from the line 3x + 4y − 8 = 0.

whyNot.B: 10 is the numerator only; it must be divided by √(3² + 4²) = 5.
whyNot.C: 18/5 leaves out the constant −8 in the numerator.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the eccentricity of the ellipse x²/25 + y²/16 = 1.
questions.explanation: Here a² = 25 and b² = 16 with a > b. For an ellipse b² = a²(1 − e²), so e² = 1 − 16/25 = 9/25 and e = 3/5. An ellipse always has e between 0 and 1.

whyNot.C: 5/3 is greater than 1, which is impossible for an ellipse.
whyNot.D: 9/25 is e², not e; take the square root.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the coordinates of the focus of the parabola y² = 12x.
questions.explanation: Compare with the standard form y² = 4ax, whose focus is (a, 0). Here 4a = 12, so a = 3 and the focus is (3, 0).

whyNot.D: 12 is 4a, not a.
whyNot.B: (0, 3) is the focus of x² = 12y, a parabola opening upwards.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A is the point (1, 2) and B is the point (7, −4). Find the point P that divides AB internally in the ratio 2 : 1.
questions.explanation: For AP : PB = m : n, P = (nA + mB)/(m + n). With m = 2, n = 1: x = (1 × 1 + 2 × 7)/3 = 15/3 = 5 and y = (1 × 2 + 2 × (−4))/3 = −6/3 = −2. So P = (5, −2), two-thirds of the way from A to B.

whyNot.B: (3, 0) divides AB in the ratio 1 : 2, nearer to A.
whyNot.D: (4, −1) is the midpoint, the ratio 1 : 1.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: The points (1, 2) and (5, 6) are the ends of a diameter of a circle. Find the equation of the circle.
questions.explanation: The centre is the midpoint (3, 4). The radius is half the diameter: r² = (5 − 3)² + (6 − 4)² = 8. So (x − 3)² + (y − 4)² = 8, which expands to x² + y² − 6x − 8y + 9 + 16 − 8 = 0, that is x² + y² − 6x − 8y + 17 = 0.

whyNot.B: This has centre (−3, −4); the signs of g and f are wrong.
whyNot.A: −7 uses the whole diameter squared (32) as r² instead of the radius squared (8).

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the length of the tangent from the point (5, 7) to the circle x² + y² − 2x − 4y − 4 = 0.
questions.explanation: The square of the tangent length from (x₁, y₁) is found by substituting the point into the circle's equation: 5² + 7² − 2(5) − 4(7) − 4 = 25 + 49 − 10 − 28 − 4 = 32. The length is √32 = 4√2 units.

whyNot.C: 6 units comes from leaving out the constant −4 (√36).
whyNot.D: 6√3 = √108 comes from adding the linear terms 10 and 28 instead of subtracting them.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Given that y = 3x⁴ − 2x² + 5, find dy/dx when x = 1.

whyNot.A: 6 is the value of y at x = 1, not the gradient.
whyNot.D: 12 forgets to differentiate the −2x² term.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Differentiate y = (2x + 1)⁵ with respect to x.
questions.explanation: Use the chain rule. Let u = 2x + 1, so y = u⁵. dy/dx = 5u⁴ × du/dx = 5(2x + 1)⁴ × 2 = 10(2x + 1)⁴.

whyNot.D: 5(2x + 1)⁴ forgets to multiply by du/dx = 2.
whyNot.C: The power must drop by one, from 5 to 4.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Evaluate ∫₀² (3x² + 2x) dx.
questions.explanation: ∫(3x² + 2x) dx = x³ + x². Evaluate from 0 to 2: (8 + 4) − (0 + 0) = 12.

whyNot.A: 8 includes only the x³ part and leaves out ∫2x dx = x².

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve y = x³ − 3x at the point where x = 2.
questions.explanation: At x = 2, y = 8 − 6 = 2. dy/dx = 3x² − 3, so the gradient is 3(4) − 3 = 9. The tangent: y − 2 = 9(x − 2), so y = 9x − 16.

whyNot.C: This has the wrong sign for the intercept; it does not pass through (2, 2).
whyNot.D: y = 3x − 4 uses gradient 3, which comes from forgetting to square x: 3(2) − 3.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the maximum value of y = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1.
questions.explanation: dy/dx = 3x² − 12x + 9 = 3(x − 1)(x − 3), so the stationary points are at x = 1 and x = 3. d²y/dx² = 6x − 12 is −6 < 0 at x = 1 (a maximum) and +6 > 0 at x = 3 (a minimum). The maximum value is y(1) = 1 − 6 + 9 + 1 = 5.

whyNot.B: 1 is the minimum value, y(3) = 27 − 54 + 27 + 1.
whyNot.D: 3 is the x-value of the minimum point, not a y-value.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find ∫(4x³ − 6x) dx.
questions.explanation: Increase each power by one and divide by the new power: ∫4x³ dx = 4x⁴/4 = x⁴ and ∫6x dx = 6x²/2 = 3x². So the integral is x⁴ − 3x² + c.

whyNot.D: 12x² − 6 is the derivative of the expression, not its integral.
whyNot.C: This raises the powers but forgets to divide by the new power.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the area of the region enclosed by the curve y = 4 − x² and the x-axis.
questions.explanation: The curve meets the x-axis where 4 − x² = 0, at x = −2 and x = 2. Area = ∫₋₂² (4 − x²) dx = [4x − x³/3] from −2 to 2 = (8 − 8/3) − (−8 + 8/3) = 16 − 16/3 = 32/3 square units.

whyNot.D: 16/3 is only half the region (from 0 to 2).
whyNot.B: 64/3 is twice the correct area.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: The region bounded by y = x², the x-axis and the line x = 2 is rotated completely about the x-axis. Find the volume of the solid formed.
questions.explanation: V = π∫₀² y² dx = π∫₀² x⁴ dx = π[x⁵/5] from 0 to 2 = 32π/5 cubic units.

whyNot.B: 8π/3 uses π∫x² dx, forgetting to square y.
whyNot.C: 32π/3 divides by 3 instead of 5 after integrating x⁴.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A particle moves in a straight line so that its displacement s metres after t seconds is s = t³ − 4t² + 3t. Find its velocity when t = 2.
questions.explanation: Velocity is ds/dt = 3t² − 8t + 3. At t = 2: 12 − 16 + 3 = −1 m s⁻¹. The negative sign means the particle is moving back towards the start.

whyNot.A: −2 is the displacement s at t = 2, not the velocity.
whyNot.D: 4 m s⁻² is the acceleration 6t − 8 at t = 2.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: The radius of a spherical balloon is increasing at 0.2 cm s⁻¹. Find the rate at which its volume is increasing when the radius is 3 cm. (V = 4πr³/3)
questions.explanation: dV/dr = 4πr². By the chain rule dV/dt = dV/dr × dr/dt = 4π(3²) × 0.2 = 36π × 0.2 = 7.2π cm³ s⁻¹.

whyNot.A: 36π is dV/dr; it still has to be multiplied by dr/dt = 0.2.
whyNot.C: 2.4π uses 4πr²/3 instead of differentiating 4πr³/3 correctly.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A and B are independent events with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.5. Find P(A ∩ B).
questions.explanation: For independent events P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15.

whyNot.D: 0.8 adds the probabilities, which is not how 'and' works.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed 4 times. Find the probability of getting exactly 3 heads.
questions.explanation: This is binomial with n = 4 and p = 1/2. P(X = 3) = ⁴C₃ (1/2)³ (1/2)¹ = 4 × 1/16 = 1/4.

whyNot.C: 1/16 is the probability of one particular order (such as HHHT); there are 4 such orders.
whyNot.B: 3/8 is P(exactly 2 heads) = 6/16.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the variance of the numbers 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10.
questions.explanation: The mean is 30/5 = 6. The squared deviations are 16, 4, 0, 4, 16, which add to 40. Variance = 40/5 = 8.

whyNot.C: 10 divides by n − 1 = 4; for a set of numbers in this syllabus divide by n = 5.
whyNot.B: 2√2 is the standard deviation, the square root of the variance.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.context:
Five students were ranked in Further Mathematics and Physics.
Student: Ada, Bola, Chidi, Dayo, Emeka
Further Mathematics rank: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Physics rank: 2, 1, 3, 5, 4
questions.stem: Using the ranks in the table, calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient.

whyNot.D: 0.2 is the fraction 6Σd²/(n(n² − 1)); it must be subtracted from 1.
whyNot.B: The rankings mostly agree, so the correlation is positive.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: X is a binomial random variable with n = 5 and p = 1/3. Find P(X = 2).

whyNot.D: 40/243 is P(X = 3): the powers of 1/3 and 2/3 are swapped.
whyNot.B: 10/243 uses (1/3)⁵ for every trial, ignoring that failures have probability 2/3.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A random variable X has a binomial distribution with n = 20 and p = 0.3. Find the mean of X.
questions.explanation: The mean of a binomial distribution is np = 20 × 0.3 = 6.

whyNot.B: 4.2 is the variance np(1 − p) = 20 × 0.3 × 0.7.
whyNot.D: 14 is n(1 − p), the mean number of failures.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A bag contains 5 red and 3 blue balls. Two balls are drawn at random one after the other without replacement. Find the probability that both are red.
questions.explanation: P(first red) = 5/8. After one red ball is removed, 4 of the 7 left are red, so P(second red) = 4/7. P(both red) = 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14.

whyNot.B: 25/64 = (5/8)² assumes the first ball is put back.
whyNot.C: 15/28 is the probability of one red and one blue.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A random variable X takes the values 1, 2 and 3 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5 and 0.3 respectively. Find E(X), the expected value of X.

whyNot.D: 2 is the middle value of X, not the weighted mean.
whyNot.B: 6 is the sum of the values 1 + 2 + 3 without weighting by probabilities.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A and B are events with P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.7. Find P(A | B), the probability of A given B.

whyNot.D: 0.2 is P(A ∩ B); it still has to be divided by P(B).
whyNot.B: 0.4 is P(B | A) = 0.2/0.5, the condition the wrong way round.
whyNot.A: 0.7 is P(A ∪ B), not a conditional probability.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Two fair dice are thrown. Given that at least one die shows a 5, find the probability that the sum of the two numbers is 8.
questions.explanation: Of the 36 equally likely outcomes, 11 have at least one 5 (6 with the first die 5, 6 with the second die 5, minus (5, 5) counted twice). Of these, only (5, 3) and (3, 5) add to 8. So the conditional probability is 2/11.

whyNot.C: 5/36 is P(sum is 8) with no condition.
whyNot.A: 1/18 = 2/36 divides by all 36 outcomes instead of the 11 that meet the condition.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Two forces of 6 N and 8 N act on a particle at right angles to each other. Find the magnitude of their resultant.
questions.explanation: At right angles, the resultant is found by Pythagoras: R = √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10 N.

whyNot.A: 14 N is the resultant only if the forces act in the same direction.
whyNot.B: 2 N is the resultant only if they act in opposite directions.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A particle of mass 4 kg rests on a smooth horizontal floor. It is pulled by a force of 20 N acting at 60° above the horizontal. Find its acceleration along the floor.
questions.explanation: Only the horizontal component moves it along the floor: 20 cos 60° = 10 N. By Newton's second law a = F/m = 10/4 = 2.5 m s⁻².

whyNot.B: 5 m s⁻² uses the whole 20 N instead of its horizontal component.
whyNot.A: 4.33 m s⁻² uses the vertical component 20 sin 60°.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A particle slides from rest down a smooth plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Find its acceleration. (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation: The component of weight along the plane is mg sin 30°. With no friction, ma = mg sin 30°, so a = 10 × 0.5 = 5 m s⁻². The mass cancels.

whyNot.A: 8.66 m s⁻² uses g cos 30°, the component perpendicular to the plane.
whyNot.D: 10 m s⁻² is free fall; the plane only lets part of g act along it.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A car of mass 2000 kg moves at 15 m s⁻¹. Find the magnitude of its momentum.
questions.explanation: Momentum = mass × velocity = 2000 × 15 = 30 000 kg m s⁻¹, which is the same unit as N s.

whyNot.C: 225 000 is the kinetic energy ½mv² in joules, not momentum.
whyNot.A: 133 comes from dividing the mass by the speed.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A ball of mass 3 kg moving at 4 m s⁻¹ collides with a ball of mass 1 kg at rest. They stick together. Find the loss in kinetic energy.
questions.explanation: Momentum is conserved: 3 × 4 = (3 + 1)v, so v = 3 m s⁻¹. KE before = ½ × 3 × 4² = 24 J. KE after = ½ × 4 × 3² = 18 J. Loss = 24 − 18 = 6 J.

whyNot.D: 18 J is the kinetic energy after the collision, not the loss.
whyNot.B: 24 J is the kinetic energy before the collision.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A uniform beam AB is 4 m long and weighs 100 N. It rests horizontally on supports at A and B. A load of 60 N is placed 1 m from A. Find the reaction at A.
questions.explanation: Take moments about B. The beam's weight acts at the centre, 2 m from B; the load is 3 m from B. R_A × 4 = 100 × 2 + 60 × 3 = 380, so R_A = 95 N. (Then R_B = 160 − 95 = 65 N.)

whyNot.C: 65 N is the reaction at B, the support further from the load.
whyNot.A: 80 N shares the total load equally, ignoring where the 60 N sits.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A lorry's engine exerts a constant driving force of 2000 N while the lorry moves at a steady 15 m s⁻¹. Find the power of the engine.
questions.explanation: Power = force × velocity = 2000 × 15 = 30 000 W = 30 kW.

whyNot.A: 3 kW is a slip of a factor of 10 in converting 30 000 W.
whyNot.C: 133 W divides force by speed instead of multiplying.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A block of mass 5 kg on a rough horizontal surface is pulled by a horizontal force of 30 N. The coefficient of friction is 0.4. Find the acceleration of the block. (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation: Normal reaction R = mg = 50 N, so friction F = μR = 0.4 × 50 = 20 N. Net force = 30 − 20 = 10 N, and a = 10/5 = 2 m s⁻².

whyNot.C: 6 m s⁻² ignores friction (30/5).
whyNot.A: 10 m s⁻² adds friction to the pull instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A ball is projected from level ground with a speed of 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. Find its horizontal range. (g = 10 m s⁻²)

whyNot.A: 40 m is the maximum possible range, at 45°.
whyNot.B: 20 m uses sin 30° instead of sin 60°.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Particles of mass 5 kg and 3 kg are connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth fixed pulley, and hang freely. Find the tension in the string. (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation: Acceleration a = (5 − 3)g/(5 + 3) = 20/8 = 2.5 m s⁻². For the 3 kg particle (moving up): T − 30 = 3 × 2.5, so T = 37.5 N. (Check with 5 kg: 50 − T = 5 × 2.5 gives the same T.)

whyNot.A: 30 N is just the weight of the lighter particle; the string must also accelerate it upward.
whyNot.C: 50 N is the weight of the heavier particle, which would mean no acceleration.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: In how many different ways can the letters of the word ABUJA be arranged?
questions.explanation: There are 5 letters with A repeated twice. Number of arrangements = 5!/2! = 120/2 = 60.

whyNot.D: 120 = 5! treats the two A's as different letters.
whyNot.B: 30 divides by 2! twice.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the coefficient of x³ in the expansion of (2 − x)⁶.
questions.explanation: The general term is ⁶Cᵣ 2^(6 − r) (−x)ʳ. For x³, r = 3: ⁶C₃ × 2³ × (−1)³ = 20 × 8 × (−1) = −160.

whyNot.A: 160 forgets that (−x)³ is negative.
whyNot.D: −20 leaves out the factor 2³ = 8.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Evaluate the determinant of the 3 × 3 matrix with rows (1, 2, 0), (3, −1, 4) and (2, 1, 1).

whyNot.C: −15 forgets the alternating minus sign on the middle term.
whyNot.D: −5 stops after the first term of the expansion.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: The function f is defined on the real numbers by f(x) = 3x + 2. Find f⁻¹(x).
questions.explanation: Let y = 3x + 2 and make x the subject: x = (y − 2)/3. Replace y with x: f⁻¹(x) = (x − 2)/3. Check: f((x − 2)/3) = x − 2 + 2 = x.

whyNot.C: This reverses the multiplication but not the addition of 2.
whyNot.B: 1/(3x + 2) is the reciprocal of f(x), not its inverse function.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: α and β are the roots of 2x² − 5x + 1 = 0. Find the value of α² + β².
questions.explanation: α + β = 5/2 and αβ = 1/2. Then α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ = 25/4 − 1 = 21/4.

whyNot.C: 29/4 adds 2αβ instead of subtracting it.
whyNot.A: 25/4 is (α + β)², without subtracting 2αβ.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Express 4/((x − 1)(x² + 1)) in partial fractions.
questions.explanation: Write 4/((x − 1)(x² + 1)) ≡ A/(x − 1) + (Bx + C)/(x² + 1), so 4 ≡ A(x² + 1) + (Bx + C)(x − 1). x = 1 gives 4 = 2A, so A = 2. Coefficients of x²: 0 = A + B, so B = −2. Constants: 4 = A − C, so C = −2. The result is 2/(x − 1) − (2x + 2)/(x² + 1).

whyNot.B: The sign is wrong: B and C are both −2.
whyNot.C: A quadratic factor x² + 1 needs a linear numerator Bx + C, not a constant.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: p is the statement "The market is open" and q is "Ada buys yam". Which sentence expresses ~p ⇒ ~q?
options: If the market is not open, then Ada does not buy yam
If the market is open, then Ada buys yam
If Ada does not buy yam, then the market is not open
The market is not open and Ada does not buy yam
questions.explanation: ~p means "The market is not open" and ~q means "Ada does not buy yam". The arrow ⇒ is read "if … then …" with ~p first, so ~p ⇒ ~q is "If the market is not open, then Ada does not buy yam".

whyNot.C: This is ~q ⇒ ~p, with the two parts the wrong way round.
whyNot.D: This is ~p ∧ ~q, a conjunction ("and"), not an implication.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A binary operation ∗ is defined on the real numbers by a ∗ b = a + b + 2ab. The identity element is 0. Find the inverse of 3 under ∗.
questions.explanation: The inverse b of 3 satisfies 3 ∗ b = 0 (the identity): 3 + b + 6b = 0, so 7b = −3 and b = −3/7. Check: 3 + (−3/7) + 2(3)(−3/7) = 21/7 − 3/7 − 18/7 = 0.

whyNot.A: −1/3 is the inverse of 3 under multiplication, a different operation.
whyNot.D: −1 uses 2b instead of 2 × 3 × b = 6b for the term 2ab.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the sum of the first 20 terms of the arithmetic progression 3, 7, 11, 15, …

whyNot.D: 780 uses (n − 2)d instead of (n − 1)d.
whyNot.C: 1640 forgets to divide by 2 in n/2.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Solve the equation log₂(x + 2) + log₂(x − 2) = 5.
questions.explanation: Combine the logs: log₂[(x + 2)(x − 2)] = 5, so x² − 4 = 2⁵ = 32 and x² = 36, giving x = ±6. x = −6 is rejected because log₂(−4) is not defined. So x = 6.

whyNot.A: x = −6 makes x + 2 and x − 2 negative, and logs of negative numbers are not defined.
whyNot.C: 36 is x², not x.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the distance between the points P(−1, 2) and Q(5, −6).

whyNot.C: 14 adds the differences 6 + 8 instead of using Pythagoras.
whyNot.B: 2√13 = √52 comes from a sign slip in the y-difference (4 instead of 8).

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the area of the triangle with vertices A(1, 1), B(4, 5) and C(7, 2).

whyNot.C: 21 forgets the factor ½.
whyNot.A: 35/2 comes from a sign slip, adding 28 instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Given a = 2i − 3j and b = −i + 5j, find 3a − 2b.

whyNot.A: 4i + j is 3a + 2b.
whyNot.D: 4i − 19j subtracts −2i wrongly as 6 − 2.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: The vectors p = 2i + kj and q = 3i − 6j are perpendicular. Find the value of k.
questions.explanation: Perpendicular vectors have a dot product of zero: p · q = 2(3) + k(−6) = 6 − 6k = 0, so k = 1.

whyNot.A: −1 comes from a sign slip in solving 6 − 6k = 0.
whyNot.C: k = −4 makes p parallel to q (2/3 = −4/−6), not perpendicular.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the acute angle between the lines y = 2x + 1 and y = −3x + 4.

whyNot.C: The lines are perpendicular only if m₁m₂ = −1, but here m₁m₂ = −6.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A circle has centre (2, −1) and touches the line 3x − 4y + 5 = 0. Find its equation.
questions.explanation: The radius is the distance from the centre to the tangent line: r = |3(2) − 4(−1) + 5|/√(9 + 16) = 15/5 = 3. So (x − 2)² + (y + 1)² = 9, which expands to x² + y² − 4x + 2y + 4 + 1 − 9 = 0, that is x² + y² − 4x + 2y − 4 = 0.

whyNot.D: This circle has centre (−2, 1); the signs are reversed.
whyNot.C: −20 uses r = 5, the value of √(3² + 4²), as the radius.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the eccentricity of the hyperbola x²/16 − y²/9 = 1.
questions.explanation: For a hyperbola b² = a²(e² − 1), so e² = 1 + b²/a² = 1 + 9/16 = 25/16 and e = 5/4. A hyperbola always has e greater than 1.

whyNot.A: √7/4 uses 1 − 9/16, the ellipse formula.
whyNot.C: 4/5 is less than 1, which is impossible for a hyperbola.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the equation of the directrix of the parabola y² = 8x.
questions.explanation: Compare with y² = 4ax: 4a = 8, so a = 2. The directrix of y² = 4ax is the line x = −a, which is x = −2.

whyNot.C: x = 2 passes through the focus (2, 0), not the directrix.
whyNot.A: −8 uses 4a instead of a.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: The position vectors of A and B are OA = 2i + 3j and OB = 6i − j. Find the unit vector in the direction of AB.

whyNot.C: (1/4)(i − j) divides by 4 instead of the magnitude 4√2, so its length is not 1.
whyNot.B: This points from B to A, the opposite direction.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the points where the line y = x + 1 meets the circle x² + y² = 13.
questions.explanation: Substitute y = x + 1: x² + (x + 1)² = 13, so 2x² + 2x − 12 = 0, giving x² + x − 6 = 0 = (x + 3)(x − 2). x = 2 gives y = 3 and x = −3 gives y = −2. The points are (2, 3) and (−3, −2).

whyNot.B: This uses the roots x = −2 and x = 3 from a sign slip in factorising; (3, 4) is not on the circle.
whyNot.A: These points lie on the circle but not on the line y = x + 1.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Evaluate the limit of (x² − 4)/(x − 2) as x tends to 2.
questions.explanation: Factorise the numerator: (x − 2)(x + 2)/(x − 2) = x + 2 for x ≠ 2. As x → 2, this tends to 2 + 2 = 4.

whyNot.B: 0 comes from putting x = 2 into the numerator only; the expression is 0/0 there, so it must be simplified first.
whyNot.C: 2 is the value x approaches, not the limit of the expression.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Given y = (x² + 1)(2x − 3), find dy/dx when x = 1.

whyNot.A: −2 is only the first part of the product rule, 2x(2x − 3).
whyNot.C: 4 is only the second part, (x² + 1) × 2.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Differentiate y = x/(x + 1) with respect to x.
questions.explanation: By the quotient rule, dy/dx = [(x + 1)(1) − x(1)]/(x + 1)² = 1/(x + 1)².

whyNot.D: This reverses the order of subtraction in the quotient rule numerator.
whyNot.C: This adds the two terms in the numerator instead of subtracting.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Evaluate ∫₁³ 2x dx.
questions.explanation: ∫2x dx = x². Evaluate from 1 to 3: 3² − 1² = 9 − 1 = 8.

whyNot.B: 9 uses only the upper limit and forgets to subtract the value at x = 1.
whyNot.A: 10 adds the values at the limits instead of subtracting.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Differentiate y = sin 3x with respect to x.
questions.explanation: By the chain rule, d/dx (sin u) = cos u × du/dx. With u = 3x, du/dx = 3, so dy/dx = 3 cos 3x.

whyNot.A: cos 3x forgets to multiply by the derivative of 3x.
whyNot.B: The derivative of sin is +cos; the minus sign belongs to the derivative of cos.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A farmer has 40 m of fencing to enclose a rectangular plot beside a long straight wall. The wall forms one side, so fencing is needed for only three sides. Find the greatest area she can enclose.
questions.explanation: Let the two sides perpendicular to the wall be x m each; the side parallel to the wall is 40 − 2x. A = x(40 − 2x) = 40x − 2x². dA/dx = 40 − 4x = 0 gives x = 10, and d²A/dx² = −4 < 0, so this is a maximum. A = 10 × 20 = 200 m².

whyNot.A: 100 m² is the area of a 10 m square, which uses all four sides of fencing.
whyNot.D: 400 m² uses 40 − x instead of 40 − 2x for the side along the wall.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: The gradient of a curve at any point is 6x − 2, and the curve passes through (1, 4). Find the equation of the curve.
questions.explanation: Integrate: y = 3x² − 2x + c. At (1, 4): 4 = 3 − 2 + c, so c = 3. The curve is y = 3x² − 2x + 3.

whyNot.D: This sets c = 4, the y-value of the point, without substituting.
whyNot.C: This leaves out the constant of integration.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the area of the region enclosed by the curve y = x² and the line y = 2x.
questions.explanation: They meet where x² = 2x, at x = 0 and x = 2. Between them the line is above the curve. Area = ∫₀² (2x − x²) dx = [x² − x³/3] from 0 to 2 = 4 − 8/3 = 4/3 square units.

whyNot.B: 8/3 is the area under y = x² alone, not between the two graphs.
whyNot.A: 20/3 adds the two areas instead of subtracting.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A particle starts from O and moves in a straight line with velocity v = 3t² − 2t m s⁻¹ after t seconds. Find its displacement from O when t = 2.
questions.explanation: Displacement s = ∫v dt = t³ − t² + c, and s = 0 at t = 0 gives c = 0. At t = 2: s = 8 − 4 = 4 m.

whyNot.A: 8 is the velocity at t = 2, not the displacement.
whyNot.C: 10 is the acceleration 6t − 2 at t = 2.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the coordinates of the minimum point of the curve y = 2x³ − 3x² − 12x + 5.
questions.explanation: dy/dx = 6x² − 6x − 12 = 6(x − 2)(x + 1) = 0 at x = 2 and x = −1. d²y/dx² = 12x − 6 is 18 > 0 at x = 2, so that is the minimum. y(2) = 16 − 12 − 24 + 5 = −15. The minimum point is (2, −15).

whyNot.D: (−1, 12) is the maximum point, where d²y/dx² = −18 < 0.
whyNot.B: (1, −8) is on the curve but is not a stationary point.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A fair die is thrown once. Find the probability that the number shown is a prime number.
questions.explanation: The primes among 1 to 6 are 2, 3 and 5, so 3 of the 6 equally likely outcomes are favourable. P = 3/6 = 1/2. (1 is not a prime number.)

whyNot.B: 2/3 counts 1 as a prime, which it is not.
whyNot.A: 1/3 misses one of the primes, usually 2.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: The mean of the numbers 3, 5, x, 9 and 10 is 7. Find the value of x.
questions.explanation: The total must be 5 × 7 = 35. The known numbers add to 3 + 5 + 9 + 10 = 27, so x = 35 − 27 = 8.

whyNot.B: 7 is the mean itself, not the missing value.
whyNot.A: 6 comes from an addition slip in the known numbers.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: X has a binomial distribution with n = 50 and p = 0.2. Find the standard deviation of X.
questions.explanation: The variance is np(1 − p) = 50 × 0.2 × 0.8 = 8. The standard deviation is √8 = 2√2 (about 2.83).

whyNot.B: 8 is the variance; take the square root.
whyNot.D: 10 is the mean np.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A and B are mutually exclusive events with P(A) = 1/3 and P(B) = 1/4. Find P(A ∪ B).
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, so P(A ∩ B) = 0 and P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) = 1/3 + 1/4 = 7/12.

whyNot.D: 1/12 multiplies the probabilities, which is P(A ∩ B) for independent events.
whyNot.B: 1/2 subtracts 1/12 as if the events were independent; mutually exclusive events have no overlap.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: For 5 pairs of values (x, y): Σx = 20, Σy = 30, Σxy = 140 and Σx² = 100. Find the least squares regression line of y on x.
questions.explanation: b = (nΣxy − ΣxΣy)/(nΣx² − (Σx)²) = (5 × 140 − 20 × 30)/(5 × 100 − 20²) = 100/100 = 1. The line passes through the means (x̄, ȳ) = (4, 6), so a = ȳ − b x̄ = 6 − 4 = 2. The line is y = x + 2.

whyNot.B: y = x + 6 uses ȳ as the intercept without subtracting b x̄.
whyNot.C: y = 1.5x is just ȳ/x̄; it forces the line through the origin.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed 3 times. Find the probability of getting at least one head.
questions.explanation: The only outcome with no head is TTT, with probability (1/2)³ = 1/8. So P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8.

whyNot.A: 3/8 is P(exactly one head).
whyNot.B: 1/8 is P(no heads), the complement.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: In a test of 6 candidates ranked by two judges, the sum of the squares of the differences in ranks is Σd² = 10. Find Spearman's rank correlation coefficient.

whyNot.A: 2/7 is the fraction being subtracted, not the coefficient.
whyNot.D: The coefficient is 1 minus a positive fraction less than 1, so it is positive here.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed 4 times. Find the probability of getting at least 2 heads.
questions.explanation: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(X = 0) − P(X = 1) = 1 − 1/16 − 4/16 = 11/16, using the binomial distribution with n = 4 and p = 1/2.

whyNot.D: 5/16 is P(X = 0 or 1), the complement.
whyNot.C: 3/8 is P(exactly 2 heads) only.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Ten cards are numbered 1 to 10. Two cards are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability that both numbers are even.
questions.explanation: There are 5 even numbers. P(first even) = 5/10 and then P(second even) = 4/9. P(both even) = 5/10 × 4/9 = 20/90 = 2/9.

whyNot.D: 1/4 = (1/2)² assumes the first card is replaced.
whyNot.B: 4/9 is the second-draw probability alone.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Box A contains 3 red and 2 white balls. Box B contains 1 red and 4 white balls. A fair coin is tossed to choose a box, and a ball is drawn from it. The ball is red. Find the probability that it came from Box A.

whyNot.D: 3/5 is P(red | A), the condition the wrong way round.
whyNot.A: 3/10 is P(A and red); it must be divided by P(red).

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A constant force of 12 N acts on a body of mass 3 kg initially at rest on a smooth horizontal surface. Find its velocity after 5 s.
questions.explanation: a = F/m = 12/3 = 4 m s⁻². Using v = u + at: v = 0 + 4 × 5 = 20 m s⁻¹.

whyNot.C: 4 m s⁻² is the acceleration, not the velocity.
whyNot.B: 60 multiplies the force by time without dividing by the mass.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A force of 40 N acts at 30° above the horizontal. Find its horizontal component.
questions.explanation: Horizontal component = F cos θ = 40 cos 30° = 40 × √3/2 = 20√3 N (about 34.6 N).

whyNot.A: 20 N is 40 sin 30°, the vertical component.
whyNot.C: 40√3 forgets the ½ in cos 30° = √3/2.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A particle of weight 20 N hangs from a light string. A horizontal force pulls the particle aside until it rests in equilibrium with the string at 30° to the vertical. Find the tension in the string.
questions.explanation: Resolve vertically: T cos 30° = 20, so T = 20/(√3/2) = 40/√3 = 40√3/3 N (about 23.1 N). (Horizontally, the pull is T sin 30° = 20√3/3 N.)

whyNot.C: 20√3/3 N is the horizontal pulling force, 20 tan 30°.
whyNot.A: 40 N uses sin 30° instead of cos 30° when resolving vertically.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A ball of mass 0.5 kg hits a wall at 8 m s⁻¹ and rebounds along the same line at 6 m s⁻¹. Find the magnitude of the impulse on the ball.
questions.explanation: Impulse = change in momentum. Taking the rebound direction as positive: 0.5 × 6 − 0.5 × (−8) = 3 + 4 = 7 N s.

whyNot.A: 1 N s ignores the reversal of direction: 0.5 × (8 − 6).
whyNot.B: 14 N s forgets to multiply the change in velocity by 0.5 kg.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A block of mass 2 kg rests without moving on a rough plane inclined at angle θ to the horizontal, where tan θ = 3/4. Find the friction force on the block. (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation: With tan θ = 3/4, sin θ = 3/5 and cos θ = 4/5. In equilibrium, friction balances the component of weight down the plane: F = mg sin θ = 20 × 3/5 = 12 N.

whyNot.D: 16 N is mg cos θ, the normal reaction.
whyNot.C: 20 N is the whole weight.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A man of mass 60 kg stands in a lift moving upwards with an acceleration of 2 m s⁻². Find the reaction of the floor on him. (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation: Taking upwards as positive: R − mg = ma, so R = m(g + a) = 60 × (10 + 2) = 720 N.

whyNot.B: 480 N = m(g − a), which is for a lift accelerating downwards.
whyNot.D: 600 N is his weight, the reaction only when the lift has no acceleration.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A uniform rod AB is 6 m long and weighs 40 N. It is pivoted at C, 2 m from A. What weight hung at A will keep the rod horizontal?
questions.explanation: The rod's weight acts at its midpoint, 3 m from A, which is 1 m beyond the pivot. Taking moments about C: W × 2 = 40 × 1, so W = 20 N.

whyNot.B: 40 N would balance only if the weight acted 2 m from C.
whyNot.A: 60 N comes from using 3 m (distance from A) instead of 1 m (distance from C).

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A particle of mass 4 kg on a smooth horizontal table is connected by a light inextensible string over a smooth pulley at the edge to a particle of mass 1 kg hanging freely. Find the tension in the string. (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation: The system's acceleration is a = (1 × g)/(4 + 1) = 10/5 = 2 m s⁻². For the particle on the table, T = 4a = 8 N. (Check with the hanging particle: 10 − T = 1 × 2.)

whyNot.A: 10 N is the weight of the hanging particle, which is only the tension if nothing accelerates.
whyNot.D: 2 m s⁻² is the acceleration, not the tension.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A stone is projected vertically upwards at 30 m s⁻¹ from the ground. How long does it take to return to the ground? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation: Use s = ut − ½gt² with s = 0: 0 = 30t − 5t² = 5t(6 − t), so t = 6 s. (It takes 3 s to rise and 3 s to fall.)

whyNot.D: 3 s is the time to reach the highest point only.
whyNot.A: 12 s doubles the correct time.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A block of mass 2 kg slides from rest a distance of 5 m down a rough plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The friction force is 4 N. Find its speed after the 5 m. (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation: It descends 5 sin 30° = 2.5 m, so gravity does mgh = 20 × 2.5 = 50 J of work. Friction removes 4 × 5 = 20 J. So ½mv² = 50 − 20 = 30 J, giving v² = 30 and v = √30 m s⁻¹ (about 5.48 m s⁻¹).

whyNot.B: √50 ignores friction.
whyNot.C: √70 adds the work done against friction instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which electronic component was the main switching and processing element of first-generation computers?
questions.explanation: First-generation computers (roughly the 1940s to mid-1950s), such as ENIAC, used thousands of vacuum tubes (valves) to switch and process signals. This made them huge, hot and power-hungry.

whyNot.C: Transistors replaced vacuum tubes in the second generation.
whyNot.D: Integrated circuits mark the third generation.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Who is widely regarded as the 'father of the computer' because he designed the Analytical Engine?
questions.explanation: Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine in the 1830s. It had a 'mill' (like a processor), a 'store' (like memory) and used punched cards for input, the same basic parts as a modern computer, so he is called the father of the computer.

whyNot.D: Blaise Pascal built an early mechanical adding machine, the Pascaline.
whyNot.B: John Napier invented logarithms and Napier's bones, a calculating aid.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A calculating aid made of numbered rods, invented by a Scottish mathematician in the early 1600s to help with multiplication, is known as
questions.explanation: John Napier, a Scottish mathematician, made a set of numbered rods (published in 1617) that reduced multiplication to adding digits read off the rods. They are called Napier's bones.

whyNot.B: The abacus uses beads on wires and is far older, from ancient times.
whyNot.C: The Pascaline was a geared adding machine built by the Frenchman Blaise Pascal in the 1640s.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A weather station in Jos records air temperature as a continuously changing quantity and shows it on a dial. Which type of computer works with data in this continuous form?
questions.explanation: Analog computers measure and process continuously varying physical quantities such as temperature, pressure or voltage. Digital computers work with discrete values (0s and 1s).

whyNot.A: A digital computer works with discrete, counted values, not continuous ones.
whyNot.C: 'Mainframe' describes size and power, not the form of data processed.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Computers built with integrated circuits (many transistors on a single silicon chip) belong to which generation?
questions.explanation: The third generation (from about the mid-1960s) used integrated circuits, which made computers smaller, faster, cheaper and more reliable than transistor machines.

whyNot.B: The first generation used vacuum tubes.
whyNot.D: The second generation used individual transistors.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which area of development is most closely associated with fifth-generation computers?
questions.explanation: Fifth-generation computing aims at machines that can reason, learn and understand natural language, that is, artificial intelligence, supported by parallel processing.

whyNot.C: Vacuum tubes belong to the first generation.
whyNot.B: Magnetic drum memory was used in first-generation machines.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A clerk types a student's score as 9 instead of 90, and the computer prints the wrong result. Which principle does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: GIGO (garbage in, garbage out) means a computer's output can only be as correct as its input. The computer processed the wrong score accurately, so the result was wrong.

whyNot.B: Diligence means a computer can work for long periods without tiring, which is unrelated to wrong input.
whyNot.D: Versatility means a computer can do many different kinds of task.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A laptop used by a student in Ibadan for assignments is best classified by size as a
questions.explanation: Microcomputers are small computers built around a single microprocessor and used by one person at a time. Desktops, laptops and tablets are all microcomputers.

whyNot.A: A mainframe is a large computer that serves many users in big organisations such as banks.
whyNot.D: A supercomputer is the fastest class, used for huge scientific calculations.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: In an intensive care unit, a machine measures a patient's heartbeat as a continuous signal and then shows the readings as numbers on a screen. Which type of computer is this?
questions.explanation: A hybrid computer combines analog and digital features. Here the analog part measures a continuous signal (the heartbeat), and the digital part converts it and displays exact numerical readings.

whyNot.B: A purely analog computer would not convert the signal into digital numbers.
whyNot.D: A purely digital computer could not take in the continuous signal directly without the analog part.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Herman Hollerith's tabulating machine, used to process the 1890 United States census, read its data from
questions.explanation: Hollerith stored each person's census details as holes in punched cards; his machine sensed the holes electrically and counted them. This greatly speeded up the 1890 census, and his company later became part of IBM.

whyNot.A: Magnetic tape storage came into use in the 1950s.
whyNot.D: Floppy disks were introduced in the 1970s.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which of the following is an input device?
questions.explanation: An input device sends data into the computer. A scanner captures printed text or pictures and sends them in as digital data.

whyNot.D: A printer produces hard copy; it is an output device.
whyNot.A: A monitor displays output on screen.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which part of the central processing unit carries out calculations and comparisons such as 'is A greater than B'?
questions.explanation: The arithmetic and logic unit (ALU) performs arithmetic (add, subtract, multiply, divide) and logical operations (comparisons such as greater than, equal to, AND, OR).

whyNot.B: The control unit directs operations; it does not do the calculations itself.
whyNot.D: Main memory stores data and programs; it does not process them.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: What is the main function of the control unit of the CPU?
options: To direct and coordinate the operations of all parts of the computer
To perform arithmetic calculations on data
To store data permanently after the computer is switched off
To convert printed documents into digital form
questions.explanation: The control unit fetches instructions from memory, decodes them and sends signals that direct the ALU, memory and input/output devices, so it coordinates the whole system.

whyNot.C: Permanent storage is the job of secondary storage such as a hard disk.
whyNot.B: Arithmetic is done by the ALU.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which type of main memory loses its contents when the power is switched off?
questions.explanation: Random access memory (RAM) is volatile: it holds the programs and data in use, but its contents are lost when power is removed. ROM and its variants keep their contents.

whyNot.A: ROM is non-volatile; it keeps its contents without power.
whyNot.C: EPROM is non-volatile; it is erased only with ultraviolet light.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: How many bits are there in 2 kilobytes? (Take 1 KB = 1024 bytes.)
questions.explanation: First change to bytes: 2 KB = 2 × 1024 = 2048 bytes. Each byte has 8 bits, so 2048 × 8 = 16 384 bits.

whyNot.D: 2048 is the number of bytes; it still has to be multiplied by 8.
whyNot.B: 16 000 uses 1 KB = 1000 bytes instead of 1024.
whyNot.C: 8192 is the number of bits in 1 KB only.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Express 3 MB in kilobytes. (Take 1 MB = 1024 KB.)
questions.explanation: Each megabyte is 1024 kilobytes, so 3 MB = 3 × 1024 = 3072 KB.

whyNot.A: 3000 KB uses 1000 instead of 1024.
whyNot.D: 3 145 728 is the number of bytes in 3 MB, not kilobytes.
whyNot.C: 384 comes from dividing by 8, which changes bits to bytes, not MB to KB.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which small, very fast memory sits between the processor and main memory and holds the data and instructions the processor uses most often?
questions.explanation: Cache memory is faster than RAM and placed close to (or inside) the CPU. Keeping frequently used items there reduces the time the processor waits for main memory.

whyNot.B: A hard disk is slow secondary storage, not a buffer for the CPU.
whyNot.A: A flash drive is portable secondary storage.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which of these printers is an impact printer?
questions.explanation: An impact printer forms characters by striking the paper. A dot-matrix printer uses pins that hit an inked ribbon against the paper, which is why it can print on carbon copies.

whyNot.A: A laser printer fuses toner onto paper with no striking.
whyNot.D: An inkjet printer sprays tiny drops of ink onto the paper.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A photographer in Enugu has a 16 GB memory card. If each photo takes up exactly 4 MB, how many photos can the card hold? (Take 1 GB = 1024 MB.)
