questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Action Group grew out of which Yoruba cultural organisation?
questions.explanation: Egbe Omo Oduduwa, a Yoruba cultural association founded by Awolowo and others in the 1940s, provided the base for the Action Group in 1951.

whyNot.D: Jam'iyyar Mutanen Arewa was the northern cultural body from which the NPC grew.
whyNot.C: The Ibo State Union was an Igbo cultural body linked to the NCNC.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Northern Elements Progressive Union (NEPU), which opposed the NPC in the North, was led by
questions.explanation: Mallam Aminu Kano led NEPU, formed in 1950. It spoke for the common people (talakawa) against the power of the emirs and allied with the NCNC.

whyNot.D: Ahmadu Bello led the NPC, NEPU's rival.
whyNot.C: Joseph Tarka led the United Middle Belt Congress (UMBC).

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The National Congress of British West Africa, formed in 1920 to demand reforms such as elected representation, was led by
questions.explanation: J. E. Casely Hayford, a lawyer from the Gold Coast, led the National Congress of British West Africa. Its demands helped push Britain towards the elective principle in the Clifford Constitution of 1922.

whyNot.C: Macaulay led the NNDP in Lagos; the Congress was led from the Gold Coast.
whyNot.A: Nkrumah became prominent only in the late 1940s.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Willink Commission (1957–58) was set up to look into
options: the fears of ethnic minorities and how to allay them
the causes of the 1945 general strike
the causes of the Aba Women's War
the results of the 1959 federal election
questions.explanation: Minority groups in each region feared domination by the major groups and asked for new states. The Willink Commission did not recommend new states but proposed that fundamental human rights be written into the constitution.

whyNot.D: The commission reported before the 1959 election took place.
whyNot.C: The Aba Women's War was in 1929, long before the commission.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Why did Northern leaders oppose the 1953 motion for self-government in 1956?
options: The North had already become independent
The British had banned all political parties in the North
They wanted the North to join French West Africa
They felt the North was not yet ready, partly because it lagged behind in Western education
questions.explanation: NPC leaders feared that with fewer Western-educated people, the North would be dominated by the South in an early self-government. They proposed self-government 'as soon as practicable', and the North became self-governing only in 1959.

whyNot.A: No part of Nigeria was independent before 1960.
whyNot.B: The NPC itself was a legal northern party in the House.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Who declared the Eastern Region an independent 'Republic of Biafra' in May 1967?
questions.explanation: Lt Col. Ojukwu, the military governor of the Eastern Region, declared Biafra on 30 May 1967. The civil war followed from July 1967 to January 1970.

whyNot.C: Gowon was the federal head of state who fought to keep Nigeria one.
whyNot.B: Effiong took over from Ojukwu at the end and announced Biafra's surrender in 1970.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: After the civil war, Gowon's programme of the '3Rs' stood for reconciliation, rehabilitation and
questions.explanation: The 3Rs were reconciliation (bringing people back together), rehabilitation (helping those affected) and reconstruction (rebuilding damaged areas), in line with the 'no victor, no vanquished' policy.

whyNot.C: Regionalism belongs to the Richards Constitution of 1946, not the post-war programme.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Who was sworn in as President on 29 May 1999, at the start of the Fourth Republic?
questions.explanation: General Abdulsalami Abubakar's military government handed over power to Chief Olusegun Obasanjo of the PDP on 29 May 1999, beginning the Fourth Republic.

whyNot.A: Abdulsalami Abubakar was the military head of state who handed over.
whyNot.C: Yar'Adua became President in 2007.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In 1976 the Murtala Mohammed government increased the number of states in Nigeria from 12 to
questions.explanation: In February 1976 Murtala Mohammed created seven new states, bringing the total from 12 to 19. The same government decided to build a new federal capital at Abuja.

whyNot.D: 21 states existed after Babangida created two more in 1987.
whyNot.C: 36 states came in 1996 under Abacha.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The meeting of January 1967 held to settle the crisis between the Federal Military Government and the Eastern Region took place at Aburi in
questions.explanation: Nigeria's military leaders met at Aburi in Ghana in January 1967. They disagreed afterwards about what had been agreed, and the crisis led to secession and civil war.

whyNot.D: Ethiopia's Addis Ababa hosted OAU peace efforts during the war, not the Aburi meeting.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Which head of state created six new states in 1996, bringing the total to 36?
questions.explanation: In October 1996 Abacha created six states (Bayelsa, Ebonyi, Ekiti, Gombe, Nasarawa and Zamfara), raising the number from 30 to 36.

whyNot.A: Babangida created states in 1987 and 1991, reaching 30.
whyNot.C: Abdulsalami Abubakar created no new states.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In 1971 Nigeria joined which organisation, reflecting the growing importance of oil to its economy?
questions.explanation: Nigeria joined the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) in 1971 as oil became its main export and source of government revenue.

whyNot.B: ECOWAS was founded in 1975.
whyNot.A: Nigeria was a founding member of the OAU in 1963.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The two political parties created by the Babangida administration for the transition to the Third Republic were the
questions.explanation: Babangida's government created the Social Democratic Party (SDP) and the National Republican Convention (NRC). Their candidates, Abiola and Tofa, contested the annulled election of 12 June 1993.

whyNot.A: The NPN and UPN were Second Republic parties (1979–83).
whyNot.B: The NCNC and AG were First Republic parties.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The only region created in the First Republic through the procedure laid down in the constitution, in 1963, was the
questions.explanation: The Mid-Western Region was carved out of the Western Region in 1963 after a referendum, following the constitutional procedure. It became Bendel State in 1976.

whyNot.D: The Eastern Region was one of the original three regions from 1946.
whyNot.B: Rivers was created as a state in 1967 by military decree, not as a region.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The War Against Indiscipline (WAI) was launched in 1984 by the military government headed by
questions.explanation: The Buhari–Idiagbon government, which came to power on 31 December 1983, launched WAI in 1984 to promote orderliness, such as queuing, punctuality and a clean environment.

whyNot.A: Obasanjo's military government ended in 1979.
whyNot.C: Abacha came to power in 1993.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Where is the headquarters of the ECOWAS Commission?
questions.explanation: The ECOWAS Commission (formerly the Executive Secretariat) is based in Abuja, Nigeria's capital.

whyNot.A: ECOWAS was founded by a treaty signed in Lagos, but its headquarters is in Abuja.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In which year was the United Nations Organisation founded?
questions.explanation: The UN was founded in 1945, at the end of the Second World War, to maintain world peace. Nigeria joined it in 1960 after independence.

whyNot.B: 1919 relates to the League of Nations after the First World War.
whyNot.C: 1960 is when Nigeria joined the UN.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) was formed in Addis Ababa in
questions.explanation: The OAU was founded on 25 May 1963 in Addis Ababa by independent African states. 25 May is still marked as Africa Day.

whyNot.D: 1975 is when ECOWAS was founded.
whyNot.B: 2002 is when the African Union replaced the OAU.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Nigeria was suspended from the Commonwealth in 1995 after the execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other Ogoni activists under the military government of
questions.explanation: The executions in November 1995 under Abacha's regime caused international outrage, and the Commonwealth suspended Nigeria. It was restored after the return to civil rule in 1999.

whyNot.D: Babangida left office in 1993.
whyNot.A: Buhari's military government ended in 1985.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: ECOMOG, the ECOWAS peacekeeping force led largely by Nigeria, first intervened in 1990 in the civil war in
questions.explanation: ECOWAS set up ECOMOG in 1990 to stop the Liberian civil war. Nigeria provided most of the troops and money. ECOMOG later also served in Sierra Leone.

whyNot.A: Ghana contributed troops but did not have a civil war needing ECOMOG.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Two heads of state given much credit for the founding of ECOWAS in 1975 were Yakubu Gowon of Nigeria and
questions.explanation: Gowon and Eyadéma of Togo worked together from the early 1970s to bring English- and French-speaking West African countries into one economic community, leading to the Treaty of Lagos in 1975.

whyNot.C: Nkrumah was overthrown in 1966 and died in 1972, before ECOWAS was formed.
whyNot.A: Tanzania is in East Africa and is not part of ECOWAS.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: When it was formed, the main aim of ECOWAS was to
options: promote economic co-operation and integration among member states
settle disputes between the Cold War superpowers
replace the national armies of members with one army
questions.explanation: ECOWAS was set up to promote economic co-operation: trade, free movement of people, and development across West Africa. Peacekeeping (ECOMOG) was added later.

whyNot.A: The fight against apartheid was mainly led through the OAU and the UN.
whyNot.D: ECOWAS never aimed to abolish national armies.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In the 1961 plebiscite supervised by the United Nations, the people of the Northern Cameroons voted to
options: remain a trust territory under Britain
questions.explanation: The British Cameroons had been a UN trust territory administered with Nigeria. In 1961 the Northern Cameroons voted to join Nigeria, while the Southern Cameroons voted to join the Republic of Cameroon.

whyNot.D: It was the Southern Cameroons that chose to join Cameroon.
whyNot.A: Independence as a separate state was not one of the choices offered.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Before the OAU was formed, Nigeria under Balewa belonged to the Monrovia Group, which favoured
options: an immediate union government for the whole of Africa
a military alliance with the Western powers
keeping colonial rule until all states were ready
gradual co-operation among African states that respected each state's sovereignty
questions.explanation: The Monrovia Group, including Nigeria and Liberia, wanted unity to grow gradually through economic and functional co-operation while each state kept its sovereignty. Nkrumah's Casablanca Group wanted immediate political union.

whyNot.A: Immediate union was the position of the Casablanca Group.
whyNot.C: Both groups supported the end of colonial rule.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Songhai Empire collapsed after its army was defeated in 1591 by invaders from
questions.explanation: A Moroccan army armed with firearms crossed the Sahara and defeated the Songhai army at Tondibi in 1591. Songhai broke up after this defeat.

whyNot.A: The Portuguese traded on the coast and did not invade Songhai.
whyNot.D: Mali had itself been overtaken by Songhai long before 1591.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.context:
When Mama Rukayat first agreed to accept bank transfers at her pepper stall in Ipata Market, Ilorin, she did it reluctantly. Her customers had been arriving without cash for months, ever since notes became hard to find, and she was tired of watching them walk away to the next stall. Her nephew opened an account for her on his phone, wrote the account number on a sheet of cardboard and nailed it to the post above her trays.

The first weeks were anxious ones. Every time a customer said "I have sent it", she would stare at her phone, waiting for the alert, while a queue grew behind. Twice the alert never came, and she had to choose between trusting a stranger and insulting a customer. She trusted, and once she was wrong.

Yet by the end of the year she would not go back. She no longer kept a tin of money under her stool, which thieves had once snatched in broad daylight. She could see at a glance how much she had sold each week, something her old notebook had never told her honestly. When the bank offered her a small loan on the strength of those records, she bought a freezer and began selling ground pepper to restaurants.

"Cash is sweet in the hand," she told her nephew, "but it does not remember anything."
questions.stem: Why did Mama Rukayat begin to accept bank transfers at her stall?
options: Customers often had no cash and she was losing sales to other stalls
The bank offered her a loan if she opened an account
Thieves had stolen the tin of money under her stool
Her nephew wanted to start a business selling phones
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says customers had been arriving without cash and she was tired of watching them walk away to the next stall, so she accepted transfers to keep their business.

whyNot.B: The loan came at the end of the year, after she had been keeping records, not at the start.
whyNot.C: The theft is mentioned as something transfers protected her from later; it is not given as the reason she started.

questions.stem: "She had to choose between trusting a stranger and insulting a customer." This means that when no alert came, Mama Rukayat
options: had to decide whether to sell to strangers or only to regular customers
had to choose between two customers who wanted the same pepper
could either believe the buyer had paid or risk offending someone who might be honest
was forced to report the buyer to the market police
questions.explanation: Without an alert she could not tell whether the money had been sent. Accepting the customer's word meant trusting a stranger; demanding proof or refusing the goods might insult a buyer who had really paid.

whyNot.A: The passage does not divide her customers into strangers and regulars; the choice is about one buyer whose payment has not shown.
whyNot.D: No police or report is mentioned.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.context:
When Mama Rukayat first agreed to accept bank transfers at her pepper stall in Ipata Market, Ilorin, she did it reluctantly. Her customers had been arriving without cash for months, ever since notes became hard to find, and she was tired of watching them walk away to the next stall. Her nephew opened an account for her on his phone, wrote the account number on a sheet of cardboard and nailed it to the post above her trays.

The first weeks were anxious ones. Every time a customer said "I have sent it", she would stare at her phone, waiting for the alert, while a queue grew behind. Twice the alert never came, and she had to choose between trusting a stranger and insulting a customer. She trusted, and once she was wrong.

Yet by the end of the year she would not go back. She no longer kept a tin of money under her stool, which thieves had once snatched in broad daylight. She could see at a glance how much she had sold each week, something her old notebook had never told her honestly. When the bank offered her a small loan on the strength of those records, she bought a freezer and began selling ground pepper to restaurants.

"Cash is sweet in the hand," she told her nephew, "but it does not remember anything."
questions.stem: The sentence "She trusted, and once she was wrong" suggests that
options: both missing alerts turned out to be bank errors
on one occasion a customer took the pepper without really paying
she stopped trusting customers after the first week
she wrongly accused an honest customer of cheating
questions.explanation: She chose to trust the customers whose alerts did not arrive. Being "wrong" once means that one of those two customers had not actually sent the money, so she lost the sale.

whyNot.C: The passage shows she kept trusting; nothing says she stopped.
whyNot.D: She did not accuse anyone; she trusted them, which is why she could be "wrong".

questions.stem: Which of the following benefits of bank transfers is NOT mentioned in the passage?
options: A clearer record of her weekly sales
Being able to obtain a loan
Less risk of losing cash to thieves
questions.explanation: The third paragraph gives three benefits: she no longer kept a tin of cash that could be stolen, she could see her weekly sales at a glance, and her records earned her a loan. Nothing is said about her suppliers' prices.

whyNot.C: The tin of money that thieves had once snatched shows that safety from theft is mentioned.
whyNot.B: The bank offered her a loan "on the strength of those records".

options: written in a language she could not read

whyNot.D: Nothing suggests the nephew took the notebook; he helped her set up the account.
whyNot.A: The point is about how reliable the records were, not about hiding them.

questions.stem: "Cash is sweet in the hand, but it does not remember anything." By this, Mama Rukayat means that cash
options: is pleasant to hold but leaves no record of what was bought and sold
loses its value quickly when prices rise
should be spent before it is stolen
is easily forgotten by careless traders
questions.explanation: "Sweet in the hand" admits that holding cash feels good. "Does not remember anything" contrasts it with bank transfers, which keep a record of every payment, the very records that got her the loan.

whyNot.B: Inflation is not discussed anywhere in the passage.
whyNot.D: It is the cash that cannot "remember", not traders who forget it.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.context:
It has become fashionable to say that young people no longer read. The charge is only half true. A typical student today reads more words in a day than her grandparents did in a week: messages, captions, comments, headlines, notes shared in class group chats. What has changed is not the amount of reading but its kind. Most of it comes in fragments, and most of it is abandoned the moment something brighter appears on the screen.

Reading a book demands a different skill. A novel or a history asks the reader to hold a long argument or a large cast of characters in mind across many pages, and to tolerate a slow chapter for the sake of a later reward. That skill, like a muscle, weakens when it is not used. Teachers notice it first: students who can summarise a two-minute video perfectly may struggle to follow a three-page essay.

The answer is not to throw away the phone, which is also a library in the pocket. It is to practise sustained reading deliberately, as athletes practise endurance. Twenty minutes a day with one text, without switching, is a modest beginning. Schools that have set aside such a period report that students complain for a fortnight and then, quietly, begin to ask for the next book.
questions.stem: What is the writer's view of the claim that young people no longer read?
options: It is partly true: they read a great deal, but mostly in short fragments
It is entirely true, because phones have replaced all reading
It is completely false, since students read more books than before
It cannot be judged without a scientific survey
questions.explanation: The writer calls the charge "only half true": students read many words every day, but the reading comes in fragments rather than long, sustained texts.

whyNot.C: The writer does not say they read more books; the extra reading is messages, captions and headlines.
whyNot.B: "Only half true" rules out "entirely true".

questions.stem: According to the passage, what has changed about young people's reading?
options: The time of day they read
The amount of reading they do
The kind of reading they do
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says directly: "What has changed is not the amount of reading but its kind."

whyNot.C: The writer says the amount has not fallen; students read more words than their grandparents.

options: students summarise better than their teachers
teachers set essays that are too long
the ability to follow long texts weakens when it is not practised
videos are a better way to learn than essays
questions.explanation: The example comes straight after the claim that the skill of sustained reading, "like a muscle, weakens when it is not used". It illustrates that weakening.

whyNot.D: The writer does not rank videos above essays; the point is about a skill that is fading.
whyNot.B: Nothing suggests the essays are unreasonable; three pages is short.

questions.stem: What is the writer's attitude to the mobile phone?

It is the only cause of poor reading
It should be banned from schools
It has no place in serious study

whyNot.C: The writer rejects throwing the phone away and never suggests a ban.
whyNot.D: Calling it "a library in the pocket" gives it a place in study.

options: a video summarised in two minutes
a library kept in the pocket
questions.explanation: The writer says we should "practise sustained reading deliberately, as athletes practise endurance": regular training builds the capacity, just as it does for a runner.

whyNot.D: "A library in the pocket" describes the phone, not sustained reading.
whyNot.C: The video is an example of short-form content, the opposite of sustained reading.

questions.stem: "Students complain for a fortnight and then, quietly, begin to ask for the next book." This suggests that
options: the reading period lasts for only two weeks
students read only to stop teachers complaining
students complain so much that the period is cancelled
early resistance to the reading period gives way to real interest
questions.explanation: After two weeks of complaint, students start asking for more books of their own accord. "Quietly" stresses that the change is genuine rather than forced: the habit has taken hold.

whyNot.C: Students asking for "the next book" shows the period continues.
whyNot.A: "A fortnight" is how long the complaining lasts, not the reading period.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.context:
Baba Audu was seventy-one when he enrolled in the adult literacy class held every Thursday evening in the primary school near his house in Bauchi. The other learners were market women and young drivers, and for the first month he sat at the back, saying nothing, his hands folded over his walking stick.

His teacher, a corps member from Ekiti, assumed he had come only for company. Then one evening, as the class was ending, the old man walked slowly to the board, took the chalk from her hand and wrote, in large uneven letters, the name of his late wife. He looked at it for a long time. "For forty years," he said, "I signed with my thumb. Now she has a name I can read."

Nobody spoke. The corps member, who had been counting the weeks until her service year ended, found that she no longer wanted to count.
questions.stem: Why did the teacher at first think Baba Audu had joined the literacy class?
options: Because his late wife had asked him to
To escort one of the young drivers
questions.explanation: The passage says the corps member "assumed he had come only for company", because he sat silently at the back for a month.

whyNot.C: His wife is mentioned only when he writes her name; nothing says she asked him to enrol.

questions.stem: How did Baba Audu behave during his first month in the class?
options: He was quiet and kept to himself
questions.explanation: For the first month "he sat at the back, saying nothing, his hands folded over his walking stick": a picture of a quiet, withdrawn learner.

whyNot.B: He said nothing, so he did not interrupt.
whyNot.A: Nothing shows him helping anyone.

questions.context:

questions.stem: "For forty years I signed with my thumb." This tells us that Baba Audu
options: had hurt his hand forty years earlier
had refused to sign any document
had not been able to write his name and used a thumbprint instead
worked as a clerk who signed documents
questions.explanation: People who cannot write often "sign" with an inked thumbprint. Combined with his joining a literacy class, the line shows he had been unable to write for forty years.

whyNot.D: A clerk would need to read and write, which he could not do.
whyNot.B: He did sign, but with his thumb rather than with a pen.

questions.context:

questions.stem: "Nobody spoke." The silence after Baba Audu wrote on the board suggests that the class was
options: confused about what he had written
deeply moved by what he had done
bored and waiting to go home
angry that he had taken the chalk
questions.explanation: The silence follows an emotional moment: an old man writing his late wife's name for the first time. Nobody speaks because they are touched, not because they object or are bored.

whyNot.D: Nothing suggests anyone was angry; the teacher's feelings change for the better.
whyNot.A: He explained clearly what the name meant, so there was nothing to be confused about.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.context:

questions.stem: The last sentence of the passage suggests that the corps member
options: had lost count of the weeks
was eager to return to Ekiti
had found new meaning in her work
had decided to extend her service year
questions.explanation: Before, she was "counting the weeks" until her service ended, a sign of impatience. Afterwards she "no longer wanted to count": the old man's achievement made her work feel worthwhile.

whyNot.D: Not wanting to count the weeks is a change of feeling, not a formal decision to extend her service.
whyNot.A: "No longer wanted to count" is about her attitude, not her memory.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The panel found the witness's story PLAUSIBLE.
questions.explanation: "Plausible" means seeming reasonable or likely to be true, so the nearest meaning is "believable".

whyNot.C: "Ridiculous" is close to the opposite of plausible.
whyNot.D: A contradictory story would not seem plausible.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The governor's AMBIVALENT remarks on the policy left journalists unsure of his position.
questions.explanation: "Ambivalent" means having mixed or contradictory feelings about something. The sentence confirms this: the remarks left journalists unsure where he stood.

whyNot.A: Hostile remarks would show a clear position against the policy.
whyNot.D: Enthusiastic remarks would show clear support, not uncertainty.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The chairman spoke with great OPTIMISM about the economy.
questions.explanation: "Optimism" is the belief that things will turn out well. Its opposite is "pessimism", the expectation that things will go badly.

whyNot.A: "Hope" is close in meaning to optimism, not opposite.
whyNot.C: Anger is a feeling, but it is not the opposite of expecting good outcomes.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: Nkechi's ADAMANT refusal to change her answer surprised the examiners.
questions.explanation: "Adamant" means firm and unwilling to change one's mind. The opposite is "yielding": willing to give way.

whyNot.B: "Stubborn" has nearly the same meaning as adamant.
whyNot.D: "Sudden" refers to timing, not firmness.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: Zainab is one of the girls who ___ in the school choir.
questions.explanation: The relative pronoun "who" refers to "the girls" (plural), not to "one". So the verb in the relative clause must be plural: "the girls who sing".

whyNot.A: "Sings" wrongly makes "who" agree with "one"; it is the girls who sing.
whyNot.C: "Has sung" is singular and also changes the meaning to a single past event.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: The number of applicants for the scholarship ___ risen sharply this year.
questions.explanation: The subject is "the number" (singular), so it takes "has". Compare "A number of applicants have applied", where "a number of" means "many" and takes a plural verb.

whyNot.D: "Have" agrees with "applicants", but the head of the subject is "the number".
whyNot.C: "Are risen" is not a correct verb form.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: Hardly ___ the bell rung when the students rushed out of the hall.
questions.explanation: When a sentence begins with "hardly", the subject and auxiliary are inverted, and the past perfect is used for the earlier action: "Hardly had the bell rung when…".

whyNot.A: "Has" is present perfect and clashes with the past tense "rushed".
whyNot.D: "Did" needs the base form ("did the bell ring"), not "rung".

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: The cashier was accused ___ fraud by the bank's auditors.
questions.explanation: In standard English we accuse someone OF a wrongdoing. (By contrast, someone is "charged with" an offence.)

whyNot.C: "Accused for" is a common error.
whyNot.B: "With" goes with "charged", not "accused".

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: Ten kilometres ___ a long distance to walk to school every day.
questions.explanation: A distance, sum of money or period of time treated as a single amount takes a singular verb, even though the noun is plural: "Ten kilometres is a long distance".

whyNot.D: "Are" treats the kilometres as separate items, but the sentence is about one total distance.
whyNot.A: "Were" is both plural and past, while "every day" points to a present habit.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: In her first week at the new school, the teacher was still LEARNING THE ROPES. This means that she was
options: learning how things are done in her new job
getting into trouble with the principal
learning to climb for a sports competition
questions.explanation: "To learn the ropes" is an idiom meaning to learn the basic procedures of a new job or situation.

whyNot.D: The idiom is not about real ropes or climbing.
whyNot.C: Nothing in the idiom suggests trouble.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Winning the national debate was A FEATHER IN ADA'S CAP. This means that the victory was
options: a reason for others to be jealous
a small prize of little value
an unfair advantage given to her
an achievement she could be proud of
questions.explanation: "A feather in one's cap" is an idiom for an achievement that earns praise and pride.

whyNot.B: The idiom stresses honour, not that the prize is worthless.
whyNot.A: Others may be jealous, but that is not what the idiom means.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: By the time the meeting started, the report ___ by the secretary.
questions.explanation: The report is the thing acted on, so a passive form is needed. The writing was finished before another past action (the meeting started), so the past perfect passive is right: "had been written".

whyNot.C: "Has been written" is present perfect and does not fit "started".
whyNot.A: "Was writing" is active: it would mean the report itself was writing something.
whyNot.D: "Had written" is active and needs an object.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: Let's go to the stadium after lunch, ___?
questions.explanation: A suggestion beginning with "Let's" (let us) takes the question tag "shall we?": "Let's go, shall we?"

whyNot.D: "Will you?" is the tag for a command to someone else ("Close the door, will you?"), not a suggestion including the speaker.
whyNot.C: "Isn't it?" is a common error; there is no "it" or "is" in the sentence.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: In the sentence "The FAST will end at sunset", the word in capitals is used as
questions.explanation: Here "fast" means a period of going without food. It follows the article "the" and is the subject of "will end", so it is a noun.

whyNot.A: "Fast" is a verb in "They fast during Ramadan", but here it follows "the" and is the subject.
whyNot.D: "Fast" is an adjective in "a fast car", but here it is not describing a noun.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: "We stayed indoors because it was raining heavily." The words "because it was raining heavily" form
questions.explanation: The clause has its own subject and verb ("it was raining") and tells us WHY we stayed indoors. A clause introduced by "because" that gives a reason is an adverbial clause of reason.

whyNot.A: An adjectival clause describes a noun, often beginning with who, which or that.
whyNot.C: A clause of time answers "when?" and usually begins with when, after, before or until.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: "Tunde is not as tall as his younger brother." This sentence means that
options: Tunde will soon be as tall as his younger brother
Tunde is taller than his younger brother
Tunde's younger brother is taller than Tunde
Tunde and his younger brother are the same height
questions.explanation: "Not as tall as" means "shorter than". If Tunde is shorter than his younger brother, the younger brother is the taller of the two.

whyNot.B: This reverses the meaning.
whyNot.D: "As tall as" would mean the same height, but the sentence says "not as tall as".

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Choose the correctly spelt word to complete the sentence: Being chosen as head girl is a great ___.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is p-r-i-v-i-l-e-g-e. There is no "d" (unlike "knowledge"), and the vowels are i, i, e, e.

whyNot.C: Adding a "d" is a common error, copied from words like "knowledge".
whyNot.B: The last vowel is "e", not "a".

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the one in "tongue".
questions.explanation: "Tongue" is /tʌŋ/, with the short vowel /ʌ/ as in "cup". "Young" is /jʌŋ/, with the same vowel.

whyNot.B: "Tone" has the diphthong /əʊ/.
whyNot.D: "Tong" has /ɒ/, as in "pot"; the spelling misleads.
whyNot.C: "Town" has the diphthong /aʊ/.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Which of these words contains the vowel sound /ɜː/, as in "bird"?
questions.explanation: "Journey" is /ˈdʒɜːni/: the "our" spelling here gives /ɜː/, the same vowel as in "bird" and "word".

whyNot.C: "Bury" is /ˈberi/, with /e/ as in "bed".
whyNot.B: "Heart" is /hɑːt/, with /ɑː/.
whyNot.D: "Board" is /bɔːd/, with /ɔː/.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Three of these words share the same vowel sound. Which one does not?
questions.explanation: "Said" /sed/, "bread" /bred/ and "friend" /frend/ all have the short vowel /e/. "Paid" /peɪd/ has the diphthong /eɪ/.

whyNot.C: "Said" looks like "paid" but is pronounced /sed/, with /e/.
whyNot.A: "Friend" is /frend/, with /e/ despite the "ie" spelling.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: In which of these words is "ch" pronounced /k/?
questions.explanation: "Stomach" is /ˈstʌmək/: the "ch" is pronounced /k/, as in many words from Greek.

whyNot.D: "Chief" begins with /tʃ/.
whyNot.A: "Chef" (from French) begins with /ʃ/.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: In which of these words is "th" pronounced /t/?
questions.explanation: In "Thomas" /ˈtɒməs/ the "th" is pronounced as a plain /t/. This happens in a few names such as Thomas and Thames.

whyNot.A: "Thought" begins with /θ/.
whyNot.B: "Though" begins with /ð/.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: In which of these words is the letter "l" silent?
questions.explanation: "Palm" is /pɑːm/: the "l" is not pronounced, as in "calm" and "half".

whyNot.A: "Bold" is /bəʊld/; the /l/ is heard.
whyNot.B: "Film" is /fɪlm/; the /l/ is heard.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: In which of these words is the "-ed" ending pronounced /ɪd/?
questions.explanation: The "-ed" ending is pronounced /ɪd/ after /t/ or /d/. "Need" ends in /d/, so "needed" is /ˈniːdɪd/.

whyNot.C: "Laughed" ends in /t/ (after the voiceless /f/).
whyNot.A: "Cleaned" ends in /d/ (after the voiced /n/).
whyNot.B: "Watched" ends in /t/ (after the voiceless /tʃ/).

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: In which of these words is the plural ending pronounced /ɪz/?
questions.explanation: The plural ending is pronounced /ɪz/ after hissing and hushing sounds such as /s/, /z/, /ʃ/, /tʃ/ and /dʒ/. "Bridge" ends in /dʒ/, so "bridges" is /ˈbrɪdʒɪz/.

whyNot.C: "Cups" ends in /s/ (after the voiceless /p/).
whyNot.D: "Bags" ends in /z/ (after the voiced /ɡ/).

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Choose the word that carries its main stress on the third syllable.
questions.explanation: "Engineer" is en-gi-NEER, /ˌendʒɪˈnɪə/: words ending in -eer are stressed on that ending.

whyNot.B: "Candidate" is stressed on the first syllable: CAN-di-date.
whyNot.C: "Government" is stressed on the first syllable: GOV-ern-ment.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Which of these words has a different stress pattern from the other three?
questions.explanation: "Decide" is stressed on the second syllable (de-CIDE). "Borrow", "village" and "carpet" are all stressed on the first syllable.

whyNot.A: BOR-row is stressed on the first syllable, like the other two.
whyNot.B: VIL-lage is stressed on the first syllable.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: In the sentence "The workers will protest against the new tax", the word "protest" is stressed on
options: the first syllable, because it is a noun
the first syllable, because it is a verb
the second syllable, because it is a verb
questions.explanation: Many two-syllable words are stressed on the first syllable as nouns (a PROtest) and on the second as verbs (to proTEST). Here "protest" follows "will", so it is a verb: pro-TEST.

whyNot.C: A verb in this group takes second-syllable stress, not first.
whyNot.A: In this sentence "protest" is a verb, not a noun.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Which of these related words is stressed on the third syllable?
questions.explanation: "Democratic" is de-mo-CRA-tic: words ending in -ic are stressed on the syllable just before the ending. The stress moves as the word changes form.

whyNot.C: "Democracy" is stressed on the second syllable: de-MOC-ra-cy.
whyNot.D: "Democrat" is stressed on the first syllable: DEM-o-crat.
whyNot.A: "Demonstrate" is stressed on the first syllable: DEM-on-strate.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem:
In the sentence below, the word in capitals carries the emphatic stress. Which question does the sentence answer?
The principal suspended THREE students yesterday.
options: When did the principal suspend three students?
How many students did the principal suspend yesterday?
Did the principal expel three students yesterday?
questions.explanation: Emphatic stress falls on the word that supplies the new or corrected information. Stressing THREE answers a question about the number of students.

whyNot.A: That question would be answered by stressing PRINCIPAL.
whyNot.B: That question would be answered by stressing YESTERDAY.
whyNot.D: That question would be answered by stressing SUSPENDED.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: "You are the new prefect, aren't you?" If the speaker says the question tag with a falling tune, the speaker
options: has no idea and genuinely wants information
is giving the listener an order
is fairly sure and expects the listener to agree
questions.explanation: In RP, a question tag with a falling tune asks for confirmation of something the speaker already believes. A rising tune on the tag shows real uncertainty and asks for information.

whyNot.A: Genuine uncertainty is shown by a rising tune on the tag.
whyNot.B: A question tag after a statement is not a command.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Which word is represented by the phonetic transcription /ˈwɪmɪn/?
questions.explanation: /ˈwɪmɪn/ has /ɪ/ in both syllables. This is "women": the first "o" is pronounced /ɪ/, an unusual spelling.

whyNot.C: "Woman" is /ˈwʊmən/, with /ʊ/ in the first syllable.
whyNot.A: "Woven" is /ˈwəʊvn/.

questions.subject: use-of-english
questions.stem: Which of these words contains the consonant sound /ʒ/?
questions.explanation: "Vision" is /ˈvɪʒn/: the "s" before "-ion" is pronounced /ʒ/, the voiced sound heard in "measure".

whyNot.C: "Mission" has the voiceless /ʃ/: /ˈmɪʃn/.
whyNot.A: "Station" has /ʃ/: /ˈsteɪʃn/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.context:
The borehole in Igbo-Ora had been broken for three months when Kehinde's grandmother announced that she would fetch water from the stream again, as she had done as a girl. Nobody believed she meant it. She was seventy, and the stream was two kilometres away, down a slope that turned to mud whenever it rained.

On the first morning, Kehinde found her already at the door with a bucket on her head. He took it from her, half in protest and half in shame, and carried it himself. The next day two of his friends came along, mainly to laugh at him. By the end of the week there were nine boys on the path every morning, and the laughter had turned into a competition to see who could carry the most without spilling a drop.

It was one of those boys, whose uncle worked at the local government secretariat, who finally carried the community's complaint to the right office. Within a month, a technician came to replace the pump.

The boys were almost disappointed. The grandmother was not. "Water that comes easily," she said, "teaches nobody anything. You have learnt something. Now go and read your books."
questions.stem: Why did Kehinde's grandmother decide to fetch water from the stream?
options: Kehinde had refused to fetch water for her
She wanted to teach the boys a lesson
The borehole had been broken for three months
The stream water was cleaner than the borehole water
questions.explanation: The first sentence links the two: the borehole had been broken for three months, so she announced she would go back to the stream.

whyNot.B: The lesson came at the end, as a result; it was not her reason for going.
whyNot.A: Kehinde took the bucket from her the first morning; he never refused.

options: She was old and the path to the stream was long and difficult

She had never fetched water in her life
She often made promises she did not keep

whyNot.B: The stream still had water; she and the boys fetched from it.

questions.stem: Kehinde took the bucket "half in protest and half in shame". This means that he
options: was angry with his grandmother and ashamed of her
protested to the local government and felt ashamed of the village
objected to her doing the work and was embarrassed that he had not done it himself
did not want to carry the bucket but was forced to
questions.explanation: "Protest" shows he did not want a seventy-year-old woman carrying water; "shame" shows he felt embarrassed that she was doing work a young man like him should be doing.

whyNot.A: His shame is about himself, not about his grandmother.
whyNot.B: The complaint to the local government came later and was carried by another boy.

They refused to come until the technician arrived
They came to laugh at him but ended up competing to carry water
They laughed at the grandmother throughout the week

whyNot.A: This reverses the order: the laughing came first.

The boys raised money to buy a new pump

questions.stem: "Water that comes easily teaches nobody anything." What does the grandmother mean by this?

Children should not be given water too easily
Water from the stream is better for learning
Borehole water is not as pure as stream water

whyNot.D: She is not comparing the quality of the water.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.context:
In the weeks before the WASSCE, many students treat sleep as a luxury they cannot afford. They read until two or three in the morning, drink strong coffee to stay awake and boast to one another about how little rest they need. It looks like dedication. In fact, it is often the surest way to waste the hours they are working so hard to gain.

Sleep is not simply a pause in the day's work. While we sleep, the brain sorts through what it has taken in, discarding some things and storing others more firmly. A student who studies a chemistry topic in the evening and then sleeps well is more likely to remember it in the morning than one who stays awake going over it again and again. Tiredness also slows thinking and shortens tempers, so the student who has not slept reads the same paragraph four times and remembers none of it.

None of this is an excuse for laziness. The student who sleeps eight hours but spends the evening scrolling through social media has gained nothing. The lesson is that rest and study are partners, not rivals. A sensible timetable makes room for both, and it starts early enough in the term that the last weeks are for revision, not for panic.
questions.stem: According to the passage, why do many students sleep very little before the WASSCE?
options: Their teachers tell them to read all night
They believe the extra hours of reading will help them
They are too anxious to fall asleep
Coffee keeps them awake against their will
questions.explanation: Students "treat sleep as a luxury they cannot afford": they give up sleep because they think the extra hours of study will improve their results.

whyNot.A: No teacher's instruction is mentioned.
whyNot.D: They drink coffee on purpose "to stay awake".

options: seems like commitment but often does more harm than good
is the best sign of a dedicated student
is only possible for very strong students

It prepares the body for the next meal
It forgets everything learnt that day

whyNot.A: The writer says sleep is "not simply a pause".
whyNot.D: Only some things are discarded; others are stored more firmly.

a student who has slept too much
the effect of tiredness on concentration
the danger of studying chemistry at night

whyNot.A: The problem is not reading speed but tiredness.

options: rest and study support each other
rest and study should be done at the same time
students should rest instead of studying
study is more important than rest
questions.explanation: Partners work together; rivals compete. The writer means that sleep helps study succeed, so the two belong together in a timetable rather than fighting for the same hours.

whyNot.C: The writer says plainly that sleep is "not an excuse for laziness".
whyNot.D: The point is that neither should crowd out the other.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the writer's main purpose in the passage?
options: To explain how the brain stores chemistry
To encourage students to spend less time on social media
To warn students against drinking coffee
To persuade students that enough sleep is part of good exam preparation
questions.explanation: Every paragraph builds one argument: giving up sleep wastes study time, sleep helps memory, and rest and study should be planned together. The coffee, chemistry and social media details only support this.

whyNot.C: Coffee is mentioned once, as part of the picture of late-night study.
whyNot.B: Social media is one example in the last paragraph, not the main point.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.context:
Harmattan Morning

The sun comes up like a coin seen through water,
pale and unhurried over Kaduna's roofs.
Dust has settled on the windscreens overnight,
writing its fine grey signature on everything.
My mother wraps her shawl twice round her shoulders
and complains, as she does every December,
that her lips have cracked like a dry riverbed.
But the children, who have never known another December,
run to school rubbing their hands together,
laughing at the cold as if they had invented it.
questions.stem: "The sun comes up like a coin seen through water." The figure of speech used in this line is
questions.explanation: The line compares the sun to a coin using the word "like". A direct comparison with "like" or "as" is a simile.

whyNot.D: A metaphor makes the comparison without "like" or "as" ("the sun is a coin").
whyNot.C: Personification gives human qualities to a thing; here the sun is compared to an object.

But the children, who have never known another December,
run to school rubbing their hands together,
laughing at the cold as if they had invented it.
questions.stem: By comparing the sun to "a coin seen through water", the poet suggests that the sun looks
options: dim and blurred through the dusty air
small and far away in the evening
questions.explanation: A coin seen through water looks faint and wavering. The next line, "pale and unhurried", and the dust of the harmattan explain why the morning sun looks dim.

whyNot.A: "Pale" contradicts "bright and burning".
whyNot.C: Harmattan is the dry season; the water is only part of the comparison.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.context:
Harmattan Morning

The sun comes up like a coin seen through water,
pale and unhurried over Kaduna's roofs.
Dust has settled on the windscreens overnight,
writing its fine grey signature on everything.
My mother wraps her shawl twice round her shoulders
and complains, as she does every December,
that her lips have cracked like a dry riverbed.
But the children, who have never known another December,
run to school rubbing their hands together,
laughing at the cold as if they had invented it.
questions.stem: "Writing its fine grey signature on everything" suggests that the dust
options: is so thick that nothing can be seen
has left a thin layer on every surface
has been used by children to write their names
has fallen only on the windscreens
questions.explanation: "Fine" means very thin and "on everything" shows how widely it has spread. The dust is pictured as signing its name on every surface it touches.

whyNot.A: "Fine" points to a thin layer, not a thick one.
whyNot.D: "On everything" goes beyond the windscreens.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.context:
Harmattan Morning

The sun comes up like a coin seen through water,
pale and unhurried over Kaduna's roofs.
Dust has settled on the windscreens overnight,
writing its fine grey signature on everything.
My mother wraps her shawl twice round her shoulders
and complains, as she does every December,
that her lips have cracked like a dry riverbed.
But the children, who have never known another December,
run to school rubbing their hands together,
laughing at the cold as if they had invented it.
questions.stem: How does the children's response to the harmattan differ from the mother's?
options: The mother finds it uncomfortable, while the children enjoy it
Both the mother and the children dislike it
The children stay indoors, while the mother goes out
The mother enjoys it, while the children complain
questions.explanation: The mother wraps up and complains about cracked lips; the poem then turns with "But" to the children, who run to school "laughing at the cold".

whyNot.D: This reverses the two responses.
whyNot.C: The children run to school; they do not stay indoors.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.context:
Harmattan Morning

The sun comes up like a coin seen through water,
pale and unhurried over Kaduna's roofs.
Dust has settled on the windscreens overnight,
writing its fine grey signature on everything.

and complains, as she does every December,
that her lips have cracked like a dry riverbed.
But the children, who have never known another December,

laughing at the cold as if they had invented it.
questions.stem: The line "who have never known another December" suggests that the children
options: are young and accept the harmattan as a normal part of life
do not know the names of the months
questions.explanation: Every December they have known has been a harmattan December, so for them the cold and dust are simply how the season is. Unlike the mother, they have nothing to compare it with and nothing to complain about.

whyNot.D: The poem gives no hint that they came from elsewhere.
whyNot.B: The line is about experience, not knowledge of the calendar.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The doctor warned that the disease was CONTAGIOUS.
questions.explanation: A contagious disease is one that spreads from person to person. The nearest meaning is "infectious".

whyNot.A: A disease can be contagious without being deadly.
whyNot.C: "Incurable" is about treatment, not spread.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The villagers were APPREHENSIVE about the arrival of the soldiers.
questions.explanation: "Apprehensive" means worried or uneasy that something bad may happen. The nearest meaning is "anxious".

whyNot.C: "Excited" suggests eager expectation, the opposite of unease.
whyNot.B: "Ignorant" means unaware; apprehensive people know something is coming.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The coach gave a TERSE reply when reporters asked about the defeat.
questions.explanation: "Terse" describes speech that uses few words, often in an abrupt way. The nearest meaning is "brief".

whyNot.C: "Lengthy" is the opposite.
whyNot.A: Nothing in "terse" suggests humour.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: Though she became famous, the singer remained HUMBLE.
questions.explanation: "Humble" means not proud. Its opposite is "arrogant": proud and acting as if one is better than others.

whyNot.B: "Modest" is nearly the same as humble.
whyNot.C: "Humble" can describe poor surroundings, but here it describes a famous person's attitude.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: After a long trial, the court ACQUITTED the accused.
questions.explanation: To acquit is to declare someone not guilty. The opposite is to convict: to declare someone guilty.

whyNot.B: "Freed" is close in meaning to acquitted.
whyNot.D: "Released" is also close in meaning.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: Farming is difficult in the ARID parts of the country.
questions.explanation: "Arid" means having very little rain, too dry to support much plant life. Its opposite is "wet".

whyNot.A: "Dry" is the meaning of arid, not its opposite.
whyNot.D: Arid areas are often hot, but "hot" is about temperature, not rainfall.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: Bread and butter ___ my usual breakfast on school days.
questions.explanation: "Bread and butter" is two nouns joined by "and", but together they name a single dish, so the verb is singular: "Bread and butter is my usual breakfast."

whyNot.D: "Are" treats bread and butter as two separate things, but here they form one meal.
whyNot.B: "Were" is plural and past, while "usual" points to a present habit.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: I ___ my homework before my father came home yesterday.
questions.explanation: Two past actions are described. The one that happened first (finishing the homework) takes the past perfect, "had finished"; the later one takes the simple past, "came".

whyNot.A: "Have finished" is present perfect and cannot be used with "yesterday".
whyNot.C: "Will finish" is future, but the sentence is about yesterday.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: If it rains tomorrow, we ___ the inter-house sports.
questions.explanation: This is a first (open) conditional about a real possibility: "if" + present tense, then "will" + base verb.

whyNot.C: "Would postponed" is never correct: "would" takes the base form.
whyNot.D: "Would have postponed" belongs to the third conditional, about the past.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: The suspect was charged ___ armed robbery.
questions.explanation: In standard English a person is charged WITH an offence. (A person is accused OF an offence.)

whyNot.A: "Charged for" is used for prices ("charged ₦500 for the book"), not offences.
whyNot.C: "Of" goes with "accused" or "convicted", not "charged".

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: Between you and ___, I don't think the plan will work.
questions.explanation: "Between" is a preposition, so the pronouns after it are objects: "between you and me".

whyNot.D: "I" is a subject pronoun; using it after a preposition is a common error.
whyNot.A: "Myself" is reflexive and needs "I" as the subject of the same clause.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: The two brothers do not SEE EYE TO EYE on politics. This means that they
options: do not see each other often
do not look at each other
questions.explanation: "To see eye to eye" is an idiom meaning to agree. Not seeing eye to eye means holding different opinions.

whyNot.A: The idiom is about opinions, not about meeting.
whyNot.C: The idiom is not about looking at each other.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: After his release from prison, Sule decided to TURN OVER A NEW LEAF. This means that he decided to
options: write a book about his life
change his behaviour for the better
questions.explanation: "To turn over a new leaf" is an idiom meaning to start behaving in a better way.

whyNot.A: The idiom has nothing to do with plants or farming.
whyNot.B: The "leaf" is a page, but the idiom does not mean writing.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: The plan to raise school fees was NIPPED IN THE BUD. This means that the plan was
questions.explanation: "To nip something in the bud" means to stop it before it can develop, as cutting off a bud stops a flower from growing.

whyNot.D: The idiom is about stopping, not secrecy.
whyNot.B: A delayed plan may go ahead later; a plan nipped in the bud is stopped.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: "What the principal said at the assembly surprised the students." The words "what the principal said at the assembly" form
options: a noun clause, object of the verb "surprised"
a noun clause, subject of the verb "surprised"
questions.explanation: The clause does the job of a noun (you could replace it with "The speech"), and it comes before the verb as the thing that surprised: it is the subject of "surprised".

whyNot.B: The object of "surprised" is "the students".
whyNot.C: The clause does not describe a noun; it names the thing that surprised them.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Ada said, "I am tired of waiting." Which option is the correct reported form of this sentence?
options: Ada said that she was tired of waiting.
Ada said that I am tired of waiting.
Ada said that she is tired of waited.
Ada said that she has been tired of waiting.
questions.explanation: In reported speech after a past reporting verb, the pronoun changes (I → she) and the tense moves back (am → was): "Ada said that she was tired of waiting."

whyNot.B: The pronoun "I" must change to "she", since Ada is not the reporter.
whyNot.C: "Tired of waited" is ungrammatical.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the correctly spelt word to complete the sentence: Power cuts are a daily ___ in many towns.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is o-c-c-u-r-r-e-n-c-e: double "c", double "r", and "-ence" at the end.

whyNot.A: "Occurence" misses the second "r", the most common error.
whyNot.D: The ending is "-ence", not "-ance".

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words contains the vowel sound /ɒ/, as in "pot"?
questions.explanation: "Quality" is /ˈkwɒləti/: after /w/, the letter "a" is often pronounced /ɒ/, as in "want" and "what".

whyNot.D: "Water" is /ˈwɔːtə/, with /ɔː/.
whyNot.A: "Walk" is /wɔːk/, with /ɔː/.
whyNot.B: "Warm" is /wɔːm/, with /ɔː/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words contains the vowel sound /iː/, as in "seat"?
questions.explanation: "People" is /ˈpiːpl/: the "eo" spelling gives the long vowel /iː/.

whyNot.A: "Pretty" is /ˈprɪti/, with short /ɪ/.
whyNot.C: "Bread" is /bred/, with /e/.
whyNot.B: "Great" is /ɡreɪt/, with /eɪ/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words has the same vowel sound as "bed"?
questions.explanation: "Any" is /ˈeni/: the "a" is pronounced /e/, the same vowel as in "bed" /bed/.

whyNot.A: "Bead" has /iː/.
whyNot.B: "Bad" has /æ/.
whyNot.D: "Bird" has /ɜː/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words contains the diphthong /əʊ/, as in "go"?
questions.explanation: "Sew" (to stitch with a needle) is /səʊ/, pronounced like "so", despite its "ew" spelling.

whyNot.A: "New" is /njuː/.
whyNot.D: "Few" is /fjuː/.
whyNot.C: "Now" is /naʊ/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words contains the diphthong /aʊ/, as in "cow"?
questions.explanation: "Drought" is /draʊt/. The "ough" spelling has several pronunciations; in "drought" it is /aʊ/, as in "cow".

whyNot.C: "Dough" is /dəʊ/.
whyNot.A: "Through" is /θruː/.
whyNot.B: "Bought" is /bɔːt/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words has the same vowel sound as "gate"?
questions.explanation: "Break" is /breɪk/, with /eɪ/ as in "gate" /ɡeɪt/. It is one of the few "ea" words pronounced this way.

whyNot.A: "Breed" is /briːd/.
whyNot.B: "Bread" is /bred/.
whyNot.C: "Breath" is /breθ/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words contains the diphthong /ɪə/, as in "here"?
questions.explanation: "Pierce" is /pɪəs/, with the centring diphthong /ɪə/, as in "here" and "fear".

whyNot.C: "Pear" is /peə/, with /eə/.
whyNot.D: "Purse" is /pɜːs/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words contains the consonant sound /tʃ/?
questions.explanation: "Nature" is /ˈneɪtʃə/: the "t" before "-ure" is pronounced /tʃ/, as in "picture".

whyNot.D: "Chef" begins with /ʃ/.
whyNot.A: "Chorus" begins with /k/.
whyNot.C: "Giant" begins with /dʒ/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words begins with the consonant sound /θ/?
questions.explanation: "Thumb" is /θʌm/: it begins with the voiceless /θ/, as in "think".

whyNot.A: "Though" begins with the voiced /ð/.
whyNot.C: "Thames" is /temz/; the "th" is pronounced /t/.
whyNot.D: "That" begins with /ð/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: In which of the following words is "ng" pronounced /ŋ/ alone, with no /ɡ/ after it?
questions.explanation: "Singer" is formed from the verb "sing" + "-er", so it keeps the /ŋ/ of "sing": /ˈsɪŋə/. In "finger", "hunger" and the comparative "longer", RP has /ŋɡ/.

whyNot.B: "Finger" is /ˈfɪŋɡə/.
whyNot.A: "Longer" (more long) is /ˈlɒŋɡə/.
whyNot.C: "Hunger" is /ˈhʌŋɡə/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: In which of the following words is the letter "h" silent?
questions.explanation: "Honest" is /ˈɒnɪst/: it begins with a vowel sound, which is why we say "an honest man".

whyNot.B: "Behind" has /h/: /bɪˈhaɪnd/.
whyNot.D: "Hotel" has /h/ in RP: /həʊˈtel/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: In which of the following words is the letter "g" silent?
questions.explanation: "Sign" is /saɪn/: the "g" is silent. In "signal" and "signature", which come from the same root, the /ɡ/ is pronounced.

whyNot.D: "Signal" is /ˈsɪɡnəl/; the /ɡ/ is heard.
whyNot.A: "Signature" is /ˈsɪɡnətʃə/; the /ɡ/ is heard.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the word whose main stress falls on the second syllable.
questions.explanation: "Develop" is de-VE-lop, /dɪˈveləp/, stressed on the second syllable.

whyNot.A: "Quality" is QUA-li-ty, stressed on the first.
whyNot.C: "Character" is CHA-rac-ter, stressed on the first.
whyNot.B: "Interval" is IN-ter-val, stressed on the first.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: In which of the following sentences is the word in capitals stressed on the first syllable?
options: The governor will PRESENT the prizes.
I OBJECT to the new timetable.
Please do not REBEL against your parents.
The OBJECT on the table is a calculator.
questions.explanation: In pairs like object, present and rebel, the noun is stressed on the first syllable and the verb on the second. Only in the first sentence is the word a noun ("the object"): OB-ject.

whyNot.B: Here "object" is a verb: ob-JECT.
whyNot.A: Here "present" is a verb: pre-SENT.
whyNot.C: Here "rebel" is a verb: re-BEL.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: In the sentence "I bought yams, rice, beans and oil", the items in the list are normally said with
options: a falling tune on every item
a rising tune on each item and a falling tune on the last
a rising tune on every item, including the last
questions.explanation: In a list, a rising tune on each item tells the listener that more is coming; a falling tune on the last item ("oil") signals that the list is complete.

whyNot.A: Falling on every item would make each one sound like the end of the list.
whyNot.D: A rise on the last item would leave the list sounding unfinished.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem:
In the sentence below, the word in capitals carries the emphatic stress. Which question does the sentence answer?
Ngozi wrote the letter in RED ink.
options: Did Ngozi type the letter in red ink?
Did Ngozi write the letter in blue ink?
Who wrote the letter in red ink?
What did Ngozi write in red ink?
questions.explanation: Emphatic stress on RED corrects or supplies information about the colour of the ink, so it answers a question about the colour.

whyNot.C: That question would be answered by stressing NGOZI.
whyNot.A: That question would be answered by stressing WROTE.
whyNot.D: That question would be answered by stressing LETTER.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.context:
Amina was the only girl who played football on the dusty field behind the primary school in Zaria, and for a long time the boys put up with her only because the ball belonged to her. They rarely passed to her, and when they did, it was usually by mistake.

Things changed on the afternoon of the inter-street match against Tudun Wada. With five minutes left and the score level, the team's goalkeeper twisted his ankle. Nobody wanted to take his place; the Tudun Wada strikers were bigger and kicked harder. Amina pushed up her sleeves and walked into the goal before anyone could argue.

She saved two shots. The second struck her in the chest so hard that she sat down in the dust, but she held on to the ball. When the referee blew the final whistle, the boys did not lift her onto their shoulders, as they would have done for one of their own. They did something she valued more. The next afternoon, when they chose sides, she was picked first.
questions.stem: Why did the boys at first allow Amina to play football with them?
options: Their goalkeeper had twisted his ankle
Their teacher had ordered them to include her
She was the best player on the field
questions.explanation: The first sentence says the boys "put up with her only because the ball belonged to her".

whyNot.D: They rarely passed to her, so they did not yet rate her as a player.
whyNot.B: The injury happened later, in the Tudun Wada match.

questions.context:

questions.stem: "They rarely passed to her, and when they did, it was usually by mistake." This shows that the boys
options: did not take her seriously as a player
wanted her to score all the goals
were poor at passing the ball
questions.explanation: Passing to her only by accident shows that the boys chose not to include her in the game: they did not think of her as a real member of the team.

whyNot.C: The sentence is about whom they passed to, not about their skill.
whyNot.B: Rarely passing to her is the opposite of wanting her to score.

questions.stem: Why did nobody want to take the injured goalkeeper's place?
options: There were only five minutes left in the match
The Tudun Wada strikers were bigger and kicked harder
They wanted Amina to play in goal
questions.explanation: The passage gives the reason after a semicolon: "the Tudun Wada strikers were bigger and kicked harder". The boys were afraid of their powerful shots.

whyNot.A: The time left is mentioned, but it is not the reason given for their fear.
whyNot.D: Amina walked in "before anyone could argue", which shows it was not their plan.

questions.stem: Amina "walked into the goal before anyone could argue". This shows that she was
questions.explanation: She acted at once, without waiting for permission and while the boys hesitated. This shows determination: a firm decision to do what was needed.

whyNot.A: Nothing suggests she acted without thinking; she then played well.
whyNot.C: Her action came from the team's need, not from a wish to show off.

questions.context:

questions.stem: "The boys did not lift her onto their shoulders, as they would have done for one of their own." This suggests that, at that moment, the boys
options: were angry that she had let in a goal
still did not fully see her as one of them
questions.explanation: "One of their own" means a boy from their group. By not celebrating her as they would have celebrated a boy, they show that she was not yet fully accepted, even after saving the match.

whyNot.A: The passage says she saved both shots; no goal is mentioned.
whyNot.B: The match had been level and she saved the shots; nothing says they lost.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.context:

questions.stem: What does the fact that Amina was picked first the next afternoon show?
options: She was now the team's captain
The boys still wanted to use her ball
She had earned the boys' respect as a player
The injured goalkeeper had asked for her
questions.explanation: Before, the boys tolerated her only for her ball. Being chosen first means they now see her as the most valuable player, something "she valued more" than being carried.

whyNot.B: The ball was the old reason for tolerating her; being picked first is a new sign of respect.
whyNot.A: Being picked first is not the same as being made captain.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.context:
Long before banks opened branches in every town, Nigerians had found ways to save. Among the Yoruba it is called esusu or ajo; the Igbo speak of isusu; in the North it is adashe. The idea is the same everywhere. A group of people, often traders or workers who trust one another, agree to contribute a fixed sum at regular intervals. Each time, the whole collection goes to one member, until everyone has had a turn.

The system has obvious weaknesses. It pays no interest, and it depends entirely on honesty: if a member who has already collected stops contributing, the others lose. Yet it has survived for generations because it solves a problem that formal banking often ignores. A market woman who earns a little each day finds it hard to save on her own; the money is always needed for something. The group gives her a reason to put money aside and a lump sum she could never have gathered alone.

Today some banks and mobile apps have copied the idea, offering "target savings" that lock money away until a chosen date. They are, in a sense, paying a compliment to the women who have run such schemes from their market stalls for generations.
questions.stem: According to the passage, how does the traditional savings scheme work?
options: Members keep their money with a bank that pays them interest
Members pay a fixed sum regularly and each one takes the whole collection in turn
The richest member lends money to the others
Each member saves alone and shows the group the savings
questions.explanation: The first paragraph explains that members "contribute a fixed sum at regular intervals" and "the whole collection goes to one member, until everyone has had a turn".

whyNot.A: The passage says the system "pays no interest".
whyNot.D: The point of the scheme is that members save together, not alone.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.context:
Long before banks opened branches in every town, Nigerians had found ways to save. Among the Yoruba it is called esusu or ajo; the Igbo speak of isusu; in the North it is adashe. The idea is the same everywhere. A group of people, often traders or workers who trust one another, agree to contribute a fixed sum at regular intervals. Each time, the whole collection goes to one member, until everyone has had a turn.

The system has obvious weaknesses. It pays no interest, and it depends entirely on honesty: if a member who has already collected stops contributing, the others lose. Yet it has survived for generations because it solves a problem that formal banking often ignores. A market woman who earns a little each day finds it hard to save on her own; the money is always needed for something. The group gives her a reason to put money aside and a lump sum she could never have gathered alone.

Today some banks and mobile apps have copied the idea, offering "target savings" that lock money away until a chosen date. They are, in a sense, paying a compliment to the women who have run such schemes from their market stalls for generations.
questions.stem: Which of the following is a weakness of the scheme mentioned in the passage?
options: The money is kept in a bank far from the market
Members may lose if someone who has collected stops paying
Members must be from the same ethnic group
questions.explanation: The second paragraph names two weaknesses: it pays no interest, and it depends on honesty, since "if a member who has already collected stops contributing, the others lose".

whyNot.C: The passage shows the scheme exists among Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa people, but says nothing about members needing to share an ethnic group.
whyNot.D: Members pay "a fixed sum".

questions.stem: According to the writer, why has the scheme survived for generations?
options: It helps people who find it hard to save on their own
It is enforced by traditional rulers
It is cheaper to join than a bank
It pays more interest than the banks
questions.explanation: The writer says it survives "because it solves a problem that formal banking often ignores": people with small daily earnings struggle to save alone, and the group gives them a reason and a lump sum.

whyNot.D: The scheme "pays no interest".
whyNot.B: Traditional rulers are not mentioned.

questions.stem: "The money is always needed for something." The writer means that
options: banks are always asking for fees
the group always needs more members
small daily earnings are easily spent on everyday needs
questions.explanation: The sentence explains why the market woman "finds it hard to save on her own": there is always some need to spend her small income on, so nothing is left over.

whyNot.C: The writer is sympathetic; the money goes on real needs, not waste.
whyNot.A: The sentence is about the woman's own spending, not bank charges.

questions.stem: The writer says that banks offering "target savings" are "paying a compliment" to the women who run such schemes. This means that the banks
options: have praised the women in their adverts
have shown, by copying the idea, that it was a good one
have asked the women to work for them
have paid the women for using their idea
questions.explanation: Copying an idea is a kind of praise: it shows you value it. The phrase is figurative; the banks have not literally paid or praised anyone.

whyNot.D: "Paying" here is figurative; no money changes hands.
whyNot.A: No advertisement is mentioned; the compliment lies in the copying.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, "a lump sum" means
options: an amount owed to the bank
money kept in a heavy box
a single large amount of money
questions.explanation: A lump sum is money received all at once, as when a member collects the whole contribution on her turn, rather than in small parts.

whyNot.B: The small daily amounts are what she pays in; the lump sum is what she receives.
whyNot.A: The scheme does not involve borrowing from a bank.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.context:
My grandfather's radio was older than my father. It was a heavy wooden box with a cracked dial, and it lived on a shelf above his chair in our compound in Abeokuta. Every evening at seven he switched it on for the news, and every evening the rest of us had to be silent until the newsreader had finished.

When my uncle bought him a smartphone that could stream any station in the world, Grandfather thanked him politely and put it in a drawer. "This one," he said, patting the wooden box, "has never told me a lie it did not believe." None of us understood what he meant, and he refused to explain.

After he died, my father took the radio to a repairer, who said it could not be fixed; the parts had not been made for forty years. My father brought it home anyway and put it back on its shelf, where it still sits, silent, every evening at seven.
questions.stem: What were the family expected to do every evening at seven?
options: Keep silent while the news was on
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says that every evening at seven Grandfather switched on the news, and "the rest of us had to be silent until the newsreader had finished".

whyNot.A: The radio was for the news, not music.
whyNot.D: Only Grandfather controlled the radio.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.context:

questions.stem: The writer says that the radio "was older than my father" in order to
options: show that the father was young
explain why the father disliked it
show how very old the radio was
suggest that the father had bought it
questions.explanation: Comparing the radio's age with a grown man's is a vivid way of stressing how old it was. The same point returns when the repairer says its parts had not been made for forty years.

whyNot.D: If it was older than the father, he could not have bought it new.
whyNot.B: The father later kept the radio, which shows he valued it.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.context:
