questions.explanation: Only the component of the force along the direction of motion does work: W = Fd cos θ = 50 × 10 × cos 60° = 50 × 10 × 0.5 = 250 J.

whyNot.A: 500 J is F × d; it treats the whole force as if it acted along the ground.
whyNot.D: 433 J uses sin 60°; the component along the horizontal is F cos θ.
whyNot.B: 25 is F cos θ, the force component in newtons; it has not been multiplied by the 10 m distance.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: The gravitational force between two masses is F. If the distance between their centres is tripled and the masses are unchanged, what does the force become?
questions.explanation: Newton's law of gravitation is an inverse-square law: F = Gm₁m₂ ÷ r². Tripling r multiplies r² by 3² = 9, so the force becomes F ÷ 9.

whyNot.C: F/3 treats the force as inversely proportional to r, not r².
whyNot.A: Gravitational force gets weaker, not stronger, as the masses move apart.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: In a hydraulic car jack, the small piston has an area of 0.02 m² and the large piston has an area of 1.0 m². What load can the large piston support when a force of 200 N is applied to the small piston?
questions.explanation: Pascal's principle: the pressure is the same throughout the liquid. Pressure = 200 ÷ 0.02 = 1.0 × 10⁴ Pa. Force on the large piston = pressure × area = 1.0 × 10⁴ × 1.0 = 1.0 × 10⁴ N.

whyNot.C: 4.0 N multiplies the effort by the small area; the force is multiplied by the ratio of the areas (1.0 ÷ 0.02 = 50).
whyNot.D: 200 N assumes the force is passed on unchanged; it is the pressure, not the force, that is transmitted.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A steel ball is released in a tall jar of glycerine. After a short time it falls with a constant speed called its terminal velocity. Which statement is true when the ball moves at its terminal velocity?
options: The viscous drag on it is zero
Its acceleration is equal to g
Its weight is balanced by the upthrust alone
Its weight is balanced by the upthrust and the viscous drag together
questions.explanation: At terminal velocity the speed is constant, so the acceleration and the net force are zero. The downward weight is balanced by the two upward forces: the upthrust from the glycerine and the viscous drag, which grows as the speed grows.

whyNot.C: If the upthrust alone balanced the weight, the ball would float or stay still; the drag is needed to balance the weight.
whyNot.A: Viscous drag is largest at terminal velocity, because drag increases with speed.
whyNot.B: At constant velocity the acceleration is zero, not g.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A block of aluminium has a mass of 0.5 kg. The specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the heat capacity of the block?
questions.explanation: Heat capacity = mass × specific heat capacity = 0.5 × 900 = 450 J K⁻¹. It is the heat needed to raise the temperature of the whole block by 1 K.

whyNot.C: 1800 J K⁻¹ divides 900 by 0.5 instead of multiplying.
whyNot.B: 900 J K⁻¹ is the specific heat capacity, which is per kilogram; the block is only 0.5 kg.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: What mass of ice at 0 °C is needed to cool 0.4 kg of water from 20 °C to 0 °C, with all the ice just melting? (specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.36 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹; ignore heat exchange with the container and surroundings)
questions.explanation: Heat lost by the water = mcΔθ = 0.4 × 4200 × 20 = 33 600 J. This heat melts the ice: m × 3.36 × 10⁵ = 33 600, so m = 33 600 ÷ 336 000 = 0.10 kg.

whyNot.A: 0.40 kg assumes equal masses are needed; ice absorbs a lot of heat when it melts, so far less is needed.
whyNot.D: 0.025 kg uses 4200 × 20 for 0.1 kg of water rather than 0.4 kg.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A fixed mass of gas has a pressure of 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa, a volume of 3.0 litres and a temperature of 27 °C. It is heated to 127 °C and its volume is reduced to 2.0 litres. What is its new pressure?
questions.explanation: Use the general gas law P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ with temperatures in kelvin: T₁ = 300 K, T₂ = 400 K. P₂ = P₁V₁T₂ ÷ (T₁V₂) = 2.0 × 10⁵ × 3.0 × 400 ÷ (300 × 2.0) = 4.0 × 10⁵ Pa.

whyNot.C: 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa allows for the change in volume but leaves out the rise in temperature.
whyNot.A: 1.4 × 10⁶ Pa uses the Celsius temperatures 27 and 127; gas-law temperatures must be in kelvin.
whyNot.D: 2.7 × 10⁵ Pa allows for the temperature change but not the change in volume.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: According to the kinetic theory, the absolute temperature of an ideal gas is a measure of the
options: average kinetic energy of its molecules
force of attraction between its molecules
questions.explanation: Kinetic theory shows that the average kinetic energy of the molecules of an ideal gas is directly proportional to its absolute (kelvin) temperature. Heating a gas makes its molecules move faster on average.

whyNot.D: The number of molecules depends on the amount of gas, not on its temperature.
whyNot.C: In an ideal gas the forces of attraction between molecules are taken as negligible.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: On a cool morning in Jos, drops of water form on the outside of a glass of cold water. The dew point of the air is the temperature at which
options: the water vapour present in the air is just enough to saturate it
the relative humidity of the air is 50%
water boils at the local atmospheric pressure
all the water vapour in the air turns to ice
questions.explanation: As air is cooled, the amount of vapour it can hold falls. The dew point is the temperature at which the vapour already present just saturates the air; below it, the extra vapour condenses as dew, as on the cold glass.

whyNot.D: Dew is liquid water; the dew point need not be at or below 0 °C.
whyNot.B: At the dew point the air is saturated, so the relative humidity is 100%, not 50%.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: The temperature of a patient is 40 °C. What is this temperature on the Fahrenheit scale?

whyNot.A: 72 °F forgets to add 32, the Fahrenheit reading of the ice point.
whyNot.B: 54.2 °F multiplies by 5/9 instead of 9/5; a Fahrenheit degree is smaller than a Celsius degree, so the number of degrees must get bigger.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A metal plate has an area of 0.5 m² at 25 °C. The linear expansivity of the metal is 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹. By how much does the area of the plate increase when it is heated to 125 °C?
questions.explanation: Area expansivity β = 2α = 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹. Temperature rise = 125 − 25 = 100 K. Increase in area = Aβθ = 0.5 × 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ × 100 = 1.2 × 10⁻³ m².

whyNot.B: 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² uses α instead of 2α; an area expands in two directions.
whyNot.A: 1.8 × 10⁻³ m² uses 3α, the cubic expansivity, which applies to volume.
whyNot.C: 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ m² is just the area expansivity; it leaves out the area and the temperature rise.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A liquid boils when its saturated vapour pressure becomes equal to the
options: pressure at the bottom of its container
saturated vapour pressure of water at 100 °C at any altitude
pressure of the vapour above an open dish of it at room temperature
questions.explanation: Bubbles of vapour can form and grow inside the liquid only when the saturated vapour pressure equals the pressure acting on the liquid surface (usually atmospheric pressure). That is why the boiling point falls where the external pressure is lower.

whyNot.A: The pressure at the bottom is larger than at the surface because of the liquid's depth; boiling is set by the pressure on the surface.
whyNot.C: Different liquids boil at different temperatures, and the external pressure changes with altitude.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A platinum resistance thermometer has a resistance of 20 Ω at the ice point and 28 Ω at the steam point. Its resistance is 23 Ω when placed in a warm liquid. What is the temperature of the liquid on the scale of this thermometer?

whyNot.D: 82.1 °C is 23 ÷ 28 × 100; it forgets to subtract the ice-point resistance.
whyNot.C: 62.5 °C is (28 − 23) ÷ 8 × 100, which measures down from the steam point instead of up from the ice point.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A liquid has an apparent cubic expansivity of 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹ when heated in a glass flask. The linear expansivity of the glass is 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹. What is the real cubic expansivity of the liquid?
questions.explanation: The flask also expands, so the liquid seems to expand less than it really does. Real expansivity = apparent expansivity + cubic expansivity of the glass. Cubic expansivity of glass = 3α = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹. Real = 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ + 0.3 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.9 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹.

whyNot.C: 1.7 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹ adds the linear expansivity; the flask's volume expands at 3α.
whyNot.A: 1.3 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹ subtracts the glass's expansion; the real expansion is larger than the apparent one.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A pipe 0.85 m long is open at both ends. What is the frequency of the fundamental note it produces? (speed of sound in air = 340 m s⁻¹, ignore end correction)
questions.explanation: For a pipe open at both ends, the fundamental has an antinode at each end, so the length is half a wavelength: λ = 2L = 1.7 m. f = v ÷ λ = 340 ÷ 1.7 = 200 Hz.

whyNot.B: 100 Hz uses λ = 4L, which is the rule for a pipe closed at one end.
whyNot.C: 400 Hz uses λ = L; the fundamental of an open pipe has λ = 2L.
whyNot.D: 289 Hz multiplies the speed by the length; frequency is speed divided by wavelength.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A danfo bus sounding its horn drives quickly towards a girl standing by the roadside. Compared with the note the driver hears, the note the girl hears is
options: lower in pitch, because the waves are stretched out
higher in pitch, because more wavefronts reach her each second
the same pitch but louder, because sound speeds up
the same pitch, because the source frequency does not change
questions.explanation: This is the Doppler effect. As the source moves towards the girl, the wavefronts are squeezed closer together in front of it, so more of them reach her each second. She hears a higher frequency (higher pitch) than the driver.

whyNot.A: Waves are stretched out behind a moving source, not in front of it.
whyNot.C: The speed of sound in air depends on the air, not on the motion of the source.
whyNot.D: Although the source frequency is fixed, the frequency received by a listener changes when the source moves towards her.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: The refractive index of water is 4/3 and that of a type of glass is 3/2. What is the refractive index for light passing from water into this glass?
questions.explanation: The relative refractive index from medium 1 to medium 2 is n₂ ÷ n₁. From water to glass: (3/2) ÷ (4/3) = 9/8 = 1.125. It is greater than 1 because light slows down as it goes from water into the denser glass.

whyNot.B: 0.889 is (4/3) ÷ (3/2), the index for light going from glass into water.
whyNot.D: 2.000 is (4/3) × (3/2); the two absolute indices must be divided, not multiplied.
whyNot.A: 0.167 is the difference 3/2 − 4/3; the indices are divided, not subtracted.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a diverging lens of focal length 20 cm. What is the magnification of the image?
questions.explanation: For a diverging lens f = −20 cm (real-is-positive). 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/20 − 1/20 = −1/10, so v = −10 cm: a virtual image 10 cm from the lens on the object side. Magnification = |v| ÷ u = 10 ÷ 20 = 0.5 (upright and diminished).

whyNot.C: 2.0 is u ÷ v, upside down; magnification is image distance ÷ object distance.
whyNot.A: 1.0 assumes the image is the same size; a diverging lens always forms a diminished image of a real object.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A glass prism has a refracting angle of 60°. The angle of minimum deviation for a beam of light passing through it is 30°. What is the refractive index of the glass?

whyNot.C: 1.73 is sin 60° ÷ sin 30°, which uses A instead of (A + D) ÷ 2.
whyNot.B: 1.22 is sin 60° ÷ sin 45°, which puts the angles the wrong way round.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: People in one room can hear a radio playing in the next room through an open doorway even when they cannot see the radio. Which wave property mainly explains this?
questions.explanation: Diffraction is the spreading of waves as they pass through a gap or round an obstacle. Sound waves have wavelengths comparable with the width of a doorway, so they spread well into the next room. Light has a far shorter wavelength and hardly spreads, so the radio cannot be seen.

whyNot.A: Polarisation applies only to transverse waves; sound in air is longitudinal.
whyNot.B: Dispersion is the splitting of waves into different wavelengths, as when a prism forms a spectrum.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded together. How many beats are heard each second?
questions.explanation: The beat frequency is the difference between the two frequencies: 260 − 256 = 4 beats per second. The loudness rises and falls four times every second.

whyNot.C: 2 is half the difference; the beat frequency is the whole difference.
whyNot.D: 258 Hz is the average frequency, which is the pitch of the note heard, not the beat frequency.
whyNot.B: 516 is the sum of the frequencies.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. When it is in normal adjustment, what is the distance between the two lenses?
questions.explanation: In normal adjustment the final image is at infinity, so the focal points of the two lenses coincide. The separation is fₒ + fₑ = 100 + 5 = 105 cm. (Its angular magnification is fₒ ÷ fₑ = 20.)

whyNot.D: 95 cm subtracts the focal lengths; in an astronomical telescope they are added.
whyNot.B: 20 is the angular magnification fₒ ÷ fₑ, not the length of the telescope.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Chidi can read his textbook clearly but cannot see the writing on the board from the back of the class. What defect does he have, and how is it corrected?
options: Short sight, corrected with a diverging lens
Short sight, corrected with a converging lens
Long sight, corrected with a diverging lens
Long sight, corrected with a converging lens
questions.explanation: Seeing near objects clearly but not distant ones is short sight (myopia): the eye focuses parallel rays in front of the retina. A diverging (concave) lens spreads the rays a little so they focus on the retina.

whyNot.B: A converging lens would make the rays meet even further in front of the retina.
whyNot.D: Long sight is the opposite problem: distant objects are clear but near ones are blurred.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A guitar and a piano each play a note of the same pitch and loudness, yet a listener can tell the two instruments apart. This is because the notes differ in
options: frequency, because the instruments are different sizes
quality, because they contain different overtones
speed, because the sounds travel differently in air
amplitude, because one instrument is struck and one plucked
questions.explanation: Quality (timbre) depends on the overtones present with the fundamental and on their relative strengths. Two notes of the same pitch have the same fundamental frequency and, at the same loudness, similar amplitude; it is the different mix of overtones that makes the instruments sound different.

whyNot.A: Same pitch means the same fundamental frequency.
whyNot.D: Same loudness means similar amplitude at the listener.
whyNot.C: All sounds travel at the same speed in the same air.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A charge of 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ C is placed in a uniform electric field of intensity 5.0 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. What force acts on the charge?
questions.explanation: Electric field intensity E is force per unit charge, so F = qE = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 5.0 × 10⁴ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹ N = 0.10 N.

whyNot.B: 2.5 × 10¹⁰ N divides E by q; the force is q multiplied by E.
whyNot.A: 4.0 × 10⁻¹¹ N divides q by E.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A parallel-plate capacitor has plates of area 0.02 m² separated by 1.0 mm of air. What is its capacitance? (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹)

whyNot.B: 1.77 × 10⁻¹³ F uses d = 1 (millimetres not converted to metres).
whyNot.D: 1.77 × 10⁻⁶ F uses the area as 200 cm² without converting it to m².
whyNot.C: 1.77 × 10⁻¹⁶ F multiplies by d instead of dividing.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: In a potentiometer experiment, a standard cell of e.m.f. 1.5 V gives a balance point at 45 cm along the wire. A second cell gives a balance point at 60 cm on the same wire. What is the e.m.f. of the second cell?
questions.explanation: With a steady current in the potentiometer wire, the p.d. along it is proportional to length, so E₁ ÷ E₂ = l₁ ÷ l₂. E₂ = 1.5 × 60 ÷ 45 = 2.0 V.

whyNot.C: 1.1 V is 1.5 × 45 ÷ 60, the ratio upside down; a longer balance length means a larger e.m.f.
whyNot.A: 1.5 V ignores the different balance lengths.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A 6 Ω resistor is connected in series with a parallel pair of 3 Ω and 6 Ω resistors. The combination is connected to a 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance. What current flows from the battery?
questions.explanation: Parallel pair: R = (3 × 6) ÷ (3 + 6) = 2 Ω. Total resistance = 6 + 2 = 8 Ω. Current I = V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 A.

whyNot.A: 0.8 A treats all three resistors as being in series (15 Ω).
whyNot.D: 2.0 A uses only the 6 Ω series resistor and leaves out the parallel pair.
whyNot.B: 4.0 A uses only the 3 Ω resistor.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: An electron moves at 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.5 T. What is the size of the magnetic force on it? (charge of electron = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.explanation: The force on a moving charge is F = qvB sin θ, with θ = 90° here. F = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁶ × 0.5 = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ N.

whyNot.B: 6.4 × 10⁻¹³ N divides by B instead of multiplying.
whyNot.A: 8.0 × 10⁻²⁰ N leaves out the speed.
whyNot.D: 1.0 × 10⁶ N is vB alone; the charge must be included.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A series a.c. circuit has a resistance of 30 Ω, an inductive reactance of 80 Ω and a capacitive reactance of 40 Ω. What is the impedance of the circuit?
questions.explanation: Z = √[R² + (X_L − X_C)²]. The reactances act in opposite senses, so they are subtracted: X_L − X_C = 40 Ω. Z = √(30² + 40²) = √2500 = 50 Ω.

whyNot.A: 150 Ω adds all three values; the voltages across R and the reactances are out of phase, so they cannot simply be added.
whyNot.C: 70 Ω adds R to (X_L − X_C) directly instead of using Pythagoras.
whyNot.B: 124 Ω adds the two reactances; inductive and capacitive reactance oppose each other.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A steady current of 2 A is passed through copper(II) sulphate solution for 30 minutes using copper electrodes. What mass of copper is deposited on the cathode? (electrochemical equivalent of copper = 3.3 × 10⁻⁷ kg C⁻¹)
questions.explanation: Faraday's first law: m = zIt, with t in seconds. t = 30 × 60 = 1800 s. m = 3.3 × 10⁻⁷ × 2 × 1800 = 1.188 × 10⁻³ kg ≈ 1.19 × 10⁻³ kg (about 1.2 g).

whyNot.D: 1.98 × 10⁻⁵ kg uses t = 30 (minutes not converted to seconds).
whyNot.B: 5.94 × 10⁻⁴ kg leaves out the current of 2 A.
whyNot.A: 2.38 × 10⁻³ kg doubles the answer, as if the time were one hour.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: The angle between the direction of the earth's magnetic field at a place and the horizontal is called the
questions.explanation: A freely suspended magnetic needle tilts so that it lies along the earth's field. The angle it makes with the horizontal is the angle of dip (inclination). It is zero at the magnetic equator and 90° at the magnetic poles.

whyNot.B: Declination is the angle between the magnetic meridian and the geographic meridian, measured in the horizontal plane.
whyNot.D: The magnetic meridian is a vertical plane containing the earth's magnetic field, not an angle.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A transformer has a primary voltage of 240 V and a primary current of 2.0 A. Its secondary delivers 36 A at 12 V. What is the efficiency of the transformer?
questions.explanation: Efficiency = output power ÷ input power × 100%. Output = 12 × 36 = 432 W. Input = 240 × 2.0 = 480 W. Efficiency = 432 ÷ 480 × 100% = 90%. The missing 10% is lost as heat in the coils and core.

whyNot.A: 111% is input ÷ output; no machine can give out more energy than it takes in.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A galvanometer has a resistance of 50 Ω and gives full-scale deflection with a current of 2 mA. What resistance must be connected in series with it to make a voltmeter reading up to 10 V?
questions.explanation: At full scale the total resistance must be V ÷ I = 10 ÷ (2 × 10⁻³) = 5000 Ω. The galvanometer already supplies 50 Ω, so the series resistor (multiplier) R = 5000 − 50 = 4950 Ω.

whyNot.B: 5000 Ω is the total resistance needed; it forgets the galvanometer's own 50 Ω.
whyNot.A: 5050 Ω adds the galvanometer resistance instead of subtracting it.
whyNot.C: A tiny resistance like 0.01 Ω is a shunt, connected in parallel to make an ammeter.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: The work function of a metal is 2.0 eV. What is the longest wavelength of light that can release photoelectrons from it? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
questions.explanation: At the threshold wavelength λ₀ the photon energy just equals the work function: hc ÷ λ₀ = W. W = 2.0 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. λ₀ = hc ÷ W = (6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.0 × 10⁸) ÷ (3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 6.2 × 10⁻⁷ m.

whyNot.A: 9.9 × 10⁻²⁶ m divides hc by 2.0 without converting electronvolts to joules.
whyNot.D: 1.6 × 10⁶ m is W ÷ hc, the formula upside down.
whyNot.C: 4.8 × 10¹⁴ is the threshold frequency W ÷ h, in hertz, not a wavelength.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A radioactive source has a half-life of 3 hours. How long does it take for its count rate to fall from 1200 counts per minute to 150 counts per minute? (ignore background radiation)
questions.explanation: Halve step by step: 1200 → 600 → 300 → 150. That is 3 half-lives. Time = 3 × 3 hours = 9 hours.

whyNot.D: 3 hours is one half-life, which would only bring the count to 600.
whyNot.C: 24 hours uses 1200 ÷ 150 = 8 as the number of half-lives; 8 is the reduction factor, which is 2³.
whyNot.B: 6 hours is two half-lives, which leaves 300 counts per minute.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: In a hydrogen atom the energy of the n = 2 level is −3.4 eV. What is the minimum energy needed to ionise a hydrogen atom whose electron is in this level?
questions.explanation: Ionisation means removing the electron completely, to the level of energy 0 eV. Energy needed = 0 − (−3.4 eV) = 3.4 eV.

whyNot.D: 13.6 eV is the ionisation energy from the ground state (n = 1), not from n = 2.
whyNot.A: 10.2 eV is the energy to raise an electron from n = 1 to n = 2.
whyNot.B: 17.0 eV adds 13.6 and 3.4; it does not match any single step.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: In the nuclear reaction ¹⁴₇N + ⁴₂He → ¹⁷₈O + X, what is the particle X?
questions.explanation: Mass numbers: 14 + 4 = 17 + A, so A = 1. Atomic numbers: 7 + 2 = 8 + Z, so Z = 1. A particle with mass number 1 and charge number 1 is a proton, ¹₁H.

whyNot.C: A neutron has atomic number 0; the atomic numbers would not balance.
whyNot.B: An electron has mass number 0; the mass numbers would not balance.
whyNot.D: An alpha particle has mass number 4, but only 1 is needed.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A p-n junction diode conducts readily when it is forward biased. In forward bias,
options: the n-side is connected to the positive terminal of the battery
the p-side is connected to the positive terminal of the battery
only minority carriers cross the junction
questions.explanation: In forward bias the p-side is made positive and the n-side negative. This pushes holes and electrons towards the junction, narrowing the depletion layer so that majority carriers flow across and a large current passes.

whyNot.A: Connecting the n-side to the positive terminal is reverse bias, in which very little current flows.
whyNot.D: The depletion layer widens in reverse bias; it narrows in forward bias.
whyNot.C: The tiny current due to minority carriers is the reverse-bias leakage current.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: In an X-ray tube, X-rays are produced when
options: light falls on the metal target and releases electrons
radioactive nuclei in the target emit gamma rays
fast-moving electrons are suddenly stopped by a metal target
questions.explanation: Electrons from a hot cathode are accelerated by a high voltage and strike a tungsten target. As they are suddenly slowed and stopped, part of their kinetic energy is given out as X-ray photons; most of the rest heats the target.

whyNot.D: The glowing filament only supplies electrons by thermionic emission; its light is not X-rays.
whyNot.A: Light releasing electrons from a metal is the photoelectric effect, the reverse kind of process.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A particle has a momentum of 3.3 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹. What is its de Broglie wavelength? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
questions.explanation: The de Broglie wavelength is λ = h ÷ p = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ ÷ 3.3 × 10⁻²⁴ = 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, which is about the size of an atom.

whyNot.D: 5.0 × 10⁹ m is p ÷ h, the formula upside down.
whyNot.A: 2.2 × 10⁻⁵⁷ m multiplies h by p instead of dividing.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: What is the energy, in electronvolts, of a photon of wavelength 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ m? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)

whyNot.C: 7.9 eV multiplies by 1.6 instead of dividing when converting joules to electronvolts.
whyNot.B: 0.32 eV is the reciprocal of the correct answer; the conversion has been done upside down.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A beam containing alpha, beta and gamma radiation passes through a strong magnetic field. The gamma rays continue in a straight line because they
options: are absorbed by the magnetic field
move more slowly than alpha particles
questions.explanation: A magnetic field exerts a force only on moving charges. Gamma rays are electromagnetic waves (photons) with no charge, so they are not deflected. Alpha particles (positive) and beta particles (negative) bend in opposite directions.

whyNot.B: Gamma photons have no rest mass; it is alpha particles that are heavy.
whyNot.D: Gamma rays travel at the speed of light, much faster than alpha particles.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: When a beam of electrons is passed through a thin crystal, a pattern of rings like a diffraction pattern is formed on a screen. This shows that
options: moving particles can behave as waves
light consists of particles called photons
questions.explanation: Diffraction is a wave effect. Electron diffraction shows that particles such as electrons have a wave nature, with a de Broglie wavelength λ = h ÷ p. This is part of wave–particle duality.

whyNot.B: Electrons have charge and mass; they show wave behaviour but are not electromagnetic waves.
whyNot.C: The particle nature of light is shown by the photoelectric effect, not by electron diffraction.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation: A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction. Displacement is distance in a stated direction, so it is a vector. Speed, mass and energy have size only, so they are scalars.

whyNot.D: Speed has no direction; velocity is the vector form of speed.
whyNot.B: Energy has magnitude only, so it is a scalar.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Two forces of 6 N and 8 N act at the same point at right angles to each other. What is the magnitude of their resultant?
questions.explanation: For two forces at right angles, use Pythagoras' theorem: R = √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 N.

whyNot.B: 14 N adds the forces as if they acted in the same direction.
whyNot.D: 2 N subtracts them as if they acted in opposite directions.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A car travelling at 30 m s⁻¹ brakes uniformly and stops after covering 75 m. What is its deceleration?
questions.explanation: Use v² = u² + 2as with v = 0: 0 = 30² + 2a × 75, so a = −900 ÷ 150 = −6.0 m s⁻². The deceleration is 6.0 m s⁻².

whyNot.C: 0.4 m s⁻² is 30 ÷ 75; speed divided by distance is not acceleration.
whyNot.B: 12 m s⁻² forgets the 2 in 2as (900 ÷ 75).
whyNot.D: 2.5 m s⁻² is 75 ÷ 30, which has the wrong units for acceleration.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A uniform plank 4 m long and weighing 200 N rests horizontally on two supports, one at each end. A bag of cement weighing 100 N is placed on the plank 1 m from the left-hand end. What is the upward force exerted by the left-hand support?
questions.explanation: Take moments about the right-hand support. Clockwise and anticlockwise moments must balance: R_L × 4 = 200 × 2 (weight at the centre, 2 m away) + 100 × 3 (bag, 3 m away) = 400 + 300 = 700. R_L = 700 ÷ 4 = 175 N. (The right support gives 300 − 175 = 125 N.)

whyNot.D: 125 N is the force at the right-hand support; the bag is nearer the left end, so the left support carries more.
whyNot.B: 150 N shares the total load of 300 N equally, ignoring where the bag is.
whyNot.C: 300 N is the total load carried by both supports together.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A screw jack has a handle of length 0.35 m and a screw of pitch 0.5 cm. What is its velocity ratio? (π = 22/7)
questions.explanation: In one turn the effort moves round a circle of radius 0.35 m (distance 2πr) while the load rises by one pitch. VR = 2πr ÷ p = (2 × 22/7 × 0.35) ÷ 0.005 = 2.2 ÷ 0.005 = 440.

whyNot.D: 220 uses πr instead of 2πr for the distance moved by the effort in one turn.
whyNot.C: 70 is r ÷ p; the effort travels the whole circumference, not the radius.
whyNot.A: 4.4 leaves the pitch in centimetres (2.2 ÷ 0.5); both lengths must be in the same unit.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A block of wood of density 600 kg m⁻³ floats in fresh water of density 1000 kg m⁻³. What fraction of the block's volume is below the water surface?
questions.explanation: A floating body displaces its own weight of liquid: ρ_wood × V × g = ρ_water × V_sub × g. So V_sub ÷ V = ρ_wood ÷ ρ_water = 600 ÷ 1000 = 0.60.

whyNot.A: 0.40 is the fraction above the surface, not below it.
whyNot.D: 1.67 is the ratio upside down; a fraction of the volume cannot be more than 1.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Bola, whose mass is 60 kg, runs up a staircase of 20 steps, each 0.2 m high, in 8 s. What average power does she develop in lifting her body? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation: Height climbed = 20 × 0.2 = 4 m. Work done = mgh = 60 × 10 × 4 = 2400 J. Power = work ÷ time = 2400 ÷ 8 = 300 W.

whyNot.C: 2400 is the work done in joules; it has not been divided by the time.
whyNot.B: 30 W uses the mass instead of the weight (it leaves out g).

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A footballer's boot exerts an average force of 500 N on a ball for 0.02 s. What impulse does the boot give the ball?
questions.explanation: Impulse = force × time = 500 × 0.02 = 10 N s. This is also the change in the momentum of the ball.

whyNot.D: 25 000 N s divides the force by the time instead of multiplying.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Which change would leave the period of a simple pendulum unchanged, if it swings through small angles at the same place?
options: Taking the pendulum to the moon
Using a heavier bob of the same size
questions.explanation: For small swings T = 2π√(l ÷ g). The period depends only on the length l and on g. The mass of the bob does not appear, so a heavier bob gives the same period.

whyNot.D: A longer string increases l, so the period increases.
whyNot.B: g on the moon is smaller, so the period would be longer.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A diver is 8 m below the surface of a lake. The atmospheric pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. What is the total pressure on the diver? (density of water = 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation: Pressure due to the water = hρg = 8 × 1000 × 10 = 8.0 × 10⁴ Pa. The atmosphere also presses on the lake surface, so total pressure = 1.0 × 10⁵ + 0.8 × 10⁵ = 1.8 × 10⁵ Pa.

whyNot.D: 8.0 × 10⁴ Pa is only the pressure due to the water; atmospheric pressure must be added.
whyNot.C: 1.08 × 10⁵ Pa leaves out g when finding the water pressure (8 × 1000 = 8000).
whyNot.A: 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa is the pressure at the surface only.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A 50 W electric heater is placed in a 1.0 kg metal block. After 3 minutes the temperature of the block has risen by 10 K. Assuming no heat is lost, what is the specific heat capacity of the metal?
questions.explanation: Electrical energy supplied = Pt = 50 × (3 × 60) = 9000 J. This equals mcΔθ, so c = 9000 ÷ (1.0 × 10) = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

whyNot.D: 15 uses the time in minutes (50 × 3 ÷ 10); the time must be in seconds.
whyNot.A: 5 leaves out the time: power is energy per second, so it must be multiplied by the time.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: While a block of ice is melting at 0 °C, heat is still being supplied to it but its temperature does not rise. The heat supplied is used to
options: break the bonds that hold the molecules in fixed positions
raise the boiling point of the water
questions.explanation: This hidden heat is latent heat of fusion. It increases the potential energy of the molecules by breaking the bonds of the solid structure. The average kinetic energy of the molecules, and hence the temperature, stays the same until all the ice has melted.

whyNot.C: Faster vibration would mean higher kinetic energy and so a higher temperature, which is not happening.
whyNot.B: Ice actually contracts when it melts, and expansion is not where the energy goes.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes evaporation?
options: It takes place only at the surface of the liquid, at any temperature
It takes place throughout the liquid at one fixed temperature
It is not affected by wind blowing over the liquid
It warms the liquid that is left behind
questions.explanation: Evaporation is the escape of the faster molecules from the surface of a liquid. It happens at all temperatures, cools the remaining liquid, and is speeded up by wind, a larger surface area and a higher temperature.

whyNot.B: Taking place throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature describes boiling.
whyNot.D: The fastest molecules escape, so the average kinetic energy of those left falls: evaporation causes cooling.
whyNot.C: Wind removes the vapour above the surface, so evaporation becomes faster, which is why clothes dry quickly on a windy day.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: In an experiment on a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, a student plots pressure P against 1/V, where V is the volume. What shape does the graph have?
options: A straight line through the origin
A straight line that cuts the 1/V axis away from the origin
A curve that falls as 1/V increases
questions.explanation: Boyle's law says PV = constant, so P = constant × (1/V). Pressure is directly proportional to 1/V, which gives a straight line through the origin.

whyNot.D: A falling curve is what you get when P is plotted against V, not against 1/V.
whyNot.A: A horizontal line would mean P does not change with volume.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A clinical thermometer has a narrow constriction in its bore just above the bulb. What is the purpose of the constriction?
options: To stop the mercury running back into the bulb before the reading is taken
To widen the range of temperatures it can measure
To protect the bulb from breaking
To make the thermometer respond more quickly
questions.explanation: When the thermometer is taken out of the patient's mouth, the mercury in the bulb cools and contracts. The thread breaks at the constriction, so the mercury above it stays in place and the highest temperature can be read. It is reset by shaking.

whyNot.D: A quick response comes from the thin glass wall of the bulb, not from the constriction.
whyNot.B: A clinical thermometer has a short range (about 35 °C to 43 °C); the constriction does not change that.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Steel railway lines are laid in lengths of 20 m. The linear expansivity of steel is 1.1 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹. What is the least gap that should be left between neighbouring lengths to allow for a temperature rise of 30 K?
questions.explanation: Expansion = lαθ = 20 × 1.1 × 10⁻⁵ × 30 = 6.6 × 10⁻³ m = 6.6 mm. A gap of at least this size stops the rails from buckling on a hot day.

whyNot.C: 0.66 mm makes a factor-of-ten slip when converting 6.6 × 10⁻³ m to millimetres.
whyNot.A: 66 mm makes a factor-of-ten slip in the other direction.
whyNot.D: 2.2 mm leaves out the factor of 30 K and uses 10 K instead.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: The air in a car tyre has a pressure of 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa at 27 °C. After a long journey on a hot road its temperature is 57 °C. Assuming the volume of the tyre does not change, what is the new pressure?
questions.explanation: Pressure law: P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂ with T in kelvin. T₁ = 300 K, T₂ = 330 K. P₂ = 2.0 × 10⁵ × 330 ÷ 300 = 2.2 × 10⁵ Pa.

whyNot.A: 4.2 × 10⁵ Pa uses the Celsius temperatures (57 ÷ 27); the pressure law needs kelvin temperatures.
whyNot.D: 1.8 × 10⁵ Pa uses T₁ ÷ T₂, which would make the pressure fall on heating.
whyNot.B: The pressure of a fixed volume of gas rises when its temperature rises.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: How much heat is given out when 2 kg of water cools from 90 °C to 40 °C? (specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)

whyNot.D: 7.6 × 10⁵ J uses 90 K as the temperature change; only the fall of 50 K counts.
whyNot.C: 3.4 × 10⁵ J uses 40 K as the temperature change.
whyNot.A: 2.1 × 10⁵ J uses a mass of 1 kg instead of 2 kg.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: In a vacuum flask, the walls facing the vacuum are silvered. The silvering mainly reduces heat transfer by
questions.explanation: Shiny silvered surfaces are poor emitters and good reflectors of radiant heat, so they cut down heat transfer by radiation across the vacuum. The vacuum itself stops conduction and convection, and the stopper reduces evaporation and convection at the top.

whyNot.D: Conduction is prevented by the vacuum (and the cork support), not by the silvering.
whyNot.A: Convection needs a fluid; the vacuum removes it.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: 0.05 kg of ice at 0 °C is dropped into 0.5 kg of water at 40 °C in a container of negligible heat capacity. What is the final temperature after all the ice has melted? (specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.36 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹)
questions.explanation: Heat lost by warm water = heat to melt ice + heat to warm the melted ice. 0.5 × 4200 × (40 − T) = 0.05 × 336 000 + 0.05 × 4200 × T. 84 000 − 2100T = 16 800 + 210T, so 2310T = 67 200 and T ≈ 29.1 °C.

whyNot.C: 36.4 °C ignores the latent heat needed to melt the ice.
whyNot.D: 32.0 °C forgets that the melted ice (now water at 0 °C) must also be warmed to the final temperature.
whyNot.A: 8.0 °C is 16 800 ÷ 2100, the temperature fall caused by melting alone, not the final temperature.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A sound wave travels in air at 330 m s⁻¹ and has a wavelength of 1.5 m. What is its frequency?
questions.explanation: The wave equation is v = fλ, so f = v ÷ λ = 330 ÷ 1.5 = 220 Hz.

whyNot.B: 495 Hz multiplies speed by wavelength; frequency is speed divided by wavelength.
whyNot.C: 0.0045 Hz is λ ÷ v, the formula upside down.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Kemi walks straight towards a large plane mirror at a steady speed of 2 m s⁻¹. At what speed does her image approach her?
questions.explanation: The image is always as far behind the mirror as Kemi is in front of it. Each second she moves 2 m closer to the mirror and the image also moves 2 m closer, so the distance between them shrinks by 4 m every second.

whyNot.A: 2 m s⁻¹ is the speed of the image relative to the mirror, not relative to Kemi.
whyNot.C: The image moves; it stays as far behind the mirror as she is in front.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: An object placed 20 cm in front of a concave mirror forms a real image 60 cm from the mirror. What is the focal length of the mirror?

whyNot.D: 40 cm is v − u; the reciprocals of the distances are added, not the distances subtracted.
whyNot.B: 80 cm is u + v, without taking reciprocals.
whyNot.C: 30 cm is half the image distance, which would be true only for an object at infinity.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Optical fibres carry internet signals as pulses of light along very thin glass threads under the sea to Lagos. Which effect keeps the light inside the fibre?
questions.explanation: The light strikes the boundary of the glass core at angles greater than the critical angle, so it is totally internally reflected again and again and is guided along the fibre with very little loss.

whyNot.B: Diffraction is the spreading of waves round obstacles; it does not trap light in a fibre.
whyNot.C: Dispersion is the splitting of light into colours; in fibres it is unwanted.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: When white light passes through a glass prism, it is split into a spectrum of colours. Which colour is deviated most, and why?
options: Red, because red light has the longest wavelength
Violet, because violet light travels fastest in glass
Violet, because glass has the greatest refractive index for violet light
Red, because glass has the greatest refractive index for red light
questions.explanation: Glass has a slightly different refractive index for each colour. It is largest for violet (which travels slowest in glass), so violet is bent and deviated most. Red has the smallest refractive index and is deviated least.

whyNot.A: Red is deviated least, not most.
whyNot.B: Violet travels slowest in glass; that is why it is refracted most.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: In a resonance-tube experiment with a tuning fork of frequency 500 Hz, the first resonance occurs at an air-column length of 16 cm and the second at 50 cm. What is the speed of sound in air?
questions.explanation: The two resonance lengths differ by half a wavelength: l₂ − l₁ = λ/2, so λ = 2 × (0.50 − 0.16) = 0.68 m. v = fλ = 500 × 0.68 = 340 m s⁻¹. Using the difference also cancels the end correction.

whyNot.B: 170 m s⁻¹ takes l₂ − l₁ as a whole wavelength; it is half a wavelength.
whyNot.C: 320 m s⁻¹ uses λ = 4l₁ and ignores the end correction.
whyNot.D: 680 m s⁻¹ takes l₂ − l₁ as a quarter wavelength.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Which change increases the speed of sound in air?
options: An increase in the frequency of the sound
An increase in the loudness of the sound
A rise in the pressure of the air at constant temperature
A rise in the temperature of the air
questions.explanation: The speed of sound in a gas is proportional to the square root of its absolute temperature, so warmer air carries sound faster. At constant temperature, changing the pressure does not change the speed, and the speed does not depend on the frequency or amplitude of the sound.

whyNot.C: Pressure and density rise together at constant temperature, so their ratio, and the speed, stay the same.
whyNot.A: All audible frequencies travel at the same speed in air; otherwise music would sound jumbled at a distance.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Which property do radio waves and X-rays have in common?
options: They travel at the same speed in a vacuum
questions.explanation: Both are electromagnetic waves, and all electromagnetic waves travel at 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum. They differ in wavelength and frequency: radio waves have long wavelengths and X-rays very short ones.

whyNot.A: Radio wavelengths are many metres; X-ray wavelengths are about 10⁻¹⁰ m.
whyNot.B: Electromagnetic waves are transverse, not longitudinal.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A pair of spectacles has diverging lenses of focal length 50 cm. What is the power of each lens?
questions.explanation: Power P = 1 ÷ f, with f in metres. For a diverging lens f is negative: f = −0.50 m. P = 1 ÷ (−0.50) = −2.0 D (dioptres).

whyNot.B: +2.0 D would be a converging lens; diverging lenses have negative power.
whyNot.A: −0.02 D uses f = 50 without converting centimetres to metres.
whyNot.D: −50 D gives the focal length in centimetres, not the power.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A fishing boat off the coast of Bonny sends a pulse of sound straight down to the sea bed. The echo returns 0.8 s later. If sound travels at 1500 m s⁻¹ in sea water, how deep is the sea at that point?
questions.explanation: In 0.8 s the pulse goes down and back up. Total distance = 1500 × 0.8 = 1200 m. Depth = 1200 ÷ 2 = 600 m.

whyNot.A: 1200 m is the total there-and-back distance; the depth is half of it.
whyNot.B: 1875 m divides the speed by the time.
whyNot.C: 300 m halves the distance twice.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A p.d. of 6 V is applied across a 12 Ω resistor. What current flows through it?
questions.explanation: Ohm's law says V = IR, so the current is I = V ÷ R = 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5 A.

whyNot.C: 2.0 A is R ÷ V, the formula upside down.
whyNot.D: 72 A multiplies V and R; current is V divided by R.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: How much work is done in moving a charge of 5 C through a potential difference of 12 V?
questions.explanation: Potential difference is work done per unit charge, so W = QV = 5 × 12 = 60 J.

whyNot.D: 2.4 J divides V by Q.
whyNot.A: 0.42 J divides Q by V.
whyNot.B: 17 J adds the numbers; work is charge multiplied by p.d.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A 2.5 kW electric cooker works on a 240 V supply. Fuses rated 3 A, 5 A, 13 A and 30 A are available. Which is the most suitable fuse for the cooker?
questions.explanation: Normal current I = P ÷ V = 2500 ÷ 240 ≈ 10.4 A. The fuse should be rated just above the normal current: 13 A lets the cooker work but blows if a fault makes the current much larger.

whyNot.A: A 3 A fuse would blow as soon as the cooker is switched on.
whyNot.C: A 5 A fuse is below the normal current of about 10.4 A.
whyNot.D: A 30 A fuse would allow a dangerously large fault current before it blows.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Two identical cells, each of e.m.f. 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω, are connected in series with a 2 Ω resistor. What current flows in the circuit?
questions.explanation: In series the e.m.f.s add: E = 3.0 V, and so do the internal resistances: r = 1.0 Ω. I = E ÷ (R + r) = 3.0 ÷ (2 + 1.0) = 1.0 A.

whyNot.A: 1.5 A ignores the internal resistance of the cells.
whyNot.B: 1.2 A includes the internal resistance of only one cell.
whyNot.C: 0.6 A uses the e.m.f. of only one cell (1.5 ÷ 2.5).

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A straight metal rod 0.5 m long moves at 10 m s⁻¹ at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.2 T, cutting the field lines. What e.m.f. is induced between its ends?
questions.explanation: The induced e.m.f. in a conductor cutting a field is E = BLv = 0.2 × 0.5 × 10 = 1.0 V.

whyNot.B: 25 V divides by B instead of multiplying (0.5 × 10 ÷ 0.2).
whyNot.C: 0.01 V divides by v instead of multiplying.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A d.c. electric motor works because
options: like magnetic poles repel each other permanently
a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force
a current produces heat in a resistor
a changing magnetic field induces an e.m.f. in a coil
questions.explanation: In a motor, the current in the coil sits in the field of a magnet. Each side of the coil feels a force (direction given by Fleming's left-hand rule); the forces on the two sides form a couple that turns the coil. The commutator keeps the turning in one direction.

whyNot.D: Induction of an e.m.f. by a changing field is the principle of the generator (dynamo) and transformer.
whyNot.C: Heating by a current is the principle of the electric iron and heater, not the motor.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Capacitors of 2 μF and 4 μF are connected in parallel across a 12 V supply. What total charge do they store?
questions.explanation: In parallel, capacitances add: C = 2 + 4 = 6 μF. Q = CV = 6 μF × 12 V = 72 μC.

whyNot.B: 16 μC uses the series combination (4/3 μF) multiplied by 12 V; the capacitors are in parallel.
whyNot.C: 2 μC divides 12 by 6 instead of multiplying.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A 2 kW water heater is switched on for 30 minutes. How much electrical energy does it use, in joules?
questions.explanation: Energy = power × time, with power in watts and time in seconds. E = 2000 × (30 × 60) = 2000 × 1800 = 3.6 × 10⁶ J (which is 1 kWh).

whyNot.A: 6.0 × 10⁴ J uses the time in minutes (2000 × 30).
whyNot.B: 1.0 × 10³ J uses kilowatts and hours (2 × 0.5 = 1 kWh) and then writes it as 10³ J.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A 100 μF capacitor is connected to a 50 Hz a.c. supply. What is its capacitive reactance? (π = 3.14)

whyNot.B: 63.7 Ω uses 1 ÷ (πfC); the formula has 2π.
whyNot.D: 3.14 × 10⁻² Ω is 2πfC without taking the reciprocal.
whyNot.A: 318 Ω uses C = 10 μF, a slip in converting microfarads.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A uniform wire has resistance R. It is stretched evenly until its length is doubled, and its volume stays the same. What is its new resistance?
questions.explanation: R = ρl ÷ A. If the length doubles at constant volume, the cross-sectional area halves. New resistance = ρ(2l) ÷ (A/2) = 4ρl ÷ A = 4R.

whyNot.A: 2R allows for the longer length but forgets that the wire has also become thinner.
whyNot.C: A longer, thinner wire has more resistance, not less.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Isotopes of an element are atoms which have the same
options: mass number but different atomic numbers
number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
number of nucleons but different numbers of electrons
number of neutrons but different numbers of protons
questions.explanation: Isotopes of one element have the same atomic number (proton number) and so the same chemical properties, but different numbers of neutrons, giving different mass numbers. For example, carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons.

whyNot.D: Atoms with different numbers of protons are different elements.
whyNot.A: Atoms with the same mass number but different atomic numbers are isobars, not isotopes.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: In a photoelectric experiment, the intensity of the light falling on a metal is doubled while its frequency is kept the same (above the threshold). What happens?
options: The same number of electrons is emitted, each with twice the kinetic energy
More electrons are emitted each second, with the same maximum kinetic energy
No electrons are emitted until the intensity passes a threshold value
More electrons are emitted, each with greater maximum kinetic energy
questions.explanation: Brighter light of the same frequency has more photons per second, but each photon has the same energy hf. So more electrons are released each second, while their maximum kinetic energy, hf − W, is unchanged.

whyNot.A: The energy of each electron depends on the photon energy hf, which has not changed.
whyNot.C: Emission depends on a threshold frequency, not a threshold intensity.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A sample contains 12 g of a radioactive isotope with a half-life of 6 hours. What mass of the isotope remains after 18 hours?
questions.explanation: 18 hours = 18 ÷ 6 = 3 half-lives. After each half-life the mass halves: 12 g → 6 g → 3 g → 1.5 g.

whyNot.B: 4.0 g divides 12 by 3, the number of half-lives; the mass halves each time, it is not divided by the count.
whyNot.A: 3.0 g is the mass after two half-lives (12 hours).

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: An electron in a hydrogen atom falls from the energy level −1.51 eV to the level −3.40 eV. What is the frequency of the photon emitted? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
questions.explanation: Photon energy = difference between the levels = −1.51 − (−3.40) = 1.89 eV = 1.89 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. f = E ÷ h = 3.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ ÷ 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ ≈ 4.6 × 10¹⁴ Hz (red light).

whyNot.A: 3.7 × 10¹⁴ Hz uses only 1.51 eV, the energy of the upper level.
whyNot.C: 8.2 × 10¹⁴ Hz uses only 3.40 eV, the energy of the lower level.
whyNot.B: 1.2 × 10¹⁵ Hz adds the two energies; the photon carries their difference.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Through a series of decays, uranium-238 (²³⁸₉₂U) changes into radium-226 (²²⁶₈₈Ra). How many alpha and beta particles are emitted?
questions.explanation: Only alpha decay changes the mass number, by 4 each time: (238 − 226) ÷ 4 = 3 alpha particles. These lower the atomic number by 3 × 2 = 6, to 86. The atomic number actually falls only to 88, so it must rise by 2 through beta decay (each beta emission raises it by 1): 2 beta particles.

whyNot.D: 3 alpha and 4 beta would end at atomic number 90, not 88.
whyNot.B: 4 alpha particles would reduce the mass number by 16, to 222.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: In a nuclear fission reactor, what is the main job of the moderator, such as graphite or water?
options: To shield workers from gamma radiation
To slow down the fast neutrons so they cause further fission
To absorb neutrons and stop the chain reaction
To carry heat away from the core to the turbines
questions.explanation: Neutrons released in fission move very fast and are unlikely to cause another uranium-235 nucleus to split. The moderator slows them down by collisions, so the chain reaction can continue.

whyNot.C: Absorbing neutrons to control or stop the reaction is the job of the control rods (e.g. boron or cadmium).
whyNot.D: Carrying heat away is the job of the coolant.
whyNot.A: Shielding is done by thick concrete around the reactor.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A single semiconductor diode is connected in series with a resistor to an a.c. supply. What is the current through the resistor like?
options: It is a perfectly steady direct current
It flows in alternating directions, as before
It flows in one direction during alternate half-cycles only
It flows during both half-cycles in the same direction
questions.explanation: The diode conducts only when it is forward biased, which happens during one half of each cycle. In the other half it is reverse biased and blocks the current. This is half-wave rectification: a one-way current in pulses.

whyNot.A: Smoothing with a capacitor is needed to make the output nearly steady; a diode alone gives pulses.
whyNot.D: Using both half-cycles needs a full-wave (e.g. bridge) rectifier with more diodes.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: The emission of electrons from the surface of a metal when it is heated to a high temperature is called
questions.explanation: When a metal (such as a filament) is heated strongly, some of its free electrons gain enough energy to escape from the surface. This is thermionic emission, used in cathode-ray tubes and X-ray tubes.

whyNot.C: Photoelectric emission is caused by light falling on the metal, not by heating it.
whyNot.A: Radioactive decay is a change in the nucleus, not the escape of surface electrons.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons emitted from a metal surface is 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What stopping potential is needed to stop them? (electronic charge = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.explanation: The stopping potential V₀ is just enough to remove the maximum kinetic energy: eV₀ = KE_max. V₀ = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ ÷ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2.0 V.

whyNot.D: 0.5 V divides e by the kinetic energy, the ratio upside down.
whyNot.C: 5.1 × 10⁻³⁸ V multiplies the energy by the charge instead of dividing.
whyNot.A: 3.2 V treats the energy in units of 10⁻¹⁹ J as if it were in electronvolts.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: When a deuterium nucleus forms from a proton and a neutron, the mass lost (the mass defect) is 4.0 × 10⁻³⁰ kg. How much energy is released? (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
questions.explanation: Einstein's equation: E = mc² = 4.0 × 10⁻³⁰ × (3.0 × 10⁸)² = 4.0 × 10⁻³⁰ × 9.0 × 10¹⁶ = 3.6 × 10⁻¹³ J. This is the binding energy of the deuteron.

whyNot.C: 1.2 × 10⁻²¹ J multiplies by c instead of c².
whyNot.D: 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ J slips one power of ten when multiplying the powers of ten.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: What is the SI unit of linear momentum?
questions.explanation: Momentum = mass × velocity, so its unit is kg × m s⁻¹ = kg m s⁻¹. This is the same as N s, the unit of impulse.

whyNot.A: kg m s⁻² is the unit of force (the newton).
whyNot.B: J s is the unit of Planck's constant (and of angular momentum), not linear momentum.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: An okada rider travels 30 km in 0.5 h along a good road, then 20 km in 1.5 h along a bad road. What is the average speed for the whole journey?
questions.explanation: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time = (30 + 20) ÷ (0.5 + 1.5) = 50 ÷ 2 = 25 km h⁻¹.

whyNot.D: 36.7 km h⁻¹ is the average of the two speeds (60 and 13.3); the rider spends much longer at the slower speed, so the speeds cannot simply be averaged.
whyNot.C: 50 is the total distance in kilometres, not a speed.
whyNot.A: 60 km h⁻¹ is the speed on the good road only.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A book rests on a table. According to Newton's third law, the force that pairs with the earth's pull on the book is the
options: push of the book on the table
pull of the book on the earth
push of the table on the book
questions.explanation: Newton's third law pairs act on different bodies, are of the same type and are equal and opposite. The earth pulls the book down by gravity; the book pulls the earth up by gravity with an equal force.

whyNot.D: The table's push on the book also acts on the book, so it cannot be the third-law partner of the book's weight; it balances the weight (first law).
whyNot.A: The book's push on the table is a contact force paired with the table's push on the book.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: On a velocity–time graph, the velocity of a lorry rises in a straight line from 4 m s⁻¹ to 16 m s⁻¹ in 3 s. What is its acceleration?
questions.explanation: Acceleration is the gradient of a velocity–time graph: a = (v − u) ÷ t = (16 − 4) ÷ 3 = 12 ÷ 3 = 4.0 m s⁻².

whyNot.C: 5.3 m s⁻² is 16 ÷ 3; it uses the final velocity instead of the change in velocity.
whyNot.B: 6.7 m s⁻² adds the velocities ((16 + 4) ÷ 3).
whyNot.D: 12 is the change in velocity in m s⁻¹, not the acceleration.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A stone is thrown vertically upwards at 15 m s⁻¹ and caught again at the point of release. How long is it in the air? (g = 10 m s⁻², ignore air resistance)
questions.explanation: Time to the top: v = u − gt, so 0 = 15 − 10t and t = 1.5 s. The fall back takes the same time, so the total time = 2 × 1.5 = 3.0 s.

whyNot.A: 1.5 s is only the time to reach the highest point.
whyNot.D: 0.67 s is g ÷ u, the ratio upside down.
whyNot.C: 11.25 is the maximum height in metres (u² ÷ 2g), not a time.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: The acceleration due to gravity on the moon is one-sixth of its value on earth. What is the weight on the moon of an astronaut whose mass is 60 kg? (g on earth = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation: Mass does not change from place to place. g on the moon = 10 ÷ 6 m s⁻². Weight = mg = 60 × 10/6 = 100 N.

whyNot.D: 600 N is the astronaut's weight on earth.
whyNot.C: 10 N divides the mass by 6 and treats the result as a weight.
whyNot.A: 60 is the mass in kilograms; weight is measured in newtons.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A hunter's gun of mass 4 kg fires a bullet of mass 0.02 kg at 400 m s⁻¹. With what speed does the gun recoil?
questions.explanation: Momentum is conserved and is zero before firing. So the gun's backward momentum equals the bullet's forward momentum: 4 × v = 0.02 × 400 = 8 kg m s⁻¹. v = 8 ÷ 4 = 2.0 m s⁻¹.

whyNot.C: 8.0 is the bullet's momentum in kg m s⁻¹; it must be divided by the gun's mass.
whyNot.A: 0.5 m s⁻¹ is the gun's mass divided by the bullet's momentum, the ratio upside down.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A lamp of weight 20 N hangs at rest from two strings. Each string makes an angle of 60° with the vertical. What is the tension in each string?
questions.explanation: Resolve vertically: the upward components of the two tensions balance the weight. 2T cos 60° = 20, so 2T × 0.5 = 20 and T = 20 N.

whyNot.C: 10 N simply halves the weight, which is true only if the strings are vertical.
whyNot.A: 11.5 N uses cos 30°; the angle given is measured from the vertical, so cos 60° is needed.
whyNot.D: 40 N (20 ÷ cos 60°) assumes one string holds the whole weight; the two strings share it.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: For a block sliding on a dry horizontal surface, which statement about friction is correct?
options: The limiting friction does not depend on the normal reaction
Friction acts in the direction of motion
Kinetic friction is greater than limiting friction
The limiting friction does not depend on the area of contact
questions.explanation: The laws of solid friction state that limiting friction is proportional to the normal reaction (F = μR) and is independent of the area of the surfaces in contact. Kinetic friction is slightly less than limiting friction, and friction opposes motion.

whyNot.A: Limiting friction is proportional to the normal reaction: pressing harder increases friction.
whyNot.C: Once sliding starts, kinetic friction is slightly less than limiting friction.
whyNot.B: Friction opposes relative motion.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A pendulum bob is pulled aside so that it is 0.2 m higher than its lowest point, then released. What is its speed as it passes through the lowest point? (g = 10 m s⁻², ignore air resistance)
questions.explanation: Potential energy lost = kinetic energy gained: mgh = ½mv². So v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 0.2) = √4 = 2.0 m s⁻¹. The mass cancels out.

whyNot.B: 4.0 m s⁻¹ is 2gh, without taking the square root.
whyNot.D: 1.4 m s⁻¹ is √(gh); it forgets the 2 from ½mv².

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: What is a temperature of −73 °C on the kelvin scale?
questions.explanation: T(K) = θ(°C) + 273 = −73 + 273 = 200 K. Kelvin temperatures are never negative.

whyNot.B: 346 K subtracts the negative sign wrongly (273 + 73).
whyNot.A: There are no negative temperatures on the kelvin scale.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A gas at 27 °C is heated at constant pressure until its volume doubles. What is its final temperature?
questions.explanation: Charles's law: V ∝ T with T in kelvin. 27 °C = 300 K. Doubling the volume doubles the kelvin temperature: 600 K. In Celsius: 600 − 273 = 327 °C.

whyNot.A: 54 °C doubles the Celsius temperature; Charles's law uses kelvin.
whyNot.C: 600 is the answer in kelvin, not in degrees Celsius.
whyNot.B: 300 is the starting temperature in kelvin.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: The thermostat in an electric iron uses a bimetallic strip. The strip bends when heated because
options: one metal melts before the other
the two metals conduct electricity differently
the two metals expand by different amounts
the two metals have different densities
questions.explanation: A bimetallic strip is made of two metals (such as brass and iron) fixed together. When heated, the metal with the larger expansivity expands more, so the strip curves with that metal on the outside. This bending opens or closes the contacts.

whyNot.D: Density does not make the strip bend; different expansion does.
whyNot.A: Neither metal melts at the temperatures of an iron.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Why is the heating element of an electric kettle placed near the bottom of the kettle?
options: So that convection currents can carry heat through all the water
Because heat travels downwards by conduction
Because hot water is denser and stays at the bottom
So that the element is protected from radiation
questions.explanation: Water heated by the element expands, becomes less dense and rises; cooler, denser water sinks to take its place. These convection currents spread the heat through all the water. An element at the top would heat only the top layer.

whyNot.B: Conduction in water is very slow; the heating relies on convection.
whyNot.C: Hot water is less dense than cold water, so it rises.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A 500 W immersion heater is placed in water that is already boiling. In 100 s, 0.02 kg of the water boils away. Assuming no heat losses, what is the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water from these results?
questions.explanation: Energy supplied = Pt = 500 × 100 = 50 000 J. This turns 0.02 kg of water into steam: L = Q ÷ m = 50 000 ÷ 0.02 = 2.5 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

whyNot.B: 1.0 × 10³ multiplies the energy by the mass instead of dividing by it.
whyNot.A: 2.5 × 10⁴ leaves out the time (500 ÷ 0.02).
whyNot.D: 5.0 × 10⁴ is the energy supplied in joules, not divided by the mass.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A 0.2 kg metal block at 100 °C is placed in 0.1 kg of water at 20 °C. Assuming no heat is lost, what is the final temperature? (specific heat capacity of the metal = 400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, of water = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)

whyNot.A: 60.0 °C is the simple average of 100 °C and 20 °C; it ignores the different masses and heat capacities.
whyNot.D: 73.3 °C weights the temperatures by mass only and ignores the specific heat capacities.
whyNot.C: 96.4 °C swaps the specific heat capacities of the metal and the water.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: On a certain day in Port Harcourt, the vapour pressure of water in the air is 1.8 kPa and the saturated vapour pressure at that temperature is 3.0 kPa. What is the relative humidity?
questions.explanation: Relative humidity = actual vapour pressure ÷ saturated vapour pressure × 100% = 1.8 ÷ 3.0 × 100% = 60%.

whyNot.D: 40% is 100% − 60%, the shortfall from saturation.
whyNot.B: 167% is the ratio upside down; relative humidity cannot exceed 100% in normal air.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: According to the kinetic theory, the pressure exerted by a gas on the walls of its container is caused by
options: the molecules expanding when they are heated
the weight of the gas molecules resting on the walls
the attraction between the gas molecules and the walls
the molecules colliding with the walls and changing momentum
questions.explanation: Gas molecules move rapidly in all directions. Each collision with a wall reverses part of a molecule's momentum, and the rate of change of momentum per unit area of the wall is the pressure.

whyNot.B: Gas pressure acts equally in all directions, including on the top wall, so it is not due to weight.
whyNot.A: The molecules themselves do not expand; they move faster when heated.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: In some cold countries salt is spread on icy roads. This helps to clear the ice because dissolved salt
options: raises the melting point of ice
raises the specific heat capacity of ice
lowers the melting point of ice
questions.explanation: Impurities such as salt lower the melting point of ice. Ice with salt on it can melt at temperatures below 0 °C, so the roads clear even when the air is slightly below freezing.

whyNot.A: Raising the melting point would make the ice harder to melt.
whyNot.B: A change in specific heat capacity would not make ice melt below 0 °C.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Two identical metal cans, one painted dull black and the other polished shiny, are filled with hot water at the same temperature and left in a cool room. Which statement is correct?
options: Both cool at the same rate, because they contain the same water
The dull black can cools faster, because dull black surfaces are better emitters of radiation
The dull black can cools slower, because black surfaces absorb heat from the water
The shiny can cools faster, because shiny surfaces are better emitters of radiation
questions.explanation: Dull black surfaces are good emitters (and good absorbers) of radiant heat; shiny surfaces are poor emitters and good reflectors. The black can therefore loses heat by radiation faster and cools more quickly.

whyNot.D: Shiny surfaces are poor emitters, which is why they are used to keep things hot.
whyNot.A: The surfaces differ, so the rate of heat loss by radiation differs.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: The amplitude of a wave is the
options: maximum displacement of a particle from its rest position
number of waves passing a point each second
time taken for one complete oscillation
questions.explanation: Amplitude is the greatest displacement of the vibrating particles from their mean (rest) position. For sound it relates to loudness and for light to brightness.

whyNot.A: The distance between neighbouring crests is the wavelength.
whyNot.C: The number of waves per second is the frequency.
whyNot.D: The time for one oscillation is the period.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A floating cork bobs up and down 120 times in one minute as water waves pass it. What is the frequency of the waves?
questions.explanation: Frequency is the number of oscillations per second. One minute = 60 s, so f = 120 ÷ 60 = 2 Hz.

whyNot.B: 120 is the number of oscillations per minute, not per second.
whyNot.C: 0.5 is the period in seconds (60 ÷ 120), not the frequency.
whyNot.D: 7200 multiplies by 60 instead of dividing.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: When a ray of light passes from air into glass, which of these stays the same?
options: Its direction, for any angle of incidence
questions.explanation: Frequency is set by the source and does not change when light enters a new medium. In glass the light slows down, so its wavelength becomes shorter (v = fλ), and it bends unless it strikes the surface normally.

whyNot.B: Light travels more slowly in glass than in air.
whyNot.C: Since v falls and f is fixed, the wavelength falls.
whyNot.A: The ray bends unless it strikes along the normal.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A ray of light in air strikes the surface of a transparent block of refractive index √3 at an angle of incidence of 60°. What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: Snell's law: n = sin i ÷ sin r, so sin r = sin 60° ÷ √3 = (√3/2) ÷ √3 = 1/2. Therefore r = 30°. The ray bends towards the normal.

whyNot.C: 60° would mean no bending, which happens only if the refractive index is 1.
whyNot.A: 45° does not satisfy sin i ÷ sin r = √3.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Why is a convex mirror used as the driving mirror of a car?
options: It gives a magnified, upright image
It gives a wide field of view with an upright image
It forms a real image on the windscreen
It gives an inverted image that is easy to judge
questions.explanation: A convex mirror always forms an upright, diminished, virtual image. Because the image is diminished, the driver sees a much wider area of the road behind than a plane mirror would show.

whyNot.A: A convex mirror diminishes; it never magnifies.
whyNot.C: A convex mirror forms only virtual images.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A converging lens has a focal length of 20 cm. Where must an object be placed so that the lens forms a real image of exactly the same size as the object?
questions.explanation: A real image of the same size (magnification 1) is formed when u = v. From 1/f = 1/u + 1/v = 2/u, u = 2f = 2 × 20 = 40 cm. The image is also 40 cm away, on the other side, and inverted.

whyNot.A: At the focal point (20 cm) the rays come out parallel and the image is at infinity.
whyNot.B: Inside the focal length the image is virtual and magnified.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A pipe closed at one end has a fundamental frequency of 150 Hz. What is the frequency of the next higher note (the first overtone) it can produce?
questions.explanation: A closed pipe has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so only odd harmonics are possible: f₀, 3f₀, 5f₀, …. The first overtone is 3 × 150 = 450 Hz.

whyNot.B: 300 Hz is the second harmonic, which a closed pipe cannot produce; it would be the first overtone of an open pipe.
whyNot.C: 600 Hz is the fourth harmonic, also an even harmonic.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: In a Young's double-slit experiment, light of wavelength 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m passes through two slits 0.5 mm apart. The fringes are seen on a screen 1.0 m away. What is the distance between neighbouring bright fringes?
questions.explanation: Fringe separation y = λD ÷ d = (6.0 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.0) ÷ (0.5 × 10⁻³) = 1.2 × 10⁻³ m = 1.2 mm.

whyNot.D: 0.12 mm uses d = 5 mm instead of 0.5 mm.
whyNot.A: 12 mm uses d = 0.05 mm, a slip in converting millimetres to metres.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: An electric bell ringing inside a glass jar can be heard clearly. As the air is pumped out of the jar, the sound becomes fainter until it can hardly be heard, although the hammer can still be seen striking the gong. This shows that
options: light needs a material medium to travel through
sound needs a material medium to travel through
questions.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave that is passed on by the vibration of particles of a medium. With almost no air in the jar, there is nothing to carry the sound. Light, an electromagnetic wave, still crosses the vacuum, so the hammer is still seen.

whyNot.A: Light travels much faster than sound.
whyNot.B: The bell is still visible, so light crosses the near-vacuum.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A mark under a glass block 6 cm thick is viewed from directly above. The refractive index of the glass is 1.5. By how much does the mark appear to be raised?
questions.explanation: Apparent depth = real depth ÷ n = 6 ÷ 1.5 = 4.0 cm. The mark appears raised by 6 − 4 = 2.0 cm. (In one step: displacement = t(1 − 1/n).)

whyNot.D: 4.0 cm is the apparent depth, not the amount by which the mark is raised.
whyNot.B: 9.0 cm multiplies the thickness by n; the apparent depth is less than the real depth.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A positively charged rod is held near an uncharged metal sphere on an insulating stand. While the rod is still near, the sphere is touched briefly with a finger; then the finger is removed, and then the rod is taken away. What charge is left on the sphere?
options: Positive on one side and negative on the other
questions.explanation: The positive rod attracts electrons to the near side of the sphere. Earthing the sphere lets electrons flow up from the earth to it. Removing the finger first traps these extra electrons. When the rod is removed they spread out, so the sphere is negatively charged: charging by induction gives the opposite sign.

whyNot.D: Charging by induction gives a charge opposite to that of the inducing rod.
whyNot.C: Electrons from the earth were trapped on the sphere, so it is not neutral.
whyNot.A: Once the rod is gone, the trapped electrons spread evenly over the sphere's surface.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Resistors of 2 Ω and 4 Ω are connected in series across a 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance. What is the p.d. across the 4 Ω resistor?
questions.explanation: Total resistance = 2 + 4 = 6 Ω, so I = 12 ÷ 6 = 2 A. The p.d. across the 4 Ω resistor = IR = 2 × 4 = 8 V. (The other 4 V is across the 2 Ω resistor.)

whyNot.A: 4 V is the p.d. across the 2 Ω resistor.
whyNot.C: 6 V shares the voltage equally; in series the larger resistor takes the larger share.
whyNot.B: 12 V is the p.d. across both resistors together.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A current of 2 A flows through a 5 Ω resistor. At what rate is heat produced in the resistor?
questions.explanation: The rate of heat production is the electrical power dissipated: P = I²R = 2² × 5 = 4 × 5 = 20 W (20 joules of heat every second).

whyNot.C: 10 W is IR (2 × 5), which is the p.d. in volts, not the power.
whyNot.A: 50 W squares the resistance instead of the current.
whyNot.D: 2.5 W divides R by I.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Two point charges repel each other with a force F. If the distance between them is halved and the charges are unchanged, what is the new force?
questions.explanation: Coulomb's law: F = kq₁q₂ ÷ r². Halving r makes r² one-quarter as large, so the force becomes 4 times as large: 4F.

whyNot.D: 2F treats the force as inversely proportional to r rather than r².
whyNot.B: F/4 is the result if the distance were doubled.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A flat coil of area 0.02 m² is placed with its plane at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.5 T. What is the magnetic flux through the coil?
questions.explanation: When the field is at right angles to the plane of the coil, flux Φ = BA = 0.5 × 0.02 = 0.01 Wb.

whyNot.C: 0.04 Wb divides A by B.
whyNot.B: 25 Wb divides B by A.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A step-down transformer changes 240 V mains to 12 V for a phone charger. Its secondary coil has 50 turns. How many turns are on the primary coil, assuming the transformer is ideal?
questions.explanation: For an ideal transformer, Vp ÷ Vs = Np ÷ Ns. Np = Ns × Vp ÷ Vs = 50 × 240 ÷ 12 = 1000 turns.

whyNot.B: 2.5 is 50 × 12 ÷ 240, which would be correct only for the secondary of a coil with 50 primary turns.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A current of 3 A flows through a 10 Ω heating coil for 2 minutes. How much heat is produced?

whyNot.B: 3.6 × 10³ J uses I instead of I² (3 × 10 × 120).
whyNot.A: 180 J uses the time in minutes (9 × 10 × 2).

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Why is the metal case of an electric pressing iron connected to the earth wire?
options: So that if a live wire touches the case, current flows safely to earth and the fuse blows
So that the iron uses less electrical energy
So that the iron heats up more quickly
So that the case does not become hot
questions.explanation: If a fault lets the live wire touch the metal case, the earth wire provides a low-resistance path to the ground. A large current flows, the fuse blows and the supply is cut off, so the user does not get a shock.

whyNot.B: Earthing does not change the energy used in normal operation.
whyNot.D: The case of an iron gets hot by conduction from the element; earthing is about electrical safety.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Two parallel metal plates 4 mm apart are connected to a 200 V supply. What is the electric field intensity between them?
questions.explanation: For a uniform field between parallel plates, E = V ÷ d with d in metres: d = 4 mm = 4 × 10⁻³ m. E = 200 ÷ (4 × 10⁻³) = 5.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹.

whyNot.C: 50 V m⁻¹ uses d = 4 (millimetres not converted to metres).
whyNot.A: 0.8 multiplies V by d (in metres) instead of dividing.
