questions.explanation: Steam adds across the C=C double bond (hydration): CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH. This is the main industrial route to ethanol from petroleum.

whyNot.B: Ethanal would need oxidation, not the addition of water.
whyNot.C: Ethane forms by adding hydrogen, not water.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Starch is completely hydrolysed by boiling with dilute acid. What is the final product?
questions.explanation: Starch is a natural polymer made of many glucose units joined together. Complete acid hydrolysis breaks all the links between the units, leaving glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆.

whyNot.B: Ethanol comes from fermenting glucose, a separate step that needs yeast.
whyNot.C: Glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol) comes from hydrolysing fats and oils, not starch.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Which compound gives a silver mirror when warmed with Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal silver trioxonitrate(V))?
questions.explanation: Alkanals (aldehydes) are easily oxidised. Ethanal reduces Ag⁺ ions in Tollens' reagent to silver metal, which coats the inside of the tube as a mirror, while ethanal is oxidised to ethanoic acid.

whyNot.D: Propanone is a ketone and is not oxidised by Tollens' reagent.
whyNot.C: Ethanoic acid is already fully oxidised and gives no mirror.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: How many moles of oxygen are needed to burn 1 mol of ethanol, C₂H₅OH, completely to carbon(IV) oxide and water?
questions.explanation: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O. The products contain 2(2) + 3(1) = 7 oxygen atoms; ethanol supplies 1, so 6 O atoms (3 mol O₂) must come from oxygen.

whyNot.A: 3.5 is the figure for ethane, which has no oxygen of its own.
whyNot.B: 6 is the number of oxygen atoms, not O₂ molecules.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: 0.1 mol of a hydrocarbon burns completely to give 0.3 mol of carbon(IV) oxide and 0.3 mol of water. What is its molecular formula?
questions.explanation: Each mole of hydrocarbon gives 0.3/0.1 = 3 mol CO₂, so it has 3 carbon atoms. Each mole gives 3 mol H₂O, containing 3 × 2 = 6 mol of H atoms, so it has 6 hydrogen atoms. The formula is C₃H₆.

whyNot.B: C₃H₈ would give 4 mol of water per mole of hydrocarbon.
whyNot.C: C₃H₃ forgets that each water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following is a natural polymer?
questions.explanation: Starch is made by plants such as cassava and yam by joining many glucose units together, so it is a natural polymer. Proteins and natural rubber are other examples.

whyNot.A: Nylon is a synthetic condensation polymer made in factories.
whyNot.D: Polythene is a synthetic addition polymer made from ethene.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Soapless detergents lather well in hard water, whereas soap forms scum. This is because
options: soap reacts with the sodium ions present in hard water
the calcium and magnesium salts of soapless detergents are soluble in water
soapless detergents contain no carbon atoms
soapless detergents remove hardness by precipitating calcium ions
questions.explanation: Hard water contains Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions. These react with soap to form insoluble calcium and magnesium salts (scum), wasting the soap. The calcium and magnesium salts of soapless detergents are soluble, so no scum forms and the detergent still lathers.

whyNot.C: Soapless detergents are organic compounds with long carbon chains.
whyNot.A: Hardness is caused by calcium and magnesium ions, not sodium ions.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which organelle modifies proteins made on the ribosomes and packages them into vesicles for secretion out of the cell?
questions.explanation: Proteins made on ribosomes of the rough endoplasmic reticulum are passed to the Golgi apparatus, which modifies them, packs them into vesicles and sends the vesicles to the cell membrane for secretion (for example, digestive enzymes from pancreatic cells).

whyNot.A: Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that break down worn-out organelles; they do not package secretions.
whyNot.C: The nucleolus makes ribosomes; it is inside the nucleus.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Cyanide stops aerobic respiration in cells. If the roots of a plant are treated with cyanide, which process in the roots will fall most sharply?
options: Uptake of mineral ions by active transport
Entry of water into root hairs by osmosis
Movement of water through the cell walls of the cortex
Passive diffusion of ions down a concentration gradient
questions.explanation: Active transport moves ions against their concentration gradient using carrier proteins and energy (ATP) from respiration. Cyanide stops aerobic respiration, so ATP runs out and active uptake of ions falls sharply. Osmosis and diffusion are passive and do not need energy from respiration.

whyNot.B: Osmosis is passive; it depends on water potential, not on ATP.
whyNot.D: Diffusion down a gradient needs no energy from the cell, so cyanide does not stop it directly.

questions.subject: biology
questions.context:
A student cut six equal strips of yam and weighed them. Each strip was placed in a different sucrose solution for two hours, then blotted dry and weighed again. Her results (percentage change in mass):
• 0.0 mol dm⁻³: +14%
• 0.1 mol dm⁻³: +8%
• 0.2 mol dm⁻³: +3%
• 0.3 mol dm⁻³: −2%
• 0.4 mol dm⁻³: −7%
• 0.5 mol dm⁻³: −11%
questions.stem: Between which two concentrations does the concentration of the yam cell sap lie?
questions.explanation: Where the solution has the same concentration as the cell sap, there is no net osmosis and no change in mass. The strips gained mass (+3%) at 0.2 mol dm⁻³ and lost mass (−2%) at 0.3 mol dm⁻³, so the zero point, and the cell sap concentration, lies between 0.2 and 0.3 mol dm⁻³.

whyNot.D: At these concentrations the strips gained a lot of mass, so the solutions were more dilute than the cell sap.
whyNot.A: At these concentrations the strips lost mass, so the solutions were more concentrated than the cell sap.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A student's drawing of a cheek cell is 18 mm long. The drawing has a magnification of ×400. What is the actual length of the cell in micrometres (µm)?
questions.explanation: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification. First change 18 mm into micrometres: 18 mm × 1 000 = 18 000 µm. Then 18 000 ÷ 400 = 45 µm.

whyNot.C: 7.2 comes from 400 × 18 ÷ 1 000, which mixes up the formula.
whyNot.D: 450 µm is ten times too big; check the unit conversion (1 mm = 1 000 µm).

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In aerobic respiration, glucose is first broken down into pyruvic acid. Where in the cell does this first stage, glycolysis, take place?
questions.explanation: Glycolysis (the splitting of glucose into two molecules of pyruvic acid) happens in the cytoplasm and does not need oxygen. The pyruvic acid then enters the mitochondria, where the Krebs cycle (in the matrix) and the electron transport chain (on the inner membrane) complete aerobic respiration.

whyNot.A: The matrix is where the Krebs cycle happens, after glycolysis.
whyNot.C: The inner membrane carries the electron transport chain, the last stage.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Enzymes speed up chemical reactions in living cells by
options: raising the temperature of the cell
supplying energy to the reacting molecules
being used up as the reaction goes on
lowering the activation energy needed for the reaction
questions.explanation: An enzyme binds its substrate at the active site and holds it in a way that makes the reaction easier, so less activation energy is needed. The reaction therefore goes faster at body temperature. The enzyme comes out unchanged and can be used again.

whyNot.B: Enzymes do not add energy; they reduce the energy barrier.
whyNot.C: Enzymes are catalysts: they are not used up and can be reused many times.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which of the following is a tissue rather than an organ?
questions.explanation: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together for one function. Xylem is a tissue made of vessels and tracheids that carry water. An organ, such as a leaf, root or kidney, is made of several different tissues working together.

whyNot.D: A leaf contains epidermis, mesophyll, xylem and phloem, so it is an organ.
whyNot.A: The kidney is made of many tissues, so it is an organ.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A body cell of an animal has a diploid number of 16 (2n = 16). How many chromatids are present in the cell at metaphase of mitosis?
questions.explanation: Before mitosis the DNA is copied during interphase, so each of the 16 chromosomes is made of two sister chromatids. At metaphase the cell therefore has 16 × 2 = 32 chromatids lined up on the equator.

whyNot.B: 16 is the number of chromosomes, not chromatids.
whyNot.C: 8 is the haploid number, found in gametes.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which change would increase the rate at which oxygen diffuses into a cell?
options: A steeper concentration gradient across the membrane
A smaller surface area of membrane
questions.explanation: The rate of diffusion increases with a steeper concentration gradient, a larger surface area, a thinner barrier and a higher temperature. A bigger difference in oxygen concentration between outside and inside makes oxygen diffuse in faster.

whyNot.C: A thicker membrane makes the diffusion distance longer, so diffusion is slower.
whyNot.A: Lower temperature makes molecules move more slowly, so diffusion is slower.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Germinating groundnut seeds took in 50 cm³ of oxygen and gave out 35 cm³ of carbon dioxide in the same time. What is their respiratory quotient (RQ), and what food are they most likely respiring?
questions.explanation: RQ = volume of CO₂ given out ÷ volume of O₂ taken in = 35 ÷ 50 = 0.7. An RQ of about 0.7 is typical of fats and oils, while carbohydrates give an RQ of 1.0. Groundnut seeds store a lot of oil, which fits.

whyNot.A: 1.4 comes from dividing the wrong way round (O₂ ÷ CO₂).
whyNot.B: The number is right, but carbohydrates give an RQ of 1.0, not 0.7.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In which part of the kidney nephron is all the glucose in the filtrate normally reabsorbed into the blood?
questions.explanation: After ultrafiltration in Bowman's capsule, the filtrate passes into the proximal convoluted tubule. Its cells have many microvilli and mitochondria and reabsorb all the glucose (and amino acids) by active transport, so normal urine contains no glucose.

whyNot.D: The loop of Henle mainly helps the kidney concentrate urine by reabsorbing water and salts.
whyNot.C: Bowman's capsule is where filtration happens, not reabsorption.

questions.subject: biology
questions.context: In an experiment, the rate of photosynthesis of a water plant was measured at increasing light intensities, at 25 °C and 0.04% carbon dioxide. The rate rose steadily at first and then levelled off above a certain light intensity. When the experiment was repeated at the same temperature with 0.1% carbon dioxide, the rate kept rising to a higher level before it levelled off.
questions.stem: What was limiting the rate of photosynthesis in the levelled-off part of the first experiment?
questions.explanation: When the rate levels off, increasing light no longer helps, so light is not the limiting factor there. Raising carbon dioxide from 0.04% to 0.1% made the rate rise higher, so carbon dioxide concentration was the factor holding the rate back.

whyNot.B: Light limits only the rising part of the curve; once the rate levels off, more light has no effect.
whyNot.A: The same plant was used, so the chlorophyll did not change, yet the rate rose when only CO₂ was increased.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A student is chased by a dog. Which hormone makes her heart beat faster and causes more glucose to be released into her blood?
questions.explanation: Adrenaline, from the adrenal glands, is the 'fight or flight' hormone. In fear or danger it increases the heart rate and breathing rate and causes the liver to change glycogen into glucose, giving the muscles more fuel quickly.

whyNot.A: Insulin lowers blood glucose; it does the opposite.
whyNot.C: Thyroxine controls the general rate of metabolism over a long time, not the sudden response to danger.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In a villus of the small intestine, most fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into the
options: muscle layer of the gut wall
questions.explanation: Each villus has a central lymph vessel called a lacteal. Fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into the epithelial cells, recombined into fats and passed mainly into the lacteal, which carries them in the lymph. Glucose and amino acids go into the blood capillaries.

whyNot.D: Blood capillaries absorb glucose and amino acids, not most of the fat.
whyNot.A: Goblet cells secrete mucus; they do not absorb digested food.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In flowering plants, one male nucleus fuses with the egg cell and the other fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the endosperm. If the leaf cells of a plant have 14 chromosomes, how many chromosomes are in each endosperm cell?
questions.explanation: Leaf cells are diploid, so 2n = 14 and n = 7. The endosperm forms from one male nucleus (n) plus two polar nuclei (n + n), so it is triploid: 3n = 3 × 7 = 21 chromosomes.

whyNot.B: 14 is the diploid number, found in the zygote and the leaf cells.
whyNot.C: 7 is the haploid number of a single gamete nucleus.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: During blood clotting at a cut, which soluble plasma protein is changed into insoluble threads that trap blood cells?
questions.explanation: Damaged tissue and platelets release thrombokinase, which (with calcium ions) turns prothrombin into thrombin. Thrombin then changes soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads, which form a mesh that traps red cells and forms a clot.

whyNot.C: Albumin is a plasma protein that helps keep water in the blood; it does not form a clot.
whyNot.B: Haemoglobin is inside red blood cells and carries oxygen.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which blood cells produce antibodies?
questions.explanation: Lymphocytes are white blood cells with a large round nucleus. When they meet a foreign antigen, some of them make antibodies that stick to that antigen and help destroy the germ.

whyNot.C: Phagocytes are also white blood cells, but they engulf germs rather than make antibodies.
whyNot.D: Platelets help blood to clot.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which events take place when a person breathes in (inspiration)?
options: The diaphragm contracts, and the ribs move down and in
The air pressure in the lungs rises above atmospheric pressure
The diaphragm relaxes and domes upwards, and the ribs move down
The diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the external intercostal muscles contract
questions.explanation: In inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the external intercostal muscles contract to pull the ribs up and out. The chest cavity gets bigger, the pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure, and air rushes in.

whyNot.C: This describes breathing out (expiration).
whyNot.B: Air flows in only when lung pressure falls below atmospheric pressure.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A student counts 18 pulse beats at her wrist in 15 seconds. What is her pulse rate?
questions.explanation: There are 60 seconds in a minute, which is 60 ÷ 15 = 4 lots of 15 seconds. Pulse rate = 18 × 4 = 72 beats per minute.

whyNot.A: 18 is the count in 15 seconds, not in a whole minute.
whyNot.C: 270 comes from multiplying 18 by 15 instead of by 4.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A person stops looking at a distant hill and starts reading a book. Which change takes place in her eyes?
options: The ciliary muscles relax, the suspensory ligaments tighten and the lens becomes thinner
The pupils widen to let in more light from the page
The ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments slacken and the lens becomes thicker
The ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments tighten and the lens becomes thicker
questions.explanation: Focusing on a near object (accommodation): the ciliary muscles contract, which reduces the pull on the suspensory ligaments so they slacken. The elastic lens then becomes thicker and more curved, bending light more so that the image of the near page falls on the retina.

whyNot.A: This is what happens when the eye focuses on a distant object.
whyNot.D: When the ciliary muscles contract, the ligaments slacken, not tighten.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which food chain would give a pyramid of numbers in which the producer bar is narrower than the bar above it?
questions.explanation: A pyramid of numbers shows how many organisms are at each level. One large mango tree supports hundreds of caterpillars, so the producer bar (1) is narrower than the primary consumer bar (500). In the other chains the producers are small and very numerous, giving an upright pyramid.

whyNot.D: 5 000 grass plants is far more than 40 grasscutters, so this pyramid is upright.
whyNot.A: Phytoplankton are tiny and very numerous, so the base is the widest bar.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: The capture–mark–recapture method is used to estimate the number of crabs in a mangrove swamp. Which assumption must hold for the estimate to be reliable?
options: The marked crabs mix freely with the rest of the population before the second sample
Marked crabs are easier to catch than unmarked ones
The marks make the crabs easier for predators to see
Many crabs are born and many die between the two samples
questions.explanation: The method assumes that the proportion of marked animals in the second sample equals their proportion in the whole population. That is only true if marked animals mix evenly with the rest, are no easier or harder to catch, are not harmed by the marks, and if few births, deaths or migrations happen between samples.

whyNot.B: If marked crabs are easier to catch, too many are recaptured and the population is underestimated.
whyNot.D: Many births and deaths change the population between samples and spoil the estimate.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In the carbon cycle, which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Green plants and algae take in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis and build it into sugars, so photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the air. Respiration, decay and burning all release carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere.

whyNot.C: Respiration releases carbon dioxide.
whyNot.D: Burning firewood (combustion) releases carbon dioxide.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In ecological succession, which organisms are usually the first to colonise bare rock?
questions.explanation: Lichens are pioneer organisms: they can cling to bare rock, survive drying out and release acids that slowly break the rock surface. As they die they add a little organic matter, starting soil formation so that mosses, then grasses and later shrubs can grow.

whyNot.A: Shrubs need deep soil and come much later in succession.
whyNot.B: Grasses need some soil, which pioneers must first help to form.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A student threw a 1 m² quadrat 10 times at random on a 200 m² school field and counted 45 Tridax plants in total. Estimate the number of Tridax plants on the whole field.
questions.explanation: Mean number per quadrat = 45 ÷ 10 = 4.5 plants per m². The field is 200 m², so the estimate is 4.5 × 200 = 900 plants.

whyNot.D: 450 uses 100 m² instead of 200 m² (or forgets to double).
whyNot.A: 9 000 multiplies the total count (45) by 200 without dividing by the number of quadrats first.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which of the following is a biotic factor in a habitat?
questions.explanation: Biotic factors are the effects of living things on one another, such as competition, predation, parasitism and disease. Soil pH, rainfall and light intensity are abiotic (non-living, physical or chemical) factors.

whyNot.A: Soil pH is a chemical (edaphic) factor, so it is abiotic.
whyNot.D: Rainfall is a climatic factor, so it is abiotic.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Yeast grown in a fixed volume of sugar solution shows an S-shaped (sigmoid) growth curve. Why does the curve level off at the stationary phase?
options: The yeast cells begin to photosynthesise
All the yeast cells stop reproducing at the same moment
The birth rate becomes equal to the death rate as food runs short and wastes build up
The death rate falls to zero
questions.explanation: At first there is plenty of food, so numbers rise quickly. As sugar is used up and wastes such as ethanol build up, fewer new cells are produced and more die. When the birth rate equals the death rate, the population stops growing and the curve becomes flat.

whyNot.B: Cells keep dividing in the stationary phase, but deaths balance the new cells.
whyNot.D: If the death rate were zero, numbers would keep rising.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Fertiliser washed from farms into a pond causes a rapid growth of algae. Soon afterwards many fish in the pond die. What is the direct cause of the fish deaths?
options: The algae eat the food of the fish
The algae raise the temperature of the water
The fertiliser poisons the fish directly
Bacteria decomposing the dead algae use up the dissolved oxygen
questions.explanation: This is eutrophication. Nitrates and phosphates make algae grow quickly (an algal bloom). The algae soon die, and large numbers of aerobic bacteria decompose them, using up the oxygen dissolved in the water. The fish suffocate for lack of oxygen.

whyNot.C: The fertiliser acts by feeding the algae; it is the oxygen shortage that kills the fish.
whyNot.A: Algae are producers; they make their own food and do not eat fish food.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: The ecological niche of an organism is best described as
options: all the populations living together in an area
its role in the community, including what it feeds on and how it interacts with other organisms
the total number of its species in a given area
the physical place where it lives
questions.explanation: A niche is the role or 'job' of an organism in its ecosystem: what it eats, what eats it, when and where it feeds, and how it affects other organisms and its surroundings. The habitat is only the place where it lives.

whyNot.D: The physical place where an organism lives is its habitat.
whyNot.A: All the populations living together in an area form a community.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which gas, released in large amounts when petrol, diesel and firewood are burned, is the main cause of the enhanced greenhouse effect?
questions.explanation: Burning fuels that contain carbon releases carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide traps heat radiated from the Earth's surface, so a rise in its level in the atmosphere increases the greenhouse effect and leads to global warming.

whyNot.C: Oxygen is used up, not produced, when fuels burn, and it is not a greenhouse gas.
whyNot.B: Nitrogen makes up most of the air but does not trap heat in this way.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In a plant, purple flowers (P) are dominant over white (p), and tall stem (T) is dominant over dwarf (t). The two genes are on different chromosomes. A plant of genotype PpTt is crossed with a plant of genotype pptt. What phenotypic ratio is expected among the offspring?
options: 1 purple tall : 1 purple dwarf : 1 white tall : 1 white dwarf
9 purple tall : 3 purple dwarf : 3 white tall : 1 white dwarf
questions.explanation: PpTt makes four kinds of gametes in equal numbers: PT, Pt, pT and pt. The pptt parent makes only pt gametes. The offspring are PpTt (purple tall), Pptt (purple dwarf), ppTt (white tall) and pptt (white dwarf), each 1/4, giving a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio.

whyNot.B: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 comes from crossing two double heterozygotes (PpTt × PpTt).
whyNot.D: This would happen only if the two genes were completely linked.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Haemophilia is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. A man with haemophilia marries a woman who is homozygous for the normal allele. What proportion of their daughters will be carriers?
questions.explanation: The father is XʰY and the mother is XᴴXᴴ. Every daughter receives the father's X chromosome, which carries h, and an Xᴴ from the mother, so every daughter is XᴴXʰ: a carrier with normal clotting. Sons receive the father's Y and are all normal.

whyNot.D: Half would apply to sons of a carrier mother, not to daughters of an affected father.
whyNot.A: Daughters must inherit their father's only X chromosome, which carries the allele.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A man of blood group AB marries a woman of blood group A whose genotype is IᴬIᴼ. What is the probability that their child will be blood group A?
questions.explanation: Father IᴬIᴮ gives Iᴬ or Iᴮ; mother IᴬIᴼ gives Iᴬ or Iᴼ. The four equally likely children are IᴬIᴬ (A), IᴬIᴼ (A), IᴮIᴬ (AB) and IᴮIᴼ (B). Two out of four are group A, so the probability is 2/4 = 1/2.

whyNot.D: 1/4 is the chance of group AB or of group B, not of group A.
whyNot.C: Group A is possible because both parents can pass on Iᴬ.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: After a new insecticide is sprayed in a town for several years, the mosquitoes there become resistant to it. Which explanation agrees with Darwin's theory of natural selection?
options: Mosquitoes that used their resistance a lot made it stronger and passed it on
A few mosquitoes already carried resistance; they survived the spraying and passed it on to their offspring
The insecticide caused every mosquito to change so that it could resist it
The insecticide made the mosquitoes reproduce faster
questions.explanation: Natural selection works on variation that already exists. A few mosquitoes happened to carry alleles for resistance. The spray killed the others, so the resistant ones survived, bred and passed on the allele. Over many generations most mosquitoes became resistant.

whyNot.C: The insecticide does not create the resistance; it selects mosquitoes that already have it.
whyNot.A: This is Lamarck's idea of use and disuse, not Darwin's theory.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Sickle-cell anaemia arises because one base in the gene for haemoglobin is replaced by a different base. This kind of change is called
questions.explanation: A change in the base sequence of a single gene is a gene (point) mutation. In sickle-cell anaemia one base is substituted, which changes one amino acid in the haemoglobin protein and makes red cells sickle when oxygen is low.

whyNot.A: A chromosome mutation changes the structure or number of whole chromosomes, as in Down's syndrome.
whyNot.D: Polyploidy means having extra complete sets of chromosomes.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Two genes that are located close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together. This is called
questions.explanation: Genes on the same chromosome travel together into the gametes during meiosis, so they tend to be inherited together. This is linkage. Only genes on different chromosomes assort independently.

whyNot.D: Independent assortment applies to genes on different chromosomes.
whyNot.B: Codominance describes two alleles of one gene both showing in the phenotype.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: One strand of a DNA molecule has the base sequence A T G C C A. What is the base sequence on the complementary strand?
options: U A C G G U
T A C G G T
G C A T T G
A T G C C A
questions.explanation: In DNA, adenine always pairs with thymine (A–T) and guanine with cytosine (G–C). So A T G C C A pairs with T A C G G T.

whyNot.A: Uracil (U) is found in RNA, not DNA.
whyNot.C: This pairs A with G and T with C, which is wrong; A pairs with T and G with C.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In four-o'clock plants, flower colour shows incomplete dominance: RR plants are red, WW plants are white and RW plants are pink. A pink-flowered plant is crossed with a white-flowered plant. What ratio of offspring is expected?
questions.explanation: Pink (RW) gives R or W gametes; white (WW) gives only W. The offspring are RW (pink) and WW (white) in equal numbers, so the ratio is 1 pink : 1 white.

whyNot.C: 1 : 2 : 1 comes from crossing pink with pink.
whyNot.D: All pink comes from crossing red (RR) with white (WW).

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A man with genotype HbAA marries a woman with genotype HbSS. What is the probability that a child of theirs will have sickle-cell anaemia (HbSS)?
questions.explanation: The father can pass on only HbA and the mother only HbS, so every child is HbAS. These children are carriers (sickle-cell trait) but none has sickle-cell anaemia, because that needs HbS from both parents. The probability of HbSS is 0.

whyNot.A: 1/4 is the chance when both parents are HbAS.
whyNot.B: Every child is HbAS, so the probability of being a carrier is 1, not of being HbSS.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: The human appendix and the tail bone (coccyx) are small structures with little or no use. They are used as evidence for evolution because they are
questions.explanation: Vestigial structures are reduced organs that were larger and useful in ancestors. Their presence suggests that humans descended from ancestors in which these organs worked, for example a tail.

whyNot.A: Analogous structures do the same job but have different origins, like bird and insect wings.
whyNot.B: Acquired characters are changes gained during an individual's life; they are not inherited.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which feature do ferns have that mosses lack?
questions.explanation: Ferns (pteridophytes) have true roots, stems and leaves with xylem and phloem, which lets them grow larger. Mosses (bryophytes) have no vascular tissue. Both groups make spores, contain chlorophyll and show alternation of generations.

whyNot.C: Mosses also reproduce by spores, made in capsules.
whyNot.D: Both mosses and ferns show alternation of generations.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which insect goes through complete metamorphosis, with egg, larva, pupa and adult stages?
questions.explanation: The housefly lays eggs that hatch into larvae (maggots); each larva becomes a pupa, from which the adult fly emerges. Grasshoppers, cockroaches and termites have incomplete metamorphosis: egg, nymph, adult, with no pupa.

whyNot.A: Grasshopper young are nymphs that look like small wingless adults; there is no pupa.
whyNot.B: The cockroach also has egg, nymph and adult stages only.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which feature shows that a plant such as hibiscus is a dicotyledon?
questions.explanation: Dicotyledons have two seed leaves, net-veined leaves, a tap root system and flower parts usually in fours or fives. Parallel veins, fibrous roots and flower parts in threes are features of monocotyledons such as maize.

whyNot.D: Parallel veins are typical of monocots such as grasses.
whyNot.C: Flower parts in threes are typical of monocots.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In the five-kingdom system of classification, bacteria are placed in the kingdom
questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes: their cells have no true nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. All prokaryotes are placed in the kingdom Monera (Prokaryotae). The other four kingdoms contain eukaryotes.

whyNot.A: Protoctista contains single-celled eukaryotes such as Amoeba and algae.
whyNot.C: Fungi are eukaryotes with a true nucleus.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Hydra is a small freshwater animal with a sac-like body, a single opening (the mouth) and tentacles armed with stinging cells. It belongs to the phylum
questions.explanation: Cnidarians (coelenterates) have a sac-like body with one opening, a body wall of two cell layers and tentacles with stinging cells (cnidoblasts) for catching prey. Hydra and jellyfish are examples.

whyNot.C: Flatworms are flattened and have no stinging tentacles.
whyNot.A: Annelids have long segmented bodies with a mouth and an anus.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Spirogyra is a filamentous green alga. Two filaments lie side by side, and the contents of a cell in one filament pass through a tube into a cell of the other. This process is called
questions.explanation: In conjugation, the cell contents of one filament move through a conjugation tube and fuse with the contents of a cell in the other filament, forming a zygospore. It is a form of sexual reproduction in Spirogyra.

whyNot.B: Fragmentation is asexual: a filament simply breaks into pieces that grow on.
whyNot.D: Binary fission is one cell splitting into two, as in Amoeba.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Apart from its lungs, which parts of its body does an adult toad use for gaseous exchange?
options: Its moist skin and the lining of its mouth
questions.explanation: Adult amphibians such as the toad have small lungs, but also exchange gases through their thin, moist, well-supplied skin and the lining of the mouth (buccal cavity). The skin must stay moist for oxygen to dissolve and diffuse in.

whyNot.C: Gills are used by tadpoles, not adult toads.
whyNot.A: Spiracles are the breathing openings of insects.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: The adult tapeworm has no mouth and no gut. How does it obtain its food?
options: It digests the lining of the host's intestine with its own enzymes
It makes its own food by photosynthesis
It absorbs digested food from the host's intestine through its body surface
It sucks blood using its hooks and suckers
questions.explanation: The tapeworm lives in the small intestine, surrounded by food the host has already digested. Its thin, flat body has a large surface area, so it simply absorbs the soluble food through its body wall. Its hooks and suckers only hold it in place.

whyNot.D: The hooks and suckers anchor the worm to the gut wall; they are not used for feeding.
whyNot.A: The tapeworm is covered in a layer that resists the host's enzymes; it does not digest the gut lining.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which three features are shared by all chordates at some stage of their life?
options: A notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord and pharyngeal (gill) slits
Hair, mammary glands and a diaphragm
A backbone, four limbs and lungs
Scales, fins and a lateral line
questions.explanation: All chordates have, at least in the embryo, a notochord (a flexible rod along the back), a hollow nerve cord on the dorsal side and gill slits in the pharynx. In vertebrates the notochord is mostly replaced by the backbone, and in land vertebrates the gill slits appear only in the embryo.

whyNot.C: Fish have no limbs and most breathe with gills, so these features are not shared by all chordates.
whyNot.B: Hair, mammary glands and a diaphragm are found only in mammals.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which list shows the levels of classification in the correct order, from the largest group to the smallest?
options: Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
Kingdom, phylum, order, class, genus, family, species
Phylum, kingdom, class, family, order, genus, species
Kingdom, class, phylum, order, family, species, genus
questions.explanation: Organisms are grouped in a hierarchy: kingdom, phylum (division in plants), class, order, family, genus and species. Each level contains fewer, more closely related organisms than the level above it.

whyNot.D: Phylum comes before class, and genus comes before species.
whyNot.B: Class comes before order, and family before genus.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: The cell wall of a plant cell is made mainly of
questions.explanation: Plant cell walls are made mainly of cellulose, a tough carbohydrate built from glucose units. Its fibres make the wall strong and fully permeable, and they stop the cell bursting when it takes in water.

whyNot.D: Chitin is found in the cell walls of fungi and in the exoskeleton of insects.
whyNot.C: Starch is the food store of plants, kept inside the cell, not used to build the wall.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Heart muscle cells contain many more mitochondria than most other cells. Why?
options: They make many proteins for export
They store large amounts of food
They need a lot of energy for continuous contraction
They divide more often than other cells
questions.explanation: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, which releases energy as ATP. Heart muscle contracts throughout life without resting, so its cells need a great deal of energy and therefore have very many mitochondria.

whyNot.A: Cells that make many proteins for export have lots of rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus.
whyNot.D: Heart muscle cells hardly divide at all in adults.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A student adds sodium hydroxide solution and a few drops of copper(II) sulphate solution to a sample of egg white. The mixture turns purple (violet). Which food substance is present?
questions.explanation: This is the Biuret test. A purple or violet colour shows that protein is present. Egg white is rich in the protein albumin.

whyNot.A: Starch is tested with iodine solution, which turns blue-black.
whyNot.D: Reducing sugars are tested with Benedict's solution and heat, giving an orange or brick-red colour.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In the emulsion test, a food sample is shaken with ethanol and the liquid is then poured into water. A cloudy white emulsion forms. What does this show?
questions.explanation: Fats and oils dissolve in ethanol but not in water. When the ethanol solution is poured into water, the fat comes out as tiny droplets that scatter light, giving a milky white emulsion. This is a positive test for fat or oil.

whyNot.D: Protein is shown by the Biuret test (purple colour).
whyNot.C: Vitamin C is shown by decolourising blue DCPIP solution.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Why do large multicellular animals need a transport system such as blood, while an amoeba does not?
options: Their cells do not need oxygen
Their surface area to volume ratio is larger than that of an amoeba
Their surface area to volume ratio is small, so diffusion alone is too slow to supply their inner cells
Diffusion does not take place in multicellular animals
questions.explanation: As an organism gets bigger, its volume grows faster than its surface area, so its surface area to volume ratio falls. Many cells are far from the surface, and diffusion over such distances is too slow. A transport system carries materials quickly to every cell. An amoeba is tiny, with a large ratio, so diffusion is enough.

whyNot.B: It is the other way round: the amoeba has the larger ratio.
whyNot.D: Diffusion still happens in multicellular animals, for example in the alveoli, but only over short distances.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A cell is viewed through a light microscope with a ×15 eyepiece lens and a ×10 objective lens. Its image measures 3 mm across. What is the actual width of the cell?
questions.explanation: Total magnification = eyepiece × objective = 15 × 10 = 150. Actual size = image size ÷ magnification = 3 mm ÷ 150 = 0.02 mm (20 µm).

whyNot.C: 0.2 mm divides by the eyepiece magnification only (3 ÷ 15).
whyNot.D: 450 mm multiplies by the magnification instead of dividing.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In a flowering plant, in which structure does meiosis take place to produce pollen grains?
questions.explanation: The anther contains pollen sacs in which pollen mother cells divide by meiosis, halving the chromosome number. The haploid cells develop into pollen grains, which carry the male gametes.

whyNot.B: The stigma receives pollen; it does not make it.
whyNot.D: The filament is the stalk that holds up the anther.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Centrioles are found in animal cells but not in the cells of flowering plants. What is their function?
options: They help to form the spindle during cell division
questions.explanation: During cell division the two centrioles move to opposite ends of an animal cell and organise the spindle fibres, which pull the chromosomes (or chromatids) apart.

whyNot.C: Proteins are made on ribosomes.
whyNot.B: Energy is released in mitochondria.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: During a 100 m race, a sprinter's leg muscles respire anaerobically for a short time. Which substance builds up in the muscles?
questions.explanation: When muscles cannot get enough oxygen, they break glucose down anaerobically into lactic acid, releasing a little energy. Lactic acid builds up and causes fatigue. It is later removed using extra oxygen (repaying the oxygen debt).

whyNot.D: Ethanol (with carbon dioxide) is made by yeast and plants in anaerobic respiration, not by human muscle.
whyNot.C: Urea is made in the liver from excess amino acids.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A mature human red blood cell has no nucleus. Which of these can it NOT do?
questions.explanation: The nucleus contains the chromosomes, which must be copied and shared out for a cell to divide. Without a nucleus a red blood cell cannot divide. It can still carry oxygen with its haemoglobin, take in glucose and respire (anaerobically). New red cells are made in the bone marrow.

whyNot.D: Carrying oxygen is the main job of red cells, using haemoglobin.
whyNot.C: Red cells respire anaerobically, since they have no mitochondria.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which teeth in an adult human are broad, have several cusps and are used mainly for grinding food?
questions.explanation: Molars are at the back of the jaw. They are broad, with several cusps and two or three roots, and they crush and grind food. Incisors are chisel-shaped for cutting, and canines are pointed for tearing.

whyNot.D: Incisors are chisel-shaped teeth for biting and cutting.
whyNot.C: Canines are pointed teeth for tearing.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which enzyme in pancreatic juice breaks down fats into fatty acids and glycerol?
questions.explanation: Lipase digests fats (lipids) into fatty acids and glycerol. Its action is helped by bile, which emulsifies fats into small droplets with a larger surface area.

whyNot.B: Amylase digests starch into maltose.
whyNot.D: Trypsin digests proteins.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which part of the human skeleton protects the brain?
questions.explanation: The cranium is the part of the skull made of fused flat bones that enclose and protect the brain.

whyNot.C: The sternum (breastbone), with the ribs, protects the heart and lungs.
whyNot.D: The vertebral column protects the spinal cord.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: The movement of manufactured food, such as sucrose, from the leaves to other parts of a plant is called
questions.explanation: Translocation is the transport of food made in the leaves (mainly sucrose and amino acids) through the phloem to growing points and storage organs such as cassava tubers.

whyNot.C: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the leaves.
whyNot.A: Guttation is the loss of liquid water drops from leaf margins.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Excess amino acids in the human body cannot be stored. In which organ is their nitrogen-containing part turned into urea?
questions.explanation: In the liver, excess amino acids are deaminated: the amino group is removed and converted into urea. The urea passes into the blood and is later removed by the kidneys in urine.

whyNot.D: The kidneys remove urea from the blood, but they do not make it.
whyNot.A: The bladder only stores urine.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which feature would you expect in a flower, such as that of maize, which is pollinated by wind?
options: Large feathery stigmas that hang outside the flower
Sticky pollen grains with spiny surfaces
questions.explanation: Wind-pollinated flowers have large, feathery stigmas (the 'silk' of maize) hanging out to catch pollen from the air. They also make large amounts of light, smooth pollen, and have small, dull petals with no scent or nectar.

whyNot.A: Bright petals attract insects, which wind-pollinated flowers do not need.
whyNot.C: Sticky, spiny pollen clings to insects; wind pollen is light and smooth.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: When a bean seed germinates, its cotyledons are carried above the soil because the hypocotyl grows longer. This type of germination is called
questions.explanation: In epigeal germination the hypocotyl (the part of the stem below the cotyledons) lengthens and pushes the cotyledons above ground, where they turn green. In hypogeal germination, as in maize, the cotyledon stays under the soil.

whyNot.B: In hypogeal germination the cotyledons stay below the soil because the epicotyl lengthens instead.
whyNot.D: Dormancy is a resting period when the seed does not germinate.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In an insect such as a grasshopper, air enters the body through openings called spiracles. How is the air carried to the tissues?
options: In the blood, inside closed vessels
Through a system of tracheae (air tubes)
questions.explanation: Insects have a tracheal system: spiracles open into tracheae, which branch into fine tracheoles that reach the cells. Oxygen diffuses directly to the tissues along these tubes, so insect blood does not carry much oxygen.

whyNot.C: Insects have an open circulation, and their blood plays little part in carrying oxygen.
whyNot.A: Gills are used by aquatic animals such as fish.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A man's urine contains 2 g of urea in every 100 cm³. If he passes 1 500 cm³ of urine in a day, how much urea does he excrete that day?
questions.explanation: 1 500 cm³ is 1 500 ÷ 100 = 15 lots of 100 cm³. Each 100 cm³ contains 2 g of urea, so the total is 15 × 2 = 30 g.

whyNot.D: 15 is the number of 100 cm³ portions, not the mass of urea.
whyNot.B: 300 g is ten times too much; check the division by 100.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: After ovulation, which hormone, made mainly by the corpus luteum, keeps the lining of the uterus thick and ready for implantation?
questions.explanation: After the egg is released, the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone. Progesterone maintains the thick, blood-rich lining of the uterus. If no pregnancy occurs, the corpus luteum breaks down, progesterone falls and menstruation begins.

whyNot.A: FSH comes from the pituitary and makes follicles develop in the ovary.
whyNot.C: LH comes from the pituitary and triggers ovulation.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In a food chain, why is much less energy available to the secondary consumers than to the primary consumers?
options: Much energy is lost at each level as heat from respiration and in undigested waste
Secondary consumers feed less often than primary consumers
Energy is destroyed whenever one organism eats another
questions.explanation: Primary consumers use most of the energy in their food for respiration (lost as heat) and movement, and some passes out in faeces or stays in parts that are not eaten. Only a small fraction (often about 10%) is stored in their bodies and passed on to the secondary consumers.

whyNot.B: Size is not the reason; the loss comes from respiration and waste.
whyNot.D: Energy is not destroyed; it is changed into heat and lost from the chain.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A student placed a quadrat measuring 0.5 m × 0.5 m at five random spots on a lawn and counted the clover plants inside it each time: 3, 5, 2, 4 and 6. Estimate the population density of clover on the lawn.
questions.explanation: Mean per quadrat = (3 + 5 + 2 + 4 + 6) ÷ 5 = 20 ÷ 5 = 4. Each quadrat covers 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25 m². Density = 4 ÷ 0.25 = 16 plants per m².

whyNot.D: 4 is the mean per quadrat, but each quadrat is only 0.25 m², not 1 m².
whyNot.B: 8 divides by 0.5 m instead of by the area 0.25 m².

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Ticks attach to the skin of cattle and suck their blood. This relationship is an example of
questions.explanation: In parasitism one organism (the parasite) lives on or in another (the host) and feeds from it, harming it. The tick gains blood while the cow loses blood and may catch diseases the tick carries.

whyNot.A: In commensalism the host is neither helped nor harmed, but here the cow is harmed.
whyNot.B: In mutualism both partners benefit.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Water lilies have large air spaces in their stems and leaf stalks. What is the main advantage of these air spaces?
options: They reduce water loss by transpiration
They store water for dry periods
They keep the leaves afloat and supply air to the submerged parts
They protect the plant from herbivores
questions.explanation: Hydrophytes such as the water lily have spongy tissue (aerenchyma) full of air. The air makes the leaves buoyant so they float in the light, and it lets oxygen reach roots and stems buried in the mud, where oxygen is scarce.

whyNot.B: A water plant is surrounded by water, so it has no need to store it.
whyNot.A: Water plants do not need to save water.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A student pours 50 cm³ of dry soil into a measuring cylinder containing 50 cm³ of water. Bubbles rise, and when they stop the level reads 85 cm³ instead of 100 cm³. What does this show, and what percentage of the soil volume was air?
questions.explanation: The bubbles show that air was trapped in the soil spaces; water took the place of the air. Volume of air = 100 − 85 = 15 cm³. Percentage of soil volume = 15 ÷ 50 × 100 = 30%.

whyNot.B: 15 cm³ is the volume of air; as a percentage of the 50 cm³ of soil it is 30%.
whyNot.C: Humus is detected by heating dry soil and weighing the loss, not by bubbles in water.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Running a petrol generator inside a closed room can kill the people sleeping there. This is because the exhaust contains carbon monoxide, which
options: makes the room too hot to breathe
dissolves in rain to form acid rain
combines firmly with haemoglobin and reduces the oxygen the blood can carry
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen does, forming carboxyhaemoglobin. Less haemoglobin is free to carry oxygen, so the body's cells are starved of oxygen, and the victim becomes unconscious and may die.

whyNot.C: Acid rain is caused mainly by sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides.
whyNot.A: Ozone is destroyed mainly by CFCs.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which farming practice helps to reduce soil erosion on a hillside farm?
options: Ploughing up and down the slope
Removing all trees from the farm
questions.explanation: Ridges made across the slope (along the contours) slow down rainwater running downhill, so it soaks in instead of washing the topsoil away. Ploughing downhill, burning and clearing trees all leave the soil more exposed to erosion.

whyNot.A: Furrows running downhill channel the water and speed up erosion.
whyNot.B: Burning removes the plant cover that protects the soil.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In the nitrogen cycle, which bacteria convert ammonium compounds into nitrites in the soil?
questions.explanation: Nitrification happens in two steps. Nitrosomonas oxidises ammonium compounds to nitrites, and then Nitrobacter oxidises the nitrites to nitrates, which plants can absorb.

whyNot.B: Nitrobacter carries out the second step, nitrites to nitrates.
whyNot.A: Rhizobium fixes nitrogen gas in root nodules of legumes.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which of the following increases the size of a population?
questions.explanation: A population grows through births and immigration (individuals moving into the area). It shrinks through deaths and emigration (individuals leaving). Predation and disease increase deaths.

whyNot.B: Emigration means individuals leave, so the population falls.
whyNot.D: Predation kills members of the population.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A Secchi disc is lowered into the water of a lagoon until it just disappears from view. What is being measured?
options: The speed of the water current
questions.explanation: A Secchi disc is a black-and-white disc on a marked rope. The depth at which it disappears shows how far light passes through the water. Cloudy water, for example with much silt or algae, gives a small depth.

whyNot.A: Water temperature is measured with a thermometer.
whyNot.B: Current speed is measured with a flow meter or by timing a float.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A pure-breeding red-flowered plant (RR) is crossed with a pure-breeding white-flowered plant (rr). Red is dominant. The F1 plants are then self-pollinated. What genotypic ratio is expected in the F2 generation?
questions.explanation: All the F1 plants are Rr. Selfing Rr × Rr: each parent gives R or r gametes. The combinations are RR, Rr, rR and rr, so the genotypic ratio is 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr. (The phenotypic ratio is 3 red : 1 white.)

whyNot.B: 3 : 1 is the phenotypic ratio (red : white), not the genotypic ratio.
whyNot.A: 1 : 1 comes from a test cross, Rr × rr.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A man with genotype HbAS (a sickle-cell carrier) marries a woman with genotype HbAA. What is the probability that a child of theirs will also be a carrier (HbAS)?
questions.explanation: The man gives HbA or HbS; the woman gives only HbA. The children are HbAA or HbAS in equal numbers, so the chance of a carrier (HbAS) is 1/2. None of the children can be HbSS.

whyNot.A: 1/4 would be the chance of HbSS if both parents were HbAS.
whyNot.B: Half the man's sperm carry HbS, so carriers are possible.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which blood group is called the universal donor because its red cells carry neither the A nor the B antigen?
questions.explanation: Group O red cells have no A or B antigens, so the antibodies in a recipient's plasma do not make them clump. In an emergency, group O blood can be given to people of any ABO group.

whyNot.C: Group AB is the universal recipient: its plasma has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies.
whyNot.A: Group A cells carry the A antigen and would be clumped by anti-A in group B or O blood.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: The particular position that a gene occupies on a chromosome is called its
questions.explanation: The locus (plural loci) is the fixed place on a chromosome where a particular gene is found. Different alleles of that gene occupy the same locus on the two members of a homologous pair.

whyNot.A: An allele is one form of a gene, not its position.
whyNot.B: A chromatid is one of the two copies of a chromosome after replication.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which application of genetics is used to settle a dispute over who is the father of a child?
questions.explanation: Every person's DNA has a pattern inherited half from the mother and half from the father. In DNA fingerprinting, the child's DNA pattern is compared with that of the mother and the alleged father; the father's DNA must account for the bands not inherited from the mother.

whyNot.C: Blood transfusion is a treatment, not a test of parentage.
whyNot.A: Artificial insemination is a way of achieving fertilisation.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Mendel concluded that the two alleles of a gene separate from each other when gametes are formed, so that each gamete carries only one of them. This is known as the law of
questions.explanation: Mendel's first law, the law of segregation, says that the pair of factors (alleles) for a characteristic separate during gamete formation, so each gamete receives only one. This happens because homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis.

whyNot.D: Independent assortment (Mendel's second law) concerns two or more different genes.
whyNot.B: Linkage is about genes on the same chromosome being inherited together; it was found after Mendel.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Identical twins have the same genes, but one twin grew up with a poor diet and is now shorter and lighter than the other. This difference is caused by
options: the mixing of genes at fertilisation
questions.explanation: Identical twins come from one zygote, so they have identical genes. Any difference between them, such as height or mass caused by diet, must come from the environment.

whyNot.B: Crossing over produces genetic differences between gametes, but identical twins come from the same zygote.
whyNot.C: Both twins came from the same fertilisation, so they share the same mix of genes.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which phrase is part of Charles Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection?
questions.explanation: Darwin argued that organisms vary, that more are born than can survive, and that those best suited to their surroundings survive and breed (survival of the fittest), passing their features on.

whyNot.A: Use and disuse is part of Lamarck's theory.
whyNot.C: Inheritance of acquired characters is also Lamarck's idea.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A couple plan to have three children. If a boy or a girl is equally likely at each birth, what is the probability that all three children will be girls?
questions.explanation: Each birth is independent, with a probability of 1/2 of a girl. The chance of three girls in a row is 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8.

whyNot.C: 1/3 wrongly divides by the number of children.
whyNot.D: 1/2 is the chance for one birth only, not for all three.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A Rhesus-negative woman is pregnant with her second Rhesus-positive baby. Her first child was also Rhesus positive, and she did not receive anti-D treatment after that birth. What problem may affect the second baby?
options: The baby's ABO blood group will change
Her anti-Rhesus antibodies may cross the placenta and destroy the baby's red blood cells
The baby will develop sickle-cell anaemia
The baby will be born Rhesus negative
questions.explanation: At the first birth some of the baby's Rh-positive cells entered the mother's blood, and she made anti-Rhesus antibodies. In the second Rh-positive pregnancy these antibodies cross the placenta and destroy the baby's red cells (haemolytic disease of the newborn). Anti-D treatment after the first birth prevents this.

whyNot.D: The baby's Rhesus group is decided by its genes; the mother's antibodies do not change it.
whyNot.C: Sickle-cell anaemia depends on haemoglobin genes, not on Rhesus groups.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: The mouthparts of a female mosquito are adapted for
options: sponging up liquid food from surfaces
questions.explanation: The female mosquito has long, needle-like mouthparts inside a sheath (the proboscis). She pierces the skin, injects saliva that stops the blood clotting, and sucks up blood, which she needs to make her eggs.

whyNot.D: Biting and chewing mouthparts are found in grasshoppers and cockroaches.
whyNot.B: Sponging mouthparts are found in the housefly.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In which way does a shark differ from a bony fish such as tilapia?
options: Its skeleton is made of cartilage, and its gill slits are not covered by an operculum
questions.explanation: Sharks are cartilaginous fish: their skeleton is cartilage, not bone, and their gill slits open separately on the side of the head. Bony fish such as tilapia have a bony skeleton and a bony flap (operculum) covering the gills.

whyNot.B: Sharks breathe with gills, like other fish.
whyNot.C: Shark skin is covered in small tooth-like (placoid) scales.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which features together show that an animal is a reptile?
options: Moist skin, and eggs laid in water
Dry skin with scales, and eggs with a leathery shell
questions.explanation: Reptiles such as the agama lizard, snakes and crocodiles have dry skin covered with scales, breathe with lungs and lay eggs with a leathery shell, usually on land.

whyNot.A: Moist skin and eggs laid in water are features of amphibians.
whyNot.D: Feathers and a beak are features of birds.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Mushrooms growing on a rotting log obtain their food by
options: feeding on the living tissue of trees (parasitism)
digesting dead organic matter outside their bodies and absorbing it (saprophytic nutrition)
taking in small animals and digesting them inside the body
questions.explanation: Mushrooms are fungi and have no chlorophyll. Their hyphae release enzymes into the dead wood, digest it outside the body and then absorb the soluble products. This is saprophytic nutrition, and it helps to recycle nutrients.

whyNot.D: Fungi have no chlorophyll, so they cannot photosynthesise.
whyNot.A: The log is dead, so the fungus is a saprophyte, not a parasite.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Ascaris, a roundworm that can live in the human intestine, belongs to the phylum
questions.explanation: Ascaris has a long, round, unsegmented body that tapers at both ends, with a mouth and an anus. These are features of roundworms, phylum Nematoda.

whyNot.D: Platyhelminthes (flatworms) such as the tapeworm have flat bodies.
whyNot.A: Annelids such as the earthworm have segmented bodies.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Amoeba moves from place to place by means of
questions.explanation: Amoeba pushes out finger-like extensions of its cytoplasm called pseudopodia. The rest of the cell flows into them, so the organism creeps along. Pseudopodia are also used to engulf food.

whyNot.C: Cilia are used by Paramecium.
whyNot.A: Flagella are used by Euglena and Chlamydomonas.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which feature separates flowering plants (angiosperms) from gymnosperms?
options: Their seeds are enclosed in a fruit formed from the ovary
They have roots, stems and leaves
questions.explanation: Angiosperm means 'enclosed seed': their ovules are inside an ovary, which becomes a fruit around the seeds. Gymnosperms such as pines have 'naked' seeds on the scales of cones. Both groups make seeds and have vascular tissue, roots, stems and leaves.

whyNot.A: Gymnosperms also produce seeds.
whyNot.D: Gymnosperms also have xylem and phloem.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: An animal found under dead leaves has a long, rounded body with many segments, two pairs of legs on most segments and one pair of antennae. To which group does it belong?
questions.explanation: Millipedes (Diplopoda) have many segments, most of which bear two pairs of legs, and one pair of antennae. They move slowly and feed on rotting plant matter.

whyNot.D: Centipedes have only one pair of legs on each segment and a flattened body.
whyNot.C: Insects have just three pairs of legs in total.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which microorganism is used to change milk into yoghurt?
questions.explanation: Lactobacillus bacteria ferment lactose (milk sugar) into lactic acid. The acid makes the milk proteins thicken and gives yoghurt its sour taste.

whyNot.B: Yeast is used in making bread and alcoholic drinks.
whyNot.C: Plasmodium is the parasite that causes malaria.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Spreading a thin film of oil over stagnant water kills mosquito larvae and pupae. Why does this work?
options: The oil makes the water too salty for them
They breathe air at the water surface through tubes, and the oil blocks these tubes
The oil kills the fish that feed on them
The oil makes the water too warm for them
questions.explanation: Mosquito larvae and pupae live in water but breathe air. They hang at the surface and take in air through breathing tubes (the siphon of the larva and the respiratory trumpets of the pupa). An oil film stops air reaching the tubes, so they suffocate.

whyNot.D: A thin film of oil does not noticeably heat the water.
whyNot.C: Killing fish that eat the larvae would increase, not reduce, the number of mosquitoes.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Rough endoplasmic reticulum is covered with ribosomes. What is its main function?
options: Making proteins and carrying them through the cell
questions.explanation: Ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum make proteins. The proteins enter the channels of the ER and are carried through the cell, often to the Golgi apparatus for packaging.

whyNot.B: Starch is stored in plastids (amyloplasts), not in the ER.
whyNot.A: Worn-out organelles are digested by lysosomes.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Chlorophyll in the chloroplasts absorbs mainly which colours of light for photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light strongly and uses that energy for photosynthesis. Green light is mostly reflected or passes through, which is why leaves look green.

whyNot.A: Green light is mostly reflected, so it is the colour chlorophyll uses least.
whyNot.B: Ultraviolet is not the light chlorophyll mainly absorbs for photosynthesis.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Osmosis is the movement of
options: any substance against a concentration gradient using energy
water molecules from a concentrated solution to a dilute solution through a partially permeable membrane
solute molecules from a concentrated solution to a dilute solution
water molecules from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
questions.explanation: Osmosis is a special kind of diffusion: water moves from a region of higher water potential (a dilute solution) to a region of lower water potential (a concentrated solution) across a partially permeable membrane.

whyNot.B: This is the wrong direction; water moves towards the more concentrated solution.
whyNot.A: Moving substances against a gradient with energy is active transport.

questions.subject: biology
questions.context: A bag made of Visking tubing (a partially permeable membrane) is filled with concentrated sucrose solution. Its open end is tied tightly round a long, narrow glass tube, and the bag is placed in a beaker of distilled water. The starting level of liquid in the glass tube is marked.
questions.stem: What will be observed in the glass tube after about an hour?
options: The liquid level falls below the mark
The liquid level rises above the mark
The liquid in the tube turns cloudy
The liquid level stays at the mark
questions.explanation: The distilled water outside has a higher water potential than the sucrose solution inside. Water moves into the bag by osmosis, increasing the volume inside, so the liquid is pushed up the glass tube.

whyNot.A: The level would fall only if the bag held a more dilute solution than the beaker.
whyNot.D: There is a water potential difference, so osmosis takes place and the level changes.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A few drops of orange juice are added to blue DCPIP solution, and the blue colour quickly disappears. What does this show?
options: The juice contains vitamin C (ascorbic acid)
questions.explanation: DCPIP is a blue dye that becomes colourless when it is reduced by vitamin C (ascorbic acid). Fast loss of the blue colour shows that the juice is rich in vitamin C.

whyNot.C: Protein is detected by the Biuret test.
whyNot.A: Starch is detected with iodine solution.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: An amoeba reproduces by dividing its nucleus and then its cytoplasm into two equal parts, forming two daughter cells. This is called
questions.explanation: In binary fission a single-celled organism divides into two equal daughter cells, each with a copy of the nucleus. It is a form of asexual reproduction used by Amoeba and bacteria.

whyNot.D: In budding a small outgrowth forms and breaks off, as in yeast and Hydra; the parts are unequal.
whyNot.C: Conjugation involves two cells or filaments exchanging material, as in Spirogyra.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A culture starts with 100 bacteria, and every bacterium divides into two every 30 minutes. Assuming none of them die, how many bacteria will there be after 3 hours?
questions.explanation: 3 hours = 180 minutes = 180 ÷ 30 = 6 divisions. Each division doubles the number, so after 6 divisions the number is 100 × 2⁶ = 100 × 64 = 6 400.

whyNot.C: 3 200 is the number after only 5 divisions (2½ hours).
whyNot.A: 1 200 adds the doublings instead of multiplying (100 × 2 × 6).

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: An enzyme from the human body was kept at 70 °C for 10 minutes and then cooled to 37 °C. It no longer worked. Why?
options: The enzyme was used up at 70 °C
Cooling it to 37 °C stopped it working
Enzymes work only at temperatures above 40 °C
The high temperature permanently changed the shape of its active site (it was denatured)
questions.explanation: Enzymes are proteins. High temperatures break the bonds that hold the protein's shape, so the active site no longer fits the substrate. This change, denaturation, is permanent, so the enzyme stays inactive even after cooling.

whyNot.A: Enzymes are not used up; they are catalysts.
whyNot.B: 37 °C is about the best temperature for human enzymes; cooling did not stop it.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Why does anaerobic respiration release much less energy from each glucose molecule than aerobic respiration?
options: No carbon dioxide is produced in any kind of anaerobic respiration
The glucose is only partly broken down, and much energy stays in products such as ethanol or lactic acid
Anaerobic respiration uses more glucose molecules at a time
Anaerobic respiration takes place only in the mitochondria
questions.explanation: Without oxygen, glucose is broken down only as far as ethanol and carbon dioxide (in yeast) or lactic acid (in muscle). These products still contain a lot of chemical energy. In aerobic respiration glucose is broken down completely to carbon dioxide and water, releasing far more energy.

whyNot.A: Yeast does produce carbon dioxide in anaerobic respiration.
whyNot.D: Anaerobic respiration takes place in the cytoplasm.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A white blood cell surrounds a bacterium with its cytoplasm and takes it into a vacuole to be destroyed. This process is called
questions.explanation: Phagocytosis ('cell eating') is the engulfing of solid particles, such as bacteria, into a vacuole by flowing cytoplasm. Enzymes from lysosomes then digest the particle.

whyNot.B: Pinocytosis ('cell drinking') is the taking in of tiny droplets of liquid, not solid particles.
whyNot.A: Osmosis is the movement of water only.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A lack of iodine in the diet can cause a swelling in the neck called goitre. Which gland is affected?
questions.explanation: The thyroid gland in the neck uses iodine to make the hormone thyroxine. Without enough iodine it cannot make enough thyroxine and it enlarges, forming a goitre. Iodised salt helps to prevent this.

whyNot.B: The adrenal glands sit on the kidneys and make adrenaline.
whyNot.C: The pituitary is at the base of the brain; it does not use iodine to make hormones.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In which part of the human alimentary canal is most of the remaining water absorbed from undigested food?
questions.explanation: After digested food is absorbed in the small intestine, the remaining material passes into the colon. The colon absorbs most of the remaining water, leaving semi-solid faeces.

whyNot.D: The stomach churns food and begins protein digestion; it absorbs very little water.
whyNot.A: The oesophagus only carries food to the stomach.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which blood vessel carries blood to the kidney to be filtered?
questions.explanation: The renal artery branches from the aorta and brings blood, carrying urea and other wastes, to each kidney. Filtered blood leaves through the renal vein.

whyNot.A: The renal vein carries filtered blood away from the kidney.
whyNot.C: The hepatic portal vein carries blood from the intestines to the liver.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: How does sweating help to cool the body on a hot day?
options: Sweat reflects sunlight away from the skin
Sweat takes heat from the skin as it evaporates
Sweat removes urea, which produces heat
Sweat closes the pores of the skin
questions.explanation: Water in sweat needs heat energy (latent heat) to evaporate. It takes this heat from the skin and the blood below it, so the body cools.

whyNot.C: Sweat does contain a little urea, but removing it does not cool the body.
whyNot.A: Sweat does not reflect sunlight; cooling comes from evaporation.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Maize plants on a farm show yellowing between the veins of their older leaves, and a lack of magnesium is suspected. Why does a lack of magnesium cause yellow leaves?
options: Magnesium is needed to make cellulose cell walls
Magnesium controls the opening of the stomata
Magnesium is part of the chlorophyll molecule
Magnesium is part of every protein in the leaf
questions.explanation: Each chlorophyll molecule has a magnesium atom at its centre. Without enough magnesium the plant cannot make enough chlorophyll, so the leaves turn yellow (chlorosis), reducing photosynthesis.

whyNot.A: Cellulose is made from glucose and contains no magnesium.
whyNot.D: Nitrogen, not magnesium, is the element found in every protein.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In a woody stem, gases are exchanged with the air through small pores in the bark called
questions.explanation: Lenticels are small areas of loosely packed cells in the bark of woody stems. The spaces between the cells let oxygen diffuse in and carbon dioxide out for the living cells inside.

whyNot.C: Stomata are pores mainly in the epidermis of leaves and young green stems, not in bark.
whyNot.A: Hydathodes are pores at leaf edges that release liquid water.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: The lower surface of a leaf has an average of 250 stomata per mm². If the area of the lower surface is 40 cm², how many stomata does it have?
questions.explanation: First change the area to mm²: 1 cm² = 10 mm × 10 mm = 100 mm², so 40 cm² = 4 000 mm². Number of stomata = 250 × 4 000 = 1 000 000.

whyNot.A: 10 000 multiplies 250 by 40 without changing cm² into mm².
whyNot.C: 100 000 uses 1 cm² = 10 mm², but 1 cm² is 100 mm².

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: What is the main function of the placenta during pregnancy?
options: To exchange food, oxygen and wastes between the mother's blood and the foetus's blood without the two bloods mixing
To cushion the foetus against knocks and jolts
To mix the mother's blood with the foetus's blood
To produce milk for the baby
questions.explanation: In the placenta the mother's blood and the foetus's blood flow very close together but stay separate. Oxygen, glucose, amino acids and antibodies diffuse to the foetus, while carbon dioxide and urea pass back to the mother. The placenta also makes hormones.

whyNot.C: The two bloods never mix; they could have different blood groups.
whyNot.B: Cushioning is done by the amniotic fluid inside the amnion.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: When ripe, the dry pods of some legumes split open suddenly and throw their seeds away from the parent plant. This method of seed dispersal is by
questions.explanation: As the pod dries, tension builds up in its walls. The pod suddenly splits and twists, flinging the seeds away. This is self (explosive) dispersal and does not need any outside agent.

whyNot.B: Wind-dispersed seeds are light, with wings or hairs.
whyNot.C: Animal-dispersed fruits are fleshy or have hooks.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which cells in the retina are sensitive to dim light but cannot detect colour?
questions.explanation: Rods work in dim light and give black-and-white vision. Cones need brighter light and detect colour; they are concentrated at the fovea (yellow spot).

whyNot.A: Cones detect colour and need bright light.
whyNot.D: The lens focuses light; it does not detect it.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Where a river meets the sea, as in the creeks of the Niger Delta, the water is a mixture of fresh water and sea water. Such water is described as
questions.explanation: Brackish water is a mixture of fresh and salt water, so its salt content is between that of rivers and that of the sea. Estuaries and mangrove swamps contain brackish water.

whyNot.C: Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium salts; it is still fresh water.
whyNot.B: Fresh water has very little salt, unlike a river mouth mixed with sea water.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which statement about ecological pyramids is correct?
options: A pyramid of energy is always upright, because energy is lost at every trophic level
A pyramid of energy is inverted when the producers are very small
A pyramid of numbers is always upright
A pyramid of biomass is always upright
questions.explanation: Energy is lost as heat at each step of a food chain, so each level always has less energy than the one below. A pyramid of energy can therefore never be inverted. Pyramids of numbers (one tree, many insects) and of biomass (small plankton, larger zooplankton at one moment) can be inverted.

whyNot.C: One large tree supporting many insects gives an inverted pyramid of numbers.
whyNot.B: Small producers can invert a pyramid of biomass, but never a pyramid of energy.

questions.subject: biology
questions.context: In a closed forest reserve, the numbers of a species of rat and of the owls that hunt it were counted every year for 20 years. Both populations rose and fell in repeated cycles. Each peak in the owl population came a year or two after a peak in the rat population.
questions.stem: Which explanation best accounts for the owl peaks coming after the rat peaks?
options: Owls and rats compete for the same food
When rats are plentiful, more owls survive and breed, so owl numbers rise after rat numbers
questions.explanation: Owls depend on rats for food. When rats become plentiful, more owls survive and raise young, so owl numbers rise, but only after a delay. The many owls then eat more rats, the rat population falls, and later owl numbers fall too as food runs short.

whyNot.A: Small rodents breed much faster than owls; that is partly why rat numbers rise first.
whyNot.C: Owls eat rats; they are predator and prey, not competitors.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A lichen growing on a rock is made of two different organisms living in close association. They are
questions.explanation: A lichen is a mutualistic partnership between an alga (or cyanobacterium) and a fungus. The alga makes food by photosynthesis; the fungus gives shelter, holds water and absorbs minerals.

whyNot.A: Mosses and ferns are separate plants, not partners in a lichen.
whyNot.B: Viruses are not partners in lichens.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A census of grasscutters in a forest reserve counted 250 animals one year and 400 the next year. What is the percentage increase in the population?
