questions.explanation: Increase = 400 − 250 = 150 animals. Percentage increase = increase ÷ starting number × 100 = 150 ÷ 250 × 100 = 60%.

whyNot.A: 37.5% divides the increase by the new number (400) instead of the starting number.
whyNot.C: 160% is 400 ÷ 250 × 100, the new population as a percentage of the old one, not the increase.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which instrument is used to measure light intensity in a habitat?
questions.explanation: A light meter (photometer) measures how bright the light is at a place, for example under a forest canopy compared with an open field.

whyNot.C: A rain gauge measures the amount of rainfall.
whyNot.D: A wind vane shows wind direction.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: The fennec fox of the Sahara Desert has very large ears that are well supplied with blood vessels. How do these ears help it survive in the desert?
options: They store water for dry periods
They give a large surface for losing body heat
They store fat for use when food is scarce
They keep sand out of the fox's eyes
questions.explanation: Large, thin ears with many blood vessels near the surface give a big surface area from which heat can radiate away, helping the fox stay cool in the hot desert.

whyNot.A: Ears do not store water.
whyNot.C: Fat is not stored in the ears.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Cutting down large areas of forest without replanting most directly leads to
options: less carbon dioxide in the air
questions.explanation: Tree roots bind the soil and the canopy breaks the force of rain. When the trees are removed, rain and wind easily carry away the fertile topsoil, so erosion increases.

whyNot.A: Erosion and leaching after deforestation make soil less fertile.
whyNot.C: Fewer trees take in less carbon dioxide, so its level in the air tends to rise.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A tiny wasp that lays its eggs inside the cassava mealybug, a pest of cassava, was released on cassava farms to reduce the number of mealybugs. This method of pest control is called
questions.explanation: Biological control uses a living natural enemy (a predator, parasite or disease) to keep a pest's numbers down. Here the wasp larvae develop inside the mealybugs and kill them, without using pesticides.

whyNot.D: Chemical control uses pesticides.
whyNot.B: Crop rotation changes the crop grown on a piece of land each season.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) released from old refrigerators and some aerosol sprays are harmful mainly because they
options: destroy the ozone layer, letting more ultraviolet radiation reach the Earth
make lakes too rich in nutrients
combine with haemoglobin in the blood
questions.explanation: In the upper atmosphere, CFCs release chlorine, which breaks down ozone. The ozone layer absorbs much of the Sun's ultraviolet radiation, so a thinner layer lets more UV through, increasing the risk of skin cancer and eye damage.

whyNot.D: Acid rain is caused by sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides.
whyNot.C: Carbon monoxide, not CFCs, combines with haemoglobin.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: The observable characteristics of an organism, such as its height or the colour of its flowers, are called its
questions.explanation: The phenotype is what an organism looks like or how it functions. It results from the genotype (the alleles it carries) acting together with the environment.

whyNot.D: The genotype is the set of alleles, such as Tt, not the visible feature.
whyNot.B: The karyotype is the picture of an organism's chromosomes, arranged in pairs.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: An organism that carries two identical alleles of a gene, such as TT or tt, is described as
questions.explanation: Homozygous means having two identical alleles for a gene (TT is homozygous dominant, tt is homozygous recessive). Homozygous organisms breed true for that feature.

whyNot.C: Heterozygous means having two different alleles, such as Tt.
whyNot.D: Haploid means having only one set of chromosomes, as in gametes.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A woman with genotype HbAS marries a man with genotype HbSS. What is the probability that their child will have sickle-cell anaemia (HbSS)?
questions.explanation: The woman gives HbA or HbS; the man gives only HbS. The children are HbAS or HbSS in equal numbers, so the chance of HbSS is 1/2.

whyNot.A: 1/4 is the chance when both parents are HbAS.
whyNot.C: The man always passes on HbS, so HbSS is possible whenever the woman passes on HbS.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Both parents are blood group AB. What fraction of their children is expected to be blood group AB?
questions.explanation: Each parent (IᴬIᴮ) gives Iᴬ or Iᴮ. The children are IᴬIᴬ (A), IᴬIᴮ (AB), IᴮIᴬ (AB) and IᴮIᴮ (B), so 2 out of 4, or 1/2, are group AB. The rest are groups A and B, 1/4 each.

whyNot.C: 1/4 is the fraction for group A or for group B.
whyNot.A: Children who receive the same allele from both parents are group A or group B, not AB.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Two plants that are both heterozygous for two genes on different chromosomes (AaBb × AaBb) are crossed. How many different genotypes can appear among the offspring?
questions.explanation: Take each gene separately. Aa × Aa gives three genotypes (AA, Aa, aa), and Bb × Bb gives three (BB, Bb, bb). Because the genes assort independently, the number of combinations is 3 × 3 = 9 genotypes.

whyNot.D: 4 is the number of phenotypes (in a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio), not genotypes.
whyNot.A: 16 is the number of boxes in the Punnett square; some boxes hold the same genotype.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Red-green colour blindness is a sex-linked recessive trait. A colour-blind man marries a woman who is homozygous for normal colour vision. What is the probability that a son of theirs will be colour blind?
questions.explanation: A son gets his Y chromosome from his father and his only X chromosome from his mother. The mother is XᴺXᴺ, so every son is XᴺY with normal vision. The probability is 0. (All the daughters will be carriers, XᴺXⁿ.)

whyNot.B: 1/2 would apply if the mother were a carrier.
whyNot.D: The father's X chromosome goes only to daughters, never to sons.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: The gametes of a species of plant each contain 12 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in a cell from one of its leaves?
questions.explanation: Gametes are haploid (n = 12). Body cells such as leaf cells come from the zygote by mitosis, so they are diploid: 2n = 2 × 12 = 24.

whyNot.A: 12 is the haploid number, found only in gametes.
whyNot.D: 6 halves the gamete number again, which does not happen.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: The wings of a bird and the wings of a butterfly both allow flight, but they have very different structures and origins. Such organs are described as
questions.explanation: Analogous organs do the same job but are built differently and evolved separately. Bird wings are modified forelimbs with bones; butterfly wings are thin outgrowths of the exoskeleton. They show convergent evolution.

whyNot.D: Homologous organs share the same basic structure and origin, even if they do different jobs.
whyNot.A: Vestigial organs are reduced and have little or no use.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of natural selection taking place today?
options: A farmer choosing the best cows to breed from
A gardener grafting orange shoots onto a lemon tree
Bacteria becoming resistant to an antibiotic that is overused
A child growing taller because of a good diet
questions.explanation: When an antibiotic is overused, the few bacteria that happen to be resistant survive and multiply, while the rest die. Over time the population becomes resistant. The environment (the antibiotic) does the selecting, so this is natural selection.

whyNot.A: When people choose which animals breed, it is artificial selection.
whyNot.D: Growth due to diet is an acquired change and is not inherited.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Crossing two different pure-bred varieties of maize often gives offspring that grow faster and yield more grain than either parent. This is called
questions.explanation: Hybrid vigour (heterosis) is the improved growth, yield or health of offspring from a cross between two different pure lines. Plant breeders use it to produce high-yielding hybrid maize seed.

whyNot.A: Inbreeding is crossing closely related plants, which usually reduces vigour.
whyNot.B: Cloning produces genetically identical copies, not crosses.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Chlamydomonas is a single-celled organism found in ponds. It has two flagella, a cup-shaped chloroplast and an eyespot. It is best described as
questions.explanation: Chlamydomonas has a true nucleus, a cell wall and a large chloroplast, so it makes its own food by photosynthesis. It is a unicellular green alga that swims with its two flagella towards light, which it detects with its eyespot.

whyNot.C: Bacteria have no nucleus and no chloroplasts.
whyNot.B: Fungi have no chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Maize and guinea grass are monocotyledons. Which type of root system do they have?
questions.explanation: Monocotyledons have a fibrous root system: many thin roots of similar size grow out from the base of the stem. Dicotyledons usually have a tap root, one main root with side branches.

whyNot.D: A tap root system is typical of dicotyledons.
whyNot.B: Root nodules with Rhizobium are found in legumes such as beans and groundnut.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A crab has a hard exoskeleton, a cephalothorax, two pairs of antennae and five pairs of legs. To which class of arthropods does it belong?
questions.explanation: Crustaceans such as crabs, prawns and crayfish have a hard exoskeleton often strengthened with calcium salts, a cephalothorax, two pairs of antennae and many pairs of jointed limbs. Most live in water and breathe with gills.

whyNot.C: Insects have one pair of antennae and three pairs of legs.
whyNot.A: Arachnids have four pairs of legs and no antennae.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Houseflies spread diseases such as typhoid and cholera mainly by
options: biting people and injecting germs into the blood
breathing germs out into the air
carrying germs on their legs and mouthparts from faeces to food
laying their eggs in drinking water
questions.explanation: Houseflies feed and breed on faeces and refuse. Germs stick to their hairy legs and mouthparts, and they also vomit and leave droppings on food. When they land on uncovered food, they contaminate it, so people swallow the germs.

whyNot.A: Houseflies do not bite; they have sponging mouthparts.
whyNot.D: Houseflies lay eggs in rubbish and dung, not in drinking water.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A starfish moves slowly over rocks on the seashore using many small tube feet. To which phylum does it belong?
questions.explanation: Echinoderms, such as starfish and sea urchins, are marine animals with a spiny skin, a body usually arranged in five parts and a water-vascular system that works hundreds of tube feet.

whyNot.C: Molluscs such as snails move on a single muscular foot.
whyNot.D: Arthropods move with jointed legs.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which feature is found only in birds?
questions.explanation: Feathers are found in birds and in no other living animals. Wings are also found in bats and insects, eggs are laid by reptiles, fish and many others, and mammals also have a four-chambered heart.

whyNot.B: Bats and insects also have wings.
whyNot.D: Mammals also have a four-chambered heart.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A whale lives in the sea and has a fish-like shape, yet it is classified as a mammal. Which feature shows that it is a mammal?
options: It feeds its young on milk from mammary glands
questions.explanation: Mammals are the only animals that feed their young on milk from mammary glands. Whales also breathe air with lungs and are warm-blooded. Fins and a streamlined body are adaptations to life in water, shared with fish.

whyNot.D: Fins are shared with fish and are an adaptation to swimming.
whyNot.C: A streamlined shape is found in many swimming animals.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which of these diseases is caused by a virus?
questions.explanation: Measles is caused by the measles virus and is prevented by vaccination. Tuberculosis and typhoid are caused by bacteria, and malaria by the protozoan Plasmodium.

whyNot.A: Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium, Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
whyNot.D: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a protozoan.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Paramecium, a slipper-shaped single-celled organism found in pond water, moves by means of
questions.explanation: Paramecium is covered with thousands of tiny hair-like cilia that beat together in waves, driving it through the water. Cilia also sweep food into its oral groove.

whyNot.C: Pseudopodia are used by Amoeba.
whyNot.B: Flagella are longer and fewer; they are used by Euglena and Chlamydomonas.

questions.subject: biology
questions.context:
A dichotomous key to four plants found around a school in southern Nigeria:
1a. Leaves with parallel veins ............ go to 2
1b. Leaves with net veins ................. go to 3
2a. Woody, with a tall unbranched trunk ..... Oil palm
2b. Not woody ............................... Maize
3a. Climbs using coiled tendrils .......... Fluted pumpkin (ugu)
3b. No tendrils ........................... Hibiscus
questions.stem: A student finds a plant with net-veined leaves and coiled tendrils that help it climb a stake. Using the key, what is the plant?
questions.explanation: Start at 1: net veins lead to 1b, so go to 3. At 3 the plant climbs with coiled tendrils, which is 3a: fluted pumpkin (ugu).

whyNot.A: Hibiscus is at 3b, for plants without tendrils.
whyNot.D: Maize has parallel-veined leaves, so it is reached through 1a, not 1b.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Economics is classified as a social science mainly because it studies
options: the natural laws that govern plants and animals
the dates and events in the history of nations
human behaviour as people live and work together in society
the physical and chemical properties of goods
questions.explanation: A social science studies people in society. Economics looks at how people, firms and governments behave when they make choices about using scarce resources, so it is a social science.

whyNot.D: Physical and chemical properties belong to the natural sciences.
whyNot.B: Dates and events of the past are the subject of history.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following is a positive statement in economics?
options: A rise in the price of kerosene reduces the quantity of kerosene demanded
Kerosene should be sold at the same price in every state
The government ought to reduce the price of kerosene
It is unfair for marketers to raise the price of kerosene
questions.explanation: A positive statement describes what is, was or will be, and it can be tested against facts. Whether a price rise reduces quantity demanded can be checked with data. The others express opinions about what ought to be (normative statements).

whyNot.C: "Ought to" expresses a value judgement, so it is normative.
whyNot.D: Whether something is fair is an opinion, not a testable fact.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The weekly wages, in thousands of naira, of eight workers in a bakery are 15, 18, 15, 20, 22, 15, 18 and 25. What is the modal wage?
questions.explanation: The mode is the value that occurs most often. 15 appears three times, 18 twice and the rest once each, so the modal wage is ₦15,000.

whyNot.B: ₦18,000 is the median: arranged in order the middle two values are 18 and 18.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A household spends ₦45,000 of its monthly budget of ₦120,000 on food. On a pie chart of the budget, what angle represents food?

whyNot.A: 45° just copies the number of thousands spent on food; it is not converted to a share of 360°.
whyNot.B: 37.5 is the percentage of the budget spent on food, not the angle.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The economic system in which resources are allocated mainly through the price mechanism, with little government control, is the
questions.explanation: In a capitalist (free market) economy, private individuals own most resources and the forces of demand and supply, working through prices, decide what, how and for whom to produce.

whyNot.D: In a socialist economy the state owns the main means of production and plans their use.
whyNot.A: A command economy is run by a central planning authority, not by prices.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The factor of production that bears the uninsurable risks of running a business is
questions.explanation: The entrepreneur starts and organises the business and bears risks that cannot be insured, such as a fall in demand or a change in fashion. Profit is the reward for bearing these risks.

whyNot.B: Labour is paid wages whether or not the business makes a profit.
whyNot.C: Capital earns interest; it is the entrepreneur who decides how to use it and carries the risk.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The mean daily sales of a kiosk over five days were 12 cartons. When the sales for a sixth day are added, the mean becomes 13 cartons. How many cartons were sold on the sixth day?
questions.explanation: Total for five days = 5 × 12 = 60. Total for six days = 6 × 13 = 78. Sixth day = 78 − 60 = 18 cartons.

whyNot.A: 13 is the new mean, not the sixth day's sales.
whyNot.D: 14 adds only 1 carton to the new mean; the sixth day must also raise the other five days' average by 1 carton each.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The economic question "for whom to produce" deals with
options: which methods of production should be used
how the goods produced are shared among members of society
where firms should locate their factories
which goods should be produced and in what quantities
questions.explanation: "For whom to produce" is the problem of distribution: deciding who gets the goods and services that have been produced, for example through incomes and prices.

whyNot.D: That is the question of what to produce.
whyNot.A: That is the question of how to produce.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A country is said to be under-populated when
options: its population is growing faster than its food supply
output per head is at its highest possible level
its population is too small to make full use of its resources, so output per head could rise with more people
most of its people live in rural areas
questions.explanation: Under-population means there are too few people to exploit the available resources fully. Adding people (and labour) would raise output per head until the optimum population is reached.

whyNot.A: Population outgrowing food supply describes over-population, as in the Malthusian view.
whyNot.B: Output per head at its maximum describes the optimum population.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: An economy is already producing on its production possibility curve. If the government wants to build more schools in the short run, it must
options: produce less of some other good
produce more of every other good as well
first raise the prices of all goods
leave some of its workers unemployed
questions.explanation: A point on the production possibility curve means all resources are fully and efficiently employed. More schools can only be produced by moving resources away from other goods, so some other output must be given up. This is opportunity cost.

whyNot.D: Leaving workers idle would move the economy inside the curve and reduce output.
whyNot.B: Producing more of everything is impossible on the curve without new resources or better technology.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: When the price of a carton of noodles falls from ₦80 to ₦60, the quantity demanded rises from 300 to 450 cartons. What is the price elasticity of demand?
questions.explanation: % change in quantity = (450 − 300) ÷ 300 × 100 = 50%. % change in price = (80 − 60) ÷ 80 × 100 = 25%. PED = 50 ÷ 25 = 2 (ignoring the sign). Demand is elastic.

whyNot.B: 0.5 is the percentage change in price divided by the percentage change in quantity: the formula upside down.
whyNot.C: 1.5 is the new quantity divided by the old quantity, not an elasticity.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: If the demand for a commodity is price elastic, a fall in its price will
options: increase the total revenue of sellers
reduce the total revenue of sellers
questions.explanation: With elastic demand, quantity demanded rises by a greater percentage than the price falls. The gain from extra sales outweighs the loss from the lower price, so total revenue rises.

whyNot.B: Revenue falls after a price cut only when demand is inelastic.
whyNot.C: Revenue stays the same only when elasticity is exactly one (unitary).

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The demand and supply functions for a commodity are Qd = 150 − 5P and Qs = 10P. The government then places a tax of ₦3 per unit on sellers, so the supply function becomes Qs = 10(P − 3). What is the new equilibrium price?
questions.explanation: With the tax: 150 − 5P = 10(P − 3) = 10P − 30, so 15P = 180 and P = ₦12. Before the tax, 150 − 5P = 10P gave P = ₦10. The price rose by ₦2, so buyers bear ₦2 and sellers ₦1 of the ₦3 tax.

whyNot.D: ₦10 is the equilibrium price before the tax.
whyNot.A: ₦13 assumes the whole tax is added to the old price, which happens only if demand is perfectly inelastic.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following will shift the demand curve for a normal good to the right?
options: A fall in the price of a substitute
A fall in the price of the good itself
A rise in the price of a complementary good
questions.explanation: For a normal good, higher incomes mean people buy more at every price, so the whole demand curve shifts to the right (an increase in demand).

whyNot.C: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the curve, not a shift.
whyNot.D: A dearer complement reduces demand, shifting the curve to the left.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A consumer's total utility from a commodity is at its maximum when the marginal utility is
questions.explanation: Total utility keeps rising as long as each extra unit adds some satisfaction (marginal utility is positive). When marginal utility falls to zero, total utility stops rising and is at its peak; after that it falls.

whyNot.C: Marginal utility is usually highest for the first unit, when total utility is still low.
whyNot.D: MU = price is the condition for consumer equilibrium, not for maximum total utility.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The income elasticity of demand for a commodity is −0.4. The commodity is
options: a Giffen good with a rising demand curve
questions.explanation: A negative income elasticity means quantity demanded falls as income rises. Goods with this property are inferior goods, which people replace with better ones as they grow richer.

whyNot.A: A luxury good has an income elasticity greater than +1.
whyNot.B: A normal necessity has a positive income elasticity between 0 and 1.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The demand and supply functions for maize are Qd = 200 − 2P and Qs = 3P − 50. If the government fixes a minimum price of ₦60, what will happen in the market?
questions.explanation: Equilibrium: 200 − 2P = 3P − 50 gives P = ₦50. At ₦60: Qd = 200 − 120 = 80 and Qs = 180 − 50 = 130. Supply exceeds demand by 130 − 80 = 50 units, a surplus.

whyNot.C: A minimum price above equilibrium creates a surplus, not a shortage.
whyNot.B: The fixed price (₦60) is above the equilibrium price (₦50), so the market does not clear.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A supply curve that is a vertical straight line has a price elasticity of supply of
options: less than one but more than zero
questions.explanation: A vertical supply curve means the same quantity is supplied whatever the price. Since quantity does not respond at all to price, supply is perfectly inelastic, with elasticity equal to zero.

whyNot.D: Infinite elasticity is shown by a horizontal supply curve.
whyNot.C: Unitary elasticity of supply is shown by a straight line through the origin.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: When cattle are slaughtered for beef, hides are also obtained for leather. Beef and hides are said to be in
questions.explanation: Goods in joint supply are produced together from the same process, so producing more of one automatically produces more of the other. Slaughtering cattle gives both beef and hides.

whyNot.A: Competitive supply means resources used for one good cannot be used for the other, such as maize and sorghum on the same land.
whyNot.C: Joint demand refers to goods bought together, such as cars and petrol.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: When the supply of a commodity is perfectly inelastic, the burden of a tax placed on it falls
questions.explanation: With perfectly inelastic supply, sellers will offer the same quantity whatever they receive. The tax cannot raise the market price (demand is unchanged and quantity is fixed), so producers must absorb the whole tax.

whyNot.C: The whole tax falls on consumers when demand is perfectly inelastic or supply is perfectly elastic.
whyNot.B: An equal split happens only when demand and supply have the same elasticity at that point.

questions.subject: economics
questions.context:
A firm's total cost (TC) at different levels of output:
Output (units): 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Total cost (₦): 50, 80, 100, 130, 180, 250
questions.stem: From the table, what is the marginal cost of producing the 4th unit?
questions.explanation: Marginal cost is the addition to total cost from producing one more unit. MC of the 4th unit = TC(4) − TC(3) = ₦180 − ₦130 = ₦50.

whyNot.A: ₦45 is the average total cost at 4 units (180 ÷ 4).
whyNot.B: ₦180 is the total cost of 4 units, not the cost of the 4th unit alone.

questions.subject: economics
questions.context:
A firm's total cost (TC) at different levels of output:
Output (units): 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Total cost (₦): 50, 80, 100, 130, 180, 250
questions.stem: From the table, at what level of output is the firm's average total cost lowest?
questions.explanation: ATC = TC ÷ output. 1 unit: ₦80; 2 units: ₦50; 3 units: ₦43.33; 4 units: ₦45; 5 units: ₦50. The lowest is at 3 units.

whyNot.D: At 2 units ATC is ₦50, higher than at 3 units.
whyNot.C: At 4 units ATC is ₦45, already rising again.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A firm in a perfectly competitive market is described as a price taker because it
options: must accept the price set by the market as a whole
is the only seller of the product
agrees prices with a few rival firms
can fix any price it wants for its product
questions.explanation: Each perfectly competitive firm is so small relative to the market that it cannot influence price. It sells at the price set by total market demand and supply.

whyNot.D: Setting its own price describes a price maker, such as a monopolist.
whyNot.C: Agreeing prices with a few rivals describes collusion in an oligopoly.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: In the long run, firms in a perfectly competitive industry earn
questions.explanation: With free entry and exit, any abnormal profit attracts new firms. Supply rises and price falls until only normal profit is left, where price equals minimum average cost.

whyNot.B: Abnormal profit can exist only in the short run, before new firms enter.
whyNot.A: Firms making persistent losses leave the industry, which raises price back to normal-profit level.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A firm doubles all its inputs and finds that its output more than doubles. The firm is experiencing
questions.explanation: Returns to scale compare the change in output with an equal proportional change in all inputs. If output rises by a greater proportion than inputs, there are increasing returns to scale.

whyNot.A: Constant returns mean output exactly doubles.
whyNot.C: Diminishing marginal returns apply in the short run, when only one input changes and others are fixed.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: In the short run, a firm making a loss should continue to produce as long as the price it receives covers its
questions.explanation: Fixed costs must be paid even if the firm shuts down. If price covers average variable cost, producing at least pays the running costs and contributes something towards fixed costs, so the loss is smaller than if it closed.

whyNot.A: If price covers average total cost, the firm is not making a loss at all.
whyNot.D: Covering average fixed cost alone does not pay for the wages and materials that production uses up.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: On a farm, the average product of labour is 20 bags when 6 workers are employed and 19 bags when 7 workers are employed. What is the marginal product of the 7th worker?
questions.explanation: Total product = average product × number of workers. With 6 workers: 6 × 20 = 120 bags. With 7: 7 × 19 = 133 bags. MP of the 7th worker = 133 − 120 = 13 bags.

whyNot.D: 19 bags is the average product with 7 workers, not the extra output of the 7th worker.
whyNot.A: 1 bag is only the fall in average product.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: In economics, production is complete only when the goods
questions.explanation: Production includes every activity needed to satisfy wants, including transporting, storing and selling. A product has not satisfied any want until it reaches the person who will use it.

whyNot.B: Distribution services such as transport and retailing are still part of production after goods leave the factory.
whyNot.D: Storage is one stage of production, but the goods have not yet reached the consumer.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A soft drinks bottling plant is usually sited close to its main market mainly because
options: its raw materials are perishable and must be processed quickly
the finished drinks are bulkier and costlier to transport than the raw materials
the government forbids factories in rural areas
it needs very large amounts of land
questions.explanation: Bottling adds a lot of water and heavy bottles to small quantities of concentrate and sugar. The finished product weighs far more than the inputs, so it is cheaper to produce near the consumers.

whyNot.A: Perishable raw materials would pull the plant towards the source of the materials, not the market.
whyNot.C: There is no general law banning factories in rural areas.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following can give a firm monopoly power by preventing other firms from entering its market?
options: A patent on a new product
Identical products sold by many firms
questions.explanation: A patent gives the inventor the legal sole right to make and sell a product for some years. It is a barrier to entry, so the patent holder can act as a monopolist.

whyNot.D: Perfect knowledge is a feature of perfect competition, which has no barriers to entry.
whyNot.C: Many firms selling identical products is the opposite of monopoly.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: When the prices of a goat, a bag of rice and a radio are all stated in naira so that their values can be compared, money is serving as a
questions.explanation: As a unit of account (measure of value), money provides a common unit in which the values of all goods can be expressed and compared.

whyNot.D: Store of value means keeping wealth in money for future use.
whyNot.B: Standard of deferred payment means settling debts in the future.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Money held by a household to meet unexpected expenses, such as hospital bills, is held for the
questions.explanation: Keynes identified three motives for holding money. The precautionary motive is holding money as a safeguard against unforeseen events such as illness or accidents.

whyNot.B: The transactions motive covers planned day-to-day spending such as food and transport.
whyNot.D: The speculative motive is holding money to take advantage of expected changes in bond prices and interest rates.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: According to Keynes, the speculative demand for money is
options: inversely related to the rate of interest
determined mainly by the level of income
directly related to the rate of interest
questions.explanation: When interest rates are high, holding idle cash means giving up a lot of interest, and bond prices are expected to rise, so people hold less money. When rates are low, they hold more. The relationship is inverse.

whyNot.C: A higher interest rate raises the cost of holding idle money, so people hold less, not more.
whyNot.B: Income mainly determines the transactions and precautionary demands, not the speculative demand.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: In the quantity theory of money MV = PT, the velocity of circulation is 4 and the volume of transactions is 1,000. If the money supply rises from ₦5,000 to ₦7,500, the price level rises from ₦20 to
questions.explanation: P = MV ÷ T. Before: 5,000 × 4 ÷ 1,000 = ₦20. After: 7,500 × 4 ÷ 1,000 = ₦30. With V and T constant, a 50% rise in money supply raises prices by 50%.

whyNot.C: ₦40 would need the money supply to double, but it rose by only half.
whyNot.B: ₦7.50 forgets to multiply by the velocity of circulation.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of commercial banks?
options: Granting loans and overdrafts to customers
Acting as lender of last resort
Controlling the money supply of the country
questions.explanation: Commercial banks accept deposits from the public and lend part of them out as loans and overdrafts, earning interest. This is one of their main functions.

whyNot.D: In Nigeria only the Central Bank of Nigeria issues the currency.
whyNot.B: Lender of last resort is a function of the central bank.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: If the banking system's credit (money) multiplier is 8, what cash reserve ratio are the banks keeping?
questions.explanation: Credit multiplier = 1 ÷ cash reserve ratio. So the ratio = 1 ÷ 8 = 0.125 = 12.5%.

whyNot.A: 8% simply copies the multiplier as a percentage.
whyNot.C: A 20% ratio gives a multiplier of 5, not 8.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A mortgage bank such as the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria mainly provides loans for
questions.explanation: Mortgage banks specialise in long-term loans for housing. The house being bought or built usually serves as security for the loan.

whyNot.D: Government borrowing is handled through the central bank and the sale of government securities.
whyNot.C: Trade finance for imports is mainly provided by commercial and merchant banks.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following measures is most suitable for reducing demand-pull inflation?
options: Raising the cash reserve ratio of commercial banks
questions.explanation: Demand-pull inflation is caused by excess spending. Raising the cash reserve ratio reduces the amount banks can lend, so credit and spending fall, easing the pressure on prices.

whyNot.C: Lower taxes leave people with more to spend, adding to demand.
whyNot.B: A lower policy rate makes borrowing cheaper and increases spending.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A bank pays 18% interest a year on a fixed deposit. If the general price level rises by 12% over the same year, what is the approximate real rate of interest?
questions.explanation: The real rate of interest is approximately the nominal rate minus the rate of inflation: 18% − 12% = 6%. This is the true gain in purchasing power for the depositor.

whyNot.C: 30% adds inflation to the interest rate instead of subtracting it.
whyNot.A: 1.5% divides the two rates, which has no economic meaning here.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A person who holds a company's debenture is
options: a customer who buys the company's goods on credit
an owner who controls the company's board
an owner who receives a share of the profits
a creditor who receives a fixed rate of interest
questions.explanation: A debenture is a long-term loan to a company. The holder is a creditor, not an owner, and is paid a fixed interest whether the company makes a profit or not.

whyNot.C: Sharing profits as dividends describes a shareholder, who is a part-owner.
whyNot.B: Debenture holders have no voting rights and do not control the board.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A country's GNP at market prices is ₦900 billion. Depreciation is ₦60 billion, indirect taxes are ₦50 billion and subsidies are ₦10 billion. What is its national income (NNP at factor cost)?
questions.explanation: NNP at market prices = GNP − depreciation = 900 − 60 = ₦840 billion. NNP at factor cost = NNP at market prices − indirect taxes + subsidies = 840 − 50 + 10 = ₦800 billion.

whyNot.D: ₦780 billion subtracts subsidies instead of adding them.
whyNot.A: ₦840 billion is NNP at market prices; taxes and subsidies have not been adjusted.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A country's consumption function is C = 20 + 0.75Y, where C is consumption and Y is income, both in billions of naira. How much is saved when income is ₦200 billion?
questions.explanation: C = 20 + 0.75 × 200 = 20 + 150 = ₦170 billion. Saving is income not consumed: S = Y − C = 200 − 170 = ₦30 billion.

whyNot.B: ₦170 billion is consumption, not saving.
whyNot.A: ₦50 billion is 25% of income, which ignores the autonomous consumption of ₦20 billion.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Pensions and scholarships paid by the government are left out when national income is calculated because they
options: are too small to be measured
are already counted as company profits
are not payments for current productive services
are paid only to people abroad
questions.explanation: Pensions and scholarships are transfer payments: money moved from taxpayers to others without any good or service being produced in return. Counting them would overstate national output.

whyNot.A: Transfer payments can be large; they are excluded because nothing is produced in exchange.
whyNot.B: They are paid by government, not counted in company profits.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A country has a comparative advantage in producing a good when it can produce that good
options: at a higher price than other countries
at a lower opportunity cost than other countries
using more labour than other countries
in larger quantities than any other country
questions.explanation: Comparative advantage depends on opportunity cost: how much of other goods must be given up. A country gains from specialising in goods it produces at a lower opportunity cost, even if it is not the cheapest producer of everything.

whyNot.D: Producing more than every other country describes absolute advantage, not comparative advantage.
whyNot.C: Using more labour means higher cost, not an advantage.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following is an injection into the circular flow of income?
questions.explanation: Injections add spending to the flow of income: investment, government spending and exports. Savings, taxes and imports take money out of the flow and are leakages (withdrawals).

whyNot.A: Savings are income not spent, so they are a leakage.
whyNot.B: Spending on imports flows to foreign producers, so it is a leakage.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: In a country's balance of payments, the capital (and financial) account records
options: payments for services such as shipping and insurance
flows of foreign loans and investment into and out of the country
the export and import of goods only
questions.explanation: The capital and financial account records the movement of funds for investment and lending: direct investment, portfolio investment and loans between residents and foreigners.

whyNot.C: Trade in goods is recorded in the current account as the balance of trade.
whyNot.A: Payments for services are invisible items in the current account.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following measures would most directly reduce a balance of payments deficit by switching spending from imports to locally made goods?
options: Raising the value of the naira against other currencies
questions.explanation: Higher tariffs make imports dearer, so buyers switch to locally made substitutes. Import spending falls, which reduces the deficit.

whyNot.A: Lower tariffs make imports cheaper and would increase spending on them.
whyNot.B: A stronger naira makes imports cheaper and exports dearer, worsening the deficit.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT included in a country's GDP for the year?
options: The value of new houses built during the year
The value of cassava grown and sold by farmers
The wages of teachers in public schools
The price paid for a used car bought from a neighbour
questions.explanation: GDP counts the value of goods and services produced in the year. A used car was produced and counted in an earlier year; selling it again only transfers ownership and adds no new output.

whyNot.C: Teachers produce a current service, so their wages are counted.
whyNot.A: New houses are new output and are counted as investment.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: When a country's national income rises from ₦100 billion to ₦150 billion, consumption rises from ₦90 billion to ₦120 billion. What is the value of the multiplier?
questions.explanation: MPC = change in consumption ÷ change in income = 30 ÷ 50 = 0.6. Multiplier = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) = 1 ÷ 0.4 = 2.5.

whyNot.A: 0.6 is the marginal propensity to consume, not the multiplier.
whyNot.D: 1.67 is 1 ÷ 0.6, which uses the MPC instead of the MPS.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which international institution's main role is to give short-term help to member countries facing balance of payments difficulties?
options: The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS)
The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC)
questions.explanation: The IMF was set up to promote exchange-rate stability and to lend to member countries with temporary balance of payments problems.

whyNot.A: The WTO sets and enforces rules for international trade.
whyNot.C: OPEC coordinates the oil policies of its member countries.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Human wants are said to be insatiable because
options: the means of satisfying them are free
as soon as some wants are satisfied, new ones arise
every want can be satisfied at once
people want only goods and not services
questions.explanation: Insatiable means wants can never be fully satisfied. When a person gets food and clothing, new wants such as a phone or a car appear. With scarce means, choices must be made.

whyNot.A: The means of satisfying wants are scarce, not free; that is the basic economic problem.
whyNot.C: If every want could be satisfied at once, there would be no need to choose.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The reward for capital as a factor of production is
questions.explanation: Each factor earns a reward: land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest and the entrepreneur earns profit.

whyNot.A: Rent is the reward for land.
whyNot.D: Profit is the reward for the entrepreneur.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: In a small workshop, 3 workers earn ₦2,000 a day, 5 workers earn ₦3,000 a day and 2 workers earn ₦4,000 a day. What is the mean daily wage?

whyNot.D: ₦3,000 is the simple average of the three wage rates, ignoring how many workers earn each, and also the mode.
whyNot.A: ₦9,000 is the sum of the three wage rates.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A major disadvantage of division of labour to the worker is that
options: it wastes time moving from one task to another
it reduces the skill of the worker in his task
repeating the same task every day can become boring
it lowers the total output of the firm
questions.explanation: When work is broken into small tasks, each worker repeats one simple operation. This monotony can lead to boredom, loss of interest and loss of craftsmanship.

whyNot.B: Repeating one task usually increases skill in that task; that is an advantage.
whyNot.A: Division of labour saves the time that would be lost moving between tasks.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: An economy moves from a point inside its production possibility curve to a point on the curve. This shows that
options: previously idle resources have been put to use
the opportunity cost of both goods has fallen to zero
the economy has discovered new technology
questions.explanation: A point inside the curve shows unemployed or inefficiently used resources. Moving onto the curve means those resources are now fully used, so output rises without any increase in resources.

whyNot.A: An increase in resources would shift the whole curve outward.
whyNot.D: New technology also shifts the curve outward rather than moving the economy onto it.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely to shift a country's production possibility curve inward?
options: The discovery of new mineral deposits
A flood that destroys many farms and factories
A rise in the number of skilled workers
questions.explanation: An inward shift means the economy can produce less of everything because its resources have shrunk. A flood that destroys farms and factories reduces productive resources.

whyNot.A: New mineral deposits add to resources and shift the curve outward.
whyNot.C: Better technology raises possible output and shifts the curve outward.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: In a mixed economy, government provides goods such as street lighting mainly because
options: private firms cannot easily charge each user, so the price mechanism may not provide them
private firms are not allowed to produce any goods
consumers do not want such goods
such goods have no cost of production
questions.explanation: Street lighting is a public good: once provided, everyone in the street benefits and no one can easily be made to pay. Private firms cannot earn enough from it, so the market fails to provide it and government steps in.

whyNot.D: Street lighting has real costs: poles, bulbs and electricity.
whyNot.B: In a mixed economy private firms produce most goods.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The term "ceteris paribus", often used in economic analysis, means
questions.explanation: Ceteris paribus is Latin for "other things being equal". Economists use it to study the effect of one factor while assuming every other factor stays the same.

whyNot.D: The long run is a time period, not an assumption about other factors.
whyNot.A: Perfect competition is a market structure.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely to reduce the geographical mobility of labour?
options: Good roads linking towns and cities
A worker's attachment to family and friends in his home town
Job vacancies advertised across the country
questions.explanation: Geographical mobility is the ease of moving from one place to another for work. Family and social ties make people reluctant to move, so they reduce mobility.

whyNot.A: Good roads make movement easier.
whyNot.D: Cheap housing in the new place encourages people to move there.

questions.subject: economics
questions.context:
A simple price index uses three groups of goods. The weights show how important each group is in household spending.
Food: weight 5, price index 140
Transport: weight 3, price index 120
Others: weight 2, price index 110
questions.stem: What is the weighted price index?
questions.explanation: Weighted index = Σ(weight × index) ÷ Σweights. (5 × 140) + (3 × 120) + (2 × 110) = 700 + 360 + 220 = 1,280. Total weight = 10. Index = 1,280 ÷ 10 = 128.

whyNot.B: 123.3 is the simple average (370 ÷ 3), which ignores the weights.
whyNot.A: 370 is just the sum of the three indices.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Effective demand refers to
options: a desire for a commodity backed by the ability and willingness to pay
the quantity sellers offer at a given price
the total quantity of a commodity produced in a year
a desire for a commodity that a person cannot afford
questions.explanation: In economics, demand means effective demand: wanting a good, being willing to pay for it and having the money to do so, at a given price and time.

whyNot.D: A desire without the ability to pay is a mere wish, not effective demand.
whyNot.B: The quantity sellers offer is supply.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following would cause the demand curve for rice to shift to the left?
options: A fall in the price of beans, a substitute
A rise in the price of beans, a substitute
A fall in the price of rice
questions.explanation: If beans become cheaper, some consumers switch from rice to beans. Less rice is demanded at every price, so the demand curve for rice shifts to the left.

whyNot.D: A fall in rice's own price causes a movement along the curve (extension), not a shift.
whyNot.C: Dearer beans would push buyers towards rice, shifting its demand to the right.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: When the price of a crate of tomatoes rises from ₦40 to ₦50, the quantity supplied rises from 200 to 260 crates. What is the price elasticity of supply?
questions.explanation: % change in quantity supplied = 60 ÷ 200 × 100 = 30%. % change in price = 10 ÷ 40 × 100 = 25%. PES = 30 ÷ 25 = 1.2, so supply is elastic.

whyNot.A: 0.83 is the formula upside down (25 ÷ 30).
whyNot.C: 6 divides the change in quantity (60) by the change in price (10) without converting to percentages.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The demand for table salt is price inelastic mainly because
options: it takes up a very small part of consumers' income
it is bought only by rich people
questions.explanation: Salt is cheap and bought in small amounts, so even a large percentage change in its price hardly affects a household's budget. It also has no close substitutes. Quantity demanded therefore changes little.

whyNot.A: Many close substitutes would make demand elastic.
whyNot.B: Luxury goods tend to have elastic demand.

questions.subject: economics
questions.context:
Market schedule for a commodity:
Price (₦): 10, 20, 30, 40, 50
Quantity demanded: 100, 80, 60, 40, 20
Quantity supplied: 20, 40, 60, 80, 100
questions.stem: If demand increases by 40 units at every price while supply stays the same, what will be the new equilibrium price?
questions.explanation: The new quantities demanded are 140, 120, 100, 80 and 60. Equilibrium is where demand equals supply: at ₦40, demand = 40 + 40 = 80 and supply = 80. The price rises from ₦30 to ₦40.

whyNot.B: ₦30 was the equilibrium price before the increase in demand.
whyNot.D: At ₦50 the new demand (60) is below supply (100).

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A minimum price fixed by the government will affect the market only if it is set
questions.explanation: A minimum price is a floor: sellers may not charge less. If it is below the equilibrium, the market price is already higher and nothing changes. Only a floor above equilibrium is binding, and it causes a surplus.

whyNot.C: A floor below equilibrium is not binding because the market price is already above it.
whyNot.A: At equilibrium the floor would not change the price or quantity.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The law of supply states that, other things being equal,
options: the higher the price, the smaller the quantity supplied
the higher the price, the greater the quantity supplied
questions.explanation: Higher prices make production more profitable, so sellers offer more for sale. This direct relationship is why the supply curve slopes upward from left to right.

whyNot.A: That describes an inverse relationship, as in the law of demand.
whyNot.C: "Supply creates its own demand" is Say's Law, not the law of supply.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: If consumers' total spending on a commodity stays exactly the same when its price changes, the price elasticity of demand is
questions.explanation: With unitary elasticity, the percentage change in quantity equals the percentage change in price, in the opposite direction. The two effects cancel, so total spending (total revenue) does not change.

whyNot.A: With elastic demand, spending rises when price falls.
whyNot.B: With zero elasticity, quantity is fixed, so spending changes in the same direction as price.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A trader sells 400 bags of sachet water a week at ₦50 per bag. She cuts the price to ₦40 and her weekly revenue becomes ₦24,000. What is the price elasticity of demand?
questions.explanation: New quantity = 24,000 ÷ 40 = 600 bags. % change in quantity = 200 ÷ 400 × 100 = 50%. % change in price = 10 ÷ 50 × 100 = 20%. PED = 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5, so demand is elastic (revenue rose when price fell).

whyNot.A: 0.4 is the formula upside down (20 ÷ 50).
whyNot.D: 1.5 is the new quantity divided by the old quantity (600 ÷ 400).
whyNot.C: 20 divides the change in quantity (200) by the change in price (₦10) without using percentages.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Palm oil is demanded for cooking, for making soap and for making body cream. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Composite demand exists when one commodity is demanded for several different uses. The total demand for palm oil is the sum of the demands for all these uses.

whyNot.A: Joint demand is when two goods are demanded together, such as cars and petrol.
whyNot.B: Derived demand is demand for something because of the demand for what it helps to produce.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of primary production?
options: Fishing in the creeks of the Niger Delta
questions.explanation: Primary production takes resources directly from nature: farming, fishing, mining and lumbering.

whyNot.C: Assembling goods in a factory is secondary production (manufacturing).
whyNot.A: Retail trade is tertiary production (commerce).

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: As more workers are added to a fixed piece of land, total product continues to rise but at a decreasing rate. During this stage, marginal product is
questions.explanation: Total product rises as long as each extra worker adds something, so MP is positive. Because each addition is smaller than the one before, total product rises at a decreasing rate: MP is falling.

whyNot.B: If MP were negative, total product would be falling.
whyNot.A: Rising MP makes total product rise at an increasing rate.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A firm's total variable cost is ₦4,800 when it produces 60 units. What is its average variable cost?
questions.explanation: Average variable cost = total variable cost ÷ output = 4,800 ÷ 60 = ₦80 per unit.

whyNot.C: ₦288,000 multiplies cost by output instead of dividing.
whyNot.A: ₦48 drops two zeros instead of dividing by 60.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A bakery has total fixed costs of ₦2,000 and an average variable cost of ₦25 per loaf. It produces and sells 100 loaves at ₦60 each. What is its profit?
questions.explanation: Total revenue = 100 × 60 = ₦6,000. Total cost = fixed cost + variable cost = 2,000 + (25 × 100) = ₦4,500. Profit = 6,000 − 4,500 = ₦1,500.

whyNot.A: ₦3,500 leaves out the fixed cost.
whyNot.B: ₦6,000 is total revenue, before any costs are subtracted.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A large firm is able to employ an accountant, a marketing manager and an engineer, each specialising in one area. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Managerial economies arise inside a large firm when it can afford to divide management work among specialists, which raises efficiency and lowers average cost.

whyNot.D: External economies come from the growth of the whole industry or area, not from the firm's own size.
whyNot.A: Financial economies refer to large firms borrowing more easily and cheaply.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A major disadvantage of the sole proprietorship as a form of business is
options: too many legal requirements for its formation
sharing of profits among many owners
questions.explanation: The sole proprietor's personal property can be taken to pay the debts of the business if it fails. This unlimited liability is a major risk.

whyNot.B: One owner can take decisions quickly; that is an advantage.
whyNot.D: The sole proprietor keeps all the profits.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A public limited company differs from a private limited company mainly in that a public limited company
options: can invite the general public to buy its shares
questions.explanation: A public limited company (Plc) may offer its shares to the general public, and its shares can be traded on the stock exchange. A private limited company cannot invite the public to subscribe for its shares.

whyNot.A: Both kinds of limited company give their shareholders limited liability.
whyNot.C: A public limited company is owned by private shareholders; it is not a public (government) corporation.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Many firms selling similar but slightly differentiated products, each using brand names and advertising, is a main feature of
questions.explanation: In monopolistic competition there are many sellers and easy entry, but each firm's product is slightly different, such as different brands of soap. Branding and advertising are used to win customers.

whyNot.A: Perfect competition has identical (homogeneous) products, so advertising is pointless.
whyNot.C: A monopsony is a market with only one buyer.

questions.subject: economics
questions.context:
A perfectly competitive firm sells its product at ₦30 per unit. Its marginal cost of each unit is:
1st unit: ₦18
2nd unit: ₦22
3rd unit: ₦26
4th unit: ₦30
5th unit: ₦35
questions.stem: How many units should the firm produce to maximise its profit?
questions.explanation: Under perfect competition price = marginal revenue = ₦30. Profit is maximised where MR = MC. Units 1 to 3 add more to revenue than to cost; the 4th unit's MC equals ₦30; the 5th unit costs ₦35 but adds only ₦30. So produce 4 units.

whyNot.B: The 5th unit would cost ₦35 but bring in only ₦30, reducing profit.
whyNot.C: The first unit has the largest gain per unit, but more units still add to total profit.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The long-run average cost curve of a firm is usually U-shaped mainly because of
options: changes in the price of the firm's product
the fall in average fixed cost as output rises
economies of scale followed by diseconomies of scale
questions.explanation: In the long run all inputs can change. As a firm grows, economies of scale lower average cost; beyond some size, diseconomies of scale (such as management problems) raise it. This gives the U shape.

whyNot.D: Diminishing returns explain the U shape of short-run cost curves, where some inputs are fixed.
whyNot.B: In the long run there are no fixed costs, so there is no average fixed cost.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A material that does not wear out or go bad easily with use has the quality of money known as
questions.explanation: Good money must be durable so that it lasts while it is passed from hand to hand and while it is stored. Perishable items such as fish make poor money.

whyNot.A: Divisibility means money can be broken into smaller units.
whyNot.B: Portability means money is easy to carry.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A customer who wants to pay by cheque must normally operate a
options: domiciliary account in foreign currency only
questions.explanation: Cheques are issued on current accounts, which are meant for frequent payments. Savings and fixed deposit accounts are mainly for keeping money and earning interest.

whyNot.B: A savings account is not normally operated with a cheque book.
whyNot.A: Money in a fixed deposit is locked up for an agreed period.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: When the Central Bank of Nigeria directs commercial banks to give a larger share of their loans to agriculture, it is using
questions.explanation: Selective credit control directs bank lending towards (or away from) particular sectors of the economy, such as agriculture or manufacturing, rather than changing the total amount of credit.

whyNot.B: Open market operations involve buying and selling government securities.
whyNot.C: Moral suasion is persuasion without a binding directive.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A commercial bank has total deposits of ₦800 million and must keep a liquidity ratio of 30%. What is the minimum value of liquid assets it must hold?
questions.explanation: Required liquid assets = liquidity ratio × deposits = 0.30 × 800 = ₦240 million.

whyNot.C: ₦560 million is the remaining 70% of deposits.
whyNot.B: ₦26.7 million divides 800 by 30 instead of taking 30% of it.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Using the quantity theory of money MV = PT, if the money supply is ₦6,000, the velocity of circulation is 3 and the price level is ₦9, what is the volume of transactions?

whyNot.D: 18,000 is MV; it has not been divided by the price level.
whyNot.B: 4,500 is 6,000 × 3 ÷ 4, a slip in the division.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which group of people is most likely to suffer during a period of inflation?
options: Owners of goods held in stock
Traders whose selling prices rise quickly
questions.explanation: Inflation reduces the purchasing power of money. People whose incomes do not rise with prices, such as pensioners on fixed pensions, can buy less and are worse off.

whyNot.C: Borrowers gain because they repay with money that is worth less.
whyNot.B: Stock holders gain as the value of their stock rises with prices.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A persistent fall in the general price level is called
questions.explanation: Deflation is a continuous fall in the general level of prices, which raises the value of money. It is the opposite of inflation.

whyNot.D: Devaluation is an official lowering of a currency's exchange rate.
whyNot.C: Depreciation refers to a fall in the value of a currency or of capital goods through wear.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A worker's monthly salary rose from ₦60,000 to ₦90,000 while the price index rose from 100 to 150 over the same period. In terms of base-period prices, his new real salary is
questions.explanation: Real salary = money salary × (base index ÷ current index) = 90,000 × 100 ÷ 150 = ₦60,000. His salary and prices both rose by 50%, so his real income is unchanged.

whyNot.D: ₦90,000 is the money (nominal) salary, not adjusted for prices.
whyNot.B: ₦135,000 multiplies by the index instead of dividing.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The money market is the market for
questions.explanation: The money market deals in short-term funds, usually for less than one year, using instruments such as Treasury bills, call money and commercial papers.

whyNot.A: Long-term funds and shares are dealt with in the capital market.
whyNot.B: Foreign currencies are traded in the foreign exchange market.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The amount of money a person holds for the transactions motive depends mainly on
options: the rate of interest on bonds
questions.explanation: Money held for transactions pays for regular purchases between paydays. The more a person earns, the more he spends and the more money he holds for this purpose.

whyNot.B: The interest rate mainly affects the speculative demand for money.
whyNot.C: The cash reserve ratio affects banks' lending, not a person's own transactions demand.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total market value of
options: all goods imported into a country in a year
all goods and services produced by a country's citizens anywhere in the world
all money in circulation in a country
all final goods and services produced within a country in a year
questions.explanation: GDP measures output produced within the country's borders, by citizens and foreigners alike, in a given year. Only final goods are counted to avoid double counting.

whyNot.B: Output by citizens wherever they are is the idea behind GNP.
whyNot.C: Money in circulation is the money supply, not output.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A country's GDP is ₦750 billion and depreciation (capital consumption) is ₦45 billion. What is its net domestic product?
questions.explanation: Net domestic product = GDP − depreciation = 750 − 45 = ₦705 billion. Depreciation is the value of capital used up in producing the output.

whyNot.D: ₦795 billion adds depreciation instead of subtracting it.
whyNot.B: ₦750 billion is GDP itself.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The value-added method of measuring national income is used mainly to avoid
questions.explanation: If the full value of output at every stage were added, raw materials would be counted many times. Adding only the value added at each stage counts each item once.

whyNot.D: Transfer payments are a problem for the income method, not the output method.
whyNot.A: Depreciation is handled when moving from gross to net figures.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A high income per head may not mean that most people in a country enjoy a high standard of living because
options: income may be very unequally distributed
per capita income ignores the size of the population
income per head includes only government workers
per capita income is calculated only for rural areas
questions.explanation: Income per head is an average. If a small group receives most of the income, the average can be high while most people remain poor.

whyNot.B: Per capita income is national income divided by population, so population is taken into account.
whyNot.D: It covers the whole population, not just rural areas.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: In a year, a country's visible exports were worth ₦2,400 billion and its visible imports ₦2,750 billion. What was its balance of trade?
questions.explanation: Balance of trade = visible exports − visible imports = 2,400 − 2,750 = −₦350 billion. A negative balance is a deficit.

whyNot.C: Imports exceed exports, so the balance is negative, not a surplus.
whyNot.B: ₦5,150 billion adds exports and imports together.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Under a floating exchange rate system, the exchange rate of a currency is determined by
options: the demand for and supply of the currency in the foreign exchange market
the price of gold set by the government
agreement among all members of ECOWAS
the central bank fixing it once every year
questions.explanation: In a floating system the exchange rate moves freely with market forces. When demand for a currency rises relative to its supply, its value rises, and the reverse.

whyNot.D: A rate fixed by the central bank describes a fixed exchange rate system.
whyNot.B: Tying a currency to gold describes the old gold standard.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following is an argument AGAINST the use of protectionist measures such as high import tariffs?
options: They raise revenue for the government
They reduce consumers' choice and may lead to higher prices
They help to reduce a balance of payments deficit
They protect infant industries from foreign competition
questions.explanation: Tariffs make imports dearer and may shelter inefficient local firms. Consumers face fewer choices and pay more, which is a major argument against protection.

whyNot.D: Protecting infant industries is a standard argument for protection.
whyNot.C: Reducing a deficit is a reason given for protection, not against it.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: International trade arises mainly because
options: countries differ in their natural resources, climate and skills
all countries produce exactly the same goods
every country has the same currency
governments want to ban local production
questions.explanation: Countries are endowed with different resources: Nigeria has crude oil and cocoa, others have different minerals or technology. These differences make specialisation and exchange beneficial.

whyNot.B: If all countries produced the same goods equally well, there would be little reason to trade.
whyNot.C: Countries use different currencies, which is why foreign exchange is needed.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Devaluation of a country's currency is most likely to reduce its balance of payments deficit when
options: its trading partners also devalue their currencies
the demand for its exports and imports is price elastic
the demand for its exports and imports is price inelastic
domestic prices rise by the same percentage as the devaluation
questions.explanation: Devaluation makes exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home. If demand is elastic, export volumes rise and import volumes fall by large amounts, so export earnings rise and import spending falls, improving the balance.

whyNot.C: With inelastic demand, volumes hardly change, so the country earns less from cheaper exports and still spends more on imports.
whyNot.A: If trading partners also devalue, the price advantage is cancelled.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A country's nominal GDP rose from ₦500 billion to ₦660 billion while its price index rose from 100 to 120. What was the rate of growth of real GDP?
questions.explanation: Real GDP in the second year = 660 × 100 ÷ 120 = ₦550 billion. Growth = (550 − 500) ÷ 500 × 100 = 10%.

whyNot.A: 32% is the growth in nominal GDP, which includes the effect of rising prices.
whyNot.D: 20% is the rise in prices, not in real output.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The branch of economics that studies the economy as a whole, such as national income, unemployment and the general price level, is
questions.explanation: Macroeconomics deals with large aggregates: total output, total employment, inflation and the balance of payments.

whyNot.A: Microeconomics studies individual units such as a single firm, household or market.
whyNot.B: Econometrics applies statistical methods to economic data.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A tractor used by a farmer to cultivate his land is an example of
options: land as a factor of production
questions.explanation: Capital goods are man-made goods used to produce other goods and services. A tractor is not wanted for its own sake but for the crops it helps to grow.

whyNot.D: Consumer goods directly satisfy wants, such as food or clothing.
whyNot.A: A tractor is scarce and has a price, so it is not a free good.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A main feature of a subsistence economy is that
options: producers consume most of what they produce
goods are produced mainly for export
money is used for all exchanges
questions.explanation: In a subsistence economy people produce mainly to meet their own needs and those of their families, with little left over for sale or exchange.

whyNot.B: Producing mainly for sale or export describes an exchange (commercial) economy.
whyNot.C: Subsistence producers usually do many different jobs rather than specialising.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of the entrepreneur?
options: Lending money to the business at a fixed interest
Supplying only physical effort to the business
Organising and combining the other factors of production
Owning the land on which the business is located
questions.explanation: The entrepreneur decides what to produce, brings land, labour and capital together, manages them and bears the risk of the business.

whyNot.B: Supplying physical effort is the role of labour.
whyNot.A: Lending money at a fixed interest is the role of a creditor providing capital.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The prices of a mudu of beans in five markets are ₦120, ₦95, ₦150, ₦80 and ₦110. What is the range?
questions.explanation: Range = highest value − lowest value = ₦150 − ₦80 = ₦70.

whyNot.C: ₦110 is the median of the five prices.
whyNot.D: ₦555 is the sum of the five prices.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The price of a bag of beans rose from ₦40,000 to ₦50,000. What is the percentage increase in price?
questions.explanation: Percentage change = (change ÷ original value) × 100 = (10,000 ÷ 40,000) × 100 = 25%.

whyNot.D: 20% divides the change by the new price (50,000) instead of the original price.
whyNot.B: 80% is the old price as a percentage of the new price.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Opportunity cost is also called real cost because it is measured in terms of
options: the market price of the good
the alternative that is given up
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made. It measures cost in terms of real goods or services sacrificed, not in money.

whyNot.A: The amount of money spent is the money cost.
whyNot.B: The market price is a money measure, not the alternative forgone.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following would most likely increase the size of a country's labour force?
options: Increasing pensions paid to retired people
Reducing the number of working hours per week
questions.explanation: The labour force is the number of people of working age who are willing and able to work. A higher retirement age keeps older workers in employment for longer, so the labour force grows.

whyNot.A: Keeping young people longer in school delays their entry into the labour force.
whyNot.C: Fewer working hours reduce hours worked, not the number of people in the labour force.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: An economy using all its resources produces 500 bags of rice and 200 bicycles. To produce 220 bicycles, it must reduce rice output to 440 bags. What is the opportunity cost of each extra bicycle?
questions.explanation: Extra bicycles = 220 − 200 = 20. Rice given up = 500 − 440 = 60 bags. Opportunity cost per bicycle = 60 ÷ 20 = 3 bags of rice.

whyNot.B: 60 bags is the total rice given up for all 20 extra bicycles.
whyNot.A: 20 is the number of extra bicycles, not their cost in rice.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A common criticism of the capitalist economic system is that it
options: gives consumers no freedom of choice
can lead to a very unequal distribution of income and wealth
has no role for private ownership
removes the profit motive from production
questions.explanation: In capitalism, incomes depend on the resources people own and their success in the market. Those who own much property earn far more, so inequality can become very large.

whyNot.A: Capitalism gives consumers wide freedom of choice.
whyNot.D: The profit motive is the driving force of capitalism.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A demand schedule is
options: a table showing the quantities of a commodity demanded at different prices
a list of firms supplying a commodity
a graph of the cost of producing a commodity
questions.explanation: A demand schedule lists the different quantities that consumers are willing and able to buy at various prices over a period. Plotting it gives the demand curve.

whyNot.C: Costs of production relate to supply, not demand.
whyNot.B: A list of firms tells us nothing about quantities demanded at each price.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A 20% rise in the price of a commodity leads to a 5% fall in the quantity demanded. What is the price elasticity of demand?
questions.explanation: PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price = 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25. As it is less than 1, demand is inelastic.

whyNot.D: 4 is the formula upside down (20 ÷ 5).
whyNot.A: 25 adds the two percentages instead of dividing.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A perfectly elastic demand curve is drawn as
options: a line that slopes upward from left to right
a curve that slopes downward from left to right
questions.explanation: Perfectly elastic demand means buyers will take any quantity at one price, but nothing at a higher price. This is shown by a horizontal line at that price.

whyNot.D: A vertical demand curve shows perfectly inelastic demand.
whyNot.B: A normal downward-sloping curve shows elasticity between zero and infinity along it.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: When the price of maize rises, farmers plant more maize and less sorghum on the same land. Maize and sorghum are in
questions.explanation: Goods are in competitive supply when the same resources can be used to produce either of them. More of one means less of the other.

whyNot.A: Joint supply is when producing one good automatically produces another, such as beef and hides.
whyNot.D: Joint demand refers to goods bought together.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The demand and supply functions for a commodity are Qd = 80 − 4P and Qs = 6P − 20. If the government fixes the price at ₦8, what is the excess demand?
questions.explanation: At ₦8: Qd = 80 − 32 = 48 and Qs = 48 − 20 = 28. Excess demand = 48 − 28 = 20 units. (The equilibrium price is ₦10, so ₦8 is below it.)

whyNot.C: 48 units is the quantity demanded at ₦8, not the excess.
whyNot.B: 28 units is the quantity supplied at ₦8.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: When consumers' incomes rise by 10%, the quantity demanded of air conditioners rises by 25%. What is the income elasticity of demand, and what kind of good is it?
questions.explanation: Income elasticity = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in income = 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5. A positive value greater than 1 shows a luxury good.

whyNot.D: 0.4 is the formula upside down; a value below 1 would indicate a necessity.
whyNot.A: An inferior good has a negative income elasticity.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Market demand for a commodity is
options: the sum of the quantities demanded by all individuals at each price
the average price paid by consumers
the quantity supplied at the equilibrium price
the quantity demanded by the richest consumer
questions.explanation: Market demand is found by adding up, at each price, the quantities that all individual consumers in the market wish to buy.

whyNot.D: One consumer's demand is individual demand, not market demand.
whyNot.C: Quantity supplied relates to sellers, not buyers.

questions.subject: economics
questions.context:
A consumer's total utility (TU) from eating oranges:
Oranges: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
Total utility (utils): 20, 35, 45, 50, 50, 46
questions.stem: What is the marginal utility of the 4th orange?
questions.explanation: Marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from one more unit: MU of the 4th orange = TU(4) − TU(3) = 50 − 45 = 5 utils.
