whyNot.A: 50 utils is the total utility from 4 oranges.
whyNot.D: 12.5 utils is the average utility (50 ÷ 4).

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A tax is placed on a commodity whose demand is inelastic and whose supply is elastic. The burden of the tax will fall
questions.explanation: The side of the market that is less responsive to price bears more of a tax. Consumers with inelastic demand keep buying even when the price rises, so sellers can pass most of the tax on to them.

whyNot.B: Producers bear most of the tax when supply is inelastic relative to demand.
whyNot.A: An equal split needs equal elasticities of demand and supply.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following would cause the supply curve of a manufactured good to shift to the right?
options: A new tax on each unit produced
A rise in the price of the good itself
A rise in the price of raw materials
questions.explanation: Better technology lowers the cost of producing each unit, so firms supply more at every price. The whole supply curve shifts to the right.

whyNot.D: Dearer raw materials raise costs and shift supply to the left.
whyNot.C: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the supply curve.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: In economics, production is best defined as
options: the creation of goods and services to satisfy human wants
the manufacture of goods in factories only
the buying and selling of goods
the growing of food crops only
questions.explanation: Production covers every activity that creates goods or services to satisfy wants: farming, manufacturing, trading, transport and personal services.

whyNot.B: Manufacturing is only one part (secondary production).
whyNot.C: Trade is part of production, but production is much wider.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of secondary production?
options: Selling petrol at a filling station
Drilling crude oil from the ground
questions.explanation: Secondary production changes raw materials into finished or semi-finished goods. Refining crude oil into petrol is manufacturing.

whyNot.B: Extracting crude oil is primary production.
whyNot.A: Selling at a filling station is tertiary production (commerce).

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A firm earns a total revenue of ₦4,500 by selling 150 units of its product. What is its average revenue?
questions.explanation: Average revenue = total revenue ÷ quantity sold = 4,500 ÷ 150 = ₦30. Average revenue is the same as the price per unit.

whyNot.B: ₦675,000 multiplies revenue by quantity instead of dividing.
whyNot.D: ₦45 divides by 100 instead of 150.

questions.subject: economics
questions.context:
Total product (TP) of a poultry farm as workers are added to a fixed number of cages:
Workers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Total product (crates of eggs): 10, 25, 45, 60, 70
questions.stem: What is the average product of labour when 4 workers are employed?
questions.explanation: Average product = total product ÷ number of workers = 60 ÷ 4 = 15 crates per worker.

whyNot.C: 60 crates is total product, not output per worker.
whyNot.A: 20 crates is the marginal product of the 3rd worker (45 − 25).

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: At an output of 50 units, a firm's total cost is ₦9,000 and its average variable cost is ₦120. What is its total fixed cost?
questions.explanation: Total variable cost = AVC × output = 120 × 50 = ₦6,000. Total fixed cost = total cost − total variable cost = 9,000 − 6,000 = ₦3,000.

whyNot.B: ₦6,000 is the total variable cost.
whyNot.D: ₦8,880 subtracts the AVC from total cost without multiplying by output.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Traffic congestion, pollution and high rents that arise when too many firms crowd into one industrial area are examples of
questions.explanation: These are disadvantages that arise from the growth of the whole industry or area, outside any single firm. They raise costs for all firms there, so they are external diseconomies.

whyNot.B: External economies are benefits from location, such as good roads or skilled labour, not costs.
whyNot.D: Internal diseconomies arise inside one firm because of its own large size.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The marginal cost curve cuts the average total cost curve at
options: the lowest point of the average total cost curve
the highest point of the average total cost curve
the point where total cost is highest
the point where output is zero
questions.explanation: When MC is below ATC it pulls the average down; when MC is above ATC it pulls the average up. So ATC is at its minimum exactly where MC crosses it.

whyNot.B: The ATC curve is U-shaped and has no highest point that MC crosses.
whyNot.C: Total cost keeps rising with output, so there is no such point.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Compared with a perfectly competitive industry with the same costs, a monopolist usually
options: charges the same price and produces the same output
has no control over the price of its product
charges a lower price and produces a larger output
charges a higher price and produces a smaller output
questions.explanation: A monopolist faces the whole downward-sloping market demand curve. To maximise profit it restricts output and raises price above what a competitive industry would charge.

whyNot.C: Lower price and greater output are typical of competition, not monopoly.
whyNot.B: Having no control over price describes a perfectly competitive firm.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: In a cooperative society, each member normally has
options: one vote, no matter how many shares he holds
votes in proportion to the shares he holds
no right to vote at meetings
the right to appoint the government's directors
questions.explanation: Cooperatives are run democratically. The principle is one member, one vote, so a member with many shares has no more voting power than one with few.

whyNot.B: Votes in proportion to shares is the rule in joint-stock companies.
whyNot.C: Members do vote; it is a democratic organisation.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Normal profit is best described as
options: any profit above the average for the industry
the minimum profit needed to keep an entrepreneur in a particular business
the profit a monopolist earns in the long run
the total revenue of a firm before costs are deducted
questions.explanation: Normal profit is the reward just enough to keep the entrepreneur in the business. Economists treat it as part of costs, so a firm earning normal profit has total revenue equal to total cost.

whyNot.A: Profit above normal is abnormal (supernormal) profit.
whyNot.D: Total revenue before costs is not profit at all.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Legal tender is money that
options: must by law be accepted in payment of debts
can be used only in foreign trade
questions.explanation: Legal tender is money that the law says must be accepted in settlement of a debt. In Nigeria, naira notes and coins issued by the Central Bank are legal tender.

whyNot.D: Legal tender is used by the general public, not only by banks.
whyNot.A: Modern money is not backed by gold.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of near money?
options: A cheque drawn on a current account balance
questions.explanation: Near money consists of assets that can be turned into cash quickly but are not themselves generally accepted as a means of payment, such as bills of exchange, Treasury bills and savings deposits.

whyNot.A: Naira notes are money itself, not near money.
whyNot.B: A cheque transfers a demand deposit, which is counted as money.

questions.subject: economics
questions.context:
Monetary data for a country (₦ billion):
Currency outside banks: 300
Demand deposits: 700
Savings and time deposits: 500
questions.stem: Broad money (M2) is narrow money plus savings and time deposits. What is broad money?
questions.explanation: Narrow money (M1) = currency outside banks + demand deposits = 300 + 700 = ₦1,000 billion. M2 = M1 + savings and time deposits = 1,000 + 500 = ₦1,500 billion.

whyNot.A: ₦1,000 billion is narrow money (M1).
whyNot.B: ₦1,200 billion leaves out currency outside banks.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following is a liability of a commercial bank?
options: Treasury bills held by the bank
questions.explanation: Customers' deposits are money the bank owes to its customers and must repay on demand or at maturity, so they are liabilities.

whyNot.D: Loans are money owed to the bank by borrowers, so they are assets.
whyNot.A: Cash held by the bank is an asset.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: When the Central Bank of Nigeria keeps the Federal Government's accounts and manages its debt, it is acting as
questions.explanation: As the government's banker, the central bank holds government accounts, receives revenue, makes payments and manages the government's borrowing.

whyNot.D: Banker to the banks means holding the commercial banks' accounts and reserves.
whyNot.A: Lender of last resort means lending to banks in difficulty.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: If the general price level rises from 100 to 125, the purchasing power of ₦1 falls to
questions.explanation: Value of money = base index ÷ current index = 100 ÷ 125 = 0.8. So ₦1 now buys what 80 kobo bought in the base period.

whyNot.A: 75 kobo assumes value falls by the same 25% as prices rose, but 1 ÷ 1.25 is 0.8.
whyNot.C: Purchasing power falls when prices rise; it does not rise to 125 kobo.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A commercial bank faces a conflict between
options: the central bank and the stock exchange
questions.explanation: To earn profit, a bank wants to lend as much as possible. To stay safe, it must keep enough cash and liquid assets to meet withdrawals. Holding more cash means lending less, so liquidity and profitability pull in opposite directions.

whyNot.C: Deposits and withdrawals are normal daily activities, not the policy conflict banks must balance.
whyNot.D: Fixed and variable costs are not the central conflict in banking.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Microfinance banks in Nigeria mainly
options: provide small loans and financial services to low-income earners and small businesses
finance large oil and gas projects
supervise all other banks in the country
questions.explanation: Microfinance banks are meant to bring banking services, especially small loans and savings facilities, to poor people and small businesses who find it hard to use conventional banks.

whyNot.A: Only the Central Bank of Nigeria issues the currency.
whyNot.D: Supervising banks is a function of the Central Bank (with the NDIC).

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: When the Central Bank appeals to commercial banks to follow its policy, without issuing a binding order, it is using
questions.explanation: Moral suasion is persuasion: the central bank uses meetings, speeches and advice to get banks to act in line with its policy, without legal force.

whyNot.C: Open market operations are the buying and selling of government securities.
whyNot.A: Special deposits are amounts banks are required to lodge with the central bank.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A situation in which an economy has high inflation together with high unemployment and slow growth is called
questions.explanation: Stagflation combines stagnation (slow growth and high unemployment) with inflation. It is difficult to fight because measures that cut inflation may worsen unemployment.

whyNot.B: Hyperinflation is extremely rapid inflation, whatever the level of unemployment.
whyNot.C: Creeping inflation is a slow, mild rise in prices.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Gross National Product is obtained by adding to Gross Domestic Product
questions.explanation: GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad. It measures the output of a country's citizens and their resources, wherever they are located.

whyNot.A: Depreciation is subtracted to move from gross to net figures.
whyNot.D: Indirect taxes are adjusted when moving between market prices and factor cost.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A household earns ₦80,000 a month and saves ₦12,000 of it. What is its average propensity to consume?
questions.explanation: Consumption = income − saving = 80,000 − 12,000 = ₦68,000. APC = consumption ÷ income = 68,000 ÷ 80,000 = 0.85.

whyNot.D: 0.15 is the average propensity to save.
whyNot.C: 0.68 drops a zero: 68,000 ÷ 100,000 instead of ÷ 80,000.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: National income figures are useful mainly because they help to
options: compare a country's standard of living over different years
decide the population of the country
measure the amount of money in circulation
fix the exchange rate of the currency
questions.explanation: National income (especially real income per head) shows how much output the country produces. Comparing figures over time shows whether living standards are rising or falling and helps in planning.

whyNot.D: Exchange rates depend on foreign exchange markets and policy, not directly on national income figures.
whyNot.C: Money in circulation is measured by monetary statistics.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A country's GDP at factor cost is ₦700 billion. Indirect taxes are ₦90 billion and subsidies are ₦30 billion. What is its GDP at market prices?
questions.explanation: GDP at market prices = GDP at factor cost + indirect taxes − subsidies = 700 + 90 − 30 = ₦760 billion.

whyNot.B: ₦640 billion subtracts taxes and adds subsidies: the wrong direction.
whyNot.A: ₦820 billion adds both taxes and subsidies.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: In an economy the marginal propensity to save is 0.2. If government spending rises by ₦15 billion, by how much will national income rise?
questions.explanation: Multiplier = 1 ÷ MPS = 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5. Change in income = multiplier × change in spending = 5 × 15 = ₦75 billion.

whyNot.A: ₦3 billion multiplies the spending by the MPS instead of dividing.
whyNot.C: ₦18.75 billion divides by the MPC (0.8) instead of the MPS.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Visible trade refers to trade in
options: physical goods such as crude oil and cocoa
services such as banking and insurance
questions.explanation: Visible trade is the export and import of goods that can be seen and touched. Trade in services such as shipping, banking and tourism is invisible trade.

whyNot.D: Banking and insurance are services, so they are invisible items.
whyNot.A: Loans are recorded in the capital and financial account.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: When a central bank rations the available foreign currency among importers and other users, it is practising
questions.explanation: Exchange control means the government or central bank restricts and allocates the use of foreign exchange, often to protect reserves and reduce a balance of payments deficit.

whyNot.C: Devaluation is an official reduction in the exchange rate, not rationing.
whyNot.A: Dumping is selling goods abroad below the home price.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Country A can produce both cloth and rice more cheaply than Country B. Both countries can still gain from trading with each other provided that
options: both countries produce exactly the same amounts
Country B has an absolute advantage in both goods
Country A stops producing both goods
the opportunity costs of producing the two goods differ between them
questions.explanation: By the theory of comparative advantage, trade is beneficial when opportunity costs differ. Each country specialises in the good it gives up least to produce, and total output rises.

whyNot.B: The question says Country A, not B, has the absolute advantage in both goods.
whyNot.A: Equal amounts of output do not create gains from trade.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Heavy dependence on a single primary export, such as crude oil, exposes a country mainly to
options: a permanent surplus in its balance of payments
sharp swings in export earnings when world prices change
the loss of its membership of international organisations
a steady rise in the prices of its imports
questions.explanation: Prices of primary products change sharply on world markets. When a country earns most of its foreign exchange from one product, a fall in that price sharply cuts its export earnings and government revenue.

whyNot.A: One-product dependence makes the balance of payments unstable, not permanently in surplus.
whyNot.D: Import prices are set elsewhere and are not caused by dependence on one export.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: In Nigeria, one worker can produce either 8 bags of cocoa or 4 radios in a day. In Japan, one worker can produce either 2 bags of cocoa or 4 radios. What is the opportunity cost of one radio in Nigeria?
questions.explanation: In Nigeria, 4 radios cost 8 bags of cocoa, so one radio costs 8 ÷ 4 = 2 bags. In Japan one radio costs only 0.5 bag, so Japan has the comparative advantage in radios and Nigeria in cocoa.

whyNot.A: 0.5 bag is the opportunity cost of a radio in Japan.
whyNot.C: 4 is the number of radios, not their cost in cocoa.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The political thinker who described life in the 'state of nature' as 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short' in his book Leviathan was
questions.explanation: Thomas Hobbes published Leviathan in 1651. He argued that without government people would live in constant fear and conflict, so they agreed to surrender their rights to an absolute sovereign who would keep order.

whyNot.D: Locke saw the state of nature as more peaceful, governed by natural law; he did not use this phrase.
whyNot.B: Machiavelli wrote The Prince, a guide on how rulers gain and keep power; he was not a social contract writer.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: John Locke argued in his Two Treatises of Government that the main purpose of government is to protect the natural rights of
options: the king, the nobles and the clergy
the ruling class over the working class
questions.explanation: Locke held that people are born with natural rights to life, liberty and property. They form a government by consent to protect these rights, and if a government violates them the people may lawfully replace it.

whyNot.A: Locke opposed the idea that government exists to serve privileged estates; he based it on the consent of all.
whyNot.C: The state as a tool of one class over another is a Marxist idea, not Locke's.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Jean-Jacques Rousseau's idea that the state should be guided by the common interest of the whole community, rather than the private interests of individuals, is known as the
questions.explanation: In The Social Contract (1762), Rousseau said that legitimate authority comes from the 'general will', the shared will of the whole people aimed at the common good. Sovereignty therefore belongs to the people as a body.

whyNot.B: Divine right says rulers get their authority from God, which Rousseau rejected.
whyNot.D: The 'invisible hand' is Adam Smith's idea about free markets, an economic rather than political concept.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In a democracy, legal sovereignty belongs to the body that makes laws, while political sovereignty ultimately lies with the
questions.explanation: A V Dicey distinguished legal sovereignty (the lawmaking authority, such as parliament) from political sovereignty (the power that the lawmakers must finally answer to). In a democracy this is the electorate, because voters can remove the lawmakers at the next election.

whyNot.C: The judiciary interprets laws; it does not hold the final political power over lawmakers.
whyNot.A: The civil service carries out policy and is answerable to ministers, not the source of sovereignty.
whyNot.B: In a democracy the armed forces are under civilian control; power taken by force is not sovereignty in the democratic sense.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The principle 'from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs' describes how goods would be shared under
questions.explanation: Karl Marx used this slogan for the final stage of communism, when production is so plentiful that goods are shared according to need. Under socialism, the earlier stage, people would be rewarded according to the work they do.

whyNot.D: Under capitalism people earn according to what the market pays for their labour or capital, not according to need.
whyNot.C: Under feudalism the produce of the land went largely to lords in return for protection.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Almond and Verba described a political culture in which most citizens have little or no awareness of the national government and its activities as
questions.explanation: In The Civic Culture, Almond and Verba identified three types: parochial (people hardly know the central government exists), subject (people know about government and obey it but do not take part) and participant (people are aware and actively involved).

whyNot.A: In a participant culture citizens are aware of the system and actively take part in it.
whyNot.D: In a subject culture citizens are aware of government and its outputs but play a passive role.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A person who becomes a citizen of a country because one or both of his or her parents are citizens of that country acquires citizenship by
questions.explanation: Jus sanguinis ('right of blood') grants citizenship through parents or grandparents, wherever the child is born. Nigeria follows this principle: a person born outside Nigeria to a Nigerian parent is a Nigerian citizen by birth.

whyNot.B: Jus soli ('right of soil') gives citizenship because of the place where a person is born, not because of the parents.
whyNot.A: Naturalisation is citizenship granted to a foreigner after a period of residence and an application.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A system of government in which power is held by the elders of the community is known as
questions.explanation: Gerontocracy comes from the Greek 'geron', meaning old man. Political power is held by the oldest members of society, as in many traditional African communities where councils of elders took decisions.

whyNot.A: Aristocracy is rule by a privileged few thought to be the best, usually by birth.
whyNot.D: Plutocracy is rule by the wealthy.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under feudalism, a vassal received land from a lord in return for
options: payment of income tax to the state
questions.explanation: Feudalism was a system in medieval Europe built on land holding. The lord granted land (a fief) to a vassal, who in return swore loyalty and provided military service. Peasants (serfs) worked the land and were tied to it.

whyNot.D: Company profits belong to capitalism, which developed after feudalism.
whyNot.A: Feudal relations were based on personal loyalty and land, not on elections.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: According to Karl Marx, the state is best understood as
options: a neutral umpire that serves all citizens equally
an institution created directly by God
an agreement freely entered into by all individuals
an instrument used by the ruling class to oppress other classes
questions.explanation: Marx argued that the state arose from class conflict and is used by the class that owns the means of production to keep other classes under control. He expected the state to 'wither away' once classes disappeared under communism.

whyNot.A: Seeing the state as a neutral umpire is a liberal or pluralist view, which Marx rejected.
whyNot.B: This is the divine right theory.
whyNot.C: This is the social contract theory of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Provisions of a constitution that can be changed only by a special and more difficult procedure than ordinary laws are called
questions.explanation: Entrenched clauses are protected parts of a constitution, such as fundamental rights or the creation of states, that require special majorities or approval by component units before they can be amended. They protect key arrangements from hasty change.

whyNot.B: Bye-laws are rules made by local councils or public bodies, not parts of the constitution.
whyNot.D: Conventions are unwritten customs that are not legally enforceable.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under section 9 of the 1999 Constitution, an ordinary amendment must be passed by a two-thirds majority of all members of each House of the National Assembly and approved by resolution of the Houses of Assembly of at least two-thirds of all the states. What is the minimum number of State Houses of Assembly needed?
questions.explanation: Nigeria has 36 states. Two-thirds of 36 is 36 × 2 ÷ 3 = 24. So at least 24 State Houses of Assembly must approve the amendment after it has passed both Houses of the National Assembly.

whyNot.D: 18 is half of 36, a simple majority figure, not two-thirds.
whyNot.B: 19 is a simple majority of 36 (more than half), not two-thirds.
whyNot.C: 26 is more than required; two-thirds of 36 is exactly 24.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The parliamentary system is said to have a dual executive because
options: two presidents rule at the same time
ministers are drawn from two different political parties
the executive is elected twice in each term
the head of state and the head of government are different persons
questions.explanation: In a parliamentary system the head of state (a monarch or ceremonial president) has nominal powers, while the head of government (the prime minister) exercises real executive power. Nigeria had this arrangement in the First Republic.

whyNot.A: There are not two presidents; one office is ceremonial and the other holds real power.
whyNot.B: A coalition may contain several parties, but that is not what 'dual executive' means.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In Nigeria's presidential system, a member of the National Assembly who is appointed a minister must
options: be confirmed by the Supreme Court
resign his or her seat in the legislature
keep the seat and vote on bills
give up membership of his or her political party
questions.explanation: Separation of personnel is a feature of the presidential system. Section 147(4) of the 1999 Constitution provides that a member of a legislative house appointed as a minister shall be deemed to have resigned his or her membership of that house.

whyNot.C: Holding both posts at once would be fusion of powers, a parliamentary feature.
whyNot.A: Ministerial nominees are confirmed by the Senate, not by the Supreme Court.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: When a court declares that a public authority acted beyond the powers given to it by law, the action is said to be
questions.explanation: Ultra vires is Latin for 'beyond the powers'. Courts use the doctrine to strike down actions and regulations of public bodies that exceed the authority granted by the constitution or the enabling Act.

whyNot.A: Sub judice means a matter is still before a court and should not be publicly discussed in a way that prejudices the case.
whyNot.C: Habeas corpus is an order that a detained person be produced in court.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A court order requiring that a person held in custody be brought before the court so that the lawfulness of the detention can be examined is called a writ of
questions.explanation: Habeas corpus ('you have the body') protects personal liberty. If the detaining authority cannot show lawful grounds for holding the person, the court orders his or her release.

whyNot.C: Mandamus orders a public official to perform a legal duty he or she has failed to perform.
whyNot.A: Certiorari brings the decision of a lower court or tribunal to a higher court to be quashed.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The principle that civil servants should serve any government in power loyally, without taking part in partisan politics, is known as
questions.explanation: Political neutrality means civil servants do not join in party politics and must carry out the policies of whichever party forms the government. This allows the civil service to remain permanent while governments change.

whyNot.A: Collective responsibility applies to cabinet ministers, who must publicly support cabinet decisions.
whyNot.D: Judicial independence concerns the freedom of judges from interference, not civil servants.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In a federal constitution, the list of matters on which both the central government and the component units may make laws is the
questions.explanation: The concurrent list contains shared subjects, such as education and agriculture in Nigeria, on which both levels may legislate. Where a federal law and a state law on a concurrent matter conflict, the federal law prevails.

whyNot.B: The exclusive list contains matters on which only the central government can legislate.
whyNot.C: Residual matters are those not on either list, and in Nigeria they belong to the states.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a unicameral legislature?
options: The Parliament of the United Kingdom
The Congress of the United States
A State House of Assembly in Nigeria
questions.explanation: A unicameral legislature has only one chamber. Each Nigerian state has a single House of Assembly. The National Assembly, the US Congress and the UK Parliament each have two chambers.

whyNot.B: The National Assembly is bicameral: the Senate and the House of Representatives.
whyNot.C: The US Congress has two chambers, the Senate and the House of Representatives.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The main function of the judiciary is to
options: collect taxes and spend public money
questions.explanation: The judiciary consists of the courts. It interprets the constitution and other laws, applies them to cases and settles disputes between individuals, between individuals and government, and between governments.

whyNot.C: Making laws is the function of the legislature.
whyNot.D: Collecting taxes and spending money are executive functions, under laws passed by the legislature.
whyNot.B: Elections are conducted by electoral bodies such as INEC.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A second round of voting held between the leading candidates when no candidate satisfied the requirements for victory in the first round is called a
questions.explanation: A run-off (second ballot) is used when the first round produces no winner under the rules, for example when no candidate wins the required spread or majority. Only the leading candidates take part, so a clear winner emerges.

whyNot.A: A by-election fills a seat that has become vacant during a term.
whyNot.C: A primary election chooses a party's candidate before the general election.
whyNot.D: A referendum asks voters to decide a specific issue, not to choose between candidates.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under the 1999 Constitution, the minimum age at which a Nigerian citizen is entitled to be registered as a voter is
questions.explanation: Section 77(2) of the 1999 Constitution entitles every Nigerian citizen who has attained the age of eighteen years, and is resident in Nigeria at the time of voter registration, to be registered as a voter.

whyNot.D: 21 was once a common voting age in many countries but is not Nigeria's.
whyNot.C: 25 is not a voting age; minimum ages for contesting offices are a different matter.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A major criticism of the one-party system is that it
options: encourages too many parties to form
limits the choice available to voters
makes elections too expensive to hold
questions.explanation: In a one-party state only one party may legally exist, so voters cannot choose between rival programmes or remove the ruling party at an election. This weakens accountability and can lead to dictatorship.

whyNot.A: Coalition governments arise in multi-party systems where no party wins a majority.
whyNot.B: A one-party state prevents other parties from forming at all.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A pressure group that tries to persuade legislators privately to support its interests is using the method known as
questions.explanation: Lobbying means contacting and persuading lawmakers and officials, often in person, to support policies the group favours. It is one of the most common methods of pressure groups.

whyNot.C: A boycott is a refusal to buy, use or take part in something as a form of protest.
whyNot.B: A filibuster is a long speech by a legislator to delay a vote; it is used by lawmakers, not pressure groups.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A pressure group formed to advance a cause that benefits society generally, such as protecting the environment, rather than the interests of its own members, is a
questions.explanation: Promotional or cause groups pursue a public cause or idea, and anyone who shares the cause can join. Protective or interest groups, such as trade unions and professional bodies, defend the interests of their own members.

whyNot.C: Protective groups defend their members' own interests, such as the pay of workers.
whyNot.B: A political party seeks to win elections and control government, which pressure groups do not.
whyNot.D: A trade union is a protective group concerned with its members' welfare.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), the Chairman is appointed by the President subject to
options: a vote of all registered parties
questions.explanation: Under section 154(1) of the 1999 Constitution, the Chairman and members of federal executive bodies such as INEC are appointed by the President, subject to confirmation by the Senate. Senate confirmation is meant to check the President's power of appointment.

whyNot.A: The Supreme Court decides cases; it does not approve appointments.
whyNot.C: Political parties take part in elections but do not appoint the electoral body.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A common disadvantage of proportional representation is that it
options: always gives one party a large majority
tends to produce many parties and coalition governments
prevents small parties from winning any seats
wastes the votes of most voters
questions.explanation: Because seats follow vote shares, even small parties win seats under proportional representation. Often no single party has a majority, so governments are formed by coalitions that may be unstable.

whyNot.D: Proportional representation reduces wasted votes; it is the first-past-the-post system that wastes many votes.
whyNot.C: It actually helps small parties win seats, the opposite of this option.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A vote in which the whole electorate is asked to accept or reject a particular proposal, such as a constitutional change, is a
questions.explanation: A referendum lets the people decide directly on an issue rather than on candidates. The 1963 creation of the Mid-Western Region, for example, followed a referendum in the area concerned.

whyNot.B: A recall removes an elected representative before the end of the term.
whyNot.A: A general election chooses representatives for public offices.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The presidential election held on 12 June 1993 in Nigeria was annulled by the military government of
questions.explanation: The 12 June 1993 election was the climax of General Ibrahim Babangida's transition programme. His government annulled it, which caused a political crisis; he stepped aside in August 1993 and handed over to an Interim National Government.

whyNot.A: Abacha took power in November 1993, after the annulment had already taken place.
whyNot.C: Obasanjo's military regime handed over power in 1979.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: One function that political parties perform by combining the many demands of different groups into a single programme is called
questions.explanation: Interest aggregation means gathering and combining many demands into broad policy choices, usually in a party manifesto. Pressure groups mainly perform interest articulation, which is expressing particular demands.

whyNot.D: Interest articulation is expressing a specific demand; it is mainly done by pressure groups.
whyNot.B: Rule adjudication is settling disputes over rules, a function of the courts.
whyNot.C: Political recruitment is selecting people for political office, a separate party function.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under Nigeria's federal arrangement, matters that are not on the Exclusive or Concurrent Legislative Lists fall within the competence of the
questions.explanation: Residual matters, those not listed in the Second Schedule, belong to the states. Section 4(7) of the 1999 Constitution empowers a State House of Assembly to make laws on any matter not on the Exclusive List, which includes these residual matters.

whyNot.B: The Federal Government can legislate only on the Exclusive and Concurrent Lists and matters incidental to them.
whyNot.C: Local governments have functions set out in the Fourth Schedule; they do not hold residual legislative powers.
whyNot.D: The Council of State is an advisory body and does not make laws.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Which of the following is on the Exclusive Legislative List of the 1999 Constitution?
questions.explanation: The Exclusive List (Part I of the Second Schedule) contains matters of national importance that only the National Assembly may legislate on, including defence, currency, foreign affairs, citizenship and the police.

whyNot.A: Chieftaincy matters are residual and are handled by the states.
whyNot.B: Markets and motor parks are local government functions under the Fourth Schedule.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Nigeria became a republic on
questions.explanation: On 1 October 1963 the Republican Constitution came into force. Nigeria replaced the British monarch with a Nigerian President as head of state while remaining in the Commonwealth.

whyNot.A: 1 October 1960 was independence; the British monarch remained head of state until 1963.
whyNot.D: 15 January 1966 was the date of the first military coup.
whyNot.B: 1 October 1979 marked the return to civilian rule and the start of the Second Republic.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The region created from part of the Western Region in 1963, the only region created in Nigeria under civilian rule, was the
questions.explanation: The Mid-Western Region was carved out of the Western Region in 1963 after a referendum. It became Nigeria's fourth region and was the only one created by the constitutional process under civilian rule.

whyNot.D: The Northern Region had existed since the Richards Constitution of 1946.
whyNot.A: The Eastern Region, like the Northern Region, was set up under the Richards Constitution of 1946.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Decree No. 34 of 1966, which abolished the regions and made Nigeria a unitary state, was issued by the government of
questions.explanation: Aguiyi-Ironsi became head of the military government after the January 1966 coup. His Unification Decree (No. 34) of May 1966 abolished the federal system. Its unpopularity in the North contributed to the counter-coup of July 1966.

whyNot.A: Gowon came to power after the July 1966 counter-coup and restored federalism.
whyNot.D: Tafawa Balewa was the civilian Prime Minister killed in the January 1966 coup; he issued no military decrees.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Nigeria's twelve states were increased to nineteen in 1976 by the government of
questions.explanation: In February 1976 the Murtala Mohammed regime created seven new states, raising the number from twelve to nineteen. The same government also began the move of the capital to Abuja.

whyNot.A: Gowon created the twelve states in 1967.
whyNot.B: Babangida created states in 1987 and 1991, raising the number to 21 and then 30.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The main purpose of the Code of Conduct Bureau established by the 1999 Constitution is to
options: allocate federal revenue among the states
train judges for the federal courts
receive and examine asset declarations of public officers
questions.explanation: The Code of Conduct Bureau enforces the Code of Conduct for public officers in the Fifth Schedule. Public officers must declare their assets on taking and leaving office, and the Bureau refers breaches to the Code of Conduct Tribunal.

whyNot.B: Local council elections are conducted by State Independent Electoral Commissions.
whyNot.A: Revenue allocation formulas are proposed by the Revenue Mobilisation Allocation and Fiscal Commission.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under section 49 of the 1999 Constitution, the House of Representatives consists of
questions.explanation: The House of Representatives has 360 members elected from federal constituencies of nearly equal population. Together with the 109 senators, the National Assembly has 469 members.

whyNot.D: 109 is the number of senators.
whyNot.B: 469 is the total membership of the National Assembly (360 + 109), not of the House alone.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Nigeria's first military coup, which ended the First Republic, took place on
questions.explanation: On 15 January 1966 a group of army officers struck, killing the Prime Minister and some regional leaders. The First Republic collapsed and Major-General Aguiyi-Ironsi took over as head of the military government.

whyNot.D: 29 July 1966 was the counter-coup that brought Gowon to power.
whyNot.A: 29 July 1975 was the coup that removed Gowon.
whyNot.C: 31 December 1983 was the coup that ended the Second Republic.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Which body is empowered by the 1999 Constitution to monitor the accruals into the Federation Account and to review revenue allocation formulae?
options: Revenue Mobilisation Allocation and Fiscal Commission
questions.explanation: The Revenue Mobilisation Allocation and Fiscal Commission (RMAFC) is a federal executive body under section 153. It monitors revenue paid into the Federation Account and reviews the formula for sharing it among the federal, state and local governments.

whyNot.D: The Federal Character Commission ensures fair distribution of public posts among states.
whyNot.A: The National Population Commission conducts the census and registers births and deaths.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The United Nations came into existence on
questions.explanation: The UN Charter entered into force on 24 October 1945, after it was ratified by the five permanent members and a majority of the other signatories. This date is celebrated every year as United Nations Day.

whyNot.D: 25 May 1963 is the date the OAU was founded.
whyNot.C: 1 September 1939 is when the Second World War began.
whyNot.A: 28 May 1975 is the date of the treaty establishing ECOWAS.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: How many members make up the United Nations Security Council?
questions.explanation: The Security Council has 15 members: 5 permanent members (China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States) and 10 non-permanent members elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms.

whyNot.B: 5 is only the number of permanent members.
whyNot.D: 10 is only the number of non-permanent members.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A negative vote by any permanent member of the UN Security Council blocks a decision on a substantive matter. This power is known as the
questions.explanation: Each of the five permanent members can block a substantive Security Council resolution by voting against it. This veto power reflects their position as the major Allied powers at the end of the Second World War.

whyNot.B: A quorum is the minimum number of members needed for a valid meeting.
whyNot.A: A filibuster is a delaying tactic of long speeches in a legislature.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The international agreement that sets out the rules on diplomatic immunity and the treatment of embassies is the
options: Charter of the Organisation of African Unity
Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations of 1961
questions.explanation: The Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations (1961) codifies the rules of diplomacy, such as the inviolability of embassy premises and the immunity of diplomats from the criminal jurisdiction of the receiving state.

whyNot.A: The Treaty of Versailles ended the First World War with Germany and created the League of Nations.
whyNot.D: The Lagos Plan of Action was an OAU plan for African economic development.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: When a host country declares that a foreign diplomat is no longer acceptable and must leave, the diplomat is said to have been declared
questions.explanation: Persona non grata means 'unwelcome person'. Under the Vienna Convention a receiving state may declare a diplomat persona non grata at any time without giving reasons, and the sending state must then recall him or her.

whyNot.D: Ultra vires means acting beyond legal powers.
whyNot.C: De jure means 'by law' or legally recognised, as in de jure recognition of a government.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The Commonwealth of Nations is made up mainly of
options: countries that produce and export petroleum
former colonies of France in Africa
Britain and countries that were formerly under British rule
all the independent states of Africa
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth is a voluntary association of independent states, most of which were once part of the British Empire. Members cooperate on democracy, development and trade. Nigeria joined at independence in 1960.

whyNot.A: This describes OPEC.
whyNot.D: All African states belong to the African Union, not the Commonwealth.
whyNot.B: Former French colonies are linked through the Francophonie, not the Commonwealth.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In 1976 Nigeria and many other African countries boycotted the Olympic Games in Montreal mainly to protest against
options: the cost of travelling to Canada
New Zealand's sporting contacts with apartheid South Africa
questions.explanation: The African boycott was a protest against New Zealand, whose national rugby team had toured apartheid South Africa. The International Olympic Committee refused to ban New Zealand, so African countries, including Nigeria, withdrew. It shows how Nigeria used sport in its anti-apartheid foreign policy.

whyNot.A: The Civil War had ended in 1970.
whyNot.C: ECOWAS, created in 1975, had nothing to do with the boycott.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The main aim of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) is to
options: unite all African states under one government
control the world price of crude oil
promote economic integration and cooperation among member states
questions.explanation: ECOWAS was set up to promote cooperation and integration in trade, transport, industry and other economic fields, so as to raise living standards in West Africa. It has since also taken on peace and security roles.

whyNot.A: No African organisation aims at one single government for the whole continent.
whyNot.B: Influencing oil prices is the concern of OPEC.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In 2002 the International Court of Justice ruled on the dispute between Nigeria and Cameroon over the Bakassi Peninsula in favour of
questions.explanation: In October 2002 the ICJ held that sovereignty over Bakassi lay with Cameroon, largely on the basis of the 1913 Anglo-German agreement. Nigeria later handed over the peninsula under the Greentree Agreement of 2006.

whyNot.D: The ICJ rejected Nigeria's claim to sovereignty over the peninsula.
whyNot.B: Equatorial Guinea took part only on maritime boundary issues and was not awarded the peninsula.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The Constitutive Act that established the African Union was adopted in 2000 at a summit held in
questions.explanation: The Constitutive Act of the African Union was adopted at the OAU summit in Lomé, Togo, in July 2000. The AU was then formally launched in Durban, South Africa, in 2002, with its headquarters in Addis Ababa.

whyNot.B: Addis Ababa is the AU's headquarters, not where the Constitutive Act was adopted.
whyNot.C: Abuja hosts the ECOWAS Commission, not the adoption of the AU's founding act.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Government by a small group of people regarded as the best qualified, usually because of birth or noble status, is
questions.explanation: Aristocracy comes from Greek words meaning 'rule of the best'. In Aristotle's classification it is the good form of rule by a few, in which the few govern for the benefit of all.

whyNot.B: Democracy is rule by the people as a whole.
whyNot.D: Anarchy is the absence of government.
whyNot.A: Gerontocracy is rule by elders, based on age rather than noble status.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A foreigner who has lived in Nigeria for the required number of years and is granted citizenship on application acquires it by
questions.explanation: Naturalisation is the legal process by which a non-citizen becomes a citizen after meeting conditions such as long residence, good character and an oath of allegiance. In Nigeria it is provided for in section 27 of the 1999 Constitution.

whyNot.D: Citizenship by birth is acquired automatically, not by application after residence.
whyNot.A: Citizenship by descent comes through one's parents.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The ability to affect the decisions of others through persuasion or example, without the use of force or formal legal authority, is known as
questions.explanation: Influence is a softer form of power. A respected religious leader or a newspaper columnist may shape government decisions through persuasion even though they hold no public office and cannot compel anyone.

whyNot.A: Coercion is the use of force or threats to compel obedience.
whyNot.B: Sovereignty is the supreme legal power of the state.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The attitudes, beliefs and values that the people of a country hold about their political system make up its
questions.explanation: Political culture is the pattern of attitudes towards politics, such as trust in government, interest in voting and respect for authority. It is formed largely through political socialisation.

whyNot.A: A constitution is a body of rules, not the attitudes of the people.
whyNot.C: The party system refers to the number and nature of parties competing for power.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A form of government in which the head of state inherits the position from a member of his or her family is
questions.explanation: In a monarchy the head of state (king, queen or emperor) usually comes to the throne by hereditary succession. In a republic, by contrast, the head of state is elected or appointed for a term.

whyNot.B: A republic has a head of state who is elected or appointed, not one who inherits the office.
whyNot.D: Oligarchy is rule by a small group, not hereditary rule by one person.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The first agent of political socialisation that a child comes into contact with is usually the
questions.explanation: From early childhood, the family teaches a child basic attitudes such as respect for authority and sometimes loyalty to a party or leader. School, peer groups, religious bodies and the mass media come later.

whyNot.C: Political parties influence people later, mostly as adults.
whyNot.A: The mass media is important but usually comes after the family's early influence.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A method of finding out the views of the public on a political issue by asking questions of a sample of people is
questions.explanation: An opinion poll measures public opinion by questioning a representative sample of the population. Governments, parties and the media use polls to judge how people feel about policies and candidates.

whyNot.B: A by-election fills a vacant seat; it is not a survey of opinion.
whyNot.D: A vote of no confidence is a legislative vote to remove a government.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The right to vote and to be voted for is an example of a
questions.explanation: Political rights allow citizens to take part in governing their country, such as voting, contesting elections and joining political parties. Social and economic rights concern things like education, health and work.

whyNot.B: Social rights include rights to education and healthcare.
whyNot.C: Economic rights include the right to work and to own property.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Which of the following is an obligation of a citizen to the state?
questions.explanation: Citizens have duties as well as rights. Paying taxes, obeying the law, defending the country and voting are obligations owed to the state. The other options are things the state provides or rights citizens enjoy.

whyNot.C: Receiving medical care is a benefit from the state, not a duty to it.
whyNot.A: Freedom of movement is a right that citizens enjoy.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A major feature of a liberal democracy is
options: unlimited powers for the head of state
questions.explanation: In a liberal democracy the people choose and can remove their rulers through regular competitive elections. Other features include the rule of law, protection of rights, a free press and several political parties.

whyNot.B: Single-party rule removes the voters' choice, which liberal democracy requires.
whyNot.D: Military decrees replace elected lawmaking and are typical of military regimes.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A constitution whose provisions are contained in a single document is described as
questions.explanation: A written constitution is set out in one formal document, such as the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria or the Constitution of the United States. An unwritten constitution is found in many sources such as statutes, court decisions and conventions.

whyNot.C: An unwritten constitution is not contained in a single document.
whyNot.B: 'Flexible' describes how easily a constitution can be amended, not whether it is in one document.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Which of the following historical documents is a source of the British constitution?
options: The Charter of the United Nations
questions.explanation: The British constitution is drawn from many sources, including historic documents such as Magna Carta (1215), Acts of Parliament, judicial decisions and conventions. Magna Carta limited the powers of the king.

whyNot.D: The Declaration of Independence is an American document that broke away from Britain.
whyNot.B: The Lyttelton Constitution was made for colonial Nigeria, not Britain.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: One feature of the presidential system of government is that the President
options: is a member of the legislature
shares executive power with a prime minister
serves a fixed term of office
can be removed by a simple vote of no confidence
questions.explanation: In a presidential system the President is elected for a fixed term, for example four years in Nigeria and the United States, and cannot be removed by an ordinary vote of the legislature; only impeachment for gross misconduct can end the term early.

whyNot.D: A vote of no confidence belongs to the parliamentary system.
whyNot.A: Separation of powers keeps the President out of the legislature.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: An advantage of a rigid constitution is that it
options: protects the constitution from hasty and frequent changes
can be amended quickly in an emergency
needs no interpretation by the courts
is easy for any government to change
questions.explanation: A rigid constitution requires a special procedure for amendment. This gives stability and protects important arrangements, such as fundamental rights and federal powers, from being changed by a passing majority.

whyNot.B: Quick amendment is an advantage of a flexible constitution; rigidity makes it slow.
whyNot.D: Ease of change describes a flexible constitution.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In a parliamentary system, the period in which members of parliament ask ministers questions about the work of their ministries is called
questions.explanation: Question time is a regular parliamentary session in which ministers answer questions from members. It is an important way for the legislature to control the executive and hold ministers accountable.

whyNot.C: Second reading is a stage in passing a bill when its general principles are debated.
whyNot.D: Prorogation ends a session of parliament without dissolving it.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A public corporation is best described as an organisation that is
options: formed by workers to protect their interests
owned by government and set up by law to provide a service
a branch of a political party
owned by shareholders and run for private profit
questions.explanation: Public corporations are created by statute, owned by government and given some independence to provide essential services such as broadcasting or ports. The Nigerian Ports Authority is an example.

whyNot.D: This describes a private company.
whyNot.A: This describes a trade union.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: An important reason for having a second chamber in a legislature is that it
options: allows the executive to make laws alone
replaces the need for a judiciary
makes the passage of laws faster
checks hasty legislation by the other chamber
questions.explanation: In a bicameral legislature each bill is considered by two houses. The second chamber can revise and delay bills passed in haste by the first. In a federation it can also give the component units equal representation, as Nigeria's Senate does.

whyNot.C: Two chambers usually make lawmaking slower, not faster.
whyNot.B: The courts remain necessary to interpret laws whatever the number of chambers.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In a parliamentary system, the cabinet is headed by the
questions.explanation: The Prime Minister, who is usually the leader of the majority party in parliament, chairs the cabinet and directs government policy. The head of state has mainly ceremonial duties.

whyNot.A: The Speaker presides over the lower house of parliament, not the cabinet.
whyNot.C: The Chief Justice heads the judiciary.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In a federation, disputes between the central government and the governments of the component units are usually settled by the
questions.explanation: Because a federal constitution divides powers between levels of government, conflicts over who controls a matter are inevitable. The courts, especially the Supreme Court, interpret the constitution and resolve such disputes. In Nigeria the Supreme Court has original jurisdiction in disputes between the Federation and a state.

whyNot.A: The police enforce laws; they do not interpret the constitution.
whyNot.B: The electoral commission conducts elections.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Which of the following countries has a unitary system of government?
questions.explanation: Ghana has a unitary system: all governmental power belongs to the central government, which may delegate functions to regional and district bodies. Nigeria, the United States and Canada are federations with constitutionally shared powers.

whyNot.D: Nigeria is a federation of 36 states and the FCT.
whyNot.C: The United States is the classic example of a federation.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A major function of an opposition party in a democracy is to
options: approve the annual budget of the government
criticise government policies and offer alternatives
appoint judges of the higher courts
questions.explanation: The opposition checks the government by scrutinising and criticising its policies and presenting alternative programmes to the voters. This keeps the government accountable and offers a replacement at the next election.

whyNot.D: Judicial appointments are made by the executive on recommendation of judicial bodies.
whyNot.A: Elections are conducted by the electoral commission.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A disadvantage of a multi-party system is that it can
options: deny voters any choice between parties
prevent minority views from being represented
questions.explanation: With many parties competing, no single party may win a majority, so several must combine to form a government. Such coalitions may break up when partners disagree, causing instability.

whyNot.C: Lack of choice is a problem of the one-party system.
whyNot.D: A multi-party system gives minority views a better chance of representation.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of electoral malpractice?
options: Stuffing ballot boxes with thumb-printed papers
Displaying the voters' register before polling day
Counting votes openly at the polling unit
questions.explanation: Ballot stuffing adds illegal votes to the box and falsifies the result, so it is electoral malpractice. The other options are normal, lawful parts of a transparent election.

whyNot.D: Open counting at the polling unit makes elections more transparent.
whyNot.C: Displaying the register lets voters check and correct their details; it is good practice.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The main purpose of voter registration is to
options: compile a list of people qualified to vote
count the votes after an election
select candidates for each political party
questions.explanation: Voter registration records the names of eligible citizens in a voters' register. On election day only registered voters may vote, which helps to prevent multiple voting and impersonation.

whyNot.D: Candidates are chosen through party primaries.
whyNot.A: Constituency boundaries are drawn through delimitation, a separate exercise.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The Unity Party of Nigeria (UPN), which contested the 1979 general elections, was led by
questions.explanation: The UPN was formed by Chief Obafemi Awolowo in 1978 and drew much of its support from the old Action Group base in the West. Awolowo was its presidential candidate in 1979 and 1983.

whyNot.A: Shagari led the National Party of Nigeria (NPN).
whyNot.D: Azikiwe led the Nigerian People's Party (NPP).
whyNot.B: Aminu Kano led the People's Redemption Party (PRP).

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The 1979 presidential election in Nigeria was won by the candidate of the
questions.explanation: Alhaji Shehu Shagari of the NPN won the 1979 presidential election and became the first executive President under the Second Republic's presidential constitution.

whyNot.B: The UPN's Obafemi Awolowo came second.
whyNot.A: The NPP's Nnamdi Azikiwe also lost; the NPP later formed an accord with the NPN.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The official in charge of conducting the election at a polling unit on election day is the
questions.explanation: The presiding officer controls voting at a polling unit: checking voters, issuing ballot papers, keeping order and counting the votes at the end. The returning officer collates results and declares the winner for a whole constituency.

whyNot.A: The returning officer declares results for a constituency, not for a single polling unit.
whyNot.D: A party agent watches proceedings on behalf of a party but does not conduct the election.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The document in which a political party sets out the programmes it intends to carry out if elected is its
questions.explanation: A manifesto lists a party's policies and promises, for example on education, health and the economy. Voters use it to compare parties and later to judge whether the party has kept its promises.

whyNot.C: A party's constitution sets out its internal rules and organisation, not its election promises.
whyNot.B: A gazette is an official government publication.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A political party that keeps its membership small and draws it mainly from influential people such as professionals and notables is described as
questions.explanation: Elite or cadre parties rely on a small group of notable and wealthy members rather than mass membership. Mass parties, by contrast, recruit large numbers of ordinary members who pay dues and take part in party activities.

whyNot.D: A mass party seeks a large membership drawn from the general population.
whyNot.A: A coalition is an alliance of parties, not a type of membership.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The electoral system in which one representative is elected from each constituency is known as the
questions.explanation: Under the single-member constituency system each electoral district returns one representative. Nigeria uses it for the Senate, House of Representatives and State Houses of Assembly, each seat going to the candidate with the most votes.

whyNot.A: In the list system parties win several seats according to their vote share.
whyNot.D: A multi-member constituency elects more than one representative.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Indirect rule was difficult to operate in Eastern Nigeria mainly because
options: the British had no officials in the area
the area lacked centralised traditional authorities
the people had no tradition of government
questions.explanation: Indirect rule worked through existing traditional rulers. Most communities in the East were governed by councils of elders and age grades without powerful kings, so the British appointed 'warrant chiefs', who lacked legitimacy and were resented.

whyNot.D: The communities had working systems of government, only decentralised ones.
whyNot.C: Most of the East was not Muslim; the Islamic emirates were in the North, where indirect rule worked best.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In the pre-colonial Hausa-Fulani emirate system, the chief adviser to the Emir, who acted somewhat like a prime minister, was the
questions.explanation: The Waziri was the most senior official in an emirate, advising the Emir and supervising the administration. Other officials had specific duties, for example the Alkali was a judge applying Islamic law and the Madawaki commanded the army.

whyNot.B: The Alkali was a judge in the Sharia courts.
whyNot.A: The Madawaki was the commander of the army.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In the pre-colonial Oyo Empire, the Oyo Mesi, the council of kingmakers that could check the Alaafin, was headed by the
questions.explanation: The Oyo Mesi was a council of seven chiefs headed by the Bashorun. It chose the Alaafin and could ask him to commit suicide if he ruled badly. The Ogboni society in turn checked the power of the Oyo Mesi.

whyNot.B: The Are-Ona-Kakanfo was the field commander of the army.
whyNot.A: The Aremo was the Alaafin's eldest son.
whyNot.D: The Ogboni was a separate secret society that checked the Oyo Mesi, not its head.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The pre-colonial political system of most Igbo communities is described as acephalous because
options: decisions were made only by the oracle
the people were ruled by foreign conquerors
power was held by a hereditary king
there was no single central ruler
questions.explanation: Acephalous means 'without a head'. Most Igbo communities had no king; authority was shared among the council of elders, age grades, title holders and the village assembly, making the system decentralised and democratic.

whyNot.C: A hereditary king would be a centralised system, the opposite of acephalous.
whyNot.B: Pre-colonial Igbo communities governed themselves.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In 1987 the number of states in Nigeria was increased from 19 to 21 by the creation of
questions.explanation: In September 1987 the Babangida government created Akwa Ibom State (from Cross River) and Katsina State (from Kaduna), bringing the total to 21. Nine more states were created in 1991 and six in 1996.

whyNot.D: Kogi and Delta were among the states created in 1991.
whyNot.A: Ekiti and Bayelsa were created in 1996.
whyNot.B: Lagos and Rivers were created in 1967.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Which of the following states was created in 1996?
questions.explanation: In October 1996 the Abacha government created six states: Bayelsa, Ebonyi, Ekiti, Gombe, Nasarawa and Zamfara, bringing the total to 36, the number in the 1999 Constitution.

whyNot.A: Akwa Ibom was created in 1987.
whyNot.C: Kogi was created in 1991.
whyNot.B: Benue was created in 1976.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under the 1999 Constitution, one function of the Council of State is to advise the President on
options: the exercise of the prerogative of mercy
the passing of bills into law
questions.explanation: The Council of State, which includes former Presidents and the state Governors, advises the President on matters such as the prerogative of mercy, national honours, the population census and appointments to bodies such as INEC and the National Judicial Council.

whyNot.C: Bills are passed by the National Assembly.
whyNot.B: Election petitions are heard by tribunals and courts.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of local governments under the Fourth Schedule of the 1999 Constitution?
options: Control of the Nigeria Police Force
Registration of births, deaths and marriages
questions.explanation: The Fourth Schedule lists local government functions, including registration of births, deaths and marriages, collection of rates, and provision of markets, motor parks and cemeteries.

whyNot.A: The police are on the Exclusive Legislative List under federal control.
whyNot.B: Currency is an exclusive federal matter handled through the Central Bank.
whyNot.C: Foreign affairs and treaties are exclusive federal matters.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The body that recommends to the President persons to be appointed as Justices of the Supreme Court and the Court of Appeal is the
questions.explanation: The National Judicial Council, established under section 153 of the 1999 Constitution, recommends judicial appointments and can recommend the removal of judicial officers. This protects the independence of the judiciary. Appointments to the Supreme Court also require Senate confirmation.

whyNot.D: The Council of State is an advisory body on matters such as the prerogative of mercy, not judicial nominations.
whyNot.B: The Federal Civil Service Commission deals with appointments in the federal civil service.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The Western and Eastern Regions of Nigeria attained self-government in
questions.explanation: Following the 1957 constitutional conference in London, the Western and Eastern Regions became self-governing in 1957. The Northern Region attained self-government in 1959, and the whole country became independent in 1960.

whyNot.C: 1959 was when the Northern Region became self-governing.
whyNot.D: 1960 was independence for the whole country.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The foreign policy of a country is best defined as
options: the principles and actions that guide its relations with other states
the rules governing its internal elections
its policy on the movement of people between its states
the way it collects taxes from foreigners
questions.explanation: Foreign policy is the set of goals, principles and strategies a state uses in dealing with other states and international organisations, aimed at protecting its national interest.

whyNot.B: Elections are a domestic matter.
whyNot.C: Movement between a country's own states is internal policy.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The head of a country's embassy in a foreign country that is not a member of the Commonwealth is called
questions.explanation: An ambassador is the highest-ranking diplomat representing a country in another state and heads its embassy. Between Commonwealth countries the equivalent official is called a high commissioner.

whyNot.C: High commissioners are used between Commonwealth members.
whyNot.A: A consul looks after the interests of citizens and trade in a particular city, below the rank of ambassador.
whyNot.B: An attaché is a junior diplomat or a specialist, such as a defence attaché.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In the United Nations General Assembly, each member state has
options: votes in proportion to its population
votes in proportion to its contribution to the UN budget
questions.explanation: All UN members are represented in the General Assembly, and each has one vote regardless of size or wealth. This reflects the principle of the sovereign equality of states.

whyNot.A: Population does not affect voting in the General Assembly.
whyNot.D: The veto exists only in the Security Council, for the five permanent members.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The headquarters of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) is in
questions.explanation: UNESCO, a specialised agency of the UN founded in 1945, has its headquarters in Paris, France. It promotes cooperation in education, science and culture and designates World Heritage Sites.

whyNot.C: Geneva hosts agencies such as the World Health Organization.
whyNot.A: Rome is the headquarters of the Food and Agriculture Organization.
whyNot.D: Nairobi hosts the UN Environment Programme.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The United Nations agency mainly concerned with the welfare and rights of children is
questions.explanation: UNICEF (the United Nations Children's Fund) provides help for children's health, nutrition, education and protection, especially in poor countries and emergencies.

whyNot.A: UNESCO deals with education, science and culture generally.
whyNot.D: The IMF deals with international monetary cooperation.
whyNot.B: The ILO deals with labour standards and workers' rights.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations has its headquarters in
questions.explanation: The FAO is based in Rome, Italy. It leads international efforts to defeat hunger, improve agriculture and promote food security.

whyNot.C: Paris is the headquarters of UNESCO.
whyNot.A: New York is the headquarters of the UN itself.
whyNot.B: Vienna hosts OPEC and some UN offices, but not the FAO.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The ECOWAS Protocol relating to Free Movement of Persons, Residence and Establishment was signed in
questions.explanation: The Protocol on Free Movement was signed in Dakar in May 1979. Its first phase allowed citizens of member states to visit other member states for up to 90 days without a visa.

whyNot.A: 1975 is when the ECOWAS Treaty itself was signed in Lagos.
whyNot.C: 1963 is the year the OAU was founded.
whyNot.D: 1990 is when ECOMOG was first deployed in Liberia.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Which of the following countries does NOT share a land border with Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Nigeria's land neighbours are Benin to the west, Niger to the north, Chad to the north-east and Cameroon to the east. Ghana lies further west, beyond Togo and Benin.

whyNot.A: Benin borders Nigeria to the west.
whyNot.C: Niger borders Nigeria to the north.
whyNot.D: Cameroon borders Nigeria to the east.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The Anglo-Nigerian Defence Pact, signed at independence, was abrogated in 1962 mainly because
options: many Nigerians, including students, saw it as a threat to Nigeria's independence
Nigeria had joined the Warsaw Pact
Britain refused to sell arms to Nigeria
the United Nations declared it illegal
questions.explanation: Critics, led by students and opposition politicians, argued that the pact tied Nigeria to Britain's military interests and conflicted with non-alignment. Under this pressure the two governments agreed to abrogate it in January 1962.

whyNot.D: The UN did not rule on the pact.
whyNot.B: Nigeria never joined the Warsaw Pact; it followed non-alignment.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Which of the following is an instrument for carrying out a country's foreign policy?
questions.explanation: States pursue their foreign policy goals through instruments such as diplomacy (negotiation), economic aid and sanctions, propaganda and, in the last resort, military force. Diplomacy is the most commonly used.

whyNot.C: A census counts a country's population; it is a domestic exercise.
whyNot.A: Delimitation of constituencies is an internal electoral matter.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A situation in which there is no government and no authority to make or enforce laws is described as
questions.explanation: Anarchy means the absence of government. Without any authority to keep order, disputes are settled by force, which is why most thinkers see government as necessary.

whyNot.D: Autocracy is rule by one person with unlimited power, so government exists.
whyNot.B: Oligarchy is rule by a small group.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under socialism, the major means of production are owned and controlled mainly by
options: the state on behalf of the people
questions.explanation: Socialism places the major means of production, such as land, large industries and banks, in public ownership, so that wealth is used for the benefit of society as a whole and inequality is reduced.

whyNot.A: Private ownership for profit is the basis of capitalism.
whyNot.B: Control by traditional rulers belongs to pre-colonial or feudal arrangements.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: An economic system in which both the government and private individuals own and run businesses is known as
questions.explanation: In a mixed economy, the public sector provides some goods and services while private firms provide others. Nigeria is an example: government owns some enterprises while most trade and many industries are private.

whyNot.C: In a command economy the state plans and controls almost all production.
whyNot.D: A subsistence economy produces mainly for the producers' own consumption.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A state that accepts responsibility for providing its citizens with social services such as health care, education and support for the unemployed is called
