questions.explanation: A welfare state uses public funds to protect citizens' wellbeing through social security, free or subsidised health and education, pensions and unemployment benefits. Britain after 1945 is a well-known example.

whyNot.A: A police state uses the police and security services to control citizens and suppress opposition.
whyNot.D: A theocratic state is governed according to religious law.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Government by one person who holds unlimited power and is not accountable to the people is
questions.explanation: In an autocracy, one ruler holds absolute power, makes decisions without consulting the people and cannot be removed by lawful means. Absolute monarchs and dictators are examples.

whyNot.C: In a democracy rulers are accountable to the people through elections.
whyNot.A: Aristocracy is rule by a privileged few.
whyNot.B: Federalism is a way of dividing power between levels of government, not rule by one person.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Section 45 of the 1999 Constitution permits certain fundamental rights to be restricted by law that is reasonably justifiable in a democratic society in the interest of
options: the ruling party winning the next election
defence, public safety, public order, public morality or public health
the personal wishes of the head of state
protecting the private business interests of public officers
questions.explanation: Rights such as private life, freedom of religion, expression, assembly and movement are not absolute. Section 45 allows laws limiting them for defence, public safety, public order, public morality or public health, or to protect the rights and freedoms of others.

whyNot.A: Restrictions to help a party win elections would be an abuse, not a lawful limitation.
whyNot.C: The constitution does not allow rights to depend on the personal wishes of any ruler.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The ancient Greek philosopher who argued in The Republic that the ideal state should be ruled by philosopher-kings was
questions.explanation: In The Republic, Plato argued that only those trained in wisdom and philosophy, the philosopher-kings, were fit to rule, because they alone understood justice and the good of the state.

whyNot.B: Aristotle, Plato's student, wrote The Politics and classified governments by who rules and in whose interest.
whyNot.A: Socrates wrote nothing himself; he is known through Plato's dialogues.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The statement that 'man is by nature a political animal' is associated with
questions.explanation: In his work The Politics, Aristotle argued that human beings naturally live in communities and can only achieve a good life within the political community, the polis.

whyNot.A: Marx focused on class struggle and economics.
whyNot.D: Hobbes saw people in the state of nature as self-interested and in conflict.
whyNot.B: Montesquieu is known for the separation of powers.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In Max Weber's classification, authority that rests on rules and laws, such as that of an elected official, is
questions.explanation: Legal-rational authority belongs to the office, not the person. People obey because the office holder was appointed or elected according to established rules, as in modern bureaucracies and democratic governments.

whyNot.C: Traditional authority rests on custom and long-established practice, such as that of a hereditary chief.
whyNot.A: Charismatic authority rests on the exceptional personal qualities of a leader.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The doctrine of laissez-faire holds that government should
options: share all property equally among citizens
fix the prices of all goods
own and control all major industries
interfere as little as possible in economic activities
questions.explanation: Laissez-faire is French for 'let do' or 'leave alone'. It is the classical liberal and capitalist idea that markets work best when government limits itself to keeping order and enforcing contracts.

whyNot.C: State ownership of major industries is a socialist idea.
whyNot.B: Price control by government is the opposite of laissez-faire.
whyNot.A: Equal sharing of property is a communist ideal.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A constitution can best be defined as
options: the record of all the decisions of the courts
the body of fundamental rules and principles by which a state is governed
a list of all the laws passed by the legislature in a year
the manifesto of the ruling political party
questions.explanation: A constitution sets out how a state is organised: the organs of government, how power is shared and limited, and the rights and duties of citizens. Other laws must conform to it.

whyNot.A: Court decisions may be a source of constitutional law but are not the constitution itself.
whyNot.D: A manifesto is a party's election programme.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The power of the President to pardon a convicted offender or reduce his or her sentence is known as the
questions.explanation: Section 175 of the 1999 Constitution gives the President the prerogative of mercy, to be exercised after consulting the Council of State. State Governors have a similar power under section 212 for state offences.

whyNot.C: The veto is the power to withhold assent from a bill.
whyNot.A: Impeachment is the legislature's power to remove the President.
whyNot.D: Judicial review is the courts' power to strike down unconstitutional laws.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The stage in the passage of a bill at which the legislature debates its general principles is the
questions.explanation: At the first reading the bill is formally introduced without debate. At the second reading its main principles are debated. It then goes to committee for detailed study, followed by the report stage and the third reading.

whyNot.A: The first reading is only a formal introduction of the bill.
whyNot.D: The report stage considers the committee's amendments.
whyNot.B: The third reading is a final review before the vote.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: When all the members of a legislative house sit as a committee to consider a bill clause by clause, it is called
questions.explanation: A committee of the whole house is the entire chamber acting as a committee, with less formal rules, to examine a bill in detail. It is often used for important bills such as the budget.

whyNot.D: A joint committee includes members of both houses of a legislature.
whyNot.A: A conference committee reconciles different versions of a bill passed by the two houses.
whyNot.B: A select committee is a small group of members set up for a particular task.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In the British parliamentary system, the group of opposition members who watch over the work of particular ministers is known as the
questions.explanation: The leader of the opposition appoints a shadow cabinet whose members each follow a government ministry, criticise its policies and present alternatives. They are ready to form a government if the opposition wins.

whyNot.A: A kitchen cabinet is an informal group of close advisers to a head of government.
whyNot.C: An inner cabinet is a small group of senior ministers in the governing party.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The union of Senegal and The Gambia that existed from 1982 to 1989 is an example of
questions.explanation: The Senegambia Confederation linked the two countries in defence and some economic matters while each kept its sovereignty and could withdraw. It was dissolved in 1989.

whyNot.B: Neither country gave up its government to a single central authority.
whyNot.A: In a federation the component units are not sovereign; in Senegambia each member remained sovereign.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A bill passed by the legislature becomes an Act when it
options: is approved by a political party
is debated by a select committee
receives the assent of the executive
questions.explanation: After passing through all stages in the legislature, a bill goes to the head of the executive for assent. Once assent is given, or the constitutional override procedure is used, it becomes an Act and is law.

whyNot.A: Newspaper publication has no legal effect on a bill.
whyNot.B: Party approval has no legal role in lawmaking.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The minimum number of members that must be present before a legislature can validly conduct its business is called
questions.explanation: A quorum prevents a few members from taking decisions on behalf of the whole house. The 1999 Constitution sets the quorum of the Senate and House of Representatives at one-third of all the members.

whyNot.D: A caucus is a meeting or group of members of a party or interest.
whyNot.C: The mace is the symbol of the authority of the legislature.
whyNot.B: A motion is a proposal put before the house for decision.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty in Britain means that
options: the courts can declare Acts of Parliament unconstitutional
Parliament can make or repeal any law and no court can set its Acts aside
Parliament cannot change laws made by earlier Parliaments
the monarch can veto any Act of Parliament
questions.explanation: In Britain, an Act of Parliament is the highest form of law. Parliament can legislate on any matter, no Parliament can bind its successors, and the courts must apply Acts rather than strike them down.

whyNot.A: Judicial review of legislation is a feature of countries with supreme written constitutions, such as Nigeria and the United States.
whyNot.C: This is the opposite of the doctrine: each Parliament can change the laws of earlier Parliaments.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In Nigeria, the administrative head and accounting officer of a federal ministry is the
questions.explanation: The Permanent Secretary is the most senior career civil servant in a ministry. He or she runs its day-to-day administration, advises the minister and is accountable for its funds. The minister is the political head.

whyNot.B: The minister is the political head who makes policy, not the career administrative head.
whyNot.C: The Auditor-General audits public accounts of all ministries; he or she is not part of a ministry's management.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Universal adult suffrage means that
options: all residents, including children, may vote
all adult citizens may vote regardless of sex, wealth or education
questions.explanation: Under universal adult suffrage every citizen who has reached the voting age, 18 in Nigeria, may vote, without qualifications based on sex, property, income, religion or education.

whyNot.B: Education qualifications restrict, rather than universalise, the franchise.
whyNot.A: A tax qualification was used in early colonial elections but is not universal suffrage.
whyNot.C: Children are excluded because suffrage is for adults.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under the 1999 Constitution, the body responsible for dividing Nigeria into federal and state constituencies is the
questions.explanation: INEC delimits constituencies and reviews them periodically so that each contains as nearly equal a number of inhabitants as practicable. Its proposals must be approved by the National Assembly before they take effect.

whyNot.D: The National Population Commission conducts the census, whose figures INEC uses.
whyNot.A: The National Assembly approves INEC's proposals but does not draw the boundaries.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A person appointed by a political party to watch the conduct of voting and counting at a polling unit on its behalf is
questions.explanation: Each party may send polling agents to observe the process, check for irregularities and sign the result sheet. They represent the party, not the electoral commission.

whyNot.D: The presiding officer is an electoral commission official in charge of the polling unit.
whyNot.C: The returning officer declares the result for a constituency.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The party official in the legislature whose duty is to ensure that party members attend and vote according to the party's position is the
questions.explanation: Party whips keep members informed of business, make sure they are present for important votes and encourage them to follow the party line. This maintains party discipline in the legislature.

whyNot.A: The clerk is a non-partisan official who keeps the records of the house.
whyNot.D: The sergeant-at-arms keeps order and security in the chamber.
whyNot.B: The speaker presides over the house and should be impartial.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under section 239 of the 1999 Constitution, a petition challenging the election of the President is first heard by the
questions.explanation: Section 239(1) gives the Court of Appeal original jurisdiction to decide whether a person has been validly elected President or Vice-President. An appeal from its decision then lies to the Supreme Court.

whyNot.B: The Supreme Court hears the final appeal, not the first hearing.
whyNot.A: The Federal High Court does not hear presidential election petitions.
whyNot.C: The Code of Conduct Tribunal tries breaches of the Code of Conduct by public officers.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In 1962 the Federal Government declared a state of emergency in the Western Region following a crisis within the
options: National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons
questions.explanation: A split in the Action Group between supporters of Obafemi Awolowo and Premier S L Akintola led to disorder in the Western House of Assembly in May 1962. The Federal Government declared an emergency and appointed an administrator for the region.

whyNot.D: The NPC controlled the Northern Region and the federal coalition; the crisis was not within it.
whyNot.A: The NCNC was based mainly in the East and was not the party that split in the West.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: An advantage of the two-party system is that it
options: usually produces a stable government with a clear majority
gives every small group its own party in parliament
questions.explanation: With only two major parties, one usually wins a majority and forms the government alone, while the other forms a strong, ready-made alternative. This tends to give stable and accountable government.

whyNot.D: Representing many small groups is a feature of multi-party systems.
whyNot.B: Power regularly alternates between the two parties.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The Nigerian Bar Association and the Nigerian Medical Association are examples of
questions.explanation: Professional associations are pressure groups formed by members of a profession. They protect their members' interests and influence government policy, but they do not put up candidates for elections.

whyNot.A: They do not contest elections to control government.
whyNot.C: Public corporations are government-owned bodies set up by statute.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A form of election in which voters choose, in a single ballot, from lists of candidates presented by each party, with seats shared according to each party's share of the vote, is the
questions.explanation: In the party list system, a form of proportional representation, voters vote for a party's list. If a party wins 30 per cent of the votes it receives about 30 per cent of the seats, filled from the top of its list.

whyNot.A: First-past-the-post awards each seat to the candidate with the most votes in a constituency.
whyNot.B: A second ballot is a run-off between leading candidates.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: One way in which political parties help to recruit leaders for a country is by
options: appointing judges of the Supreme Court
selecting and presenting candidates for elections
questions.explanation: Political recruitment is a key party function. Parties identify, train and nominate people for public office, and the electorate then chooses among the parties' candidates.

whyNot.B: Judges are appointed on the recommendation of judicial bodies, not by parties.
whyNot.C: Voter registration is done by the electoral commission.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The presiding officer of the Senate of Nigeria is the
questions.explanation: Section 50 of the 1999 Constitution provides for a President and Deputy President of the Senate, elected by the senators from among themselves. The Senate President presides over its sittings.

whyNot.A: The Speaker presides over the House of Representatives.
whyNot.D: The Clerk is the chief administrative officer, not a presiding officer.
whyNot.C: Unlike in the United States, Nigeria's Vice-President does not preside over the Senate.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under the 1999 Constitution, a person who has been elected Governor of a state at two previous elections
options: is not qualified to contest for the office again
may contest for a third term with Senate approval
may stay in office until the age of 70
may contest again after waiting four years
questions.explanation: A Governor serves a term of four years (section 180), and section 182(1)(b) disqualifies a person who has been elected to the office at any two previous elections. This limits a Governor to two elected terms.

whyNot.D: The two-election limit applies for life; it is not lifted by waiting.
whyNot.B: The Senate has no power to grant a third term.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The day-to-day administration of the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja, is carried out by
options: the Speaker of the House of Representatives
a Minister appointed by the President
the Chief Judge of the FCT
questions.explanation: The FCT has no Governor or House of Assembly. The President holds its executive powers and, under section 302, may delegate them to a Minister of the Federal Capital Territory. The National Assembly makes its laws.

whyNot.A: The FCT has no elected Governor; only the 36 states do.
whyNot.B: The Speaker is a legislative officer with no executive role in the FCT.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Nigeria became an independent country on
questions.explanation: Nigeria gained independence from Britain on 1 October 1960 under the Independence Constitution, with a parliamentary system and Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa as Prime Minister.

whyNot.C: 1 January 1914 is the date of the amalgamation of the Northern and Southern Protectorates.
whyNot.A: 1 October 1963 is when Nigeria became a republic.
whyNot.D: 29 May 1999 marked the return to civilian rule under the Fourth Republic.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A major criticism of the Richards Constitution of 1946 was that
options: it granted Nigeria full independence too early
Nigerians were not consulted in drawing it up
questions.explanation: Governor Arthur Richards drew up the constitution with little consultation with Nigerians, which nationalists, especially the NCNC, strongly opposed. This led to the wide consultations that preceded the Macpherson Constitution.

whyNot.A: Independence came only in 1960.
whyNot.C: The Richards Constitution created the regions rather than abolishing them.
whyNot.B: The presidential system was introduced in 1979.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In which year did Nigeria return to civilian rule, beginning the Fourth Republic?
questions.explanation: On 29 May 1999 the military handed over power to an elected civilian government under the 1999 Constitution. This began the Fourth Republic, which is still in existence.

whyNot.C: 1979 began the Second Republic.
whyNot.A: 1993 saw the annulled election and a short-lived Interim National Government.
whyNot.B: 1983 saw the end of the Second Republic by a military coup.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The Nigerian Civil War was fought between
questions.explanation: The Civil War began in July 1967, after the Eastern Region declared itself the Republic of Biafra in May 1967, and ended in January 1970 with Biafra's surrender.

whyNot.B: 1966 saw the two coups and the crises that led to the war, which started in 1967.
whyNot.C: The war had ended by January 1970.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under section 150 of the 1999 Constitution, the Chief Law Officer of the Federation is the
options: President of the Court of Appeal
questions.explanation: The Attorney-General of the Federation, who is also the Minister of Justice, is the government's chief legal adviser and can begin, take over or discontinue criminal proceedings in federal matters.

whyNot.A: The Chief Justice heads the judiciary and the Supreme Court.
whyNot.B: The Inspector-General heads the police.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The fundamental human rights of citizens are contained in which chapter of the 1999 Constitution?
questions.explanation: Chapter IV (sections 33 to 46) guarantees fundamental rights such as the rights to life, dignity, personal liberty, fair hearing and freedom of expression. Unlike Chapter II, these rights can be enforced in court.

whyNot.B: Chapter II contains the Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy.
whyNot.D: Chapter VI deals with the Executive.
whyNot.A: Chapter VIII deals with the Federal Capital Territory and general supplementary provisions.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Why was the Supreme Military Council during the military era in Nigeria regarded as combining legislative and executive powers?
options: It was elected by the people every four years
It made decrees and also directed their implementation
It shared power with a civilian parliament
questions.explanation: Military regimes suspended the legislature and parts of the constitution. The Supreme Military Council (later bodies under other names) made laws by decree and, through the head of state and the federal executive, carried them out. This fusion of powers is a major feature of military rule.

whyNot.A: Military councils were not elected.
whyNot.C: Military regimes suspended the parliament, so there was no civilian legislature to share power.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The operations of the United Nations Trusteeship Council were suspended in 1994 because
options: all the territories placed under it had become self-governing or independent
the General Assembly refused to fund it
it was merged with the International Court of Justice
the Security Council abolished the United Nations
questions.explanation: The Trusteeship Council supervised territories placed under UN trusteeship, helping them towards self-government. When Palau, the last trust territory, became independent in 1994, the Council suspended its operations.

whyNot.D: The UN still exists.
whyNot.C: The ICJ is a separate organ and no merger took place.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The regular meeting of the leaders of Commonwealth countries to discuss common issues is known as
options: the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM)
questions.explanation: CHOGM brings together the heads of government of Commonwealth member states, usually every two years, to discuss issues such as democracy, trade and development. Nigeria hosted CHOGM in Abuja in 2003.

whyNot.C: The Security Council is a UN organ.
whyNot.D: The ECOWAS Authority is the meeting of West African heads of state.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Nigeria's first participation in a United Nations peacekeeping operation, starting in 1960, took place in
questions.explanation: Soon after independence Nigeria sent troops and police to the UN operation in the Congo (ONUC), which began in 1960. This started Nigeria's long record of contributing to peacekeeping.

whyNot.C: Nigeria led ECOMOG in Liberia from 1990, an ECOWAS rather than UN operation.
whyNot.A: Nigeria served in Lebanon later, from 1978.
whyNot.D: Nigeria's role in Sierra Leone came in the 1990s.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In the 'concentric circles' approach to Nigeria's foreign policy, the innermost circle is concerned with
options: Nigeria's own security and that of its immediate neighbours
relations with Europe and North America
questions.explanation: The concentric circles idea ranks Nigeria's foreign policy priorities. The innermost circle covers Nigeria's security and its relations with neighbouring states; the next covers West Africa, then Africa, and the outer circle the rest of the world.

whyNot.B: The Commonwealth lies in the outer circles of wider international relations.
whyNot.C: Relations with Europe and North America belong to the outermost circle.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A diplomatic official who mainly looks after the trade interests and the welfare of his or her country's citizens in a particular foreign city is
questions.explanation: Consuls work in consulates, often in commercial cities. They issue visas and passports, help citizens in difficulty and promote trade. Ambassadors and high commissioners handle political relations with the whole state.

whyNot.D: An ambassador represents his or her country to the government of the host state as a whole.
whyNot.C: A secretary-general heads an international organisation such as the UN.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), formed in 1949, is best described as
options: an economic community of African states
a specialised agency of the UN
questions.explanation: NATO is a collective defence alliance of North American and European countries. Its members agree that an armed attack against one of them is an attack against all.

whyNot.B: Economic communities in Africa include ECOWAS.
whyNot.C: Oil-producing countries are grouped in OPEC.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Measures such as trade bans or the freezing of assets imposed on a country to force it to change its policies are called
questions.explanation: Sanctions are penalties applied by states or international organisations to pressure a government. For example, many countries applied economic and sporting sanctions against apartheid South Africa.

whyNot.C: A treaty is a formal agreement between states.
whyNot.A: A protocol is an agreement that adds to or amends a treaty.
whyNot.D: An alliance is an agreement to cooperate, usually for defence.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The ECOWAS Community Court of Justice has its seat in
questions.explanation: The ECOWAS Court of Justice sits in Abuja, Nigeria, which also hosts the ECOWAS Commission. The Court interprets ECOWAS treaties and hears certain human rights cases.

whyNot.B: Accra is the capital of Ghana and does not host the court.
whyNot.D: Lomé hosts the ECOWAS Bank for Investment and Development, not the Court.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The main purpose of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) is to
options: promote international monetary cooperation and help countries with balance of payments problems
questions.explanation: The IMF, created at the Bretton Woods conference in 1944, promotes stable exchange rates and monetary cooperation and lends to member countries facing balance of payments difficulties, often with conditions attached.

whyNot.D: Peacekeeping troops are provided by member states under UN or regional missions.
whyNot.A: Legal disputes between states go to the International Court of Justice.
whyNot.C: Refugees are the concern of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Nigeria became a member of the Commonwealth in
questions.explanation: Nigeria joined the Commonwealth on attaining independence on 1 October 1960. It remained a member after becoming a republic in 1963.

whyNot.B: In 1914 Nigeria was amalgamated as a British colony; it was not an independent member.
whyNot.D: Becoming a republic in 1963 did not end or start Commonwealth membership.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: "On the stove, the kettle hissed and the pot of beans bubbled." The words "hissed" and "bubbled" are examples of
questions.explanation: Onomatopoeia is the use of words whose sounds imitate the sounds they describe. 'Hissed' sounds like steam escaping and 'bubbled' sounds like boiling liquid.

whyNot.C: An oxymoron joins two words of opposite meaning; 'hissed' and 'bubbled' are not opposites.
whyNot.A: Litotes is understatement by denying the opposite, such as 'not bad'; nothing is understated here.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: "At the motor park, Funke lost her purse and her temper." The device in which one verb ("lost") is applied to two words in different senses is
questions.explanation: Zeugma uses one word to govern two others, with a different sense for each. Funke 'lost' her purse (it went missing) and 'lost' her temper (she became angry): one verb, two meanings.

whyNot.A: An oxymoron joins opposites such as 'open secret'; 'purse' and 'temper' are not opposites.
whyNot.C: Chiasmus reverses the order of words in two parallel phrases (A–B, B–A), which this sentence does not do.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: "In the flood, Baba Sule lost his house, his farm, his two cows and his favourite pen." The sudden fall from serious losses to a trivial one at the end of this sentence is
questions.explanation: Anticlimax (also called bathos) arranges ideas so that a serious list ends with something unimportant, producing a comic or ironic effect. A house, a farm and cows are major losses; a pen is trivial.

whyNot.D: Climax arranges ideas in rising order of importance; here the last item is the least important.
whyNot.C: Apostrophe addresses an absent person or a thing directly; no one is addressed.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: A tailor in Aba complained, "Since the new market opened, business has been only sew-sew." The play on "sew-sew" and "so-so" is a
questions.explanation: A pun is a play on words that sound alike (or one word with two meanings) for a humorous effect. 'Sew-sew' sounds like 'so-so' (just average) and also fits the tailor's work of sewing.

whyNot.A: A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as', which is not done here.
whyNot.B: A refrain is a line repeated at regular intervals in a poem or song.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: "Eat to live; do not live to eat." The device in which the words of the first phrase are repeated in reverse order in the second is
questions.explanation: Chiasmus repeats words or ideas in reverse order (A–B, then B–A). 'Eat ... live' becomes 'live ... eat', which makes the advice balanced and memorable.

whyNot.C: Zeugma uses one word to govern two others in different senses, which is not the pattern here.
whyNot.B: A euphemism is a mild expression for something unpleasant; this is not a softened expression.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: A poem of mourning written in memory of a particular person who has died is called
questions.explanation: An elegy is a serious, reflective poem lamenting the death of a person. It often moves from grief to some form of consolation.

whyNot.A: An ode is a formal poem of praise addressed to a person, object or idea, not mainly a lament for the dead.
whyNot.C: A ballad tells a story in short, song-like stanzas.
whyNot.B: An epic is a long narrative poem about heroic deeds.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: The attitude of a writer towards his or her subject or audience, shown through the choice of words, is the
questions.explanation: Tone is the writer's (or speaker's) attitude, for example angry, mocking, tender or bitter, revealed through diction. Mood is the feeling the work creates in the reader.

whyNot.C: Mood is the atmosphere or feeling produced in the reader, not the writer's own attitude.
whyNot.A: Theme is the central idea or message of the work.
whyNot.B: Setting is the time and place of the action.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: In a novel, images of fire appear again and again, each time linked to anger and destruction. Such a recurring image or idea that helps develop the theme of a work is a
questions.explanation: A motif is an image, symbol, idea or phrase that recurs throughout a work and helps to build its theme. The repeated fire images, always tied to anger, form a motif.

whyNot.B: A prologue is an introductory section at the start of a work, not something that recurs.
whyNot.C: A caesura is a pause within a line of verse.
whyNot.A: The plot is the sequence of events, not a repeated image.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: In a poem the speaker says, "I am the River Niger; I have carried canoes for a thousand years." The imagined voice speaking in a poem, which is not the poet's own, is called the
questions.explanation: The persona is the speaker or 'voice' a poet creates. Here the poet speaks as the River Niger, so the river is the persona, not the poet himself.

whyNot.C: The audience is the people the poem is addressed to or read by, not the speaker.
whyNot.B: A chorus is a group in a play that comments on the action.
whyNot.D: An antagonist is the character opposing the hero in a story or play.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: "The more a man boasts, the less he has done." A short, witty and memorable statement of this kind is
questions.explanation: An epigram is a brief, clever saying that expresses an idea neatly, often with a twist. This sentence sums up a truth about boasting in a short, balanced form.

whyNot.A: An epitaph is an inscription on a tomb or a short text in memory of a dead person.
whyNot.C: An epilogue is a closing section or speech at the end of a work.
whyNot.D: An epithet is a descriptive word or phrase attached to a name, such as 'Ade the Strong'.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:
Read the poem below and answer the questions that follow.

Our Mango Tree

Our mango tree stood guard beside the well,
Its arms spread wide to shelter all who came;
Beneath it Grandpa sat with tales to tell,
And every child who passed there knew its name.

But yesterday the men with saws arrived;
They spoke of roads, of progress and of gain.
The tree that sixty rainy seasons thrived
Fell in an hour, and left us to the rain.
questions.stem: In line 2, "Its arms spread wide to shelter all who came", the poet uses
questions.explanation: Personification gives human qualities to non-human things. The tree is given 'arms' that it spreads to shelter people, like a welcoming human being.

whyNot.C: Onomatopoeia uses words that imitate sounds; there are none in this line.
whyNot.B: An oxymoron joins two contradictory words, which the line does not do.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:
Read the poem below and answer the questions that follow.

Our Mango Tree

Our mango tree stood guard beside the well,
Its arms spread wide to shelter all who came;
Beneath it Grandpa sat with tales to tell,
And every child who passed there knew its name.

But yesterday the men with saws arrived;
They spoke of roads, of progress and of gain.
The tree that sixty rainy seasons thrived
Fell in an hour, and left us to the rain.
questions.stem: Each stanza of the poem, made up of four lines, is called a
questions.explanation: A quatrain is a stanza of four lines. Each stanza of 'Our Mango Tree' has four lines rhyming abab (well/tell, came/name).

whyNot.C: A couplet has two lines.
whyNot.A: A sestet has six lines.
whyNot.B: A tercet has three lines.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:
Read the poem below and answer the questions that follow.

Our Mango Tree

Our mango tree stood guard beside the well,
Its arms spread wide to shelter all who came;
Beneath it Grandpa sat with tales to tell,
And every child who passed there knew its name.

But yesterday the men with saws arrived;
They spoke of roads, of progress and of gain.
The tree that sixty rainy seasons thrived
Fell in an hour, and left us to the rain.
questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main concern of the poem?
options: The joy of children playing in a village
The loss of something valued in the community to the demands of development
The danger of drinking water from an open well
The skill of the workmen who build roads
questions.explanation: The first stanza shows the tree as a protector and a centre of community life; the second shows it cut down in the name of 'roads' and 'progress'. The poem is concerned with what is lost when development destroys something valued.

whyNot.A: Children are mentioned only in passing in line 4; the poem is about the tree's destruction.
whyNot.C: The well is only the tree's location; water safety is not discussed.
whyNot.D: The workmen are not admired; the speaker regrets what they do.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:
Read the poem below and answer the questions that follow.

Our Mango Tree

Our mango tree stood guard beside the well,
Its arms spread wide to shelter all who came;
Beneath it Grandpa sat with tales to tell,
And every child who passed there knew its name.

But yesterday the men with saws arrived;
They spoke of roads, of progress and of gain.
The tree that sixty rainy seasons thrived
Fell in an hour, and left us to the rain.
questions.stem: The tone of the second stanza is best described as
questions.explanation: The speaker sadly records how a tree that grew for sixty years was destroyed in an hour and 'left us to the rain'. These details express sorrow and regret for the loss.

whyNot.A: Nothing is celebrated; 'progress' and 'gain' are reported with disappointment.
whyNot.C: The speaker clearly cares about the loss, so the tone is not indifferent.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:
Read the poem below and answer the questions that follow.

Our Mango Tree

Our mango tree stood guard beside the well,
Its arms spread wide to shelter all who came;
Beneath it Grandpa sat with tales to tell,
And every child who passed there knew its name.

But yesterday the men with saws arrived;
They spoke of roads, of progress and of gain.
The tree that sixty rainy seasons thrived
Fell in an hour, and left us to the rain.
questions.stem: In lines 7–8 the poet sets "sixty rainy seasons" against "an hour" mainly in order to
options: prove that the workmen were lazy and slow
stress how quickly something that took very long to grow was destroyed
show that the tree was too old to bear fruit
suggest that the rainy season had been unusually long
questions.explanation: The contrast between sixty years of growth and one hour of cutting emphasises how quick and careless the destruction was compared with the long time the tree took to grow, deepening the sense of loss.

whyNot.C: The poem says nothing about the tree's fruit; age is mentioned to show how long it had served the people.
whyNot.A: Cutting the tree in one hour shows speed, not slowness.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:
Read the poem below and answer the questions that follow.

Exam Hall

The clock on the wall is a judge
with no mercy in its face.
Forty heads bend like rice in the wind.
Someone's pen dies.
Someone's prayer rises.
And I,
who read all night,
cannot remember my own name.
questions.stem: The poet describes the clock as "a judge / with no mercy in its face" mainly to suggest
options: that the clock on the wall is broken
the pressure of time on the candidates
that the invigilator is very strict
questions.explanation: A merciless judge decides people's fate without pity. Calling the clock such a judge shows that time keeps running regardless of the candidates' needs, which creates pressure and fear.

whyNot.D: The lines describe the clock, not the invigilator.
whyNot.A: A clock acting as a judge is clearly working; nothing suggests it has stopped.
whyNot.C: 'No mercy' stresses harshness, not fairness.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:
Read the poem below and answer the questions that follow.

Exam Hall

The clock on the wall is a judge
with no mercy in its face.
Forty heads bend like rice in the wind.
Someone's pen dies.
Someone's prayer rises.
And I,
who read all night,
cannot remember my own name.
questions.stem: "Forty heads bend like rice in the wind" (line 3) contains
questions.explanation: A simile makes a direct comparison using 'like' or 'as'. The bowed heads of the candidates are compared to rice stalks bending in the wind using the word 'like'.

whyNot.A: A metaphor compares without 'like' or 'as'; this line uses 'like'.
whyNot.C: Apostrophe addresses someone or something absent; nobody is addressed here.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:
Read the poem below and answer the questions that follow.

Exam Hall

The clock on the wall is a judge
with no mercy in its face.
Forty heads bend like rice in the wind.
Someone's pen dies.
Someone's prayer rises.
And I,
who read all night,
cannot remember my own name.
questions.stem: "Someone's pen dies" (line 4) most likely means that
options: a pen has been thrown out of the hall
a candidate's pen has run out of ink
a candidate has fainted in the hall
the invigilator has seized a pen
questions.explanation: In an exam setting, a pen 'dying' figuratively means it stops writing, usually because the ink has run out. The line adds to the picture of small crises happening in the hall.

whyNot.C: It is the pen, not the candidate, that 'dies'.
whyNot.D: Nothing in the poem mentions the invigilator taking anything.

cannot remember my own name.
questions.stem: The claim in the last three lines that the speaker "cannot remember my own name" is an example of
questions.explanation: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration for effect. The speaker does not literally forget his or her name; the exaggeration shows how badly panic has wiped out what was studied.

whyNot.C: A euphemism softens something unpleasant; here the speaker exaggerates rather than softens.
whyNot.A: Litotes is understatement, the opposite of exaggeration.

questions.stem: Lines 4 and 5 both begin with the word "Someone's". The repetition of the same word at the beginning of successive lines is called
questions.explanation: Anaphora is the repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive lines or clauses. 'Someone's pen dies. / Someone's prayer rises.' builds a rhythm that pictures many candidates at once.

whyNot.A: Enjambment is the running on of a sentence from one line into the next, not repetition.
whyNot.D: A caesura is a pause in the middle of a line.
whyNot.C: Assonance is the repetition of vowel sounds inside words.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:
Read the drama extract below and answer the questions that follow.

(The village square at Umudike. The drums stop suddenly. The CHIEF ELDER rises.)
CHIEF ELDER: People of Umudike, the oracle has spoken. The new road will not pass through the shrine of our fathers.
OBI: (stepping forward) With respect, Elder, the road will bring a hospital. Must our children die so that a shrine may stand?
CHIEF ELDER: Young man, the goat that butts the wall breaks only its own horns.
(Murmurs among the crowd. OBI's MOTHER pulls him back by the arm.)
MOTHER: (whispering) Obi, you have said enough.
questions.stem: The disagreement between the Chief Elder and Obi is mainly a conflict between
options: the people of Umudike and a neighbouring village
a mother and her disobedient son
respect for tradition and the desire for modern development
questions.explanation: The Chief Elder defends the shrine because 'the oracle has spoken', while Obi argues that the road will bring a hospital. Their clash is between tradition and progress.

whyNot.D: No dispute over family land is mentioned.
whyNot.B: Obi's mother only restrains him; the main conflict is with the Chief Elder.
whyNot.A: No other village is involved.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:

MOTHER: (whispering) Obi, you have said enough.
questions.stem: The Chief Elder's reply, "the goat that butts the wall breaks only its own horns", is
options: a proverb warning Obi that his stubbornness will bring trouble on himself
a prayer asking the gods to forgive the village
a song of praise for Obi's courage
a joke meant to calm the angry crowd
questions.explanation: The Chief Elder answers with a proverb, a traditional saying used to give wisdom indirectly. It means that a person who stubbornly attacks something stronger than himself will only hurt himself, so it warns Obi.

whyNot.B: He is speaking to Obi, not praying to the gods.
whyNot.C: The Elder disapproves of Obi; he does not praise him.

questions.context:

MOTHER: (whispering) Obi, you have said enough.
questions.stem: The stage direction "Murmurs among the crowd" after the Chief Elder's reply mainly shows that
options: the drummers are about to start playing again
the crowd is uneasy at the open challenge to the Elder
the crowd has decided to build the road
questions.explanation: Murmuring is low, uneasy talk. Coming after Obi publicly questions the oracle and the Elder rebukes him, it shows the crowd's discomfort and tension at the exchange.

whyNot.C: No decision is taken; murmurs show reaction, not agreement.
whyNot.A: The direction refers to the crowd talking, not to the drums.

questions.context:

MOTHER: (whispering) Obi, you have said enough.
questions.stem: Obi's mother pulls him back and whispers, "Obi, you have said enough." Her action suggests that she
options: is angry that the drums have stopped
wants Obi to go and fetch a doctor
fears that Obi has offended the elders and wants to protect him
questions.explanation: Pulling him back and speaking quietly shows she is worried about the consequences of challenging the Elder in public. She wants to stop him before he gets into deeper trouble.

whyNot.A: If she agreed with him she would not stop him from speaking.
whyNot.B: Her words are about Obi's speech, not about the drums.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:
Read the drama extract below and answer the questions that follow.

(A barber's shop in Ibadan. LATEEF is shaving a customer, MR OGUNDELE, who is reading a newspaper.)
LATEEF: Oga, they say the price of fuel will go up again.
OGUNDELE: Hmm.
LATEEF: And they say the suya man at the junction has married a third wife.
OGUNDELE: Hmm.
LATEEF: (shaving faster) And they say barbers who talk too much end up cutting their customers.
OGUNDELE: (lowering the paper quickly) Lateef! Face your work!
questions.stem: The extract is most likely taken from
questions.explanation: The everyday setting, the talkative barber, the customer's bored 'Hmm' and the funny warning about cutting customers all create humour, which marks the extract as comedy.

whyNot.D: Nothing serious or disastrous happens; the tone is light.
whyNot.A: An elegy is a poem of mourning, not a dramatic scene.
whyNot.C: An epic is a long heroic narrative poem.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:

OGUNDELE: Hmm.
LATEEF: (shaving faster) And they say barbers who talk too much end up cutting their customers.
OGUNDELE: (lowering the paper quickly) Lateef! Face your work!
questions.stem: Mr Ogundele's repeated reply, "Hmm", shows that he
options: is not interested in Lateef's gossip
strongly agrees with every point Lateef makes
has not heard anything Lateef said
questions.explanation: He keeps reading his newspaper and answers only 'Hmm', a polite but uninterested sound. He does not engage with the news about fuel prices or the suya man until his own safety is mentioned.

whyNot.B: Strong agreement would be shown in words; 'Hmm' is noncommittal.
whyNot.D: He is relaxed and reading until the last line; he speaks sharply when alarmed.
whyNot.C: His quick reaction to the last remark shows he has been hearing Lateef.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:

(A barber's shop in Ibadan. LATEEF is shaving a customer, MR OGUNDELE, who is reading a newspaper.)
LATEEF: Oga, they say the price of fuel will go up again.

LATEEF: And they say the suya man at the junction has married a third wife.
OGUNDELE: Hmm.
LATEEF: (shaving faster) And they say barbers who talk too much end up cutting their customers.
OGUNDELE: (lowering the paper quickly) Lateef! Face your work!
questions.stem: The humour of Lateef's last speech comes mainly from the fact that
options: he refuses to accept payment for the shave
he warns about barbers cutting customers while shaving his own customer faster
he reveals a secret about the suya man's wife
he reads the newspaper aloud to Mr Ogundele
questions.explanation: Lateef holds a razor to Ogundele's face, speeds up, and then mentions barbers who cut their customers. The audience sees the danger at once, and Ogundele's alarmed reaction makes the moment funny.

whyNot.C: The suya man's marriage is mentioned earlier and gets no reaction.
whyNot.A: Payment is never mentioned.
whyNot.D: It is Ogundele who holds the newspaper, not Lateef.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: An introductory speech or scene that comes before the main action of a play, often giving background or setting the mood, is the
questions.explanation: A prologue opens a play and prepares the audience, for example by giving background or introducing the theme, before the main action begins.

whyNot.D: An epilogue comes at the end of a play, after the main action.
whyNot.A: The climax is the point of highest tension in the plot.
whyNot.B: The denouement is the final unravelling of the plot.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: A play that mixes serious and comic elements, in which the main characters face danger but the play ends happily, is a
questions.explanation: A tragicomedy combines features of tragedy (serious events, threat of disaster) with those of comedy, and usually ends happily for the main characters.

whyNot.C: A farce is pure comedy built on absurd situations and physical humour, without serious threat.
whyNot.B: A tragedy ends in disaster for the hero, not happily.
whyNot.A: A melodrama relies on exaggerated emotions and clear-cut heroes and villains.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: In a play, a wealthy chief who is about to win a chieftaincy title is suddenly exposed as a thief and loses everything. This sudden reversal of the hero's fortune is known as
questions.explanation: Peripeteia (Aristotle's term) is a sudden reversal of fortune, usually from good to bad in tragedy. The chief moves from near-triumph to ruin in one turn of events.

whyNot.D: Anagnorisis is the hero's moment of recognition or discovery of the truth, not the reversal itself.
whyNot.B: Hubris is excessive pride that may cause a downfall, not the reversal.
whyNot.C: Exposition is the opening part of a play that gives background information.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:
Read the prose extract below and answer the questions that follow.

The letter from Ibadan lay unopened on the table for three days. Nkechi dusted around it, cooked around it and prayed around it. On the fourth morning her son Uche, home from the farm, tore it open before she could stop him. "Mama," he said slowly, "they have offered me a place to study medicine." Nkechi sat down on the floor, right there in the dust she had just swept, and laughed until she cried.
questions.stem: "Nkechi dusted around it, cooked around it and prayed around it." This sentence mainly shows that Nkechi
options: did not know how to read
had already guessed that the news was bad
was anxious about what the letter might say
was too busy to care about the letter
questions.explanation: She keeps the letter in view while doing everything else but does not open it, and even prays around it. The repeated 'around it' shows that the letter dominates her thoughts and that she is anxious about its contents.

whyNot.A: Nothing suggests she cannot read; she simply avoids opening it.
whyNot.D: Praying around it shows she cares a great deal.
whyNot.B: She is uncertain, not sure the news is bad; she laughs with joy when it turns out good.

questions.subject: literature-in-english

Nkechi sat down on the floor, right there in the dust she had just swept, and laughed until she cried.
questions.stem: Nkechi "laughed until she cried" because she was
questions.explanation: The news is that Uche has been offered a place to study medicine. Laughing until she cried shows joy so great that it overflows into tears.

whyNot.B: The news is good, so she has no reason for disappointment.
whyNot.A: Although Uche opened the letter, her reaction is to the good news, not anger at him.

On the fourth morning her son Uche, home from the farm, tore it open before she could stop him. "Mama," he said slowly, "they have offered me a place to study medicine." Nkechi sat down on the floor, right there in the dust she had just swept, and laughed until she cried.
questions.stem: By keeping the letter unopened for three days before revealing its contents, the writer mainly creates
questions.explanation: Suspense is the reader's uncertainty and eagerness to know what will happen. Delaying the opening of the letter makes the reader wonder what it contains.

whyNot.B: Satire ridicules faults in people or society; nothing is ridiculed here.
whyNot.D: A flashback moves back to earlier events; the extract moves forward in time.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:
Read the prose extract below and answer the questions that follow.

Councillor Bassey loved the people of his ward so much that he built himself a second house, just to be closer to them. He loved their children so much that he named the new primary school after himself, so that they would never forget whom to thank. When the school's roof blew off in the first storm of the rainy season, he made a moving speech about the cruelty of nature.
questions.stem: The tone of the extract is best described as
questions.explanation: The writer pretends to praise the Councillor ('loved the people ... so much') while showing his selfishness. Mocking wrongdoing through irony in this way gives the passage a satirical tone.

whyNot.D: The 'praise' is ironic; the actions described are selfish.
whyNot.C: The writer clearly takes a critical attitude, so the tone is not neutral.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:
Read the prose extract below and answer the questions that follow.

Councillor Bassey loved the people of his ward so much that he built himself a second house, just to be closer to them. He loved their children so much that he named the new primary school after himself, so that they would never forget whom to thank. When the school's roof blew off in the first storm of the rainy season, he made a moving speech about the cruelty of nature.
questions.stem: "Councillor Bassey loved the people of his ward so much that he built himself a second house." The writer's real attitude to the Councillor, shown through this ironic statement, is that he is
options: selfish and uses public office for his own benefit
generous and devoted to his people
poor and in need of a bigger house
questions.explanation: The sentence claims love for the people but describes him building a house for himself. The gap between the stated motive and the action is verbal irony, exposing his selfishness.

whyNot.B: That is what the words seem to say, but the irony shows the opposite.
whyNot.D: Naming the school after himself shows he seeks praise, not humility.
whyNot.C: He is building a second house, so he is not poor.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:
Read the prose extract below and answer the questions that follow.

Councillor Bassey loved the people of his ward so much that he built himself a second house, just to be closer to them. He loved their children so much that he named the new primary school after himself, so that they would never forget whom to thank. When the school's roof blew off in the first storm of the rainy season, he made a moving speech about the cruelty of nature.
questions.stem: The last sentence of the extract suggests that the Councillor
options: plans to resign because of the storm
is a skilled builder who was simply unlucky
blames nature to hide the poor quality of the school he built
has decided to rebuild the school with his own money
questions.explanation: A roof that blows off in the very first storm points to poor construction. Instead of accepting responsibility, he makes a 'moving speech' blaming nature, which the writer presents ironically.

whyNot.B: The irony of the passage shows the writer does not see him as innocent.
whyNot.A: Nothing suggests he will resign; he simply makes a speech.
whyNot.D: No plan to rebuild is mentioned.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: A short story opens with the words: "The bullet had already left the gun when Kunle remembered that the safety catch was off." Beginning a story in the middle of the action in this way is called
questions.explanation: In medias res (Latin for 'into the middle of things') means beginning a narrative in the middle of the action, with earlier events explained later.

whyNot.A: The denouement is the resolution at the end of a story.
whyNot.C: Foreshadowing gives hints of what will happen later; this opening plunges straight into a key event.
whyNot.B: An epilogue is a section at the end of a work.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: A character who is complex, has many sides to his or her personality and may surprise the reader is described as
questions.explanation: E. M. Forster's term 'round character' describes a character drawn in depth, with complex and sometimes contradictory qualities, who can surprise the reader convincingly.

whyNot.D: A flat character is built around a single idea or quality.
whyNot.B: A stock character is a familiar type, such as the wicked stepmother, with little individuality.
whyNot.C: A foil is a character who contrasts with another to highlight that character's qualities.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: A narrative technique that presents the continuous, unbroken flow of a character's thoughts, feelings and memories as they pass through the mind is
questions.explanation: Stream of consciousness tries to record a character's thoughts as they actually occur, often jumping between ideas and memories without normal logical order.

whyNot.B: A dramatic monologue is a poem in which one speaker addresses a silent listener.
whyNot.C: Objective narration reports only what can be seen and heard, never thoughts.
whyNot.D: Epistolary narration tells a story through letters.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: A short story in which animals such as the tortoise and the hare speak and act like humans in order to teach a moral lesson is
questions.explanation: A fable is a short tale, usually with animal characters given human qualities, that ends with a moral lesson.

whyNot.A: A biography is the true account of a real person's life.
whyNot.C: An elegy is a poem of mourning.
whyNot.B: A novella is a work of prose fiction longer than a short story, not specifically a moral animal tale.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: Arrow of God, the novel about Ezeulu, the chief priest of Ulu, was written by
questions.explanation: Arrow of God (1964) is Chinua Achebe's third novel. Its hero, Ezeulu, is the chief priest of the god Ulu, and the novel explores his clash with his people and the British colonial administration.

whyNot.B: Wole Soyinka is mainly known as a playwright; his novels include The Interpreters.
whyNot.A: Elechi Amadi wrote The Concubine.
whyNot.D: Cyprian Ekwensi wrote People of the City and Jagua Nana.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: Death and the King's Horseman, a play about Elesin Oba, the king's horseman of Oyo, was written by
questions.explanation: Death and the King's Horseman (1975) is by Wole Soyinka. It is based on a real event in colonial Oyo, when a British officer interfered with the horseman's ritual duty to follow the dead king.

whyNot.D: Ola Rotimi wrote The Gods Are Not to Blame and Kurunmi.
whyNot.B: J. P. Clark wrote Song of a Goat.
whyNot.C: Femi Osofisan wrote Once Upon Four Robbers.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: Ayi Kwei Armah, author of The Beautyful Ones Are Not Yet Born, a novel about corruption after independence, is from
questions.explanation: Ayi Kwei Armah is a Ghanaian novelist. The Beautyful Ones Are Not Yet Born (1968) is set in Ghana and attacks the corruption of the post-independence period.

whyNot.D: The well-known Kenyan novelist is Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o.
whyNot.B: Senegalese writers include Mariama Bâ and Léopold Sédar Senghor.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: Alan Paton's novel Cry, the Beloved Country (1948), about the pastor Stephen Kumalo searching for his son, is set mainly in
questions.explanation: Cry, the Beloved Country is set in South Africa. Kumalo travels from his rural village to Johannesburg, and the novel deals with racial injustice there.

whyNot.A: The novel has no Nigerian setting.
whyNot.D: Kenyan settings are found in Ngũgĩ's novels, not Paton's.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: The Joys of Motherhood (1979), whose heroine Nnu Ego gives her life to her children, was written by
questions.explanation: The Joys of Motherhood is a novel by Buchi Emecheta. The title is ironic: Nnu Ego sacrifices everything for her children and dies alone.

whyNot.B: Flora Nwapa wrote Efuru.
whyNot.A: Adichie wrote Purple Hibiscus and Half of a Yellow Sun.
whyNot.D: Zulu Sofola was a playwright, author of The Wedlock of the Gods.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: In Yoruba oral literature, oriki is best described as
options: a song of mourning sung only at burials
a folktale about the tricks of the tortoise
praise poetry that celebrates the qualities and achievements of a person or lineage
a hunters' chant performed at hunting festivals
questions.explanation: Oriki are Yoruba praise poems or praise names. They recall and celebrate the qualities, deeds and ancestry of a person, family, town or deity.

whyNot.D: The Yoruba hunters' chant is ijala.
whyNot.A: A song of mourning is a dirge.
whyNot.B: Tortoise stories are folktales, a prose form, not praise poetry.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: In 1991, Ben Okri's novel The Famished Road, narrated by the spirit-child Azaro, won the
questions.explanation: The Famished Road won the Booker Prize in 1991, one of the best-known literary prizes for fiction in English.

whyNot.D: The Nobel Prize is given for a writer's whole body of work, and Okri has not won it.
whyNot.B: The Caine Prize, first awarded in 2000, is for African short stories, not novels.
whyNot.A: That prize is for poetry, and The Famished Road is a novel.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: In his book Decolonising the Mind (1986), the Kenyan writer Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o announced that he would
options: stop writing novels and write only plays
write only in French for a wider audience
write his creative works in Gikuyu instead of English
move to Nigeria to teach literature
questions.explanation: In Decolonising the Mind, Ngũgĩ argued that African writers should write in African languages, and he bade farewell to English as the language of his creative writing, choosing Gikuyu instead.

whyNot.A: He went on writing novels, such as Matigari, in Gikuyu.
whyNot.B: Kenya is an English-speaking country; Ngũgĩ argued for African languages, not French.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: Camara Laye, whose autobiographical novel The African Child (L'Enfant noir) describes his childhood, was from
questions.explanation: Camara Laye was a Guinean writer. The African Child (1953), first written in French as L'Enfant noir, recalls his childhood in Kouroussa, Guinea.

whyNot.C: The book was written in French; Ghana is English-speaking.
whyNot.D: The well-known Ugandan writer is Okot p'Bitek.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: Wole Soyinka's poem "Telephone Conversation", in which an African man phones a landlady about renting a room, is mainly about
questions.explanation: In 'Telephone Conversation' the landlady is more interested in how dark the caller's skin is than in him as a tenant. Soyinka uses irony and humour to expose racial prejudice.

whyNot.A: The poem is about a phone call over a room, not war.
whyNot.D: No government or official is involved.
whyNot.B: Marriage is not a subject of the poem.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: "Big Bola bought blue buckets at Bodija market." The repetition of the "b" sound at the start of several words is
questions.explanation: Alliteration is the repetition of the same consonant sound at the beginning of nearby words. Big, Bola, bought, blue, buckets and Bodija all begin with 'b'.

whyNot.B: Assonance is the repetition of vowel sounds, not initial consonants.
whyNot.D: Onomatopoeia uses words that imitate sounds.
whyNot.C: Rhyme is the matching of sounds at the ends of words.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: "The more he gave away, the richer he became." A statement like this, which seems to contradict itself but contains a deeper truth, is
questions.explanation: A paradox appears self-contradictory but reveals a truth. Giving away should make one poorer, yet the man becomes 'richer', for example in friendship, respect or happiness.

whyNot.C: A pun plays on words with similar sounds or double meanings.
whyNot.A: A euphemism softens something unpleasant.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: A serious and dignified lyric poem that addresses and praises a person, object or idea, such as "To the River Benue", is
questions.explanation: An ode is a formal, elevated lyric poem that addresses and celebrates its subject, often a person, natural object or abstract idea.

whyNot.B: A ballad tells a story in simple song-like stanzas.
whyNot.D: A limerick is a short, humorous five-line poem.
whyNot.A: An epic is a long narrative poem of heroic deeds.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: A narrative poem in short stanzas, often with a refrain, that tells a story in simple language and was originally meant to be sung is
questions.explanation: A ballad tells a story (it is narrative), uses simple language and short stanzas, often has a refrain, and comes from a tradition of songs passed on orally.

whyNot.D: A sonnet is a 14-line lyric poem, not a sung story.
whyNot.B: An ode praises its subject rather than telling a story.
whyNot.C: An epigram is a short witty statement.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: A long narrative poem in an elevated style about the heroic deeds of a great warrior or nation is
questions.explanation: An epic is a long narrative poem celebrating the deeds of a hero of great importance to a people, often involving supernatural forces and told in a grand style.

whyNot.A: A lyric is a short poem expressing personal feeling.
whyNot.D: An elegy mourns the dead.
whyNot.B: A sonnet has only 14 lines.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: A writer's choice and use of words, for example formal or slang, simple or difficult, is called
questions.explanation: Diction means a writer's selection of words. It shapes the tone and style of a work, for example by being formal, colloquial, plain or ornate.

whyNot.B: Rhythm is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables.
whyNot.A: Plot is the sequence of events.
whyNot.D: Setting is time and place.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: In a poem about the end of a war, a white dove lands on a broken gun. The white dove stands for peace. An object used to represent an idea in this way is a
questions.explanation: A symbol is an object, person or action that represents a larger idea. The white dove is a widely recognised symbol of peace.

whyNot.B: A simile is a comparison using 'like' or 'as'.
whyNot.D: A refrain is a repeated line in a poem.
whyNot.C: Rhyme is the matching of end sounds.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: "Ifeoma was a good student, a fine prefect, a great leader and finally a national hero." The arrangement of ideas in rising order of importance is
questions.explanation: Climax (as a figure of speech) arranges words or ideas so that each is stronger or more important than the last, building up to the most important: from 'good student' to 'national hero'.

whyNot.D: Anticlimax ends with something less important; here the last item is the greatest.
whyNot.B: Zeugma uses one word in two senses.
whyNot.C: Litotes is understatement by denying the opposite.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: "Musa spent a sleepless night before his interview." It is Musa, not the night, who could not sleep. Attaching a description to the wrong noun in this way is called
questions.explanation: A transferred epithet moves an adjective from the person or thing it really describes to another noun close to it. 'Sleepless' really describes Musa but is attached to 'night'.

whyNot.A: An oxymoron joins two words with opposite meanings, such as 'sweet sorrow'.
whyNot.D: A pun is a play on words with two meanings or similar sounds.
whyNot.C: Metonymy names something by a thing closely associated with it.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: "The new governor promised to be our Moses and lead us out of poverty." The reference to the Bible story of Moses is an example of
questions.explanation: An allusion is a brief reference to a well-known person, event or text from history, religion or literature. Moses, who led the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt, is alluded to here.

whyNot.D: An oxymoron joins contradictory words; none appear here.
whyNot.B: Litotes is deliberate understatement.
whyNot.C: Onomatopoeia uses words that imitate sounds.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:
Read the poem below and answer the questions that follow.

To My Mother

You walked ten miles to market, rain or sun,
With yams upon your head and me behind;
You never rested till the day was done,
Yet always found a word that was gentle and kind.
Now I have shoes, a car, a city flat;
You sleep for ever under the cashew tree.
I'd trade them all, the car, the shoes, the flat,
To walk to market once more, you and me.
questions.stem: Line 6, "You sleep for ever under the cashew tree", is a gentle way of saying that the mother
options: likes to rest in the shade
questions.explanation: To 'sleep for ever' under a tree is a euphemism for being dead and buried there. The poet avoids the harsh word 'dead'.

whyNot.D: Sleeping 'for ever' shows this is not ordinary rest.
whyNot.B: Nothing suggests she moved; she lies under a tree.
whyNot.A: Illness is not mentioned; 'for ever' points to death.

whyNot.C: A limerick is a humorous five-line poem.

questions.stem: The contrast between lines 1–4 and lines 5–8 mainly brings out the theme that
options: children should not walk to market
material comfort cannot replace the love of a lost parent
hard work always leads to wealth
city life is better than village life
questions.explanation: The first half shows a poor life rich in the mother's love; the second shows wealth (shoes, car, flat) without her. The speaker would trade everything for one more walk, showing that possessions cannot replace her.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:
Read the poem below and answer the questions that follow.

Generator

Every evening at seven
the light goes, as always,
and the generators begin their argument:
the big one next door shouts,
the small one across the road stammers,
ours just coughs and clears its throat
like a shy schoolboy
called to answer in class.
questions.stem: In line 3, "the generators begin their argument", the poet uses
questions.explanation: Personification gives human actions to non-human things. Generators cannot argue; the poet presents their combined noise as a human quarrel.

whyNot.B: There is no repetition of initial consonant sounds.
whyNot.D: Litotes is understatement by denying the opposite.

options: is small and struggles weakly to start
is the loudest on the street
questions.explanation: A shy schoolboy hesitates, coughs and speaks softly. The simile shows that the family's generator splutters and makes only a weak, hesitant noise compared with the others.

whyNot.C: The big generator next door 'shouts'; theirs only 'coughs'.
whyNot.B: A coughing, hesitant machine is not presented as powerful.

the order in which the generators were bought

the distance of each house from the road

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:
Read the drama extract below and answer the questions that follow.

(A hospital corridor at midnight. DR ADEBAYO paces up and down. NURSE HALIMA enters.)
HALIMA: Doctor, the generator is out of diesel, and the boy in Ward 3 is getting worse.
DR ADEBAYO: Then we will work with torches. Find every torch in this building.
HALIMA: And if the batteries run down?
DR ADEBAYO: Then we will work by the light of our phones. That boy is not going to die tonight because of diesel.
(HALIMA hesitates, then hurries out. DR ADEBAYO looks up at the dark ceiling.)
DR ADEBAYO: (quietly) God, if You are awake, now would be a good time.
questions.stem: Dr Adebayo's replies to Nurse Halima show him to be
questions.explanation: Faced with no diesel, he immediately thinks of torches, then phones, and insists the boy will not die. This shows determination and the ability to find solutions.

whyNot.A: He is working hard at midnight to save a patient.
whyNot.D: He is fighting to save the boy's life.
whyNot.B: He gives clear, quick orders.

whyNot.A: He asks for help rather than praising himself.

(The parlour of a small flat in Enugu. RISI comes in from the front door.)
MAMA RISI: (calling from the kitchen) Risi! Who was that at the door?
RISI: Nobody, Mama. Just a man selling brooms.
(She hides a white envelope behind her back. Her brother DAPO, sitting in the corner, sees it.)
DAPO: (aside) A man selling brooms, with a white envelope?
questions.stem: Risi's reply to her mother, "Nobody, Mama. Just a man selling brooms", shows that Risi
options: is too tired to answer properly
is hiding something from her mother
does not know who came to the door
wants her mother to buy a broom
questions.explanation: Immediately after this reply she hides a white envelope behind her back. This shows that her answer is a cover story to keep something secret.

whyNot.A: She answers quickly with a ready excuse; tiredness is not shown.
whyNot.D: She says nothing about buying.
whyNot.C: She clearly received something from whoever came.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.context:
Read the prose extract below and answer the questions that follow.

My uncle came back from Lagos with a shining car and a bag full of gifts. Everybody in the village said he had become a big man. He gave Papa an envelope, gave Mama a wrapper and gave me a ball that bounced higher than the church roof. On the third night, two policemen came for him. Mama said they were his friends from Lagos, and I believed her, because why else would they hold his hands so tightly?
questions.stem: The narrator believes the policemen are the uncle's friends, but the reader realises that he is being arrested. This gap between the narrator's understanding and the reader's is an example of
options: irony created by a naive narrator
questions.explanation: The child narrator is naive and takes Mama's explanation at face value. Readers understand that holding his hands 'so tightly' means arrest. The difference between what the narrator says and what the reader knows creates irony.

whyNot.B: The narrator is a child in the story ('I'), not an all-knowing outsider.
whyNot.A: The events are told in a simple sequence, with no flashback inside another.
whyNot.D: The narration is orderly, not a free flow of thoughts.

questions.stem: "a ball that bounced higher than the church roof" is an example of
questions.explanation: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration. A ball could hardly bounce higher than a church roof; the exaggeration shows the child's excitement at the gift.

whyNot.A: Litotes is understatement, the opposite of exaggeration.
whyNot.C: A euphemism softens something unpleasant; here a pleasant thing is exaggerated.

questions.stem: The atmosphere created in the extract is best described as
questions.explanation: Morning mist, an 'old shawl', silent abandoned mines, forbidden green ponds and a grieving father create a still, sad atmosphere.

whyNot.A: The mines are silent and abandoned; nothing is busy.
whyNot.B: Nothing violent or noisy happens.
whyNot.D: A father mourning his drowned son is not comic.

whyNot.C: A narrator is the voice telling the story, not a type of character development.

questions.explanation: In third-person limited narration the narrator stands outside the story but sees events through one character, sharing only that character's thoughts and feelings.

whyNot.D: First-person narration uses 'I' and the narrator is a character.
whyNot.B: Second-person narration addresses the reader as 'you'.

questions.explanation: In an autobiography the writer tells the story of his or her own life ('auto' means self). A biography is written about someone else.

whyNot.B: A fable is a short moral tale, often with animals.
whyNot.D: A novella is a short novel, a work of fiction.

whyNot.D: A legend is a traditional story about a hero, believed to have some historical basis.
whyNot.B: A myth explains origins or natural events, usually through gods or supernatural beings.
whyNot.C: Satire ridicules folly or vice in society.

questions.subject: literature-in-english

questions.explanation: No Longer at Ease (1960) continues the story of Okonkwo's family. Obi returns from England, works in the civil service in Lagos, and is eventually tried for taking a bribe.

whyNot.B: A Man of the People is narrated by Odili and centres on the politician Chief Nanga.
whyNot.C: Anthills of the Savannah is set in the fictional state of Kangan.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: The Concubine (1966), about the beautiful Ihuoma whose husbands and suitors die mysteriously, was written by
questions.explanation: The Concubine is Elechi Amadi's first novel. It is set in a traditional Ikwerre village, and Ihuoma's misfortunes are explained by her being the wife of a sea-king in the spirit world.

whyNot.A: Flora Nwapa wrote Efuru.
whyNot.B: Buchi Emecheta wrote The Joys of Motherhood.
whyNot.C: Cyprian Ekwensi wrote Jagua Nana.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: The historical plays Kurunmi and Ovonramwen Nogbaisi were written by
questions.explanation: Ola Rotimi wrote both plays. Kurunmi is about the Ijaye war in nineteenth-century Yorubaland; Ovonramwen Nogbaisi is about the Oba of Benin at the time of the British expedition of 1897.
