whyNot.B: Soyinka's plays include The Lion and the Jewel and Death and the King's Horseman.
whyNot.C: J. P. Clark wrote Song of a Goat.
whyNot.A: Zulu Sofola wrote The Wedlock of the Gods.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: Once Upon Four Robbers, a play that examines armed robbery and public executions in Nigeria, was written by
questions.explanation: Once Upon Four Robbers is by Femi Osofisan. It uses a storyteller, songs and a magic charm to question society's response to robbery and the inequality that breeds it.

whyNot.D: Ola Rotimi's plays include The Gods Are Not to Blame.
whyNot.A: Soyinka's plays include The Trials of Brother Jero.
whyNot.C: Zulu Sofola wrote The Wedlock of the Gods.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: The Yoruba novel Ògbójú Ọdẹ nínú Igbó Irúnmalẹ̀, translated into English by Wole Soyinka as The Forest of a Thousand Daemons, was written by
questions.explanation: D. O. Fagunwa wrote the novel in Yoruba in 1938. Wole Soyinka translated it into English as The Forest of a Thousand Daemons (1968).

whyNot.A: Amos Tutuola wrote in English; his best-known book is The Palm-Wine Drinkard.
whyNot.B: Ola Rotimi was a playwright.
whyNot.C: Femi Osofisan is a playwright born long after the novel was written.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: Gabriel Okara's poem "Piano and Drums" is mainly about
options: the joy of a wedding celebration
the horrors of the slave trade
the speaker's confusion between African tradition and Western culture
questions.explanation: In 'Piano and Drums' the drums stand for the simple, traditional African world and the piano for complex Western culture. The speaker is left torn and 'lost' between the two.

whyNot.A: No wedding is described.
whyNot.B: The slave trade is not its subject.
whyNot.C: The instruments are symbols, not real musicians quarrelling.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: Ferdinand Oyono, whose novel Houseboy is written as the diary of a servant named Toundi, was from
questions.explanation: Ferdinand Oyono was a Cameroonian novelist and diplomat. Houseboy (Une vie de boy, 1956) exposes the cruelty and hypocrisy of French colonial rule in Cameroon.

whyNot.A: Houseboy was written in French, as Oyono was from French-speaking Cameroon.
whyNot.D: The famous Kenyan novelist is Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: Nervous Conditions (1988), a novel about a girl named Tambu seeking an education, was written by Tsitsi Dangarembga of
questions.explanation: Tsitsi Dangarembga is a Zimbabwean writer. Nervous Conditions is set in colonial Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe) and follows Tambu's struggle for education.

whyNot.D: Ghanaian women writers include Ama Ata Aidoo.
whyNot.A: The Senegalese woman writer often studied is Mariama Bâ.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: Heinemann's African Writers Series, launched in 1962 with Things Fall Apart as its first title, had which writer as its first general editor?
questions.explanation: Chinua Achebe was the founding editor of Heinemann's African Writers Series and helped bring many African writers to international readers.

whyNot.A: Soyinka was not the series editor.
whyNot.D: Ngũgĩ was published in the series (Weep Not, Child) but was not its editor.

questions.subject: literature-in-english
questions.stem: In African oral literature, a song of lament performed at a funeral is called a
questions.explanation: A dirge is a song or chant of mourning for the dead. In many African communities dirges are performed at burials to express grief and honour the dead.

whyNot.C: A lullaby is sung to put a child to sleep.
whyNot.A: A work song accompanies labour such as farming or rowing.
whyNot.B: A praise song celebrates a living person's qualities.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A straight road measures 12 cm on a map of scale 1:25,000. What is the length of the road on the ground?
questions.explanation: 1:25,000 means 1 cm on the map stands for 25,000 cm on the ground. 12 × 25,000 = 300,000 cm. There are 100,000 cm in 1 km, so 300,000 cm = 3 km.

whyNot.B: 30 km comes from dividing by 10,000 instead of 100,000 when changing centimetres to kilometres.
whyNot.C: 12 km treats every centimetre on the map as 1 km, which would be a scale of 1:100,000.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A map carries the statement scale '2 cm represents 1 km'. What is this scale written as a representative fraction (R.F.)?
questions.explanation: 1 km = 100,000 cm. If 2 cm stands for 100,000 cm, then 1 cm stands for 100,000 ÷ 2 = 50,000 cm. The R.F. is therefore 1:50,000.

whyNot.D: 1:100,000 would mean 1 cm (not 2 cm) represents 1 km.
whyNot.B: 1:200,000 multiplies by 2 instead of dividing by 2.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Two schools are 4.5 km apart on the ground. How far apart will they be on a map of scale 1:50,000?
questions.explanation: Change the ground distance to centimetres: 4.5 km = 4.5 × 100,000 = 450,000 cm. On a 1:50,000 map, divide by 50,000: 450,000 ÷ 50,000 = 9 cm.

whyNot.D: 4.5 cm treats the map as 1 cm to 1 km, which is 1:100,000, not 1:50,000.
whyNot.A: 90 cm uses 1,000,000 cm in a kilometre instead of 100,000 cm.

questions.subject: geography
questions.context: On a map of scale 1:50,000, a hilltop R has a spot height of 600 m. A bridge S, which is 450 m above sea level, is 6 cm from R on the map.
questions.stem: What is the average gradient from R to S?
questions.explanation: Vertical interval (VI) = 600 − 450 = 150 m. Horizontal equivalent (HE) = 6 × 50,000 = 300,000 cm = 3,000 m. Gradient = VI ÷ HE = 150 ÷ 3,000 = 1/20, which is written 1 in 20.

whyNot.A: 1 in 2,000 divides 300,000 cm by 150 m without first putting both distances in the same unit.
whyNot.D: 1 in 4 compares the height of R (600 m) with the vertical interval; it does not use the horizontal distance at all.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The bearing of village X from village Y is 300°. What is the bearing of Y from X?
questions.explanation: A back bearing differs from the forward bearing by 180°. Since 300° is more than 180°, subtract: 300° − 180° = 120°.

whyNot.C: 060° is 360° − 300°, which mirrors the line across north instead of reversing its direction.
whyNot.A: 240° has no rule behind it; reversing a direction always changes the bearing by exactly 180°.

questions.subject: geography
questions.context: On a map, a set of closed, roughly circular contour lines lie one inside another. Their values rise from 300 m on the outermost ring to 500 m on the innermost ring, and the rings are evenly spaced on all sides.
questions.stem: Which relief feature do these contours show?
questions.explanation: Closed contours whose values increase towards the centre show land rising on every side to a top. Because the spacing is even all round, the slopes are equal, giving a conical hill.

whyNot.A: In a depression the values decrease towards the centre, not increase.
whyNot.C: A plateau has a broad, flat top, so the middle would have a wide space with no contours.
whyNot.D: An escarpment has closely packed contours on one side and widely spaced ones on the other.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: On which type of slope can a person standing at the top usually see a person standing at the foot?
options: A slope with a knoll halfway down
A slope with a ridge across it
questions.explanation: A concave slope is steep at the top and gentle at the bottom, curving inwards. Nothing rises between the top and the foot, so the two points are intervisible.

whyNot.D: A convex slope bulges outwards, so the bulge hides the foot from a person at the top.
whyNot.A: A knoll is a small hill; one halfway down would block the line of sight.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A rectangular forest reserve measures 5 cm by 2 cm on a map of scale 1:20,000. What is its actual area?
questions.explanation: On a 1:20,000 map, 1 cm = 20,000 cm = 0.2 km. Length = 5 × 0.2 = 1 km; width = 2 × 0.2 = 0.4 km. Area = 1 × 0.4 = 0.4 km². Always change each side to kilometres before multiplying.

whyNot.A: 4 km² puts the decimal point in the wrong place; each side is under 1 km, so the area must be less than 1 km².
whyNot.D: 10 km² multiplies 5 × 2 and treats each centimetre as 1 km.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A cross-section is drawn from a map of scale 1:50,000, using a vertical scale of 1 cm to 100 m. What is the vertical exaggeration?
questions.explanation: Write the vertical scale as an R.F.: 100 m = 10,000 cm, so it is 1:10,000. Vertical exaggeration = horizontal scale denominator ÷ vertical scale denominator = 50,000 ÷ 10,000 = 5 times.

whyNot.C: 500 divides 50,000 by 100 without changing 100 m to 10,000 cm.
whyNot.D: 2 times has no basis; the two scales must both be written in centimetres and compared.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which method of showing relief uses short lines drawn in the direction of the steepest slope, drawn thicker and closer together where the slope is steep?
questions.explanation: Hachures are short lines drawn down the slope. Where the land is steep they are thick and close together; on gentle slopes they are thin and far apart. They show steepness but not exact heights.

whyNot.C: Layer tinting uses different colours for bands of height, not lines.
whyNot.A: Spot heights are dots with numbers giving the height of single points.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Town P is on longitude 75°W. What is the local time at P when it is 12.00 noon at Greenwich (0°)?
questions.explanation: The earth turns 15° every hour. 75° ÷ 15° = 5 hours. Places west of Greenwich are behind it, so subtract: 12.00 noon − 5 hours = 7.00 a.m.

whyNot.A: 5.00 p.m. adds 5 hours, which is the rule for places east of Greenwich.
whyNot.C: 5.00 a.m. subtracts 7 hours; the difference is only 75 ÷ 15 = 5 hours.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The local times of two places differ by 3 hours 20 minutes. What is the difference between their longitudes?
questions.explanation: The earth turns 1° in 4 minutes (360° in 1,440 minutes). 3 hours 20 minutes = 200 minutes. 200 ÷ 4 = 50°.

whyNot.C: 200° assumes 1 minute for each degree; it actually takes 4 minutes to turn 1°.
whyNot.B: 45° converts only the 3 hours (3 × 15°) and forgets the 20 minutes, which add another 5°.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which rock forms when lava cools quickly on the earth's surface, giving it very small crystals?
questions.explanation: Basalt is an extrusive igneous rock. Lava pours out on the surface and cools fast, so its crystals have little time to grow and are very small.

whyNot.C: Granite is igneous too, but it cools slowly deep underground and has large crystals.
whyNot.A: Sandstone is a sedimentary rock made of cemented sand grains.
whyNot.B: Marble is a metamorphic rock formed from limestone.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: In hot deserts, the outer layers of exposed rock peel off in thin sheets like the skin of an onion. Which process is mainly responsible?
options: Abrasion by sand carried in the wind
Solution of the rock by rainwater
Plant roots growing into rock joints
Repeated heating by day and cooling by night
questions.explanation: This is exfoliation, a form of mechanical weathering. The rock surface expands in the hot day and contracts in the cold night. Repeated many times, this stress makes the outer layers break away in sheets.

whyNot.B: Solution is chemical weathering that needs plenty of water, which deserts lack.
whyNot.A: Wind abrasion wears rock by blasting, producing features like rock pedestals, not peeling sheets.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A long, narrow ridge of sand or shingle joined to the land at one end and stretching out into the sea at the other is called a
questions.explanation: A spit forms where longshore drift carries sand along the coast and keeps depositing it beyond a bend in the coastline. One end stays attached to land; the other end lies free in the sea.

whyNot.B: A tombolo is a ridge of sand that joins an island to the mainland, so both ends are attached.
whyNot.D: A stack is a pillar of rock left standing in the sea by erosion, not a deposit of sand.
whyNot.C: A bar stretches across a bay, joining land at both ends.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The heavy afternoon thunderstorms common in equatorial regions are mainly which type of rainfall?
questions.explanation: Strong heating of the ground in the morning warms the air above it. The warm, moist air rises, cools, condenses into tall cumulonimbus clouds and falls as heavy rain with thunder in the afternoon. This is convectional rainfall.

whyNot.D: Relief rainfall needs moist air forced to rise over high land.
whyNot.C: Frontal rainfall happens where warm and cold air masses meet, mainly in temperate latitudes.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which instrument is used in a weather station to measure atmospheric pressure?
questions.explanation: A barometer measures the pressure (weight) of the air. Pressure readings are used to draw isobars and forecast weather changes.

whyNot.C: A hygrometer measures humidity.
whyNot.A: An anemometer measures wind speed.
whyNot.B: A wind vane shows wind direction.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The temperature at the top of a mountain 2,000 m high is 10 °C. If temperature falls with height at 6.5 °C per 1,000 m, what is the temperature at sea level at the foot of the mountain?
questions.explanation: Going down 2,000 m, the temperature rises by 6.5 × 2 = 13 °C. Temperature at sea level = 10 + 13 = 23 °C.

whyNot.B: −3 °C subtracts the 13 °C; the air gets warmer, not colder, as you go down.
whyNot.A: 16.5 °C adds the rate for only 1,000 m instead of 2,000 m.
whyNot.D: 13 °C is the change in temperature, not the temperature at sea level.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The earth's axis is tilted away from the vertical (a line at right angles to the plane of its orbit) by about
questions.explanation: The axis leans 23½° from the vertical. This tilt, kept as the earth goes round the sun, causes the seasons and the changing lengths of day and night.

whyNot.A: 66½° is the angle between the axis and the plane of the orbit itself, not the tilt from the vertical.
whyNot.D: 90° would mean no tilt from the plane at all, lying the axis flat.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The point on the earth's surface directly above the focus of an earthquake is called the
questions.explanation: The focus is where the earthquake starts underground. The epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it, where shaking is usually strongest.

whyNot.A: A crater is the opening at the top of a volcano.
whyNot.C: A seismograph is the instrument that records earthquake waves.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A local government area has a population density of 250 people per km² and an area of 3,600 km². What is its population?
questions.explanation: Population density = population ÷ area, so population = density × area = 250 × 3,600 = 900,000 people.

whyNot.D: 90,000 drops a zero in the multiplication.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A town of 2,000,000 people grows at 3% per year. What will its population be after one year?

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A town has 54,000 males and 45,000 females. What is its sex ratio, expressed as the number of males per 100 females?
questions.explanation: Sex ratio = (males ÷ females) × 100 = (54,000 ÷ 45,000) × 100 = 1.2 × 100 = 120 males per 100 females.

whyNot.B: 83 is the number of females per 100 males (45,000 ÷ 54,000 × 100), the ratio turned upside down.
whyNot.D: 99 is the total population in thousands, not a ratio.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which condition most encourages a dispersed settlement pattern in a rural area?
options: Water can be found almost anywhere in the area
The area is often attacked by raiders
Good farmland is limited to one small area
Water is found only at a few springs
questions.explanation: In a dispersed pattern, homesteads are scattered far apart. This happens when families can settle anywhere because water, farmland and security are available all over the area.

whyNot.B: Insecurity makes people cluster together for defence, giving a nucleated pattern.
whyNot.D: Few water points draw people together around them, giving a nucleated pattern.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: An industry that is not tied to the location of its raw materials or power supply, and can be set up in many different places, is described as
questions.explanation: Footloose industries, such as electronics assembly, use light, high-value components and electricity that can reach almost anywhere. Transport costs matter little, so they are free to locate in many places.

whyNot.D: Extractive industries, such as mining, must be where the mineral is found.
whyNot.C: Weight-losing industries are usually tied to their raw materials to save transport costs.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: What is the main advantage of water transport over road transport for moving bulky goods such as grain or coal?
options: It is the fastest form of transport
It is not affected by weather or seasons
It is cheaper per tonne over long distances
questions.explanation: Ships and barges carry very large loads using little fuel per tonne, so they are the cheapest way to move heavy, bulky goods over long distances, even though they are slow.

whyNot.A: Water transport is slow; air transport is the fastest.
whyNot.D: Ships can only load at ports and jetties; road transport gives door-to-door service.
whyNot.B: Rivers can become too shallow in the dry season, and storms affect shipping.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: In international trade, the term 'visible trade' refers to the buying and selling of
options: services such as banking and insurance
physical goods such as crude oil and cocoa
questions.explanation: Visible trade is trade in goods that can be seen and touched, such as crude oil, cocoa and machinery. The difference between visible exports and visible imports is the balance of trade.

whyNot.B: Services such as banking, shipping and tourism are invisible trade.
whyNot.A: Trade within one country is home (internal) trade, not international trade.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: In which farming system does a farmer clear a piece of land, farm it for a few years and then move to new land when the soil loses its fertility?
questions.explanation: In shifting cultivation the farmer clears and burns the bush, farms the plot until yields fall, then abandons it and moves on. The old plot is left to recover its fertility naturally.

whyNot.D: Mixed farming keeps crops and animals on the same farm permanently.
whyNot.A: Plantations are permanent large estates growing one cash crop.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which problem is a direct result of rapid urban growth in cities such as Lagos?
options: A drop in the price of city land
Traffic congestion and the growth of slums
A shortage of workers for city jobs
A fall in the demand for housing
questions.explanation: When people move into a city faster than roads, houses and services can be provided, roads become jammed and many people end up in overcrowded, poorly serviced slums.

whyNot.D: More people means more demand for housing, not less.
whyNot.A: Crowding raises the price of city land.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A population pyramid has a narrow base, and its bars stay wide all the way up to the older age groups. What does this show?
options: A high birth rate and many young people
A rapidly growing number of school children
A low birth rate and many elderly people
A high birth rate and short life expectancy
questions.explanation: The base shows the youngest age groups; a narrow base means few births. Wide upper bars mean many people survive into old age. This is an ageing population, typical of rich industrial countries.

whyNot.D: A high birth rate and short life expectancy give a broad base that narrows quickly upwards.
whyNot.A: Many young people would make the base wide, not narrow.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Nigeria lies approximately between latitudes
questions.explanation: Nigeria stretches from the Atlantic coast at about 4°N to its northern border at about 14°N. Its longitudes run from about 3°E to about 15°E. It lies wholly in the northern hemisphere, within the tropics.

whyNot.A: Nigeria is north of the Equator, so its latitudes are north, not south.
whyNot.D: 14°N to 24°N would place the country in the Sahara, well north of Nigeria.
whyNot.B: The Equator (0°) passes far south of Nigeria's coast.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Jos is generally cooler than Makurdi, although both are in the middle belt of Nigeria. What is the main reason?
options: Jos gets more hours of sunshine
Jos is closer to the sea
Jos lies further south than Makurdi
Jos stands on a high plateau
questions.explanation: Temperature falls with height. Jos is on the Jos Plateau, over 1,000 m above sea level, while Makurdi lies low in the Benue valley. The higher altitude gives Jos its cooler climate.

whyNot.B: Jos is actually further from the sea than Makurdi, so this cannot be the reason.
whyNot.C: Jos is north of Makurdi, not south of it.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Shiroro hydroelectric dam in Niger State is built across which river?
questions.explanation: The Shiroro Dam is on the River Kaduna, a tributary of the Niger, in Niger State. With Kainji and Jebba on the Niger, it is one of Nigeria's main hydroelectric stations.

whyNot.B: The Benue flows through the north-east and middle belt, not through the Shiroro gorge.
whyNot.C: The River Ogun is in the south-west.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which tree crop is most widely grown in the rainforest belt of south-eastern Nigeria, in states such as Imo, Abia and Akwa Ibom?
questions.explanation: The oil palm thrives in the hot, wet rainforest of the south-east. It provides palm oil and palm kernels and has long been the chief cash crop of that area.

whyNot.C: Cotton needs a drier savanna climate in the north.
whyNot.A: Groundnut is a savanna crop of the north.
whyNot.B: Sorghum (guinea corn) is a grain crop of the drier north.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Obudu Plateau, known for its cattle ranch and cool climate, is in which state?
questions.explanation: The Obudu Plateau is in the north of Cross River State, near the border with Cameroon. Its height gives it a cool climate that suits cattle ranching and tourism.

whyNot.A: Plateau State contains the Jos Plateau, not the Obudu Plateau.
whyNot.C: Taraba State contains the Mambilla Plateau, a different highland.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Ajaokuta Steel Complex was planned to obtain its iron ore mainly from deposits at
questions.explanation: Iron ore is mined at Itakpe in Kogi State, not far from Ajaokuta. A rail line was built to carry the ore from Itakpe to the steel complex.

whyNot.C: Ewekoro is known for limestone used in making cement.
whyNot.B: Enugu is known for coal, not iron ore.
whyNot.D: Jos is known for tin and columbite.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which environmental problem is most closely linked with crude-oil production in the Niger Delta?
options: Oil spills that pollute creeks and farmland
questions.explanation: Leaking pipelines, damaged wellheads and illegal refining spill crude oil into creeks, mangroves and farms in the Niger Delta, killing fish, ruining farmland and polluting drinking water. Gas flaring also pollutes the air.

whyNot.B: Desertification and overgrazing are problems of the dry far north.
whyNot.D: Spreading sand dunes affect the Sahel states of the north-east and north-west.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Agulu–Nanka area, known for some of Nigeria's most severe gully erosion, is in which state?
questions.explanation: Agulu and Nanka are in Anambra State in the south-east. Heavy rainfall on loose, sandy soils and steep slopes has cut deep gullies that destroy homes, roads and farmland.

whyNot.D: Sokoto State suffers more from desertification than from gully erosion.
whyNot.B: Lagos State is low-lying and coastal; its main problems are flooding and coastal erosion.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Desertification is most serious in which group of Nigerian states?
questions.explanation: Desertification affects the far north, which borders the Sahara and has low, unreliable rainfall. Overgrazing, tree felling for firewood and drought turn farmland into desert in states such as Yobe, Borno and Sokoto.

whyNot.A: These south-western states are in the rainforest and derived savanna belt.
whyNot.C: These Niger Delta states are wet and swampy.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Counting the six area councils of the Federal Capital Territory, how many local government areas does Nigeria have?
questions.explanation: The 1999 Constitution (as amended) lists 768 local government areas in the 36 states and 6 area councils in the FCT, giving 774 in all.

whyNot.B: 747 swaps the last two digits of 774.
whyNot.D: 536 has no basis in the Constitution.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which is the longest river in Africa?
questions.explanation: The Nile, at about 6,650 km, is the longest river in Africa. It flows northwards from East Africa through Sudan and Egypt to the Mediterranean Sea.

whyNot.C: The Congo carries more water than the Nile but is shorter.
whyNot.B: The Niger is West Africa's longest river but is much shorter than the Nile.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The River Congo empties into which body of water?
questions.explanation: The Congo flows through central Africa in a great curve and enters the Atlantic Ocean on the west coast, at the border of the DR Congo and Angola.

whyNot.D: Rivers such as the Zambezi and Limpopo, not the Congo, flow into the Indian Ocean.
whyNot.B: The Nile, not the Congo, flows into the Mediterranean Sea.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The temperate grasslands known as the steppes are found mainly in
questions.explanation: The steppes are wide, treeless temperate grasslands stretching across Eurasia, from Ukraine through southern Russia into Kazakhstan. They are important wheat-growing and grazing lands.

whyNot.C: The grasslands of Argentina and Uruguay are the pampas.
whyNot.B: The grasslands of North America are the prairies.
whyNot.A: The grasslands of South Africa are the veld.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Gezira irrigation scheme in Sudan, between the Blue Nile and the White Nile, was developed mainly for growing
questions.explanation: The Gezira scheme uses water from the Blue Nile to irrigate a flat clay plain in a dry climate. Long-staple cotton was its main cash crop, grown in rotation with food crops.

whyNot.B: Cocoa needs a hot, wet forest climate like southern Ghana or Nigeria.
whyNot.D: Rubber needs an equatorial climate with rain all year.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Large rubber plantations, such as the Firestone plantation at Harbel, are an important part of the economy of
questions.explanation: Liberia's hot, wet climate suits rubber trees. The Firestone plantation at Harbel, opened in the 1920s, is one of the largest rubber plantations in the world, and rubber is a major export.

whyNot.C: Niger is a dry Sahel country where rubber cannot grow.
whyNot.A: Egypt is a desert country whose farming depends on the Nile; rubber is not grown there.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Atlas Mountains, a range of fold mountains, are found in which part of Africa?
questions.explanation: The Atlas Mountains run through Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia in north-west Africa. They were formed by folding as the African and Eurasian plates pushed together.

whyNot.D: East Africa's highlands are mainly volcanic and rift features, such as Kilimanjaro.
whyNot.B: Southern Africa has the Drakensberg, an old plateau edge, not the Atlas.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Rotterdam, one of the world's busiest seaports, owes much of its importance to its position near the mouth of which river?
questions.explanation: Rotterdam lies in the delta of the Rhine in the Netherlands. Barges carry goods up the Rhine to the industrial Ruhr and other parts of Germany, so Rotterdam serves a huge hinterland.

whyNot.D: The Danube flows east into the Black Sea.
whyNot.B: The Volga is in Russia and flows into the Caspian Sea.
whyNot.A: The Thames flows through London in England.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The St Lawrence Seaway in North America is important because it
options: lets ocean-going ships reach the Great Lakes from the Atlantic
links the Atlantic Ocean with the Pacific Ocean
carries crude oil from Canada to Mexico
joins the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea
questions.explanation: The St Lawrence Seaway is a system of locks and canals along the St Lawrence River. It allows ships to sail from the Atlantic deep into the Great Lakes, carrying grain, iron ore and other bulky goods.

whyNot.B: The Panama Canal, not the St Lawrence Seaway, links the Atlantic and the Pacific.
whyNot.D: The Suez Canal joins the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Why is cattle rearing limited in the forest belt of West Africa?
options: The tsetse fly spreads sleeping sickness among cattle
Rainfall there is too low for pasture
The grass there is too short for cattle
There is no market for beef in the south
questions.explanation: The tsetse fly breeds in the warm, humid, shady forest and wetter savanna. It spreads trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness), which kills most breeds of cattle, so large herds are kept mainly in the drier north.

whyNot.C: Forest areas have tall, coarse grasses or thick undergrowth, not short grass.
whyNot.B: The forest belt has the highest rainfall in West Africa.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A monsoon climate, such as that of India, is mainly marked by
options: a seasonal reversal of winds that brings a wet season and a dry season
heavy rainfall spread evenly through every month
cold, snowy winters and short cool summers
hot dry summers and mild wet winters
questions.explanation: In summer the land heats up and moist winds blow in from the ocean, bringing very heavy rain. In winter the winds reverse and blow out from the cool land, bringing dry weather. This reversal is the monsoon.

whyNot.B: Rain in every month describes the equatorial climate.
whyNot.D: Hot dry summers and mild wet winters describe the Mediterranean climate.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: On a map of scale 1:250,000, the distance between two towns is 3.2 cm. What is the actual distance between them?
questions.explanation: 1 cm on the map = 250,000 cm = 2.5 km on the ground. 3.2 × 2.5 = 8 km.

whyNot.D: 80 km uses 10,000 cm in a kilometre instead of 100,000 cm.
whyNot.C: 32 km has no basis; 3.2 cm × 2.5 km per cm is 8 km.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which of these map scales will show a small area in the greatest detail?
questions.explanation: The smaller the number after the colon, the larger the scale. At 1:10,000, 1 cm stands for only 100 m, so streets and buildings can be drawn clearly. It is the largest scale of the four.

whyNot.B: At 1:50,000, 1 cm stands for 500 m, so less detail can be shown.
whyNot.D: 1:1,000,000 is the smallest scale here, used for whole countries, with very little detail.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A footpath is 2.5 km long on the ground. How long will it be on a map of scale 1:25,000?

whyNot.B: 1 cm uses 10,000 cm in a kilometre instead of 100,000 cm.
whyNot.D: 100 cm uses 1,000,000 cm in a kilometre.

questions.subject: geography
questions.context: On a map of scale 1:20,000, a church C stands at 320 m above sea level and a well W at 240 m. The distance from C to W on the map is 8 cm.
questions.stem: What is the average gradient between C and W?
questions.explanation: Vertical interval = 320 − 240 = 80 m. Horizontal equivalent = 8 × 20,000 = 160,000 cm = 1,600 m. Gradient = 80 ÷ 1,600 = 1/20, written as 1 in 20.

whyNot.D: 1 in 2,000 divides 160,000 cm by 80 m without changing both to metres.
whyNot.B: 1 in 4 compares the height of C (320 m) with the vertical interval (80 m).

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The bearing of a mast from a school is 215°. What is the bearing of the school from the mast?
questions.explanation: The back bearing differs by 180°. Since 215° is more than 180°, subtract: 215° − 180° = 035°.

whyNot.D: 145° is 360° − 215°, which reflects the line across north instead of reversing it.
whyNot.B: 395° adds 180° but bearings cannot exceed 360°; subtracting 360° gives 035°.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A bearing is measured from
options: due east in a clockwise direction
true north in a clockwise direction
true north in an anticlockwise direction
due south in an anticlockwise direction
questions.explanation: A bearing gives direction as an angle from 000° to 360°, measured clockwise from true north. East is 090°, south is 180° and west is 270°.

whyNot.C: Measuring anticlockwise would make east 270°, which is wrong.
whyNot.A: Bearings always start from north, not east.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A rectangular lake measures 3 cm by 1.5 cm on a map of scale 1:100,000. What is its actual area?
questions.explanation: On a 1:100,000 map, 1 cm = 100,000 cm = 1 km. The lake is 3 km by 1.5 km, so its area = 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 km².

whyNot.A: 45 km² puts the decimal point in the wrong place.
whyNot.B: 9 km² adds the sides twice (3 + 1.5 + 3 + 1.5) to get the perimeter, then treats it as an area.

questions.subject: geography
questions.context: On a contour map, the contours on the eastern side of a highland are packed very closely together, while on the western side they are widely spaced and fall gradually to lower ground.
questions.stem: Which relief feature is shown?
questions.explanation: An escarpment (cuesta) has a steep scarp slope on one side, shown by closely packed contours, and a gentle dip slope on the other, shown by widely spaced contours.

whyNot.D: A conical hill has evenly spaced contours on all sides.
whyNot.C: A col is a low gap between two hills on a ridge.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: In map reading, the contour interval is
options: the difference in height between two neighbouring contour lines
the height of the highest point on the map
the number of contour lines on the map
the horizontal distance between two contour lines
questions.explanation: Contours are drawn at regular vertical steps, such as every 20 m or 50 m. That fixed difference in height between one contour and the next is the contour interval.

whyNot.D: The horizontal distance between contours changes with steepness; it is not fixed.
whyNot.B: The highest point is shown by a spot height or trigonometrical station.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A road measures 12 cm on a map of scale 1:100,000. How long will a cyclist travelling at 16 km per hour take to ride its full length?
questions.explanation: 1 cm = 1 km on this map, so the road is 12 km long. Time = distance ÷ speed = 12 ÷ 16 = 0.75 hours. 0.75 × 60 = 45 minutes.

whyNot.B: 1 hour 20 minutes comes from 16 ÷ 12, dividing the wrong way round.
whyNot.D: 7 hours 30 minutes uses 1:1,000,000, making the road 120 km long.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Town K is on longitude 60°W. When it is 3.00 p.m. at Greenwich (0°), what is the local time at K?
questions.explanation: 60° ÷ 15° per hour = 4 hours. K is west of Greenwich, so its time is behind: 3.00 p.m. − 4 hours = 11.00 a.m.

whyNot.D: 7.00 p.m. adds 4 hours, the rule for places east of Greenwich.
whyNot.A: 12.00 noon subtracts only 3 hours; the difference is 4 hours.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A traveller crosses the International Date Line going eastwards, from Asia towards America. What should the traveller do to the calendar?
options: Put it back by one day
Put it forward by one day
Put it back by one hour
questions.explanation: Travelling east, a traveller gains time at every time zone. To correct this, the date is set back one day on crossing the Date Line eastwards; going westwards a day is added.

whyNot.C: Putting the calendar forward one day is done when crossing westwards, from America towards Asia.
whyNot.D: The date line changes the date by a whole day, not one hour.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which condition most favours the formation of a delta at the mouth of a river?
options: The river flows fast into deep water with strong currents
The river carries a large load and the sea's currents are weak
The river carries very little sediment
The sea at the mouth has a very large tidal range
questions.explanation: A delta grows when a river brings down plenty of sediment and drops it as it slows on entering the sea. Weak tides and currents allow the deposits to build up instead of being carried away.

whyNot.A: Strong currents and deep water sweep sediment away, so no delta forms.
whyNot.D: A large tidal range scours the mouth, which usually produces an estuary, not a delta.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: In deserts, rock pedestals (mushroom rocks) are formed mainly by
options: wind abrasion, which is strongest close to the ground
questions.explanation: Wind lifts sand only a short distance off the ground, so sand-blasting is strongest near the base of a rock. The base is worn away faster than the top, leaving a narrow neck under a wide cap.

whyNot.A: Rivers are rare in deserts and do not undercut rocks in this way.
whyNot.B: Chemical weathering needs plenty of water, which deserts lack.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which instrument records both the highest and the lowest temperatures reached in a day?
questions.explanation: Six's thermometer (the maximum and minimum thermometer) has small markers that are pushed along by the mercury and stay at the highest and lowest temperatures reached until they are reset.

whyNot.D: A barometer measures air pressure.
whyNot.A: A rain gauge measures rainfall.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which of these ocean currents is a cold current?
questions.explanation: The Canary Current flows southwards from cooler latitudes along the north-west coast of Africa, so it is cold. It cools the coast and helps keep the western Sahara dry.

whyNot.C: The Gulf Stream is a warm current flowing from the Gulf of Mexico across the Atlantic.
whyNot.D: The Guinea Current is a warm current flowing eastwards along the West African coast.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which type of cloud is most often associated with thunderstorms and heavy showers?
questions.explanation: Cumulonimbus clouds are huge, towering clouds built by strongly rising air. They bring heavy rain, thunder, lightning and sometimes hail.

whyNot.B: Cirrus are thin, wispy clouds high in the sky that do not give rain.
whyNot.C: Stratus are low, flat grey layers that bring dull weather or drizzle.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Every fourth year has 366 days instead of 365 days. This is because
options: the earth takes about 24 hours to turn once on its axis
the earth takes about 365¼ days to go round the sun
the moon takes about 29½ days to go round the earth
the earth's axis is tilted at 23½°
questions.explanation: One revolution of the earth round the sun takes about 365¼ days. The extra quarter-days add up to one full day every four years, which is added as 29 February in a leap year.

whyNot.A: The 24-hour rotation causes day and night, not leap years.
whyNot.D: The tilt of the axis causes the seasons.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: On which two dates are day and night about equal in length all over the world?
questions.explanation: On the equinoxes, about 21 March and 23 September, the midday sun is overhead at the Equator and the circle of light passes through both poles, so every place has about 12 hours of day and 12 hours of night.

whyNot.D: 21 June and 22 December are the solstices, when the difference between day and night is greatest.
whyNot.B: 22 December is a solstice, so this pair is only half right.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A weather station records a maximum temperature of 33 °C and a minimum temperature of 21 °C on one day. What is the mean daily temperature?
questions.explanation: Mean daily temperature = (maximum + minimum) ÷ 2 = (33 + 21) ÷ 2 = 54 ÷ 2 = 27 °C.

whyNot.B: 12 °C is the daily range (33 − 21), not the mean.
whyNot.A: 54 °C is the sum of the two readings before dividing by 2.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The seasonal movement of Fulani herders and their cattle between dry-season and rainy-season pastures is known as
questions.explanation: Transhumance is the regular seasonal movement of herders and their animals. In the dry season they move south or to river valleys for grass and water; when the rains come they return north.

whyNot.B: Rural–urban migration is the movement of people from villages to towns to live and work.
whyNot.D: Shifting cultivation is a crop-farming system, not the movement of livestock.
whyNot.C: Emigration is leaving one's country to live in another.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The population of a town rose from 120,000 in 2010 to 150,000 in 2020. What was the percentage increase?
questions.explanation: Increase = 150,000 − 120,000 = 30,000. Percentage increase = (increase ÷ original population) × 100 = (30,000 ÷ 120,000) × 100 = 25%.

whyNot.D: 20% divides the increase by the new population (150,000) instead of the original one.
whyNot.C: 30% is just the increase in thousands, not a percentage.

questions.subject: geography
questions.context: Four local government areas have these figures. LGA A: population 180,000, area 600 km². LGA B: population 240,000, area 1,200 km². LGA C: population 150,000, area 300 km². LGA D: population 400,000, area 2,000 km².
questions.stem: Which local government area has the highest population density?
questions.explanation: Density = population ÷ area. A: 180,000 ÷ 600 = 300 per km². B: 240,000 ÷ 1,200 = 200. C: 150,000 ÷ 300 = 500. D: 400,000 ÷ 2,000 = 200. C is the most densely populated even though it has the fewest people.

whyNot.C: D has the largest population but also the largest area, giving only 200 per km².
whyNot.A: A has 300 per km², less than C's 500.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which pair of factors best explains why many manufacturing industries are found in Lagos?
options: A cool climate and rich pasture land
A large market and good seaport facilities
Nearness to coal and iron-ore mines
A small population and cheap land
questions.explanation: Lagos has millions of consumers, a large labour force, banks, and the busy Apapa and Tin Can Island ports for importing raw materials and machinery. These attract many factories.

whyNot.C: Lagos has no coal or iron-ore mines nearby.
whyNot.D: Lagos has a very large population and expensive land.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Compared with road transport, a major disadvantage of rail transport is that it
options: can only run in the dry season
is badly affected by traffic jams
questions.explanation: Trains can only run on fixed tracks between stations, so goods must usually be moved by road at both ends. Lorries can deliver straight from the sender's door to the receiver's door.

whyNot.A: Railways are well suited to carrying heavy, bulky goods.
whyNot.C: Trains run on their own tracks, so they avoid road traffic jams.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A farmer who grows maize and cassava and also keeps goats and poultry on the same farm is practising
questions.explanation: Mixed farming combines crop growing and livestock keeping on one farm. Animal droppings manure the crops, and crop remains feed the animals.

whyNot.D: Monoculture is growing only one crop.
whyNot.B: Pastoral nomadism is moving about with herds and growing no crops.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which of these is a characteristic of plantation agriculture?
options: Moving the farm to new land every few years
Herding animals from place to place
Small plots farmed mainly to feed the family
A large estate growing one cash crop with much capital
questions.explanation: Plantations are large estates that specialise in one cash crop, such as rubber or oil palm. They need heavy capital, many workers, scientific methods and often their own processing factory.

whyNot.C: Small family plots describe subsistence farming.
whyNot.A: Moving the farm describes shifting cultivation.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which method of mining is used when a mineral lies close to the surface, as with much of the tin worked on the Jos Plateau?
questions.explanation: In open-cast mining the soil and rock above a shallow deposit are stripped away and the mineral is dug from an open pit. It is cheap where the mineral is near the surface, but leaves pits and ponds on the land.

whyNot.B: Shaft mining sinks vertical shafts to reach deep deposits.
whyNot.A: Drift mining drives a sloping or level tunnel into a hillside to reach a seam, as at the Enugu coal mines.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Abuja, the seat of the Federal Government of Nigeria, is best described by its main function as
questions.explanation: Abuja was built to house the Presidency, the National Assembly, the Supreme Court and federal ministries. Its main function is government (administration).

whyNot.B: Abuja did not grow up around a mine.
whyNot.D: Abuja is far inland, so it cannot be a fishing port.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: A town of 120,000 people recorded 3,600 live births in one year. What is its crude birth rate?
questions.explanation: Crude birth rate = (live births ÷ total population) × 1,000 = (3,600 ÷ 120,000) × 1,000 = 0.03 × 1,000 = 30 per 1,000 people per year.

whyNot.A: 3 per 1,000 multiplies by 100 instead of 1,000.
whyNot.B: 300 per 1,000 multiplies by 10,000 instead of 1,000.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Nigeria's total area is about
questions.explanation: Nigeria covers about 923,768 km², which rounds to about 924,000 km². It is one of the larger countries in West Africa.

whyNot.C: 92,400 km² is ten times too small, about the size of just one large Nigerian state such as Niger State.
whyNot.B: 9,240,000 km² is ten times too large, bigger than the whole of West Africa.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Apart from the Federal Capital Territory, how many states make up Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Nigeria has 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja. The last six states were created in 1996, bringing the number from 30 to 36.

whyNot.C: 19 was the number of states created in 1976, before later state creations.
whyNot.B: 30 was the number of states between 1991 and 1996.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Jebba hydroelectric dam is built across which river?
questions.explanation: The Jebba Dam is on the River Niger downstream of the Kainji Dam, on the border of Kwara and Niger States. Both dams use the flow of the Niger to produce electricity.

whyNot.D: The River Kaduna is the site of the Shiroro Dam.
whyNot.B: Jebba lies on the Niger in Kwara and Niger States, not on the Benue.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which part of Nigeria receives the highest annual rainfall?
options: The Sokoto Basin in the north-west
The south-eastern coast, around Bonny and Calabar
The Jos Plateau in the middle belt
The Chad Basin in the north-east
questions.explanation: Rainfall in Nigeria decreases from the coast inland. The south-eastern coast faces the moist south-west winds first, and the Cameroon highlands nearby add relief rain, so places like Bonny and Calabar get about 3,000 mm of rain or more a year.

whyNot.A: The Sokoto Basin is in the dry far north, with one of the lowest rainfalls.
whyNot.D: The Chad Basin borders the Sahara and is among the driest parts of Nigeria.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Nigeria's large deposits of bitumen (tar sand) are found mainly in
questions.explanation: Nigeria's bitumen belt runs across the south-west, through Ondo, Ogun, Edo and Lagos States, with the largest deposits in Ondo State. Bitumen can be used for road surfacing and as a source of oil.

whyNot.C: Sokoto State is in the far north-west and is known for limestone, not bitumen.
whyNot.D: Kano State has no major bitumen deposits.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Most of Nigeria's cattle are reared in the northern part of the country mainly because the north
options: has the largest number of rivers
has the highest rainfall in the country
is largely free from the tsetse fly
questions.explanation: The tsetse fly, which carries trypanosomiasis, cannot survive well in the drier, more open savanna of the north. Open grassland also provides pasture, so cattle rearing is concentrated there.

whyNot.C: The north has the lowest, not the highest, rainfall.
whyNot.A: Rainforest is in the south; the north is savanna.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which river flows from Nigeria into Lake Chad?
questions.explanation: The Komadugu-Yobe river system rises in the north of Nigeria (from rivers such as the Hadejia and Jama'are) and flows north-east along the Niger border into Lake Chad.

whyNot.D: The Ogun flows south into the Lagos Lagoon.
whyNot.A: The Gongola flows south into the River Benue, not into Lake Chad.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The rain-bearing wind that blows into Nigeria from the Atlantic Ocean is the
options: south-east trade wind from the Indian Ocean
questions.explanation: The south-west monsoon is moist tropical maritime air that has crossed the warm Atlantic. It brings the rainy season to Nigeria as it moves inland.

whyNot.A: The harmattan is dry, dusty air from the Sahara.
whyNot.C: The Indian Ocean is on the far side of Africa and does not supply Nigeria's rain.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The start of the rainy season in northern Nigeria is mainly linked to
options: the arrival of the north-east trade wind
the southward movement of the Inter-Tropical Discontinuity
the northward movement of the Inter-Tropical Discontinuity
the cold Canary Current off the coast
questions.explanation: The Inter-Tropical Discontinuity (ITD) is the boundary between dry Saharan air and moist Atlantic air. As it moves north following the overhead sun, moist air spreads over the north and the rains begin.

whyNot.B: When the ITD moves south, dry air returns and the dry season begins.
whyNot.A: The north-east trade wind is the dry harmattan, which ends the rains.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Apapa port, one of Nigeria's busiest seaports, is in which state?
questions.explanation: Apapa port is in Lagos State, beside the Lagos harbour. It handles a large share of Nigeria's imports because Lagos is the country's largest commercial centre.

whyNot.C: Rivers State has the Port Harcourt and Onne ports.
whyNot.A: Delta State has the Warri and Sapele ports.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Victoria Falls, on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe, are on which river?
questions.explanation: The Victoria Falls are on the River Zambezi, which forms part of the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe before flowing into the Indian Ocean.

whyNot.A: The Limpopo forms the border of South Africa with Botswana and Zimbabwe further south.
whyNot.D: The Orange River flows through South Africa and Namibia to the Atlantic.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which is the largest country in Africa by area?
questions.explanation: Algeria, with about 2.38 million km², has been Africa's largest country by area since South Sudan separated from Sudan in 2011. Much of it is in the Sahara.

whyNot.C: Nigeria has the largest population in Africa, but its area is far smaller than Algeria's.
whyNot.A: Egypt is about 1 million km², less than half the size of Algeria.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Blue Nile has its source in Lake Tana, which is in
questions.explanation: Lake Tana lies on the Ethiopian Highlands. The Blue Nile flows out of it and joins the White Nile at Khartoum in Sudan.

whyNot.B: Uganda contains the outlet of Lake Victoria, a source of the White Nile, not the Blue Nile.
whyNot.D: Sudan is where the Blue Nile meets the White Nile, not where it starts.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which group of crops is typical of lands with a Mediterranean climate?
questions.explanation: Mediterranean lands have hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters. Grapes, olives and citrus fruits have deep roots or thick skins that let them survive the summer drought.

whyNot.C: Cocoa, rubber and oil palm need hot, wet equatorial conditions all year.
whyNot.B: Jute, rice and tea are typical of monsoon lands.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Which of these West African countries is landlocked?
questions.explanation: Mali has no coastline. It depends on ports in neighbouring countries such as Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire for its imports and exports.

whyNot.A: Ghana has a coast on the Gulf of Guinea.
whyNot.D: Senegal has a long Atlantic coastline.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Tundra vegetation, made up mainly of mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs, is found
options: in hot deserts with very little rain
in equatorial lowlands with rain all year
along coasts with a Mediterranean climate
near the Arctic, where winters are very long and cold
questions.explanation: Tundra lies around the Arctic Ocean in northern Canada, Alaska, Scandinavia and Russia. The growing season is very short and the subsoil is frozen, so only low plants can grow.

whyNot.B: Equatorial lowlands have dense tropical rainforest.
whyNot.A: Hot deserts have scattered drought-resistant plants such as cacti and thorny shrubs.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: Hot deserts such as the Sahara have a very large daily range of temperature mainly because
options: the sun is never overhead there
clear skies let heat escape quickly at night
thick cloud traps heat at night
sea breezes cool the land by day
questions.explanation: With almost no cloud or moisture in the air, the ground heats up strongly by day. At night there is nothing to hold the heat in, so it radiates away fast and temperatures drop sharply.

whyNot.A: The sun is high in the sky in the Sahara, especially in summer, which is why the days are so hot.
whyNot.C: Thick cloud would keep nights warm and reduce the range; deserts have very little cloud.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Prairie Provinces of Canada are especially famous for growing
questions.explanation: The prairies have rich black soils, flat land and warm summers, ideal for large-scale, machine-based wheat farming. Canada is one of the world's leading wheat exporters.

whyNot.C: Cocoa needs a hot, wet tropical climate.
whyNot.A: Rice needs flooded fields and a warm, wet climate.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The Strait of Gibraltar separates
questions.explanation: The Strait of Gibraltar is a narrow channel joining the Atlantic Ocean to the Mediterranean Sea. Spain lies on its northern side and Morocco on its southern side.

whyNot.D: Egypt and Saudi Arabia are separated by the Red Sea.
whyNot.C: France and England are separated by the English Channel.

questions.subject: geography
questions.stem: The coniferous forests (taiga) of Canada and Russia are important mainly as a source of
options: softwood for timber, pulp and paper
hardwoods such as mahogany and iroko
questions.explanation: The taiga is made up of large stands of a few kinds of conifer, such as pine, spruce and fir. Their soft, light wood is easy to cut and float, making it ideal for timber, wood pulp and paper.

whyNot.D: Mahogany and iroko are tropical hardwoods from rainforests.
whyNot.A: Latex comes from rubber trees in hot, wet tropical lands.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Nigeria sells cocoa beans, sesame seeds and cashew nuts to buyers in Europe and Asia. This shows that agriculture helps the economy by
options: supplying raw materials to local textile mills
questions.explanation: When farm produce is exported, the country is paid in foreign currencies such as dollars and euros. Agriculture therefore earns foreign exchange, which Nigeria uses to import machines and other goods.

whyNot.C: The produce here is sold abroad, not used by local factories; textile mills also use cotton, not cocoa or cashew.
whyNot.D: Cocoa, sesame and cashew are not used as fuel for power stations.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Each year, Fulani herders in northern Nigeria move their cattle southwards in the dry season in search of pasture and water, and return north when the rains come. This system of livestock keeping is called
questions.explanation: Nomadic herding (pastoralism) is the movement of herders and their animals from place to place following the seasonal availability of grass and water. The animals are not kept on a fixed, fenced farm.

whyNot.A: Ranching keeps animals on a large fixed area of fenced pasture.
whyNot.D: In zero grazing animals are confined and cut fodder is carried to them.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: When the government pays part of the cost of fertiliser so that farmers can buy it below its market price, it is giving farmers a
questions.explanation: A subsidy is a payment by government that lowers the cost of an input or product to the user. Fertiliser subsidies help poor farmers afford inputs and raise yields.

whyNot.C: A tariff is a tax on imported goods; it raises prices rather than lowering them.
whyNot.D: A guaranteed minimum price is a price promised for the farmer's produce, not a reduction in the cost of inputs.
whyNot.A: A loan must be repaid; a subsidy does not.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: In many villages in Ekiti State most farmers are now over 55 years old because young people have moved to Lagos and other cities in search of jobs. The main effect of this on agriculture is
options: a fall in the price of farm produce
questions.explanation: Rural-urban migration takes away the young, strong people who do most farm work. The ageing farmers left behind cannot cultivate large areas, so labour becomes scarce and food output falls.

whyNot.D: Fragmentation results from sharing land among heirs, not from young people leaving.
whyNot.A: Less labour usually means less food produced, which tends to raise, not lower, prices.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Mr Okafor pays a landowner an agreed sum so that he can farm a piece of land for 10 years, after which the land goes back to the owner. This form of land tenure is
questions.explanation: Under leasehold, the tenant pays rent to use land for a fixed period agreed in a lease. At the end of the period the right to use the land returns to the owner.

whyNot.A: Freehold means owning the land outright with no time limit.
whyNot.B: Communal land belongs to a whole community or family, not rented from one owner.
whyNot.C: Inheritance is receiving land from a parent or relative after death.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which of the following is an edaphic (soil) factor affecting crop production?
questions.explanation: Edaphic factors are properties of the soil itself, such as soil pH, texture, structure, fertility and soil water. Soil pH affects how available nutrients are to plant roots.

whyNot.A: Relative humidity is a climatic factor, a property of the air.
whyNot.C: Light intensity is a climatic factor.
whyNot.D: Wind is a climatic factor.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Under the Land Use Act, the document that a state Governor issues as evidence of a person's statutory right to occupy a piece of land is the
questions.explanation: The Land Use Act empowers the Governor to grant statutory rights of occupancy. The grant is evidenced by a Certificate of Occupancy (C of O), which holders can also use as security for loans.

whyNot.B: A deed of gift transfers property from one person to another as a gift; it is not issued by the Governor.
whyNot.C: A survey plan shows the boundaries and size of the land but does not grant the right to occupy it.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The Harmattan, a dry, dusty wind from the Sahara that blows over Nigeria in the dry season, affects crops mainly by
options: adding nitrogen to the soil through dust
raising the relative humidity of the air
washing away the topsoil from farmland
increasing water loss from plants and drying out the soil
questions.explanation: The Harmattan air is very dry. It increases the rate of transpiration from leaves and evaporation from the soil, so crops that are not irrigated wilt and young plants may die.

whyNot.C: Washing away topsoil is water erosion caused by heavy rain, not a dry wind.
whyNot.B: The Harmattan lowers relative humidity; it is a dry wind.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A farmer in Kaduna State plants maize after the first heavy showers of the season, but the rains then stop for three weeks and most seedlings die. The problem is mainly one of
questions.explanation: The total amount of rain in the year may be enough, but it did not fall evenly: a dry spell followed the early showers (a false start to the rains). How rainfall is spread over the season is as important as the total, which is why farmers wait until the rains are established before planting.

whyNot.B: The question is about a break in the rains soon after planting, not about how much rain falls in the whole year.
whyNot.D: Soil acidity does not explain seedlings dying during a dry spell.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Some soybean varieties grown in Nigeria flower early or late depending on the length of day and night. This response of plants to day length is called
questions.explanation: Photoperiodism is the response of a plant, especially its flowering, to the relative lengths of day and night. Short-day plants flower when days become shorter than a critical length; long-day plants flower when days are longer.

whyNot.B: Phototropism is growth of a shoot towards light, not flowering in response to day length.
whyNot.C: Photosynthesis is the making of food from carbon dioxide and water using light energy.
whyNot.D: Geotropism is growth in response to gravity.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The breaking down of rocks into smaller pieces by heating and cooling, running water and wind, without any change in their chemical composition, is called
questions.explanation: Physical (mechanical) weathering breaks rock into smaller fragments by forces such as expansion and contraction from temperature changes, and abrasion by water and wind. The minerals are not chemically changed.

whyNot.D: Chemical weathering changes the minerals, for example by solution, oxidation or hydrolysis.
whyNot.C: Leaching is the washing of nutrients down the soil by water, not the breaking of rocks.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: In a soil profile, the dark upper layer that is mixed with humus and in which most crop roots feed is the
questions.explanation: The A horizon, or topsoil, contains most of the organic matter (humus), soil organisms and plant nutrients, so it is dark in colour and is where most crop roots are found.

whyNot.C: The B horizon is the subsoil below, where clay and materials leached from above accumulate; it has little humus.
whyNot.D: The C horizon is partly weathered rock with little organic matter.
whyNot.A: The R horizon is the solid bedrock.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A fresh soil sample weighed 60 g. After drying in an oven at 105 °C, it weighed 50 g. What is its moisture content as a percentage of the oven-dry weight?
questions.explanation: Water lost = 60 − 50 = 10 g. Moisture content (dry-weight basis) = water ÷ dry soil × 100 = 10 ÷ 50 × 100 = 20%.

whyNot.A: 16.7% divides the water by the fresh weight (10 ÷ 60), not the oven-dry weight.
whyNot.C: 10 is the mass of water in grams, not a percentage.
whyNot.D: 83.3% is the dry soil as a percentage of the fresh weight.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Kenaf, grown in parts of northern Nigeria, is cultivated mainly for its
questions.explanation: Kenaf is a fibre crop. Its stems yield a strong bast fibre used for making sacks, ropes, twine and similar products.

whyNot.B: Oil crops include groundnut, oil palm and sesame.
whyNot.C: Starchy tubers come from crops such as yam and cassava.
whyNot.D: Latex is obtained from the rubber tree.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A herbicide that a rice farmer sprays on her field to kill broad-leaved weeds without harming the rice is described as
questions.explanation: A selective herbicide kills certain kinds of plants (here broad-leaved weeds) but leaves others, such as the grass crop rice, unharmed. A non-selective herbicide kills almost any green plant it touches.

whyNot.D: A non-selective herbicide would kill the rice as well as the weeds.
whyNot.A: Pre-planting describes when a herbicide is applied, not which plants it kills.
whyNot.B: Systemic describes how a herbicide moves inside a plant, not whether it spares the crop.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The maize weevil (Sitophilus zeamais) causes most of its damage to maize
options: in storage, by boring into and eating the grains
in the field, by feeding on the roots
in the field, by sucking sap from the leaves
in the nursery, by cutting seedlings at ground level
questions.explanation: The maize weevil is a storage pest. Adults and larvae feed inside the grains, leaving them hollow and full of holes, which lowers their weight, quality and germination.

whyNot.C: Sap-sucking is done by insects such as aphids, not weevils feeding on grain.
whyNot.D: Cutting seedlings at ground level is typical of cutworms.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Rice blast, which produces diamond-shaped grey-centred spots on rice leaves and can rot the neck of the panicle, is caused by a
questions.explanation: Rice blast is a fungal disease (caused by Magnaporthe oryzae, also known as Pyricularia oryzae). Its spores spread by wind; resistant varieties and fungicides help control it.

whyNot.B: Virus diseases of crops include maize streak and cassava mosaic, not rice blast.
whyNot.C: Bacterial leaf blight of rice is a different disease with long water-soaked streaks.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A farmer needs 54 kg of P₂O₅ per hectare for 2 ha of cowpea. He uses single superphosphate, which contains 18% P₂O₅. How many 50 kg bags of single superphosphate does he need?
questions.explanation: Fertiliser per hectare = 54 ÷ 0.18 = 300 kg. For 2 ha: 300 × 2 = 600 kg. Number of bags = 600 ÷ 50 = 12 bags.

whyNot.A: 6 bags is enough for only 1 ha.
whyNot.C: 2 bags treats 54 × 2 = 108 kg as the amount of fertiliser, forgetting that it is only 18% P₂O₅.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The older leaves of a plantain crop show yellowing and then brown, dry, scorched edges, while the younger leaves look normal. The nutrient most likely lacking is
questions.explanation: Potassium is mobile in the plant, so a shortage shows first on older leaves. The typical sign is yellowing and scorching (browning) of the leaf margins. Plantain and banana need a lot of potassium.

whyNot.D: Nitrogen deficiency causes general yellowing of older leaves, starting along the midrib, not scorched margins.
whyNot.A: Iron is immobile, so its deficiency shows as yellowing between the veins of young leaves.
whyNot.B: Sulphur deficiency shows as yellowing of the young leaves.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: One reason crop rotation helps to control pests and diseases is that it
options: makes every crop on the farm resistant to disease
kills all insects in the soil before planting
breaks the life cycle of pests that attack only one kind of crop
removes the need for weeding the farm
questions.explanation: Many pests and pathogens depend on one particular crop. When a different, unrelated crop is grown the next season, they find no host, so their numbers fall.

whyNot.B: Rotation does not kill soil insects directly; it starves host-specific ones.
whyNot.A: Resistance is a property of the variety, not something rotation gives a crop.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A young female pig that has not yet given birth to piglets is called a
questions.explanation: A gilt is a young female pig that has not farrowed (given birth). After farrowing she is called a sow.

whyNot.A: A sow is a female pig that has already farrowed.
whyNot.C: A boar is an uncastrated male pig.
whyNot.B: A barrow is a castrated male pig.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: In the digestive system of a chicken, the muscular organ that grinds food with the help of small stones (grit) is the
questions.explanation: Chickens have no teeth. The gizzard has thick muscular walls and contains grit, and its contractions grind grains into small particles for digestion.

whyNot.D: The crop stores and softens food; it does not grind it.
whyNot.C: The proventriculus (true stomach) secretes digestive juices.
whyNot.A: The caeca help in the fermentation of fibre.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The oestrous cycle of a cow, the time from one heat period to the next, lasts about
questions.explanation: A cow that is not pregnant comes on heat about every 21 days (range 18–24 days). Farmers watch for heat at this interval so that the cow can be mated or inseminated.

whyNot.C: About 283 days is the gestation period of a cow, not the oestrous cycle.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The gestation period of a goat is about
questions.explanation: Goats carry their young for about five months, roughly 150 days (145–155 days), so a doe can kid about three times in two years.

whyNot.C: About 114 days is the gestation period of a sow.
whyNot.A: About 283 days is the gestation period of a cow.
whyNot.D: About 31 days is the gestation period of a rabbit.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Foot-and-mouth disease, which causes blisters in the mouth and between the claws of cattle, making them drool and limp, is caused by a
questions.explanation: Foot-and-mouth disease is a highly contagious viral disease of cloven-hoofed animals. Antibiotics cannot cure it; control is by vaccination, quarantine and restricting animal movement.

whyNot.A: Bacterial diseases of cattle include anthrax and brucellosis.
whyNot.C: Protozoan diseases include trypanosomiasis and babesiosis.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Ticks on cattle are harmful mainly because they suck blood and
options: destroy the rumen microbes that digest grass
cause the animal's horns to break
transmit organisms that cause diseases such as babesiosis (redwater)
lay their eggs inside the animal's intestine
questions.explanation: Ticks are external parasites. Besides causing blood loss and damaging hides, they are vectors of disease organisms, for example Babesia (redwater) and the agents of anaplasmosis and heartwater.

whyNot.D: Ticks live on the skin and lay eggs on the ground, not in the intestine.
whyNot.A: Ticks feed on the skin surface and do not affect rumen microbes.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which of these feed ingredients is used in poultry rations mainly as a source of energy?
questions.explanation: Maize grain is rich in starch (carbohydrate), so it is the main energy source in most poultry feeds in Nigeria.

whyNot.C: Groundnut cake is mainly a protein source.
whyNot.A: Fish meal is a high-quality protein source.
whyNot.B: Bone meal supplies minerals, mainly calcium and phosphorus.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A hatchery sets 400 eggs. Candling shows that 360 are fertile, and 324 chicks hatch. What is the hatchability of the fertile eggs?
questions.explanation: Hatchability of fertile eggs = chicks hatched ÷ fertile eggs × 100 = 324 ÷ 360 × 100 = 90%.

whyNot.C: 81% is chicks hatched as a percentage of all eggs set (324 ÷ 400), not of fertile eggs.
whyNot.B: 10% is the share of infertile eggs (40 ÷ 400).

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A fish farmer in Delta State has a pond measuring 20 m by 15 m. He stocks it with catfish fingerlings at 5 per square metre. How many fingerlings does he need?
questions.explanation: Pond area = 20 × 15 = 300 m². Number of fingerlings = 300 × 5 = 1,500.

whyNot.A: 300 is the area of the pond in square metres, not the number of fish.
whyNot.D: 175 adds the two sides and multiplies by 5: (20 + 15) × 5.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Cattle that graze heavily on young, lush legume pasture may develop a swollen left side and difficulty in breathing. This condition, called bloat, is caused by
options: a virus spread by biting flies
gas building up in the rumen faster than it can be belched out
a shortage of calcium in the blood after calving
questions.explanation: Fermentation in the rumen always produces gas, which is normally belched. Lush legumes can produce a stable froth that traps the gas, so pressure builds up in the rumen (on the left side) and presses on the lungs.

whyNot.D: A shortage of blood calcium after calving is milk fever.
whyNot.C: Worms cause poor growth and anaemia rather than sudden swelling of the rumen.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The law of diminishing returns states that as more units of a variable input are added to a fixed input,
options: the price of the product rises steadily
the extra output from each additional unit eventually falls
total output always rises at an increasing rate
questions.explanation: When more and more of a variable input (for example labour or fertiliser) is applied to a fixed input such as land, a point is reached after which each extra unit adds less output than the one before. Marginal product declines.

whyNot.C: Output may rise at an increasing rate at first, but the law says the additional output eventually falls.
whyNot.A: The law is about physical output, not prices.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which of the following is a special characteristic of land as a factor of production?
options: It is produced by human effort
Its supply rises when rent rises
It can be moved from place to place
questions.explanation: Land is a gift of nature. Its total quantity cannot be increased, and it cannot be moved from one location to another, although its quality can be improved.

whyNot.D: Land is immobile; it cannot be moved.
whyNot.A: Land is a free gift of nature, not man-made like capital.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Seeds, fertiliser and agrochemicals that are completely used up within one cropping season are classified as
questions.explanation: Working or circulating capital consists of inputs that are used up in a single production cycle and must be bought again, such as seeds, feed, fertiliser and fuel.

whyNot.C: Fixed capital, such as tractors and buildings, lasts for many seasons.
whyNot.B: Liquid capital is cash or assets that can quickly be turned into cash.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A broiler farmer in Abeokuta sold 500 birds at ₦6,000 each. His total variable cost was ₦2,100,000 and his fixed cost was ₦400,000. What was his gross margin?
questions.explanation: Total revenue = 500 × ₦6,000 = ₦3,000,000. Gross margin = total revenue − total variable cost = ₦3,000,000 − ₦2,100,000 = ₦900,000. Fixed cost is not subtracted in gross margin.

whyNot.A: ₦500,000 is the net profit (after also subtracting the fixed cost), not the gross margin.
whyNot.D: ₦3,000,000 is the total revenue.
whyNot.B: ₦2,500,000 is the total cost.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A farmer borrows ₦500,000 from a microfinance bank at 9% simple interest per year. How much interest will she pay after 2 years?
questions.explanation: Simple interest = principal × rate × time = ₦500,000 × 9/100 × 2 = ₦90,000.

whyNot.B: ₦45,000 is the interest for only one year.
whyNot.A: ₦590,000 is the total amount repaid (principal plus interest), not the interest.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Bad roads linking farming villages to towns are a marketing problem mainly because they
options: make farmers produce more than buyers want
force farmers to grade their produce
reduce the amount of rain on the farms
raise transport costs and cause perishable produce to spoil
questions.explanation: On poor roads vehicles travel slowly, break down and charge more. Perishable produce such as tomatoes and vegetables may rot before reaching the market, and farmers receive lower prices.

whyNot.A: Over-production is not caused by the state of the roads.
whyNot.B: Grading is a useful marketing function, not a problem caused by roads.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: At the peak of the harvest season, large quantities of oranges arrive in markets in Benue State and their price falls sharply. This is mainly because
options: the government has fixed a low price for oranges
the cost of producing oranges has risen
supply has increased greatly while demand has changed little
demand for oranges has risen sharply
questions.explanation: When supply increases a lot and demand stays about the same, sellers must lower their prices to sell the extra quantity. This is why prices of seasonal crops fall at harvest.

whyNot.D: A rise in demand would push prices up, not down.
whyNot.B: Higher production costs tend to raise prices, not lower them.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: An extension agent goes to a farmer's own farm and home to discuss the farmer's particular problems with him. This extension method is called
questions.explanation: A farm and home visit is an individual contact method. The agent sees the farmer's real situation and can give advice suited to him, which builds trust, although it reaches few farmers.

whyNot.A: A method demonstration shows a group how to carry out a practice.
whyNot.D: Mass media (radio, TV, newspapers) reaches many people at once without personal contact.
whyNot.B: An agricultural show displays produce and technologies to the public at one location.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A poultry farm has fixed costs of ₦600,000 for a season. Each crate of eggs sells for ₦3,500 and has a variable cost of ₦2,000. How many crates must be sold to break even?
questions.explanation: Each crate contributes ₦3,500 − ₦2,000 = ₦1,500 towards fixed costs. Break-even quantity = fixed cost ÷ contribution per crate = ₦600,000 ÷ ₦1,500 = 400 crates.
