questions.explanation: People who cannot read or do not know their rights are easily cheated or abused and rarely seek redress. Civic education and legal aid help to overcome this problem.

whyNot.A: Rural areas usually have too few courts, not too many.
whyNot.C: A free press helps to protect rights by exposing abuses.
whyNot.B: A written constitution sets out and protects rights.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Human rights are described as "inalienable". What does this mean?
options: They are enjoyed only by citizens of the country
They are granted by the President and can be withdrawn by him
They cannot be taken away from a person except in situations allowed by law
They apply only to adults who pay tax
questions.explanation: Inalienable rights belong to people because they are human. They cannot be given away or arbitrarily taken away; they may only be restricted in the limited circumstances the law allows, such as a lawful court sentence.

whyNot.A: Many human rights protect everyone, including foreigners.
whyNot.B: Human rights are not gifts of the government that it can freely withdraw.
whyNot.D: Human rights belong to all persons, including children and non-taxpayers.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Mr Adebayo, a Yoruba trader, buys land in Kano, but community leaders say that only indigenes may own land there. Which right in section 43 of the Constitution protects him?
options: Right to acquire and own immovable property anywhere in Nigeria
Right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Right to dignity of the human person
questions.explanation: Section 43 states that every citizen of Nigeria shall have the right to acquire and own immovable property anywhere in Nigeria. Being a non-indigene does not take away this right.

whyNot.C: Section 38 concerns belief and worship.
whyNot.D: Section 34 protects against torture and degrading treatment.
whyNot.A: Section 35 protects against unlawful arrest and detention.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: How many articles does the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) contain?
questions.explanation: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights has a preamble and 30 articles setting out basic civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights for all people.

whyNot.C: Ten is the number of amendments in the US Bill of Rights, not the UDHR articles.
whyNot.A: Forty-five is not the number of UDHR articles.
whyNot.B: Sixty is not the number of UDHR articles.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: A school refuses to admit a pupil only because her parents were not married when she was born. Which right is violated?
options: Right to private and family life
questions.explanation: Section 42(2) provides that no citizen shall be subjected to any disability or deprivation merely because of the circumstances of his or her birth. Refusing admission for this reason is discrimination.

whyNot.A: Private and family life protects homes, letters and communications from interference.
whyNot.B: Personal liberty protects against unlawful arrest and detention.
whyNot.C: Freedom of movement is about moving and living freely within Nigeria.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: A judge hears a land dispute in which his own brother is one of the parties. Which principle of fair hearing is broken?
options: No one should be a judge in his own cause (nemo judex in causa sua)
Hear the other side (audi alteram partem)
The welfare of the people is the supreme law (salus populi)
questions.explanation: Nemo judex in causa sua means no one should judge a case in which he has an interest. A judge whose brother is a party may be biased, so he should step aside. Section 36 requires a court that is independent and impartial.

whyNot.C: Audi alteram partem requires both sides to be heard; the problem here is the judge's interest, not refusing to hear a side.
whyNot.A: Caveat emptor is a rule of commercial law about buying goods.
whyNot.D: Salus populi is a political maxim, not a rule of fair hearing.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Under section 35(3) of the 1999 Constitution, what must a person who is arrested be told, in writing, within twenty-four hours and in a language he understands?
options: The date on which his trial will end
The facts and grounds for his arrest or detention
The punishment he will receive if convicted
The names of all witnesses against him
questions.explanation: Section 35(3) requires that any person arrested or detained be informed in writing within twenty-four hours, in a language he understands, of the facts and grounds for the arrest or detention. This helps him to prepare a defence and to challenge an unlawful arrest.

whyNot.A: No one can know in advance when a trial will end.
whyNot.D: The Constitution does not require the names of witnesses within 24 hours of arrest.
whyNot.C: Punishment is decided by a court only after conviction.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: A Nigerian claims that her human rights were violated by an ECOWAS member state. Which sub-regional court, based in Abuja, can hear her case?
options: The ECOWAS Community Court of Justice
The African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights
questions.explanation: The ECOWAS Community Court of Justice, based in Abuja, can hear cases of human rights violations in member states, and individuals may bring such cases directly to it.

whyNot.A: The International Court of Justice at The Hague hears disputes between states, not individual complaints.
whyNot.C: The African Court is a continental court and sits in Arusha, Tanzania.
whyNot.D: The Federal High Court is a national court, not a sub-regional one.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which arm of government is responsible for carrying out (implementing) laws?
questions.explanation: The executive, headed in Nigeria by the President at the federal level and governors in the states, implements laws and runs the day-to-day business of government.

whyNot.D: The legislature makes laws.
whyNot.B: The judiciary interprets laws and settles disputes.
whyNot.C: The electorate (voters) chooses leaders; it is not an arm of government.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: A. V. Dicey stated three principles of the rule of law. Which of the following is one of them?
questions.explanation: Dicey's three pillars are the supremacy of the law (no arbitrary power), equality before the law, and the protection of individual rights by the ordinary courts.

whyNot.C: Party supremacy over law is the opposite of the rule of law.
whyNot.D: Fusion of powers is a feature of parliamentary systems, not a principle of the rule of law.
whyNot.B: Immunity is a limitation on the rule of law, not one of its principles.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Why is voting by secret ballot important in elections?
options: It lets party agents see how each person voted
It allows voters to choose freely without fear of intimidation
It makes counting the votes unnecessary
It allows only literate people to vote
questions.explanation: With a secret ballot no one knows how a particular voter voted. Voters can therefore choose freely without fear of threats, punishment or pressure.

whyNot.A: Revealing each person's vote would destroy secrecy.
whyNot.C: Votes still have to be counted.
whyNot.D: Secret ballot does not restrict who may vote.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: After an election, the winning party forms the government, but opposition parties are free to criticise its policies and campaign for the next election. Which democratic principle does this show?
options: Majority rule with respect for minority rights
questions.explanation: In a democracy the majority governs, but the minority keeps its rights: it may criticise, organise and seek to win the next election.

whyNot.A: One-party rule does not allow opposition parties.
whyNot.B: Separation of powers divides government functions among three arms.
whyNot.C: Federal character concerns fair spread of appointments among states.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Under the rule of law, when may a person lawfully be punished?
options: Whenever the police suspect him of a crime
Whenever a traditional ruler orders it
Whenever a government official is displeased with him
Only for a breach of the law proved before a court
questions.explanation: Dicey taught that no one should be punished except for a distinct breach of law established in the ordinary courts. Suspicion or the anger of officials is not enough.

whyNot.C: Punishing people at the will of officials is arbitrary rule.
whyNot.A: Suspicion must be proved in court before punishment.
whyNot.B: Traditional rulers cannot lawfully order punishment outside the court process.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which condition is most necessary for an election to be free and fair?
options: Allowing only party members to vote
A single candidate for each office
Voting by a show of hands under supervision of party agents
An independent and impartial electoral commission
questions.explanation: An independent and impartial electoral body that is not controlled by the government or any party can organise elections honestly, so that the results reflect the will of the voters.

whyNot.B: A single candidate gives voters no real choice.
whyNot.C: Open voting exposes voters to intimidation; a secret ballot is needed.
whyNot.A: Every qualified adult citizen should be allowed to vote, not only party members.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: A court grants bail to Ali, but the security agency holding him refuses to release him for several months. Which principle is most directly undermined?
questions.explanation: Under the rule of law, government and its agencies must obey the law and court orders like everyone else. Ignoring a court order granting bail puts the agency above the law and undermines the rule of law.

whyNot.A: Federal character concerns fair representation of states in appointments.
whyNot.C: Delegated legislation is law-making by subordinate bodies.
whyNot.D: Collective responsibility is about ministers standing together on cabinet decisions.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: For how many years does an elected President of Nigeria hold office before he must seek re-election?
questions.explanation: Section 135 provides that the President holds office for four years from the date of taking the oath of office. He may be re-elected only once (section 137), so the maximum is two terms.

whyNot.A: Five years is the term in some other countries, not Nigeria.
whyNot.B: Six years is not the term under the 1999 Constitution.
whyNot.D: Seven years is not the term under the 1999 Constitution.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Under section 9 of the 1999 Constitution, an ordinary amendment to the Constitution needs the support of two-thirds of all members of each House of the National Assembly and approval by the Houses of Assembly of at least two-thirds of all the states. What is the minimum number of states needed?
questions.explanation: Nigeria has 36 states. Two-thirds of 36 is 36 × 2 ÷ 3 = 24, so at least 24 State Houses of Assembly must approve the amendment. This difficult procedure makes the Constitution rigid. (Amending section 8 or Chapter IV needs even more: four-fifths of each House of the National Assembly.)

whyNot.C: 18 is only half of the 36 states.
whyNot.A: 19 is a simple majority of 36, not two-thirds.
whyNot.B: 27 is three-quarters of 36.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: During the impeachment of a state governor, who appoints the seven-member panel that investigates the allegations of misconduct?
options: The Chief Judge of the state
The Speaker of the State House of Assembly
questions.explanation: Section 188(5) provides that the Chief Judge of the state, at the request of the Speaker of the House of Assembly, appoints a panel of seven persons of unquestionable integrity to investigate the allegations against the governor.

whyNot.D: The Speaker requests the panel but does not appoint it.
whyNot.A: The President has no role in impeaching a governor.
whyNot.B: The Chief Justice of Nigeria plays no part in a state governor's impeachment; for the President, the panel is appointed by the Chief Justice (section 143).

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which agency controls the manufacture, importation and sale of food and drugs in Nigeria?
options: National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP)
National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC)
questions.explanation: NAFDAC regulates and controls the manufacture, importation, distribution, advertisement and sale of food, drugs, cosmetics and chemicals in Nigeria, and fights fake and substandard medicines.

whyNot.D: The NDLEA fights illegal hard drugs such as cocaine and heroin.
whyNot.A: SON sets and enforces quality standards for manufactured products in general.
whyNot.B: NAPTIP fights human trafficking.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which of the following could be a warning sign that a student is abusing drugs?
options: Red eyes, sudden fall in grades and withdrawal from family
Eating balanced meals and sleeping well
questions.explanation: Common signs of drug abuse include red or glassy eyes, mood swings, loss of interest in school, falling grades, keeping bad company, stealing money and withdrawing from family.

whyNot.C: Regular attendance and improving grades are signs of a healthy student.
whyNot.A: Joining a club is a healthy activity.
whyNot.D: Good eating and sleeping habits are not warning signs.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: What does the abbreviation HIV stand for?
questions.explanation: HIV stands for Human Immunodeficiency Virus. It attacks the body's immune system, and if untreated it can lead to AIDS (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome).

whyNot.A: There is no vaccine against HIV, and 'V' stands for virus.
whyNot.D: This is not what the letters stand for.
whyNot.C: HIV is a virus, not a vitamin.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which of the following is an effect of human trafficking on Nigeria as a country?
options: It reduces the spread of diseases
It improves the country's relations with other nations
It increases the number of skilled workers at home
It damages the country's international image and robs it of young human resources
questions.explanation: Human trafficking makes Nigeria look bad abroad, leads to the loss of young people who could contribute to national development, and exposes victims to abuse, disease and death.

whyNot.C: Trafficking takes young people away; it does not add skilled workers.
whyNot.B: It strains relations with other countries.
whyNot.A: Victims are often exposed to diseases such as HIV, which can spread.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which federal agency coordinates Nigeria's national response to HIV and AIDS?
options: National Agency for the Control of AIDS (NACA)
National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC)
questions.explanation: NACA coordinates and oversees the national response to HIV and AIDS, working with government agencies, health workers and civil society on prevention, treatment and care.

whyNot.D: NAFDAC regulates food and drugs generally.
whyNot.B: NOA handles public enlightenment and national values.
whyNot.C: NEMA handles disasters and emergencies.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which of the following is the best way to help a person who is addicted to drugs?
options: Giving the person more money to buy drugs
Driving the person away from home
Taking the person for counselling and treatment at a rehabilitation centre
questions.explanation: Drug addiction is a health problem. Counselling, medical treatment and rehabilitation, together with support from family, help the person to stop drug use and return to normal life.

whyNot.B: Rejection pushes the person deeper into drugs and bad company.
whyNot.A: More money feeds the addiction.
whyNot.C: Mockery causes shame and does not help the person recover.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: In a NECO examination, a man is caught writing a paper in place of a registered candidate. Which form of examination malpractice is this?
questions.explanation: Impersonation is when someone sits for an examination on behalf of the real candidate, pretending to be that person. It is a serious examination offence.

whyNot.A: Collusion is candidates helping each other or copying in the hall.
whyNot.D: Leakage is exposing the questions before the examination.
whyNot.C: Smuggling foreign materials is bringing notes or textbooks into the hall.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Sniffing glue, petrol or other solvents to get "high" is the abuse of which class of substances?
questions.explanation: Inhalants are substances whose fumes are breathed in to produce a high, such as glue, petrol, paint thinners and some aerosols. They can cause brain damage and sudden death.

whyNot.D: Hallucinogens, such as LSD, mainly cause hallucinations.
whyNot.A: Narcotics, such as heroin, relieve pain and cause drowsiness.
whyNot.B: Stimulants, such as cocaine, speed up the nervous system.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Trafficked women abroad are told they owe their traffickers a large "debt" for travel costs and must work without pay until it is repaid. What is this method of control called?
questions.explanation: Debt bondage is forcing a person to work to pay off a debt that is made so large, or so unclear, that it can never really be paid. Traffickers use it, along with threats and seizure of passports, to keep victims under control.

whyNot.A: Collective bargaining is negotiation between workers' unions and employers.
whyNot.B: Apprenticeship is learning a trade under a master, usually by agreement.
whyNot.D: Cooperative saving is a voluntary arrangement for members to save together.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Tramadol, a prescription painkiller widely abused by young people in Nigeria, belongs to which class of drugs?
questions.explanation: Tramadol is an opioid painkiller. Like other opioids, it acts on the brain to reduce pain and can cause drowsiness, dependence, seizures and death from overdose when misused.

whyNot.B: Stimulants, such as cocaine and amphetamine, speed up the nervous system.
whyNot.D: Hallucinogens, such as LSD, distort perception.
whyNot.C: Inhalants are fumes breathed in, such as glue and petrol.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which of the following is a political office holder rather than a civil servant?
options: A clerical officer in a ministry
questions.explanation: A minister is a political appointee who heads a ministry for a period and leaves with the government. Permanent Secretaries, directors and clerical officers are career civil servants.

whyNot.C: A Permanent Secretary is the most senior civil servant in a ministry.
whyNot.B: A director is a career civil servant.
whyNot.D: A clerical officer is a career civil servant.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which of the following is a professional association that also acts as a pressure group?
questions.explanation: The Nigerian Medical Association is a body of medical doctors. It protects its members' interests and tries to influence government health policies, so it acts as a pressure group.

whyNot.C: The Ministry of Health is a government ministry.
whyNot.A: The Army is a government institution for defence.
whyNot.B: INEC is a government body that conducts elections.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: An association places adverts in newspapers and holds radio talk shows to win public support for its campaign. Which method of pressure group activity is this?
questions.explanation: Pressure groups use newspapers, radio, television and social media to inform the public and win support for their cause, which in turn puts pressure on government.

whyNot.D: A strike is workers stopping work.
whyNot.C: Litigation is going to court.
whyNot.B: A boycott is refusing to buy, use or take part in something.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Under Nigeria's Contributory Pension Scheme, which body regulates and supervises pension matters?
questions.explanation: The National Pension Commission (PenCom) regulates and supervises the Contributory Pension Scheme, under which employers and employees contribute to retirement savings accounts managed by licensed pension fund administrators.

whyNot.B: The CBN regulates banks and monetary policy.
whyNot.D: The FIRS collects federal taxes.
whyNot.C: The SEC regulates the capital market (shares and other securities), not pensions.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: An officer in a ministry delays the files of people who are not from his own ethnic group. Which principle of the civil service is he breaking?
questions.explanation: Impartiality requires civil servants to treat all citizens fairly and equally, without favouring anyone because of ethnic group, religion or other personal ties.

whyNot.C: Anonymity means civil servants are not publicly credited or blamed for policies.
whyNot.A: Permanence means civil servants stay in office when governments change.
whyNot.D: Hierarchy is the chain of command in the service.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: A director in a government agency fills all new vacancies with his relatives, ignoring better-qualified applicants. Which problem is this?
questions.explanation: Nepotism is favouring one's relatives in giving jobs, contracts or promotions. It ignores merit, lowers efficiency and is a form of corruption.

whyNot.B: Red tape is excessive rules and slow procedures.
whyNot.D: Anonymity is a principle of the civil service, not a problem.
whyNot.C: Delegation is passing tasks to subordinates, which is normal management.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Local non-governmental organisations send trained observers to polling units and publish reports on irregularities. Which role of civil society does this show?
options: Promoting transparency and accountability in elections
Making electoral laws for the country
Declaring the official results of the elections
Conducting the elections on behalf of INEC
questions.explanation: Civil society organisations act as watchdogs. By observing elections and reporting problems, they promote transparency and help to hold the electoral body and politicians accountable.

whyNot.D: INEC, not NGOs, conducts elections.
whyNot.C: Only the electoral commission's returning officers declare official results.
whyNot.B: Electoral laws are made by the National Assembly.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which institution in Badagry, Lagos State, was set up to train senior managers in the public service in Nigeria?
options: The National Institute for Policy and Strategic Studies
The Administrative Staff College of Nigeria (ASCON)
questions.explanation: The Administrative Staff College of Nigeria (ASCON), located at Topo, Badagry, trains public servants in management and administration to improve efficiency in the public service.

whyNot.A: The National Institute for Policy and Strategic Studies is at Kuru, near Jos.
whyNot.D: The Nigerian Defence Academy is in Kaduna and trains military officers.
whyNot.C: The Nigerian Law School trains law graduates for the Bar.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: The office of the ombudsman, on which Nigeria's Public Complaints Commission is modelled, first developed in which country?
questions.explanation: The ombudsman began in Sweden in 1809 as an official who receives complaints from citizens against government officials. Many countries copied it; Nigeria's version is the Public Complaints Commission.

whyNot.C: The USA did not originate the ombudsman office.
whyNot.A: France adopted a similar office much later.
whyNot.D: Ghana has its own commission but did not originate the idea.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between the public service and the civil service?
options: The public service is wider; it includes the civil service as well as public corporations, the armed forces and other government agencies
They are completely separate, with no officials in common
The public service is made up only of elected politicians
The civil service is wider; it includes the public service as one of its departments
questions.explanation: The public service covers everyone employed by government: civil servants in ministries plus staff of public corporations and parastatals, the armed forces, the police, the judiciary's staff and others. The civil service is the part of it that works in ministries and departments.

whyNot.D: This reverses the relationship: the civil service is part of the public service.
whyNot.B: Civil servants are themselves public servants, so the two overlap.
whyNot.C: Politicians are political office holders, not career public servants.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A small retailer in Ibadan cannot afford to buy a whole carton of 48 tins of milk, so the wholesaler sells him 6 tins at a time. This service of the wholesaler is called
questions.explanation: Breaking bulk means buying goods in large quantities from producers and dividing them into the smaller quantities that retailers can afford and sell. Selling 6 tins out of a carton of 48 is breaking bulk.

whyNot.C: Warehousing is storing goods until they are needed, not dividing them into smaller lots.
whyNot.D: Grading is sorting goods into classes by quality or size.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A trader who carries goods on her head and moves from street to street selling to anyone who calls her is best described as
questions.explanation: A hawker is an itinerant (moving) retailer who has no fixed shop. She carries her goods around and sells small quantities directly to consumers wherever she finds them.

whyNot.D: A wholesaler buys in bulk and sells mainly to retailers, usually from a warehouse.
whyNot.A: A broker brings buyers and sellers together for a commission and does not carry the goods himself.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A provision shop made sales of ₦600,000 in a year. Its average stock, valued at selling price, was ₦75,000. What was its rate of turnover?
questions.explanation: When stock is valued at selling price, rate of turnover = sales ÷ average stock at selling price = ₦600,000 ÷ ₦75,000 = 8. The stock was sold and replaced 8 times in the year.

whyNot.A: 0.125 divides average stock by sales, which is the wrong way round.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which of the following is an invisible import for Nigeria?
options: A Nigerian student paying school fees to a university in Britain
Foreign tourists spending money at a resort in Calabar
Nigeria buying tractors from a factory in Brazil
A Nigerian firm selling cocoa beans to a buyer in the Netherlands
questions.explanation: Invisible trade is trade in services. When a Nigerian pays for a service provided abroad (education in Britain), money leaves Nigeria, so it is an invisible import.

whyNot.C: Tractors are physical goods coming in, so they are a visible import.
whyNot.B: Foreign tourists bring money into Nigeria, so this is an invisible export.
whyNot.D: Cocoa is a physical good going out, so it is a visible export.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A trader's sales for the month were ₦500,000 and her gross profit margin was 20% of sales. What was her cost of sales?
questions.explanation: Gross profit = 20% of ₦500,000 = ₦100,000. Cost of sales = sales − gross profit = ₦500,000 − ₦100,000 = ₦400,000.

whyNot.B: ₦100,000 is the gross profit, not the cost of sales.
whyNot.D: ₦416,667 treats 20% as a mark-up on cost (500,000 ÷ 1.2), but the question gives a margin on sales.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: An agent who sells goods on behalf of a principal and, for an extra commission, guarantees that the buyers he introduces will pay is called
options: a commission agent who bears no risk
questions.explanation: A del credere agent receives an additional commission (the del credere commission) in return for guaranteeing his principal against bad debts from the customers he finds. If a buyer fails to pay, the agent pays.

whyNot.D: A broker only brings buyers and sellers together; he does not guarantee payment.
whyNot.A: An auctioneer sells to the highest bidder in public; guaranteeing buyers' debts is not part of his work.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Several independent shop owners in Kaduna agree with one wholesaler to buy all their stock through him, display a common sign and share advertising costs, while each still owns his shop. This arrangement is a
questions.explanation: In a voluntary chain, independent retailers link up with a wholesaler. They gain bulk-buying prices and joint advertising, while each retailer keeps ownership and control of his own shop.

whyNot.A: A multiple shop (chain store) has many branches all owned and controlled by one company.
whyNot.D: A department store is one large shop with many departments under one owner.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which of the following is a disadvantage of the self-service method of retailing?
options: It needs more sales assistants than counter service
It makes customers wait longer to be attended to
It prevents goods from being displayed openly
It increases the risk of goods being stolen by shoppers
questions.explanation: In self-service, goods are on open shelves and customers handle them freely. This saves labour and time, but makes shoplifting easier, so the shop must spend on security and checks.

whyNot.A: Self-service reduces the number of sales assistants needed; that is one of its advantages.
whyNot.C: Self-service depends on displaying goods openly on shelves.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A government agency disposes of used vehicles by inviting the public to a sale where each vehicle goes to the person who offers the highest price. This method of selling is
questions.explanation: At an auction, goods are offered publicly and buyers bid against one another; the goods are sold to the highest bidder.

whyNot.C: Hire purchase is buying by instalments, not bidding.
whyNot.D: Barter is exchanging goods for goods without money.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A trader adds 20% to cost to get her selling price. Her opening stock was ₦30,000 and her closing stock ₦50,000, both at cost. Sales for the year were ₦480,000. What was her rate of stock turnover?
questions.explanation: Stock is at cost, so use cost of sales. Selling price = 120% of cost, so cost of sales = ₦480,000 ÷ 1.2 = ₦400,000. Average stock = (₦30,000 + ₦50,000) ÷ 2 = ₦40,000. Rate of turnover = ₦400,000 ÷ ₦40,000 = 10 times.

whyNot.A: 12 comes from dividing sales (₦480,000) by average stock at cost, which mixes selling price with cost.
whyNot.D: 8 comes from dividing cost of sales by closing stock (₦50,000) instead of average stock.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Mrs Adeyemi's shop is insured against fire with a policy excess of ₦20,000. A fire causes damage worth ₦250,000, and the claim is accepted. How much will the insurer pay?
questions.explanation: An excess is the first part of every claim that the insured must bear herself. The insurer pays the loss minus the excess: ₦250,000 − ₦20,000 = ₦230,000.

whyNot.A: ₦250,000 ignores the excess that the insured must bear.
whyNot.B: ₦270,000 wrongly adds the excess instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A shipping company insures the ship itself against damage or loss at sea. This class of marine insurance is called
questions.explanation: Marine insurance has three main parts: hull (the ship itself), cargo (the goods carried) and freight (the payment due for carrying the goods). Insuring the vessel is hull insurance.

whyNot.A: Cargo insurance covers the goods on board, not the ship.
whyNot.B: Freight insurance covers the money the shipowner would earn for carrying the goods.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A supermarket owner wants protection against losses caused by cashiers who steal money from the tills. Which type of insurance should he buy?
questions.explanation: Fidelity guarantee insurance protects an employer against loss of money or goods through the dishonesty (fraud, theft, embezzlement) of his own employees.

whyNot.D: Burglary insurance covers theft by people who break into the premises, not by employees.
whyNot.B: Public liability insurance covers claims by members of the public injured on the premises.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A trader wants a bank account from which she can pay her suppliers by cheque. Which account should she open?
questions.explanation: A current account is designed for businesses and people who make frequent payments. The holder is given a cheque book and can withdraw or pay out money at any time.

whyNot.A: A fixed deposit account keeps money for a fixed period to earn interest; no cheques are drawn on it.
whyNot.C: A savings account is for saving and earning interest; it does not normally come with a cheque book.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which means of transport is most suitable for carrying heavy, bulky goods such as cement and steel rods over long distances on land at a low cost per tonne?
questions.explanation: Trains can pull many wagons at once, so the cost per tonne of carrying heavy bulky goods over long distances on land is low.

whyNot.B: Air transport is fast but very expensive and has limited space for heavy goods.
whyNot.A: Pipelines carry only liquids and gases, not solid goods like cement.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A television advert says, 'Brand Z soap washes whiter than any other soap.' This is mainly an example of
questions.explanation: Competitive (persuasive) advertising tries to win customers from rival brands by claiming that the product is better than the others.

whyNot.A: Informative advertising simply gives facts such as price, location or uses without comparing brands.
whyNot.D: Collective advertising is done jointly by a group of producers to promote a whole product type, not one brand.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A trader borrows ₦500,000 from a bank at 18% simple interest per year and repays it after 8 months. How much interest does she pay?
questions.explanation: Simple interest = principal × rate × time. Time = 8 months = 8/12 year. Interest = ₦500,000 × 18/100 × 8/12 = ₦60,000.

whyNot.D: ₦90,000 is the interest for a full year, not 8 months.
whyNot.B: ₦72,000 treats 8 months as 0.8 of a year; 8 months is 8/12 of a year.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which life assurance policy pays the sum assured at the end of a fixed period, or earlier if the insured person dies before then?
options: Term policy that pays only on death
questions.explanation: An endowment policy is both a form of saving and protection: the insured receives the sum assured at the end of the agreed period, or his dependants receive it if he dies earlier.

whyNot.B: A whole life policy pays only when the insured dies, whenever that is.
whyNot.D: A term policy pays only if death occurs within the term; nothing is paid if the insured survives.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: After paying premiums on a life policy for eight years, Mr Obi decides to end the policy before it matures. The amount the insurer pays him on ending it is called the
questions.explanation: When a life policy holder ends (surrenders) the policy before maturity, the insurer pays back part of the value built up from the premiums. This amount is the surrender value, and it is usually less than the sum assured.

whyNot.A: The sum assured is the full amount payable at maturity or on death, not on early termination.
whyNot.B: The premium is what the insured pays the insurer, not what he receives.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Bayo has only third-party motor insurance. He carelessly drives into Tunde's parked car, damaging both cars. What will Bayo's insurer pay for?
options: The damage to Tunde's car only
Nothing, because Bayo caused the accident
The damage to Bayo's car only
questions.explanation: Third-party insurance covers the insured's legal liability to other people (third parties) for injury or damage to their property. It does not cover damage to the insured's own vehicle; that needs a comprehensive policy.

whyNot.D: The insured's own car is not covered by a third-party policy.
whyNot.C: Covering both cars would require a comprehensive policy.
whyNot.B: Third-party cover exists precisely to pay when the insured is liable for harming others.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of a sole proprietorship?
options: The business can raise capital by selling shares to the public
The business continues even after the owner dies
The owner can take decisions quickly without consulting anyone
The owner has limited liability for the debts of the business
questions.explanation: A sole proprietor is the only owner and manager, so he can make and carry out decisions at once without waiting for partners or a board.

whyNot.D: A sole proprietor has unlimited liability.
whyNot.A: Only public companies can sell shares to the public.
whyNot.B: A sole proprietorship has no separate legal existence and usually ends with the owner's death.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which of the following can bring an ordinary partnership to an end?
options: A fall in the firm's profit for one year
The employment of a new manager
The opening of a new branch
The death of one of the partners
questions.explanation: An ordinary partnership is based on the personal relationship of the partners, so the death, bankruptcy or insanity of a partner dissolves it unless the deed says otherwise.

whyNot.B: Employing a manager is a normal business decision; it does not dissolve the firm.
whyNot.A: A fall in profit for one year does not end a partnership.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which document, issued by the Corporate Affairs Commission, shows that a company has been legally formed and exists as a separate legal person?
questions.explanation: Once the registration documents are approved, the Corporate Affairs Commission issues a certificate of incorporation. From that date the company is a legal person that can own property, sue and be sued.

whyNot.B: A prospectus invites the public to buy shares; it does not create the company.
whyNot.D: A partnership deed is an agreement between partners, not a company document.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A company's shares sell on the stock market at ₦4.00 each. It pays a dividend of 20 kobo per share. What is the dividend yield?
questions.explanation: Dividend yield = dividend per share ÷ market price per share × 100. 20 kobo = ₦0.20, so yield = 0.20 ÷ 4.00 × 100 = 5%.

whyNot.C: 20% treats 20 kobo as if it were a percentage.
whyNot.A: 0.5% comes from a slip with the decimal point (0.20 ÷ 40).

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: At the end of the year, a consumers' cooperative shop shares its surplus among members according to
options: the number of shares each member's family holds in other firms
the value of goods each member bought from the shop
the number of years each member has been in the society
questions.explanation: In a consumers' cooperative, the surplus is returned to members as a dividend on purchases: the more a member bought from the society, the larger his share.

whyNot.D: Length of membership does not decide a member's share of the surplus.
whyNot.A: Age has nothing to do with sharing the surplus.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which of the following is a common problem of public corporations in Nigeria?
options: Unlimited liability of the managers for their debts
Inefficiency caused by political interference in their management
Lack of any capital because government cannot fund them
Too much competition from many shareholders' meetings
questions.explanation: Public corporations are owned and controlled by government. Appointments and decisions are often influenced by politics rather than merit, which leads to inefficiency and losses.

whyNot.C: Public corporations are financed by government, so a total lack of capital is not their typical problem.
whyNot.A: Managers of public corporations do not have unlimited liability.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Ngozi and Emeka are partners sharing profits and losses in the ratio 3 : 2 after Ngozi receives a salary of ₦40,000 a year. If the firm's profit for the year is ₦240,000, what is Ngozi's total share?

whyNot.B: ₦144,000 is 3/5 of the whole ₦240,000, ignoring the salary.
whyNot.D: ₦120,000 leaves out her salary.
whyNot.C: ₦184,000 adds the salary to 3/5 of the whole profit, counting the salary twice.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A well-known businessman allows a partnership to use his name to attract customers but contributes no capital and takes no part in running it. He is called
questions.explanation: A nominal (quasi) partner only lends his name and reputation to the firm. He contributes no capital and does not manage, but he can be held liable to outsiders who dealt with the firm because of his name.

whyNot.D: A general partner has unlimited liability and usually takes part in managing the firm.
whyNot.C: A limited partner contributes capital and has limited liability; the businessman here contributes no capital.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A company keeps part of its profit each year instead of paying it all out as dividends, and uses it to buy new machines. This source of finance is called
questions.explanation: Retained profit (ploughing back profit) is the part of profit kept in the business rather than shared out. It is an internal source of finance and need not be repaid.

whyNot.D: An overdraft is borrowed from a bank and must be repaid with interest.
whyNot.A: A debenture issue raises a long-term loan from outside lenders.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Two banks agree to combine and form one bank, with the shareholders of both becoming shareholders of the new bank. This is called
questions.explanation: A merger (amalgamation) is the coming together of two or more firms, by agreement, to form a single business.

whyNot.A: Privatisation is the sale of government-owned enterprises to private owners.
whyNot.C: Nationalisation is government taking over private businesses.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which document goes with the goods when the seller's van delivers them, and is signed by the buyer as proof that the goods have been received?
questions.explanation: The delivery note travels with the goods. The buyer checks the goods against it and signs a copy, which the driver returns to the seller as proof of delivery.

whyNot.D: A pro forma invoice is sent before the goods, often to request payment in advance.
whyNot.A: A letter of enquiry is sent by the buyer to ask about goods and prices.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A seller replies to a buyer's letter of enquiry with a document stating the prices, terms of payment and delivery of the goods requested. This document is a
questions.explanation: A quotation is the seller's answer to an enquiry. It tells the buyer the price of the goods and the terms on which they can be supplied.

whyNot.A: A credit note reduces an amount already charged, for example for returned goods.
whyNot.C: A receipt acknowledges payment that has already been made.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: In a cheque, the bank on which the cheque is drawn and which is ordered to pay is called the
questions.explanation: A cheque has three parties: the drawer (account holder who writes it), the drawee (the bank told to pay) and the payee (the person to be paid).

whyNot.B: The drawer is the customer who writes and signs the cheque.
whyNot.A: The payee is the person named to receive the money.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A seller sends a buyer a document telling him that the goods he ordered have been dispatched and when they are expected to arrive. This document is
questions.explanation: An advice note is sent separately from the goods to inform the buyer that they are on the way, so that he can prepare to receive them and check them on arrival.

whyNot.C: An invoice is the bill showing the amount the buyer owes for the goods.
whyNot.A: An order comes from the buyer, not the seller.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: On 2 March, Musa wrote a cheque to his supplier but dated it 30 March. The bank should not pay the cheque before 30 March because it is
questions.explanation: A post-dated cheque carries a date later than the day it was written. The bank will not pay it until the date written on it arrives.

whyNot.C: A stale cheque is one presented too long after its date, not before it.
whyNot.B: Crossing affects how a cheque is paid (into an account), not when it is paid.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A buyer orders 40 cartons of noodles at ₦2,500 per carton. The seller allows a 15% trade discount and adds ₦5,000 for carriage. What is the invoice total?
questions.explanation: Gross price = 40 × ₦2,500 = ₦100,000. Trade discount = 15% × ₦100,000 = ₦15,000, leaving ₦85,000. Add carriage of ₦5,000: invoice total = ₦90,000. Trade discount is taken off the price of the goods only, not the carriage.

whyNot.A: ₦85,000 leaves out the carriage charge.
whyNot.D: ₦89,250 wrongly takes the trade discount off the carriage as well.
whyNot.C: ₦105,000 ignores the trade discount.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A trader in Kano hands goods to a road haulage company for delivery to a buyer in Port Harcourt. Which document, filled in by the sender, travels with the goods and gives the carrier details of the consignment?
questions.explanation: A consignment note (waybill) is used when goods are sent by road or rail through a carrier. It names the sender and receiver and describes the goods, and it accompanies them on the journey.

whyNot.C: A bill of lading is used for goods carried by sea.
whyNot.B: An air waybill is used for goods carried by air.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A written, signed and unconditional promise by one person to pay a stated sum of money to another person on demand or at a fixed future date is
questions.explanation: A promissory note is made by the debtor himself, promising to pay. A bill of exchange and a cheque are orders given to someone else to pay.

whyNot.A: A bill of exchange is an order drawn by the creditor on the debtor, not a promise by the debtor.
whyNot.C: A cheque is an order to a bank to pay, not a personal promise.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A wholesaler's catalogue price for a freezer is ₦50,000. A retailer is given trade discounts of 20% and then a further 10%. What does the retailer pay?
questions.explanation: Successive discounts are taken one after the other. After 20%: ₦50,000 × 0.80 = ₦40,000. After a further 10% of ₦40,000: ₦40,000 × 0.90 = ₦36,000.

whyNot.D: ₦35,000 wrongly adds the two discounts to 30% of ₦50,000.
whyNot.C: ₦40,000 applies only the first discount.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Mr Bello signs an authority allowing his insurance company to collect each month, from his bank account, whatever premium falls due, even if the amount changes. This method of payment is a
questions.explanation: Under a direct debit, the payee (here the insurer) claims the money from the payer's account using the payer's signed authority, and the amount may vary. Under a standing order, the payer instructs his own bank to pay a fixed sum.

whyNot.A: A standing order is set up by the payer for a fixed amount; it does not let the payee collect varying sums.
whyNot.C: A bank draft is a single cheque drawn by a bank on itself, used for one payment.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A car manufacturer calls back all cars of one model sold in Nigeria to replace faulty brakes free of charge. This mainly protects the consumer's right to
questions.explanation: A product recall removes or repairs goods that could cause harm. Faulty brakes endanger life, so the recall protects the consumer's right to safety.

whyNot.C: The right to choice is about having a variety of products and sellers to choose from.
whyNot.D: The right to be heard is about consumers' views being considered in decisions.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Traders keep large quantities of sugar in their stores and refuse to sell, waiting for the price to rise because of scarcity. This unfair practice is called
questions.explanation: Hoarding is deliberately keeping goods off the market to create artificial scarcity, so that prices rise and the hoarder can sell later at a high profit. It harms consumers.

whyNot.C: Branding is giving a product a distinctive name or mark.
whyNot.B: Breaking bulk is dividing large quantities into small lots for sale, which helps consumers.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A trader mixes palm oil with cheap coloured vegetable oil and sells it as pure palm oil. This practice is known as
questions.explanation: Adulteration is lowering the quality of a product by mixing it with inferior or harmful substances while selling it as pure. It cheats consumers and can endanger their health.

whyNot.A: Standardisation means making products meet set quality standards, the opposite of this practice.
whyNot.B: Grading is sorting goods into quality classes honestly.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A filling station's pump showed that 40 litres of fuel had been sold at ₦900 per litre, but an inspection proved that only 37.5 litres were actually delivered. By how much was the customer overcharged?
questions.explanation: Litres missing = 40 − 37.5 = 2.5 litres. Overcharge = 2.5 × ₦900 = ₦2,250. (The customer paid ₦36,000 but received fuel worth only ₦33,750.)

whyNot.C: ₦36,000 is what the customer paid in total, not the overcharge.
whyNot.D: ₦33,750 is the value of the fuel actually delivered.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: The organised effort of consumers, together with government and other bodies, to protect buyers against unfair practices of sellers is known as
questions.explanation: Consumerism is the movement that seeks to protect and promote the rights and interests of consumers, for example through laws, agencies and consumer associations.

whyNot.C: Mercantilism is an old economic idea of building national wealth through exports.
whyNot.B: Protectionism is shielding home industries from foreign competition, for example through tariffs.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of misleading advertising?
options: A bank publishing its new branch address
A school advertising the date of its open day
A shop announcing its new opening hours
A drink advertised as a cure for malaria without any proof
questions.explanation: Misleading advertising makes false or unproven claims that may cause consumers to buy a product. Claiming a drink cures malaria without proof is false and dangerous to health.

whyNot.C: Announcing opening hours is plain, factual information.
whyNot.A: Publishing a branch address is informative, not misleading.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Kunle tells a paint seller that he needs paint for the outside walls of his house. The seller recommends a brand, but it washes off in the first rain. Under the Sale of Goods law, which implied condition has the seller broken?
options: That the goods correspond with a sample shown
That the seller has the right to sell the goods
That the buyer will enjoy quiet possession of the goods
That the goods are fit for the purpose made known to the seller
questions.explanation: When a buyer tells the seller the particular purpose for which goods are needed and relies on the seller's skill, there is an implied condition that the goods will be reasonably fit for that purpose. Paint that washes off is not fit for outside walls.

whyNot.A: No sample was involved in this sale.
whyNot.B: Nothing suggests the seller did not own the paint.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Government fixes a maximum price above which a basic food item may not be sold. This price control mainly protects consumers against
questions.explanation: A maximum (ceiling) price prevents sellers from charging more than the fixed price, protecting consumers, especially the poor, from being exploited when goods are scarce.

whyNot.C: Packaging quality is controlled by standards, not by a price limit.
whyNot.A: Ingredient safety is checked by regulatory agencies, not by price control.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Why should a consumer keep the receipt after buying an electric iron?
options: It allows her to sell the iron to someone else at a profit
It reduces the price she will pay on her next visit
It is proof of purchase if she needs to complain or claim a refund
It shows that the iron is genuine and approved
questions.explanation: A receipt proves where, when and for how much the goods were bought. Without it, a seller may refuse to repair, replace or refund faulty goods.

whyNot.B: A receipt does not give a discount on future purchases.
whyNot.D: A receipt shows a sale took place; it does not prove the product is genuine or approved.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Pack A of detergent weighs 500 g and costs ₦1,200. Pack B weighs 750 g and costs ₦1,650. Which pack gives better value, and what is its price per kilogram?
questions.explanation: Price per kg of A = ₦1,200 ÷ 0.5 kg = ₦2,400. Price per kg of B = ₦1,650 ÷ 0.75 kg = ₦2,200. B is cheaper per kilogram, so it is the better buy even though its pack costs more.

whyNot.A: ₦2,400 per kg is A's unit price, which is higher than B's.
whyNot.C: B's unit price is ₦2,200, not ₦2,400.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which of the following services does a wholesaler commonly give to retailers?
options: Selling goods to them on credit
Collecting taxes for government on their behalf
questions.explanation: Wholesalers often allow retailers to take goods and pay later (trade credit). This helps small retailers who lack capital to stock their shops.

whyNot.C: Production is done by manufacturers, not wholesalers.
whyNot.B: Collecting taxes for government is not a service wholesalers render to retailers.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: An agent who is given possession of his principal's goods, sells them in his own name and may sell on credit is called
questions.explanation: A factor (mercantile agent) holds the principal's goods, sells them in his own name, may fix prices and give credit, and receives a commission called factorage.

whyNot.D: A broker brings buyer and seller together but does not hold the goods or sell in his own name.
whyNot.B: An auctioneer sells publicly to the highest bidder on behalf of the owner; he does not trade in his own name on credit.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A middleman who brings buyers and sellers together and earns a commission called brokerage, without ever taking possession of the goods, is
questions.explanation: A broker is an agent who only arranges contracts between buyers and sellers. He does not hold the goods and is paid a commission known as brokerage.

whyNot.D: A factor takes possession of the goods.
whyNot.A: A wholesaler buys the goods and owns them before reselling.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which of the following is a visible export of Nigeria?
options: Insurance cover sold by a Nigerian firm to a Ghanaian trader
Freight charges earned by a Nigerian ship
Money spent by foreign tourists in Calabar
Crude oil sold to a refinery in India
questions.explanation: Visible exports are physical goods sold abroad, which can be seen and recorded at the ports. Crude oil is a good, so its sale abroad is a visible export.

whyNot.A: Insurance is a service, so selling it abroad is an invisible export.
whyNot.C: Tourism earnings are an invisible export.
whyNot.B: Shipping (freight) earnings are an invisible export.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A shoe costs a retailer ₦8,000 and she adds a mark-up of 30% on cost. What is her selling price?
questions.explanation: Mark-up = 30% of cost = 0.30 × ₦8,000 = ₦2,400. Selling price = cost + mark-up = ₦8,000 + ₦2,400 = ₦10,400.

whyNot.B: ₦2,400 is the mark-up (profit) only, not the selling price.
whyNot.A: ₦11,429 treats 30% as a margin on selling price (8,000 ÷ 0.7).

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A supermarket's cost of sales for the year was ₦720,000 and its rate of stock turnover was 6 times. What was its average stock at cost?
questions.explanation: Rate of turnover = cost of sales ÷ average stock, so average stock = cost of sales ÷ rate of turnover = ₦720,000 ÷ 6 = ₦120,000.

whyNot.D: ₦4,320,000 multiplies instead of dividing.
whyNot.C: ₦60,000 divides by 12, as if the turnover rate were 12.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A trader's sales for the year were ₦400,000, cost of sales ₦260,000 and expenses ₦85,000. What was her net profit?
questions.explanation: Gross profit = sales − cost of sales = ₦400,000 − ₦260,000 = ₦140,000. Net profit = gross profit − expenses = ₦140,000 − ₦85,000 = ₦55,000.

whyNot.D: ₦140,000 is the gross profit, before expenses are deducted.
whyNot.B: ₦315,000 subtracts only the expenses from sales.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Government charges an import duty of 20% of the value of every imported car. This type of customs duty is called
questions.explanation: An ad valorem duty is charged as a percentage of the value of the goods. A specific duty is a fixed amount per unit (for example ₦5,000 per car) whatever the value.

whyNot.A: A specific duty is a fixed sum per unit or weight, not a percentage of value.
whyNot.D: Excise duty is charged on goods produced within the country, not on imports.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Tola pays an international fast-food company for the right to open a restaurant in Abuja using its name, recipes and methods of operation. This arrangement is called
questions.explanation: In franchising, the franchisor allows the franchisee to use its brand name, products and system in return for fees or a share of sales, while the franchisee owns and runs the outlet.

whyNot.C: Hire purchase is buying goods by instalments.
whyNot.A: Entrepot trade is importing goods in order to re-export them.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Despite competition from supermarkets, small neighbourhood shops in Nigeria continue to survive mainly because they
options: buy goods in larger quantities than supermarkets
enjoy lower prices from manufacturers than supermarkets
give personal service and small credit to customers they know
spend more on advertising than large retailers
questions.explanation: Small shops are close to homes, open long hours, sell in very small quantities and know their customers personally, often allowing them to buy on credit. These advantages keep them in business.

whyNot.A: Supermarkets, not small shops, buy in larger quantities.
whyNot.B: Large retailers usually get better prices because they buy in bulk.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: During a storm, the captain of a ship throws part of the cargo overboard to save the ship and the rest of the cargo. Under marine insurance, this loss is shared by all the parties to the voyage as
questions.explanation: A general average loss is a sacrifice made deliberately for the safety of the whole voyage, such as jettisoning cargo. Because everyone benefits, the shipowner and all cargo owners contribute to the loss.

whyNot.B: A particular average loss is an accidental partial loss borne only by the owner of the damaged property.
whyNot.C: A total loss means the ship or cargo is completely lost; here most was saved.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which life assurance policy pays the sum assured only when the insured person dies, whenever that happens?
questions.explanation: A whole life policy runs for the insured's entire life; the sum assured is paid to his dependants or estate on his death, at whatever age.

whyNot.D: An endowment policy pays at the end of a fixed period, or on earlier death.
whyNot.B: Fidelity guarantee insurance protects employers against dishonest employees.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: The main advantage of using telephone and e-mail in business is that they
options: remove the need to keep any business records
allow messages and orders to be passed quickly over long distances
guarantee that every customer will pay promptly
carry goods from producers to consumers
questions.explanation: Communication links traders who are far apart. Telephone and e-mail let orders, enquiries and replies travel almost instantly, which speeds up business.

whyNot.A: Businesses still need to keep records.
whyNot.D: Communication carries messages, not goods; goods are carried by transport.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which means of transport is generally the cheapest per tonne but the slowest for carrying very bulky goods over long distances between continents?
questions.explanation: Ships carry huge loads at a low cost per tonne, which suits bulky goods such as crude oil, grain and vehicles, but they move slowly compared with aircraft.

whyNot.B: Air transport is the fastest but the most expensive.
whyNot.C: Road transport cannot cross oceans and is costly per tonne over long distances.
whyNot.D: Rail transport cannot cross oceans between continents.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which of the following is a disadvantage of advertising?
options: It creates jobs in the media industry
It informs consumers about new products
It helps producers to increase their sales
Its cost may be added to the price consumers pay
questions.explanation: Advertising is expensive, and producers often recover the cost by charging higher prices. It can also persuade people to buy things they do not need.

whyNot.B: Informing consumers about products is an advantage.
whyNot.C: Increasing sales is an advantage to producers.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Large boards carrying adverts placed along highways and at busy junctions are an example of
questions.explanation: Billboards and posters displayed in public places are outdoor advertising. They are seen repeatedly by motorists and pedestrians.

whyNot.C: Press advertising appears in newspapers and magazines.
whyNot.B: Direct mail advertising is sent to people by post or e-mail.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A trader saves ₦200,000 in a bank at 6% simple interest per year. How much will she have in the account after 3 years?
questions.explanation: Simple interest = ₦200,000 × 6/100 × 3 = ₦36,000. Amount = principal + interest = ₦200,000 + ₦36,000 = ₦236,000.

whyNot.A: ₦36,000 is the interest only, not the total in the account.
whyNot.B: ₦212,000 includes the interest for just one year.
whyNot.D: ₦238,203 is the compound interest amount, but the question says simple interest.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which document, issued by a dock or warehouse keeper for goods in his care, is a document of title that can be transferred by endorsement to a buyer?
questions.explanation: A dock (warehouse) warrant gives its holder the right to collect the stored goods. Because it is a document of title, the owner can sell the goods simply by endorsing and handing over the warrant.

whyNot.A: A delivery note only accompanies goods being delivered; it gives no title.
whyNot.C: An advice note merely tells a buyer that goods have been sent.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which class of motor insurance must every vehicle owner in Nigeria have by law before using the vehicle on a public road?
questions.explanation: Nigerian law makes third-party motor insurance compulsory so that people injured or whose property is damaged by a vehicle can be compensated. Comprehensive cover is optional.

whyNot.C: Comprehensive cover is wider but it is optional, not the legal minimum.
whyNot.A: Goods-in-transit insurance covers goods being carried, and is not required for every vehicle.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which of the following risks can an insurance company NOT normally insure?
options: Damage to a warehouse by fire
Losses caused by a change in fashion that makes goods unpopular
Injury to a worker in a factory accident
Theft of goods from a shop by burglars
questions.explanation: Insurers cover risks whose chances can be calculated from past experience. Losses from changes in fashion, poor management or competition cannot be measured this way, so they are non-insurable risks that the business itself must bear.

whyNot.A: Fire is a common insurable risk.
whyNot.D: Burglary is insurable.
whyNot.C: Industrial accidents to workers can be covered, for example by employer's liability insurance.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: In a limited partnership, there must be at least one partner who
options: has unlimited liability for the debts of the firm
is a member of the public who bought shares
is appointed by the Corporate Affairs Commission
contributes no capital to the firm
questions.explanation: A limited partnership allows some partners to have limited liability, but at least one general partner must have unlimited liability for the firm's debts. Limited partners usually take no part in management.

whyNot.D: Partners in a limited partnership contribute capital; a partner who contributes nothing is a nominal partner.
whyNot.B: Partnerships do not sell shares to the public.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of a private limited company?
options: Its owners have unlimited liability for its debts
Its shares cannot be freely transferred or offered to the public
It is owned and run by the government
It must be quoted on the stock exchange
questions.explanation: A private limited company has limited liability, but it restricts the transfer of its shares and may not invite the general public to subscribe for them.

whyNot.A: Shareholders of a limited company have limited liability.
whyNot.D: Only public companies can be quoted on the stock exchange.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A company gives its existing shareholders extra shares free of charge, paid for out of its reserves. This is called
questions.explanation: A bonus (scrip) issue turns part of a company's reserves into new shares given free to existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings.

whyNot.C: In a rights issue, shareholders must pay for the new shares, usually at a discount.
whyNot.D: A debenture issue raises a loan; it gives no free shares.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Aisha owns 8,000 shares in a company that makes a bonus issue of 1 new share for every 4 held. How many shares will she own after the issue?
questions.explanation: Bonus shares = 8,000 ÷ 4 × 1 = 2,000. Total after the issue = 8,000 + 2,000 = 10,000 shares.

whyNot.A: 2,000 is the number of new bonus shares only.
whyNot.B: 32,000 multiplies by 4 instead of dividing.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A company has ₦300,000 of 10% cumulative preference shares. It paid no dividend last year. This year, how much must it pay preference shareholders before ordinary shareholders receive anything?
questions.explanation: Each year's preference dividend = 10% × ₦300,000 = ₦30,000. Because the shares are cumulative, last year's unpaid ₦30,000 is carried forward. Total due this year = ₦30,000 + ₦30,000 = ₦60,000.

whyNot.D: ₦30,000 is only this year's dividend; cumulative shares also carry the arrears.
whyNot.A: ₦90,000 counts three years of dividend instead of two.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Workers in a Lagos factory form a society into which they save part of their salaries every month, and from which members can borrow at low interest. This is a
questions.explanation: A thrift and credit cooperative encourages members to save regularly and lends to members at low interest from the pooled savings.

whyNot.C: A consumers' cooperative runs a shop that sells goods to its members.
whyNot.D: A producers' cooperative is formed by producers to produce or market goods together.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A major problem of the sole proprietorship is that
options: decision-making is slow because of many meetings
profits must be shared among many owners
it must publish its accounts every year
capital is limited to what the owner can save or borrow
questions.explanation: A sole trader relies on his own savings, loans from family and friends, and small bank loans. This limited capital makes it hard for the business to expand.

whyNot.B: A sole trader keeps all the profit.
whyNot.A: A sole trader decides alone, so decisions are quick.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A government-owned enterprise is told to operate on business lines, charge economic prices and make a profit, while government remains its owner. This policy is called
questions.explanation: Commercialisation means reorganising a public enterprise to run profitably and without depending on government subsidies, while ownership stays with government. In privatisation, ownership passes to private persons.

whyNot.D: Privatisation transfers ownership (shares) to private individuals and firms.
whyNot.B: Nationalisation is government taking over privately owned businesses.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of a partnership over a sole proprietorship?
options: Each partner can act without considering the others
The business can sell shares on the stock exchange
More capital and a wider range of skills are available
The partners enjoy limited liability by law
questions.explanation: In a partnership, several people contribute capital, ideas and skills, so the business can be bigger and better managed than one owned by a single person.

whyNot.D: Ordinary partners have unlimited liability.
whyNot.B: Partnerships cannot sell shares on the stock exchange.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: At which meeting do the shareholders of a public company usually elect directors, approve the accounts and declare the dividend?
questions.explanation: The annual general meeting (AGM) is held every year for shareholders. There they receive and approve the accounts, elect or re-elect directors, appoint auditors and approve dividends.

whyNot.C: The board meeting is for directors, not the general body of shareholders.
whyNot.A: A staff meeting involves employees, not the owners.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: After accepting a seller's quotation, the buyer sends a document formally requesting the goods. This document is
questions.explanation: An order is the buyer's written request for goods. It states the quantity, description, price and delivery terms, and it forms the basis of the contract of sale.

whyNot.D: An invoice is sent by the seller to bill the buyer.
whyNot.B: A credit note is sent by the seller to reduce an amount charged.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A customer pays cash for goods and is given a document acknowledging that the money has been received. This document is
questions.explanation: A receipt is written evidence that payment has been made. It protects the buyer from being asked to pay twice.

whyNot.B: A quotation gives prices before any sale.
whyNot.A: A delivery note shows that goods, not money, have been received.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A customer wants to put cash into her bank account at the counter. Which form does she fill?
questions.explanation: A deposit or pay-in slip records the account number, name and amount being paid in. The bank stamps the customer's copy as evidence of the deposit.

whyNot.A: A cheque is used to withdraw or pay out money, not to deposit cash.
whyNot.D: A proposal form is used to apply for insurance.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A retailer bought 40 bags of cement listed at ₦3,000 each, less 10% trade discount. He returned 5 damaged bags. What is the value of the credit note he should receive?
questions.explanation: The credit note is for the price actually charged for the returned bags. Net price per bag = ₦3,000 × 0.90 = ₦2,700. Credit note = 5 × ₦2,700 = ₦13,500.

whyNot.D: ₦15,000 uses the list price and ignores the trade discount the buyer actually received.
whyNot.A: ₦108,000 is the net value of the whole order, not of the returned bags.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A cheque that has no crossing on it and can therefore be cashed over the bank counter is called
questions.explanation: An open (uncrossed) cheque may be paid in cash over the counter to the payee. A crossed cheque must be paid into a bank account.

whyNot.D: A crossed cheque cannot be cashed over the counter.
whyNot.B: A stale cheque is one presented too long after its date.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A cheque has the name of a particular bank written between two parallel lines across its face. This means the cheque
options: can be paid only into an account at the bank named
is payable only after a future date
can be cashed by anyone who holds it
has been refused payment by the drawer's bank
questions.explanation: This is a special crossing. The paying bank will pay only through the bank named between the lines, which gives extra protection against fraud.

whyNot.C: That describes an open bearer cheque, not a crossed one.
whyNot.B: A future date makes a cheque post-dated; the crossing does not.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: An exporter sends urgent medical supplies to Accra by aeroplane. Which document does the airline issue as a receipt for the goods and evidence of the contract of carriage?
questions.explanation: The air waybill is the transport document for goods carried by air. Unlike the bill of lading, it is not a document of title.

whyNot.A: A bill of lading is used for goods carried by sea.
whyNot.B: A dock warrant relates to goods stored at a dock, not goods carried by air.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A trader in a village without internet access pays her supplier by dialling a short code on her basic mobile phone. This method of payment uses
questions.explanation: USSD (Unstructured Supplementary Service Data) banking lets customers transfer money by dialling short codes such as *123#. It works on basic phones and does not need internet data.

whyNot.C: A cheque is a paper order to a bank, not a phone code.
whyNot.B: A bill of exchange is a written order to pay, not an electronic phone service.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: An invoice for ₦80,000 offered a cash discount for prompt payment. The buyer paid within the period and settled the invoice with ₦78,000. What was the rate of cash discount?

whyNot.C: 2% would be a discount of ₦1,600, not ₦2,000.
whyNot.B: 25% comes from a slip with the decimal point.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: How does a credit card differ from a debit card?
options: With a credit card, money is taken at once from the holder's current account
A credit card is issued only to companies, not to individuals
A credit card can be used only to withdraw cash from an ATM
With a credit card, the card issuer pays the seller and the holder repays the issuer later
questions.explanation: A credit card lets the holder buy now and pay later: the issuer settles with the seller, then bills the holder, who pays within an agreed period or pays interest. A debit card takes the money straight from the holder's own account.

whyNot.A: Taking money at once from the holder's account describes a debit card.
whyNot.C: Credit cards are used mainly to pay for goods and services, not only for ATM withdrawals.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Funmi receives a text message, apparently from her bank, asking her to reply with her card number and PIN to 'avoid her account being blocked'. What should she do?
options: Send only the PIN but not the card number
Reply quickly so that her account is not blocked
Forward the message to her friends to confirm it
Refuse to share the details and report the message to her bank
questions.explanation: This is phishing: fraudsters pose as banks to steal secret details. Banks never ask customers for their PIN. She should keep her details secret and report the message to the bank through its official channels.

whyNot.B: Replying would give fraudsters access to her money.
whyNot.A: The PIN is the most secret detail of all; it must never be shared.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Which of the following is a duty of a consumer?
options: To fix the selling prices of goods in the market
To register new businesses with government
To read and follow the instructions for using a product
To test drugs before they are sold to the public
questions.explanation: Consumers have duties as well as rights. They should read labels and instructions, check expiry dates, keep receipts and report bad products.

whyNot.A: Prices are set by sellers or by government control, not by individual consumers.
whyNot.D: Testing and approving drugs is done by regulatory agencies.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A trader sells bags labelled with the name and logo of a famous foreign brand, although they were made in a backyard workshop. This practice is
questions.explanation: Counterfeiting is making or selling fake copies of genuine branded goods and passing them off as the real thing. It cheats consumers who pay for quality they do not get.

whyNot.D: Branding is a producer giving its own product a distinctive name; using another firm's brand falsely is counterfeiting.
whyNot.B: Advertising is making goods known to the public.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A shopkeeper paid ₦36,000 for a carton of 20 packets of flour, each labelled 1 kg. On checking, each packet contained only 900 g. Based on the labelled weight, what is the value of the flour she did not receive?
questions.explanation: Price per kg = ₦36,000 ÷ 20 kg = ₦1,800. Each packet is 100 g short, so the shortfall is 20 × 0.1 kg = 2 kg. Value = 2 × ₦1,800 = ₦3,600.

whyNot.B: ₦1,800 is the price of 1 kg, but 2 kg are missing in total.
whyNot.D: ₦32,400 is the value of the flour she actually received.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A shop raised the price of a phone from ₦20,000 to ₦25,000 and then advertised '20% off – now only ₦20,000!' Compared with the price before the increase, how much does a customer actually save?
questions.explanation: 20% off ₦25,000 = ₦25,000 × 0.80 = ₦20,000, which is exactly the original price. The 'discount' saves nothing; it is a misleading price claim.

whyNot.B: ₦5,000 is the discount on the inflated price, not a real saving.
whyNot.A: ₦4,000 is 20% of the original price, but no discount was actually given on that price.

questions.subject: commerce
