questions.stem: A written promise by a manufacturer to repair or replace a television free of charge if it develops a fault within one year is called
questions.explanation: A guarantee (warranty) states that the maker will repair or replace faulty goods within a stated period. It protects consumers against defective products.

whyNot.D: An invoice is a bill for goods sold.
whyNot.B: A premium is the amount paid for insurance.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Members of a national association of bakers agree on a code of conduct requiring correct weights and clean premises, and punish members who break it. This method of consumer protection is
questions.explanation: Self-regulation happens when traders or producers in a trade association set and enforce their own rules of fair dealing without being forced by law.

whyNot.D: Legislation is law made by the legislature, not rules agreed by a trade association.
whyNot.A: A consumer association is formed by consumers, not by producers.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Usman bought a generator from a dealer. The police later proved it was stolen and returned it to its true owner. Usman can claim his money back from the dealer because the dealer broke the implied condition that
options: the seller has the right to sell the goods
the goods are fit for a particular purpose
the goods are delivered within a reasonable time
the goods correspond with a sample
questions.explanation: In every sale, there is an implied condition that the seller has the right to sell (title). A dealer who sells stolen goods has no good title, so the buyer may recover the price from him.

whyNot.B: The generator may have worked well; the problem is ownership, not fitness.
whyNot.D: No sample was involved.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: A recommended retail price printed on a packet of biscuits mainly helps consumers to
options: know when a retailer is overcharging them
know the date the biscuits were made
identify the agency that approved the product
questions.explanation: A recommended retail price tells the consumer what the manufacturer expects the product to sell for. A buyer can then tell when a retailer is charging far above it.

whyNot.C: Ingredients are shown in a separate list on the label.
whyNot.B: The production date is shown separately, not by the price.

questions.subject: commerce
questions.stem: Ada was injured when a new gas cylinder she bought from a retailer exploded because of a manufacturing defect. Under the law of negligence, can she claim damages from the manufacturer?
options: Yes, because a manufacturer owes a duty of care to the final consumer of its product
No, because she had no contract with the manufacturer
No, because the rule of caveat emptor protects every manufacturer
Yes, but only if she bought the cylinder directly from the factory
questions.explanation: In negligence, a manufacturer owes a duty of care to the people who will finally use its products. A consumer injured by a defect can sue the manufacturer even though she bought from a retailer and has no contract with the maker.

whyNot.B: A claim in negligence does not depend on a contract between the parties.
whyNot.C: Caveat emptor does not allow a manufacturer to escape liability for injuries caused by defective products.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Danladi's pharmacy has total assets of ₦1,640,000 and the owner's capital is ₦1,175,000. What are the total liabilities of the business?
questions.explanation: Assets = Capital + Liabilities, so Liabilities = Assets − Capital = ₦1,640,000 − ₦1,175,000 = ₦465,000.

whyNot.D: ₦2,815,000 adds capital to assets; liabilities are the part of the assets not financed by the owner.
whyNot.B: ₦1,175,000 is the capital, not what the business owes outsiders.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Mrs Ibekwe pays ₦300,000 of her personal savings into her business bank account as additional capital. What is the effect on the business's accounting equation?
questions.explanation: The bank balance (an asset) rises by ₦300,000, and the owner's claim on the business (capital) rises by the same ₦300,000. Both sides of Assets = Capital + Liabilities go up equally.

whyNot.B: The money is not owed to an outsider, so it is not a liability; it is the owner's investment.
whyNot.D: Money coming into the business increases assets; it does not reduce them.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: An accountant refuses to record a sale until there is a signed invoice and delivery note to support it. Which accounting concept is the accountant applying?
questions.explanation: The objectivity concept requires that accounting records be based on verifiable evidence, such as invoices, receipts and delivery notes, rather than on personal opinion. Supporting documents allow anyone to check the entry.

whyNot.C: Materiality is about whether an amount is large enough to need separate treatment.
whyNot.B: Going concern assumes the business will continue to operate in the foreseeable future.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A business measures its profit and prepares financial statements every twelve months, even though it expects to operate for many years. Which concept explains this practice?
questions.explanation: The accounting period concept divides the life of a business into equal periods, usually one year, so that profit can be measured and reported regularly to owners and other users.

whyNot.A: Business entity separates the owner's private affairs from the business.
whyNot.C: Dual aspect says every transaction has a debit and a credit of equal value.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Who wrote the first printed description of the double-entry bookkeeping system, published in Venice in 1494?
questions.explanation: Luca Pacioli, an Italian mathematician and friar, described the double-entry method used by Venetian merchants in his book 'Summa de Arithmetica' published in 1494. He is often called the father of accounting.

whyNot.D: Adam Smith was an economist who wrote 'The Wealth of Nations' in 1776.
whyNot.B: Keynes was a twentieth-century economist, not the author of the first bookkeeping text.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Kelechi does not keep full books. His capital was ₦900,000 at the start of the year and ₦840,000 at the end. During the year he brought in extra capital of ₦100,000 and took drawings of ₦120,000. What was the result for the year?
questions.explanation: Profit = Closing capital − Opening capital + Drawings − Capital introduced = ₦840,000 − ₦900,000 + ₦120,000 − ₦100,000 = −₦40,000. A negative figure means a net loss of ₦40,000.

whyNot.A: The sign is wrong: closing capital plus drawings (₦960,000) is less than opening capital plus new capital (₦1,000,000).
whyNot.D: ₦60,000 is just the fall in capital; it ignores drawings and the new capital.
whyNot.B: ₦160,000 adds the new capital instead of deducting it.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Financial information should be free from material error and bias, so that users can depend on it to represent faithfully what it claims to show. Which qualitative characteristic is described?
questions.explanation: Reliable information is free from material error and bias and faithfully represents the transactions and events it describes. Users can then depend on it when making decisions.

whyNot.B: Understandability means information is presented so that users with reasonable knowledge can grasp it.
whyNot.A: Comparability means users can compare information across periods or businesses.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A business pays its electricity bill of ₦18,000 in cash. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
questions.explanation: Cash (an asset) falls by ₦18,000. Electricity is an expense, and expenses reduce profit and therefore reduce the owner's capital by ₦18,000. Both sides fall by the same amount.

whyNot.D: No liability is settled here; the bill is an expense paid as it falls due.
whyNot.A: Paying cash reduces assets; nothing is received in exchange that is an asset.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Rukayat starts a business with ₦500,000 cash. She then buys goods on credit for ₦120,000, and sells goods that cost ₦80,000 for ₦110,000 cash. What are the total assets of the business after these transactions?

whyNot.C: ₦620,000 ignores the sale, which turned ₦80,000 of goods into ₦110,000 of cash.
whyNot.B: ₦530,000 is the capital after the profit, not the total assets.
whyNot.A: ₦730,000 adds the sale proceeds but does not remove the goods that were sold.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Which branch of accounting involves an independent examination of a company's records and financial statements in order to give an opinion on whether they show a true and fair view?
questions.explanation: Auditing is the independent examination of financial records and statements by a qualified person (the auditor), who then reports whether the statements show a true and fair view.

whyNot.D: Cost accounting works out the cost of products, jobs or services.
whyNot.C: Management accounting prepares information to help managers plan and control the business.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Goods with a list price of ₦200,000 are sold to Amaka Ventures at a trade discount of 20%. Amaka also gets a cash discount of 5% because she pays within the credit period. How much cash does she pay?

whyNot.C: ₦150,000 adds the two rates (25%) and applies them to the list price; cash discount is worked on the invoice amount.
whyNot.A: ₦160,000 is the invoice amount before the cash discount.
whyNot.B: ₦190,000 ignores the trade discount.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: How is trade discount treated in the books of the seller?
options: It is credited to the discount received account
It is debited to the discount allowed account
It is deducted on the invoice and not entered in any ledger account
It is entered in the discount column of the cash book
questions.explanation: Trade discount is a reduction from the list price given to traders. It is deducted on the invoice, and only the net amount is recorded in the books, so it never appears in a ledger account.

whyNot.B: Discount allowed is cash discount for prompt payment, not trade discount.
whyNot.D: The cash book discount columns record cash discounts only.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A trader withdraws ₦60,000 from the business bank account for office use. How is this recorded in a two-column cash book?
options: Debit the cash column and credit the bank column
Debit the bank column and credit the cash column
Credit both the cash and bank columns
Debit both the cash and bank columns
questions.explanation: Cash in the office increases, so the cash column is debited; the bank balance decreases, so the bank column is credited. Both entries are in the cash book, so this is a contra entry marked 'C'.

whyNot.B: This is the entry for paying office cash into the bank, the opposite transaction.
whyNot.D: Every transaction needs one debit and one credit; the bank balance falls, so the bank column must be credited.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: At the end of the month, the bank column of Halima's cash book shows a credit balance. What does this mean?
options: The bank statement contains an error
The business has a bank overdraft
The bank owes the business interest
The business has money in the bank
questions.explanation: In the cash book, the bank column is debited with money paid in and credited with money paid out. A credit balance means more has been paid out than paid in, so the business owes the bank: an overdraft.

whyNot.D: Money in the bank (a favourable balance) is shown by a debit balance.
whyNot.A: A credit balance is a normal position when an account is overdrawn; it does not by itself suggest an error.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Olumide's cash book shows a debit bank balance of ₦156,000. The bank statement shows bank charges of ₦2,400, a standing order for insurance of ₦15,000 and a credit transfer of ₦27,000 received from a customer, none of which is in the cash book. What is the adjusted cash book balance?
questions.explanation: Bank charges and the standing order reduce the bank balance; the credit transfer increases it. Adjusted balance = ₦156,000 − ₦2,400 − ₦15,000 + ₦27,000 = ₦165,600.

whyNot.A: ₦170,400 adds the bank charges instead of deducting them.
whyNot.D: ₦138,600 leaves out the credit transfer from the customer.
whyNot.C: ₦200,400 adds all three items, but charges and the standing order are payments.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Under the traditional classification of accounts, the wages account is a
questions.explanation: Nominal accounts record expenses, losses, incomes and gains. Wages are an expense, so the wages account is a nominal account.

whyNot.C: Real accounts record assets such as buildings, machinery and inventory.
whyNot.B: Personal accounts record people and firms, such as customers and suppliers.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Sadiq keeps an analytical petty cash book with columns for travelling, stationery and postage. During the week he pays: bus fare ₦1,500; envelopes ₦2,200; taxi fare ₦3,000; printing paper ₦4,800; okada fare ₦800. What is the total of the travelling column?
questions.explanation: Travelling items are the bus fare, taxi fare and okada fare: ₦1,500 + ₦3,000 + ₦800 = ₦5,300. Envelopes and printing paper belong in the stationery column.

whyNot.A: ₦7,000 is the stationery column (₦2,200 + ₦4,800).
whyNot.D: ₦12,300 is the total of all payments.
whyNot.B: ₦4,500 leaves out the okada fare.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Nnamdi returns damaged goods to his supplier. Which document does Nnamdi send to the supplier to show the amount he is claiming?
questions.explanation: A debit note is sent by the buyer to the seller when goods are returned or an overcharge is found. It tells the seller that the buyer is reducing (debiting) the seller's account.

whyNot.C: A credit note is issued by the seller to the buyer to confirm the reduction.
whyNot.B: An invoice is sent by the seller to record a sale on credit.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Bola starts a business with cash of ₦200,000 and equipment worth ₦350,000. She also takes over a debt of ₦90,000 owed to a supplier for the equipment. In the opening journal entry, how much is credited to her capital account?
questions.explanation: Capital = Assets − Liabilities = (₦200,000 + ₦350,000) − ₦90,000 = ₦460,000. The journal debits cash and equipment, credits the supplier ₦90,000 and credits capital with the balance of ₦460,000.

whyNot.A: ₦550,000 is total assets; the debt owed to the supplier must be deducted.
whyNot.D: ₦640,000 adds the liability instead of deducting it.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: In the books of Adigun Stores, Uzo Ltd's account (a supplier) shows on the credit side purchases of ₦240,000 and ₦65,000. On the debit side it shows payments of ₦180,000, returns of ₦12,000 and discount received of ₦4,500. What is the balance on the account?
questions.explanation: Credit side = ₦240,000 + ₦65,000 = ₦305,000. Debit side = ₦180,000 + ₦12,000 + ₦4,500 = ₦196,500. The credit side is larger by ₦108,500, so the balance brought down is a credit balance of ₦108,500: Adigun Stores still owes Uzo Ltd.

whyNot.B: The credit side is larger, so the balance brought down is on the credit side; a supplier's account normally has a credit balance.
whyNot.D: ₦125,000 deducts only the payments.
whyNot.C: ₦113,000 ignores the discount received.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A payment of ₦12,000 by cash to Obi, a supplier, was debited to the cash account and credited to Obi's account. What type of error is this?
questions.explanation: The correct accounts were used and the amount is right, but the debit and credit were swapped: Obi's account should be debited and cash credited. This is an error of complete reversal.

whyNot.C: An error of commission uses the wrong account of the right class, such as the wrong supplier.
whyNot.B: Compensating errors are two separate errors that cancel each other out.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Rent paid of ₦52,000 was correctly entered in the cash book but was posted to the rent account as ₦25,000. By how much will the trial balance totals differ?
questions.explanation: The credit in the cash book is ₦52,000 but the debit in the rent account is only ₦25,000. The debit total is short by ₦52,000 − ₦25,000 = ₦27,000. Like every transposition difference, ₦27,000 is divisible by 9.

whyNot.D: ₦52,000 would be the difference only if the rent account had been left out completely.
whyNot.C: ₦77,000 adds the two figures instead of finding the difference.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A trial balance failed to agree and the difference was put in a suspense account. Only two errors were later found: the sales journal had been overcast by ₦6,000, and electricity of ₦3,000 paid in cash had been entered in the cash book but not posted to the electricity account. What was the balance on the suspense account?
questions.explanation: Overcasting sales made the credit side ₦6,000 too large. The missing electricity posting made the debit side ₦3,000 too small. Debits were therefore short by ₦6,000 + ₦3,000 = ₦9,000, so a debit of ₦9,000 was put in suspense to make the totals agree.

whyNot.D: The suspense entry goes on the side that is short; here the debit side was short.
whyNot.A: ₦3,000 deals with only the electricity error.
whyNot.B: ₦3,000 credit takes the difference between the errors, but both errors made the debit side smaller relative to the credit side.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Which of the following errors will NOT be revealed by the trial balance?
options: A credit sale was entered in the customer's account but not in the sales account
The purchase of a computer for office use was debited to the purchases account
Rent of ₦4,500 was posted to the rent account as ₦5,400, with the cash book correct
The wages account was added up ₦1,000 too much
questions.explanation: Debiting the computer to purchases is an error of principle: a debit and an equal credit are still made, only in the wrong class of account, so the trial balance still agrees. The other errors give unequal debits and credits.

whyNot.A: Posting only one side of a transaction makes the trial balance disagree.
whyNot.D: An overcast account gives a wrong balance on one side only.
whyNot.C: Posting ₦5,400 against a ₦4,500 credit makes the debit side larger by ₦900.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A trader's draft net profit is ₦480,000. It is then found that equipment costing ₦60,000 was debited to the purchases account, and that discount allowed of ₦5,000 was omitted from the books completely. What is the corrected net profit?
questions.explanation: Charging equipment to purchases overstated cost of sales, so profit rises by ₦60,000 when corrected. The omitted discount allowed is an expense, so profit falls by ₦5,000. Corrected profit = ₦480,000 + ₦60,000 − ₦5,000 = ₦535,000.

whyNot.C: ₦425,000 reverses both adjustments.
whyNot.B: ₦545,000 adds the discount allowed, but it is an expense.
whyNot.D: ₦540,000 ignores the omitted discount allowed.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Ade Stores is both a customer and a supplier of Okon Enterprises. Okon agrees to set off ₦15,000 owed by Ade against the amount Okon owes Ade. How is this recorded in Okon's control accounts?
options: Debit sales ledger control account and credit cash account
Debit suspense account and credit sales ledger control account
Debit sales ledger control account and credit purchases ledger control account
Debit purchases ledger control account and credit sales ledger control account
questions.explanation: The set-off (contra) reduces both what Okon owes and what Ade owes. Reducing a liability is a debit to the purchases ledger control account; reducing a debtor is a credit to the sales ledger control account.

whyNot.C: This would increase both balances instead of reducing them.
whyNot.A: No cash changes hands in a set-off.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: In a sales ledger control account, bad debts written off are entered on the
options: credit side of the purchases ledger control account
debit side of the purchases ledger control account
questions.explanation: Writing off a bad debt reduces the amount owed by customers. The sales ledger control account is an asset-type account, so reductions go on the credit side, just as they would in the customer's own account.

whyNot.D: The debit side records increases in amounts owed, such as credit sales.
whyNot.B: Bad debts concern customers, not suppliers, so they do not go into the purchases ledger control account.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Which of the following balances appears on the debit side of a trial balance?
questions.explanation: Drawings reduce the owner's capital, so the drawings account has a debit balance and appears on the debit side of the trial balance.

whyNot.A: Returns outwards reduce purchases and have a credit balance.
whyNot.D: Provision for depreciation is a credit balance deducted from the cost of assets.
whyNot.B: A bank loan is a liability, which is a credit balance.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: From the following, find the closing balance on the sales ledger control account: opening debit balance ₦210,000; credit sales ₦640,000; cash sales ₦90,000; cash and cheques received from customers ₦580,000; returns inwards ₦18,000; customers' cheques dishonoured ₦12,000; bad debts written off ₦7,000.
questions.explanation: Debits: ₦210,000 + ₦640,000 + ₦12,000 (dishonoured cheques put the debts back) = ₦862,000. Credits: ₦580,000 + ₦18,000 + ₦7,000 = ₦605,000. Closing balance = ₦862,000 − ₦605,000 = ₦257,000. Cash sales are left out because they create no debtors.

whyNot.C: ₦233,000 deducts the dishonoured cheques; they increase what customers owe.
whyNot.A: ₦347,000 includes the cash sales, which never pass through the debtors' accounts.
whyNot.D: ₦264,000 forgets to deduct the bad debts written off.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Which of the following is a main purpose of keeping control accounts?
options: To replace the need for a trial balance
To show the profit earned from credit sales
To help locate errors within a particular ledger
To record cash sales and cash purchases
questions.explanation: A control account summarises all the entries in a ledger. If its balance agrees with the total of the individual balances in that ledger, that ledger is probably correct, so errors can be traced to a particular ledger quickly.

whyNot.B: Profit is measured in the income statement, not in control accounts.
whyNot.A: Control account balances are themselves used in the trial balance; they do not replace it.
whyNot.D: Cash sales and purchases do not involve individual customers or suppliers, so they are left out of control accounts.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A trader's sales for the year are ₦800,000 and she earns a gross profit margin of 25% on sales. What is her cost of sales?
questions.explanation: Gross profit = 25% × ₦800,000 = ₦200,000. Cost of sales = Sales − Gross profit = ₦800,000 − ₦200,000 = ₦600,000.

whyNot.B: ₦640,000 treats 25% as a mark-up on cost (₦800,000 ÷ 1.25); a margin is a percentage of sales.
whyNot.D: ₦200,000 is the gross profit, not the cost of sales.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: In the trading account, carriage inwards is
options: charged as a selling expense in the income statement
added to purchases in arriving at cost of sales
questions.explanation: Carriage inwards is the cost of bringing purchased goods into the business. It is part of the cost of the goods, so it is added to purchases when calculating cost of sales.

whyNot.A: Carriage outwards (delivering goods to customers) is the selling expense, not carriage inwards.
whyNot.B: Returns outwards, not carriage inwards, are deducted from purchases.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A business's financial year ends on 31 December. On 1 January it paid ₦96,000 for insurance covering the 15 months to 31 March of the following year. How much insurance should be charged in the income statement for the year?
questions.explanation: Monthly cost = ₦96,000 ÷ 15 = ₦6,400. The year has 12 of those months, so the charge = 12 × ₦6,400 = ₦76,800. The remaining 3 months (₦19,200) is a prepayment shown as a current asset.

whyNot.B: ₦96,000 includes the 3 months that belong to next year.
whyNot.C: ₦19,200 is the prepayment, not the year's expense.
whyNot.D: ₦115,200 adds the prepayment instead of deducting it.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Ebube Ltd has inventory ₦145,000, trade receivables ₦98,000, cash ₦37,000, trade payables ₦112,000, accrued expenses ₦8,000 and a bank loan of ₦300,000 repayable in five years. What is its working capital?
questions.explanation: Current assets = ₦145,000 + ₦98,000 + ₦37,000 = ₦280,000. Current liabilities = ₦112,000 + ₦8,000 = ₦120,000. Working capital = ₦280,000 − ₦120,000 = ₦160,000. The five-year loan is a non-current liability.

whyNot.B: −₦140,000 wrongly treats the five-year loan as a current liability.
whyNot.A: ₦168,000 leaves out the accrued expenses.
whyNot.C: ₦280,000 is the current assets alone.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A machine costing ₦1,800,000 was bought on 1 April. It is depreciated at 20% per annum on the straight-line method, on a time basis. The year ends on 31 December. What is the depreciation charge for the first year?
questions.explanation: Full-year depreciation = 20% × ₦1,800,000 = ₦360,000. The machine was owned for 9 months (April to December), so the charge = ₦360,000 × 9/12 = ₦270,000.

whyNot.A: ₦360,000 is a full year's charge; the machine was owned for only 9 months.
whyNot.C: ₦90,000 is for 3 months, the part of the year before the machine was bought.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: At the year end trade receivables are ₦400,000 and the allowance for doubtful debts is to be 4% of receivables. The allowance brought forward from last year is ₦22,000. How is the change in the allowance shown in the income statement?
questions.explanation: Required allowance = 4% × ₦400,000 = ₦16,000. The existing allowance is ₦22,000, so it must fall by ₦6,000. A decrease in the allowance is credited to the income statement as a gain, increasing profit.

whyNot.D: An expense arises only when the allowance has to be increased.
whyNot.A: ₦16,000 is the new allowance; only the change goes to the income statement.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: From the following, calculate the prime cost of a manufacturer: opening inventory of raw materials ₦60,000; purchases of raw materials ₦340,000; closing inventory of raw materials ₦45,000; direct wages ₦210,000; direct expenses ₦25,000; factory rent ₦80,000.
questions.explanation: Raw materials consumed = ₦60,000 + ₦340,000 − ₦45,000 = ₦355,000. Prime cost = materials consumed + direct wages + direct expenses = ₦355,000 + ₦210,000 + ₦25,000 = ₦590,000. Factory rent is an overhead, added after prime cost.

whyNot.D: ₦670,000 includes factory rent, which is a factory overhead, not a direct cost.
whyNot.A: ₦575,000 uses purchases instead of materials consumed.
whyNot.B: ₦680,000 adds the closing inventory instead of deducting it.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: In its first year, Unity Social Club received ₦450,000 in members' subscriptions. This includes ₦30,000 paid in advance for next year. At the year end, members still owe ₦20,000 for the current year. What subscription income should be shown in the income and expenditure account?
questions.explanation: Income for the year = cash received − subscriptions in advance + subscriptions in arrears = ₦450,000 − ₦30,000 + ₦20,000 = ₦440,000. Income belongs to the year it relates to, not the year cash is received.

whyNot.C: ₦460,000 adds the advance and deducts the arrears, the wrong way round.
whyNot.A: ₦450,000 is just the cash received.
whyNot.D: ₦500,000 adds both the advance and the arrears.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: In the accounts of a not-for-profit organisation such as a social club, the equivalent of a trader's capital is called the
questions.explanation: The accumulated fund is the excess of a club's assets over its liabilities. It grows with each surplus and falls with each deficit, just as a trader's capital changes with profits and losses.

whyNot.B: The consolidated revenue fund belongs to government accounting.
whyNot.D: Share premium is a capital reserve of a company.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Ayo's net profit for the year is ₦126,000 on sales of ₦900,000. What is his net profit margin?
questions.explanation: Net profit margin = Net profit ÷ Sales × 100 = ₦126,000 ÷ ₦900,000 × 100 = 14%.

whyNot.D: 12.6% puts the decimal point in the wrong place.
whyNot.A: 86% is the percentage of sales taken up by costs, not the profit.
whyNot.C: 7.14% divides sales by profit instead of profit by sales.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A partnership's profits for the last three years were ₦420,000, ₦360,000 and ₦480,000. Goodwill is valued at two years' purchase of the average profit. What is the value of goodwill?

whyNot.C: ₦420,000 is the average profit, or only one year's purchase.
whyNot.B: ₦1,260,000 is the total profit for three years.
whyNot.A: ₦960,000 uses the highest year's profit instead of the average.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Under the Partnership Act 1890, where there is no agreement, a partner who lends money to the firm beyond his agreed capital is entitled to interest on the loan at
options: the same rate as interest on capital
questions.explanation: Section 24 of the Partnership Act 1890 provides that a partner who advances money to the firm beyond the capital he agreed to contribute is entitled to interest at 5% per annum, unless the partners agree otherwise.

whyNot.A: The Act sets 5%, not 10%.
whyNot.B: Without an agreement, no interest at all is allowed on capital, so this cannot be the rule for loans.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Tobi, a partner, lent ₦600,000 to the firm on the first day of the year. There is no partnership agreement. How much interest is he entitled to for the year, and where is it charged?
options: ₦30,000, charged as an expense in the income statement
₦60,000, charged as an expense in the income statement
questions.explanation: Under the Partnership Act 1890 the interest is 5% × ₦600,000 = ₦30,000. Interest on a partner's loan is a cost of borrowing, like interest to any lender, so it is charged against profit in the income statement before the profit is appropriated.

whyNot.C: The appropriation account shares out profit (interest on capital, salaries); loan interest is an expense deducted before that.
whyNot.B: ₦60,000 uses 10%; the Act allows 5% when there is no agreement.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Ada and Bimpe share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. They admit Chidi, who is to receive one-fifth of future profits. Ada and Bimpe will share the rest in their old ratio. What is the new profit-sharing ratio of Ada, Bimpe and Chidi?
questions.explanation: After Chidi's 1/5, 4/5 remains. Ada gets 3/5 × 4/5 = 12/25, Bimpe gets 2/5 × 4/5 = 8/25 and Chidi gets 1/5 = 5/25. The ratio is 12 : 8 : 5.

whyNot.D: 3 : 2 : 1 would give Chidi one-sixth, not one-fifth.
whyNot.A: 3 : 2 : 5 would give Chidi half of the profits.
whyNot.C: 2 : 2 : 1 ignores the old 3 : 2 ratio between Ada and Bimpe.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: When a new partner is admitted, land is revalued from ₦2,000,000 to ₦2,600,000 and inventory is reduced by ₦80,000. What is the net profit on revaluation to be shared by the old partners?
questions.explanation: Gain on land = ₦2,600,000 − ₦2,000,000 = ₦600,000. Loss on inventory = ₦80,000. Net revaluation profit = ₦600,000 − ₦80,000 = ₦520,000, credited to the old partners' capital accounts in their old ratio.

whyNot.D: ₦600,000 ignores the fall in the value of inventory.
whyNot.C: ₦680,000 adds the inventory loss instead of deducting it.
whyNot.A: ₦260,000 is half of the profit, one partner's share if they share equally.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: When a partnership is dissolved, the account opened to record the sale of its assets and to find the profit or loss on the sale is the
questions.explanation: On dissolution, the assets are transferred to a realisation account, the proceeds of sale and expenses are entered, and the balance shows the profit or loss on realisation shared among the partners.

whyNot.A: A revaluation account is used when a partner is admitted or retires and the business continues.
whyNot.C: The appropriation account shares the normal profit of a continuing partnership.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: In a company limited by shares, if the company cannot pay its debts, a shareholder can be made to contribute no more than
options: his share of the company's total debts
any amount still unpaid on his shares
the market value of his shares
questions.explanation: Limited liability means a shareholder's liability is limited to the amount unpaid on the shares he holds. Once his shares are fully paid, he cannot be asked to pay any more towards the company's debts.

whyNot.A: Shareholders are not personally responsible for the company's debts; that is the point of limited liability.
whyNot.D: Dividends already received properly are not a measure of a shareholder's liability.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A company has ₦2,500,000 of 12% debentures. Interest for the first half of the year has been paid, but interest for the second half is still owing at the year end. How much debenture interest is accrued?
questions.explanation: Annual interest = 12% × ₦2,500,000 = ₦300,000. Half a year's interest is still owing: ₦300,000 ÷ 2 = ₦150,000, shown as a current liability. The full ₦300,000 is charged as an expense.

whyNot.D: ₦300,000 is the full year's interest, half of which has been paid.
whyNot.A: ₦125,000 uses 10% instead of 12%.
whyNot.C: ₦75,000 is only three months' interest.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Which of the following is a capital reserve of a company?
questions.explanation: Share premium comes from issuing shares above their nominal value, not from trading profits, so it is a capital reserve and cannot be paid out as cash dividends.

whyNot.D: A general reserve is set aside from profits, so it is a revenue reserve.
whyNot.C: Retained earnings are undistributed profits, a revenue reserve.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Under which policy are all the revenues of Federal Government ministries, departments and agencies paid into a single account at the Central Bank of Nigeria?
options: Integrated Payroll and Personnel Information System (IPPIS)
questions.explanation: The Treasury Single Account brings all Federal Government receipts into one account (a unified structure of accounts) at the Central Bank of Nigeria, so that government can see and control all its cash in one place.

whyNot.A: IPPIS is a system for paying the salaries of government workers.
whyNot.C: The Excess Crude Account held oil revenue above the budget benchmark price.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Ifeoma sells goods that cost ₦50,000 to a customer on credit for ₦70,000. What is the overall effect of this sale on her accounting equation?
options: Assets increase by ₦70,000 and liabilities increase by ₦70,000
Assets increase by ₦20,000 and capital increases by ₦20,000
Assets increase by ₦20,000 and liabilities increase by ₦20,000
Assets decrease by ₦50,000 and capital decreases by ₦50,000
questions.explanation: Inventory falls by ₦50,000 and trade receivables rise by ₦70,000, so total assets rise by ₦20,000. The ₦20,000 profit belongs to the owner, so capital rises by ₦20,000.

whyNot.A: The customer owes Ifeoma; that is an asset of hers, not a liability.
whyNot.C: The extra ₦20,000 is profit, which increases capital, not liabilities.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A customer pays ₦45,000 in cash to settle his debt to the business. What is the effect on the total assets of the business?
questions.explanation: Cash (an asset) rises by ₦45,000 and trade receivables (another asset) fall by ₦45,000. One asset replaces another, so total assets stay the same.

whyNot.B: This counts the cash received but forgets that the debtor balance falls.
whyNot.A: The business receives money; it does not lose assets.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A delivery van bought on hire purchase is recorded as an asset of the business, although legal ownership passes only after the last instalment is paid. Which principle explains this treatment?
questions.explanation: Substance over form means transactions are recorded according to their economic reality rather than their legal form. The business uses and controls the van as if it owned it, so it is shown as an asset.

whyNot.B: Money measurement only requires items to be measurable in money.
whyNot.A: Realisation deals with when revenue is earned, not with recording assets.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Goods are sent to a customer on 'sale or return'. At the year end the customer has not yet said whether he will keep them. Under the realisation concept, how should the goods be treated?
options: They are written off as a loss
They are recorded as a cash sale at cost
They are recorded as a credit sale at selling price
They are not yet a sale and are included in closing inventory at cost
questions.explanation: Revenue is realised only when the buyer accepts the goods and becomes liable to pay. Until then the goods still belong to the seller, so they are part of its closing inventory, valued at cost.

whyNot.C: No sale has taken place because the customer has not accepted the goods.
whyNot.A: The goods have not been lost; they are still the seller's property.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Which of the following is part of accounting but NOT part of bookkeeping?
options: Entering invoices in the sales journal
questions.explanation: Bookkeeping is the recording side: entering transactions in the books of original entry and the ledger. Accounting goes further, by summarising, analysing and interpreting the records for users.

whyNot.A: Entering invoices in journals is routine recording, which is bookkeeping.
whyNot.C: Posting to the ledger is a bookkeeping task.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Which group of users mainly looks at a company's financial statements when deciding whether to buy, hold or sell its shares?
questions.explanation: Investors (present and potential shareholders) study profit, dividends and growth to decide whether to buy, hold or sell shares in the company.

whyNot.A: Employees are mainly interested in job security and the ability to pay wages.
whyNot.C: Suppliers want to know whether they will be paid on time.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: At the end of the year Hadiza's capital was ₦1,340,000. During the year she made a net profit of ₦285,000, took drawings of ₦160,000 and introduced extra capital of ₦50,000. What was her capital at the start of the year?
questions.explanation: Closing capital = Opening capital + Capital introduced + Profit − Drawings. So Opening capital = ₦1,340,000 − ₦50,000 − ₦285,000 + ₦160,000 = ₦1,165,000.

whyNot.C: ₦1,215,000 forgets to deduct the capital introduced.
whyNot.D: ₦1,515,000 reverses every adjustment: it adds the profit and new capital and deducts the drawings.
whyNot.B: ₦1,055,000 deducts the profit but ignores the drawings and the new capital.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Femi starts a business by paying ₦800,000 cash into it. He then borrows ₦300,000 from a bank and uses ₦650,000 cash to buy a van. What are the total assets of the business?

whyNot.D: ₦1,750,000 adds the van but does not take out the cash spent on it.
whyNot.A: ₦800,000 is the capital only; the loan also brought in assets.
whyNot.B: ₦450,000 is the remaining cash, leaving out the van.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A business is expected to close down in two months' time. How should its assets be valued in its final statement of financial position?
options: At original cost, because of the historical cost concept
At the amounts they are expected to fetch on sale, because the going concern assumption no longer applies
At replacement cost, because of the prudence concept
At cost less depreciation, because of the consistency concept
questions.explanation: Cost less depreciation is used because a going concern will keep using its assets. When a business is about to close, the assets will be sold, so they should be valued at what they are expected to realise.

whyNot.A: Historical cost relies on the business continuing; it is not suitable when the assets are about to be sold.
whyNot.D: Consistency cannot justify a method once the going concern basis has failed.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Which source document is evidence that a customer has paid cash to a business?
questions.explanation: A receipt is issued when money is received. It is the written evidence that the customer has paid, and the copy is used to record the cash received.

whyNot.D: An invoice shows what the customer owes, not that he has paid.
whyNot.C: A delivery note shows that goods have been delivered.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Three customers settle their debts within the discount period and each is allowed a cash discount of 2.5%. They owed ₦80,000, ₦120,000 and ₦40,000. What is the total of the discount allowed column in the cash book?

whyNot.D: ₦2,000 is the discount on the first customer only.
whyNot.C: ₦3,000 is the discount on the second customer only.
whyNot.A: ₦234,000 is the cash actually received after discount.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: In a bank reconciliation, 'unpresented cheques' are cheques that
options: the business has received but not yet entered in the cash book
customers have paid directly into the bank
the business has issued and entered in the cash book but the bank has not yet paid
the bank has returned unpaid to the business
questions.explanation: Unpresented cheques have been sent to suppliers and credited in the cash book, but the suppliers have not yet presented them, so they do not yet appear on the bank statement.

whyNot.D: Cheques returned unpaid are dishonoured cheques.
whyNot.B: Payments made directly by customers are credit transfers.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: After adjustment, Gloria's cash book shows a debit bank balance of ₦310,000. Unpresented cheques total ₦54,000 and lodgements not yet credited by the bank total ₦86,000. What balance should the bank statement show?
questions.explanation: Start from the adjusted cash book balance. Unpresented cheques have not left the bank yet, so add ₦54,000; uncredited lodgements have not reached the bank yet, so deduct ₦86,000. Bank statement balance = ₦310,000 + ₦54,000 − ₦86,000 = ₦278,000.

whyNot.B: ₦342,000 deducts the unpresented cheques and adds the lodgements, the wrong way round.
whyNot.A: ₦450,000 adds both items.
whyNot.D: ₦170,000 deducts both items.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: In which ledger would you find the wages account and the sales account?
questions.explanation: The general (nominal) ledger holds the impersonal accounts: expenses such as wages, incomes such as sales, assets and capital. Customers' and suppliers' personal accounts are kept in the sales and purchases ledgers.

whyNot.D: The sales ledger holds the personal accounts of credit customers, not the sales account itself.
whyNot.A: The purchases ledger holds the personal accounts of credit suppliers.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A petty cashier works on an imprest of ₦35,000. During the month she pays out ₦28,400 on business expenses. She also receives ₦3,000 from a member of staff for a private phone call, which she puts in the petty cash box. How much must the chief cashier give her to restore the imprest?
questions.explanation: Cash left in the box = ₦35,000 − ₦28,400 + ₦3,000 = ₦9,600. Amount needed to restore the imprest = ₦35,000 − ₦9,600 = ₦25,400 (the expenses less the cash received).

whyNot.C: ₦28,400 ignores the ₦3,000 received, which is still in the box.
whyNot.B: ₦31,400 adds the ₦3,000 instead of deducting it.
whyNot.A: ₦6,600 is the cash that would be left if nothing had been received.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Goods bought on credit are returned to the supplier because they are the wrong size. In which book is this first recorded by the buyer?
questions.explanation: Goods sent back to a supplier are returns outwards. The buyer records them first in the returns outwards (purchases returns) journal, from the debit note.

whyNot.A: Returns inwards are goods sent back by customers to the business.
whyNot.B: No cash is involved, so the cash book is not used.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Under the traditional classification of accounts, the owner's capital account is a
questions.explanation: The capital account records the amount the business owes to its owner, a person. It is therefore treated as a personal account.

whyNot.C: Real accounts record assets such as land, buildings and equipment.
whyNot.A: Nominal accounts record incomes and expenses.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: How are the individual invoices listed in the sales journal posted to the ledger?
options: To the debit side of the sales account
To the credit side of each supplier's account in the purchases ledger
To the debit side of each customer's account in the sales ledger
To the credit side of each customer's account in the sales ledger
questions.explanation: Each customer now owes the business, so each invoice is debited to that customer's personal account. The total of the journal is then credited to the sales account.

whyNot.D: Customers' accounts are credited when they pay or return goods, not when they buy.
whyNot.A: The sales account is credited, not debited, with the journal total.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: While reconciling, Kabir finds that the bank wrongly debited his business account with ₦15,000 for a cheque drawn by another customer. How should this be dealt with?
options: Treat it as bank charges in the income statement
Show it in the bank reconciliation statement and ask the bank to correct it
questions.explanation: The cash book is correct; the error is the bank's. The cash book is not changed. The ₦15,000 is shown as an adjustment in the bank reconciliation statement, and the bank is asked to correct its records.

whyNot.D: Crediting the cash book would record a payment the business never made.
whyNot.A: It is not a genuine charge, so it is not an expense of the business.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: At the start of the month the bank column of a cash book shows an overdraft of ₦45,000. During the month ₦230,000 is paid into the bank and cheques totalling ₦160,000 are paid out. What is the bank balance at the end of the month?
questions.explanation: Start at −₦45,000 (overdraft). Add receipts: −₦45,000 + ₦230,000 = ₦185,000. Deduct payments: ₦185,000 − ₦160,000 = ₦25,000. A positive bank balance is a debit balance in the cash book.

whyNot.C: The business now has money in the bank, so the balance is no longer an overdraft.
whyNot.B: ₦115,000 treats the opening overdraft as money in the bank.
whyNot.D: ₦70,000 ignores the opening overdraft.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A credit sale of ₦18,000 to Danjuma was completely left out of the books. What is the effect on net profit when the error is corrected?
questions.explanation: The correction debits Danjuma ₦18,000 and credits sales ₦18,000. Sales rise, so gross profit and net profit both increase by ₦18,000.

whyNot.A: Adding a sale increases income, so profit cannot fall.
whyNot.C: Only the sales side affects profit; the debit to Danjuma is an asset.
whyNot.B: Sales are income, so recording the missing sale does change profit.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: The purchases account was overcast by ₦4,000 and the difference in the trial balance was put in a suspense account. Which entry corrects the error?
options: Debit suspense account, credit trade payables
Debit cash account, credit purchases account
Debit suspense account, credit purchases account
Debit purchases account, credit suspense account
questions.explanation: Overcasting purchases made its debit balance ₦4,000 too large. To reduce it, purchases is credited ₦4,000, and the other side goes to the suspense account as a debit, clearing it.

whyNot.D: Debiting purchases would make the overstated balance even larger.
whyNot.A: Suppliers' balances were not affected by an addition error in the purchases account.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A trader's draft net profit is ₦350,000. Later it is found that: (i) closing inventory was understated by ₦15,000; (ii) rent paid in advance of ₦12,000 was charged as an expense of this year; (iii) cash drawings of ₦20,000 were debited to the wages account. What is the corrected net profit?
questions.explanation: Each error understated profit. Raising closing inventory adds ₦15,000; removing the prepaid rent from expenses adds ₦12,000; moving drawings out of wages adds ₦20,000. Corrected profit = ₦350,000 + ₦15,000 + ₦12,000 + ₦20,000 = ₦397,000.

whyNot.B: ₦303,000 deducts all three adjustments instead of adding them.
whyNot.C: ₦377,000 ignores the drawings wrongly charged as wages.
whyNot.D: ₦365,000 corrects only the inventory.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.context: Trial balance of Okoro Ventures (extract). Debit balances: equipment ₦400,000; inventory ₦120,000; trade receivables ₦85,000; cash ₦45,000; drawings ₦30,000; purchases ₦260,000; expenses ₦70,000. Credit balances: trade payables ₦75,000; sales ₦455,000; capital (missing).
questions.stem: Using the trial balance, what is the missing capital figure?

whyNot.A: ₦540,000 treats drawings as a credit balance; drawings are a debit.
whyNot.C: ₦1,010,000 is the total of the debit side.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Which of the following is an error of principle?
options: A cheque from Ike Okafor was credited to the account of Ike Okonkwo
The cost of fuel for the delivery van was debited to the motor vehicles account
Sales of ₦3,600 were entered in both accounts as ₦6,300
A purchase invoice was lost and never entered in the books
questions.explanation: An error of principle records an item in the wrong class of account. Fuel is revenue expenditure but was put in an asset account (capital expenditure).

whyNot.A: Using the wrong account of the right class (two customers) is an error of commission.
whyNot.D: A transaction left out of the books entirely is an error of omission.
whyNot.C: A wrong amount entered on both sides from the start is an error of original entry.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: The figure for credit sales in a sales ledger control account is obtained from the
questions.explanation: All credit sales are first recorded in the sales journal, so its total for the period gives the credit sales figure for the debit side of the sales ledger control account.

whyNot.D: The cash book gives cash received from customers and cash sales, not credit sales.
whyNot.A: The returns inwards journal gives sales returns, which go on the credit side.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: In the sales ledger, one customer's account shows a credit balance. Which of the following could explain this?
options: The customer bought more goods on credit
The customer paid more than he owed
The customer's debt was written off as bad
questions.explanation: A customer's account normally has a debit balance (he owes the business). If he overpays, or returns goods after paying, the credits exceed the debits and the business now owes him.

whyNot.A: Credit purchases by the customer increase the debit balance.
whyNot.C: A dishonoured cheque is debited back to the customer, increasing what he owes.
whyNot.D: Writing off a bad debt brings the balance to nil, not to a credit.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A trial balance is out by ₦540, and the bookkeeper suspects that two adjacent digits of one figure were swapped when it was posted. Which of the following postings could explain the whole difference?

whyNot.C: Swapping the last two digits here gives a difference of only ₦9.
whyNot.B: This swap gives ₦270, half the difference.
whyNot.D: This swap gives ₦90.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: From the following, find the closing balance on the purchases ledger control account: opening credit balance ₦130,000; credit purchases ₦520,000; cash purchases ₦60,000; payments to suppliers ₦470,000; discount received ₦9,000; returns outwards ₦14,000; set-off against the sales ledger ₦11,000.
questions.explanation: Credits: ₦130,000 + ₦520,000 = ₦650,000. Debits: ₦470,000 + ₦9,000 + ₦14,000 + ₦11,000 = ₦504,000. Closing credit balance = ₦650,000 − ₦504,000 = ₦146,000. Cash purchases are left out because no supplier is owed.

whyNot.A: ₦206,000 includes cash purchases, which never pass through suppliers' accounts.
whyNot.D: ₦157,000 forgets the set-off, which reduces the amount owed to suppliers.
whyNot.B: ₦168,000 adds the set-off instead of deducting it.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Rent of ₦40,000 received in cash from a tenant was not recorded at all. Which journal entry corrects this error?
options: Debit rent received account, credit cash account
Debit cash account, credit suspense account
Debit suspense account, credit rent received account
Debit cash account, credit rent received account
questions.explanation: This is an error of omission. Cash has come in, so cash is debited; rent received is income, so the rent received account is credited. No suspense account is needed because the trial balance was not affected.

whyNot.A: This reverses the entry and would show rent as paid out.
whyNot.C: An error of omission does not affect the agreement of the trial balance, so there is no suspense balance to clear.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A trader fixes her selling prices by adding a mark-up of 50% to cost. What is her gross profit as a percentage of sales (margin)?
questions.explanation: If cost is ₦100, gross profit is ₦50 and sales are ₦150. Margin = ₦50 ÷ ₦150 × 100 = 33⅓%.

whyNot.B: 50% is the mark-up on cost; the margin is worked on sales.
whyNot.A: 150% is selling price as a percentage of cost.
whyNot.C: 66⅔% is cost of sales as a percentage of sales.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: In the trading account, returns inwards are
questions.explanation: Returns inwards are goods sent back by customers, so they cancel part of the sales. They are deducted from sales to give net sales (turnover).

whyNot.A: Returned goods reduce sales; they do not increase them.
whyNot.D: Returns outwards, not returns inwards, are deducted from purchases.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: At the start of the year, commission of ₦20,000 was owing to a business. During the year it received ₦215,000 in commission, and at the end of the year a further ₦35,000 was owing. What commission income belongs to the year?
questions.explanation: Of the ₦215,000 received, ₦20,000 was for last year, so deduct it. The ₦35,000 earned but not yet received belongs to this year, so add it. Income = ₦215,000 − ₦20,000 + ₦35,000 = ₦230,000.

whyNot.D: ₦200,000 adds the opening amount and deducts the closing amount, the wrong way round.
whyNot.A: ₦270,000 adds both amounts owing.
whyNot.B: ₦215,000 is just the cash received.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A vehicle bought on 1 January 2022 for ₦2,000,000 was depreciated at 20% per annum on the straight-line method. It was sold on 1 January 2025 for ₦950,000. What was the result of the sale?
questions.explanation: Annual depreciation = 20% × ₦2,000,000 = ₦400,000. Three full years (2022, 2023, 2024) give ₦1,200,000. Net book value = ₦2,000,000 − ₦1,200,000 = ₦800,000. Sale proceeds ₦950,000 exceed this, so profit = ₦150,000.

whyNot.B: The proceeds are more than the net book value, so this is a profit, not a loss.
whyNot.D: ₦250,000 compares the proceeds with the total depreciation instead of the net book value.
whyNot.C: ₦550,000 assumes four years of depreciation.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A debt written off as bad two years ago is unexpectedly paid by the former customer. How is the amount recovered treated in the income statement?
options: It is added to income as bad debts recovered
It is added to the allowance for doubtful debts
questions.explanation: The debt was charged as an expense in an earlier year. When it is recovered, the amount is treated as a gain, shown as 'bad debts recovered' and added to gross profit in the income statement.

whyNot.C: The allowance for doubtful debts is a provision for future losses, not a place to record recoveries.
whyNot.B: The recovery is not a sales return; it increases profit.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Nkem's business earned a net profit of ₦180,000 for the year. Her capital employed was ₦1,200,000. What is her return on capital employed?
questions.explanation: Return on capital employed = Net profit ÷ Capital employed × 100 = ₦180,000 ÷ ₦1,200,000 × 100 = 15%.

whyNot.B: 6.67% divides capital employed by profit instead of profit by capital employed.
whyNot.C: 1.5% misplaces the decimal point.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A manufacturer's prime cost is ₦780,000 and factory overheads are ₦220,000. Work in progress was ₦40,000 at the start of the year and ₦65,000 at the end. What is the cost of production (cost of goods manufactured)?
questions.explanation: Factory cost = Prime cost + Factory overheads = ₦780,000 + ₦220,000 = ₦1,000,000. Add opening work in progress and deduct closing work in progress: ₦1,000,000 + ₦40,000 − ₦65,000 = ₦975,000.

whyNot.D: ₦1,000,000 ignores work in progress.
whyNot.A: ₦1,025,000 deducts opening and adds closing work in progress, the wrong way round.
whyNot.C: ₦935,000 deducts closing work in progress but forgets to add the opening figure.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A receipts and payments account of a social club is
options: a statement of its assets and liabilities at a date
an account showing the growth of its accumulated fund
a summary of its cash and bank transactions for the period
an account showing its surplus or deficit for the period
questions.explanation: The receipts and payments account is a summary of the club's cash book. It starts with the opening cash and bank balance, lists all receipts and payments, and ends with the closing balance.

whyNot.A: Assets and liabilities are shown in the statement of financial position.
whyNot.D: Surplus or deficit is found in the income and expenditure account, which follows the accruals concept.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Mallam Sani takes goods costing ₦25,000 from his shop for his family's use. Which entry records this?
questions.explanation: Goods taken by the owner are drawings, so the drawings account is debited. They are no longer available for sale, so purchases is credited (reduced) at cost.

whyNot.C: This reverses the entry and would increase purchases.
whyNot.B: The goods were not sold; crediting sales would overstate turnover.
whyNot.D: No cash was taken; the owner took goods.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: At the start of the year, Progress Youth Club had equipment ₦350,000 and cash ₦85,000. Members owed subscriptions of ₦12,000 and had paid ₦9,000 in advance. The club owed its drinks supplier ₦30,000. What was its accumulated fund at the start of the year?
questions.explanation: Assets = ₦350,000 + ₦85,000 + ₦12,000 (subscriptions in arrears) = ₦447,000. Liabilities = ₦9,000 (subscriptions in advance) + ₦30,000 = ₦39,000. Accumulated fund = ₦447,000 − ₦39,000 = ₦408,000.

whyNot.D: ₦426,000 treats subscriptions in advance as an asset; they are a liability.
whyNot.C: ₦447,000 is the total assets, before deducting liabilities.
whyNot.B: ₦384,000 treats subscriptions in arrears as a liability; they are an asset.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Xavier and Yemisi share profits equally. They admit Zainab, and the new ratio is Xavier 2, Yemisi 2, Zainab 1. Goodwill valued at ₦300,000 is created and then written off in the new ratio. By how much is Zainab's capital account debited?
questions.explanation: Goodwill is written off in the new ratio 2 : 2 : 1. Zainab's share = 1/5 × ₦300,000 = ₦60,000, debited to her capital account. In effect she pays the old partners for her share of the goodwill they built.

whyNot.C: ₦100,000 would be one-third, as if the three partners shared equally.
whyNot.A: ₦150,000 is each old partner's share of goodwill under the old equal ratio.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: The written agreement that sets out how partners will share profits, how much capital each will contribute and other terms of the partnership is called the
questions.explanation: A partnership deed (articles of partnership) is the agreement among the partners. It usually covers capital, profit-sharing ratio, interest on capital and drawings, salaries and what happens on dissolution.

whyNot.B: A memorandum of association is a company document.
whyNot.A: A certificate of incorporation is issued when a company is registered.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Tolu and Musa share residual profits in the ratio 2 : 1. Net profit is ₦720,000. Interest on drawings charged totals ₦18,000, interest on capital allowed totals ₦90,000, and Musa receives a salary of ₦150,000. What is Tolu's share of the residual profit?

whyNot.A: ₦320,000 ignores the interest on drawings, which is added to profit before sharing.
whyNot.C: ₦480,000 shares the whole net profit without any appropriations.
whyNot.B: ₦308,000 deducts the interest on drawings instead of adding it.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Where partners' capital accounts are fluctuating (no separate current accounts are kept), their drawings are debited to the
questions.explanation: With fluctuating capitals, all adjustments, including shares of profit, interest, salaries and drawings, go directly into the capital accounts. Drawings reduce what the firm owes each partner, so they are debited there.

whyNot.D: Drawings are not an appropriation of profit; they are withdrawals by the partners.
whyNot.C: Drawings are not an expense of the business.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A partner withdrew ₦120,000 on 1 July. The firm charges interest on drawings at 10% per annum, and its year ends on 31 December. How much interest is charged on this drawing?
questions.explanation: Interest on drawings is charged for the time the money was out of the business: from 1 July to 31 December is 6 months. Interest = ₦120,000 × 10% × 6/12 = ₦6,000.

whyNot.C: ₦12,000 is a full year's interest.
whyNot.A: ₦3,000 is for only 3 months.
whyNot.B: ₦9,000 is for 9 months.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: A company has 2,000,000 fully paid ordinary shares of 50 kobo each. The directors declare an ordinary dividend of 15%. What is the total dividend?
questions.explanation: Dividend percentages are based on the nominal (par) value of the shares. Nominal value = 2,000,000 × ₦0.50 = ₦1,000,000. Dividend = 15% × ₦1,000,000 = ₦150,000.

whyNot.C: ₦300,000 assumes the shares have a nominal value of ₦1 each.
whyNot.B: ₦75,000 uses 7.5% instead of 15%.
whyNot.D: ₦1,000,000 is the share capital, not the dividend.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: In relation to a company, a debenture holder is
options: an owner of the company who receives dividends
an auditor who reports to the shareholders
a director who manages the company
a lender to the company who is paid interest
questions.explanation: A debenture is a written acknowledgement of a long-term loan to a company. The debenture holder is a creditor who receives a fixed rate of interest, whether or not the company makes a profit.

whyNot.A: Shareholders are the owners and receive dividends.
whyNot.C: Directors are appointed to manage the company.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Lekki Foods Plc issues 300,000 ordinary shares of ₦1 each at ₦1.80 per share, payable in full on application. All the shares are taken up and paid for. How much cash does the company receive?
questions.explanation: Cash received = 300,000 × ₦1.80 = ₦540,000. Of this, ₦300,000 (300,000 × ₦1) is credited to ordinary share capital and ₦240,000 (300,000 × ₦0.80) to share premium.

whyNot.D: ₦300,000 is the nominal value only, the amount credited to share capital.
whyNot.C: ₦240,000 is the share premium only.
whyNot.B: ₦840,000 adds the premium to the full issue price.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Which law currently governs the registration and regulation of companies in Nigeria?
options: Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act
questions.explanation: The Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA) 2020 replaced CAMA 1990. It governs the incorporation, management and winding up of companies, administered by the Corporate Affairs Commission.

whyNot.D: The Partnership Act 1890 deals with partnerships, not companies.
whyNot.B: BOFIA regulates banks and other financial institutions specifically.

questions.subject: financial-accounting
questions.stem: Which public officer is responsible for preparing the annual financial statements of the Federal Government of Nigeria?
options: Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria
Chairman of the Revenue Mobilisation Allocation and Fiscal Commission
questions.explanation: The Accountant-General of the Federation heads the treasury's accounting and prepares the Federal Government's annual financial statements. The Auditor-General for the Federation then audits them and reports to the National Assembly.

whyNot.D: The Auditor-General audits the statements; he does not prepare them.
whyNot.B: The CBN Governor runs the central bank, which is the government's banker, not its accountant.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: After the baby Moses was placed in a basket among the reeds of the Nile, who found him?
questions.explanation: Exodus 2:5-6 says Pharaoh's daughter came down to bathe at the river, saw the basket among the reeds and took pity on the crying Hebrew child. She later named him Moses and raised him as her son, while his own mother nursed him.

whyNot.A: Miriam stood at a distance to watch what would happen and then offered to find a Hebrew nurse (Exodus 2:4, 7); she did not find him.
whyNot.B: Zipporah became Moses' wife many years later in Midian (Exodus 2:21).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Why did Moses flee from Egypt to the land of Midian as a young man?
options: Pharaoh had ordered all Hebrew leaders to be arrested
He refused to make bricks without straw
He had killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew
God told him in a dream to go and find Jethro
questions.explanation: Exodus 2:11-15 tells how Moses saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his own people. He killed the Egyptian and hid him in the sand. When Pharaoh heard of it he sought to kill Moses, so Moses fled to Midian, where he met Jethro's daughters at a well.

whyNot.B: The order to make bricks without straw came later, after Moses and Aaron first spoke to Pharaoh (Exodus 5).
whyNot.D: God's call came later at the burning bush; Moses met Jethro only after fleeing.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: The Gibeonites tricked Joshua into making a peace treaty by pretending to come from a far country with worn-out sacks and dry, mouldy bread. According to Joshua 9:14, what mistake did the Israelite leaders make?
options: They did not ask counsel from the LORD
They made the treaty without Aaron's approval
They refused to share the spoil of Jericho with the Gibeonites
They attacked Gibeon without sending spies
questions.explanation: Joshua 9:14 says the men of Israel examined the Gibeonites' provisions but did not ask counsel from the LORD. Relying only on what they could see, they made a covenant that they had to keep even after discovering the trick three days later. The lesson is that leaders should seek God's guidance before making important decisions.

whyNot.D: Israel did not attack Gibeon at all; they made a treaty with it.
whyNot.B: Aaron had died before Israel entered Canaan (Numbers 20:28), so his approval was not involved.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Why did God reduce Gideon's army to only three hundred men before the battle against the Midianites?
options: Because Gideon could not find enough weapons for more men
So that Israel could not boast that their own strength had saved them
So that the Midianites would be tempted to attack first
Because the rest of the soldiers had worshipped Baal
questions.explanation: In Judges 7:2 the LORD told Gideon that he had too many men, lest Israel boast that their own hand had saved them. The fearful went home, and the rest were tested at the water until only the three hundred who lapped remained. The victory would then clearly be God's.

whyNot.D: The men were sent home for being afraid or by the water test, not for worshipping Baal.
whyNot.A: The Bible gives no shortage of weapons as the reason; the reason given is to prevent boasting.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Who persuaded Samson to reveal the secret of his great strength and then handed him over to the Philistines?
questions.explanation: Judges 16 tells how the Philistine lords paid Delilah to discover the source of Samson's strength. After she pressed him day after day, he told her that no razor had ever touched his head because he was a Nazirite. She had his hair shaved while he slept, and the Philistines seized him.

whyNot.A: Jael killed Sisera with a tent peg (Judges 4:21); she had nothing to do with Samson.
whyNot.D: Rahab hid Joshua's spies at Jericho (Joshua 2).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Which sin of Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli, is described in 1 Samuel 2:12-17?
options: They took the people's sacrifices by force and treated the LORD's offering with contempt
They carried the ark of the covenant into Egypt
They set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan
They refused to fight against the Philistines
questions.explanation: 1 Samuel 2:12-17 calls Eli's sons worthless men who did not know the LORD. Their servant took meat from the pot with a fork and demanded raw meat before the fat was burnt, taking it by force if refused, so the sin of the young men was very great because they treated the LORD's offering with contempt. Both later died on the same day when the Philistines captured the ark (1 Samuel 4:11).

whyNot.C: Golden calves at Bethel and Dan were set up by Jeroboam much later (1 Kings 12:28-29).
whyNot.D: They did go out to battle against the Philistines and died there (1 Samuel 4:11).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: When God no longer answered him, King Saul consulted a medium at Endor. Whom did he ask her to bring up?
questions.explanation: 1 Samuel 28 records that Saul, afraid of the Philistine army and receiving no answer from the LORD by dreams, Urim or prophets, disguised himself and went to a medium at Endor. He asked her to bring up Samuel, who had died. Samuel told him that the LORD had torn the kingdom from him and that he and his sons would die.

whyNot.C: Eli had died long before, but Saul did not ask for him.
whyNot.B: Jonathan was Saul's son and was still alive at this time; he died in the battle that followed (1 Samuel 31:2).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: As David was bringing the ark of God to Jerusalem on a new cart, Uzzah was struck dead. What had Uzzah done?
options: He opened the ark to look inside it
He mocked David for dancing before the ark
He took hold of the ark when the oxen stumbled
He refused to walk in front of the ark
questions.explanation: 2 Samuel 6:6-7 says that when they came to the threshing floor of Nacon the oxen stumbled, and Uzzah put out his hand to the ark and took hold of it. God's anger was kindled against him and he died there. The ark was holy and was not to be handled carelessly; David later had it carried properly.

whyNot.A: Looking into the ark is linked to the men of Beth-shemesh (1 Samuel 6:19), not Uzzah.
whyNot.B: It was Michal, Saul's daughter, who despised David for dancing (2 Samuel 6:16).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: How did Absalom 'steal the hearts' of the people of Israel before he rebelled against his father David?
options: He gave the elders of Israel gold from David's treasury
He rebuilt the walls of Hebron at his own cost
He met people at the city gate and said that if he were judge he would give them justice
He married the daughter of the king of the Philistines
questions.explanation: 2 Samuel 15:1-6 says Absalom rose early and stood beside the road to the gate. When anyone came with a case for the king, he said there was no one appointed by the king to hear them and wished aloud that he were judge so that he could give everyone justice. He kissed those who bowed to him, and so he won the people's loyalty away from David.

whyNot.A: The Bible does not say Absalom used treasury gold; he won support by flattery and promises.
whyNot.B: Absalom did proclaim himself king at Hebron, but the passage says nothing of rebuilding its walls.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Two women came to King Solomon, each claiming the same living baby as her own. How did Solomon discover the real mother?
options: He told the priest to cast lots between the two women
He gave the child to the woman who spoke first
He ordered the child cut in two and saw which woman begged for its life
He asked the neighbours which woman had given birth first
questions.explanation: In 1 Kings 3:16-28 Solomon called for a sword and ordered the child divided between the two women. The real mother, moved with love, begged him to give the baby to the other woman rather than kill it, while the other agreed to the division. Solomon gave the child to the first woman, and Israel saw that God had given him wisdom to do justice.

whyNot.D: The two women lived alone in the house with no one else present (1 Kings 3:18), so there were no witnesses to ask.
whyNot.A: No lots were cast; the judgement came from Solomon's wise test.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: During the drought, Elijah stayed with a widow at Zarephath. What miracle provided food for her household?
options: Her empty jars filled with oil that she sold to pay her debts
Her jar of flour and jug of oil did not run out
Manna fell around her house each morning
Ravens brought her bread and meat every day
questions.explanation: In 1 Kings 17:8-16 the widow used her last flour and oil to make a small cake for Elijah first. Elijah promised that the jar of flour would not be used up and the jug of oil would not run dry until the LORD sent rain, and it happened as he said. Her faith and generosity were rewarded.

whyNot.D: Ravens fed Elijah himself at the brook Cherith (1 Kings 17:6), not the widow.
whyNot.A: Jars filling with oil to pay a debt was Elisha's miracle for a prophet's widow (2 Kings 4:1-7).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Before Elijah was taken up into heaven, he asked Elisha what he could do for him. What did Elisha ask for?
options: Elijah's chariot and horses of fire
A long life and great riches
A double portion of Elijah's spirit
The right to anoint the next king of Israel
questions.explanation: 2 Kings 2:9-10 records that Elisha asked for a double portion of Elijah's spirit. Elijah said it was a hard thing, but Elisha would have it if he saw Elijah taken away. Elisha saw the chariot and horses of fire and the whirlwind, took up Elijah's cloak and struck the Jordan, and the waters parted.

whyNot.A: The chariot of fire separated the two men; Elisha did not ask for it.
whyNot.B: Asking for riches or long life is the opposite of the request; compare Solomon, who also did not ask for these (1 Kings 3:11).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: What did Elisha tell Naaman, the commander of the Syrian army, to do to be healed of his leprosy?
options: Wash seven times in the river Jordan
Bathe in the rivers of Damascus for seven days
Offer a burnt offering at the temple in Jerusalem
Touch the bones of the prophet Elijah
questions.explanation: In 2 Kings 5:10 Elisha sent a messenger telling Naaman to go and wash in the Jordan seven times. Naaman was angry at first and said the rivers of Damascus were better, but his servants persuaded him to obey. He dipped seven times and his flesh became clean like that of a little child (2 Kings 5:14).

whyNot.B: Naaman mentioned the Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, in anger, but Elisha had named the Jordan.
whyNot.D: A dead man revived when he touched Elisha's bones (2 Kings 13:21); this has nothing to do with Naaman.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Gehazi, Elisha's servant, ran after Naaman and lied to obtain silver and clothing from him. What happened to Gehazi?
options: He was made the new commander of the Syrian army
He was swallowed by the earth
He was struck blind for three days
questions.explanation: 2 Kings 5:20-27 tells how Gehazi falsely claimed that Elisha wanted a talent of silver and two changes of clothing for visiting prophets. When he returned, Elisha knew what he had done and declared that Naaman's leprosy would cling to him and his descendants for ever. Gehazi left Elisha's presence a leper, as white as snow. Greed and lying brought judgement.

whyNot.C: Blindness for three days happened to Saul of Tarsus (Acts 9:9).
