whyNot.B: The earth swallowed Korah and his followers in the wilderness (Numbers 16:31-33).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In a vision, the LORD showed Amos a basket of summer fruit (Amos 8:1-2). What message did this vision carry?
options: The end had come upon God's people Israel
The exile in Babylon would last only one summer
Israel should bring the first fruits to Bethel
A rich harvest would follow Israel's repentance
questions.explanation: After showing Amos the basket of summer (ripe) fruit, the LORD said that the end had come upon His people Israel and He would never again pass by them. In Hebrew the words for 'summer fruit' and 'end' sound alike. Israel was ripe for judgement because of its injustice, as the following verses about cheating the poor show (Amos 8:4-6).

whyNot.D: The vision announced judgement, not a reward for repentance.
whyNot.B: Amos prophesied to the northern kingdom, which fell to Assyria, and he did not speak of a short Babylonian exile.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Amos addressed some people as 'cows of Bashan' on the mountain of Samaria (Amos 4:1). Who were they?
options: Priests who served at the altar in Bethel
Wealthy women of Samaria who oppressed the poor
Shepherds who refused to pay their taxes
questions.explanation: Bashan was famous for its well-fed cattle. In Amos 4:1-3 the prophet uses the picture for the rich women of Samaria, who crushed the needy and demanded that their husbands bring them drinks. Amos warned that they would be dragged away into captivity. He condemned luxury built on oppressing the poor.

whyNot.A: Amos does attack worship at Bethel (Amos 4:4), but the 'cows of Bashan' are the luxurious women, not the priests.
whyNot.C: Amos himself was a herdsman; the phrase is not about shepherds or taxes.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In Hosea 3, God told Hosea to go again and love a woman who had been unfaithful, and Hosea bought her back. What did this action show?
options: God still loved unfaithful Israel and would restore her
Prophets should marry only women from the tribe of Levi
God had finally divorced Israel for ever
Israel could buy God's favour with silver and barley
questions.explanation: Hosea 3:1 says the LORD told Hosea to love the woman 'even as the LORD loves the children of Israel', though they turned to other gods. Hosea paid silver and barley to bring her back and told her to stay faithful. The act pictured God's patient, redeeming love: Israel would return and seek the LORD (Hosea 3:5).

whyNot.C: Buying her back shows restoration, not a final rejection.
whyNot.D: Hosea paid the price; the point is God's grace towards Israel, not Israel paying God.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: To which king of Judah did Isaiah give the sign that a child would be born and called Immanuel?
questions.explanation: In Isaiah 7 Judah was threatened by the kings of Syria and Israel. Isaiah told King Ahaz to ask the LORD for a sign, and when Ahaz refused, Isaiah announced that a child would be born and called Immanuel, which means 'God with us' (Isaiah 7:10-14). Matthew 1:23 applies this sign to the birth of Jesus.

whyNot.A: Hezekiah, Ahaz's son, received a different sign: the shadow going back ten steps (Isaiah 38:7-8).
whyNot.D: Uzziah is the king whose death year is linked with Isaiah's call (Isaiah 6:1).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Jeremiah 31:31-34 speaks of a new covenant that God would make with Israel and Judah. What would be special about it?
options: God would put His law within them and write it on their hearts
It would apply only to the priests and Levites
It would be kept only by those who returned to Egypt
It would be written on new tablets of stone
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 31:33 says that under the new covenant God would put His law within the people and write it on their hearts; He would be their God and they would be His people. Everyone, from the least to the greatest, would know the LORD, and He would forgive their sin. Hebrews 8:8-12 quotes this passage of the covenant brought by Christ.

whyNot.D: Tablets of stone belonged to the old covenant at Sinai (Exodus 34:1); the new covenant is inward.
whyNot.B: Jeremiah says all would know the LORD, from the least to the greatest.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: God made Ezekiel a 'watchman' for the house of Israel (Ezekiel 3:17-19). What would happen if Ezekiel failed to warn a wicked man who then died in his sin?
options: The man's children would be punished in his place
God would hold Ezekiel responsible for that man's death
The wicked man would be forgiven because he was not warned
Ezekiel would be sent back to Jerusalem as a punishment
questions.explanation: In Ezekiel 3:18 God said that if Ezekiel did not warn the wicked, that wicked person would die in his iniquity, but his blood God would require at Ezekiel's hand. If Ezekiel warned him and he did not turn, Ezekiel would have delivered his own soul. The passage teaches the heavy responsibility of those called to speak God's word.

whyNot.C: The passage says the wicked man would still die in his sin; failure to warn did not save him.
whyNot.A: Ezekiel teaches that each person dies for his own sin (Ezekiel 18:20), not that children are punished instead.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In which town was Jesus born?
questions.explanation: Matthew 2:1 says Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, and Luke 2:4-7 explains that Joseph went there from Nazareth for the census because he was of the house and family of David. This fulfilled Micah 5:2, which named Bethlehem as the birthplace of the ruler of Israel.

whyNot.B: Nazareth was the town where Jesus grew up, so he was called Jesus of Nazareth, but he was not born there.
whyNot.C: Jerusalem is where Jesus was presented in the temple, not where he was born.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Which disciple was sitting at the tax booth when Jesus said to him, 'Follow me'?
questions.explanation: Matthew 9:9 says Jesus saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth and said, 'Follow me', and he rose and followed him. Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27 call him Levi. Tax collectors were despised, so Jesus' call showed that he came to call sinners.

whyNot.D: Andrew was a fisherman called by the Sea of Galilee with his brother Simon Peter.
whyNot.C: Philip, from Bethsaida, was called in John 1:43; he was not a tax collector.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: When Jesus fed the five thousand, what food did the disciples have at the start?
options: Seven loaves and a few small fish
questions.explanation: All four Gospels record that only five loaves and two fish were available (for example Mark 6:38). Jesus looked up to heaven, blessed and broke the loaves, and the disciples gave them to the people. All ate and were satisfied, and twelve baskets of fragments were left over (Mark 6:42-43).

whyNot.D: Seven loaves and a few small fish fed the four thousand in a separate miracle (Matthew 15:34).
whyNot.C: Twelve is the number of baskets of leftovers, not loaves at the start.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In the parable of the sower, whom does the seed that fell on rocky ground represent?
options: People who receive the word with joy but fall away when trouble comes because they have no root
People whose faith is choked by the worries and riches of this life
People who never understand the word, so the evil one snatches it away
People who hear the word, understand it and bear much fruit
questions.explanation: Jesus explained in Matthew 13:20-21 that the seed on rocky ground is the one who hears the word and at once receives it with joy, but has no root and endures only for a while. When tribulation or persecution comes because of the word, he quickly falls away. Faith needs deep roots to survive hardship.

whyNot.C: This describes the seed along the path (Matthew 13:19).
whyNot.B: This describes the seed among thorns (Matthew 13:22).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In the parable of the prodigal son, what did the elder son complain about when his brother returned?
options: His father had given the younger son a larger share of the property than him
His brother had stolen his own share of the inheritance
He had served for years without disobeying, yet was never given even a young goat to celebrate with his friends
The hired servants in the house were treated better than he was
questions.explanation: In Luke 15:28-30 the elder son was angry and refused to go in. He told his father that he had served him many years and never disobeyed, yet was never given a young goat to celebrate with his friends, while the fattened calf was killed for the son who had wasted the property. The father replied that all he had was the elder son's, but it was right to celebrate because his brother was lost and was found.

whyNot.A: The younger son asked for his own share; the elder son did not say the division was unequal.
whyNot.D: Thinking about hired servants having plenty of bread was the younger son's thought in the far country (Luke 15:17).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Which of these miracles most clearly shows Jesus' power over nature?
options: Casting out demons from the man in the tombs
Calming the storm on the Sea of Galilee
questions.explanation: In Mark 4:35-41 a great windstorm arose while Jesus slept in the boat. He rebuked the wind and said to the sea, 'Peace! Be still!', and there was a great calm. The disciples asked who this was, that even the wind and the sea obeyed him. The other miracles show his power over disease, death and evil spirits.

whyNot.C: Healing leprosy shows power over disease.
whyNot.B: Raising Jairus's daughter shows power over death.
whyNot.A: Casting out demons shows power over evil spirits.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Jairus fell at Jesus' feet and begged him to come and heal his dying daughter. What was Jairus's position?
questions.explanation: Mark 5:22 and Luke 8:41 describe Jairus as one of the rulers of the synagogue. While Jesus was on the way, a woman with a flow of blood was healed, and news came that the girl had died. Jesus told Jairus not to fear but only believe, then took the girl by the hand and raised her.

whyNot.D: A centurion asked Jesus to heal his servant at Capernaum (Luke 7:2-10); that is a different story.
whyNot.A: Zacchaeus was the chief tax collector at Jericho (Luke 19:2).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Jesus' entry into Jerusalem on a donkey fulfilled a prophecy that Zion's king would come humble and mounted on a donkey. In which Old Testament book is this prophecy?
questions.explanation: Zechariah 9:9 tells the daughter of Zion to rejoice because her king comes to her, righteous and having salvation, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey. Matthew 21:4-5 and John 12:14-15 say Jesus' entry fulfilled this word. It showed him as a humble, peaceful king rather than a warrior.

whyNot.C: Micah 5:2 is the prophecy about Bethlehem as the birthplace of Israel's ruler.
whyNot.A: Malachi 3:1 speaks of a messenger preparing the way, linked with John the Baptist.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: At the Last Supper Jesus washed his disciples' feet (John 13). What lesson did he say this taught them?
options: They must wash before every meal to be ceremonially clean
They should serve one another humbly, as he had served them
Peter would deny him three times before morning
Only the apostles were fit to share the Passover meal
questions.explanation: In John 13:12-15 Jesus explained that if he, their Lord and Teacher, had washed their feet, they also ought to wash one another's feet. He had given them an example to follow. Leadership in God's kingdom means humble service, not seeking honour.

whyNot.A: Jesus was not teaching a washing ritual; he said he was giving an example of service.
whyNot.C: Jesus did foretell Peter's denial (John 13:38), but that was not the lesson of the foot-washing.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: When Jesus was arrested in the garden, Peter cut off the right ear of the high priest's servant. What name does John's Gospel give to this servant?
questions.explanation: John 18:10 names both people: Simon Peter drew a sword, struck the high priest's servant and cut off his right ear, and the servant's name was Malchus. Jesus told Peter to put his sword away, and Luke 22:51 adds that Jesus touched the ear and healed him. Jesus did not resist arrest by force.

whyNot.B: Bartimaeus was the blind beggar healed near Jericho (Mark 10:46).
whyNot.A: Barabbas was the prisoner whom Pilate released instead of Jesus (Mark 15:15).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: As the apostles watched Jesus being taken up into heaven, two men in white robes spoke to them. What did they say?
options: Jesus would come back in the same way as they saw him go
They should return to fishing in Galilee
They must choose a successor to Judas at once
Jesus would appear to them again on the road to Emmaus
questions.explanation: Acts 1:10-11 records that two men in white robes asked the men of Galilee why they stood looking into heaven. They said that this Jesus, who had been taken up from them, would come in the same way as they had seen him go. The ascension carries the promise of Christ's return.

whyNot.C: Matthias was later chosen to replace Judas (Acts 1:26), but the men in white did not command it.
whyNot.D: The Emmaus appearance happened before the ascension (Luke 24:13-35).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: After Peter's sermon on the day of Pentecost, about how many people were baptised and added to the believers?
questions.explanation: Acts 2:41 says those who received Peter's word were baptised, and about three thousand souls were added that day. Peter had called them to repent and be baptised in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and they would receive the gift of the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:38).

whyNot.A: Acts 4:4 says the number of men who believed rose to about five thousand later, after Peter's sermon at the temple.
whyNot.B: About one hundred and twenty believers were gathered when Matthias was chosen (Acts 1:15), before Pentecost.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: When the Jewish council saw the boldness of Peter and John (Acts 4:13), what astonished them?
options: They were uneducated, ordinary men, yet spoke with great confidence
They were trained by Gamaliel but had turned against him
They had come from Rome with letters from Caesar
They quoted the law of Moses better than the scribes
questions.explanation: Acts 4:13 says the council perceived that Peter and John were uneducated, common men and were astonished, and they recognised that they had been with Jesus. Their boldness came from the Holy Spirit and their time with Jesus, not from formal training. They went on to say they could not stop speaking about what they had seen and heard (Acts 4:20).

whyNot.B: It was Paul, not Peter and John, who had studied under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3).
whyNot.C: Peter and John were Galilean fishermen with no letters from Caesar.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Tabitha, also called Dorcas, was raised from death by Peter at Joppa. What was she known for?
options: Good works and acts of charity, such as making clothes for widows
Selling purple cloth in the city of Thyatira
Hiding the apostles from Herod's soldiers
questions.explanation: Acts 9:36-41 describes Tabitha as a disciple full of good works and acts of charity. When she died, the widows showed Peter the tunics and other garments she had made for them. Peter prayed and said, 'Tabitha, arise', and she came back to life, and many in Joppa believed.

whyNot.C: Selling purple goods from Thyatira describes Lydia at Philippi (Acts 16:14).
whyNot.A: Philip the evangelist had four unmarried daughters who prophesied (Acts 21:9).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: When Saul came to Jerusalem after his conversion, the disciples were afraid of him. Who took him and brought him to the apostles?
questions.explanation: Acts 9:26-27 says the disciples did not believe Saul was a disciple. Barnabas took him, brought him to the apostles and told them how Saul had seen the Lord on the road and had preached boldly in Damascus in the name of Jesus. Barnabas, the 'son of encouragement', vouched for him.

whyNot.A: Silas joined Paul later, on the second missionary journey (Acts 15:40).
whyNot.B: Stephen had already been stoned to death before Saul's conversion (Acts 7:58-60).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Whom did the Lord send in a vision to lay hands on Saul in Damascus so that he would regain his sight?
questions.explanation: Acts 9:10-18 says the Lord told a disciple in Damascus named Ananias to go to Straight Street and find Saul. Ananias was afraid because of Saul's reputation, but the Lord said Saul was a chosen instrument to carry His name to the Gentiles. Ananias laid his hands on Saul, something like scales fell from his eyes, he regained his sight and was baptised.

whyNot.B: Barnabas met Saul later in Jerusalem (Acts 9:27).
whyNot.C: Philip was preaching in the coastal towns after baptising the Ethiopian eunuch (Acts 8:40).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Why did Paul and Barnabas separate before Paul's second missionary journey?
options: Barnabas wanted to preach in Rome while Paul wanted to go to Spain
Paul was arrested in Jerusalem and Barnabas went on alone
They disagreed about taking John Mark, who had left them on the first journey
They disagreed about whether Gentile believers should be circumcised
questions.explanation: Acts 15:36-40 says Barnabas wanted to take John Mark with them, but Paul thought it best not to take one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia. The disagreement was so sharp that they parted: Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus, while Paul chose Silas. Later Paul spoke well of Mark as useful to him (2 Timothy 4:11).

whyNot.D: On circumcision Paul and Barnabas were on the same side at the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15:2).
whyNot.B: Paul's arrest in Jerusalem came at the end of his third journey (Acts 21).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Before Paul saw the vision of the man of Macedonia at Troas, what does Acts 16:6 say the Holy Spirit had prevented him and his companions from doing?
options: Going up to Jerusalem for Pentecost
Speaking the word in the province of Asia
questions.explanation: Acts 16:6-10 says Paul and his companions went through Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. They also tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them. At Troas Paul saw a man of Macedonia begging him to come and help, so they crossed into Europe. God directs mission work by closing as well as opening doors.

whyNot.C: Rome was not in view here; Paul reached Rome much later as a prisoner (Acts 28).
whyNot.A: Paul's wish to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost belongs to his third journey (Acts 20:16).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Acts 17:11 says the Jews of Berea were more noble-minded than those in Thessalonica. Why?
options: They gave Paul and Silas money for their journey
They forced the city officials to release Paul and Silas
They received the message eagerly and examined the Scriptures daily to see if it was true
They refused to listen to Paul until he was circumcised
questions.explanation: Acts 17:11-12 says the Bereans received the word with all eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day to see whether these things were so. Many of them believed. Their example teaches believers to welcome teaching gladly but also to test it against the word of God.

whyNot.B: Releasing prisoners by officials happened at Philippi (Acts 16:35-39), not Berea.
whyNot.D: Paul was already circumcised as a Jew (Philippians 3:5), and the Bereans welcomed the message.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: At Troas, a young man named Eutychus fell from a third-storey window while Paul was preaching late into the night. Why did he fall?
options: The floor of the upper room collapsed
He tried to climb down to escape the crowd
Soldiers pushed him for listening to Paul
He sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked on
questions.explanation: Acts 20:7-12 says that Paul, who was leaving the next day, talked until midnight. Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep, fell from the third storey and was taken up dead. Paul went down, embraced him and said his life was in him, and the people were greatly comforted.

whyNot.C: No soldiers were involved; the meeting was a gathering of believers to break bread.
whyNot.A: The text says nothing of the floor collapsing; Eutychus fell from the window.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: According to Romans 3:23, who has sinned and fallen short of the glory of God?
options: Only those who have never been baptised
questions.explanation: Romans 3:22-23 says there is no distinction: all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. Paul had already shown that both Jews and Gentiles are under sin (Romans 3:9). Because everyone needs salvation, all are justified freely by God's grace through faith in Christ Jesus (Romans 3:24).

whyNot.A: Paul insists that Jews too are under sin, not just Gentiles.
whyNot.D: Paul argues that Gentiles without the law are also guilty (Romans 1:18-32).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Ngozi's neighbour poured dirty water in front of her shop to annoy her. Which teaching of Paul in Romans 12:21 should guide Ngozi's response?
options: Pour dirty water in front of the neighbour's door
Report the neighbour to the elders and demand payment
Stop greeting the neighbour until he apologises
Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good
questions.explanation: Romans 12:17-21 tells believers not to repay evil for evil, to live peaceably with all as far as possible, never to take revenge, and even to feed a hungry enemy. Verse 21 sums it up: do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good. Ngozi should respond with kindness rather than revenge.

whyNot.A: Paying back evil for evil is exactly what Romans 12:17 forbids.
whyNot.C: Withholding greetings is a quiet form of revenge; Paul calls for active good towards those who wrong us.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In 1 Corinthians 15, what does Paul say would follow if Christ had not been raised from the dead?
options: The believers' faith would be futile and they would still be in their sins
The law of Moses would have to be kept by all Gentiles
Believers would be raised on the third day instead
The apostles would become the new high priests
questions.explanation: Some in Corinth denied the resurrection of the dead. Paul argues in 1 Corinthians 15:14-17 that if Christ has not been raised, apostolic preaching is in vain, their faith is futile and they are still in their sins. But Christ has been raised, the firstfruits of those who have died (1 Corinthians 15:20). The resurrection is central to the Christian faith.

whyNot.B: Paul does not link the resurrection to Gentiles keeping the law here.
whyNot.C: Paul teaches that believers will be raised at Christ's coming (1 Corinthians 15:23), not on a third day.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Why did Paul rebuke the Corinthian church about the way it celebrated the Lord's Supper (1 Corinthians 11:17-22)?
options: They celebrated it only once a year at Passover
They allowed Gentile believers to take part
They used leavened bread instead of unleavened bread
Some ate their own meals first while others went hungry, and some even got drunk
questions.explanation: In 1 Corinthians 11:20-22 Paul says that when they met, it was not really the Lord's Supper they ate, because each one went ahead with his own meal; one went hungry and another got drunk. This humiliated the poor and despised the church of God. Paul reminded them of what Jesus did on the night he was betrayed and told them to wait for one another (1 Corinthians 11:33).

whyNot.C: Paul says nothing about the kind of bread; his complaint is selfishness and division.
whyNot.B: Gentile believers were full members of the Corinthian church; Paul did not object to their sharing.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Paul wrote in Galatians 3:28 that there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male and female, for all are one in Christ Jesus. What does this teach a church in Nigeria with members from many ethnic groups?
options: Each ethnic group should worship in its own separate church
Differences of language must be removed before people can be saved
Church leaders should come only from the largest ethnic group
All believers are equal members of one family in Christ, whatever their background
questions.explanation: In Galatians 3:26-28 Paul says all who are baptised into Christ are sons of God through faith and have put on Christ. Race, social status and gender do not decide a person's standing before God. A church with Hausa, Igbo, Yoruba and other members should therefore welcome all as equal members of one body.

whyNot.A: Separating believers by ethnic group goes against the unity Paul teaches.
whyNot.B: Paul does not require people to give up their language; salvation is by faith in Christ.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: According to Ephesians 2:8-9, how are believers saved?
options: By keeping the law of Moses without failing
By giving generously to the poor and the church
By being born into a Christian family
By grace through faith, not by works, so that no one can boast
questions.explanation: Ephesians 2:8-9 says that by grace believers have been saved through faith; this is not their own doing but the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast. Good works follow salvation as the life God prepared for His people (Ephesians 2:10), but they do not earn it.

whyNot.A: Paul teaches that no one is justified by works of the law (Galatians 2:16).
whyNot.B: Generosity is a fruit of faith, not the means of salvation.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In Ephesians 6:1-3, which commandment does Paul describe as the first commandment with a promise?
options: You shall have no other gods before me
Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy
questions.explanation: Ephesians 6:1-3 tells children to obey their parents in the Lord, then quotes the commandment, 'Honour your father and mother', calling it the first commandment with a promise: that it may go well with you and you may live long in the land (compare Exodus 20:12). Respect for parents is a Christian duty.

whyNot.C: The Sabbath commandment gives a reason (God rested), but Paul does not call it the first with a promise.
whyNot.A: This is the first of the Ten Commandments, but it is not attached to a promise of long life.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In Philippians 2:5-8, Paul tells believers to have the same mind as Christ Jesus. What example of Christ does he describe?
options: He commanded his followers to rule over the Gentiles
He used his miracles to become king over Israel
He refused to suffer and called on angels to defend him
Though he was in the form of God, he humbled himself, took the form of a servant and was obedient to death on a cross
questions.explanation: Philippians 2:3-8 calls believers to do nothing from selfish ambition but in humility to count others more significant than themselves. Christ is the model: though in the form of God, he did not hold on to equality with God but emptied himself, took the form of a servant, was born in human likeness and humbled himself to death on a cross. God therefore highly exalted him (Philippians 2:9).

whyNot.C: Jesus said he could call on angels but chose not to (Matthew 26:53).
whyNot.B: Jesus withdrew when people wanted to make him king by force (John 6:15).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In 1 Peter 5:7, what are believers told to do with their anxieties, and why?
options: Hide them from others, because worry shows weak faith
Ignore them, because suffering will soon end
Share them only with the elders, because elders can solve them
Cast them all on God, because He cares for them
questions.explanation: 1 Peter 5:6-7 tells believers to humble themselves under God's mighty hand and to cast all their anxieties on Him, because He cares for them. Peter was writing to Christians facing suffering, assuring them that God is concerned for them personally.

whyNot.A: Peter does not tell believers to hide their worries; he tells them to bring them to God.
whyNot.B: Peter does not tell believers to ignore their worries; he points them to God's care.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In James 3, to which of these does James compare the tongue, showing that a small thing can control a great deal?
options: A mustard seed that becomes a tree
The small rudder that steers a large ship
Salt that has lost its taste
A lamp placed on a stand
questions.explanation: James 3:3-5 compares the tongue to the bit in a horse's mouth and the very small rudder that turns a large ship wherever the pilot wishes. So the tongue is a small member but boasts of great things, and like a small fire it can set a great forest ablaze. James teaches believers to control their speech.

whyNot.D: A lamp on a stand is Jesus' picture of letting one's light shine (Matthew 5:15).
whyNot.A: The mustard seed is Jesus' picture of the growth of the kingdom of God (Matthew 13:31-32).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: When Moses feared the Israelites would not believe him, God gave him a sign with his staff. What happened when Moses threw it on the ground?
questions.explanation: In Exodus 4:1-5 God told Moses to throw his staff on the ground and it became a serpent. When Moses took it by the tail, it became a staff again. This was a sign so that the people would believe that the LORD had appeared to him.

whyNot.B: Aaron's staff budded and produced almonds in the wilderness (Numbers 17:8); that was a different sign.
whyNot.C: Fire is linked to the burning bush, not to the staff.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: On the night of the first Passover, what did each Israelite household put on its doorposts and lintel?
options: The blood of the Passover lamb
questions.explanation: Exodus 12:7 and 12:13 say the Israelites were to take some of the blood of the lamb and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel of their houses. When the LORD struck the firstborn of Egypt, He would see the blood and pass over those houses. Christians see the Passover lamb as a picture of Christ (1 Corinthians 5:7).

whyNot.C: Palm branches are linked with the Feast of Booths and Jesus' entry into Jerusalem, not the Passover doors.
whyNot.D: The Nile's water had been turned to blood in the first plague, but it was not put on the doors.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: While Moses was on Mount Sinai, the people asked for gods to go before them. Who made the golden calf?
questions.explanation: Exodus 32:1-4 says that when Moses delayed on the mountain, the people gathered around Aaron and asked him to make gods for them. Aaron collected their gold earrings, fashioned a golden calf, and they said, 'These are your gods, O Israel.' Moses later rebuked Aaron for bringing such a great sin on the people (Exodus 32:21).

whyNot.D: Joshua was with Moses on the mountain and heard the noise as they came down (Exodus 32:17).
whyNot.C: Korah led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron later (Numbers 16).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Moses sent twelve spies to explore Canaan. Which two of them urged the people to trust God and go in to take the land?
questions.explanation: Numbers 13-14 records that ten spies spread a bad report about giants and strong cities, and the people wept and wanted to go back to Egypt. Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh said the land was very good and that the LORD would bring them in. Because of the people's unbelief, only Joshua and Caleb of that generation entered Canaan (Numbers 14:30).

whyNot.A: Aaron and Hur held up Moses' hands in the battle against Amalek (Exodus 17:12); they were not among the spies.
whyNot.C: Nadab and Abihu were Aaron's sons who died for offering unauthorised fire (Leviticus 10:1-2).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: After Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground, what did Joshua set up at Gilgal so that future generations would ask about it?
options: A golden lampstand with seven branches
A bronze serpent on a pole
An altar made of cedar wood
Twelve stones taken from the bed of the Jordan
questions.explanation: Joshua 4:1-8 and 4:20-24 say that one man from each of the twelve tribes took a stone from the middle of the Jordan where the priests stood. Joshua set up the twelve stones at Gilgal, so that when children later asked what they meant, they would be told how the LORD dried up the Jordan for Israel to cross.

whyNot.B: The bronze serpent was made by Moses in the wilderness (Numbers 21:9).
whyNot.A: The golden lampstand belonged to the tabernacle (Exodus 25:31), not a memorial at Gilgal.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: How did God tell Joshua to march around Jericho before its walls fell?
options: Once a day for seven days without stopping
Three times on a single day
Once a day for six days, then seven times on the seventh day
Seven times a day for seven days
questions.explanation: In Joshua 6:3-4 the LORD commanded the army to march around the city once a day for six days, with seven priests blowing trumpets before the ark. On the seventh day they marched around seven times, the priests blew the trumpets, the people shouted, and the wall fell down flat (Joshua 6:15-20). Victory came through obedience to God's instructions.

whyNot.D: They marched seven times only on the seventh day, not every day.
whyNot.A: On the seventh day they marched seven times, not once.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Why did Gideon ask God for the sign of the fleece, first wet with dew while the ground was dry and then dry while the ground was wet (Judges 6:36-40)?
options: To decide which of his brothers should lead the army
To be sure that God would save Israel by his hand as He had promised
To test whether the altar of Baal still had power
To find out where the Midianites were camped
questions.explanation: Judges 6:36-37 says Gideon told God that if He would save Israel by Gideon's hand as He had said, He should make the fleece wet and the ground dry. God did it, and the next night He did the opposite at Gideon's request. Gideon wanted assurance that God's call and promise were real before leading Israel against Midian.

whyNot.D: Gideon later learned of the Midianites' fear by overhearing a dream in their camp (Judges 7:13-15), not through the fleece.
whyNot.C: Gideon had already pulled down the altar of Baal (Judges 6:27); the fleece was not about Baal.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: What did Hannah vow when she prayed for a son at Shiloh?
options: She would name the child after Eli the priest
She would take the child back to Ramah to be a king
She would offer the child as a sacrifice on the altar
She would give the child to the LORD all the days of his life
questions.explanation: 1 Samuel 1:11 records Hannah's vow: if the LORD would remember her and give her a son, she would give him to the LORD all the days of his life, and no razor would touch his head. When Samuel was weaned, she brought him to Eli at Shiloh to serve the LORD, keeping her promise (1 Samuel 1:24-28).

whyNot.A: She named the boy Samuel, saying she had asked him from the LORD (1 Samuel 1:20).
whyNot.C: Giving the child to the LORD meant lifelong service, not a sacrifice on the altar.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Saul dressed David in his own armour before David went out to fight Goliath. Why did David take it off?
options: The priest said armour was unclean for battle
He had not tested it and could not walk in it
It belonged to Jonathan, who wanted it back
It was too small for David's large body
questions.explanation: 1 Samuel 17:38-39 says David put on Saul's helmet and coat of mail and tried to walk, but said he could not go with them because he had not tested them. He took them off and went with his staff, five smooth stones and his sling, trusting the LORD who had delivered him from the lion and the bear.

whyNot.C: The armour was Saul's, and the passage does not mention Jonathan wanting it.
whyNot.D: David was a youth, and the text says nothing about the armour being too small for him.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Which king of Tyre supplied Solomon with cedar and cypress timber for building the temple?
questions.explanation: 1 Kings 5:1-10 says Hiram king of Tyre had always loved David. Solomon asked him for cedars from Lebanon, and Hiram's servants brought the timber down to the sea and floated it in rafts. In return Solomon sent wheat and oil to Hiram's household each year (1 Kings 5:11).

whyNot.C: Ben-hadad was a king of Syria who fought against Israel (1 Kings 20).
whyNot.D: Nebuchadnezzar was king of Babylon, who destroyed Solomon's temple centuries later (2 Kings 25:9).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: On Mount Carmel, before he prayed for fire, what did Elijah order to be poured on the offering and the wood?
questions.explanation: 1 Kings 18:33-35 says Elijah had four jars filled with water and poured on the burnt offering and the wood three times, until the water ran around the altar and filled the trench. This made it clear that no human trick could light the fire. When Elijah prayed, the fire of the LORD fell and consumed the offering, wood, stones, dust and water (1 Kings 18:38).

whyNot.A: Oil would have helped the fire burn, the opposite of what Elijah wanted to show.
whyNot.B: Elijah cut up the bull and laid it on the wood; the liquid poured on it was water.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: A woman of Shunem and her husband made a small room on their roof for Elisha. What did Elisha later promise her?
options: She would be given a house in Samaria
She would have a son about that time the next year
Her land would never again suffer drought
Her husband would become a captain in the army
questions.explanation: In 2 Kings 4:8-17 the Shunammite woman, who had no son and whose husband was old, prepared a room with a bed, table, chair and lamp for Elisha. To reward her kindness Elisha said that about that time the following year she would embrace a son, and she bore a son as he had said. Later Elisha raised that son to life (2 Kings 4:32-37).

whyNot.D: Elisha offered to speak to the king or the army commander for her, but she declined (2 Kings 4:13).
whyNot.C: Elisha later warned her of a coming famine (2 Kings 8:1); he did not promise that drought would never come.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: One of the sons of the prophets dropped a borrowed axe head into the Jordan. What did Elisha do?
options: He paid the owner for a new axe head
He told the man to dive in seven times
He struck the water with Elijah's cloak
He cut a stick and threw it in, and the iron floated
questions.explanation: 2 Kings 6:1-7 says that while the sons of the prophets were cutting trees by the Jordan to build a larger place to live, an axe head fell into the water. The man cried out because it was borrowed. Elisha cut off a stick, threw it in at the spot, and made the iron float, and the man picked it up. God cares even about small needs.

whyNot.C: Elisha struck the Jordan with Elijah's cloak to part it after Elijah was taken up (2 Kings 2:14).
whyNot.B: Dipping seven times in the Jordan was Elisha's instruction to Naaman (2 Kings 5:10).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: A prophet's widow told Elisha that a creditor was coming to take her two sons as slaves. How did God provide for her through Elisha?
options: Elisha asked the king to cancel all debts in Israel
Ravens brought her food and money every morning
Her little oil filled many borrowed jars, and she sold it to pay her debt
She found silver hidden in her late husband's house
questions.explanation: In 2 Kings 4:1-7 Elisha told the widow to borrow many empty vessels from her neighbours, shut the door and pour her small jar of oil into them. The oil kept flowing until every vessel was full. Elisha told her to sell the oil, pay her debts, and live on the rest with her sons.

whyNot.B: Ravens fed Elijah at the brook Cherith (1 Kings 17:6).
whyNot.A: Elisha did not go to the king; the provision came through a miracle of oil.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In Amos 3:2 God says to Israel, 'You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.' What does this teach?
options: God does not care about nations other than Israel
Being God's chosen people brings greater responsibility, not freedom from judgement
Only the families of priests would be punished
Israel would be spared because God had chosen them
questions.explanation: Many in Israel believed that being God's chosen people guaranteed safety. Amos turned this around: because God had specially known Israel and brought them out of Egypt, He would hold them accountable for their sins. Privilege brings responsibility. Amos also shows God judging other nations (Amos 1-2), so He is Lord of all.

whyNot.A: Amos 1-2 shows God judging the sins of many nations, and Amos 9:7 says God brought up other peoples too.
whyNot.D: This is the very belief Amos was correcting: election would not shield Israel from punishment.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In Hosea 4:6 God says, 'My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge.' What knowledge were they lacking?
options: Knowledge of God and His law
questions.explanation: Hosea 4:1 says there was no faithfulness, steadfast love or knowledge of God in the land. In 4:6 God blames the priests for rejecting knowledge and forgetting the law of God, so the people were ruined. Hosea teaches that true knowledge of God, shown in obedience, is essential for a nation's life.

whyNot.C: Hosea's concern was spiritual and moral, not economic skills.
whyNot.A: Hosea did not blame Israel's ruin on a lack of military knowledge; he blamed their turning from God.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Isaiah 1:18 says that though Israel's sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow. What does this verse teach?
options: God is willing to cleanse and forgive those who turn to Him
Sin can be washed away by ritual bathing
Only sins committed in ignorance can be forgiven
God will ignore sin as long as sacrifices are offered
questions.explanation: Isaiah 1:16-18 calls the people to wash themselves, stop doing evil, learn to do good, seek justice and help the oppressed. God then invites them to reason together and promises that sins like scarlet will become white as snow. Verses 19-20 add that the willing and obedient will be blessed, but the rebellious will be judged. Forgiveness goes with true repentance.

whyNot.D: Isaiah 1:11-15 says God was weary of their sacrifices because their hands were full of blood.
whyNot.B: The washing in Isaiah 1:16 is a picture of turning from evil, not a ritual bath.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In his letter to the exiles in Babylon, Jeremiah said the LORD would bring them back after a set time. How long was it?
questions.explanation: In Jeremiah 29:10 the LORD says that when seventy years are completed for Babylon, He will visit His people and bring them back to their place (see also Jeremiah 25:11-12). Meanwhile the exiles were to build houses, plant gardens, marry, and seek the welfare of the city where they lived (Jeremiah 29:5-7).

whyNot.C: Forty years was the time Israel wandered in the wilderness (Numbers 14:33-34).
whyNot.D: Four hundred years is linked with Israel's stay in Egypt, as foretold to Abraham (Genesis 15:13).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In Ezekiel 34, God condemns the 'shepherds of Israel'. Who were they, and what was their fault?
options: Herdsmen of Tekoa, who let their flocks stray into Judah
The Levites, who refused to offer lambs at the temple
Foreign kings, who stole Israel's sheep in war
Israel's leaders, who cared for themselves instead of the people
questions.explanation: In Ezekiel 34:2-4 the shepherds are Israel's rulers. They fed themselves, ate the fat and clothed themselves with the wool, but did not strengthen the weak, heal the sick or seek the lost, and ruled with force and harshness. God declared that He Himself would search for His sheep and set over them one shepherd, His servant David (Ezekiel 34:11, 23). The passage is a warning to all leaders.

whyNot.A: Tekoa was Amos's home town; Ezekiel's shepherds are a picture, not real herdsmen.
whyNot.B: Ezekiel's charge is about neglecting and exploiting the people, not about temple offerings.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: When the book of the law was found in the temple during King Josiah's reign, which prophetess did the king's officials consult?
questions.explanation: 2 Kings 22:8-14 says Hilkiah the high priest found the book of the law while the temple was being repaired. When it was read to Josiah he tore his clothes, and he sent officials to enquire of the LORD. They went to Huldah the prophetess in Jerusalem, who confirmed that disaster would come on the nation, but that Josiah would be spared from seeing it because he humbled himself (2 Kings 22:15-20).

whyNot.B: Deborah was a prophetess who judged Israel in the time of the judges (Judges 4:4).
whyNot.D: Anna was an elderly prophetess who saw the infant Jesus in the temple (Luke 2:36-38).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Which angel was sent to Mary in Nazareth to tell her that she would bear a son named Jesus?
questions.explanation: Luke 1:26-31 says that in the sixth month of Elizabeth's pregnancy the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a town of Galilee called Nazareth, to a virgin named Mary, who was betrothed to Joseph. He told her she would conceive and bear a son and call his name Jesus. Gabriel had also announced John's birth to Zechariah (Luke 1:19).

whyNot.C: Michael is called an archangel who contends with the devil (Jude 9), but he did not appear to Mary.
whyNot.A: Raphael does not appear in the Gospel accounts of Jesus' birth.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Who were the parents of John the Baptist?
questions.explanation: Luke 1:5-13 introduces Zechariah, a priest, and his wife Elizabeth, both righteous before God but childless and old. While Zechariah served in the temple, the angel Gabriel told him that Elizabeth would bear a son to be named John, who would prepare the people for the Lord.

whyNot.D: Elkanah and Hannah were the parents of Samuel (1 Samuel 1:19-20).
whyNot.C: Simeon and Anna both met the infant Jesus in the temple, but they were not husband and wife.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus stood up to read and was handed a scroll. Which prophet's book was it?
questions.explanation: Luke 4:16-21 says Jesus was given the scroll of the prophet Isaiah and read the passage about the Spirit of the Lord anointing him to preach good news to the poor, proclaim liberty to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind (Isaiah 61:1-2). He then said, 'Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.'

whyNot.A: Jeremiah's book was not the one read; the passage about good news to the poor is from Isaiah 61.
whyNot.D: Malachi is the last of the prophets, but the passage Jesus read is in Isaiah.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:5), what does Jesus say the meek will receive?
questions.explanation: Matthew 5:5 says, 'Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.' Meekness means gentle strength and humble trust in God rather than pride or violence. Each Beatitude pairs a quality with a particular blessing.

whyNot.A: Seeing God is promised to the pure in heart (Matthew 5:8).
whyNot.C: Comfort is promised to those who mourn (Matthew 5:4).
whyNot.D: Mercy is promised to the merciful (Matthew 5:7).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Right after teaching the Lord's Prayer, what did Jesus say would happen to those who do not forgive others (Matthew 6:14-15)?
options: Their prayers will be answered more slowly
They must offer a sacrifice in the temple
They will lose their place in the synagogue
Their Father will not forgive their trespasses
questions.explanation: Matthew 6:14-15 says that if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive others, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses. This explains the line 'forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors' (Matthew 6:12). Those forgiven by God must forgive others.

whyNot.C: Jesus' warning concerns God's forgiveness, not synagogue membership.
whyNot.B: Jesus did not prescribe a sacrifice; he linked receiving forgiveness with giving it.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: What is the main lesson of the parable of the lost sheep in Luke 15:3-7?
options: Shepherds should never leave their flocks unattended
Sinners must find their own way back to God
There is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents
Only the righteous are welcome in God's kingdom
questions.explanation: Jesus told this parable when the Pharisees and scribes grumbled that he received sinners and ate with them (Luke 15:1-2). A shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to look for the one lost sheep and rejoices when he finds it. Jesus said that in the same way there is more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance (Luke 15:7).

whyNot.D: The parable shows God seeking sinners, the opposite of welcoming only the righteous.
whyNot.B: In the parable the shepherd goes out to find the sheep; it does not find its own way back.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: A rich man asked Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life. Why did he go away sad (Mark 10:17-22)?
options: Jesus refused to speak to him because he was a tax collector
Jesus told him he had broken all the commandments
Jesus told him to sell what he had and give to the poor, and he had great possessions
Jesus said he was too young to follow him
questions.explanation: The man said he had kept the commandments from his youth. Jesus, looking at him, loved him and said he lacked one thing: to sell all he had, give to the poor, and come and follow him. The man was disheartened and went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. Jesus then taught how hard it is for those who trust in riches to enter the kingdom of God (Mark 10:23-25).

whyNot.B: The man claimed to have kept the commandments, and Jesus did not call him a lawbreaker.
whyNot.A: He is not described as a tax collector; Jesus welcomed tax collectors such as Zacchaeus.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In the parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14-30), why was the servant who received one talent condemned?
options: He spent it on wild living in a far country
He lent it to the other servants without the master's permission
He lost it to robbers on the way to market
He hid it in the ground out of fear and did not use it to gain anything
questions.explanation: The servants with five and two talents traded and doubled them, and were praised. The one-talent servant said he was afraid of his hard master, so he hid the talent in the ground and returned it unchanged. The master called him wicked and slothful, saying he should at least have put the money with the bankers to earn interest. The parable teaches that God expects us to use faithfully the gifts He gives.

whyNot.A: Wasting money in wild living describes the prodigal son (Luke 15:13).
whyNot.C: The servant kept the talent safe and returned it; his fault was that he did nothing with it.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Jesus healed ten men with leprosy on the way to Jerusalem (Luke 17:11-19). How many came back to thank him, and who was he?
options: Nine, and they were all Jews
One, and he was a Samaritan
Two, and they were both Galileans
One, and he was a priest
questions.explanation: Jesus told the ten lepers to go and show themselves to the priests, and as they went they were cleansed. Only one, seeing he was healed, turned back, praised God with a loud voice and fell at Jesus' feet giving thanks; he was a Samaritan. Jesus asked where the other nine were, noting that only this foreigner had returned to give praise to God. The story teaches gratitude.

whyNot.D: The lepers were sent to the priests; none of them is said to be a priest.
whyNot.A: Nine did not return; Jesus asked, 'Where are the nine?'

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: When Jesus told the paralysed man let down through the roof, 'Son, your sins are forgiven', why did some scribes object (Mark 2:5-7)?
options: They thought that only God can forgive sins, so Jesus was blaspheming
They were angry that the roof of the house had been broken
They believed the man was being punished for his parents' sin
They said healing was not allowed on the Sabbath
questions.explanation: Mark 2:6-7 says some scribes questioned in their hearts why this man spoke like that, calling it blasphemy, since no one can forgive sins but God alone. Jesus answered by healing the man, so that they would know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins (Mark 2:10-12). The miracle pointed to Jesus' divine authority.

whyNot.D: This healing at Capernaum is not said to be on a Sabbath; Sabbath disputes come in other stories (Mark 3:1-6).
whyNot.C: The idea that sickness comes from parents' sin was raised about the man born blind (John 9:2).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In Acts 1:8 Jesus promised the apostles power when the Holy Spirit came upon them. What would they then be?
options: Priests serving in the temple in place of the Levites
His witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and to the end of the earth
Soldiers who would free Israel from Rome
Rulers over the twelve tribes of Israel in Jerusalem
questions.explanation: Acts 1:6-8 says the apostles asked whether Jesus would now restore the kingdom to Israel. He replied that the times were not for them to know, but they would receive power when the Holy Spirit came upon them and would be his witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth. The rest of Acts follows this pattern.

whyNot.D: The apostles hoped for a restored kingdom, but Jesus redirected them to witnessing.
whyNot.C: Jesus' kingdom was not to be won by armed revolt against Rome.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: How does Acts 2:44-45 describe the way the first believers in Jerusalem shared their goods?
options: The apostles collected taxes from every believer
Each family kept its goods and gave a tenth to the temple
Only the rich were allowed to join the fellowship
They had all things in common and sold possessions to give to anyone in need
questions.explanation: Acts 2:44-45 says all who believed were together and had all things in common. They sold their possessions and belongings and distributed the proceeds to all, as any had need. Acts 2:42 adds that they devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread and prayers. Their sharing showed love and unity.

whyNot.B: The passage describes generous sharing, not a fixed tithe to the temple.
whyNot.A: Giving was voluntary; the apostles did not tax believers (compare Acts 5:4).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: As Stephen was being stoned, he knelt and cried, 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them' (Acts 7:60). What did this prayer show?
options: He was asking God to punish the Sanhedrin later
He wanted the crowd to free him
He was admitting that he had blasphemed
He forgave his killers, following the example of Jesus
questions.explanation: Stephen's last words echo Jesus' prayer on the cross, 'Father, forgive them' (Luke 23:34). Even while being killed, Stephen prayed for those stoning him and committed his spirit to the Lord Jesus (Acts 7:59). He is a model of Christian forgiveness under persecution.

whyNot.A: He asked God not to count the sin against them, the opposite of seeking punishment.
whyNot.C: Stephen boldly defended his message and did not admit to blasphemy.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: After Stephen's death, a great persecution scattered the believers throughout Judea and Samaria. What was the result (Acts 8:4)?
options: The believers returned to the Jewish sacrifices
Those who were scattered preached the word wherever they went
The church in Jerusalem closed down completely
questions.explanation: Acts 8:1 says all except the apostles were scattered, and Acts 8:4 adds that those who were scattered went about preaching the word. Philip, for example, went to Samaria and proclaimed Christ (Acts 8:5). Persecution, meant to stop the church, spread the gospel further.

whyNot.D: The apostles remained in Jerusalem (Acts 8:1), so the church there did not close.
whyNot.C: The apostles stayed in Jerusalem; they did not flee to Egypt.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: After an angel freed Peter from prison, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark. What did the servant girl Rhoda do when she recognised his voice at the gate?
options: She opened the gate at once and hid him in the house
She ran to tell Herod's soldiers that Peter had escaped
In her joy she ran in to tell the others without opening the gate
She refused to believe it was Peter and went back to sleep
questions.explanation: Acts 12:12-16 says many were praying in the house. Rhoda recognised Peter's voice and was so overjoyed that she did not open the gate but ran in and reported that Peter was standing outside. The others told her she was out of her mind, but Peter kept knocking, and when they opened they were amazed. God had answered the church's prayer.

whyNot.A: She did not open the gate at first; Peter was left knocking.
whyNot.D: Rhoda believed it was Peter; it was the people inside who doubted her.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Cornelius, the centurion to whom Peter preached the gospel (Acts 10), lived in which city?
questions.explanation: Acts 10:1 says Cornelius was a centurion of the Italian Cohort at Caesarea, a devout man who feared God. An angel told him to send men to Joppa for Peter. Peter came to Caesarea, preached, and the Holy Spirit fell on the Gentile listeners, who were then baptised (Acts 10:44-48).

whyNot.C: Peter was staying at Joppa in the house of Simon the tanner when Cornelius's men came for him.
whyNot.D: Damascus is where Saul was going when he was converted (Acts 9:3).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Which church, while worshipping the Lord and fasting, was told by the Holy Spirit to set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work to which He had called them?
questions.explanation: Acts 13:1-3 lists prophets and teachers in the church at Antioch. As they worshipped and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, 'Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.' After more fasting and prayer they laid hands on them and sent them off on the first missionary journey.

whyNot.A: The Jerusalem church sent Barnabas to Antioch earlier (Acts 11:22), but the missionary sending was from Antioch.
whyNot.D: Ephesus was reached later, on Paul's second and third journeys.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Why were Paul and Silas beaten and thrown into prison at Philippi?
options: They had preached in the synagogue on the Sabbath
The owners of a slave girl lost their income after Paul cast a spirit of divination out of her
They were accused of bringing a Gentile into the temple
They refused to bow to the image of the emperor
questions.explanation: Acts 16:16-24 says a slave girl with a spirit of divination brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling. She followed Paul for many days, until he commanded the spirit to come out of her. When her owners saw their hope of gain was gone, they dragged Paul and Silas before the magistrates, who had them beaten with rods and imprisoned.

whyNot.D: No image of the emperor is mentioned in Acts 16.
whyNot.C: The charge of bringing Gentiles into the temple was made against Paul later in Jerusalem (Acts 21:28).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Who stirred up the riot at Ephesus against Paul's preaching, and why?
options: Demetrius, a silversmith who made shrines of Artemis and feared losing trade
Elymas, a magician who wanted to keep the proconsul's favour
Tertullus, a lawyer hired by the high priest
Gallio, the proconsul, who hated the Jews
questions.explanation: Acts 19:23-27 says Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought much business to the craftsmen. He gathered them and warned that Paul's teaching that gods made with hands are not gods would ruin their trade and the honour of the great goddess Artemis. The crowd filled the theatre shouting, 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!'

whyNot.D: Gallio was proconsul of Achaia at Corinth and refused to judge the Jews' case against Paul (Acts 18:12-17).
whyNot.B: Elymas opposed Paul at Paphos in Cyprus (Acts 13:8).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: After the shipwreck, Paul landed on the island of Malta (called Melita in some older translations). What happened when a viper fastened on his hand as he put sticks on the fire?
options: He shook it off into the fire and suffered no harm
The islanders killed him, thinking he was a murderer
He became very ill until Publius prayed for him
He died for a short while and was raised
questions.explanation: Acts 28:3-6 says that when the viper fastened on Paul's hand, the islanders thought he must be a murderer whom justice would not allow to live. But Paul shook the creature into the fire and suffered no harm. When they saw nothing happened to him, they changed their minds and said he was a god. Paul later healed Publius's father (Acts 28:8).

whyNot.C: It was Publius's father who was sick, and Paul prayed for him, not the other way round.
whyNot.B: The islanders only thought he was a murderer; they did not harm him.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: According to Romans 10:9, what must a person do to be saved?
options: Keep all the commandments and be circumcised
Be baptised by an apostle and give alms to the poor
Fast for forty days and pray at the temple
Confess with the mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in the heart that God raised him from the dead
questions.explanation: Romans 10:9-10 says that if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. With the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved. Salvation comes through faith in the risen Christ.

whyNot.A: Paul teaches that righteousness comes by faith, not by the law or circumcision (Romans 10:4).
whyNot.C: Fasting and temple prayer are not the conditions Paul gives.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Tunde lost his job but held on to Romans 8:28. What does this verse assure believers?
options: Believers will never face any hardship
Every loss will be repaid double within a year
God works all things together for good for those who love Him
Suffering always shows that a person has sinned
questions.explanation: Romans 8:28 says that for those who love God, all things work together for good, for those who are called according to His purpose. It does not promise that troubles will not come; Paul lists hardships in Romans 8:35. It assures believers that God is at work even in painful events for their final good.

whyNot.A: Paul himself lists tribulation, distress and persecution as things believers face (Romans 8:35).
whyNot.D: The verse speaks of God's good purpose, not of suffering as proof of sin.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: What does Paul teach about temptation in 1 Corinthians 10:13?
options: Temptation comes from God to punish the disobedient
Giving in to small temptations is not sinful
Believers who are truly saved will never be tempted
God will not let believers be tempted beyond what they can bear but will provide a way of escape
questions.explanation: 1 Corinthians 10:13 says no temptation has overtaken believers that is not common to man. God is faithful and will not let them be tempted beyond their ability, but with the temptation He will also provide the way of escape, so that they may be able to endure it. Believers can resist temptation with God's help.

whyNot.C: Paul says temptation is common to all, so believers are not exempt.
whyNot.A: Paul presents God as faithful helper in temptation; James 1:13 says God tempts no one.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Some Corinthian believers knew that idols are nothing and freely ate food offered to idols. What did Paul tell them in 1 Corinthians 8:9-13?
options: They should force weaker believers to eat it too
They must never eat meat again under any circumstances
They should not let their freedom become a stumbling block to a weaker believer
Eating such food would make them lose their salvation
questions.explanation: Paul agreed that an idol is nothing, but warned that a believer with a weak conscience might see them eating in an idol's temple and be led to sin. Sinning against a brother in this way is sinning against Christ. Paul said that if food made his brother stumble, he would never eat meat rather than cause him to fall (1 Corinthians 8:13). Love limits liberty.

whyNot.B: Paul's 'never eat meat' was a personal choice for the sake of others, not a rule for all situations.
whyNot.A: Forcing weaker believers would damage their conscience, which is exactly what Paul warns against.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In 2 Corinthians 9:7, what kind of giver does Paul say God loves?
questions.explanation: 2 Corinthians 9:7 says each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver. Paul was encouraging the Corinthians to complete their gift for the poor believers in Jerusalem. What matters is a willing heart, not the size of the gift.

whyNot.A: Paul stresses the attitude of the heart, not the amount; compare the poor widow's offering (Mark 12:43).
whyNot.C: Jesus taught giving in secret (Matthew 6:3-4), but that is not the quality named in 2 Corinthians 9:7.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Which of the following does Paul list among the works of the flesh in Galatians 5:19-21?
questions.explanation: Galatians 5:19-21 lists the works of the flesh, including sexual immorality, idolatry, sorcery, enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, envy and drunkenness, and warns that those who practise such things will not inherit the kingdom of God. Patience, faithfulness and self-control belong to the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22-23).

whyNot.A: Patience is part of the fruit of the Spirit, the opposite list.
whyNot.D: Self-control is the last item in the fruit of the Spirit.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: How does Paul tell husbands to love their wives in Ephesians 5:25?
options: As Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her
Only as long as their wives obey them
In the same way as they love their parents
As a master cares for the servants in his house
questions.explanation: Ephesians 5:25 commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. Verse 28 adds that husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. The standard is Christ's self-giving, sacrificial love, not control or convenience.

whyNot.D: Paul uses Christ and the church as the pattern, not master and servant.
whyNot.B: Paul's command to husbands has no such condition attached.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Amaka, a clerk in a Lagos office, works hard only when her supervisor is watching. Which teaching from Colossians 3:23 corrects her attitude?
options: Whatever you do, work heartily as for the Lord and not for men
Do not work at all if your wages are too small
Let those who do not work go without food
Work hard only for employers who are believers
questions.explanation: Colossians 3:22-24 tells servants to obey their earthly masters not only when being watched, to please people, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord. Verse 23 says whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, since it is the Lord Christ they serve. A Christian worker should be diligent whether seen or unseen.

whyNot.D: Paul's teaching covers all work, not just work for believing employers.
whyNot.C: This rule from 2 Thessalonians 3:10 is about idle people refusing to work, not eye-service.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In 1 Peter 4:15-16, Peter distinguishes between two kinds of suffering. What does he teach?
options: All suffering is a punishment that believers must accept in silence
Believers should not suffer as wrongdoers, but if they suffer as Christians they should not be ashamed
Believers who suffer have lost God's favour
Christians should avoid suffering by hiding their faith
questions.explanation: 1 Peter 4:15-16 says none of the believers should suffer as a murderer, thief, evildoer or meddler. But if anyone suffers as a Christian, he should not be ashamed but glorify God in that name. Suffering earned by wrongdoing brings no credit; suffering for faithfulness to Christ is an honour (compare 1 Peter 4:14).

whyNot.A: Peter separates suffering for wrongdoing from suffering for Christ; not all suffering is punishment.
whyNot.C: Peter says those insulted for Christ's name are blessed (1 Peter 4:14).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In 1 Timothy 6:10, what does Paul describe as a root of evil that has led some to wander from the faith?
questions.explanation: 1 Timothy 6:9-10 warns that those who desire to be rich fall into temptation and harmful desires. Paul says the love of money is a root of evil, and through this craving some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs. It is the craving for money, not money itself, that he condemns; he tells Timothy that godliness with contentment is great gain (1 Timothy 6:6).

whyNot.D: Paul does not condemn money itself; he tells the rich to use their wealth to do good (1 Timothy 6:17-18).
whyNot.A: Paul elsewhere commends honest work (Ephesians 4:28), so work is not the root of evil.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which surah of the Qur'an is also called Umm al-Kitab (the Mother of the Book) and is recited in every rak'ah of salat?
questions.explanation: Surah al-Fatihah (Surah 1) sums up the main themes of the Qur'an: praise of Allah, His mercy, the Day of Judgement, worship of Him alone and the prayer for guidance. For this reason it is called Umm al-Kitab, and it is recited in every rak'ah of salat.

whyNot.A: Al-Ikhlas is greatly valued for teaching tawhid, but it is not called Umm al-Kitab and is not compulsory in every rak'ah.
whyNot.C: Al-Baqarah is the longest surah; it is not recited in every rak'ah.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which surah of the Qur'an is the only one that does NOT begin with 'Bismillahir-Rahmanir-Rahim'?
questions.explanation: Surah at-Tawbah, also called Bara'ah, is the ninth surah and the only one of the 114 surahs that does not open with the basmalah. It begins with a declaration of disassociation from the idolaters who broke their treaties.

whyNot.C: Al-Anfal, the surah just before at-Tawbah, does begin with the basmalah.
whyNot.A: Al-Fatihah opens with the basmalah; many scholars count it as its first verse.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which is the longest surah of the Qur'an, with 286 verses?
questions.explanation: Surah al-Baqarah (Surah 2), revealed in Madinah, is the longest surah with 286 verses. It contains Ayat al-Kursi (2:255) and many rulings on fasting, marriage, divorce and trade.

whyNot.D: Al 'Imran (Surah 3) has 200 verses.
whyNot.A: An-Nisa' (Surah 4) has 176 verses.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: For ease of recitation, especially in Ramadan, the Qur'an is divided into how many equal parts (ajza', singular juz')?
questions.explanation: The Qur'an is divided into 30 parts (ajza'). Reading one juz' a day lets a Muslim complete the whole Qur'an in the month of Ramadan.

whyNot.C: There are 60 hizb (half-parts), not 60 ajza'.
whyNot.A: 114 is the number of surahs, not of ajza'.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which surah of the Qur'an was revealed in Madinah?
questions.explanation: Surah al-Baqarah was revealed in Madinah after the Hijrah. Like other Madinan surahs, it is long and gives laws for the Muslim community, such as fasting, zakat, marriage and trade. Al-'Alaq, al-Fil and Quraysh are short Makkan surahs about faith and Allah's favours.

whyNot.A: Al-'Alaq contains the very first revelation, received in the Cave of Hira near Makkah.
whyNot.C: Al-Fil recalls the attack on the Ka'bah by Abrahah's army, told to the people of Makkah.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: In Surah al-Kawthar (Surah 108), what does Allah command the Prophet (SAW) to do in return for the abundance given to him?
options: Migrate and fight in Allah's cause
Pray to his Lord and sacrifice
questions.explanation: Surah al-Kawthar says: 'Surely We have given you abundance (al-Kawthar). So pray to your Lord and sacrifice. Surely it is your enemy who is cut off.' The command is to pray and to offer sacrifice to Allah alone.

whyNot.C: Fasting and feeding the poor are taught elsewhere in the Qur'an, not in al-Kawthar.
whyNot.A: Al-Kawthar is a short Makkan surah; it does not command migration or fighting.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which surah speaks of the coming of Allah's help and victory, and of people entering Allah's religion in crowds?
questions.explanation: Surah an-Nasr (Surah 110) says that when Allah's help and victory come and people enter His religion in multitudes, the Prophet should glorify his Lord and seek His forgiveness. Many scholars link it to the conquest of Makkah and see it as a sign that the Prophet's mission was nearly complete.

whyNot.D: Al-Falaq is a prayer for refuge from evils such as darkness and envy.
whyNot.C: At-Takathur warns against being distracted by competing for more worldly things.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: The well-known short commentary on the Qur'an called Tafsir al-Jalalayn was written by
options: Jalal ad-Din al-Mahalli and Jalal ad-Din as-Suyuti
Usman dan Fodio and Abdullahi dan Fodio
questions.explanation: Tafsir al-Jalalayn means 'the commentary of the two Jalals'. Jalal ad-Din al-Mahalli began it and, after his death, Jalal ad-Din as-Suyuti completed it. It is widely studied in Nigerian Islamic schools.

whyNot.C: Al-Bukhari and Muslim are famous compilers of hadith, not the authors of this tafsir.
whyNot.A: Ibn Kathir and at-Tabari each wrote their own large tafsir, not al-Jalalayn.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Surah az-Zalzalah (Surah 99) ends by teaching that whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it. What lesson does this teach?
options: Only large deeds are recorded by the angels
Every deed, however small, will be accounted for on the Day of Judgement
Reward and punishment happen only in this world
Good deeds cancel the need to perform salat
questions.explanation: The surah describes the earthquake of the Last Day, when the earth will bring out its burdens. Verses 7–8 teach that nothing is too small to be counted: even an atom's weight of good or evil will be shown to its doer. A Muslim should therefore not look down on any good deed or any sin.

whyNot.A: The verses say the opposite: even an atom's weight is recorded.
whyNot.C: The surah is about the Day of Judgement, the reckoning after this world.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: According to Qur'an 25:32, why was the Qur'an revealed gradually rather than all at once?
options: So that the Companions could vote on each verse
Because the Prophet could not read or write
To strengthen the heart of the Prophet (SAW)
Because Arabic had no written alphabet at the time
questions.explanation: The unbelievers asked why the Qur'an was not sent down all at once. Qur'an 25:32 answers: 'Thus (it is revealed) so that We may strengthen your heart with it, and We have recited it in stages.' Gradual revelation over about 23 years also made it easier to memorise and answered events as they happened.

whyNot.B: The Prophet was unlettered, but the verse gives strengthening his heart as the reason.
whyNot.D: Arabic did have a script; the Qur'an was written down by scribes as it was revealed.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: After the Qur'an, what is the second source of the Shari'ah (Islamic law)?
questions.explanation: Muslims take their law first from the Qur'an and then from the Sunnah, the sayings, actions and approvals of the Prophet (SAW), recorded in the hadith. Ijma' and qiyas come after these two primary sources.

whyNot.A: Ijma' is the third source and must itself rest on the Qur'an and Sunnah.
whyNot.B: Qiyas is used only when the Qur'an, Sunnah and ijma' give no direct ruling.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: A Companion washed his face in a certain way in front of the Prophet (SAW), and the Prophet saw it and said nothing against it. What type of sunnah is this?
