questions.explanation: v = ∫(6t − 4) dt = 3t² − 4t + c. It starts from rest, so v = 0 at t = 0 and c = 0. At t = 3: v = 27 − 12 = 15 m s⁻¹.

whyNot.A: 14 is the acceleration at t = 3, not the velocity.
whyNot.B: 27 leaves out the −4t term.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the area of the finite region enclosed by the curve y = x² − 4x and the x-axis.
questions.explanation: The curve meets the x-axis where x(x − 4) = 0, at x = 0 and x = 4, and lies below the axis in between. ∫₀⁴ (x² − 4x) dx = [x³/3 − 2x²]₀⁴ = 64/3 − 32 = −32/3. Area = 32/3 square units.

whyNot.C: 64/3 is only the x³/3 part at x = 4.
whyNot.D: 32 is only the 2x² part at x = 4.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A rectangle has a perimeter of 24 m. Find the greatest possible area of the rectangle.
questions.explanation: Let the sides be x and 12 − x. Area A = x(12 − x) = 12x − x². dA/dx = 12 − 2x = 0 gives x = 6, and d²A/dx² = −2 < 0, so this is a maximum. A = 6 × 6 = 36 m².

whyNot.C: 32 m² comes from sides 8 and 4, which is not the maximum.
whyNot.D: 144 m² squares 12, the half-perimeter, instead of 6.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: The side of a square metal plate is expanding at 0.3 cm s⁻¹ when heated. Find the rate at which its area is increasing when the side is 5 cm.
questions.explanation: A = x², so dA/dx = 2x. dA/dt = 2x × dx/dt = 2 × 5 × 0.3 = 3 cm² s⁻¹.

whyNot.C: 1.5 forgets the 2 in dA/dx = 2x.
whyNot.A: 10 is dA/dx at x = 5, not yet multiplied by dx/dt.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find ∫(2x + 3)⁴ dx.
questions.explanation: Increase the power by 1 and divide by the new power and by the coefficient of x: ∫(2x + 3)⁴ dx = (2x + 3)⁵/(5 × 2) + c = (2x + 3)⁵/10 + c. Check: d/dx[(2x + 3)⁵/10] = 5(2x + 3)⁴ × 2/10 = (2x + 3)⁴.

whyNot.A: Dividing by 5 alone forgets the factor 2 from the inner function.
whyNot.D: Multiplying by 2 instead of dividing by 2 doubles the error.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: The region under the curve y = √x from x = 0 to x = 4 is rotated completely about the x-axis. Find the volume of the solid generated.
questions.explanation: V = π∫₀⁴ y² dx = π∫₀⁴ x dx = π[x²/2]₀⁴ = π × 16/2 = 8π cubic units.

whyNot.A: 16π forgets to divide x² by 2 when integrating.
whyNot.B: 16π/3 integrates y = √x instead of y² = x.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: The mean of 8 numbers is 12. When one of the numbers is removed, the mean of the remaining 7 numbers is 11. Find the number removed.
questions.explanation: Total of 8 numbers = 8 × 12 = 96. Total of the remaining 7 = 7 × 11 = 77. The number removed is 96 − 77 = 19.

whyNot.D: 1 is the change in the mean, not the number removed.
whyNot.B: 23 uses 12 + 11, adding the two means.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A letter is chosen at random from the word ILORIN. Find the probability that it is a vowel.
questions.explanation: ILORIN has 6 letters: I, L, O, R, I, N. The vowels are I, O and I, which is 3 letters. Probability = 3/6 = 1/2.

whyNot.A: 1/3 counts I only once (I and O = 2 of 6).
whyNot.B: 1/6 counts a single vowel letter.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A and B are independent events with P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.25. Find P(A ∪ B).
questions.explanation: For independent events, P(A ∩ B) = 0.4 × 0.25 = 0.1. Then P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) = 0.4 + 0.25 − 0.1 = 0.55.

whyNot.C: 0.65 adds P(A) and P(B) without subtracting the overlap; the events are not mutually exclusive.
whyNot.B: 0.1 is P(A ∩ B), not P(A ∪ B).

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: X is a binomial random variable with n = 4 and p = 1/4. Find P(X = 1).

whyNot.B: 27/256 leaves out the factor ⁴C₁ = 4.
whyNot.D: 1/4 is just p, the probability of one success in a single trial.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the standard deviation of the numbers 4, 8, 10, 12 and 16.
questions.explanation: Mean = 50/5 = 10. Squared deviations: 36, 4, 0, 4, 36, total 80. Variance = 80/5 = 16, so standard deviation = √16 = 4.

whyNot.D: 16 is the variance; the standard deviation is its square root.
whyNot.A: √20 divides by n − 1 = 4 instead of n = 5.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Emeka, Fatima, Tunde and Ngozi sit at random in a row of 4 chairs. Find the probability that Emeka and Fatima sit next to each other.
questions.explanation: There are 4! = 24 arrangements. Treat Emeka and Fatima as one block: 3! = 6 arrangements of the block and the other two, and the pair can sit in 2 orders, giving 12. Probability = 12/24 = 1/2.

whyNot.A: 1/4 forgets that the pair can sit in 2 orders (6/24).

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A and B are events with P(B) = 0.5 and P(A | B) = 0.3. Find P(A ∩ B).

whyNot.B: 0.6 divides 0.3 by 0.5 instead of multiplying.
whyNot.A: 0.8 adds the two probabilities.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: The masses of bags of garri packed at a mill are normally distributed with mean 60 kg and standard deviation 5 kg. Given that P(Z < 2) = 0.9772, find the probability that a bag chosen at random weighs more than 70 kg.

whyNot.A: 0.9772 is P(X < 70); the question asks for more than 70 kg.
whyNot.C: 0.4772 is P(0 < Z < 2), the area between the mean and z = 2.
whyNot.B: 0.0456 counts both tails, P(|Z| > 2).

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: For a set of paired data, x̄ = 4, ȳ = 10 and the regression coefficient of y on x is b = 1.5. Find the regression line of y on x.
questions.explanation: The least squares line y = a + bx passes through (x̄, ȳ). So 10 = a + 1.5 × 4, giving a = 10 − 6 = 4. The line is y = 4 + 1.5x.

whyNot.C: y = 10 + 1.5x uses ȳ as the intercept, but the line must pass through (4, 10).
whyNot.B: y = 16 + 1.5x adds b x̄ instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.context:
A random variable X has this probability distribution:
x: 0, 1, 2, 3
P(X = x): 0.1, 0.3, k, 0.2
questions.stem: Using the table, find the variance of X.

whyNot.C: 3.7 is E(X²); [E(X)]² must be subtracted.
whyNot.B: 1.7 is E(X), the mean.
whyNot.D: 0.9 is the standard deviation, √0.81.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ is brought uniformly to rest in 4 s. Find the magnitude of the braking force.
questions.explanation: Deceleration a = (20 − 0)/4 = 5 m s⁻². Force F = ma = 1200 × 5 = 6000 N.

whyNot.A: 4800 N multiplies the mass by the time 4 s instead of by the deceleration.
whyNot.C: 24000 N multiplies the mass by the speed, which gives momentum (in kg m s⁻¹), not force.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Find the kinetic energy of a ball of mass 0.4 kg moving at 15 m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy = ½mv² = ½ × 0.4 × 15² = 0.2 × 225 = 45 J.

whyNot.D: 90 J forgets the ½ in ½mv².
whyNot.B: 6 is the momentum mv = 0.4 × 15, not the kinetic energy.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A trader lifts a 50 kg bag of rice from the ground onto a shelf 3 m high. Find the gain in potential energy of the bag. (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation: Gain in potential energy = mgh = 50 × 10 × 3 = 1500 J.

whyNot.B: 150 J leaves out g, using m × h only.
whyNot.D: 500 J is the weight of the bag in newtons, not the energy gained.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: Two forces, each of magnitude 10 N, act at a point with an angle of 120° between them. Find the magnitude of their resultant.

whyNot.C: 20 N would need the forces to act in the same direction.
whyNot.B: 17.3 N is the resultant when the angle between them is 60°.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A ball is thrown vertically upwards with a speed of 20 m s⁻¹. Find the greatest height it reaches. (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation: At the greatest height v = 0. Using v² = u² − 2gh: 0 = 400 − 20h, so h = 20 m.

whyNot.A: 40 m uses u²/g, forgetting the 2 in 2gh.
whyNot.B: 2 m is the time to reach the top (u/g), not the height.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A stone is thrown horizontally at 15 m s⁻¹ from the top of a cliff 80 m high. How far from the foot of the cliff does it land? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation: Vertically: 80 = ½ × 10 × t², so t² = 16 and t = 4 s. Horizontally the speed stays 15 m s⁻¹, so the distance is 15 × 4 = 60 m.

whyNot.D: 120 m uses t = 8 s, from 80 = 10t instead of 80 = 5t².
whyNot.A: 80 m is the height of the cliff, not the horizontal distance.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: On a see-saw, Ada (weight 300 N) sits 2 m from the pivot. How far from the pivot, on the other side, must Bayo (weight 400 N) sit to balance it?
questions.explanation: For balance, clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment: 400 × d = 300 × 2 = 600, so d = 600/400 = 1.5 m. The heavier person sits nearer the pivot.

whyNot.B: 2.67 m swaps the weights (400 × 2 ÷ 300); the heavier person must sit nearer.
whyNot.C: 2 m would only balance two equal weights.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A sledge moving at 8 m s⁻¹ on rough horizontal ground slides 16 m before coming to rest, slowed only by friction. Find the coefficient of friction. (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation: v² = u² − 2as: 0 = 64 − 32a, so a = 2 m s⁻². Friction is the only horizontal force: μmg = ma, so μ = a/g = 2/10 = 0.2.

whyNot.C: 0.5 is 8/16, speed over distance, which is not a deceleration.
whyNot.B: 2 is the deceleration in m s⁻²; μ = a/g.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A constant force of 20 N acts for 0.3 s on a body of mass 2 kg that is initially at rest. Find the speed of the body afterwards.
questions.explanation: Impulse = Ft = 20 × 0.3 = 6 N s, which equals the change in momentum. So 2v = 6 and v = 3 m s⁻¹.

whyNot.A: 6 is the impulse in N s; it must be divided by the mass.
whyNot.B: 1.5 m s⁻¹ divides the impulse by 4 instead of 2.

questions.subject: further-mathematics
questions.stem: A lift of mass 500 kg is moving downwards and slowing down at 1 m s⁻². Find the tension in the lift cable. (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation: Moving down and slowing down means the acceleration is 1 m s⁻² upwards. Taking upwards as positive: T − 500g = 500 × 1, so T = 5000 + 500 = 5500 N.

whyNot.B: 4500 N treats the acceleration as downwards; slowing while moving down means it points up.
whyNot.A: 5000 N is the weight, which is the tension only at constant velocity.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: The German mathematician Gottfried Leibniz built a mechanical calculator that could multiply and divide as well as add. What is it called?
questions.explanation: In the 1670s–1690s Leibniz designed the Stepped Reckoner. It used a stepped drum so that it could repeat additions to multiply and repeat subtractions to divide, going beyond Pascal's adding machine.

whyNot.D: The Pascaline was Blaise Pascal's earlier machine, mainly for addition and subtraction.
whyNot.B: The Difference Engine was designed by Charles Babbage in the 1820s.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Joseph Marie Jacquard's weaving loom of the early 1800s is important in computing history because it was controlled by
questions.explanation: Jacquard's loom used chains of punched cards: holes in each card decided which threads were lifted, so the pattern was 'programmed'. Babbage later borrowed the punched-card idea for his Analytical Engine.

whyNot.B: Magnetic tape storage came more than a century later.
whyNot.D: Vacuum tubes were used in first-generation electronic computers of the 1940s.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which ancient counting device is made of beads that slide along rods or wires set in a frame?
questions.explanation: The abacus is one of the oldest calculating aids. Each rod stands for a place value (units, tens, hundreds…) and numbers are shown and added by moving beads.

whyNot.A: Napier's bones are numbered rods, not beads.
whyNot.C: A slide rule uses sliding scales marked in logarithms.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of a computer?
options: It cannot think or decide what to do without instructions
It works at very high speed
It can store large amounts of data
It gives accurate results from correct data
questions.explanation: A computer only follows the instructions (programs) given to it. It has no intelligence or judgement of its own, so it cannot decide what to do by itself. Speed, storage and accuracy are strengths, not limitations.

whyNot.B: High speed is a characteristic (advantage) of computers.
whyNot.C: Large storage capacity is an advantage of computers.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: The Nigerian Meteorological Agency needs a computer that can carry out trillions of calculations each second to model the weather. Which class of computer is designed for such work?
questions.explanation: Supercomputers are the fastest and most powerful computers. They are used for very heavy calculations such as weather forecasting, climate modelling and scientific simulation.

whyNot.D: A microcomputer (personal computer) is far too slow for national weather models.
whyNot.B: An embedded computer controls a single device such as a microwave oven.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Second-generation computers mainly used which of the following as their main (internal) memory?
questions.explanation: Second-generation computers (late 1950s to mid-1960s) used transistors for processing and tiny magnetised rings called magnetic cores for main memory. Semiconductor memory chips came later with integrated circuits.

whyNot.B: Semiconductor RAM chips replaced core memory from the third and fourth generations.
whyNot.D: Paper tape was an input/storage medium, not main memory.
whyNot.A: Flash memory is a much later invention.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Very large-scale integration (VLSI), which puts many thousands or millions of transistors on one chip, is a feature of which generation of computers?
questions.explanation: Fourth-generation computers (from the 1970s) used large-scale and very large-scale integration, which made the microprocessor and personal computers possible.

whyNot.C: Second-generation machines used separate transistors.
whyNot.D: Third-generation machines used integrated circuits with far fewer components per chip (small- and medium-scale integration).

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: The computer in a school office is used for typing letters, preparing spreadsheets, browsing the internet and playing videos. By purpose, it is a
questions.explanation: A general-purpose computer can do many different jobs simply by running different programs. A special-purpose computer is built for one task only, such as controlling a traffic light.

whyNot.A: A special-purpose computer does one fixed job.
whyNot.C: Analog describes the form of data (continuous), not the range of jobs.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: The slide rule, a calculating device that uses sliding scales based on logarithms, was invented in the early 1600s by
questions.explanation: The English mathematician William Oughtred made the first slide rule around 1622, placing two logarithmic scales side by side so that sliding them multiplied numbers.

whyNot.D: Napier invented logarithms and Napier's bones, which the slide rule built on, but not the slide rule itself.
whyNot.C: Pascal built the Pascaline adding machine in the 1640s.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: The idea that a computer should keep its program in memory together with the data it works on (the stored-program concept) is mostly credited to
questions.explanation: In 1945 John von Neumann described a design in which instructions and data are both held in the same memory. This 'von Neumann architecture' is still the basis of most computers.

whyNot.D: Hollerith built punched-card tabulating machines for the census.
whyNot.B: Ada Lovelace wrote an early program for Babbage's Analytical Engine.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: An architect in Abuja wants to print large, accurate building drawings on wide sheets of paper. Which output device is best suited for this?
questions.explanation: A plotter draws lines with pens or prints on very wide paper, making it ideal for building plans, maps and engineering drawings.

whyNot.D: A dot-matrix printer prints small pages at low quality.
whyNot.A: A scanner is an input device.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which input method is used to read the shaded boxes on objective-test answer sheets so that they can be marked by computer?
questions.explanation: OMR detects the position of pencil marks on a specially printed form. It is used to mark multiple-choice answer sheets quickly.

whyNot.C: OCR reads printed letters and turns them into editable text.
whyNot.B: MICR reads magnetic-ink numbers on cheques.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: How many bytes are there in 5 MB? (Take 1 MB = 1024 KB and 1 KB = 1024 bytes.)

whyNot.A: 5120 is the number of kilobytes, not bytes.
whyNot.C: 5 000 000 uses 1000 instead of 1024.
whyNot.B: 40 960 is 5 × 1024 × 8, mixing up bytes and bits.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A teacher in Owerri has an 8 GB flash drive. How many video clips of 256 MB each can it hold? (Take 1 GB = 1024 MB.)

whyNot.D: 31 would leave 256 MB unused; 32 clips fit exactly.
whyNot.C: 3 comes from dividing 8 by 256 without converting GB to MB properly.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which CPU register temporarily holds the results of calculations carried out by the arithmetic and logic unit?
questions.explanation: The accumulator is a register in which the ALU stores intermediate and final results of arithmetic and logic operations.

whyNot.D: The program counter holds the address of the next instruction.
whyNot.A: The memory address register holds the address of the memory location being accessed.
whyNot.B: The instruction register holds the instruction currently being decoded.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A ticket machine at a Lagos bus terminal has a touch screen. Why is a touch screen described as both an input and an output device?
options: It stores data and also processes it
It shows information and also accepts the user's touches as commands
It prints tickets and also scans them
It connects to the network and also supplies power
questions.explanation: The screen displays menus and results (output) and senses where the user touches to receive choices (input), so one device does both jobs.

whyNot.C: Printing and scanning are done by other devices, not the touch screen.
whyNot.A: Storing and processing are jobs of storage and the CPU.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which unit of storage is equal to 1024 gigabytes?
questions.explanation: Going up in steps of 1024: 1024 bytes = 1 KB, 1024 KB = 1 MB, 1024 MB = 1 GB, and 1024 GB = 1 TB (terabyte).

whyNot.B: A megabyte is smaller than a gigabyte.
whyNot.D: A petabyte is 1024 terabytes.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: In what order does the CPU carry out the steps of the machine cycle for each instruction?
questions.explanation: The CPU first fetches the instruction from memory, then decodes it to work out what it means, and then executes it. The cycle then repeats for the next instruction.

whyNot.D: An instruction cannot be decoded before it has been fetched.
whyNot.A: The instruction must be decoded before the CPU knows how to execute it.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which secondary storage device stores data on flash memory chips and has no moving parts?
questions.explanation: An SSD keeps data in flash memory chips. With no spinning disks or moving heads it is quieter, faster and more resistant to knocks than a hard disk.

whyNot.D: A hard disk has spinning platters and moving read/write heads.
whyNot.C: A DVD drive spins the disc and moves a laser.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A computer has a word length of 32 bits. How many bytes can it handle as one unit?
questions.explanation: 1 byte = 8 bits, so a 32-bit word = 32 ÷ 8 = 4 bytes.

whyNot.A: 32 is the number of bits, not bytes.
whyNot.C: 8 is the number of bits in one byte.
whyNot.B: 256 is 32 × 8, multiplying instead of dividing.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Cells B2 to B5 of a spreadsheet contain 12, 15, 18 and 15. What does =AVERAGE(B2:B5) return?
questions.explanation: AVERAGE adds the values and divides by how many there are: (12 + 15 + 18 + 15) ÷ 4 = 60 ÷ 4 = 15.

whyNot.C: 60 is the SUM, not the average.
whyNot.B: 18 is the largest value (MAX).

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Cell C2 contains a student's score of 48. What does cell D2 show if it contains =IF(C2>=50,"Pass","Fail")?
questions.explanation: IF tests the condition C2>=50. Since 48 is not greater than or equal to 50, the condition is false, so the third argument, "Fail", is shown.

whyNot.A: "Pass" is shown only when the condition is true.
whyNot.C: IF returns the chosen text, not the word FALSE, because both results are given.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which language translator converts and runs a high-level program one statement at a time, stopping at the first error it meets?
questions.explanation: An interpreter translates each statement and executes it immediately before moving on. It stops when it finds an error, which makes it handy for testing.

whyNot.D: A compiler translates the whole program before it is run.
whyNot.B: An assembler translates assembly language, not a high-level language.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A program written with mnemonics such as LDA, ADD and STA must be converted into machine code by
questions.explanation: Mnemonics like LDA (load accumulator) belong to assembly language, a low-level language. An assembler translates assembly language into machine code.

whyNot.B: An interpreter translates high-level languages line by line.
whyNot.D: A compiler translates high-level languages such as C.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Software whose source code is made freely available for anyone to study, change and share, such as Linux, is called
questions.explanation: Open-source software publishes its source code under a licence that lets users read, modify and redistribute it. Linux and the LibreOffice suite are examples.

whyNot.C: Proprietary software keeps its source code private and is controlled by its owner.
whyNot.A: Custom-written software is made for one particular client.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A program that reduces the size of files so that they take less storage space and can be sent faster by email is a
questions.explanation: File compression utilities (for example, programs that make ZIP files) squeeze data into fewer bytes. They are utility software because they help maintain and manage the computer.

whyNot.C: A device driver lets the operating system control a piece of hardware.
whyNot.A: A compiler translates source code into machine code.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: The principal of a school in Kaduna wants to send the same letter to 300 parents, with each parent's name and address filled in automatically from a list. Which word-processing feature should she use?
questions.explanation: Mail merge combines one main document with a data source (the list of names and addresses) to produce a personalised copy for each person on the list.

whyNot.D: Find and replace changes words in one document; it does not create personalised copies.
whyNot.B: Word wrap only moves text to the next line at the margin.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Cells A1 to A6 of a spreadsheet hold 10, the text "absent", 25, nothing (blank), 40 and 7. What does =COUNT(A1:A6) return?
questions.explanation: COUNT counts only cells that contain numbers. The numbers are 10, 25, 40 and 7, so the result is 4. The text cell and the blank cell are ignored.

whyNot.C: 6 counts every cell, including the text and the blank.
whyNot.D: 5 counts the text cell as well (that is what COUNTA would do).
whyNot.A: 82 is the SUM of the numbers.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Cell C2 contains the formula =$A1*B$1. If the formula is copied to cell D3, what formula will D3 contain?
questions.explanation: Copying from C2 to D3 moves one column right and one row down. In $A1 the column is fixed ($A) but the row changes, giving $A2. In B$1 the row is fixed ($1) but the column changes, giving C$1. So D3 holds =$A2*C$1.

whyNot.B: This keeps the row in $A1 fixed, but only the column is locked there.
whyNot.C: This changes the locked parts ($A and $1) and leaves the free ones.
whyNot.D: This forgets that the column B in B$1 is free to change.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which of the following is database management software?
questions.explanation: Microsoft Access is a database management system used to create tables, forms, queries and reports for storing and finding records.

whyNot.A: PowerPoint is presentation software.
whyNot.B: Photoshop is graphics (image-editing) software.
whyNot.D: Firefox is a web browser.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Convert 10011₂ to base ten.
questions.explanation: Place values from the right are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. 10011₂ = 16 + 0 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 19.

whyNot.C: 11 reads the digits as if the leftmost 1 were worth 8.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Convert 57 in base ten to base eight (octal).
questions.explanation: Divide by 8: 57 ÷ 8 = 7 remainder 1; 7 ÷ 8 = 0 remainder 7. Reading the remainders from the last to the first gives 71₈. Check: 7 × 8 + 1 = 57.

whyNot.C: 17 reads the remainders in the wrong order.
whyNot.A: 57 is the number unchanged in base ten.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Convert the hexadecimal number 3A₁₆ to binary.
questions.explanation: Write each hex digit as four bits: 3 = 0011 and A (10) = 1010. Together 0011 1010 = 111010₂ after dropping the leading zeros.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Subtract 1101₂ from 11010₂.
questions.explanation: 11010₂ = 26 and 1101₂ = 13. 26 − 13 = 13, and 13 = 8 + 4 + 1 = 1101₂. (Doing it in binary with borrowing gives the same answer.)

whyNot.A: 10111 is 23, which comes from errors in borrowing.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A two-input logic gate gives an output of 0 only when both inputs are 1, and 1 for every other input. Which gate is it?
questions.explanation: NAND means NOT-AND: it is an AND gate followed by NOT. AND gives 1 only for inputs 1 and 1, so NAND gives 0 only for 1 and 1 and gives 1 otherwise.

whyNot.A: AND gives 1 only when both inputs are 1, the opposite.
whyNot.D: NOR gives 1 only when both inputs are 0.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which logic gate has only one input and gives an output that is the opposite of the input?
questions.explanation: The NOT gate (inverter) has one input. When the input is 1 the output is 0, and when the input is 0 the output is 1.

whyNot.C: AND has two or more inputs.
whyNot.A: OR has two or more inputs.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A finite set of clear, ordered steps for solving a problem is called
questions.explanation: An algorithm is a step-by-step method that solves a problem in a limited number of steps. It can then be written as pseudocode, drawn as a flowchart or coded in a programming language.

whyNot.B: A flowchart is one way of drawing an algorithm; a single symbol is only one step.
whyNot.C: A compiler is a translator program.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.context:
10 LET S = 0
20 FOR I = 1 TO 4
30 LET S = S + I * I
40 NEXT I
50 PRINT S
60 END
questions.stem: What value does the BASIC program above print?
questions.explanation: The loop adds the square of I for I = 1, 2, 3 and 4: S = 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 = 30. Line 50 prints 30.

whyNot.A: 10 is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4, forgetting to square I.
whyNot.B: 16 is only the last square, 4 × 4.
whyNot.C: 14 stops after I = 3.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A school's registration program rejects any age typed in that is less than 10 or greater than 25. Which type of validation check is this?
questions.explanation: A range check makes sure a value lies between a lower and an upper limit, here 10 to 25.

whyNot.C: A presence check only makes sure the field is not left empty.
whyNot.D: A format check tests the pattern of the data, such as a date written DD/MM/YYYY.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.context:
N ← 1
WHILE N < 20 DO
    N ← N * 3
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT N
questions.stem: What is the output of the pseudocode above?
questions.explanation: N starts at 1. 1 < 20, so N = 3. 3 < 20, so N = 9. 9 < 20, so N = 27. Now 27 < 20 is false, so the loop stops and 27 is output.

whyNot.A: 9 is the value before the last pass; the loop still runs because 9 < 20.
whyNot.C: 20 is the limit in the condition, not a value N ever takes.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A bank links the computers in its branches in Lagos, Abuja, Kano and Port Harcourt so that they share one customer database. This network is a
questions.explanation: A WAN covers a large geographical area such as a country, linking networks in different cities, usually through telecommunication links.

whyNot.D: A LAN covers only a building or a small site.
whyNot.B: A PAN covers a few metres around one person, such as a phone and earbuds.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: In which network topology is each computer connected to exactly two neighbours so that the cables form a closed loop?
questions.explanation: In a ring topology the devices form a circle. Data passes from one computer to the next around the loop until it reaches its destination.

whyNot.A: In a star each computer has its own cable to a central hub or switch.
whyNot.D: In a bus all computers share one main cable with two ends.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: In the web address https://www.example.com/results.html, what does 'https' identify?
options: The name of the file requested
The protocol used to transfer the page
The domain name of the website
The country where the server is
questions.explanation: A URL begins with the protocol. HTTPS is the secure (encrypted) version of HTTP, the protocol for transferring web pages. 'www.example.com' is the domain name and 'results.html' is the file.

whyNot.C: The domain name is www.example.com.
whyNot.A: The file name is results.html.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A school downloads a 1.5 GB software update over a connection that transfers 2 megabytes per second. How long does the download take? (Take 1 GB = 1024 MB and ignore delays.)
questions.explanation: 1.5 GB = 1.5 × 1024 = 1536 MB. Time = size ÷ rate = 1536 ÷ 2 = 768 seconds (12.8 minutes).

whyNot.A: 750 uses 1 GB = 1000 MB.
whyNot.C: 3072 multiplies by 2 instead of dividing.
whyNot.B: 96 divides by 8 as well, as if the rate were given in megabits.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Unwanted email messages sent in bulk to very many people, often to advertise something, are called
questions.explanation: Spam is unsolicited bulk email. It wastes time and storage and is often used to spread scams and malware.

whyNot.C: An attachment is a file sent along with an email.
whyNot.B: A cookie is a small file a website stores in the browser.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which of these is the strongest password for an online school portal account?
questions.explanation: A strong password is long and mixes capital and small letters, digits and symbols, and does not contain names, dates or common words. Kw7#pL9!vRz2 meets all of these.

whyNot.A: 'password123' is one of the most commonly guessed passwords.
whyNot.D: A name followed by a birth year is easy for others to guess.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which device forwards data packets between different networks, for example between a school's LAN and the internet, choosing a path for each packet?
questions.explanation: A router connects separate networks and uses IP addresses to decide where to send each packet next.

whyNot.B: A hub only repeats signals to all devices on the same LAN.
whyNot.A: A repeater just boosts a weak signal on a cable.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which type of malware copies itself and spreads across a network on its own, without needing to attach itself to another file or program?
questions.explanation: A worm is self-replicating and spreads through networks by itself. A virus, by contrast, needs a host file or program and spreads when that host is run or shared.

whyNot.B: A virus attaches to a host file and needs that file to be run.
whyNot.D: A Trojan horse pretends to be useful software and does not copy itself.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which type of fire extinguisher is safest to use on a fire involving computers and other electrical equipment?
questions.explanation: A CO₂ extinguisher smothers the fire with gas, does not conduct electricity and leaves no residue on equipment. Water and foam conduct electricity and can cause electric shock.

whyNot.C: Water conducts electricity and can electrocute the user.
whyNot.A: Foam contains water, so it conducts electricity too.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A trader at Computer Village copies a licensed accounting program onto CDs and sells them without the owner's permission. This offence is called
questions.explanation: Software piracy is the illegal copying, distribution or sale of software in breach of its copyright and licence.

whyNot.C: Phishing tricks people into revealing personal details.
whyNot.D: Hacking is gaining unauthorised access to a computer system.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: UNIVAC I, delivered to the United States Census Bureau in 1951 as one of the first commercial computers, belongs to which generation?
questions.explanation: UNIVAC I used vacuum tubes for processing, the defining feature of first-generation computers (1940s to mid-1950s).

whyNot.B: Second-generation computers used transistors, which came into wide use in the late 1950s.
whyNot.D: Third-generation computers used integrated circuits from the mid-1960s.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: The same computer in a Benin City office is used to prepare payroll, design posters, play music and send emails. Which characteristic of computers does this show?
questions.explanation: Versatility means a computer can do many different kinds of work, simply by running different programs.

whyNot.A: Diligence means working for long periods without tiring.
whyNot.C: Accuracy means giving correct results from correct data.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A computer that combines the features of both analog and digital computers is called a
questions.explanation: A hybrid computer can accept continuous (analog) signals, convert them, and process them digitally. It is used in places like hospitals and scientific labs.

whyNot.B: Mainframe describes size and power, not the type of data handled.
whyNot.C: Supercomputer also describes size and speed.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: In a microcomputer, the whole central processing unit is built on a single chip called a
questions.explanation: A microprocessor is a CPU on one integrated-circuit chip. Its arrival in the 1970s made small, cheap microcomputers (personal computers) possible.

whyNot.D: The motherboard is the main circuit board that the microprocessor plugs into.
whyNot.A: A hard disk is a storage device.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Charles Babbage's first calculating machine, designed in the 1820s to compute and print mathematical tables automatically, was the
questions.explanation: Babbage first designed the Difference Engine to produce error-free tables of numbers by the method of differences. He later designed the more general Analytical Engine.

whyNot.A: The Analytical Engine came later and was a general-purpose design.
whyNot.B: The Stepped Reckoner was built by Leibniz.
whyNot.C: The Tabulating Machine was Hollerith's census machine.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Herman Hollerith's Tabulating Machine Company was later merged with other firms into the company that is now known as
questions.explanation: In 1911 Hollerith's company merged with others to form the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company, which was renamed International Business Machines (IBM) in 1924.

whyNot.A: Microsoft was founded in 1975 as a software company.
whyNot.C: Apple was founded in 1976.
whyNot.D: Intel was founded in 1968 to make chips.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: The term 'hardware' refers to
options: the data stored on a computer
the programs that tell a computer what to do
the people who operate a computer
the physical parts of a computer that can be seen and touched
questions.explanation: Hardware is the physical equipment: the system unit, monitor, keyboard, mouse, printer and the parts inside them.

whyNot.B: Programs are software.
whyNot.C: The people who use and run computers are called users or liveware (humanware).

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: The Harvard Mark I, completed in 1944 by Howard Aiken with IBM, is best described as
options: a third-generation computer using integrated circuits
an electromechanical computer using switches, relays and shafts
a fully electronic computer using transistors
questions.explanation: The Harvard Mark I was a large electromechanical machine: it used relays, switches and a long rotating shaft rather than purely electronic parts. Transistors had not yet been invented.

whyNot.D: The transistor was invented only in 1947.
whyNot.A: Microprocessors appeared in the 1970s.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A person whose main job is to write, test and correct computer programs is called a
questions.explanation: A programmer designs, codes, tests and debugs programs, usually following a specification from a systems analyst.

whyNot.A: A data entry clerk types data into the computer.
whyNot.B: A computer engineer designs and repairs hardware.
whyNot.C: A systems administrator keeps computers and networks running.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which statement best describes the difference between analog and digital computers?
options: Analog computers measure continuous quantities; digital computers count discrete values
Analog computers are always faster than digital computers
Digital computers measure continuous quantities; analog computers count discrete values
Analog computers store data on disks; digital computers store data on paper
questions.explanation: Analog computers work with continuously varying physical quantities such as voltage or temperature. Digital computers work with separate (discrete) values, usually 0s and 1s.

whyNot.C: This reverses the two definitions.
whyNot.D: Storage medium is not what separates analog from digital computers.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which device keeps a computer running for a short time when mains power suddenly fails, giving the user time to save work and shut down properly?
questions.explanation: A UPS contains a battery that takes over immediately when mains power fails, so the computer does not switch off suddenly and lose unsaved work.

whyNot.C: A stabiliser evens out voltage but has no battery to supply power during an outage.
whyNot.A: A surge protector only blocks sudden voltage spikes.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which input device converts a printed photograph or document into a digital image that can be stored on a computer?
questions.explanation: A scanner shines light on the page and records the reflected light as a digital image, which is sent to the computer.

whyNot.B: A plotter is an output device for large drawings.
whyNot.C: A speaker is an output device for sound.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A secretary scans a typed letter and wants the computer to turn it into text that she can edit in a word processor. Which technology does this?
questions.explanation: OCR software recognises the shapes of printed letters in a scanned image and converts them into editable characters.

whyNot.A: OMR only detects the position of marks on a form.
whyNot.C: MICR reads special magnetic-ink characters such as those on cheques.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: How many kilobytes are there in 0.5 MB? (Take 1 MB = 1024 KB.)
questions.explanation: Each megabyte is 1024 kilobytes, so half a megabyte is 0.5 × 1024 KB = 512 KB.

whyNot.A: 500 uses 1000 instead of 1024.
whyNot.C: 2048 divides 1024 by 0.5 instead of multiplying.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: An external hard drive has a capacity of 2 TB. Express this in gigabytes. (Take 1 TB = 1024 GB.)
questions.explanation: Each terabyte is 1024 gigabytes, so 2 TB = 2 × 1024 GB = 2048 GB.

whyNot.D: 2000 uses 1000 instead of 1024.
whyNot.A: 512 divides by 2 instead of multiplying.
whyNot.C: 2 097 152 multiplies by 1024 twice, which gives megabytes.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Bisi's phone has 3 GB of free space. If each song takes exactly 4 MB, how many songs can she store in that space? (Take 1 GB = 1024 MB.)

whyNot.A: 750 uses 1 GB = 1000 MB.
whyNot.C: 12 multiplies 3 by 4 without converting units.
whyNot.B: 3072 is the free space in MB, not the number of songs.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which non-impact printer uses a laser beam, a drum and powdered toner to produce high-quality pages quickly?
questions.explanation: A laser printer uses a laser to draw the page as an electric charge on a drum; toner sticks to the charged areas and is then fused onto the paper by heat.

whyNot.A: An inkjet printer sprays liquid ink through tiny nozzles.
whyNot.B: A dot-matrix printer is an impact printer that strikes an inked ribbon.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A processor has an address bus with 16 lines. How many different memory locations can it address?
questions.explanation: Each address line carries one bit, so 16 lines can form 2¹⁶ different addresses. 2¹⁶ = 65 536 memory locations.

whyNot.A: 256 is 2⁸, which would need only 8 lines.
whyNot.D: 16 is the number of lines, not the number of addresses.
whyNot.B: 32 is 16 × 2, doubling instead of raising 2 to the power 16.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which type of read-only memory can be erased by shining ultraviolet light on it and then reprogrammed?
questions.explanation: EPROM (Erasable Programmable ROM) has a small quartz window; ultraviolet light through the window erases the chip so it can be programmed again.

whyNot.D: PROM can be programmed only once and cannot be erased.
whyNot.A: Mask ROM has its contents fixed during manufacture.
whyNot.C: DRAM is a type of RAM, not ROM.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: The smallest single dot of light that makes up the picture on a computer screen is called a
questions.explanation: A pixel (picture element) is the smallest point on a screen. Screen resolution, such as 1920 × 1080, gives the number of pixels across and down.

whyNot.C: A byte is a unit of storage (8 bits).
whyNot.A: The cursor marks where the next character will appear.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which of the following is system software?
questions.explanation: Linux is an operating system, and operating systems are system software because they control the hardware and run other programs. The other three are application packages.

whyNot.A: Excel is a spreadsheet application.
whyNot.D: CorelDRAW is a graphics application.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Cells D1 to D4 of a spreadsheet contain 63, 48, 71 and 55. What does =MIN(D1:D4) return?
questions.explanation: MIN returns the smallest value in the range. Comparing 63, 48, 71 and 55, the smallest is 48.

whyNot.D: 71 is the largest value (MAX).
whyNot.A: 237 is the SUM of the values.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: In a spreadsheet, B2 = 7 and C2 = 5. What value does the formula =(B2+C2)*2 give?
questions.explanation: Brackets are worked out first: B2 + C2 = 7 + 5 = 12. Then 12 × 2 = 24.

whyNot.D: 17 ignores the brackets and works 7 + 5 × 2.
whyNot.A: 70 multiplies 7 by 5 and then by 2.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: While typing in a word processor, the text automatically moves to the next line when it reaches the right margin. This feature is called
questions.explanation: Word wrap moves a word that does not fit to the start of the next line, so the user does not need to press Enter at the end of each line.

whyNot.C: Mail merge produces personalised copies of a document.
whyNot.B: Justification lines text up evenly with both margins; it does not move text to a new line.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: An air traffic control system must respond to radar data immediately, within strict time limits. Which type of operating system does it need?
questions.explanation: A real-time operating system processes input and responds within guaranteed, very short time limits, which is essential where delays are dangerous.

whyNot.A: Batch processing collects jobs and runs them later, which is far too slow here.
whyNot.D: Single-tasking cannot handle many radar signals at once.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Software that is stored permanently on a ROM chip and controls a device at a basic level, such as a computer's BIOS, is called
questions.explanation: Firmware is software built into hardware, usually in ROM or flash memory. The BIOS that starts a computer is firmware.

whyNot.C: Freeware is software that is given away free of charge.
whyNot.B: Shareware can be tried free for a while before paying.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: In a spreadsheet, the box formed where a column and a row meet, such as B4, is called a
questions.explanation: A cell is the intersection of one column and one row. Its address is the column letter followed by the row number, for example B4.

whyNot.C: A range is a group of cells, such as B4:B9.
whyNot.A: A worksheet is the whole grid of cells.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: After compiling, which program joins several object-code modules and library routines into one executable program?
questions.explanation: A linker (link editor) combines separately compiled object files and the library routines they call into a single file that can be loaded and run.

whyNot.C: An interpreter translates and runs source code line by line; it produces no executable file.
whyNot.D: A debugger helps find errors in a program.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A church in Onitsha wants to design its weekly bulletin with pictures, columns and different page layouts. Which type of application software is best for this?
questions.explanation: Desktop publishing (DTP) software, such as Microsoft Publisher, gives detailed control of page layout, columns, text frames and pictures for newsletters, bulletins and flyers.

whyNot.B: Database software stores and searches records.
whyNot.D: Spreadsheet software works with numbers in rows and columns.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Cell A1 of a spreadsheet contains 23.461. What does =ROUND(A1,1) return?
questions.explanation: ROUND(A1,1) rounds to 1 decimal place. The digit after the first decimal place is 6, which is 5 or more, so 23.4 rounds up to 23.5.

whyNot.C: 23.4 cuts off the digits instead of rounding up.
whyNot.D: 23 rounds to 0 decimal places.
whyNot.B: 23.46 rounds to 2 decimal places.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Convert 1010.1₂ to base ten.
questions.explanation: Before the point: 1010₂ = 8 + 2 = 10. After the point, the first place is worth 2⁻¹ = 0.5, so .1₂ = 0.5. Total = 10.5.

whyNot.A: 10.1 copies the fractional digit without converting it.
whyNot.B: 5.5 reads the whole-number part as 101₂.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Convert 64 in base ten to hexadecimal.
questions.explanation: 64 ÷ 16 = 4 remainder 0, and 4 ÷ 16 = 0 remainder 4. Reading upwards gives 40₁₆. Check: 4 × 16 + 0 = 64.

whyNot.B: 64 is the number in base ten, unchanged.
whyNot.C: 100 is 64 written in base eight.
whyNot.D: 3F₁₆ is 63.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Convert 754₈ to base ten.
questions.explanation: Place values in base eight are 64, 8 and 1. 754₈ = 7 × 64 + 5 × 8 + 4 × 1 = 448 + 40 + 4 = 492.

whyNot.D: 754 leaves the number in base eight.
whyNot.A: 124 uses place values 16, 4, 1 wrongly.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Add 1111₂ and 1₂.
questions.explanation: 1 + 1 = 10₂, so write 0 and carry 1 into each column in turn: every column becomes 0 with a carry, giving 10000₂. Check: 15 + 1 = 16 = 10000₂.

whyNot.C: '2' is not a binary digit.
whyNot.A: 1110 is 14, which is subtraction, not addition.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Multiply 101₂ by 11₂.
questions.explanation: 101₂ = 5 and 11₂ = 3, so the product is 15 = 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 1111₂. In binary: 101 + 1010 = 1111.

whyNot.B: 1000 is 8, which is 5 + 3, adding instead of multiplying.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A two-input logic gate gives an output of 1 only when both inputs are 0. Which gate is it?
questions.explanation: NOR is NOT-OR. OR gives 0 only when both inputs are 0, so NOR gives 1 only in that case and 0 for every other input pair.

whyNot.A: NAND gives 0 only when both inputs are 1.
whyNot.D: AND gives 1 only when both inputs are 1.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: In ASCII code, the capital letter A is stored as 65 (in base ten). What is the ASCII code of the capital letter D?
questions.explanation: Capital letters have consecutive ASCII codes: A = 65, B = 66, C = 67, D = 68.

whyNot.D: 69 is the code for E.
whyNot.A: 67 is the code for C.
whyNot.C: 100 is the code for small d.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: In a flowchart, which symbol is used to mark the START and STOP of the algorithm?
questions.explanation: The terminal symbol, an oval or rounded rectangle, shows where a flowchart begins and ends.

whyNot.B: The diamond is for decisions.
whyNot.D: The rectangle is for processes such as calculations.
whyNot.A: The parallelogram is for input and output.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.context:
10 LET A = 15
20 LET B = 4
30 LET C = A MOD B
40 PRINT C
50 END
questions.stem: What does the BASIC program above print?
questions.explanation: MOD gives the remainder after division. 15 ÷ 4 = 3 remainder 3, so 15 MOD 4 = 3.

whyNot.A: 3.75 is 15 ÷ 4, ordinary division.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: To reduce typing errors, every exam score is typed into the computer twice by two different clerks and the computer compares the two entries. This method is called
questions.explanation: Verification checks that data has been copied or typed correctly from the source, for example by double entry. Validation instead checks that data is sensible or allowed (such as a range check), not that it matches the source.

whyNot.D: Validation checks that data obeys rules, but cannot tell whether a sensible value was mistyped.
whyNot.A: Encryption scrambles data for security.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which hardware component must a computer have so that it can be connected to a network by cable or wireless link?
questions.explanation: A network interface card (NIC), wired or wireless, provides the connection between the computer and the network and gives it a unique hardware (MAC) address.

whyNot.B: A sound card handles audio.
whyNot.C: A graphics card produces the display image.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: In a full mesh network every computer has its own direct link to every other computer. How many links are needed to connect 5 computers in a full mesh?
questions.explanation: Each of the 5 computers links to the other 4, giving 5 × 4 = 20 link-ends. Each link joins two computers, so the number of links = 20 ÷ 2 = 10, from the formula n(n − 1) ÷ 2.

whyNot.C: 5 links would only form a ring.
whyNot.B: 20 counts every link twice.
whyNot.D: 25 is 5 × 5, which links each computer to itself as well.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A company that provides customers with access to the internet, usually for a fee, is called
questions.explanation: An ISP connects homes, schools and businesses to the internet through cable, fibre, wireless or mobile networks, and usually charges for the service.

whyNot.A: A search engine finds web pages; it does not provide the connection.
whyNot.C: A web browser is a program for viewing web pages.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A home Wi-Fi link transfers data at 20 megabits per second. How many megabytes can it transfer in one minute? (Take 1 byte = 8 bits and ignore delays.)
questions.explanation: In 60 seconds the link carries 20 × 60 = 1200 megabits. Dividing by 8 bits per byte: 1200 ÷ 8 = 150 megabytes.

whyNot.D: 1200 is megabits; it has not been divided by 8.
whyNot.A: 9600 multiplies by 8 instead of dividing by 8.
whyNot.B: 2.5 MB is the amount in one second only.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Gaining access to another person's computer system or account without permission is called
questions.explanation: Hacking is unauthorised entry into a computer system, network or account. It is a crime in Nigeria and in most countries.

whyNot.A: Downloading is copying files from the internet to your device.
whyNot.B: Browsing is viewing web pages.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: Which Nigerian law, passed in 2015, deals specifically with offences such as hacking, identity theft and cyberstalking?
questions.explanation: The Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act 2015 created offences such as unlawful access to computers, identity theft, cyberstalking and computer fraud.

whyNot.B: The Freedom of Information Act (2011) gives the public access to government records.
whyNot.D: The Nigeria Data Protection Act (2023) governs how personal data is collected and processed.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A document file that is sent together with an email message is called
questions.explanation: An attachment is any file, such as a document, picture or spreadsheet, sent along with an email. It is usually shown with a paper-clip icon.

whyNot.B: The subject line is a short title for the email.
whyNot.C: The recipient is the person the email is sent to.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A web designer in Ibadan uploads the files of a new site to the web server at example.com. Which protocol is designed for transferring files between computers in this way?
questions.explanation: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is used to upload and download files between a client and a server, for example when publishing a website.

whyNot.D: SMTP is used to send email.
whyNot.B: POP3 is used to download email from a mail server.
whyNot.A: DNS converts domain names to IP addresses.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: After typing her password correctly, a bank customer must also enter a one-time code sent to her phone before she can log in. This security measure is called
questions.explanation: Two-factor authentication requires two different kinds of proof: something you know (the password) and something you have (the phone receiving the code). A stolen password alone is then not enough.

whyNot.D: Encryption scrambles data so it cannot be read; it does not check who is logging in.
whyNot.B: A firewall filters network traffic.

questions.subject: computer-studies
questions.stem: A student who spends many hours at a computer complains of tired, sore eyes and blurred vision. Which practice would best reduce this problem?
options: Working in a dark room with only the screen lit
Turning the screen brightness to maximum
Using an anti-glare screen and looking away from the screen regularly
Sitting closer to the screen to see it more clearly
questions.explanation: Eye strain is reduced by cutting glare and giving the eyes regular rests, for example by looking at something far away every few minutes, and by keeping the screen at a comfortable distance and brightness.

whyNot.D: Sitting closer increases eye strain.
whyNot.A: A bright screen in a dark room creates strong contrast that tires the eyes.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Which animal was the chief means of transport for goods carried across the desert in the trans-Saharan trade?
questions.explanation: The camel can travel for days with little water and carries heavy loads over sand, so camel caravans carried goods between North Africa and the states of the western and central Sudan, such as Kanem-Bornu and the Hausa states.

whyNot.C: Horses were themselves an important import from the north, but they need much water and could not carry trade goods across the desert.
whyNot.D: Donkeys were used for local trade in the savanna, not for crossing the Sahara.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The archaeological site of Igbo-Ukwu, in present-day Anambra State, is famous for
options: life-size stone statues of ancient kings
the oldest terracotta heads found in Nigeria
finely made bronze objects cast by the lost-wax method
the remains of huge earth walls around a capital city
questions.explanation: Excavations at Igbo-Ukwu uncovered very detailed bronze bowls, ornaments and other objects, together with thousands of beads, dating back over a thousand years. They show that skilled metalworking existed in Igboland long before European contact.

whyNot.D: Great earth walls are associated with Benin and with the Hausa cities, not Igbo-Ukwu.
whyNot.B: The oldest terracotta figures in Nigeria belong to the Nok culture.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In the Benin Kingdom, the famous brass plaques and heads made for the Oba were produced by
options: traders who brought them from North Africa
ordinary farmers working in their spare time
a guild of craftsmen organised under the palace
questions.explanation: Benin brass casting was a royal art. The brass casters formed a guild that worked for the Oba and lived in their own quarter of Benin City, and the skill was passed down within the guild.

whyNot.A: The works were made in Benin itself; North African traders did not supply them.
whyNot.B: The Portuguese traded brass (manillas) to Benin, but the casting was done by Benin craftsmen.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Among the pre-colonial Igbo, the ofo staff held by the head of a lineage was a symbol of
options: authority and truth, linking the holder with the ancestors
membership of a trading company on the coast
victory in war over a neighbouring town
the power of the Oba over his chiefs
questions.explanation: The ofo was a sacred staff passed down in a lineage. The elder who held it spoke for the lineage, and it was believed to carry the authority of the ancestors, so oaths sworn on it were taken very seriously.

whyNot.B: Trading companies belonged to the Niger Delta house system, not the ofo.
whyNot.D: Most Igbo communities had no Oba; authority was spread among elders and other groups.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In pre-colonial Igbo communities, age grades usually served to
options: choose and crown the king of the community
carry out public works and help enforce community decisions
judge cases according to Islamic law
collect tribute for an overlord in another kingdom
questions.explanation: Age grades grouped people born within a few years of one another. Younger grades cleared paths, built markets and guarded the town, while older grades helped keep order and carry out the decisions of the elders and village assembly.

whyNot.A: Most Igbo communities had no king to crown; government was by elders and assemblies.
whyNot.C: Islamic law was applied in the emirates of the North, not in Igbo age grades.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Old Oyo's military strength rested largely on its cavalry. This helps to explain why Oyo found it difficult to
options: obtain horses from its northern neighbours
fight effectively in the thick forest zone to the south
defend its capital against small raids
control the open savanna close to its capital
questions.explanation: Horses work well in open grassland but not in dense forest, where tsetse flies also kill them. So Oyo dominated the savanna but its cavalry was much less effective against forest peoples to the south.

whyNot.D: The open savanna was exactly where the cavalry was strongest.
whyNot.A: Oyo did obtain horses from the north; the problem was using them in the forest.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Leaders who received flags from Uthman dan Fodio and carried the jihad into their own areas later became
options: kings of the old Hausa ruling families
emirs of the emirates of the Sokoto Caliphate
questions.explanation: Uthman dan Fodio gave flags to trusted followers, who led the jihad in places such as Kano, Zaria and Adamawa. After victory they ruled those areas as emirs who owed loyalty to Sokoto.

whyNot.A: The jihad overthrew the old Hausa ruling families.
whyNot.C: Mai was the title of the rulers of Bornu, which resisted the jihad.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In the emirates of the Sokoto Caliphate, the official who judged cases according to Islamic law was the
questions.explanation: The Alkali was the Islamic judge. He heard cases and applied the Sharia, which made the courts of the emirates a separate arm of government from the emir's council.

whyNot.B: The Waziri was the chief adviser or chief minister.
whyNot.C: The Madawaki was a senior military title, often the commander of the army.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Afonja's revolt at Ilorin in the early nineteenth century helped bring about the collapse of Old Oyo. Which office did Afonja hold?
questions.explanation: Afonja was the Are-Ona-Kakanfo, the head of the Oyo army in the provinces. He turned against the Alaafin and called on Fulani Muslims for help; they later took control of Ilorin, which became an emirate of the Sokoto Caliphate.

whyNot.B: The Bashorun headed the Oyo Mesi in the capital.
whyNot.C: The Aremo was the crown prince.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In the political system of the Benin Kingdom, the Uzama were
options: palace servants who carried messages to the provinces
hereditary chiefs who served as kingmakers
priests of the earth goddess in each village
foreign traders allowed to settle at the coast
questions.explanation: The Uzama were the highest-ranking hereditary chiefs of Benin. Their positions passed from father to son, and they played a central part in installing a new Oba, so they acted as kingmakers.

whyNot.A: Palace officials were organised in palace associations; the Uzama were senior hereditary nobles.
whyNot.C: The Uzama held political, not village priestly, office.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In which year did British forces capture Sokoto and bring the caliphate under British control?
questions.explanation: After capturing Kano early in 1903, Lugard's forces took Sokoto in March 1903. The British then ruled the North through the emirs under indirect rule.

whyNot.C: 1900 is when the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria was proclaimed, before the conquest was complete.
whyNot.B: 1914 was the year of amalgamation.
whyNot.D: 1897 was the year of the British expedition against Benin.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: During the colonial period, which export crop was grown mainly in Northern Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Groundnuts (and cotton) grew well in the drier savanna of the North and were exported in large amounts, especially after the railway reached Kano. Cocoa came mainly from the West and palm produce mainly from the East.

whyNot.D: Cocoa was the main export crop of the Western Region.
whyNot.A: Palm oil and kernels came mainly from the East and the Niger Delta.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Before 1900, Western-style schools in Southern Nigeria were provided mainly by
questions.explanation: Missions such as the Church Missionary Society, the Methodists and the Church of Scotland Mission set up schools so that converts could read the Bible. The colonial government only gradually began to fund and run schools.

whyNot.D: The Royal Niger Company was a trading and governing company, not an educational body.
whyNot.B: The emirs supported Qur'anic schools, not Western schools, and were in the North.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: One major reason the British amalgamated Northern and Southern Nigeria in 1914 was to
options: prepare Nigeria for independence within a few years
use the revenue surplus of the South to offset the deficit of the North
end the use of indirect rule in the North
allow Nigerians to elect a national parliament
questions.explanation: The North had little revenue and depended on grants from Britain, while the South earned customs duties from its trade. Joining them let the colonial government use Southern revenue for the North and run both more cheaply.

whyNot.A: Independence was not considered in 1914; it came 46 years later.
whyNot.D: There was no elected national parliament after amalgamation.
whyNot.C: Indirect rule continued in the North and was extended to the South.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The railway line from Lagos reached Kano in 1912. Its main economic purpose was to
options: take crude oil from the North to the ports
carry export crops such as groundnuts and cotton to the coast
carry passengers to the new federal capital
move troops for the war against Germany
questions.explanation: Colonial railways were built to move raw materials cheaply to the ports for export and to carry imported goods inland. The Lagos–Kano line opened up the groundnut and cotton areas of the North.

whyNot.C: There was no federal capital in 1912; Lagos was the capital.
whyNot.A: Crude oil was not produced in commercial quantities until the 1950s, and in the Niger Delta.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The West African Currency Board, set up in 1912, was responsible for
options: issuing a common currency for the British West African colonies
collecting taxes for the Native Authorities
fixing the prices paid to cocoa farmers
questions.explanation: The Board issued West African coins and notes used in Nigeria, the Gold Coast, Sierra Leone and the Gambia. These replaced older currencies such as cowries and manillas.

whyNot.D: Fixing crop prices was later the work of the marketing boards.
whyNot.C: Taxes for Native Authorities were collected through the Native Treasuries.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Christian missionary work in nineteenth-century Nigeria began at Badagry in 1842 with the arrival of
options: Richard Lander, the explorer of the Niger
Mary Slessor of the Calabar mission
Thomas Birch Freeman of the Methodist mission
Hope Waddell of the Church of Scotland mission
questions.explanation: Thomas Birch Freeman, a Methodist missionary, arrived at Badagry in September 1842. Missionary work then spread from Badagry to Abeokuta and other towns.

whyNot.D: Hope Waddell began the Church of Scotland mission at Calabar in 1846.
whyNot.B: Mary Slessor arrived in Calabar much later, in 1876.
whyNot.A: Richard Lander was an explorer who traced the course of the Niger, not a missionary.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Nigerian Council set up by Lugard in 1914 was criticised mainly because it
options: was made up entirely of elected Nigerians
gave the North no representation at all
was only advisory and had no real power to make laws
met every week and slowed down government
questions.explanation: The Nigerian Council was a large body of mostly British officials with a few nominated Nigerian members. It met rarely and could only discuss and advise, so it gave Nigerians no real say in government. It was abolished by the Clifford Constitution of 1922.

whyNot.A: None of its members was elected; the Nigerian members were nominated.
whyNot.D: It met only about once a year.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Adubi War (the Egba uprising) of 1918 in Abeokuta was largely a reaction against
options: the introduction of direct taxation and forced labour under indirect rule
the arrival of Christian missionaries in Abeokuta
the building of the railway from Lagos to Kano
questions.explanation: After Egbaland lost its separate status in 1914, the British extended indirect rule there, increasing the power of the Alake and introducing direct taxation and forced labour. Anger at these measures led to the uprising of 1918.

whyNot.C: Missionaries had worked in Abeokuta since the 1840s and were not the cause of the 1918 rising.
whyNot.A: Dahomey's wars with the Egba belonged to the nineteenth century.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Lagos Treaty of Cession of 1861, by which Lagos became a British colony, was signed by
questions.explanation: Oba Dosunmu (Docemo), son of Akitoye, signed the treaty in August 1861 under British pressure, handing Lagos over to the British Crown in return for a pension.

whyNot.D: Kosoko had been driven out of Lagos by the British in 1851.
whyNot.A: Akitoye was restored in 1851 but died in 1853, before the cession.
whyNot.B: Ovonramwen was Oba of Benin, not Lagos.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Who is often called the 'father of Nigerian nationalism'?
questions.explanation: Herbert Macaulay criticised colonial policies in Lagos from the late nineteenth century, founded the NNDP in 1923 and was the first president of the NCNC in 1944. His long struggle earned him this title.

whyNot.A: Ahmadu Bello led the NPC in the 1950s, much later.
whyNot.C: Balewa was the first Prime Minister, not an early nationalist pioneer.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: During the 1950s and early 1960s, the Premier of the Northern Region was
questions.explanation: Sir Ahmadu Bello, the Sardauna of Sokoto and leader of the NPC, chose to remain Premier of the Northern Region and sent his deputy, Tafawa Balewa, to the centre as Prime Minister.

whyNot.C: Balewa was federal Prime Minister.
whyNot.A: Aminu Kano led the opposition party NEPU.
whyNot.D: Okpara was Premier of the Eastern Region.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In the 1950s, the National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC) drew its strongest support from the
questions.explanation: Although the NCNC began as a national body, under Azikiwe it became strongest in the Eastern Region, which it governed. The NPC dominated the North and the Action Group the West.

whyNot.A: The NPC dominated the Northern Region.
whyNot.C: The Action Group controlled the Western Region, though the NCNC had support there too.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In 1947 an NCNC delegation travelled to London mainly to protest against
questions.explanation: Nationalists objected that the Richards Constitution of 1946 had been drawn up without consulting Nigerians and kept most power with officials. The NCNC toured Nigeria to raise funds and then sent a delegation to London in 1947 to protest.

whyNot.D: The Macpherson Constitution came in 1951, after the protest.
whyNot.A: The Lyttelton Constitution came in 1954.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Atlantic Charter of 1941 encouraged African nationalists because it
options: set a date for the independence of British colonies
ended the slave trade in West Africa
created the United Nations Trusteeship Council
declared the right of all peoples to choose their own form of government
questions.explanation: In the Atlantic Charter, Britain and the United States declared that all peoples had the right to choose their government. African nationalists argued that this principle should apply to the colonies too.

whyNot.A: The Charter set no dates for independence; Churchill later said it was not meant for the British Empire.
whyNot.C: The United Nations was founded in 1945, after the Charter.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Zikist Movement of the late 1940s is best described as
options: a trade union for railway workers
a cultural society for the Yoruba people
a party formed by Northern emirs
a radical youth movement that demanded immediate independence
questions.explanation: Inspired by Azikiwe's ideas, the Zikists were young militants who called for 'positive action' to end colonial rule quickly. Some members were jailed for sedition and the movement was banned in 1950.

whyNot.B: The Yoruba cultural society was Egbe Omo Oduduwa.
whyNot.C: Northern leaders formed the NPC, not the Zikist Movement.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: After the federal elections of 1959, the federal government was formed by a coalition of the
questions.explanation: No party won an overall majority in 1959. The NPC, which won the most seats, formed a coalition with the NCNC, and Tafawa Balewa remained Prime Minister. The Action Group became the opposition, led by Awolowo.

whyNot.A: The Action Group became the opposition party.
whyNot.C: An NCNC–AG alliance was discussed but did not form the government.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Lagos Weekly Record, an early newspaper that criticised colonial rule, was founded in 1891 by
questions.explanation: John Payne Jackson, a Liberian-born journalist, founded the Lagos Weekly Record in 1891. It became one of the boldest critics of colonial policy in Lagos for decades.

whyNot.D: Azikiwe founded the West African Pilot in 1937.
whyNot.B: Macaulay was a politician and journalist, but he did not found the Weekly Record.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: When Obafemi Awolowo moved to the federal House of Representatives after the 1959 elections, who succeeded him as Premier of the Western Region?
questions.explanation: Awolowo left the Western premiership to lead the opposition in the federal House. His deputy in the Action Group, S. L. Akintola, became Premier. Their later quarrel led to the Western Region crisis of 1962.

whyNot.C: Osadebay later became Premier of the Mid-Western Region.
whyNot.A: Okpara succeeded Azikiwe as Premier of the Eastern Region.
whyNot.B: Adelabu was an NCNC politician in Ibadan who died in 1958.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: At which conference did Britain agree that Nigeria would become independent on 1 October 1960 if the new federal parliament asked for it?
questions.explanation: At the resumed constitutional conference in London in 1958, the British government promised independence on 1 October 1960, provided the federal parliament elected in 1959 passed a resolution asking for it, which it did.

whyNot.B: The 1950 Ibadan conference discussed proposals for the Macpherson Constitution.
whyNot.C: The 1953 London conference prepared the Lyttelton Constitution and set no independence date.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Second Republic ended with the military coup of 31 December 1983, which brought to power
questions.explanation: The coup of 31 December 1983 overthrew President Shehu Shagari. Major-General Muhammadu Buhari became head of state, until he was himself overthrown by Babangida in August 1985.

whyNot.D: Babangida took power in 1985 by overthrowing Buhari.
whyNot.C: Abacha announced the 1983 coup on radio but did not become head of state until 1993.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In October 1979 the military handed power to an elected civilian government. The military head of state who handed over was
questions.explanation: General Olusegun Obasanjo completed the transition programme begun by Murtala Mohammed and handed power to President Shehu Shagari on 1 October 1979.

whyNot.B: Gowon was overthrown in 1975 after postponing the return to civil rule.
whyNot.D: Murtala Mohammed was killed in 1976, before the handover.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Structural Adjustment Programme (SAP) introduced in 1986 is associated with the government of
questions.explanation: Faced with falling oil prices and debt, the Babangida government launched SAP in 1986. It devalued the naira, cut subsidies and encouraged privatisation.

whyNot.B: Shagari's civilian government ended in 1983.
whyNot.C: Gowon ruled from 1966 to 1975, during the oil boom.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: General Murtala Mohammed was killed in February 1976 during an unsuccessful coup led by
questions.explanation: On 13 February 1976, Lt-Col. Dimka led a failed coup in which Murtala Mohammed was shot in Lagos. Dimka was later caught and executed, and Obasanjo became head of state.

whyNot.B: Nzeogwu was a leader of the January 1966 coup.
whyNot.D: Orkar led the failed coup of April 1990 against Babangida.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The census controversy of 1962–63 was politically explosive mainly because
options: population figures decided each region's share of seats in the federal House
it was the first census ever held in Nigeria
it decided which region would host the capital
the census was conducted by foreign experts
questions.explanation: Seats in the House of Representatives were shared according to population. A larger count meant more seats and more power for a region, so each region was accused of inflating its figures and the results were bitterly disputed.

whyNot.B: Censuses had been held in the colonial period, for example in 1952–53.
whyNot.C: The capital was Lagos; the move to Abuja came decades later.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Udoji Commission of 1972–74 is remembered for
options: recommending large salary increases in the public service
questions.explanation: The Public Service Review Commission headed by Jerome Udoji reviewed the civil service. Its pay awards, paid with arrears during the oil boom, sharply raised wages and are often blamed for the inflation that followed.

whyNot.A: The 1979 Constitution was drafted by the Constitution Drafting Committee.
whyNot.C: States were created in 1976 after the Irikefe panel.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Operation Feed the Nation (1976) and the Green Revolution (1980) were both programmes aimed at
options: reducing the size of the army
questions.explanation: Operation Feed the Nation, launched by the Obasanjo government, and Shagari's Green Revolution both encouraged farming to reduce Nigeria's growing dependence on imported food.

whyNot.C: Primary education was the aim of the Universal Primary Education scheme.
whyNot.D: Public discipline was the aim of the War Against Indiscipline (1984).

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: After General Babangida stepped aside in August 1993, the Interim National Government was headed by
