questions.explanation: Babangida handed over to an Interim National Government led by Chief Ernest Shonekan on 26 August 1993. It lasted less than three months before General Sani Abacha took over in November 1993.

whyNot.B: Abiola won the annulled election but was never allowed to take office.
whyNot.C: Abacha removed Shonekan in November 1993.
whyNot.D: Tofa was the NRC candidate in the June 1993 election.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: During the Western Region crisis of 1962, the federal government declared a state of emergency and appointed as administrator
questions.explanation: Fighting broke out in the Western House of Assembly in May 1962 between supporters of Awolowo and Akintola. The federal government declared an emergency and appointed Dr Moses Majekodunmi, the federal health minister, to run the region.

whyNot.D: Akintola was one of the two sides in the dispute; he was later restored as Premier.
whyNot.B: Awolowo was restricted and later jailed for treasonable felony.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Nigerian Enterprises Promotion Decree of 1972, known as the indigenisation decree, aimed to
options: ban the import of all manufactured goods
nationalise all farms in the country
move the federal capital from Lagos to Abuja
transfer ownership of certain businesses from foreigners to Nigerians
questions.explanation: The decree reserved some kinds of business entirely for Nigerians and required Nigerian part-ownership of others, so that Nigerians would control more of their economy.

whyNot.B: Farms were not nationalised under the decree.
whyNot.C: The Abuja decision was taken in 1976, under a different decree.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Who led the Gold Coast to independence as Ghana in 1957?
questions.explanation: Kwame Nkrumah and his Convention People's Party led the struggle for independence. He became Ghana's first Prime Minister in 1957 and later its first President.

whyNot.B: Sékou Touré led Guinea to independence in 1958.
whyNot.D: Tubman was President of Liberia, which was never a colony.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Freetown, in present-day Sierra Leone, was founded in the late eighteenth century as a settlement for
questions.explanation: British abolitionists founded Freetown as a home for freed Africans, including poor black people from London, black Loyalists from Nova Scotia and, later, Africans freed from slave ships.

whyNot.D: Portuguese traders were active on the coast earlier, but Freetown was not founded for them.
whyNot.B: Sierra Leone was a British, not French, settlement.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Commonwealth of Nations is an association made up mainly of
options: the oil-producing countries of the world
all the independent countries of Africa
Britain and countries that were formerly under British rule
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth grew out of the British Empire. Nigeria joined at independence in 1960. Members cooperate freely on trade, education and other matters.

whyNot.C: That describes the African Union.
whyNot.A: That describes OPEC.
whyNot.B: That describes ECOWAS.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The capital of the ancient Ghana Empire was
questions.explanation: Kumbi Saleh, in the south of present-day Mauritania, was the capital of ancient Ghana. It had separate towns for the king and for Muslim traders.

whyNot.A: Gao was the capital of the Songhai Empire.
whyNot.D: Niani was the capital of the Mali Empire.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In 1958, which French West African territory voted against joining the French Community and became independent at once?
questions.explanation: In de Gaulle's 1958 referendum, Guinea, led by Sékou Touré, voted 'No' and became independent in October 1958. France withdrew its staff and aid immediately.

whyNot.B: Senegal voted 'Yes' and became independent in 1960.
whyNot.D: Côte d'Ivoire, under Houphouët-Boigny, voted 'Yes'.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Askia Muhammad, who made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca and reorganised the government of his empire, was a ruler of
questions.explanation: Askia Muhammad (Askia the Great) seized power in Songhai in 1493. He promoted Islam and learning, made a pilgrimage to Mecca and divided the empire into provinces under governors.

whyNot.D: The famous pilgrim king of Mali was Mansa Musa.
whyNot.B: Kanem-Bornu's rulers were called Mai, not Askia.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Which of these was a principle written into the Charter of the Organisation of African Unity in 1963?
options: A common currency for all member states
Election of a continental president by all Africans
A single army for the whole continent
Non-interference in the internal affairs of member states
questions.explanation: The OAU Charter stressed the sovereign equality of states, non-interference in their internal affairs and respect for their territorial integrity. Plans for a continental government, army or currency were not adopted.

whyNot.C: A continental army was a Casablanca Group idea that was not adopted.
whyNot.A: No common currency was set up by the OAU.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The founder of the Mali Empire, remembered for defeating Sumanguru of the Sosso, was
questions.explanation: Sundiata Keita defeated Sumanguru at the Battle of Kirina in the thirteenth century and built the Mali Empire on the ruins of Ghana's former lands.

whyNot.B: Mansa Musa was a later ruler of Mali, famous for his pilgrimage of 1324.
whyNot.A: Sunni Ali built up the Songhai Empire in the fifteenth century.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The French policy of assimilation, under which Africans could become French citizens, was applied most fully in
options: the interior of the French Sudan
questions.explanation: Inhabitants of the Four Communes (Saint-Louis, Gorée, Dakar and Rufisque) had French citizenship rights and could elect a deputy to the French parliament. In 1914 Blaise Diagne became the first black African elected.

whyNot.A: Northern Nigeria was British and was ruled through indirect rule.
whyNot.D: In the interior most Africans remained subjects, not citizens.
whyNot.B: The Gold Coast was a British colony.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In 1979 Nigeria nationalised the assets of British Petroleum (BP) in the country mainly as a protest against
options: Britain's policies on white-minority rule in southern Africa
Britain's support for Biafra during the civil war
BP's refusal to pay workers' salaries
BP's pollution of the Niger Delta
questions.explanation: Nigeria's foreign policy made African liberation a priority. In 1979 it seized BP's interests to pressure Britain over Rhodesia (Zimbabwe) and over fears that Nigerian oil was reaching apartheid South Africa.

whyNot.B: Britain supported the Federal Government, not Biafra, during the civil war.
whyNot.D: Pollution was not the stated reason for the 1979 action.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: According to Yoruba tradition, the ancestor of the Yoruba who established his rule at Ile-Ife was
questions.explanation: Yoruba traditions name Oduduwa as the founder of Ile-Ife and the ancestor of the Yoruba kings. His descendants were said to have founded other Yoruba kingdoms.

whyNot.C: Oranmiyan is remembered as a descendant of Oduduwa who founded Oyo.
whyNot.B: Bayajidda appears in the Hausa origin legend.
whyNot.D: Tsoede is the founder hero of Nupe.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In the Bayajidda legend about the origin of the Hausa states, Bayajidda killed a snake and married the queen of
questions.explanation: In the legend, Bayajidda killed a snake that guarded the well at Daura and married its queen. Their descendants were said to found the seven Hausa states.

whyNot.D: Kano was one of the states founded by the descendants, not the queen's town.
whyNot.A: Zazzau (Zaria) was also founded by a descendant.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The traditional ruler of the Itsekiri kingdom of Warri bears the title
questions.explanation: The Itsekiri kingdom is ruled by the Olu of Warri. Its royal line traces its origin to a prince from Benin.

whyNot.D: Etsu is the title of the Nupe ruler.
whyNot.B: Obi is the title of rulers in some Igbo towns such as Onitsha.
whyNot.A: Amanyanabo is a title of rulers of Ijaw city-states such as Bonny.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Benin tradition holds that the present dynasty of Obas began with
questions.explanation: Benin tradition says that Oranmiyan of Ife came to Benin, and that his son Eweka became the first Oba of the present dynasty, replacing the earlier Ogiso rulers.

whyNot.A: Ewuare was a later Oba of the fifteenth century.
whyNot.C: Ovonramwen ruled in the 1890s and was exiled by the British.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Which fifteenth-century Oba of Benin is remembered for expanding the kingdom and rebuilding Benin City with walls and wide streets?
questions.explanation: Oba Ewuare (Ewuare the Great), who came to the throne in the mid-fifteenth century, conquered many towns, reorganised the government and rebuilt Benin City.

whyNot.C: Eweka I founded the dynasty much earlier.
whyNot.D: Akenzua II reigned in the twentieth century.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The ruling dynasty of Kanem-Bornu for many centuries, until the mid-nineteenth century, was the
questions.explanation: The Saifawa dynasty ruled Kanem and later Bornu for about a thousand years. It ended in 1846, when power passed fully to the family of al-Kanemi.

whyNot.D: The Keita dynasty ruled Mali.
whyNot.A: The Askia dynasty ruled Songhai.
whyNot.B: The Sunni dynasty also ruled Songhai, before the Askias.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Pre-colonial Kano was especially famous for its
options: brass casting for a royal court
questions.explanation: Kano was a great trading and craft city. Its indigo dye pits produced dyed cloth, and its tanned leather goods were sold across the Sahara.

whyNot.D: Royal brass casting is associated with Benin.
whyNot.B: Kola nuts came from the forest zone to the south and were imported by the Hausa.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The city-states of the Niger Delta grew rich in the pre-colonial period mainly by
options: mining gold and selling it across the Sahara
raising cattle for the northern markets
acting as middlemen between European traders and the peoples of the hinterland
growing cocoa for export to Europe
questions.explanation: States such as Bonny, Brass and Elem Kalabari controlled the creeks and river mouths. They bought slaves and later palm oil from the interior and sold them to European ships, keeping the profit as middlemen.

whyNot.A: The Delta had no gold, and trans-Saharan trade passed through the North.
whyNot.D: Cocoa was a colonial crop of the West.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In many pre-colonial Igbo communities, the Ozo title was
options: an office given by the Oba of Benin to his governors
the title of a single king ruling all of Igboland
a costly title taken by respected men that gave influence in community affairs
the name of a court that judged by Islamic law
questions.explanation: Ozo was a title society. A man paid heavy fees and had to be of good character to take it, and titled men were respected and had a strong voice in making decisions.

whyNot.B: There was no single king of all Igboland.
whyNot.D: Islamic courts were a feature of the northern emirates.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Tsoede (Edegi) is remembered in tradition as the founder of which kingdom?
questions.explanation: Nupe traditions say that Tsoede (also called Edegi) came from Idah, united the Nupe people and became their first Etsu, bringing royal symbols such as bronze figures and canoe chains.

whyNot.C: Tsoede is said to have come from Idah, the Igala capital, but he founded the Nupe kingdom.
whyNot.B: The Jukun kingdom of Kwararafa was centred in the Benue valley and has its own founding traditions.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: During the colonial period, cocoa was grown for export mainly in
questions.explanation: Cocoa grew well in the forest belt of the West, around Ibadan, Ife, Ondo and Abeokuta. Cocoa earnings helped to pay for the Western Region's development in the 1950s.

whyNot.B: The North's main export crops were groundnuts and cotton.
whyNot.D: The East's main exports were palm oil and kernels.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Which of these was used as currency in parts of the Niger Delta before British coins replaced it?
options: The manilla, a brass or copper ring
questions.explanation: Manillas, horseshoe-shaped rings of brass or copper brought by European traders, were used as money in the Delta and its hinterland. The British withdrew them in the late 1940s.

whyNot.D: The kobo was introduced in 1973.
whyNot.A: The West African pound was the British coinage that replaced the manilla.
whyNot.B: The naira was introduced in 1973.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Under British colonial administration, a province of Nigeria was headed by a British official called the
questions.explanation: Each province was headed by a Resident, who advised the emirs or chiefs and supervised the Native Authorities. Provinces were divided into divisions under District Officers.

whyNot.B: District Officers headed divisions, smaller units within a province.
whyNot.D: The Governor-General headed the whole of Nigeria.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In 1851 the British bombarded Lagos, drove out Oba Kosoko and restored
questions.explanation: The British accused Kosoko of supporting the slave trade. After the bombardment they placed Akitoye, who had promised to end the trade, back on the throne.

whyNot.C: Dosunmu, Akitoye's son, became Oba later and signed the cession of 1861.
whyNot.D: Ovonramwen was Oba of Benin.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The British expedition against Ijebu in 1892 was launched mainly because the Ijebu
options: sided with the Germans in a war
blocked trade routes between Lagos and the interior
had killed the British consul at Calabar
questions.explanation: The Ijebu controlled routes between Lagos and the Yoruba interior and charged tolls or closed them. The British wanted free trade inland, so they attacked and defeated Ijebu in 1892.

whyNot.D: The Ijebu were reluctant to accept missionaries, but the main reason for the attack was trade.
whyNot.A: No European war was involved in 1892.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Aro Expedition of 1901–1902 was aimed mainly at
options: punishing Benin for the killing of British officials
breaking the power of the Aro and their Ibini Ukpabi oracle
questions.explanation: The British saw the Aro network and its oracle as a barrier to their control and trade in the Igbo interior. The expedition destroyed the oracle shrine at Arochukwu and opened the area to British rule.

whyNot.C: Sokoto was conquered by Lugard's forces in 1903.
whyNot.A: The Benin expedition took place in 1897.
whyNot.B: Jaja was removed in 1887.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The commodity marketing boards set up by the colonial government from the late 1940s
options: built the railway from Lagos to Kano
issued the currency used in Nigeria
bought export crops such as cocoa from farmers at fixed prices
trained Nigerians for the civil service
questions.explanation: Starting with the Cocoa Marketing Board in 1947, the boards were the only legal buyers of certain export crops. They paid farmers fixed prices and kept surpluses, which were later used for regional development.

whyNot.A: The Lagos–Kano railway was completed in 1912.
whyNot.B: Currency was issued by the West African Currency Board.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In 1849 Britain appointed John Beecroft as
options: head of the Royal Niger Company
consul for the Bights of Benin and Biafra
the first Governor of the Lagos Colony
questions.explanation: Beecroft became the first British consul for the Bights of Benin and Biafra in 1849. Consuls protected British traders and interfered in local politics, as in the attack on Lagos in 1851.

whyNot.C: Lagos only became a colony in 1861.
whyNot.A: The Royal Niger Company received its charter in 1886.
whyNot.D: Provinces under Residents came after the conquest of the North in the 1900s.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Ekumeku movement, which resisted British and Royal Niger Company rule from the late 1890s, was based among the
questions.explanation: Ekumeku was a secret resistance movement of western Igbo towns west of the Niger, near Asaba. It fought the Royal Niger Company and then the colonial government for over a decade.

whyNot.D: The Brass people attacked the Company at Akassa in 1895, but that was not the Ekumeku.
whyNot.C: The Egba rising was the Adubi War of 1918.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Satiru rising of 1906, near Sokoto, is best described as
options: a women's protest against taxation in the East
a war between Bornu and the Sokoto Caliphate
a strike by railway workers in Lagos
a Mahdist revolt against British rule, crushed with the Sultan's support
questions.explanation: In 1906 villagers at Satiru, inspired by Mahdist beliefs, rose against British rule and defeated a small British force. The British, supported by the Sultan of Sokoto, crushed the revolt, showing how indirect rule tied the emirs to the colonial government.

whyNot.C: Labour strikes in Lagos came later and were not religious revolts.
whyNot.A: That describes the Aba Women's War of 1929.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Abubakar Tafawa Balewa was a leading member of which political party?
questions.explanation: Balewa was deputy leader of the NPC under Ahmadu Bello. He became federal Prime Minister in 1957 and led Nigeria at independence in 1960.

whyNot.D: The Action Group was Awolowo's party.
whyNot.B: NEPU was the opposition party in the North, led by Aminu Kano.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Nnamdi Azikiwe served in the 1950s as Premier of which region?
questions.explanation: Azikiwe, leader of the NCNC, was Premier of the Eastern Region from 1954 until 1959, when he moved to the centre. He later became Governor-General and then President.

whyNot.A: Awolowo and then Akintola were Premiers of the West.
whyNot.C: The Mid-Western Region was only created in 1963.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The slogan 'Africa for the Africans', which inspired many West African nationalists, is most closely associated with
questions.explanation: Marcus Garvey, a Jamaican leader, preached black pride and 'Africa for the Africans' in the 1910s and 1920s. His ideas influenced young nationalists such as Azikiwe and Nkrumah.

whyNot.B: Lugard was a British colonial administrator.
whyNot.D: Mungo Park was a Scottish explorer of the Niger.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti is remembered for leading the Abeokuta Women's Union in protests against
options: unfair taxation of women under the Alake's administration
the annulment of the June 1993 election
the building of the Kainji Dam
the creation of the Mid-Western Region
questions.explanation: In the 1940s the Abeokuta Women's Union protested that market women were being heavily taxed by the Native Authority under the Alake. The protests forced the Alake to leave the throne for a time in 1949.

whyNot.D: The Mid-West was created in 1963 by constitutional referendum.
whyNot.B: The 1993 annulment came long after; she died in 1978.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Nigerian soldiers returning from the Second World War helped the nationalist movement mainly because they
options: brought back large sums of money for political parties
had seen that Europeans were not superior and expected fairer treatment
had been trained as lawyers in Britain
were given seats in the Legislative Council
questions.explanation: Ex-servicemen had fought alongside and against Europeans, seen other countries and been promised a better life. When they returned to poor jobs and colonial rule, many supported demands for self-government.

whyNot.D: Ex-servicemen were not given special seats in the Legislative Council.
whyNot.C: Soldiers were not trained as lawyers.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Ibadan General Conference of January 1950 was held to
options: discuss proposals for a constitution to replace the Richards Constitution
settle the dispute that led to the civil war
questions.explanation: Governor Macpherson invited Nigerians to discuss constitutional reform at village, provincial and regional levels. The proposals went to a General Conference at Ibadan in 1950, leading to the Macpherson Constitution of 1951.

whyNot.A: Independence came in 1960, after conferences in London.
whyNot.D: The crisis before the civil war was discussed at Aburi in 1967.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Northern Region attained internal self-government in
questions.explanation: The Eastern and Western Regions became self-governing in 1957, but the Northern Region asked for more time and became self-governing in March 1959.

whyNot.C: 1957 is when the East and West became self-governing.
whyNot.B: 1956 was the date in the 1953 self-government motion, which the North opposed.
whyNot.D: 1960 was the year of full independence.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The general strike of 1945, which showed the strength of organised labour in the nationalist struggle, is most closely associated with the labour leader
questions.explanation: Michael Imoudu, a railway union leader, was a central figure in the 1945 general strike over wages and the cost of living. The strike linked workers' grievances to the wider demand for self-government.

whyNot.D: Macaulay was a party leader, not a labour leader.
whyNot.B: Ikoli was a journalist and Nigerian Youth Movement leader.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Kano riots of May 1953 followed
options: the creation of new states in 1967
the crisis over the motion for self-government in 1956
questions.explanation: Northern members who opposed the 1953 self-government motion were insulted in Lagos. When an Action Group delegation later went to Kano to campaign, tension led to riots in which many people died.

whyNot.C: The 1966 coup was followed by later violence, not the 1953 riots.
whyNot.A: States were created in 1967, fourteen years later.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The United Middle Belt Congress (UMBC), which campaigned for a separate Middle Belt region, was led by
questions.explanation: Joseph Tarka, a Tiv politician, led the UMBC, which spoke for minority groups in the southern part of the Northern Region and allied with the Action Group.

whyNot.C: Aminu Kano led NEPU.
whyNot.A: Okpara was an NCNC leader and Premier of the Eastern Region.
whyNot.B: Ahmadu Bello led the NPC, which opposed a separate Middle Belt region.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Who was head of the Federal Military Government throughout the Nigerian Civil War of 1967–1970?
questions.explanation: Lt-Col. (later General) Yakubu Gowon became head of state after the counter-coup of July 1966 and led the Federal side through the war, which ended in January 1970.

whyNot.A: Murtala Mohammed became head of state in 1975.
whyNot.B: Ironsi was killed in July 1966, before the war.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In 1973 Nigeria changed its currency from the pound to the
questions.explanation: On 1 January 1973 Nigeria introduced the naira and kobo, a decimal currency, in place of the Nigerian pound, shillings and pence.

whyNot.A: The cedi is Ghana's currency.
whyNot.B: The CFA franc is used by many former French colonies.
whyNot.C: The dalasi is the currency of the Gambia.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The 1979 Constitution changed Nigeria's system of government from the parliamentary system to
questions.explanation: The 1979 Constitution, like that of the United States, created an executive President elected by the people, separate from the National Assembly, in place of a Prime Minister responsible to parliament.

whyNot.A: The constitution allowed several registered political parties.
whyNot.D: It ended military rule and returned power to civilians.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Gowon was overthrown in a bloodless coup in July 1975 while he was attending an OAU summit in
questions.explanation: While Gowon was at the OAU summit in Kampala, Uganda, officers removed him and installed Brigadier Murtala Mohammed as head of state.

whyNot.D: Addis Ababa was the OAU headquarters, but the 1975 summit met in Kampala.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Universal Primary Education (UPE) scheme was launched nationwide in 1976 under the government of
questions.explanation: UPE was planned under Gowon but launched in September 1976 by the Obasanjo government, which made primary education free across the country.

whyNot.A: Shagari became President in 1979, after UPE began.
whyNot.C: Gowon announced the plan but was overthrown in 1975, before its launch.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The Second World Black and African Festival of Arts and Culture (FESTAC '77) was hosted by
options: Ghana, with Accra as the main venue
Nigeria, with Lagos as the main venue
Senegal, with Dakar as the main venue
Ethiopia, with Addis Ababa as the main venue
questions.explanation: Nigeria hosted FESTAC in 1977. Festac Town and the National Theatre in Lagos were built for it. The first such festival had been held in Dakar, Senegal, in 1966.

whyNot.C: Dakar hosted the first festival in 1966, not FESTAC '77.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Who became head of state after the death of General Sani Abacha in June 1998?
questions.explanation: General Abdulsalami Abubakar became head of state in June 1998. He carried out a short transition and handed power to President Obasanjo on 29 May 1999.

whyNot.A: Obasanjo became President in 1999, after Abubakar's transition.
whyNot.C: Shonekan headed the Interim National Government in 1993.
whyNot.B: Diya, Abacha's deputy, had been arrested in 1997.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In 1991 the Babangida government increased the number of states in Nigeria to
questions.explanation: Babangida created two states in 1987 (making 21) and nine more in August 1991, making 30. Abacha created six more in 1996, making 36.

whyNot.C: 21 was the total after the 1987 creation of Akwa Ibom and Katsina.
whyNot.A: 19 was the total from 1976 to 1987.
whyNot.B: 36 was reached in 1996 under Abacha.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: General Aguiyi-Ironsi was killed in the counter-coup of July 1966 while on a visit to
questions.explanation: Ironsi was staying at Government House, Ibadan, as the guest of the Western Region's military governor, Lt-Col. Adekunle Fajuyi, when mutinous soldiers seized and killed both men on 29 July 1966.

whyNot.A: Kaduna was the Northern capital, where the January coup had killed Ahmadu Bello.
whyNot.B: Enugu was the Eastern capital.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The presidential election of 2015 was historic because
options: it was the first election held under military rule
it was the first time women were allowed to vote
a sitting president was defeated by an opposition candidate for the first time
questions.explanation: In 2015 Muhammadu Buhari of the APC defeated the sitting president, Goodluck Jonathan, and Jonathan accepted the result. It was the first time power passed peacefully to an opposition party through an election in Nigeria.

whyNot.B: In 2015 Nigeria was under civilian rule.
whyNot.C: Women had voted in Nigerian elections long before 2015.
whyNot.A: The civil war ended in 1970.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: In the Middle Ages, the city of Timbuktu was famous as a centre of
questions.explanation: Timbuktu, on the Niger bend, prospered under the Mali and Songhai empires. Its mosques and the Sankore scholars made it a famous centre of Islamic learning, and it was a key trans-Saharan market.

whyNot.A: European missionaries did not work there in the Middle Ages.
whyNot.D: Timbuktu was linked to the trans-Saharan, not the Atlantic, trade.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Léopold Sédar Senghor, a poet and statesman, was the first president of
questions.explanation: Senghor led Senegal to independence in 1960 and was its president until 1980. He was also a famous poet of the Négritude movement.

whyNot.A: Guinea's first president was Sékou Touré.
whyNot.C: Ghana's first president was Kwame Nkrumah.
whyNot.B: Côte d'Ivoire's first president was Félix Houphouët-Boigny.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Which West African country was never colonised by a European power?
questions.explanation: Liberia declared its independence in 1847 and kept it throughout the scramble for Africa, though it lost some land to neighbouring colonies.

whyNot.D: Ghana was the British colony of the Gold Coast.
whyNot.B: Sierra Leone was a British colony.
whyNot.C: Togo was a German and then French colony.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Which item was mainly carried southwards across the Sahara into West Africa in the trans-Saharan trade?
questions.explanation: West Africa sent gold, ivory, kola nuts and slaves northwards. In return it received salt from Saharan mines, along with horses, cloth and other goods. Salt was in great demand because it was scarce in the savanna and forest.

whyNot.C: Gold went northwards from West Africa.
whyNot.D: Kola nuts were grown in the West African forest and sent north.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The first Europeans to establish trading contact with the Benin Kingdom, in the late fifteenth century, were the
questions.explanation: Portuguese sailors reached Benin in the 1480s. They traded brass, cloth and other goods for pepper, ivory and cloth, and Oba Esigie sent an ambassador to Portugal.

whyNot.B: The British came later and dominated the coast in the nineteenth century.
whyNot.D: The Dutch traded with Benin later, in the seventeenth century.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: The political party that led the Gold Coast to independence in 1957 was the
options: National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC)
questions.explanation: Nkrumah broke away from the UGCC in 1949 and formed the CPP, which demanded 'self-government now'. The CPP won the elections of the 1950s and led the country to independence.

whyNot.A: The UGCC was the older, more moderate party that Nkrumah left.
whyNot.B: The NCNC was a Nigerian party.
whyNot.C: The PDG was Sékou Touré's party in Guinea.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: How many West African states signed the Treaty of Lagos that created ECOWAS in 1975?
questions.explanation: Fifteen states signed the Treaty of Lagos on 28 May 1975. Cape Verde joined in 1977, bringing the membership to sixteen at that time.

whyNot.D: Sixteen was the membership after Cape Verde joined in 1977.
whyNot.B: 36 is the number of states in Nigeria.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Which of these countries is a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council with the power of veto?
questions.explanation: The five permanent members with veto power are the United States, Russia, China, the United Kingdom and France. Other countries, including Nigeria, serve only as elected non-permanent members for two-year terms.

whyNot.A: Nigeria has served several terms as an elected non-permanent member, not a permanent one.
whyNot.D: Germany is not a permanent member.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Nigeria's first major peacekeeping commitment after independence was the United Nations operation in
questions.explanation: Soon after independence, Nigerian troops and police joined the UN force in the Congo. In 1964 Major-General Aguiyi-Ironsi commanded the whole UN force there.

whyNot.B: Liberia (1990) was an ECOWAS operation that came thirty years later.
whyNot.A: Sierra Leone also came much later, under ECOMOG.

questions.subject: history
questions.stem: Which was the last of Britain's West African colonies to gain independence, in 1965?
questions.explanation: The order of independence was Ghana (1957), Nigeria (1960), Sierra Leone (1961) and finally the Gambia (February 1965).

whyNot.C: Sierra Leone became independent in 1961.
whyNot.A: Ghana was the first, in 1957.
whyNot.B: Nigeria became independent in 1960.
